From the early Pharaonic era, about 3000 BCE, copper and gold were mined there for tools and jewellery, and iron began to be mined around 1000 BCE. Emeralds and amethysts were mined too, and limestone, granite and marble were quarried. Trade routes ran from the Nile to the Red Sea, among them one to the ancient Egyptian port of Mersa Gawasis, where boats were carried in pieces across the desert through the wadis and assembled for expeditions.

Trade grew under the Romans, from 30 BCE to 395 CE, and Red Sea ports were points of embarkation for trade with India. The chief port during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods was Berenice Troglodytica, and the Via Hadriana led from it to Antinoöpolis on the Nile. Imperial porphyry was quarried at Mons Claudianus into the Byzantine era. Roman soldiers lived and worked at the ports, eating mainly pigs, donkeys and camels.

The mountains support golden eagles, bearded vultures, the Nubian ibex and the aoudad, a mountain sheep, while the plateaus hold small mammals such as the fennec fox and jerboa. Mining continues, now mainly for crude oil and natural gas. In March 2025 archaeologists of the French Institute of Oriental Archaeology found two sets of iron ankle shackles from the 3rd century BCE at the Ghozza gold mine, evidence of forced labour in gold mining in the Ptolemaic period.
eastern-europe: Eastern Europe is a subregion of the European continent, and the term is largely ambiguous. Its eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains, while its western boundary is defined in many ways and has shifted over time. Much of the region lies on the East European Plain, whose highest point, in the Valdai Hills northwest of Moscow, reaches only 343 metres. It is drained by long rivers such as the Volga, the longest in Europe, the Dnieper and the Danube. The historian Larry Wolff has argued that the idea of Eastern Europe was created in the 18th century by Enlightenment thinkers.

The region's history was shaped by the migrations of the Slavs in the 6th and 7th centuries and by the Christianization of its peoples from both Rome and Constantinople. A treaty of 681 recognizing the rule of the Bulgars marks the beginning of the Bulgarian state. In 882 Oleg made Kyiv the capital of Kievan Rus', the first East Slavic state, and in 964–965 Sviatoslav destroyed the Khazar capitals. The Mongol invasions, and later the Ottoman, Habsburg and Russian empires and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, shaped its political map.

In 1526 Suleiman destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, and the Ottoman advance in Central Europe ended at the siege of Vienna in 1683. In June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia with about 600,000 troops, of whom fewer than 30,000 returned. After the First World War new or restored states emerged, among them Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union divided the region into spheres of influence.

From 1945 to 1989 most of the region was under communist rule, and during the Cold War the term Eastern Europe was used almost as a synonym for the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc; historians generally regard definitions based on that usage as outdated. After the Revolutions of 1989 many countries joined NATO and the European Union: the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia entered the Union on 1 May 2004, Bulgaria and Romania on 1 January 2007, and Croatia on 1 July 2013. The region's traditions include Orthodox icon painting, the literature of Alexander Pushkin and Adam Mickiewicz, and the music of Frédéric Chopin.
eastern-orthodox-church: The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that it is the one, holy, catholic and apostolic church established by Jesus Christ, with bishops who are successors of the apostles, and its own official name is the Orthodox Catholic Church. The churches of Constantinople, Alexandria, Jerusalem and Antioch shared communion with Rome until the East-West Schism of 1054. Before the Council of Ephesus in 431 the Church of the East shared it too, and so did the Oriental Orthodox Churches before the Council of Chalcedon in 451, both separating mainly over differences in Christology.

In the ninth and tenth centuries Christianity made great inroads among the Slavs, including Bulgaria in 864 and Kievan Rus' in 988, made possible by the brothers Cyril and Methodius of Thessaloniki. They translated the liturgy and the Gospels into the local language, from which arose the literary language Church Slavonic. The Great Schism of 1054 separated the Catholic Church from the Byzantine churches, over issues such as the filioque clause and the authority of the pope, sharpened by political and cultural differences.

The Byzantine Empire never fully recovered from the sack of Constantinople in 1204 and fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453. In 1547 Ivan IV took the title Tsar of All Rus, and in 1589 the Patriarchate of Constantinople granted autocephalous status to Moscow, which came to call itself the Third Rome. After the October Revolution of 1917 part of the Russian clergy fled abroad, and 28 bishops and 1,200 priests were executed in the next five years.

The church is a communion of autocephalous, or self-headed, churches, each governed by its bishops through local synods. It has no central authority comparable to the pope, and the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople is recognised only as first among equals. Its theology rests on scripture and holy tradition, including the decrees of the seven ecumenical councils. It recognises seven major sacraments, called holy mysteries, of which the Eucharist is the principal one. The main service is the Divine Liturgy. Many churches take a national title, such as Greek, Russian or Serbian Orthodox.
eastern-settlement: Despite its name, the Eastern Settlement lay more to the south than to the east of the Western Settlement. Both were on the south-western tip of Greenland, at the heads of long fjords such as Eiriksfjord (Tunulliarfik Fjord), Einarsfjord (Igaliku) and Sermilik Fjord. About 500 groups of Norse farm ruins survive in the area, with 16 church ruins, among them Brattahlíð, Dyrnæs, Garðar, Hvalsey and Herjolfsnes. The Vatnahverfi district south-east of Einarsfjord had some of the colony's best grazing and a tenth of its known farms. Major parts of the settlement, including Brattahlíð, the homestead of Erik the Red, were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2017 as Kujataa Greenland.

The settlers came from Iceland, and at its height the colony had about 4,000 inhabitants. They lived mainly by keeping sheep and cattle, with some seal hunting. The Little Ice Age of the 14th century may have raised the need for winter fodder while making hay meadows less productive. Isotope analysis of excavated bones shows a shift towards the sea: the first settlers took about 80 percent of their food from farming, while from the 14th century 50 to 80 percent of the diet came from the sea. The settlement outlasted the more northerly Western Settlement by some 50 to 100 years.

Why it ended is debated. A Greenlandic Inuit legend tells of a blood feud between the Norse chieftain Ungortoq and the Inuk warrior K'aissape, whose men came to Hvalsey disguised as an iceberg and burned the houses, but archaeologists have found no sign of a fire. Other explanations include soil erosion from overgrazing and the effects of the Black Death.
eastern-thrace: Eastern Thrace is the eastern part of the historical region of Thrace and the part of Turkey that lies in south-east Europe, with an area of 23,764 km2, about 3% of the country's land. The Dardanelles, the Sea of Marmara and the Bosphorus separate it from Anatolia. It includes the provinces of Edirne, Tekirdağ and Kırklareli and the European parts of Çanakkale and Istanbul. Its southernmost part is the Gallipoli peninsula. Greece lies to the west and Bulgaria to the north, with the Aegean Sea to the south-west and the Black Sea to the north-east. Its position beside a major sea trade corridor has long given it importance.

Myth placed Hero and Leander at the ancient city of Sestus and made Aeneas the founder of Aenus. After the death of Alexander the Great, his general Lysimachus (360 to 281 BCE) became king of Thrace and made Lysimachia his capital. The Battle of Adrianople in 378 was a turning point in the decline of the Roman Empire. Çimpe Castle, taken in 1352, was the first European territory held by the Ottoman Empire, and Edirne became its second capital after Bursa. The Gallipoli Campaign of the First World War was fought on the peninsula.

Ottoman Rumelia was lost piecemeal from 1699, and the bulk of it in the First Balkan War of 1912. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878 and the Balkan Wars, Muslim refugees (muhacir) of various origins were forced to flee from the Balkans towards Eastern Thrace through expulsions, violence and massacres, and further emigration followed the population exchange between Greece and Turkey that followed. The land borders were defined by the Treaty of Constantinople of 1913 and the Bulgarian-Ottoman convention of 1915, and were reaffirmed by the Treaty of Lausanne.

Its largest city is Istanbul. Edirne holds the Selimiye Mosque, the Üç Şerefeli Mosque, the Old Mosque, the Muradiye Mosque and the Grand Synagogue. The Kırkpınar oil-wrestling tournament has been held near Edirne every year since 1360, and the Romani festival Kakava is held annually in Edirne and Kırklareli. A large part of the population descends from the muhacir who settled there.
eastern-turkestan: East Turkestan is a loosely defined geographical region in what is now the north-west of the People's Republic of China, at the crossroads of East and Central Asia. The name was coined in the 19th century by Russian Turkologists, among them Nikita Bichurin, to replace the Western term 'Chinese Turkestan', which referred to the Tarim Basin in southern Xinjiang. From the 17th century the Uyghur name for the Tarim Basin was Altishahr, Six Cities. Chinese dynasties from the Han to the Tang called an overlapping area the Western Regions. Until the 20th century local people tended to name themselves after their cities or oases, such as Kashgaria out of Kashgar.

In 60 BCE the Han dynasty established the Protectorate of the Western Regions over the oasis states of the Tarim Basin, ruled indirectly through small agricultural military colonies. Chinese authority lapsed after the Western Han, was restored in 94 CE and lasted officially until 107 CE. The Western Turkic Khaganate inherited the region after the Gökturks, and western Tujue territory later became part of the Tang dynasty until the ninth century. In the sixteenth century the Chagatai Khanate completed the conversion to Islam and Turkification of western Xinjiang, then known as Moghulistan, while the Ming dynasty held the eastern areas.

In 1755 the Qing dynasty defeated the Dzungar Khanate and took two territories: Dzungaria in the north, where the Dzungars lived, and the southern areas, called Huijiang or Altishahr. In 1764 the Qianlong Emperor made Xinjiang an official name for the two together, and after General Tso suppressed the Dungan revolt, Xinjiang was reorganised as a province in 1882. Russia occupied the Ili valley between 1851 and 1881. After the Qing fell in 1912, Yang Zengxin took control and acceded to the Republic of China.

On 12 November 1933 Uyghur separatists in the Kashgar region declared the East Turkestan Republic, which lasted until 16 April 1934 and was recognised by no country; the warlord Sheng Shicai defeated it. A second East Turkestan Republic existed in the Ili region from 12 November 1944 to 27 June 1946, with Soviet support. In 1949 the Communist leadership persuaded both the Kuomintang and Republic governments in Xinjiang to surrender, and on 1 October 1955 Xinjiang was made the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
eastern-turkic-khaganate: The Göktürks replaced the Rouran Khaganate as the dominant power on the Mongolian Plateau in 552 to 555, forming the First Turkic Khaganate, which soon spread west to the Caspian Sea. In about 460 the Rouran had moved the Ashina family east to the Altai, an important source of metalwork. Bumin demanded a royal bride from the Rouran and was denounced as a blacksmith slave.

He took a bride from the Western Wei instead, defeated the Rouran ruler and took the title of khagan in 552. He died the same year, and his brother Istämi (552 to 575) and then Istämi's son Tardu ruled the west, reaching the Caspian and the Oxus. The Göktürks gained the Tarim Basin, the Silk Road trade and the Sogdian merchants who managed it.

Muqan Qaghan (553 to 572) finished off the Rouran and pushed the Kitans east. After Taspar Qaghan died in 581, the year the Sui dynasty was founded, rival claimants fought, and the Sui supported or bribed one faction against another. The empire separated into east and west between 581 and 603. Ishbara Qaghan submitted to the Sui, and Tardu briefly reunified the empire from 599 to 603 before the Sui drove him back. In 603 the east passed to Yami Qaghan, a sort of Sui vassal.

As Sui power waned, Shibi Qaghan (609 to 619) besieged Emperor Yang of Sui in Shanxi. Illig Qaghan (620 to 630), the last independent ruler, raided the new Tang dynasty every year and in 626 reached the gates of Chang'an. Emperor Taizong of Tang paid an enormous ransom. Unusual cold in 627 to 629 caused mass livestock deaths and famine, and Illig raised taxes instead of lowering them. The Xueyantuo, Uyghurs, Bayegu and some of his own people rebelled, the Khitans and Taizong joined them in 629, and six Tang armies attacked along a front of 1,200 km. Illig was captured in 630.

After 630 Taizong made the Ashina settle in the Ordos Loop, and the Xueyantuo ruled much of the north. Chebi Khan tried to revive the khaganate and was captured by the Chinese and Uyghurs in 650, and two further attempts in 679 to 681 failed. Turkic power was restored by the Second Turkic Khaganate (682 to 744) and then by the Uyghur Khaganate (744 to 840). The Orkhon inscriptions call the Eastern Turks the Kök Türük, the Blue or Heavenly Turks.
eastphalia: Eastphalia covered the eastern shires (Gaue) of the stem duchy of Saxony, roughly between the River Leine in the west and the Elbe and Saale in the east, in what is now south-eastern Lower Saxony, western Saxony-Anhalt and northern Thuringia. Its name probably means east plain: falen is a Germanic word for flat or level ground. The North German Plain of Eastphalia and Westphalia contrasts with the hilly Central Uplands of Franconia and Thuringia to the south. Its shires included Astfala around Hildesheim, the Harzgau around Halberstadt, the Salzgau and the Hassegau around Mansfeld.

According to the Royal Frankish Annals and the Saxon Poet, the Eastphalians under Hessi gave hostages and swore loyalty to Charlemagne at the river Oker in 775. Hessi later became a Christian and was made a count, and the bishoprics of Halberstadt and Hildesheim were founded east of the Oker in 804 and 815. The lands around the Harz were the hereditary lands of Henry the Fowler, the first Saxon duke to become King of the Romans in 919, and of the Ottonian dynasty that followed him.

Bordering the lands of the Polabian Slavs along and beyond the Elbe and Saale, Eastphalia became the starting point of the German Ostsiedlung. Sometime after 965 Otto I entrusted the defence of its north-eastern parts, later called the Altmark, to Dietrich of Haldensleben. After Henry the Lion was placed under the imperial ban in 1180, the region broke up into smaller states, among them the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg, the counties of Anhalt, Wernigerode and Blankenburg, the Imperial city of Goslar, the Archbishopric of Magdeburg and the prince-bishoprics of Hildesheim and Halberstadt.

Unlike Westphalia, whose name lived on in the archbishops of Cologne's Duchy of Westphalia, the name Eastphalia fell out of use after 1180. Linguists revived it in the 19th century for the Eastphalian dialect of West Low German. The Ottonian abbeys and castles of the region include three World Heritage Sites: the medieval town of Goslar, Quedlinburg, and St. Mary's Cathedral with St. Michael's Church at Hildesheim.
eberhard-i-duke-of-wurttemberg: Eberhard was born at Urach on 11 December 1445, the son of Count Ludwig I and Mechthild of the Palatinate; Württemberg had been divided since 1442. He succeeded his older brother as a minor under the guardianship of Rudolph von Ehingen, but in 1459, with the help of Frederick I, Elector Palatine, he threw off the guardian and took up the government of Urach. Until 1468 he neglected his duties and lived recklessly; in 1467 Hans Talhoffer made a fencing manual for him, now in the Bavarian State Library.

In 1468 he travelled to Jerusalem, became a knight of the Order of the Holy Sepulchre and took the palm as his emblem. In Italy he met scholars, and on 12 April 1474 he married Barbara, daughter of Ludovico III Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua; their only child died in infancy. Though he could not speak Latin, he had many Latin texts translated into German, and part of his library survives. His motto was attempto, I dare. He expelled all the Jews of Württemberg, invited the Brethren of the Common Life into the country, founded collegiate churches in Urach, Herrenberg and elsewhere and took an interest in reforming the church and monasteries.

By the Treaty of Münsingen of 14 December 1482 his cousin Eberhard VI was made his heir, and Eberhard moved the capital to Stuttgart. Pope Sixtus IV gave him the Golden Rose that year. He helped found the Swabian League in 1488, helped free Maximilian I from imprisonment in Bruges, and in 1492 received the Order of the Golden Fleece. At the Diet of Worms on 21 July 1495 Maximilian invested him with a sword, and Württemberg ranked above all margraves and counts but below the existing duchies.

Eberhard died at Tübingen on 24 February 1496 and was succeeded by his cousin as Duke Eberhard II. He was buried first at Saint Peter auf dem Einsiedel and later in the collegiate church of Tübingen. Patriotic historians of the 19th and 20th centuries idealised him; his bust stands in the Walhalla, and Justinus Kerner's song Preisend mit viel schönen Reden praises him as the prince who could rest his head safely in the lap of any of his subjects.
ebla: Ebla is a tell, now called Tell Mardikh, about 55 kilometres south-west of Aleppo. The name may derive from a Semitic word meaning white rock, possibly the limestone outcrop on which the city stood. In its first kingdom it covered 56 hectares behind mud-brick fortifications, with a raised acropolis in the centre and a lower town divided into four districts, each with its own gate. The city's patron god was Kura.

Ebla was first settled around 3500 BCE, and its growth was supported by satellite agricultural settlements and its role in growing international trade, which probably began with demand for wool in Sumer. Its first kingdom, between about 3000 and 2300 BCE, was the most prominent among the Syrian states. Its government consisted of a king, styled Malikum, and a grand vizier who headed a council of elders, and the queen shared the running of state affairs. The population in 2400 to 2300 BCE is estimated at about 40,000 in the capital. The palace was destroyed by fire during an Akkadian conquest.

A second kingdom continued the first under a new dynasty and was destroyed at the end of the 3rd millennium BCE. Amorites then formed a third kingdom, rebuilt as a planned city, whose first known king was Ibbit-Lim. It became a subject and ally of Yamhad until the Hittite king Mursili I destroyed Ebla around 1600 BCE.

Italian archaeologists directed by Paolo Matthiae began excavating Tell Mardikh in 1964. In 1968 they recovered a statue dedicated to the goddess Ishtar bearing the name of Ibbit-Lim, king of Ebla, which identified the city. The palace archive held about 20,000 cuneiform tablets dated to 2500 to 2350 BCE, in Sumerian and in Eblaite. They had been shelved by subject, and the positions of those that fell when the palace burned let the excavators reconstruct the shelving. Early claims of references to Yahweh and the Biblical Patriarchs are now widely discredited.
ebony: Ebony is a dense black-brown hardwood that comes from several species of the genus Diospyros, which also includes the persimmon. Some species, such as macassar and mun ebony, are dense enough to sink in water. The wood is finely textured and takes a mirror finish when polished, which made it valuable as an ornamental wood. The species include Diospyros ebenum, the Ceylon ebony of southern India and Sri Lanka, D. crassiflora, the Gabon ebony of western Africa, D. blancoi, the Philippine ebony or kamagong, and D. celebica, the Sulawesi ebony of Indonesia, prized for its multi-coloured grain. The Dutch largely exploited the Mauritius ebony, D. tessellaria, in the 17th century. The word comes from the Ancient Egyptian hbny, through Greek ébenos and Latin ebenus.

Ebony has a long history of use, and carved pieces have been found in Ancient Egyptian tombs. By the end of the 16th century, makers in Antwerp were producing fine ebony cabinets for the luxury trade. The hard, dense wood suited refined mouldings framing panels carved in very low relief, usually with allegorical subjects or scenes from classical or Christian history. Such cabinets were soon made in Paris too, where their makers became known as ébénistes, which remains the French word for a cabinetmaker.

Ebony was traditionally used for black chess pieces, with boxwood or ivory for the white. Today its uses are largely small items, among them crucifixes, parts of clarinets, oboes and piccolos, piano, organ and harpsichord keys, fingerboards and tuning pegs of stringed instruments, lace-making bobbins and the butts of pool cues.

Ebony trees are generally small and grow slowly, and high demand and low supply have led to severe overharvesting. Many species are listed in the appendices of CITES, which requires a permit for international trade, and some countries ban the export of species such as the Ceylon ebony. Illegal logging in Madagascar has focused on ebony and rosewood. Sustainable alternatives include other dark woods and black plastic, and wood can be ebonised with a solution of iron acetate or with dyes.
eboracum: The name comes from the Common Brittonic Eburākon, of disputed meaning: one view reads it as yew tree place, while linguists such as Andrew Breeze and Peter Schrijver dispute the link with the yew. Its first known written mention is on a wooden tablet from Vindolanda dated about 95 to 104. The fortress stood on flat ground above the River Ouse near its junction with the Foss, built when Quintus Petillius Cerialis led the Ninth Legion north from Lincoln against the Brigantes, whose leaders had turned hostile to Rome.

The fortress covered 50 acres. Its turf ramparts of 71 to 74 were refurbished by Agricola in 81 and rebuilt in stone from 107 and 108, and the Sixth Legion took over the garrison, possibly by 118; Hadrian probably visited in 122. A civilian town grew up beside it and across the Ouse. Septimius Severus made it his base for campaigning in Caledonia from 208, and his court stayed there until his death. In 306 Constantius I also died there, and his son Constantine was at once proclaimed by the troops; the surviving Multangular Tower is probably Constantine's work.

By 237 Eboracum was a colonia, the highest status a Roman city could reach and the only one of Britain's four not founded for retired soldiers, with a council of rich locals. In 296 it became capital of Britannia Secunda. It was the main centre for working Whitby jet into jewellery, and its people worshipped the genius of the city, the Mother Goddess, Mithras and Serapis among others. Bishop Eborius of Eboracum attended the Council of Arles in 314.

The site developed into the city of York, and the name survives as Ebor in the official title of the Archbishop of York. Remains of the basilica of the headquarters building can be seen in the undercroft of York Minster, the Multangular Tower stands in the York Museum Gardens with Roman sarcophagi, and the Roman Bath pub shows part of the military bath-house. Many finds are in the Yorkshire Museum.
ebro-river: The Ebro rises at Fontibre in the Cantabrian Mountains of Cantabria, only 42 kilometres from the Bay of Biscay, and flows almost entirely east-south-east to the Mediterranean. It is the longest river entirely within Spain. Much of its water comes from northern tributaries that drain about two thirds of the southern slopes of the Pyrenees, and all of Andorra drains into it through the Segre. The valley is cut off from the sea by mountains, so the climate is dry and continental, with hot summers and cold winters.

The Greeks called the river Ibēr and the Romans Hibēr or Ibērus, and the Iberian Peninsula and its people took their names from it. After the First Punic War (264-241 BCE) it served as the dividing line between Roman expansion to the north and Carthaginian expansion to the south. When the Roman Republic, alarmed by Hannibal's growing influence, made the city of Saguntum, well south of the river, a protectorate of Rome, Hannibal saw a breach of that arrangement and used it as the occasion for the Second Punic War.

The Cistercian monastery of Nuestra Señora de Rueda, founded on the river's bank in Aragon in 1202, used one of the first large waterwheels built for power in Spain and diverted Ebro water to heat its buildings. In 1938 the river was the starting ground of the Battle of the Ebro, a Republican offensive of the Spanish Civil War that enjoyed early success but ended in defeat, the Republican forces never reaching their objective of Gandesa.

In Catalonia the river passes through gorges below the cliffs of the Serra de Cardó, turns east near Tortosa and reaches the sea close to Amposta. Dams were built at Flix in 1948 and at Mequinenza and Riba-roja in 1955. The delta in the Terres de l'Ebre region, about 340 square kilometres, is one of the largest wetlands of the western Mediterranean and has formed entirely from sediment carried downriver; Amposta, a seaport in the 4th century, now lies well inland. Part of it is protected as the Ebro Delta Natural Park, and it is farmed for rice, citrus fruit and vegetables.
ebroin: Ebroin was mayor of the palace of Neustria on two occasions, first from 658 until his deposition in 673 and again from 675 until his death. After the failed coup of the Austrasian mayor Grimoald the Elder, the Merovingian court resided in Neustria. According to the Liber historiae Francorum, a council of Franks elected Ebroin in 659 to replace Erchinoald, who had died in the reign of Chlothar III. Queen Balthild served as regent for her son Chlothar III and, after a power struggle with Ebroin, withdrew to the Abbey of Chelles in 664.

Bede records that in 668 Ebroin waylaid an Englishman returning from Rome, for fear that the Byzantine emperor Constans II was plotting an alliance against him. When Chlothar III died in 673, Ebroin raised another brother, Theuderic III, to the throne of Neustria without consulting the nobles. He tried to keep Neustria and Burgundy united, but the Burgundian nobles, led by Bishop Leodegar of Autun and Adalrich, Duke of Alsace, offered the crown to Childeric II of Austrasia. Childeric replaced Ebroin with his own mayor, Wulfoald. Ebroin was tonsured and confined to Luxeuil. A proclamation then declared that each kingdom would keep its own laws and that no one should again set up a tyranny like Ebroin's.

Childeric II was murdered at Bondi, and Ebroin and Leodegar left their cloister. Ebroin proclaimed a false Merovingian as king, had the mayor Leudesius murdered and made himself mayor again. About 675 he reimposed his authority over Neustria and most of Burgundy and took Autun, where Leodegar's eyes were put out. Ebroin persuaded the king that Childeric's murder had been Leodegar's doing, and Leodegar was tried and exiled. On 12 October 678 he was led away and murdered. Ebroin also defeated the Austrasians at the Battle of Bois-du-Fays, near Laon. Duke Martin, lured to Ecry with false assurances of talks with Theuderic, was killed there with his supporters.

Ebroin was assassinated in a combined attack by his many enemies. In 684 Ansoald, bishop of Poitiers, commissioned a Life of Leodegar that presented Ebroin as an enemy of God driven only by ambition and a lust for power. It became so well established in the Church that Leodegar was canonised as Saint Leger. The Austrasians, whose own ambitious mayoral family commissioned the continuations of the chronicle of Fredegar, also found tales of Ebroin's infamy useful.
ebussuud-efendi: Ebussuud Efendi was born on 30 December 1490, the son of Iskilipli Sheikh Muhiddin Muhammad Efendi. He was also called El-İmâdî because his family came from Imâd, a village near İskilip. In the 1530s he served as a judge in Bursa, Istanbul and Rumelia, where he brought local laws into line with sharia, before Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent made him Shaykh al-Islām in 1545. He held that office until his death on 23 August 1574 and brought it to the peak of its power.

As Shaykh al-Islām Ebussuud turned the issuing of fatwās, until then largely informal, into an organised procedure. He set up a department, the fatwā-khāna, in which scribes (fatwā katibi) with legal training drafted questions to fixed technical and rhetorical standards and clerks (fatwā emini), scholars holding senior madrasa posts, sometimes prepared provisional answers before they reached him. His manual Advice to Fetva Scribes (Fetva Katiblerine Tenbih) taught how to frame a query so that it could be answered precisely and in the fewest words. The reform gave Ottoman fatwā documents a standard style and let the office issue them in large numbers.

His rulings covered ritual prayer, ablution, contracts, religious foundations, the practices of Sufis, family matters and the affairs of non-Muslim communities. He shaped the imperial land and tax systems in line with Hanafi tradition and the institution of the cash-waqf. His opinions did not always side with the state: he declared that collecting poll tax from landless peasants, torturing suspects and taxing pigs went against religious law. He also issued rulings that legitimised the attack on Cyprus by Suleiman's successor Selim, and a contested fatwā permitting dealings involving interest (riba) in certain cases, which modern Muslim modernists often cite.

His fatwā collections, known as Ma‘ruḍāt and also as Fetava-yı Ebussuud, survive in several versions compiled by different hands in Turkish archives and libraries, and were cited by generations of later jurists. His Qur'an commentary, Irshādu-l-‘Aqqli-s-Saleem ilā Mazāyā Al-Kitaabi-l-Kareem, earned him awards from Suleiman, who sent copies to Mecca and Medina; later scholars such as Muhammad Taqi Usmani count it among the four leading commentaries. He also wrote on mysticism, Arabic grammar, literature and poetry, and commentaries on al-Taftazānī's Talweeḥ and al-Nasafī's Manār.
ecbatana: Ecbatana lay in the Zagros Mountains, at the foot of Mount Alvand, on the royal road that connected Persepolis to Sardis. Its position on the main east–west highway, together with a local reputation for horses and wheat, is credited with its wealth in antiquity. Ancient authors called it Caput Mediae, the Royal Seat and the Great City. The site is identified with the present city of Hamadan, and scholars now regard that identification as secure, although a lack of Median and Achaemenid remains once prompted suggestions of other sites, among them Takht-i Suleiman and Tabriz.

According to Herodotus, the first Median ruler Deioces chose Ecbatana as his capital in 678 BCE and built a palace there within seven concentric walls, each with battlements of a different colour, the last two coated in silver and gold. Some archaeologists have attributed the construction to Phraortes, the second Median king. Assyrian sources never mention the city, which suggests that Assyria did not penetrate east of the Alvand range. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that Cyrus the Great seized the royal residence after the army of Astyages handed its king to him in fetters, and carried its silver and gold to Anšan.

Under the Achaemenids Ecbatana lost its former importance but served as a summer capital, a treasury and a royal archive; the Bible mentions its citadel (Ezra 6:2) as holding national records in the time of Darius I. In 330 BCE Alexander the Great took its treasury and stripped the palace of its gold and silver decoration, and he had the general Parmenion killed there. Seleucus I ruled the city in 305 BCE, and Demetrius I Soter kept a mint there. The Parthians made it a summer capital and their main mint. Ardashir I conquered it in 226 CE. It fell to the Muslims after the battle of Nahavand in 642, was destroyed in the Mongol invasion around 1220 and sacked by Timur in 1386.

Excavation has been limited because the modern town covers most of the ancient site. Charles Fossey dug at Ecbatana in 1913, and work on the mound of Tell Hagmatana, thought to correspond to the ancient citadel, began in 1983. Few finds can be firmly dated to the Median period. They include a massive mud-brick defensive wall and a small room with four corner columns, and excavations in 2006 on a limited area of the hill found nothing older than the Parthian period. Many of the finds are kept in the Ecbatana Museum, opened in 1994.
ecclesiastes: The English title is a Latin transliteration of the Greek Ekklēsiastēs, which the Septuagint used to translate the Hebrew Kohelet, from a word for assembly. Most scholars today understand it to mean someone speaking before an assembly, hence Teacher or Preacher. Rabbinic tradition ascribes the book to King Solomon in his old age, but critical scholars have long rejected a pre-exilic origin. Persian loanwords and numerous Aramaisms point to the Persian period or later, and scholars dispute whether it belongs to the Achaemenid or the Hellenistic period, depending on how much Greek influence they find in it.

An unnamed narrator introduces the words of Kohelet and returns in the epilogue at 12:9–14. Kohelet declares that all is hevel, a Hebrew word for vapour or breath that is translated as vanity, futility or meaninglessness. He asks what profit people gain from their toil under the sun. As a king he has experienced everything and concludes that death levels the wise and the foolish alike. His advice is to take pleasure in eating, drinking and work in the present, since enjoyment is a gift from God.

The book contains the passage in chapter 3 that begins with a time to be born and a time to die. It ends with the instruction to fear God and keep his commandments. Many modern commentators regard the epilogue as the addition of a later scribe. Scholars disagree whether the book is positive or pessimistic, and the Talmud records that the rabbis considered withholding it because of its apparent contradictions.

In Judaism the book is read on Shemini Atzeret in some rites and on the Shabbat of the intermediate days of Sukkot among Ashkenazim. Jerome wrote a commentary on it, and Augustine cited it in his City of God. Its phrases, such as eat, drink and be merry and nothing new under the sun, entered English, and the song Turn! Turn! Turn! by Pete Seeger takes its words from chapter 3.
ecclesiastical-history-of-the-english-pe: Bede wrote the work in Latin and is believed to have completed it in 731, when he was about 59. Its first twenty-one chapters, on the time before the mission of Augustine, were compiled from earlier writers such as Orosius, Gildas and Prosper of Aquitaine, from the letters of Pope Gregory I and from legends and traditions. After 596 he used documentary sources that he took pains to obtain from England and Rome, and oral testimony. His title echoes Eusebius's Historia Ecclesiastica, and like Eusebius he took the Acts of the Apostles as his model.

In 725 Bede had written The Reckoning of Time, using a form of the anno Domini era devised by Dionysius Exiguus in 525, and he continued to use it throughout the History, which helped to bring about its adoption in Western Europe.

The work has five books. The first sketches the history of Britain from Julius Caesar's invasion in 55 BCE, with a brief account of Christianity in Roman Britain, including the martyrdom of St Alban, and the mission of Augustine in 597. The second begins with the death of Gregory the Great in 604 and tells how Penda, the pagan king of Mercia, killed the newly Christian Edwin of Northumbria around 632. The third follows Christianity under the Northumbrian kings Oswald and Oswy and climaxes in the Council of Whitby. The fourth opens with the consecration of Theodore as Archbishop of Canterbury.

Bede had a clear polemical and didactic purpose. He was a partisan of his native Northumbria and gave Mercia less attention. He held that the conversion of Britain was the work of Irish and Italian missionaries, not of the native Britons, and that the Anglo-Saxon settlement was God's punishment for their failure to evangelise and to accept the Roman date of Easter. He wrote at length about that date. The parable of the sparrow, told of Edwin's council in 627, is one of its best-known passages.

About 160 manuscripts of the History survive, roughly half of them on the Continent, and about 100 more hold parts of it. It was translated into Old English between the end of the 9th century and about 930; the attribution to King Alfred is no longer accepted. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle drew heavily on it for the chronological framework of its early parts. It was first printed in the later 15th century, probably at Strasbourg.
For many years early Anglo-Saxon history was essentially a retelling of the History, but recent scholarship has looked as much at what Bede did not write as at what he did.
ecgfrith-of-northumbria: Ecgfrith was born in 645, or less likely 646, to King Oswiu of Northumbria and his wife Eanflæd. At about the age of 10 he was held as a hostage at the court of Queen Cynewise, wife of King Penda of Mercia. Penda was later defeated and killed by Oswiu at the Battle of the Winwaed, a victory that greatly enhanced Northumbrian power. To secure his hegemony over the other English kingdoms, Oswiu arranged a marriage between Ecgfrith and Æthelthryth, a daughter of Anna of East Anglia.

In 671 Ecgfrith defeated the Picts at the Battle of Two Rivers, and the Northumbrians took control of Pictland for the next fourteen years. About 672 Æthelthryth persuaded him to let her become a nun. She entered the monastery of the Abbess Æbbe, Ecgfrith's aunt, at Coldingham, and a year later became founding abbess of Ely. Her taking the veil may have led to a long quarrel with Wilfrid, Bishop of York, who was expelled from his see; Ecgfrith's second wife, Eormenburg, and Wilfrid became bitter enemies.

Ecgfrith supported Benedict Biscop. In 674 he gave him 70 hides of land near the mouth of the River Wear for a monastery dedicated to St Peter, and about ten years later 40 hides on the River Tyne at Jarrow for a sister house dedicated to St Paul. These became the monastery of Wearmouth and Jarrow, Bede's lifelong home. Ecgfrith also appears to have been the earliest Northumbrian king, and perhaps the earliest Anglo-Saxon ruler, to issue the silver penny, which became the mainstay of English coinage for centuries. His pennies, also known as sceattas, were thick, cast in moulds and issued on a large scale.

In June 684 Ecgfrith sent a raiding party under his general Berht to Brega in Ireland, which seized a large number of slaves and sacked many churches and monasteries. Ecgberht of Ripon had warned against it, and Bede and other churchmen condemned it. In 685, against the advice of Cuthbert of Lindisfarne, Ecgfrith led a force against the Picts of Fortriu, led by his cousin Bridei. Lured into the mountains by a feigned flight, he was killed on 20 May. Most of his army was lost. He was buried on Iona and succeeded by his illegitimate half-brother Aldfrith.

Bede dated the beginning of Northumbria's decline from Ecgfrith's death. The Northumbrians never regained the dominance of northern Britain lost in 685, but the kingdom remained one of the most powerful states of Britain and Ireland well into the Viking Age.
echigo-province: Echigo Province was an old province in north-central Japan, on the shores of the Sea of Japan. It bordered Uzen, Iwashiro, Kōzuke, Shinano and Etchū Provinces and corresponds today to Niigata Prefecture without the island of Sado. Its abbreviated name was Esshū, a name it shared with Echizen and Etchū Provinces. Under the Engishiki classification it ranked as one of the 35 superior countries in importance and one of the 30 far countries in distance from the capital Kyoto. Together with Kōzuke Province it formed the Jōetsu region.

In the late 7th century, in the reign of Emperor Monmu, the ancient province of Koshi was divided into three: Echizen, Etchū and Echigo. The new Echigo consisted of Iwafune and Nutari Districts and was one of two border provinces of the Yamato state with the Emishi, the other being Mutsu. In 702 it received four districts from Etchū: Kubiki, Koshi, Uonuma and Kanbara. When Japan extended its territory northward in 708, Dewa District was established under Echigo, but in 712 it became Dewa Province. Sado Province was merged with Echigo between 743 and 752, and from the division of Sado in 752 the territory of Echigo stayed constant until the Meiji period.

The provincial capital stood in Kubiki District, in what is now the city of Jōetsu, but its exact location is unknown. The temple of Gochikokubun-ji in Jōetsu claims to be the successor of the provincial temple, though its records date only to 1562, when Uesugi Kenshin relocated it to its present site. Two Shinto shrines dispute the title of ichinomiya of the province: Yahiko Shrine and Kota Shrine.

The Hōjō clan ruled Echigo directly in the Kamakura period, followed by the Uesugi clan from the start of the Muromachi period to the late Sengoku period. Under the Tokugawa shogunate of the Edo period the province was divided among several feudal domains. The Hokurikudō highway passed through it, with numerous post stations, and the port of Niigata was of major importance in the coastal kitamaebune trading system.

The area became a battleground during the Battle of Hokuetsu in the Boshin War of the Meiji Restoration. After the establishment of the Meiji government the domains and provinces became prefectures with the abolition of the han system in 1871, and these prefectures merged to form Niigata Prefecture in 1876. The province had consisted of fifteen districts, several of which, such as Nakakanbara and Higashikubiki, have since been dissolved.
echizen-province: Echizen Province lay in what is today the northern portion of Fukui Prefecture in the Hokuriku region, and was part of the Hokurikudō Circuit. It bordered Kaga, Wakasa, Hida and Ōmi Provinces. It was strategically important because of its nearness to Kyoto and Nara and its place on the Sea of Japan, with contacts to the Asian continent. The province was known for washi paper, which a text of 774 mentions, and for ceramics: Echizen is one of the six old kiln sites of Japan, with Shigaraki, Bizen, Seto, Tanba and Tokoname.

Koshi Province, one of the original provinces listed in the Nihon Shoki, gave Japan its 26th emperor, Emperor Keitai, when its king was chosen during a succession crisis in 507. Under the reforms of the Taihō Code in 701, Koshi was divided into Echizen, Etchū and Echigo. In 718 four northern districts were separated to form Noto Province, and in 823 the districts of Kaga and Enuma formed Kaga Province, giving Echizen its later borders. The governor Fujiwara no Tametoki took his daughter Murasaki Shikibu to the province for just over a year, a stay said to have influenced The Tale of Genji.

The Shiba clan ruled as shugo for most of the Muromachi period and were displaced by the Asakura clan, who made Ichijōdani their headquarters. Under Asakura Yoshikage the province enjoyed a peace far greater than the rest of Japan, partly through his negotiations with the Ikkō-ikki, and became a refuge for people fleeing the violence to the south. Oda Nobunaga defeated the Asakura, burned Ichijōdani Castle and divided the province among his generals. After his death it passed to Shibata Katsuie, later defeated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

After the Battle of Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu awarded the whole province to his second son, Yūki Hideyasu, daimyō of Echizen Domain at Fukui Castle. Much of it stayed under the Matsudaira clan until the Meiji Restoration, as a buffer between Kyoto and the Maeda clan of Kaga, though internal conflicts reduced Fukui Domain and much land became shogunal territory.

Matsudaira Shungaku, the 17th daimyō of Fukui Domain, played a major role in national politics in the Bakumatsu period and helped negotiate the surrender of pro-Tokugawa forces at the end of the Boshin War. Fukui Prefecture and Tsuruga Prefecture were established on 29 August 1871. Echizen still existed legally for certain purposes: it is named in treaties of 1894 between Japan and the United States and between Japan and the United Kingdom.
ecija: Écija lies in the countryside 85 kilometres east of the city of Seville, on the left bank of the Genil, the main tributary of the Guadalquivir. The Roman town stood on the river's terraces, a position suited to controlling the river and its meadows. Its economy rests on agriculture, cattle and textiles, and its most distinctive feature is its Baroque bell towers.

Iberian finds go back to the 8th century BCE. Astigi stood firmly on Julius Caesar's side at the Battle of Munda, and as a reward Caesar ordered its fortification and refounded it as a colony, whose name under Octavian was settled as Colonia Iulia Augusta Firma Astigitana. Pliny the Elder and Pomponius Mela call it the rival of Córdoba and Seville. It was the seat of one of four conventi of Hispania Baetica, where leading men met under the proconsul to oversee justice, and an early diocese. Suevi and Visigoths ruled it after the Romans.

An Islamic army conquered the town in 711 after a resistance of six months. Known as Istiǧǧa, it became the capital of an extensive district and fed Córdoba and Seville. Its walls were demolished in the early 10th century as punishment for local support of the rebellion of Umar ibn Hafsun against Umayyad rule. Christians seized the place on 3 May 1240, and its nearness to the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada made it a border town. Most of its Mudéjar population was expelled in 1263. It received the title of city in 1402 and stopped being a frontier in 1410, with the conquest of Antequera.

Écija prospered in the 17th and 18th centuries, with a wool trade and a mixed society, and the earthquake of 1755 forced a deep urban renewal. It is a town of the province of Seville in Andalusia, with 40,100 people at the 2008 census. Its landmarks include the Church of Santa María and the Benamejí Palace. Astigi was among the most complete Roman cities discovered, but in 1998 the city council decided to bulldoze its Roman remains for a car park.
ecole-francaise-dextreme-orient: The school was founded on 20 January 1900, with its headquarters in Hanoi, then in the Tonkin protectorate of French Indochina. Its first director was Louis Finot, followed by Alfred Foucher in 1905 and Claude-Eugène Maitre in 1908. Finot returned as director in 1920, and George Cœdès led the school from 1929 to 1947. Paul Mus joined it in 1927 and worked in Hanoi as its secretary and librarian until 1940.

After Vietnam became independent the school moved its headquarters away from Hanoi, and it later settled in Paris. Later directors included Louis Malleret, Jean Filliozat, Léon Vandermeersch and Denys Lombard. Its main fields are archaeology, philology and the study of modern Asian societies, and it is now an associated college of PSL University.

The school devised its own romanization of Mandarin Chinese, which shared some features with Wade–Giles and Hanyu Pinyin and was later superseded by Pinyin. Its catalogue of publications holds some 600 titles in archaeology, history, anthropology, literature and philology, covering Asia from India to Japan.

It publishes five scholarly journals. The Bulletin de l'École française d'Extrême-Orient has appeared since 1901. Arts Asiatiques is published with the Musée Guimet and the CNRS, the Cahiers d'Extrême-Asie in Kyoto, Aséanie, on Southeast Asian studies, in Bangkok, and Sinologie française in Chinese in Beijing. The journals are aimed at specialists and at a wider public interested in Asian civilizations and societies.
ecomog: The members of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) agreed a Protocol on Mutual Defence Assistance at Freetown on 29 May 1981, which provided for an allied armed force when needed. ECOMOG itself was created by the Standing Mediation Committee at its meeting in Banjul on 6 and 7 August 1990. The Nigerian scholar Adekeye Adebajo has written that this body stood on shaky legal foundations, that the guidelines of the defence protocol were not followed, and that the force was justified largely on humanitarian grounds.

It was the English-speaking members of ECOWAS that acted, intervening in the Liberian civil war that had begun in 1989. Several French-speaking members strongly opposed the deployment, and the leaders of Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire supported Charles Taylor in his attempt to depose Samuel Doe.

Unlike the usual United Nations mission of the time, the force had to fight its way into a many-sided civil war to hold the factions apart. Most of its men and resources came from the Nigerian Armed Forces, with smaller units from Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone, The Gambia and others. Its first commander was the Ghanaian Lieutenant General Arnold Quainoo; after Samuel Doe was killed by Prince Johnson's Independent National Patriotic Front of Liberia on 9 September 1990, Major General Joshua Dogonyaro took over, the first of an unbroken line of Nigerian commanders.

Senegal sent 1,500 soldiers with some financial support from the United States, but withdrew them all by mid-January 1993, after six were killed in a confrontation with Taylor's supporters at Vahun on 28 May 1992. Corruption and organised looting by its troops led some Liberians to read the acronym as Every Car or Movable Object Gone. After Taylor was elected president on 19 July 1997, the last field commander, General Timothy Shelpidi, withdrew the force fully by the end of 1998.

Within Africa the force was the first credible attempt at a regional security initiative since the Organisation of African Unity tried to send an Inter-African Force to Chad in 1981. A deployment of 1,700 men planned in 2001 for the border between Guinea and Liberia never took place, for lack of funds and because of fighting in Liberia. In 2003, under pressure from the United States, ECOWAS launched a similar mission, ECOMIL, to halt the rebel occupation of Monrovia during the Second Liberian Civil War; it was soon succeeded by the United Nations mission UNMIL.
ecuadorian-peruvian-war: The dispute dated from before Ecuador's independence, as part of a wider quarrel between Gran Colombia and Peru. It turned on whether Ecuador's territory reached beyond the Andes to the Marañón (Amazon) river and so included the Amazon basin. Several attempts at settlement failed and produced conflicting treaties, and war came more than once: the Gran Colombia–Peru War of 1828 and the first Ecuadorian–Peruvian War of 1857 to 1860. The Salomón–Lozano Treaty, signed in secret by Colombia and Peru in March 1922, set their boundary at the Putumayo River and so recognised Peruvian control of much of the disputed region. By December 1940 President Manuel Prado had authorised a Northern Army Detachment, ready for operations by July 1941.

Fighting began on 5 July 1941 on the Zarumilla river, and each side blamed the other for the first shot. Ecuadorian Colonel Luis A. Rodríguez said Peruvian policemen fired on a border patrol; Peruvian accounts said Ecuadorian soldiers from Huaquillas attacked a police patrol at Aguas Verdes. By 6 July Peru was bombing Ecuadorian border posts. Its offensive under General Eloy G. Ureta began on 23 July, with 11,500 to 13,000 men, and overran the post at Chacras the next day. Ecuador had no armour and few aircraft, and Peru's navy and air force had the advantage.

A ceasefire took effect on 31 July, but that day Peruvian paratroopers captured Puerto Bolívar, and fighting continued in the Amazon, where Second Lieutenant Hugo Ortiz Garcés was killed at the Santiago river on 2 August. By the end of August Peru held El Oro, Loja and Zamora Chinchipe and had begun a blockade of Guayaquil. The Talara Accord of 2 October ended the clashes and set up a demilitarised zone watched by representatives of the United States, Brazil and Argentina.

Ecuador and Peru signed the Rio Protocol on 29 January 1942, and Ecuador gave up its claim to a sovereign outlet to the Amazon. Peruvian troops left El Oro on 12 February 1942. Ecuador withdrew from the boundary commissions in 1948, arguing that the Protocol did not fit the geography, and some 78 kilometres of the border stayed unmarked for fifty years. In 1960 President José María Velasco declared the Protocol void, as signed under occupation, but Peru and four other countries held it valid. The disputes ended only with the Cenepa War of 1995 and the Brasilia Presidential Act of October 1998.
ecumenical-patriarch-of-constantinople: The see of Byzantium, whose foundation was later ascribed to Andrew the Apostle, was originally a common bishopric. When Emperor Constantine enlarged Byzantium into a second capital and named it Constantinople, its bishop, once a suffragan of the Metropolitan of Heraclea, was raised to an archbishopric. For many decades the heads of the church of Rome opposed this, in defence of the principle that all patriarchates derived from Saint Peter.

In 381 the First Council of Constantinople declared that its bishop should have the primacy of honour after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 set up a patriarchate with jurisdiction over Asia Minor and Thrace, and Canon 28 granted it honours equal to Rome's, with Rome keeping its seniority. Leo I refused to accept this canon, since it was made in the absence of his legates. The patriarch has been called ecumenical since the sixth century.

The Latin patriarchate was created after the Latin capture of Constantinople in 1204, during the Fourth Crusade. When the Ottoman Turks took the city in 1453 the patriarchate ceased to function. Sultan Mehmed II restored it, wishing to present his dynasty as heirs of the Eastern Roman emperors, and in 1454 he gave the office to the scholar-monk Gennadius Scholarius, known for his opposition to union with the Latin West, who became Patriarch Gennadius II. The patriarch was made ethnarch of the Millet of Rum, which included all Orthodox Christians under Ottoman rule. Several patriarchs were executed, most notably Gregory V, who was lynched on Easter Monday 1821 in revenge for the outbreak of the Greek Revolution.

In the 19th century nationalism among the Balkan Christian nations led to several autocephalous national churches, leaving the ecumenical patriarch with direct control over the Orthodox Christians of Turkey, parts of Greece and the dioceses of the Greek diaspora.

The ecumenical patriarch is first among equals among the Orthodox bishops. He presides over councils of primates or bishops in which he takes part and has the right to convene extraordinary synods, but he has no direct jurisdiction over the other patriarchs or autocephalous churches. The Orthodox Church has no central authority or single head, and its system is synodical, unlike the papal supremacy of the Catholic Church. The monastic communities of Mount Athos are directly under his jurisdiction. His full style is Archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, and Ecumenical Patriarch.
edda: Edda is an Old Norse term that modern scholars apply to two medieval Icelandic works, the Prose Edda and an older collection of poems, the Poetic Edda, which had no original title. Historically the word referred only to the Prose Edda, but that usage has fallen out of favour because of confusion with the other work. Both were recorded in Iceland in the 13th century, though they contain material from earlier traditional sources reaching back into the Viking Age. They are the main sources for the skaldic tradition of medieval Iceland and for Norse mythology.

At least five explanations of the word have been proposed. One links it to a word meaning great-grandmother in the poem Rígsþula, another to Old Norse óðr, poetry, and a third, put forward in 1895 by Eiríkr Magnússon, to the place name Oddi, where Snorri Sturluson was educated. The most widely accepted derives it from the Latin edo, I compose, though this may reflect modern usage more than history. A fifth treats it as a bird title, little eider duck, like the legal code Grágás.

The Prose Edda is an Icelandic manual of poetics that also contains many mythological stories. Its purpose was to enable Icelandic poets and readers to understand the subtleties of alliterative verse and the mythological allusions behind the many kennings of skaldic poetry. The Icelandic scholar and historian Snorri Sturluson wrote it around 1220. It survives in four known manuscripts and three fragments, written from about 1300 to about 1600. It consists of a Prologue and three books: Gylfaginning, on the creation and foretold destruction and rebirth of the Norse world, Skáldskaparmál, a dialogue between the sea god Ægir and the god of poetry Bragi, and Háttatal, a demonstration of verse forms.

The Poetic Edda comes from the manuscript Codex Regius. Its first part has ten songs about gods, narrating the creation, destruction and rebirth of the mythological world, and its second has nineteen about heroes and heroines such as Sigurd, Brynhildr and Gunnar. Nothing is known of the manuscript's whereabouts until 1643, when it came into the possession of Brynjólfur Sveinsson, Bishop of Skálholt. Scholars had speculated that an Elder Edda once existed containing the pagan poems Snorri quotes, and the find seemed to confirm it. Brynjólfur attributed it to the 12th-century priest Sæmundr the Learned, a view modern scholars reject. He sent it to King Christian IV of Denmark, and in 1971 it was returned to Iceland.
edfu: Edfu, called Behedet in ancient Egyptian and Apollonopolis Magna in Hellenistic and Roman times, lies on the west bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, between Esna and Aswan. The ancient settlement, Tell Edfu, lies about 50 m west of the Ptolemaic temple. The ruins of one of seven small provincial step pyramids built along the Nile Valley, loosely attributed to King Huni of the Third Dynasty, stand about 5 km to the south; the purpose of these pyramids is unknown.

Tell Edfu preserves a continuous sequence of occupation from the Old Kingdom to the Graeco-Roman period, more than 3,000 years, in places up to 20 m high, and holds evidence reaching back to the Predynastic Period. The settlement was the capital of the Second Upper Egypt nome. Its oldest datable part belongs to the late Old Kingdom, and it flourished and expanded westward during the First Intermediate Period, one of the few southern settlements to thrive while the north, especially the delta, seems to have been in economic decline.

Excavations have uncovered the administrative centre, a columned hall of the late Middle Kingdom, and a granary courtyard of the Second Intermediate Period with at least seven round silos, the largest found in an ancient Egyptian urban centre. A Sixth Dynasty governor, Izi, was worshipped as a god in the Middle Kingdom.

The god Horus was worshipped here as Horus Behedet. The Ptolemaic temple was built over the site of a smaller New Kingdom temple, which left the ruined pylon of the older building on the east side of the first court. Under the Roman emperors the city was the headquarters of the Legio II Traiana, and it later became a Christian bishopric, now a titular see of the Catholic Church.

The Temple of Horus is the most completely preserved of all temple remains in Egypt. In 1860 the French archaeologist Auguste Mariette had the sand, rubbish and mud-brick houses cleared from its precinct, which showed it to be largely intact. In 1848 the town had about 2,000 inhabitants, whose homes stood around and even on the ancient ruins, and who made earthenware vessels like those found in ancient tombs. The temple drew visitors through the 19th century, among them the Prince of Wales in 1862, and the 20th. Excavation at Tell Edfu has been directed since 2001 by Nadine Moeller.
edgar-degas: Degas was born in Paris on 19 July 1834, the oldest of five children of the banker Augustin De Gas and Célestine Musson De Gas, a Creole from New Orleans. He adopted the less grandiose spelling Degas as an adult. His mother died when he was thirteen. After a baccalauréat in literature in 1853 he registered as a Louvre copyist, though his father expected him to study law, and he enrolled at the University of Paris with little effort. In 1855 he met Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, whose advice to draw lines and still more lines he never forgot, and he was admitted to the École des Beaux-Arts. From July 1856 he spent three years in Italy copying Renaissance masters.

Back in Paris in 1859 he began The Bellelli Family, unfinished until 1867, and several history paintings, among them Sémiramis Building Babylon and Young Spartans Exercising. He first exhibited at the Salon in 1865. Within a few years, influenced chiefly by Édouard Manet, whom he had met in 1864, he turned to contemporary subjects. In 1870 he enlisted in the National Guard for the defence of Paris, and a rifle test showed that his eyesight was defective, a worry for the rest of his life. A Cotton Office in New Orleans, painted there from 1872, was the only work a museum bought in his lifetime.

In 1877 Degas invited Mary Cassatt to join the third Impressionist exhibition, and they worked closely on a planned prints journal in 1879 and 1880 until he withdrew from it. His pastel nudes at the eighth exhibition in 1886 drew the most critical writing on him in his lifetime, most of it favourable.

Degas rejected painting outdoors and denied that his art was spontaneous. He said that nothing in it was less so, and that it came from reflection and study of the great masters. He is nonetheless described more accurately as an Impressionist than as a member of any other movement. His one sculpture shown in his lifetime, The Little Dancer of Fourteen Years, a nearly life-size wax with real hair and a cloth tutu, appeared in 1881. Critics found its realism extraordinary but many called it ugly. His heirs found about 150 wax sculptures in his studio, and the foundry owner Adrien Hébrard judged that 74 could be cast in bronze. He influenced Jean-Louis Forain and Walter Sickert.
edgar-king-of-england: Edgar was the younger son of King Edmund I and his first wife, Ælfgifu, who was buried and venerated as a saint at Shaftesbury Abbey. He was brought up by Ælfwynn, the wife of Æthelstan Half-King, whose household was close to the circle of monastic reform around Dunstan. Edmund was killed in 946, and his brother Eadred ruled until 955, when Edgar's older brother Eadwig became king. In 957 the kingdom was divided along the River Thames, with Eadwig keeping Wessex and Edgar ruling Mercia. Historians disagree whether this followed a revolt against Eadwig or an earlier agreement.

Edgar became king of the whole of England when Eadwig died on 1 October 959. Dunstan became Archbishop of Canterbury at the start of the reign, and Edgar's former tutor Æthelwold became Bishop of Winchester in 963. Only two Benedictine monasteries existed when Edgar came to the throne, and the historian Stenton judged that the king's enthusiasm was the decisive factor in the re-establishment of English monasticism. The reform brought a flowering of learning and art centred on Winchester. Monasteries also acquired estates from lay landowners with the king's help, which later caused disorder.

His law codes mainly aimed at better enforcement of existing law, and a standardised coinage of the early 970s replaced the earlier decentralised system. No Viking attacks on England are recorded in his reign. Edgar and his queen, Ælfryth, were consecrated at Bath on Whit Sunday, 11 May 973. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle recorded the event in verse and implies it was a first coronation, though historians debate whether it was a second, and Janet Nelson argues that it was meant to display his claim to imperial status as overlord of Britain.

Edgar died on 8 July 975 and was buried at Glastonbury Abbey. The throne was then disputed between supporters of his two surviving sons. Edward became king with the backing of Dunstan and Æthelwine, while Æthelred had the support of his mother and Bishop Æthelwold. Edward was murdered in 978 and Æthelred succeeded him. Later chroniclers presented Edgar's reign as a golden age, and modern historians such as Judith Green call it the apogee of Old English kingship, though they disagree about his political legacy.
edict-of-gulhane: In the decades before 1839 the Ottoman Empire faced military defeat, an inefficient decentralised government and a tax system, the iltizam, that failed to collect revenue and widened the gap between Muslim and non-Muslim subjects. Janissary revolts had deposed Selim III in 1807, and Mahmud II abolished the Janissaries in 1826, replacing them with the Mansure army. Losses in the Greek War of Independence and high desertion in border conflicts with Russia exposed the weakness of the new force, and long terms of conscription were among the problems the edict was meant to address.

The reformers hoped to modernise the empire so that it could compete with the Great Powers of Europe, and to win over disaffected regions, above all the largely Christian Ottoman lands in Europe. The millets, communal law-courts, had gained wide religious autonomy that seemed to threaten the central government.

The edict rested on three demands. The first guaranteed the security of every subject's life, on the reasoning that people in fear for their lives become a danger to others and to the sultan. The second promised a regular system of assessing taxes, levying troops and fixing the length of service: taxes by means rather than at a flat rate, and a shorter military term so that industries would suffer less while men were away. The third concerned justice: public trials, the free possession and disposal of property, so that the innocent heirs of a criminal kept their rights, and punishments fitting the deed whatever the offender's rank.

A Council of Justice, joined by ministers and notables, was to draft the fundamental laws, and the Military Council those on military service. A law against the traffic in favours and offices was promised, and minorities, made liable to conscription, could avoid it by paying the jizya. The text appeared in Ottoman Turkish in the Takvim-i Vekayi and in Greek and French, the French in Le Moniteur ottoman.

The promises were never fully carried out, in the face of Christian nationalism and resentment among Muslim populations. Even so the edict changed how the state dealt with its subjects, began a state criminal law alongside sharia and enlarged a bureaucracy whose officials now received salaries and education. With the edict of 1856 it was an early step towards Ottomanism, a shared legal and national Ottoman identity.
edict-of-milan: The Romans attributed their success to their collective piety in keeping good relations with the gods. Christians held that their god was the only God and that all others were false, which could not be fitted into the system. They would not swear loyalty oaths to the emperor's divinity, and persecution followed. Emperor Decius (r. 249–251) imposed hard restrictions, and under Gallienus (r. 253–268) came nearly forty years without official sanctions. On 30 April 311 Emperor Galerius posted at Nicomedia an edict of toleration, which ended the persecutions but did nothing to restore confiscated Christian property.

Constantine I, who ruled in the West, and Licinius, who controlled the Balkans, met at Mediolanum, modern Milan, and agreed on 13 February 313 to change policy towards Christians. No edict survives. The text is known from Lactantius's On the Deaths of the Persecutors, which gives a letter of Licinius to the governor of Bithynia posted at Nicomedia on 13 June 313, and from a Greek version in Eusebius of Caesarea's History of the Church, with marked differences between the two.

The agreement was in effect aimed at Maximinus Daza, the Caesar in the East. After Galerius's death Maximinus renewed persecution, and one petition against Christians survives in a stone inscription at Arycanda in Lycia. Licinius issued his letter after defeating Maximinus.

The letter grants Christians and everybody the free power to follow the religion of their choice, and extends to other religions the right of open worship. It orders the return of meeting places and other properties taken from Christians, with the state compensating present owners. It gave Christianity legal status but did not make it the state church, which happened in 380 with the Edict of Thessalonica. Licinius, a pagan, composed it, so it reflects his policy more than that of Constantine, who was already a Christian and later promoted Christianity while tolerating other religions. Scholars no longer debate seriously whether a formal Edict of Milan existed as church history describes it.
edict-of-nantes: The edict aimed primarily to end the long-running French Wars of Religion. Thirty-six years earlier Catherine de Médici's Edict of Saint-Germain had granted limited tolerance to the Huguenots, but events overtook it: it was not formally registered until after the Massacre of Vassy on 1 March 1562, which set off the first of the wars. Henry IV had been a Protestant before taking the throne in 1589, and it was widely believed that he converted to Catholicism in 1593 only to secure his position. Restoring royal authority required internal peace, based on limited toleration enforced by the crown.

The edict, signed on 18 April 1598, consisted of four basic texts: a main text of 92 articles, 56 particular, secret articles on Protestant rights and obligations, and two brevets, letters patent holding the military and pastoral clauses. It gave general freedom of conscience to individuals, amnesty and the restoration of their civil rights, including the right to work in any field, even for the state. Protestant worship was limited to specified areas, and Catholicism stayed the established religion.

The brevets granted safe havens, military strongholds such as La Rochelle, for which the king paid 180,000 écus a year, and a further 150 emergency forts maintained at Huguenot expense. Pope Clement VIII is reported to have protested on hearing of the edict, This crucifies me. The Parlement of Paris delayed ten months before registering it, in 1599, and the Parlement of Rouen registered it without reservation only in 1609.

The edict restored peace and unity but pleased neither side. Catholics rejected the apparent recognition of Protestantism as a permanent element of French society, and Protestants wanted full parity, which it did not give. In 1629 Louis XIII withdrew the brevets after the siege of La Rochelle, which Cardinal Richelieu blockaded for fourteen months.

In October 1685 Louis XIV, Henry's grandson, revoked the edict with the Edict of Fontainebleau and declared Protestantism illegal. Persecution drove as many as 400,000 people to flee, most to Great Britain, Prussia, the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, South Africa and the colonies in North America. Civil rights for non-Catholics in France were restored only with the Edict of Versailles, signed by Louis XVI on 7 November 1787.
edict-of-potsdam: On 22 October 1685 King Louis XIV of France issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, part of a programme of persecution that closed Huguenot churches and schools. It followed the dragonnades, used since 1681 to intimidate Huguenots into converting to Catholicism. Estimates of the Protestants who left France over the next two decades range from 210,000 to 900,000. Across the Rhine, the Holy Roman Empire is estimated to have lost a third of its population through slaughter, famine and plague during the Thirty Years' War. The western part of Brandenburg-Prussia lay within the empire, and the badly depopulated territory faced a desperate labour shortage in the second half of the seventeenth century.

Encouraged by the French theologian-philosopher Jakob Abbadie, Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, issued the edict in Potsdam on 29 October 1685. It provided for Prussian diplomats in Amsterdam to ship refugees who had reached Cadzand and other Dutch ports to the Free City of Hamburg, where Prussian representatives would organise transport up the Elbe. People fleeing eastern and southern France were to travel by land via Sedan and the Duchy of Cleves, which had become a territory of Brandenburg-Prussia in 1666.

Migrants were promised free choice of settlement, no customs duties or taxes on the assets they brought, and abandoned properties free of debts. Settlers received a six-year tax holiday on property taxes, and farmers on abandoned land a ten-year one. Officials were to hire town houses where families could live rent free for up to four years. Once settled, migrants were to enjoy full legal and civic equality with the elector's subjects, free of any discriminatory droit d'aubaine. They could hold services in French and set up their own schools. On 9 November 1685 translations were printed in German, French and Dutch and sent into France by secret couriers and local Protestant networks.

About 20,000 Huguenots are estimated to have moved to Brandenburg-Prussia. The contrast between the edict and Louis XIV's was widely remarked, and the state became a centre of European immigration that also drew the persecuted of Russia, the Netherlands and Bohemia. The immigrants helped to restore an economy damaged by the wars of the century. The edict also served the elector's interests: a large immigrant community bound to him by religion strengthened him against the landed nobility and powerful Lutheran interests, and it returned land abandoned since the Thirty Years' War to use. In Uckermark the farmer Jean Harlan of Calais was given an empty farmstead, two horses, a cow and 50 Thalers.
edicts-of-ashoka: The Edicts are more than thirty inscriptions on pillars, boulders and cave walls, attributed to Emperor Ashoka of the Mauryan Empire. They are found across modern India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and provide the first tangible evidence of Buddhism. They are the earliest written and datable texts from India, and since they were cut in stone they survive exactly as inscribed, whereas earlier texts such as the Vedic texts were handed down orally. Ashoka called them Dhaṃma Lipi, inscriptions of the Dharma, and refers to himself as Beloved of the Gods. The identification with Ashoka was confirmed by an inscription found in 1915 at Maski, which uses his name with his titles. James Prinsep deciphered them.

The Edicts fall into four groups: Minor Rock Edicts, Minor Pillar Edicts, fourteen Major Rock Edicts with two further ones in Odisha, and seven Major Pillar Edicts. The minor rock edicts are the earliest and are the most religious; they mention the Buddha, the Sangha and Buddhist scriptures. The earliest dated, the Kandahar Bilingual Rock Inscription in Greek and Aramaic, was written in the tenth year of his reign, in 260 BCE. The major rock edicts give practical instructions for running the empire, such as irrigation, and set out his belief in peaceful moral conduct, with little personal detail. The Major Pillar Edicts date from his twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh years, and the last is testamental in nature.

The dhamma they promote is largely ecumenical and non-sectarian. Romila Thapar summarises its main principles as non-violence, tolerance of all sects, obedience to parents, respect for brahmins and other teachers, and humane treatment of servants. Ashoka reports medical treatment for people and cattle, better roadside facilities, and officers to oversee the welfare of the people and the spread of the Dharma. He also records that he sent emissaries and medicinal plants to Hellenistic kings, naming Antiochos and Ptolemy, as far as the Mediterranean.

Most inscriptions are in Prakrit in the Brahmi script, with Kharoshthi in the northwest and Greek and Aramaic inscriptions in the northwestern areas. The two Indian scripts had become extinct by about the 5th century CE and were undeciphered when the Edicts were investigated in the 19th century. The inscriptions may show Achaemenid influence: lipi, the word used for his writings, is thought to come from an Old Persian word for inscription. They contain the first examples of the Brahmi numerals that were ancestors of the Hindu–Arabic numerals. The Chinese traveller Fa Hian described a pillar with an inscription by Ashoka. Christopher I. Beckwith distinguishes Ashoka from the Piyadasi of the major edicts, a view that mainstream scholarship does not accept.
edigu: Edigu, also written Edigü or Edigey, was a Turco-Mongol emir from the Manghit tribe. His father, Kutlukiya, was a noble who was defeated and killed by Khan Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde in 1378. Edigu became known as a highly successful general of Tokhtamysh before turning his arms against his master, and by 1396 he was a sovereign ruler of a large area between the Volga and Ural rivers. According to the Epic of Edigu his paternal lineage goes back to the first caliph, Abu Bakr, but the historian István Vásáry considers this lineage, with its fifteen generations, to have been falsified for political legitimacy.

In 1397 Edigu allied himself with Timur-Qutlugh and was appointed commander-in-chief of the Golden Horde armies. In 1399 he inflicted a crushing defeat on Tokhtamysh and Vytautas of Lithuania at the Battle of the Vorskla River. Tokhtamysh lost the throne and fled to Siberia, and Edigu united all of Jochi's lands under his rule, for the last time in history. He also took control of Khwarazm, which he ruled until 1412, and deposed Timur-Qutlugh in favour of a more loyal khan. In 1406 his agents found and killed Tokhtamysh in Siberia.

In 1408 Edigu staged a destructive invasion of Russia because tribute had not been paid in several decades. He burned Nizhny Novgorod, Rostov, Serpukhov and other towns and besieged Moscow, but accepted a ransom from its inhabitants and returned to the steppe. By 1412 or 1413 he had lost control of Astrakhan, Bolghar, Crimea and Sarai, and the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh expelled him from Khwarazm. Within a few years he held only the Manghit homeland on the lower Ural River and the north-eastern shore of the Caspian Sea. He still ravaged Kiev under Lithuanian rule in 1416.
