Edigu was killed in 1419 by Qadir Berdi, a son of Tokhtamysh, who led a campaign deep into Manghit territory and died of his wounds shortly afterwards. Edigu came to be regarded as the founder of the Manghit ulus, later the Nogai Horde, whose dynasty continued for about two centuries, until his last descendants moved to Moscow, where they were baptized and became known as Princes Urusov and Yusupov. The Mamluk-era historian al-Maqrizi described him as courageous and generous, a righteous Muslim who loved Islamic scholars, and said he prohibited the Tatars from selling their sons.
edinburgh: Edinburgh lies in Scotland's Central Belt on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth, between the firth to the north and the Pentland Hills to the south. The modern city is often said to be built on seven hills, among them Calton Hill, Arthur's Seat and the Castle Rock, which gave rise to comparisons with Rome. Castle Rock is a volcanic plug, and the crag and the hollows around it formed an ideal natural strongpoint on which Edinburgh Castle was built. The nickname Auld Reekie, Scots for Old Smoky, refers to the smoke over the Old Town.

The earliest known human habitation in the area was at Cramond, where a Mesolithic camp site dates to about 8500 BCE. The name comes from Eidyn, the name of the region in Cumbric, a Brittonic Celtic language, centred on the stronghold of Din Eidyn, believed to have stood on Castle Rock. A siege of Din Eidyn by Oswald, king of the Angles of Northumbria, in 638 began three centuries of Germanic influence in south-east Scotland, and the town was subsumed in 954 by the kingdom the English called Scotland. As Cumbric gave way to Northumbrian Old English and then Scots, din was replaced by burh, producing Edinburgh.

In 1603 James VI of Scotland succeeded to the English throne, and in 1650 Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army occupied the city. The Acts of Union of 1706 and 1707 united the two kingdoms as Great Britain from 1 May 1707, and the Parliament of Scotland merged into that of Great Britain at Westminster. Many Scots opposed the Union, and there were riots in the city.

The population rose from 49,000 in 1751 to 136,000 in 1831, mostly by migration from the countryside. Overcrowding in the Old Town's tenements and poor sanitation brought cholera outbreaks in 1832, 1848 and 1866. Glasgow overtook Edinburgh as Scotland's largest city by 1821. Improvements under Lord Provost William Chambers in the 1860s began to transform the Old Town, and major slum clearance followed in the 1960s and 1970s.

Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas, recognised as the capital since at least the 15th century. It is the seat of the Scottish Parliament and Government and of the highest courts in Scotland. The Palace of Holyroodhouse is the monarch's official residence in Scotland. The Old Town and the New Town together are a World Heritage Site, and the University of Edinburgh was founded in 1582.
edirne: Edirne lies in the northwestern part of the province of Edirne in Eastern Thrace, 7 km from the Greek border and 20 km from the Bulgarian border. Its position in the border region between Asia and Europe gave rise to the claim that it is the most frequently contested spot on earth. The through highway that connects Europe to Istanbul, Anatolia and the Middle East passes through it, and the surrounding lowlands are productive farmland.

The city was founded on an earlier Thracian settlement. A Greek city, Orestias, stood on the site, and the Roman emperor Hadrian re-established it, adorned it with monuments and renamed it Hadrianopolis, anglicised as Adrianople. Constantine I defeated Licinius there in 324, and the Emperor Valens was killed by the Goths at the Battle of Adrianople in 378. After the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Versinikia in 813, Khan Krum of Bulgaria seized the city and moved its inhabitants to the Bulgarian lands north of the Danube. In 1077 Nikephoros Bryennios rebelled there against Emperor Michael VII Doukas.

In the period of the Latin Empire of Constantinople, the Bulgarian Emperor Kaloyan defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Adrianople in 1205. The Latin regime gave the city to the Byzantine aristocrat Theodore Branas as a hereditary fief in 1206, and Theodore Komnenos, Despot of Epirus, took it in 1227. In 1321 Andronikos III made it his base for the First Palaiologan civil war against his grandfather, Emperor Andronikos II.

The city fell to the Ottomans around 1369. Its church declined, its properties were confiscated and its Metropolitan was taken prisoner and died in captivity. A document of 1389 states that the new Metropolitan could not enter the city and had to carry out his duties from Constantinople. Edirne was the second capital of the Ottoman Empire from the 1360s to 1453.

Edirne is the seat of Edirne Province and a commercial centre for woven textiles, silks, carpets and agricultural products. The Selimiye Mosque, built in 1575 to the design of Mimar Sinan for Sultan Selim II, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011. Two earlier mosques also stand in the centre: the Eski Cami, begun in 1403 and finished in 1422, and the Üç Şerefli Mosque, built between 1437 and 1447 for Sultan Murad II. The Kırkpınar oil-wrestling tournament, held each year in late June or early July, was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2010.
edmund-allenby: Edmund Allenby was born on 23 April 1861, the son of Hynman Allenby, who owned 2,000 acres in Norfolk, and Catherine Anne Cane, and was educated at Haileybury College. He had little desire to be a soldier and failed the examination for the Indian Civil Service, but passed that for Sandhurst in 1880 and was commissioned in the 6th (Inniskilling) Dragoons on 10 May 1882.

He served in the Bechuanaland Expedition of 1884–85 and in the Second Boer War, in which Lord Kitchener described him as a popular and capable cavalry brigadier. A tendency to sudden bellowing rages at his subordinates, combined with his powerful frame, earned him the nickname The Bull.

In the First World War he commanded the cavalry division of the British Expeditionary Force, covering the retreat after the Battle of Mons and fighting at the First Battle of Ypres. He led the Cavalry Corps from 1914, and in May 1915 took command of V Corps at the Second Ypres, where his policy of continual counterattacks defeated the German assault but at controversially heavy cost. In May 1917 the War Cabinet was divided over resources for the Western Front and other fronts, and David Lloyd George appointed Allenby to replace Sir Archibald Murray in command of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force after Jan Smuts refused the post.

From October to December 1917 his forces captured Beersheba, Jaffa and Jerusalem, and in the summer of 1918 they occupied the Jordan Valley. At the Battle of Megiddo they defeated the Ottoman Eighth Army, and the Desert Mounted Corps then captured Damascus and advanced into northern Syria. T. E. Lawrence and Faisal's forces took part in the pursuit, and the Battle of Aleppo was fought five days before the Armistice of Mudros ended the campaign on 30 October 1918.

Made a field marshal on 31 July 1919, Allenby became Special High Commissioner of Egypt that year, as demonstrations against British rule disrupted the country and leaders such as Saad Zaghlul had been exiled to Malta. He first took a conciliatory line, persuading the Colonial Office to let Zaghlul's delegation travel to France, and as High Commissioner he favoured negotiations, after which the Milner Mission was begun.

He remained a hated figure in Egypt, and at Port Said the burning of an effigy of him became a spring tradition. His only child, Horace, was killed in action in 1917. Allenby died of a ruptured cerebral aneurysm on 14 May 1936 at his house in Kensington, and his ashes were buried in Westminster Abbey.
edmund-barton: Edmund Barton was born on 18 January 1849 in Glebe, Sydney, the eleventh of twelve children of English parents, William and Mary Louisa Barton, who had arrived in New South Wales in 1827. His father worked as an accountant, stockbroker and estate agent and was once bankrupt; his mother ran a boarding school for girls in hard times. Barton attended Sydney Grammar School, where he was dux and school captain in 1863 and 1864, and matriculated at the University of Sydney in 1865. He was a member of the Sydney University Cricket Club and a founder of the Sydney Rowing Club, and married Jane Mason Ross in 1877.

After losing a university seat in 1876, Barton won a by-election to the New South Wales Legislative Assembly in 1879. In 1882, aged 33, he became Speaker, the youngest presiding officer of any Australian legislative chamber. He entered the Legislative Council in 1887 and served as Attorney General in 1889. An early supporter of federation, he was a delegate to the National Australasian Convention of March 1891 and helped to produce a draft constitution substantially similar to the one enacted in 1900. After the fall of Henry Parkes's government in October 1891, Parkes persuaded him to lead the federal movement in New South Wales.

In 1897 Barton topped the poll of New South Wales delegates to the Constitutional Convention. Sir Samuel Griffith wrote most of the text of the constitution, but Barton was the political leader who carried it through, and he led the campaign for a yes vote in the referendum. He became prime minister on 1 January 1901, the day federation took effect. His ministry was described as a 'cabinet of kings', and after the March 1901 election he stayed in office with the support of the Australian Labor Party. His government set up the Australian Defence Force and the Commonwealth Public Service, introduced nation-wide women's suffrage, and passed the Immigration Restriction Act 1901. In November 1901 Parliament approved Australian control of British New Guinea.

Barton resigned on 24 September 1903 and was sworn in to the High Court on 7 October with Samuel Griffith and Richard O'Connor. On the court he joined Griffith in almost every case and delivered only twelve separate judgments in the 44 cases heard in 1904 and 1905. In 1919 he was disappointed to be passed over as Chief Justice on Griffith's retirement. He died of heart failure on 7 January 1920 at Medlow Bath, New South Wales, and was survived by his wife and six children.
edmund-burke: Edmund Burke was born in Dublin on 12 January 1729. His mother Mary, née Nagle, was a Roman Catholic from a County Cork family, and his father Richard, a successful solicitor, was a member of the Church of Ireland. Burke adhered to his father's faith and remained a practising Anglican all his life. His political enemies repeatedly accused him of secret Catholic sympathies, at a time when Catholic membership disqualified a man from public office under the Penal Laws in Ireland.

His first published work, A Vindication of Natural Society, appeared in the spring of 1756. It imitated the style and ideas of Lord Bolingbroke to show the absurdity of his arguments for deistic rationalism. Lord Chesterfield and Bishop Warburton at first took it as Bolingbroke's own, and in 1757 Burke stated in the preface to the second edition that it was a satire.

In December 1765 Burke entered the House of Commons for Wendover, a pocket borough in the gift of an ally of Rockingham. After his maiden speech William Pitt the Elder said he had spoken in such a manner as to stop the mouths of all Europe. He sat as a Whig, and for Bristol from 1774. His first great subject was the dispute with the American colonies. On 19 April 1774 he spoke On American Taxation, urging that Britain leave America to tax itself and warning that no body of men will be argued into slavery. He supported the colonists' right to resist metropolitan authority, though not their independence. In March 1782 he became Paymaster of the Forces and a Privy Counsellor.

Burke held that manners underpin virtue and that religious institutions matter for the moral stability of the state. He argued against unrestricted ruling power and for the ability of parties to maintain a principled opposition. He long supported Catholic emancipation and led the attempt to impeach Warren Hastings of the East India Company.

In Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) he argued that the revolution was destroying the fabric of good society and the traditional institutions of the state, and he condemned its persecution of the Catholic Church. He became the leading figure of the conservative Whigs, the Old Whigs, against the New Whigs led by Charles James Fox. He died on 9 July 1797. In the 20th century he came to be regarded, especially in Britain and the United States, as a philosophical founder of conservatism.
edmund-hillary: Edmund Hillary was born in Auckland on 20 July 1919, and the family moved to Tuakau, south of Auckland, in 1920. He was small and shy at first, and grew to 6 feet 2 inches (188 cm) after taking up boxing. A school trip to Mount Ruapehu in 1935 first interested him in climbing. After two unsuccessful years at Auckland University College he gave up study in 1938 and worked as a beekeeper with his father and brother, climbing in winter. He made his first major climb in 1939, the summit of Mount Ollivier, and in 1943 joined the Royal New Zealand Air Force as a navigator on Catalina flying boats.

In 1951 Hillary joined the British reconnaissance of Everest led by Eric Shipton, and from Pumori gained the first clear view of the Western Cwm, which identified what became the standard Nepalese route. For the 1953 expedition, led by John Hunt, he forged a route through the Khumbu Icefall. After Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans turned back on 26 May when Evans's oxygen system failed, Hunt directed Hillary and Tenzing Norgay to make the attempt. They pitched a tent at 27,900 feet (8,500 m), and on 29 May Hillary climbed the 40-foot rock face later called the Hillary Step. They reached the summit at 11:30 am and stayed about fifteen minutes.

He was appointed a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire on 6 June 1953. He led the New Zealand section of the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition and reached the South Pole on 4 January 1958, the first party to do so overland since Amundsen and Scott and the first to use motor vehicles. In 1985 he landed at the North Pole, becoming the first man to stand at both poles and on the summit of Everest.

From 1960 Hillary devoted himself to the Sherpa people of Nepal through the Himalayan Trust, which he established and led until his death; his efforts are credited with the construction of many schools and hospitals. His wife Louise and younger daughter Belinda were killed in a plane crash near Kathmandu on 31 March 1975. He died of heart failure at Auckland City Hospital on 11 January 2008, aged 88, and was given a state funeral. Lukla Airport in Nepal was renamed Tenzing–Hillary Airport in 2008.
edmund-ironside: Edmund was the third of the six sons of King Æthelred the Unready and his first wife. He was probably born in Wessex and raised by his grandmother Ælfthryth. His elder brother Æthelstan, who was close to him, died in June 1014 and left Edmund the sword of Offa and estates in the Danelaw, as well as his connections in the Five Boroughs.

In early 1015, at an assembly in Oxford, Edmund's allies Sigeferth and Morcar were tricked and executed by Eadric Streona, with the complicity of Æthelred. Edmund rescued Sigeferth's widow from the monastery at Malmesbury and married her against the king's will. He occupied the Five Boroughs, and in one of two charters he called himself king. The revolt ended when Cnut invaded in the summer of 1015, and Edmund's early attempts to raise armies against him collapsed amid mistrust.

Æthelred died on 23 April 1016. The citizens and councillors of London chose Edmund as king, while most of the English magnates, meeting at Southampton, elected Cnut. Edmund fought several battles with Cnut, at Penselwood, Sherston and Brentford, and probably Otford, and relieved the siege of London. His decision to take Eadric back into his ranks was heavily criticised by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. At Assandun he was backed by the whole English nation, but Eadric fled, which caused a decisive English defeat.

The English magnates then pressed for peace, and Edmund met Cnut on an island in the River Severn at Alney. They exchanged hostages, declared their friendship and fixed a payment for the Danish army. Edmund kept Wessex and Cnut took the north. Edmund died on 30 November after ruling for 222 days, and was buried at Glastonbury Abbey.

Cnut secured all England, executed Eadric Streona in 1017 and exiled or executed Edmund's family and supporters. He then married Emma of Normandy. His dynasty lasted until 1042, when Edward the Confessor restored the House of Wessex. Medieval writers praised Edmund as an indefatigable warrior, contrasting him with his father, and modern historians generally regard him as a capable leader who fought Cnut to a standstill.
edmund-the-martyr: Edmund was king of East Anglia from about 855. Few facts are known, since the Vikings destroyed the contemporary evidence, including the charters. Coins show that he succeeded Æthelweard, because they shared moneyers, and the number of coins suggests a reign of several years. The only contemporary written references are the records of his death in Asser's life of Alfred the Great and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

The 12th-century Annals of St Neots says he succeeded on Christmas Day 855 aged fourteen, but no source for this is known. His origin is not certain: Abbo of Fleury says he was descended from the ancient Saxon nobility, and 12th-century writers invented accounts of his family.

In the autumn of 865 a force of probably over 5,000, called by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle a great heathen army, came to East Anglia. Edmund made peace and gave them horses and supplies, and they moved on to York in the summer of 866. They returned in 869. The Chronicle says the army took winter quarters at Thetford, that Edmund fought against them that winter and that the Danes won, killed the king and conquered the land.

Where Edmund died, and whether in battle or murdered afterwards, is not known. Abbo of Fleury wrote his passio around 986 for the monks of Ramsey Abbey, from a story Dunstan had heard from an old man who claimed to have been Edmund's sword-bearer. In it the king refused to fight and was bound, beaten, shot with arrows like Saint Sebastian and beheaded by Hinguar, probably Ivar the Boneless.

His head, found clasped between a wolf's paws, answered the searchers: Her, her, her. The historian Antonia Gransden called Abbo's account little more than a hotch-potch of hagiographical commonplaces, and Ridyard says the martyrdom cannot be proven. A stone cross at Hoxne marks one supposed site of the death.

After Guthrum, king of East Anglia, died around 890, the same moneyers who had struck his coins began to make memorial pennies reading SCE EADMVND REX, the earliest evidence that Edmund was venerated as a saint. More than 70 moneyers made them and over 1,800 specimens were found in the Cuerdale Hoard in 1840. His body was moved from Haegelisdun to Beodricesworth, now Bury St Edmunds, probably under Æthelstan, who founded the monastery there in 925.

It was taken to London in 1010 for safety and returned three years later. The abbey became one of the best-known and wealthiest places of pilgrimage in England. Edmund and Edward the Confessor were patron saints of medieval England until Saint George replaced them in the 15th century. His shrine was destroyed in 1539 during the dissolution of the monasteries. His feast day is 20 November.
edo-castle: The warrior Edo Shigetsugu built a residence on the site of the later Honmaru and Ninomaru around the end of the Heian period or the start of the Kamakura period. His clan left in the 15th century after uprisings in the Kanto region, and Ota Dokan, a retainer of the Ogigayatsu Uesugi family, built Edo Castle in 1457. Tokugawa Ieyasu established the Tokugawa shogunate there, and the castle was the residence of the shogun and headquarters of the military government through the Edo period (1603-1867). It is also called Chiyoda Castle.

The plan was large and elaborate. The grounds were divided into wards separated by moats and large stone walls carrying keeps, defence houses and towers: the Honmaru at the centre, the Ninomaru and Sannomaru extending east, the Nishinomaru to the west and the Kitanomaru to the north. East of the Sannomaru an outer moat enclosed the districts of Otomachi and Daimyo-Koji. There were 36 major gates, and Ote-mon was the main one and the most heavily armed. The circumference is debated, with estimates from 6 to 10 miles.

The Spanish governor Rodrigo de Vivero y Velasco described the castle in 1608-1609, remarking on its huge stones and the crowds within: he claimed to have seen 20,000 servants between the first gate and the shogun's palace, and to have passed two ranks of 1,000 musketeers. The Honmaru held the keep and residence of the shogun; its main halls were said to cover 33,000 square metres in the Kan-ei era (1624-1644). Its five-storey keep, 51 metres high and the tallest castle tower in Japan, was built in 1607, rebuilt in 1623 and 1638, and destroyed in the Fire of Meireki of 1657 and never reconstructed. Fujimi-yagura took over its role from 1659.

Fires repeatedly destroyed the Honmaru, and after each one the shogun normally moved into the Nishinomaru. The main palace was destroyed in 1863 and not rebuilt, and the Nishinomaru itself burned in 1853 and again on 5 May 1873, after which the imperial palace of the Meiji era was built on its site. The castle's corridor Matsu no Orōka was the scene in 1701 of the events that led to the forty-seven ronin incident.

After the resignation of the shogun and the Meiji Restoration the castle became the Tokyo Imperial Palace. Some moats, walls and ramparts survive, including the Fujimi-yagura, the Fujimi-tamon and the Ote-mon, which took its present form in the 1620s, when Date Masamune helped with the repairs. The grounds in the Edo period were more extensive than today's, since Tokyo Station and the Marunouchi district lay inside the outermost moat. Many Tokyo place names derive from the castle, among them Otemachi, Toranomon and Marunouchi.
edo-people: The Edo speak the Edo language, which belongs to the Edoid group, and are the descendants of the founders of the Benin Kingdom, the Ogiso. Other Edoid peoples, among them the Esan, the Etsakọ, the Isoko, the Owan and the Urhobo, as well as some other southern groups, migrated from the Benin kingdom. Most of these related groups trace their history back to the old city centre of the Benin people, Benin City.

The name Benin is a Portuguese corruption of Ubini, a word that came into use during the reign of the Oba Ewuare, around 1440. Ubini was later corrupted to Bini by the mixed ethnicities living together at the centre, and then to Benin around 1485, when the Portuguese began trading with Ewuare and gave him coral beads, which the Edo call ivie.

Edo State in Nigeria takes its name from the Edo and from Benin City, their central homeland. The state was formerly part of the old Bendel State, also called the Mid-Western Region, and its culture reflects that of the Edo, Urhobo, Esan and related peoples. The Edo are prominent in the Edo South senatorial district, which comprises seven local government areas.

In traditional belief an invisible world of supernatural beings acts as intercessor for the human world, and offerings are made to them at shrines. Osanobua is the creator and supreme god. His child Olokun rules the waters and gives prosperity and fertility, and another son, Ogun, is the patron god of metalworkers. Shango, the god of thunder, and Osun, the god of medicine, are also honoured.

Coral beads mark Edo dress at weddings and coronations. Women wear a beaded cape or blouse called the ewu-ivie, necklaces called ivie-uru and bracelets called ivie-obo, while men wear a striped cloth over a white shirt and a cap or headdress, which may be made of a mesh of coral beads. Traditional art consists of sculptures, plaques and masks, including the mask of the Queen Mother Idia and the Benin Bronzes, which are now dispersed through museums around the world.
edo-period: In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu prevailed at the Battle of Sekigahara and established hegemony over most of Japan, and in 1603 Emperor Go-Yōzei gave him the title of shogun. He had profited from his transfer to the rich Kantō area, where he made Edo, a strategically situated castle town and the future Tokyo, his headquarters. He resigned two years later in favour of his son Hidetada but kept his power, and in 1615 he defeated his main rival, Toyotomi Hideyori, at the Siege of Osaka. He died in 1616. Peace generally prevailed from then on, which made the samurai largely redundant.

The political system is called bakuhan, a joining of bakufu and han, the domains: the shogun held national authority and some 300 daimyo held regional authority. The Tokugawa came to hold nearly seven million koku of land and control of the most important cities. In 1635 Shogun Iemitsu made the system of sankin-kōtai compulsory. It required about 260 daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo, while their wives and heirs stayed there permanently as hostages. Social order was rigid and based on inherited position; scholars since about 1995 have argued that peasants, craftsmen and merchants were a classification rather than a ladder of rank.

Foreign contact was curtailed step by step. Japanese vessels were forbidden to travel abroad without certification in 1633, and the Closed Country Edict of 1635 forbade any Japanese to leave. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637, which the shogunate blamed on Christian influence, an edict of 1639 expelled the Portuguese. The Dutch were confined from 1636 to the island of Dejima in Nagasaki.

The period passed on a flourishing commercial sector, a well-educated elite, productive agriculture and a national network of roads, among them the five highways of the Gokaidō. Merchants prospered and laid the foundation of the later zaibatsu. By the mid-18th century Edo had more than one million people, probably the biggest city in the world at the time, and Osaka and Kyoto each had more than 400,000. A commoner culture grew in these cities, with kabuki and ukiyo-e, while Neo-Confucianism became the major intellectual development and the dominant legal philosophy by the mid-17th century.

The period ended after Commodore Matthew C. Perry's squadron appeared in Edo Bay in July 1853. The Treaty of Peace and Amity, or Treaty of Kanagawa, of March 1854 opened two ports to American ships. The shogunate modernised its army and navy in its last years, but the Meiji Restoration and the Boshin War restored imperial rule in 1868.
edo-state: Edo State lies in the South-South geopolitical zone of Nigeria. It borders Kogi State to the north, across the Niger River to the north-east, Anambra State to the east, Delta State to the south-east and south, and Ondo State to the west. Benin City is its capital. The state has a tropical wet and dry climate, and its resources include crude oil, limestone and other minerals.

Its modern borders encompass regions that were formerly the site of various empires and kingdoms, among them the Benin Empire, formed in the 11th century. The ancient city of Edo, on the site of modern Benin City, was home to some of the largest earthworks in the world. In 1897 the British Empire conducted a punitive expedition and invasion, destroying most of the ancient city of Edo and incorporating the territory into what became the Southern Nigeria Protectorate.

The Mid-Western Region came into being in June 1963, formed from the Benin and Delta provinces of the Western Region of Nigeria, with Benin City as its capital. When a twelve-state structure was introduced in 1967 it became Midwest State, and in 1976 the territory was renamed Bendel State. During the Nigerian Civil War, Biafran forces negotiated a passage through the Mid-Western state on the way to Lagos, and under Biafran occupation the state was declared the Republic of Benin, which collapsed a day after the declaration as Nigerian troops took Benin City. Edo State was established on 27 August 1991, when Bendel State was split into Edo and Delta States.

The traditional political organisation of the Edo people rests on a three-tier age-group system that makes age rather than lineage the criterion of authority. Benin City itself is organised by age-grades, by wards and by chiefs, hereditary and non-hereditary, who serve the Oba in specialised functions. The Oba is the focal point of the Benin political system, which rests on divine kingship.

The state is inhabited mainly by Edoid peoples, including the Edo or Bini, Esan, Owan, Afemai (Etsako and Akoko-Edo) and Ora, with the Igala and others. Edo-speaking people make up the largest share, and the Edo language is commonly spoken in Benin City, while English is the official language. Christianity was introduced by Portuguese missionaries in the 15th century and is dominant in the south; Islam is dominant in the north, and traditional religions are also practised. The state consists of eighteen local government areas and has about five million inhabitants. Benin City is the centre of the country's rubber industry.
edo-tokyo: The name Edo means bay-entrance. The city was laid out as a castle town around Edo Castle, at the tip of the Musashino terrace. Samurai and daimyo residences lay nearest the castle and occupied up to 70 percent of the city's area, while the townspeople (chonin) lived to the east and northeast in a far more densely populated district of gated communities called machi.

This organisation for the samurai class defined Edo in contrast to Kyoto, shaped by the Imperial Court and its temples, and Osaka, the commercial centre dominated by merchants. A daimyo might hold an upper, a middle and a lower residence, the last on the outskirts as a pleasure retreat with gardens. Water carried the bulk cargo of rice, timber, charcoal and salt along a network of rivers, canals and moats, and the Gokaido, the Five Highways, radiated from the bridge at Nihonbashi.

Before the 10th century Edo is not mentioned in the records. Its development began in the late 11th century, when a branch of the Taira clan, the Chichibu, settled the area, and a descendant took the name Edo Shigetsugu and built a fortified residence that would become Edo Castle.

His son Edo Shigenaga sided with the Taira against Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1180 but later surrendered and became a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate. When Tokugawa Ieyasu entered Edo in 1590 it was not yet a town: a small fortified residence stood on the edge of the plateau, with wetlands and marshes to the east. He had the surroundings surveyed, altered the Hibiya inlet, and began diverting the Hirakawa River and digging moats and canals.
After his victory at Sekigahara in October 1600 he founded the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603 and made Edo his headquarters. Kyoto remained the de jure capital as the seat of the emperor.

Under the nationwide programme of civil works called Tenka-Bushin, the castle was expanded into one of the largest fortified complexes in the world, coasts were reclaimed and the Kanda River was cut. The population is estimated to have reached 1 million by 1721. The Great Fire of Meireki in 1657 killed an estimated 100,000 people and destroyed the keep of Edo Castle, which was never rebuilt, and about 100 major fires struck the city during the Edo period.
After the overthrow of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868 the city was renamed Tokyo, meaning Eastern Capital, and the emperor's residence moved there from Kyoto, making it the capital of Japan.
edouard-manet: Manet's father, Auguste Manet, a judge, expected him to study law, but an uncle, Edmond Fournier, encouraged painting and took him to the Louvre. After a training voyage to Rio de Janeiro in 1848 and two failed naval examinations, he was allowed to study art. He opened a studio in 1856 and, following the realism of Gustave Courbet, painted The Absinthe Drinker and other contemporary subjects such as beggars, singers and bullfights. In 1862 he exhibited Music in the Tuileries, a crowd of friends in the Tuileries Garden that drew fury for its thick brushwork, with Eugène Delacroix among its few defenders.

The Salon rejected The Luncheon on the Grass in 1863, and Manet showed it at the Salon des Refusés. Its fully dressed men beside a nude woman, and its sketch-like handling, caused controversy, while Antonin Proust praised it. Olympia, painted in 1863 on the pose of Titian's Venus of Urbino, was accepted by the Salon in 1865, where its frank portrayal of a self-assured courtesan caused a scandal. Caricatured in the press, it was championed by the avant-garde, among them Courbet, Paul Cézanne and Claude Monet.

Manet painted café scenes, the races, the streets of Paris and war. His The Execution of Emperor Maximilian, in three versions between 1867 and 1869, treated the shooting of a Habsburg emperor installed by Napoleon III, and neither the paintings nor a lithograph could be shown in France. Through Berthe Morisot he came to know Edgar Degas, Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir.

Unlike the core Impressionist group he held that modern artists should exhibit at the Salon, and he refused to take part in their independent exhibitions. He abandoned the layered method of his teacher Thomas Couture for a direct, alla prima method on a light ground, which the Impressionists adopted.

In his mid-forties Manet's health declined, with severe pain and partial paralysis in his legs. His last major work, A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, hung in the Salon of 1882, after which he worked in small formats. His left foot was amputated in April 1883 because of gangrene, and he died 11 days later, on 30 April, in Paris. The art historian Beatrice Farwell says he has been universally regarded as the Father of Modernism.
eduard-bernstein: Eduard Bernstein was born in Schöneberg, now part of Berlin, on 6 January 1850, the seventh of fifteen children of Jakob Bernstein, a railway engine driver. The family was of Polish-Jewish origin but secular. He left school at sixteen and worked as a bank clerk from 1869 to 1878. The Franco-Prussian War awakened his politics, and in 1872 he joined the Social Democratic Workers' Party. After Chancellor Otto von Bismarck enacted the Anti-Socialist Laws in 1878, he moved to Zurich as secretary to the wealthy sympathiser Karl Höchberg. The stay became an exile of over twenty years. Engels's Anti-Dühring, he recalled, converted him to Marxism. In 1888 he moved to London, where he lived for thirteen years.

In London Bernstein worked in the British Museum, wrote for the SPD's Vorwärts and Karl Kautsky's Die Neue Zeit, and wrote the tactical sections of the Erfurt Program of 1891. His contact with the Fabian Society and his view of the stability of late Victorian capitalism led him to doubt orthodox Marxism. He returned to Germany in February 1901, sat in the Reichstag in 1902–1906, 1912–1918 and 1920–1928, and voted for war credits on 4 August 1914, which he later called the darkest day of his political life. He opposed the war as Germany's aims became known, helped found the Independent Social Democratic Party, and rejoined the SPD on 24 December 1918.

His articles in Die Neue Zeit between 1896 and 1898 grew into Evolutionary Socialism (1899). He rejected the Hegelian dialectic and treated socialism as an ethical ideal, not a historical inevitability. Using statistics, he argued that capital was not concentrating in fewer hands, that credit and cartels let capitalism adapt instead of collapsing, and that the working class was not growing poorer. Socialists should therefore work through democratic institutions, trade unions and cooperatives.

The SPD condemned his views, and Rosa Luxemburg answered them in Social Reform or Revolution?, yet the party's practice was largely reformist. Bernstein died in Berlin on 18 December 1932, weeks before the Nazi seizure of power. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern democratic socialism.
eduard-morike: Mörike was born in Ludwigsburg on 8 September 1804, the seventh child of the district medical councillor Karl Friedrich Mörike and Charlotte Mörike, née Bayer. He had 13 siblings, of whom seven died young.

After his father's death in 1817 he lived with his uncle Eberhard Friedrich von Georgii, president of the Württemberg Supreme Tribunal in Stuttgart, who meant him to become a clergyman. In 1818 he entered the Evangelical Seminary at Urach, where he made friends who stayed close for life, among them Wilhelm Hartlaub and the poet Wilhelm Waiblinger. From 1822 to 1826 he studied theology and classics at the Tübinger Stift, and there, with Ludwig Amandus Bauer, he invented the imaginary land of Orplid, which they later developed into a literary work.

After his theological examination in October 1826 Mörike served as a Lutheran pastor in Oberboihingen, Möhringen and Köngen. In 1828 he took an extended leave to write, hoping to live as a freelance, but the attempt failed, and his return to a vicarage at Pflummern in 1829 brought a conflict of conscience, since he believed that serving the Church with a heart like his was a sin.

A transfer to Plattenhardt that May relieved it, and he met Luise Rau there. In 1834 he became pastor of Cleversulzbach. Poor health and money problems followed, and in 1851 he moved to Stuttgart as teacher of German literature at the Katharinenstift girls' school. He received the title of professor in 1856 and retired in 1866. He separated from his wife Margarethe in 1873 and died in Stuttgart on 4 June 1875.

Mörike belonged to the Swabian school around Ludwig Uhland, Gustav Schwab and Justinus Kerner. His Gedichte of 1838 are mostly lyrical, often humorous and written in simple, apparently everyday German, and his ballad Schön Rotraut became a favourite. His first published work was the novel Maler Nolten (1832), the life of a painter. The novella Mozart auf der Reise nach Prag, a humorous look at the problems of artists in a world uncongenial to art, is often cited as his finest achievement. He also wrote the fairy tale Das Stuttgarter Hutzelmännlein (1855) and translated Anacreon and Theocritus into German.

Many poems were set to music by Hugo Wolf, and Hugo Distler composed 48 settings in his Mörike-Chorliederbuch. Several became established folk songs. The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein recommended him to Bertrand Russell as a great poet whose beauty was closely related to Goethe's.
eduard-shevardnadze: Eduard Shevardnadze was born on 25 January 1928 in Mamati, in the Transcaucasian SFSR. His father, Ambrose, was a teacher and a devoted communist and party official. In 1937, during the Great Purge, his father was arrested but later released because an NKVD officer who had been his pupil intervened. In 1948 Eduard joined the Georgian Communist Party and the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, and rose through the Georgian Komsomol to become its First Secretary, meeting Mikhail Gorbachev in those years. He was demoted in 1961 after offending a senior official.

After two years out of the public eye he returned as First Secretary of a Tbilisi city district and charged the Tbilisi First Secretary with corruption. He became head of the Georgian interior ministry, and appointed First Secretary of the Georgian Communist Party in 1972, he was tasked with suppressing black-market capitalism. Georgia grew economically while the Soviet Union stagnated, and his Abasha experiment of 1973, returning agricultural decisions to the local level, became the model for nationwide agricultural organisations set up by decree in 1982.

Gorbachev appointed him foreign minister in 1985. Shevardnadze advocated glasnost and perestroika, negotiated nuclear arms treaties with the United States, helped to end the war in Afghanistan, allowed the reunification of Germany and withdrew Soviet forces from Eastern Europe. He resigned in December 1990, saying that dictatorship was coming, and returned briefly in November 1991 before resigning with Gorbachev the following month.

Zviad Gamsakhurdia, Georgia's first president, was deposed in a coup in January 1992, and the Military Council asked Shevardnadze to lead the country. He became Chairperson of the State Council in March 1992 and was elected president in 1995 with 70 per cent of the vote, winning a second term in April 2000 in an election marred by accusations of vote-rigging. War in Abkhazia broke out in August 1992 and Georgia lost it; the Sochi agreement ended hostilities in South Ossetia, though Georgia lost effective control of much of that territory.

He won the civil war of 1993 against Gamsakhurdia's supporters with substantial help from Russia, and Georgia joined the Council of Europe in 1999. Allegations of fraud in the election of 2 November 2003 led to protests known as the Rose Revolution, and he agreed to resign. He died on 7 July 2014.
eduardo-frei-montalva: Eduardo Frei Montalva was born in Santiago on 16 January 1911, the son of Eduard Frei Schlinz, an immigrant born in Feldkirch, Austria, and Victoria Montalva Martínez. The family moved to Lontué in 1914, where his father worked as an accountant at a winery, and returned to Santiago in 1919. He graduated as a lawyer in 1933 and married María Ruiz-Tagle, with whom he had seven children. His eldest son, Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle, was president of Chile from 1994 to 2000.

He began in the Conservative Party but in 1938 was among the young men who founded the Falange Nacional. He was minister of Public Works in 1945 and in 1949 was elected senator for Atacama and Coquimbo. On 27 July 1957 the Falange became the Christian Democratic Party, and he was its undisputed leader. He stood for president in 1958 and came third. He ran again in 1964 under the slogan Revolución en Libertad and defeated the Socialist Salvador Allende, taking 56 per cent of the vote against 39.

Frei took office on 4 November 1964. His main projects were Promoción Popular, agrarian reform, education reform and neighbourhood associations. Total school enrolment rose by 46 per cent between 1964 and 1970, and about 250,000 houses were built, mostly for the poor. An agrarian reform law signed in July 1967 made all farms of more than eighty basic hectares liable to expropriation, and expropriated estates became asentamientos run jointly by the state and the peasants who had lived on them. Rural unionisation accelerated, and in 1966 pacts on Chilean copper were signed.

Eight workers were killed at the El Salvador mine and eleven squatters in the Massacre of Puerto Montt, for which his interior minister Edmundo Pérez Zujovic was politically blamed. On 21 October 1969 General Roberto Viaux led the brief, non-violent Tacnazo demonstration of an artillery regiment. Frei left office on 4 November 1970 and handed the presidency to Allende.

Frei became convinced that Allende's government pursued a totalitarian project, and in 1973 he was elected senator for Santiago and President of the Senate, leading the opposition. After the coup of 11 September 1973 his party supported the armed forces' intervention, and in November he wrote a letter endorsing it. He later became an opponent of Augusto Pinochet's military government and in 1981 led a rally against the extension of Pinochet's presidency. He died in Santiago on 22 January 1982 after surgery, and was buried in the Cementerio General.
edvard-benes: Edvard Beneš was born on 28 May 1884 in Kožlany, Bohemia, the youngest son and tenth child of a peasant family. He attended grammar school in the Vinohrady district of Prague and studied at the Sorbonne, receiving his doctorate of law at Dijon in 1908. He became a lecturer in sociology at Charles University in 1912. During the First World War he was one of the leading organisers of Czechoslovak independence from abroad. He went into exile in Paris in September 1915 and worked for recognition from France and Britain, together with Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and Milan Rastislav Štefánik, who organised the Czechoslovak Legion.

From 1918 to 1935 Beneš was the first and longest-serving foreign minister of Czechoslovakia, holding the post through ten governments, one of which he headed himself as prime minister from 1921 to 1922. He represented the country at the 1919 peace conference in Paris. When Masaryk retired in 1935 Beneš became president. During the Sudeten crisis of 1938 he rejected the demands of Konrad Henlein's Karlsbad programme and offered a plan for 20 cantons with substantial autonomy, which Henlein refused. He was unwilling to fight Germany alone. After the Munich Agreement he went into exile in London on 22 October 1938.

In exile Beneš organised the Czechoslovak National Liberation Committee in October 1939, which declared itself the provisional government. In 1942 he persuaded the British Foreign Office to revoke the Munich Agreement. He had decided that the Sudeten Germans were collectively guilty of treason and that they should be expelled, and the Košice programme of April 1945 provided for the expulsion of the Germans and of the Hungarians in Slovakia. After returning, he was elected president again on 19 June 1946.

Beneš presided over a National Front coalition led by the Communist Klement Gottwald. The Communists won 38 per cent in the elections of May 1946. On 21 February 1948 twelve non-Communist ministers resigned over the Communist packing of the police, expecting Beneš to side with them. He hesitated, while Gottwald threatened a general strike, and a Communist-dominated government was formed. Beneš had been in poor health since a minor stroke in 1945 and suffered two more in 1947. He died at his villa in Sezimovo Ústí on 3 September 1948, seven months after the coup. Assessments of his character and policy remain controversial.
edvard-grieg: Edvard Hagerup Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in Bergen. His father, Alexander Grieg, was a merchant and the British vice-consul in Bergen, and his mother, Gesine Hagerup, was a music teacher who taught him the piano from the age of six. The family name, originally spelled Greig, is associated with the Scottish Clan Gregor. In 1858 the violinist Ole Bull, a family friend, recognized the fifteen-year-old's talent and persuaded his parents to send him to the Leipzig Conservatory. Grieg disliked its discipline. In the spring of 1860 he survived pleurisy and tuberculosis, and his health was impaired for life by a destroyed left lung.

Grieg made his debut as a concert pianist in Karlshamn, Sweden, in 1861. From 1863 he spent three years in Copenhagen, where he met Niels Gade and Rikard Nordraak, composer of the Norwegian national anthem; he wrote a funeral march for Nordraak, who died in 1866. On 11 June 1867 he married his first cousin Nina Hagerup, a lyric soprano. In the summer of 1868 he wrote his Piano Concerto in A minor, premiered in Copenhagen on 3 April 1869. Franz Liszt, who had written a testimonial for him, met him in Rome in 1870 and sight-read the concerto from the manuscript. He was music director of the Bergen orchestra Harmonien from 1880 to 1882.

Grieg wrote the incidental music for Henrik Ibsen's play Peer Gynt at the author's request, and it became familiar as two orchestral suites; it includes Morning Mood and In the Hall of the Mountain King, of which he wrote in 1874 that it reeked of exaggerated Norwegian nationalism. He also wrote the Holberg Suite, three violin sonatas, a cello sonata, songs to poems by Heine, Goethe, Ibsen and Hans Christian Andersen, and sixty-six Lyric Pieces for piano in ten books. His use of Norwegian folk music brought the music of Norway to fame, as Sibelius's did in Finland.

He died of heart failure at the Municipal Hospital in Bergen on 4 September 1907, and 30,000 to 40,000 people lined the streets for his funeral. His ashes were entombed in a mountain crypt near his house, Troldhaugen, now the Edvard Grieg Museum.
edvard-munch: Edvard Munch was born on 12 December 1863 in a farmhouse in the village of Ådalsbruk in Løten, to Laura Catherine Bjølstad and Christian Munch, a doctor and medical officer. His sister Laura Catherine suffered mental illness and was confined in an institution, and Munch often expressed a fear of inheriting insanity. In 1879 he enrolled at a technical college, but he left it the next year, to his father's disappointment, determined to become a painter. He studied at the Royal School of Art and Design in Kristiania and joined the Kristiania Bohème, a circle of writers and artists, where the painter Christian Krohg gave him instruction and support.

The nihilist Hans Jæger urged Munch to paint his own emotional and psychological state, and from this emerged his distinctive style. He arrived in Paris during the Exposition Universelle of 1889 and learned from the colour of Paul Gauguin, Vincent van Gogh and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec. In 1892 an exhibition in Berlin caused such controversy, called the Munch Affair, that it closed after a week. There he met August Strindberg, and in December 1893 he showed the paintings that began the cycle he later called the Frieze of Life, with motifs such as Madonna, Anxiety and Death in the Sickroom.

The Scream exists in four versions, two pastels and two paintings, made between 1893 and 1910, as well as lithographs. In autumn 1908, after heavy drinking and brawling, he suffered a breakdown and spent eight months in a clinic. His work afterwards became more colourful, and in 1916 he completed eleven paintings for the Aula of the University of Oslo.

Munch spent most of his last two decades in solitude at his estate at Ekely, in Oslo. He died there on 23 January 1944, aged 80, of a respiratory illness. His works had been banned in Nazi-occupied Europe, but most survived the war. He bequeathed his remaining works to the city of Oslo, which opened the Munch Museum at Tøyen in 1963; it holds about 1,100 paintings, 4,500 drawings and 18,000 prints.
edward-augustus-freeman: Freeman was born on 2 August 1823 at Metchley Abbey in Harborne, Warwickshire, and his parents named him after the month of his birth. Both died in November 1824, and he was raised by his paternal grandmother at Weston-super-Mare. He won a scholarship to Trinity College, Oxford, became a fellow of the college in 1845 and, though drawn to the High Church movement, gave up the idea of taking orders. In 1847 he married Eleanor Gutch, daughter of his former tutor, and in 1860 settled at Somerleaze, near Wells.

His first book was a History of Architecture (1849), and his essay on window tracery of 1851 proposed the terms Flowing and Flamboyant. He published 239 distinct works, among them William Rufus (1882) and the unfinished History of Sicily, on whose fourth volume he worked with his son-in-law Arthur Evans. He insisted on the unity of history and on the right use of original authorities, though he did not use manuscripts, and he often said that "History is past politics and politics present history." The saying marks the limit of his work, which was almost wholly political history and dealt little with other sides of a nation's life.

A follower of Gladstone, he stood unsuccessfully for Mid-Somerset in 1868 and took a prominent part in the agitation over the Bulgarian atrocities of the April Uprising. He expressed an antipathy for the Turks and sympathy for the subject nations of eastern Europe, and he and Evans were activists in the uprising in Bosnia and Herzegovina. His private letters show disdain for Jews: he called Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli "the dirty Jew".

From 1886 ill health kept him abroad for much of the time. On a visit to Spain in 1892 he fell ill with smallpox and died at Alicante on 16 March, where he was buried in the Protestant cemetery under a Latin inscription by Evans. His library of some 6,500 volumes went to Owens College, Manchester, and most of his papers, including 6,200 architectural sketches of European churches, are in the University of Manchester Library.
edward-balliol: Edward Balliol was the eldest son of John Balliol and Isabella de Warenne. In 1295, when his father negotiated an alliance with France, Edward was betrothed to Joan of Valois, eldest daughter of Charles, Count of Valois, but the betrothal was cancelled when John resigned the Scottish throne in 1296. After his father's abdication Edward was a prisoner in the Tower of London until 1299, when he was released into the custody of his grandfather John de Warenne, 6th Earl of Surrey. He possibly married Margaret of Taranto around 1331; if so, the marriage was childless and had been annulled by 1332.

After the death of Robert I in June 1329 left the six-year-old David II as king, Balliol was recruited by the disinherited, men whose Scottish lands and titles Robert had confiscated after the Battle of Bannockburn. With covert support from Edward III of England, they invaded in 1332, and Balliol's force defeated the regent, the Earl of Mar, at the Battle of Dupplin Moor on 11 August 1332. He was crowned at Scone on 24 September, but three months later a surprise attack by nobles loyal to David II at the Battle of Annan drove him back to England.

In 1333 Edward III openly declared for Balliol, and they returned with an English army, captured Berwick and defeated the Scots at the Battle of Halidon Hill. Under the Treaty of Newcastle in 1334 Balliol ceded Lothian to Edward and paid homage to him. His position stayed insecure because of quarrels among his supporters and fighting by pro-Bruce forces. A pro-Balliol army under Strathbogie was defeated at the Battle of Culblean on 30 November 1335, which was the effective end of his attempt, and by 1338 the tide had turned against him. After David II's defeat at the Battle of Neville's Cross in 1346 he raised an insurrection in Galloway, but held only part of it, and his power there diminished until 1355.

On 20 January 1356 Balliol surrendered his claim to the Scottish throne to Edward III in exchange for an English pension of 2,000 pounds a year. He spent the rest of his life near Yorkshire and died childless in January 1364 at Wheatley, Doncaster. The location of his grave has been speculated to lie under a Doncaster post office.
edward-braddock: Braddock was born in London in January 1695, the son of Major-General Edward Braddock of the 2nd Regiment of Foot Guards. He was commissioned ensign in his father's regiment on 11 October 1710, at the age of 15, and became lieutenant of its grenadier company in 1716. On 26 May 1718 he fought a duel in Hyde Park with a colonel named Waller. Promotion was slow: he became captain only in 1736, at 41, major in 1743 and lieutenant colonel on 21 November 1745.

In the War of the Austrian Succession he took part in the siege of Bergen op Zoom in 1747. He was made colonel of the 14th Regiment of Foot on 17 February 1753 and major general the next year. He landed at Hampton, Virginia, with two infantry regiments on 20 February 1755, and at the Congress of Alexandria on 14 April colonial governors persuaded him to attack the French on four fronts: Fort Niagara, Fort Saint-Frédéric at Crown Point under William Johnson, Fort Beausejour under Colonel Robert Monckton, and Fort Duquesne under Braddock himself.

Delayed by confusion and by supplies the colonies had promised and not delivered, he had to cut a road for his artillery. Benjamin Franklin's autobiography describes helping him gather wagons and warning him of ambush. After crossing the Monongahela, his column met a French and Indian force from Fort Duquesne that worked down its flanks and caught it in crossfire. The causes of the defeat are still debated; one likely factor was that he underestimated how quickly his enemies could react and how fast his own men's discipline could fail.

Shot through the chest, he was carried from the field by Washington and Colonel Nicholas Meriwether and died on 13 July. He left Washington his sash and two pistols, and the sash is kept at Mount Vernon. He was buried in the road near Great Meadows, with wagons driven over the grave to hide it. Remains believed to be his were found in 1804 and reburied, and the Coldstream Guards raised a monument in 1913. Braddock in Pennsylvania and several roads bear his name.
edward-bruce: Edward was one of five sons of Robert de Brus and Marjorie, Countess of Carrick, though the order is uncertain. His date of birth is unknown, but he was old enough to fight in 1307. The Irish medievalist Seán Duffy suggests that he was fostered in Ireland as a child, probably by the O'Neills of Ulster. He fought alongside Robert throughout the struggle for the Scottish throne. His younger brothers Nigel, Thomas and Alexander were captured and executed by the English, but Edward survived, and with Robert's daughter Marjorie captive he was apparently heir.

After the Battle of Barra in May 1308 he laid waste to the Earldom of Buchan, the power base of the Comyns, for several months. He recaptured Rutherglen Castle in 1313 and commanded a Scottish schiltrom at Bannockburn on 23 and 24 June 1314. He became Earl of Carrick between 1309 and 1313.

In 1315 Domhnall mac Briain Ó Néill, king of Tír Eóghain, and about twelve allies asked Scotland for help against Anglo-Irish incursions. The Bruce brothers agreed on condition that the Irish accept Edward as king of Ireland. Edward landed near Larne on 26 May 1315 with a fleet carrying an estimated 6,000 men or more. The Irish annals say the northern lords took him as king, though he never received more than nominal recognition from the more powerful Irish kings. He nonetheless ruled much of eastern and mid-Ulster.

His army destroyed Castle Roche and on 29 June attacked Dundalk, whose Anglo-Irish and Gaelic inhabitants were massacred alike. Edward avoided battle with the armies of Richard Óg de Burgh and Edmund Butler, and by September de Burgh had been defeated at Connor. In December Edward defeated Roger Mortimer at the Battle of Kells. By 1317 famine had stricken most of the country, making it hard to feed his men. Ó Néill and his allies sent a remonstrance to Pope John XXII in 1317, but the papacy did not recognise Edward's claim.

In the late summer of 1318 Sir John de Bermingham marched against Edward. On 14 October 1318 the Scots-Irish army was badly defeated at the Battle of Faughart. Edward was killed, his body quartered and sent to various towns in Ireland, and his head delivered to Edward II. The Annals of Ulster call him the destroyer of Ireland, both Foreigners and Gaels, and say his time brought death and loss of people throughout Ireland for three and a half years. His illegitimate son Alexander Bruce later inherited the earldom.
edward-elgar: Elgar's father, William Henry Elgar, was raised in Dover and apprenticed to a London music publisher. In 1841 he moved to Worcester, where he worked as a piano tuner and kept a shop selling sheet music and instruments. Edward was the fourth of seven children. His mother, Ann Elgar, had converted to Roman Catholicism shortly before his birth, and he was baptised and brought up in that faith, to his father's disapproval. William Elgar was a violinist of professional standard and organist of St George's Roman Catholic Church, Worcester, from 1846 to 1885.

At 29 Elgar took a pupil, Caroline Alice Roberts, eight years his senior. They married on 8 May 1889 at Brompton Oratory. Her family was horrified, and she was disinherited. She acted as his business manager and social secretary, and their daughter Carice Irene was born on 14 August 1890.

During the 1890s Elgar built a reputation with works for the choral festivals of the English Midlands, among them The Black Knight (1892), King Olaf (1896) and Caractacus (1898), and gained a long-standing publisher in Novello and Co. For the Birmingham Triennial Music Festival of 1900 he set Cardinal John Henry Newman's poem The Dream of Gerontius. Hans Richter conducted the premiere, in which a poorly prepared chorus sang badly. Performances in Düsseldorf in 1901 and 1902 drew an enthusiastic German press, and Richard Strauss proposed a toast to him in his presence.

Some of the Anglican establishment disliked the Catholic text. Charles Villiers Stanford complained that it stank of incense, and the dean of Gloucester banned it from his cathedral in 1901. Elgar was knighted in 1904, appointed to the Order of Merit in June 1911 and created a baronet in 1931. Alice Elgar died of lung cancer on 7 April 1920.

Elgar was contemptuous of folk music. The continental composers who most influenced him were Handel, Dvořák and, to some degree, Brahms, and his orchestration owes much to French composers, above all Delibes. His best-known works were written between 1899 and 1920, most of them orchestral, among them Cockaigne (1900–1901) and the Introduction and Allegro for Strings (1905). He completed no large-scale works after the Cello Concerto.

Between 1914 and 1925 he conducted acoustic recordings of his music, and after the moving-coil microphone arrived in 1923 he re-recorded most of his major orchestral works. His reputation fell after the First World War and revived significantly from the 1960s.
edward-heath: Edward Richard George Heath was born at Broadstairs, Kent, on 9 July 1916, the son of William George Heath, a carpenter who later became a builder and a small businessman, and Edith Anne Heath, a lady's maid. He was educated at Chatham House Grammar School in Ramsgate and in 1935 went up to Balliol College, Oxford, with a county scholarship. A talented musician, he won the college's organ scholarship and graduated in philosophy, politics and economics in 1939. In 1941 he was commissioned in the Royal Artillery, serving with anti-aircraft guns, and he became a civil servant after the war.

Heath was elected Member of Parliament for Bexley in 1950. As Chief Whip from 1955 he kept out of the Suez controversy, and his report on Conservative opinion helped secure the premiership for Harold Macmillan in 1957. He served as Minister of Labour and as President of the Board of Trade. In July 1965 he unexpectedly won the leadership of the Conservative Party, with 150 votes to Reginald Maudling's 133 and Enoch Powell's 15, and he remained leader after the defeat of 1966. In 1970 his party won 330 seats to Labour's 287.

As prime minister he completed the decimalisation of British coinage and reformed local government in 1972. Unemployment passed one million in January 1972, and Heath reversed course in what became known as the Barber Boom. The Industrial Relations Act 1971 set up a special court whose imprisonment of striking dockworkers was a public relations disaster. His government took the United Kingdom into Europe on 1 January 1973. During the Troubles he held unofficial talks with the Provisional IRA in July 1972, which failed, and later pressed for a settlement with parties committed to nonviolence.

Heath called an election for 28 February 1974 under the slogan Who governs Britain? The result gave the Conservatives the most votes but Labour slightly more seats. Talks with Jeremy Thorpe's Liberal Party failed and Heath resigned on 4 March. After a second defeat in October 1974 he lost the leadership to Margaret Thatcher in February 1975.

Heath campaigned with Thatcher for the yes side in the 1975 referendum on the European Economic Community and served on the Brandt Commission. He later opposed Thatcherism. A keen yachtsman, he won the 1969 Sydney to Hobart race and captained Britain's winning Admiral's Cup team in 1971 while prime minister. He was also an organist, pianist and conductor. He never married, published The Course of My Life in 1998 and left the Commons in 2001. He died on 17 July 2005, aged 89.
edward-hyde-1st-earl-of-clarendon: Edward Hyde was born on 18 February 1609 at Dinton in Wiltshire, the third son of Henry Hyde and Mary Langford. His father and two uncles were lawyers. He entered Magdalen Hall, Oxford, in 1622, and the death of his elder brothers made him his father's heir. He was called to the bar on 22 November 1633 and married twice, first Anne Ayliffe, who died of smallpox in 1629, then Frances Aylesbury in 1634. He belonged to the Great Tew Circle of intellectuals around his best friend Lord Falkland.

Elected to the Long Parliament in November 1640, Hyde was at first a moderate critic of Charles I but grew more supportive as the King accepted reforming bills. He joined the King at York shortly before the First English Civil War began in August 1642. After the royalist defeat he fled to Jersey in 1646, and he kept out of the Second English Civil War because it involved alliances with the Scots. He began writing his History of the Rebellion in this period and served Charles II in exile as a diplomat in Paris and Madrid.

After the Restoration of 1660 he was effectively chief minister, helped draft the Declaration of Breda and worked for mercy to the King's enemies except the regicides, largely achieved in the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion. The Clarendon Code is named after him, though he disapproved of much of it. His daughter Anne married the King's brother James, Duke of York, which he found an unwelcome shock. In 1663 he was one of eight Lords Proprietor of Carolina.

Ill health, enemies at court and the Second Anglo-Dutch War brought him down. The Plague, the Great Fire and the Dutch raid on the Medway in June 1667 were the final blow, and he was removed from office though he had opposed the war. The Commons impeached him, and he fled to France in November 1667, without the King's defence. In exile he expanded his History, the classic account of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, and wrote an autobiography and a critique of Hobbes's Leviathan. He died at Rouen on 9 December 1674 and was buried in Westminster Abbey on 4 January 1675.
edward-i-of-england: Edward was born on the night of 17 to 18 June 1239 at the Palace of Westminster, the eldest son of Henry III and Eleanor of Provence. In 1259 he briefly sided with the baronial reformers behind the Provisions of Oxford, but he reconciled with his father and stayed loyal in the Second Barons' War. After the Battle of Lewes in 1264 he was held hostage by the rebels, escaped, and defeated their leader Simon de Montfort at the Battle of Evesham in 1265. In 1270 he sailed on the Ninth Crusade, and he was on his way home in 1272 when he heard of his father's death. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey after reaching England in 1274.

Edward spent much of his reign reforming royal administration and the law. In 1274 he named Robert Burnell chancellor, replaced most local officials and ordered an inquest into abuses by royal officers. A series of statutes regulated criminal and property law, and the coinage, in poor state by 1279, was overhauled. After the Statute of the Jewry of 1275 and the arrest of the heads of Jewish households in 1279, about 300 people were executed, and in 1290 all Jews were expelled from England.

In Wales, Edward conquered the principality of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in the war of 1282 to 1283, then built castles and towns and settled them with English people. The death of Margaret, the child heir to the Scottish throne, in 1290 left a succession dispute known as the Great Cause. Edward claimed feudal suzerainty over Scotland and invaded; William Wallace and Andrew de Moray defeated an English army at Stirling Bridge in 1297, and Edward beat Wallace at Falkirk on 22 July 1298. The wars required heavy taxation, which brought opposition in England.

In 1307 Robert Bruce renewed resistance in Scotland and defeated Valence at Loudoun Hill. Edward marched north, fell ill with dysentery and died on 7 July 1307 at Burgh by Sands, near the border, leaving his son Edward II a war with Scotland and financial burdens.

Historians are divided about him. He is credited with restoring royal authority and making Parliament a permanent institution through which taxes could be raised and the law reformed. He is condemned for vindictiveness and untrustworthiness towards Wales and Scotland and for the expulsion of the Jews. In the 17th century the lawyer Edward Coke called him the English Justinian.
edward-ii-of-england: Edward was born at Caernarfon Castle in north Wales on 25 April 1284, less than a year after his father Edward I conquered the region, and is sometimes called Edward of Caernarfon. He became heir after the death of his older brother Alphonso. He was probably given a religious education by Dominican friars and trained in riding and military skills by Guy Ferre. He was betrothed to Isabella, daughter of Philip IV of France, in the hope of ending the dispute over Gascony. Piers Gaveston joined his household in 1300.

Edward I died on 7 July 1307, and Edward was proclaimed king on 20 July. He recalled Gaveston from exile and made him Earl of Cornwall. The barons saw Gaveston as arrogant, and a chronicler complained of two kings reigning in one kingdom. They forced the Ordinances of 1311 on the king, and Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster, led the nobles who seized and executed Gaveston in 1312. In 1314 Edward led an army of 15,000 to 20,000 to relieve Stirling Castle and was beaten by Robert the Bruce at Bannockburn.

Hugh Despenser the Younger became the king's chamberlain and closest adviser, and in 1321 civil war broke out when Lancaster and many barons turned against the Despensers. Edward put down the rebellion, executed Lancaster and punished the so-called Contrariants through special courts in which the accused could not speak in their own defence. A parliament at York in May 1322 revoked the Ordinances. Isabella, sent to France to negotiate in 1325, refused to return and with the exiled Roger Mortimer invaded England in 1326. Edward's regime collapsed, and he was captured in Wales.

Edward was forced to give up his crown in January 1327 in favour of his son Edward III. He was held at Berkeley Castle and died there on 21 September 1327, probably murdered on the orders of the new regime. A story that he was killed with a red-hot iron spread after Mortimer's execution in 1330, but most historians now dismiss it. He was buried at Gloucester Abbey on 20 December 1327.

Contemporary chroniclers were highly critical of him. The historian Michael Prestwich calls him lazy and incompetent, while Pierre Chaplais argues that he was a reluctant king who preferred to rule through a powerful deputy such as Gaveston or Despenser. Christopher Marlowe's play Edward II, first performed about 1592, focuses on his relationship with Gaveston, the precise nature of which is uncertain.
edward-iii-of-england: Edward was born at Windsor Castle on 13 November 1312, and was created Earl of Chester when only twelve days old. His father, Edward II, had alienated the nobility by favouring a few courtiers such as Piers Gaveston and Hugh Despenser the Younger, and his Scottish campaigns had failed. Edward II's wife, Isabella of France, was publicly humiliated in September 1324 when she was declared an enemy alien, and she and her lover Roger Mortimer deposed the king. Edward was crowned at fourteen. Under the tutelage of Richard de Bury, Bishop of Durham, he learned to read and write French and Latin.

Mortimer became the de facto ruler and made himself unpopular, not least through the defeat at Stanhope Park and the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton of 1328. At seventeen the king acted against him and began his personal reign. He then backed Edward Balliol's claim in Scotland, defeated a large relieving army at Halidon Hill and reinstated Balliol, but forces loyal to David II regained control, and in 1338 he agreed a truce.

In 1337 Philip VI of France confiscated the Duchy of Aquitaine and the county of Ponthieu, and Edward responded by claiming the French crown as grandson of Philip IV. This began the Hundred Years' War. His early policy of buying alliances with continental rulers cost too much and achieved little. Victories at Crécy and Poitiers led to the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360, under which England made territorial gains and Edward renounced his claim to the French throne.

The middle years saw much legislation, including the Statute of Labourers of 1351, which fixed wages at their pre-plague level after the Black Death and eventually failed. Parliament developed into two houses, and the Good Parliament of 1376 created the procedure of impeachment and the office of the Speaker. His later years were marked by inertia and military failure, and by 1375 England had lost most of his conquests except the Pale of Calais.

Edward III played a limited part in government after about 1375. He died of a stroke at Sheen on 21 June 1377, after outliving his eldest son, Edward the Black Prince. He and Philippa of Hainault had seven sons and five daughters, and his endowment of his sons as dukes created dynasties that later bedevilled the Lancastrian line. Contemporaries admired him; Jean Froissart wrote that his like had not been seen since King Arthur. Nineteenth-century Whig historians accused him of neglecting his duties, but modern historians credit him with significant achievements.
edward-iv-of-england: Edward was born on 28 April 1442 at Rouen, the eldest surviving son of Richard, 3rd Duke of York, and Cecily Neville, and was known as the Earl of March until his father's death. Both parents descended from Edward III. By seventeen he was a political and military leader in his own right, and after the Yorkist defeat at Ludford Bridge in 1459 he withdrew to Calais with the Earls of Salisbury and Warwick. When his father was killed at Wakefield on 30 December 1460, Edward became head of the Yorkist party.

On 2 February 1461 Edward won the Battle of Mortimer's Cross, which was preceded by a parhelion, or three suns, that he took as his emblem, the sun in splendour. He was hastily appointed king in London, and the Yorkists won the Battle of Towton on 29 March in a snowstorm; estimates of the dead range from 9,000 to 20,000. He was crowned on 28 June 1461. His secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville in 1464 angered Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick.

In July 1469 Warwick and Edward's brother George, Duke of Clarence, defeated a royal army at Edgecote Moor and held the king at Middleham Castle, but found little support and released him in September. After the Lincolnshire Rebellion of March 1470 they fled to France, where Louis XI brought Warwick together with Margaret of Anjou. Warwick landed on 9 September 1470 to restore Henry VI, and Edward took refuge in Flanders. He landed near Hull in March 1471, entered London unopposed, and won the battles of Barnet on 14 April, where Warwick was killed, and Tewkesbury on 4 May. Henry VI died within days, and it is generally assumed that he was killed on Edward's orders.

Clarence was executed in the Tower on 18 February 1478. In 1475 Edward invaded France but agreed the Treaty of Picquigny with Louis XI, receiving 75,000 crowns at once and a yearly pension of 50,000 crowns. Edward fell ill at Easter 1483, added a codicil naming his brother Richard, Duke of Gloucester, as Protector, and died on 9 April 1483; the cause is uncertain.

His twelve-year-old son Edward V was never crowned, and Gloucester became Richard III in July. The biographer Charles Ross concluded that Edward was the only English king since 1066 in active possession of his throne who failed to secure the safe succession of his son.
edward-james-roye: Roye was born free on 3 February 1815 in Newark, Ohio, the son of John and Nancy Roye, formerly enslaved African Americans who had moved there from Kentucky and were reportedly of Igbo origin. His father ran a ferry across the Wabash River at Terre Haute, Indiana, and owned property in three towns, so the son could attend Ohio University. After his father's death in 1836 he moved to Terre Haute and ran the African-American community's largest barbershop.

Drawn by the American Colonization Society's promotion of emigration, Roye moved to Liberia with his family in 1846, reportedly bringing $1,000 of capital. Within three years he was in politics, serving as speaker of the House of Representatives in 1849–1850, as Secretary of the Treasury and later as Chief Justice from 1865 to 1868; he lost the presidential election of 1855. In 1857 he bought the brig Eusebia to trade camwood, palm oil and ivory between Monrovia and New York City, and by 1870 his fortune was put at $200,000.

Inaugurated on 3 January 1870, he was the first member of the True Whig Party to become president. Liberia's imports cost far more than its exports of coffee, rice, palm oil, sugarcane and timber earned. Roye sought to lengthen the presidential term from two years to four; a referendum passed the change, but the Republican Party disputed the result and held an election in May 1871, which Roye boycotted and which its candidate Joseph Jenkins Roberts claimed unopposed. The speaker William Spencer Anderson negotiated a loan of $500,000 from British financiers, on terms worse than the legislature had approved.

News of the loan set off riots in Monrovia, and Roye was removed on 26 October 1871, in what some allies called a coup d'état. Charged with treason, he was convicted on 10 February 1872 and sentenced to hang. He died a few days later in uncertain circumstances: a 1926 history says a mob beat him to death after an escape attempt, while contemporary despatches from the U.S. minister in Liberia say he drowned swimming for an English ship. Royesville is named after him, his portrait appeared on the five-dollar note, and the True Whig Party's headquarters was called the Edward J. Roye Building.
edward-lhuyd: Lhuyd was born in 1660 at Loppington in Shropshire, the illegitimate son of Edward Llwyd of Llanforda, near Oswestry, and Bridget Pryse of Llansantffraid in Cardiganshire. His family belonged to the gentry of south-west Wales and was well established but not wealthy; his father experimented with agriculture and industry in the spirit of the new science. Lhuyd attended and later taught at Oswestry Grammar School, and in 1682 went up to Jesus College, Oxford, but left before graduating. His surname is an archaic spelling of Lloyd or Llwyd, from the Welsh for grey.

In 1684 he became assistant to Robert Plot, Keeper of the Ashmolean Museum, then on Broad Street. A visit to Snowdonia in 1688 let him list the region's flora for John Ray's Synopsis Methodica Stirpium Britannicarum. In 1699, with funding from his friend Isaac Newton, he published the Lithophylacii Britannici Ichnographia, the first catalogue of fossils. It includes the first written record of a trilobite, which he took for the skeleton of a flat fish, and he gave the first scientific description of what is now recognised as a dinosaur tooth, Rutellum impicatum.

After 1697 he visited every county in Wales and then Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall, Brittany and the Isle of Man. Invited by a group of Cornish scholars led by John Keigwin of Mousehole, he studied Early Modern Cornish and published a paper on it in 1702. In the first volume of his Archæologia Britannica, prepared with the help of Moses Williams, he grouped Breton, Cornish and Welsh as one family and Irish, Manx and Scottish Gaelic as another. He derived the first from Gaulish and the second from Celtiberian, and called their speakers Celts. Oxford gave him an honorary MA in 1701, and the Royal Society elected him a fellow in 1708.
