Asthma, which he developed on his travels, led to his death from pleurisy in his room at the Ashmolean on 30 June 1709. He was buried in the Welsh aisle of St Michael at the Northgate. From the 18th century the peoples he had grouped together were increasingly known as Celts. Cymdeithas Edward Llwyd, the National Naturalists' Society of Wales, bears his name, and a bronze bust by John Meirion Morris was unveiled in Aberystwyth in 2001.
edward-said: Edward Said was born on 1 November 1935 into a Protestant Palestinian Christian family in Jerusalem, then under the British Mandate. His father, Wadie Said, a businessman, had served in the American Expeditionary Forces in the First World War and so earned United States citizenship for himself and his family. His mother, Hilda, was half Palestinian and half Lebanese and was raised in Nazareth. His father had founded a stationery business in Cairo in 1919. After the war of 1948 the family moved to Egypt, where Said attended Victoria College, and then to the United States, where he attended Northfield Mount Hermon School. He graduated from Princeton University in 1957 and received a doctorate in English literature from Harvard in 1964.

Said's first book, Joseph Conrad and the Fiction of Autobiography (1966), grew out of his doctoral dissertation, and Beginnings: Intention and Method (1974) examined the theoretical bases of literary criticism. His study Orientalism (1978) argued that much Western study of Islamic civilisation served the self-affirmation of European identity rather than objective scholarship, and that Oriental studies thereby worked as a method of cultural discrimination and imperial domination. It proposed a persistent Eurocentric prejudice against Arabo-Islamic peoples, rooted in a long tradition of romanticised and false images of the Orient. Said wrote that such images had served as implicit justification for the colonial ambitions of the European powers and the United States.

He later wrote The World, the Text, and the Critic (1983), Culture and Imperialism (1993) and the Reith Lectures of 1993, published as Representations of the Intellectual. After the Six-Day War of 1967 he became a public intellectual by challenging how American news media explained the Arab-Israeli conflict, and he wrote The Question of Palestine (1979). In the essay Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims he argued for the legitimacy of the claim to a Jewish homeland while asserting the Palestinian people's equal right of self-determination.

Said was also an accomplished pianist and a music critic for The Nation, and wrote four books on music. With the conductor Daniel Barenboim he founded the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra in 1999, made up of young Israeli, Palestinian and Arab musicians, and the Barenboim-Said Foundation in Seville. He lectured at more than 200 universities and received about twenty honorary degrees. He had struggled for twelve years with chronic lymphocytic leukemia when he died in 2003, and was buried in the Protestant Cemetery in Broumana in Lebanon. Birzeit University renamed its music school the Edward Said National Conservatory of Music in 2004, and Columbia University has an Edward Said Chair.
edward-seaga: Edward Philip George Seaga was born on 28 May 1930 in Boston, Massachusetts. His father, Philip George Seaga, was of Lebanese Jamaican descent and had gone to the United States hoping to profit from the prosperity of the Roaring Twenties, but the Wall Street crash of 1929 ended those hopes. His mother, Erna, was Jamaican of African and Scottish descent. The family returned to Jamaica three months after his birth, and he was baptised in Kingston's Anglican Parish Church on 5 December 1930.

Seaga's research led him to Jamaican popular music. In 1955 he supervised an album of ethnic Jamaican music, and in the late 1950s he set up West Indies Records Limited, which released early recordings by Higgs and Wilson and by Byron Lee and the Dragonaires and became the most successful record company in the West Indies. From 1961 he lived in West Kingston and recorded artists from its music scene. After his election to Parliament in 1962 he sold the company to Byron Lee, and it was renamed Dynamic Sounds.

His political career began in 1959, when Alexander Bustamante, founder of the Jamaica Labour Party, nominated him to the Legislative Council, later the Senate. At 29 he was its youngest appointee. In the Senate he made a widely reported speech about the haves and the have nots. He led the party from 1974 to 2005.

Seaga became prime minister after the general election of 30 October 1980, in which the Labour Party won 51 of the 60 seats against nine for the People's National Party. In 1983 it won again; the opposition boycotted that election, protesting the refusal to update the voter register amid allegations of fraud. He remained in office until February 1989.

His government made agreements with the International Monetary Fund and pursued free-market policies and privatisation; critics argue that austerity and unemployment fell hardest on the working class. A strong anti-communist, he reversed his predecessor's engagement with Cuba and Grenada, cut ties with Cuba soon after winning, formed a close relationship with Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher and sent a small force to support the United States invasion of Grenada in 1983. By then Jamaica was the third largest recipient of United States aid per head, after Egypt and Israel.
The Labour Party lost the 1989 election by 45 seats to 15, and Seaga served again as Leader of the Opposition until January 2005. He died on 28 May 2019, his eighty-ninth birthday.
edward-the-black-prince: Edward of Woodstock was born at Woodstock, Oxfordshire, on 15 June 1330, the eldest son of Edward III of England and Queen Philippa. He was made Duke of Cornwall, the first English dukedom, in 1337, the year his father declared war on France and began the Hundred Years' War, and Prince of Wales in 1343. English contemporaries regarded him as a model of chivalry, while French sources remember him for his brutality. The name Black Prince is first recorded in the 1530s or early 1540s, about 165 years after his death.

In July 1346 Edward sailed with his father, who knighted him at Quettehou, and he commanded the vanguard at the Battle of Crécy. In 1355 he became the king's lieutenant in Gascony and led a chevauchée that sacked Avignonet, Castelnaudary, Carcassonne and Narbonne. In 1356 a second chevauchée ravaged Auvergne, Limousin and Berry, and near Poitiers his forces routed the French army and captured King John II of France. He took the principal part on the English side in negotiating the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360.

On 19 July 1362 his father granted him Aquitaine and Gascony as a principality, but the Lord of Albret and other Gascon nobles did not recognise his suzerainty. In 1367 he defeated Henry of Trastámara at Nájera in support of King Peter of Castile, though Peter never repaid the debt. A hearth tax of 1368 alienated Albret and other nobles, and Charles V of France encouraged the Gascon lords to disaffection.

The death of his eldest son, Edward of Angoulême, in 1371 caused him great grief, and his health continued to deteriorate. He returned to England in January 1371 and resigned the principality in 1372. In 1376 he led the Commons in their attack on the Lancastrian administration. After the Good Parliament he knew he was dying, with fits of dysentery so violent that he sometimes fainted; his illness likely began after Nájera. He died on 8 June 1376 and was buried in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 September. His son Richard II therefore succeeded Edward III. His alternative arms of three ostrich feathers are believed to have inspired the badge of later Princes of Wales.
edward-the-confessor: Edward was the seventh son of Æthelred the Unready and the first by his second wife, Emma of Normandy, and was born between 1003 and 1005 at Islip, Oxfordshire. After Sweyn Forkbeard seized the throne in 1013, Emma fled to Normandy with Edward and his brother Alfred, and in 1016 Cnut became undisputed king. Edward spent about twenty-five years in exile, probably mainly in Normandy. His mother married Cnut in 1017 and favoured her son by Cnut, Harthacnut. In 1036 Alfred was captured by Godwin, Earl of Wessex, and died of his injuries, which is thought to be the source of much of Edward's hatred for Godwin. In 1041 Harthacnut, who had not long to live, invited Edward back to England, probably as his heir.

After Harthacnut died on 8 June 1042, Godwin supported Edward, who was crowned at Winchester on Easter Sunday, 3 April 1043. His position was weak, as he had to keep on terms with the three leading earls, Leofric of Mercia, Godwin and Siward of Northumbria, and had no personal power base. He married Godwin's daughter Edith on 23 January 1045. In 1051 a quarrel over the appointment of the Archbishop of Canterbury and an affray at Dover led to the Godwins' flight, but they returned in 1052 with an army and Edward had to restore them.

From the later 1050s the Godwin brothers controlled nearly all the earldoms, and Edward seems to have withdrawn from active politics. Historians disagree about the reign: some see the decline of royal power, while the biographers Frank Barlow and Peter Rex portray a successful king. He had no children, and historians have long puzzled over his intentions for the succession. Edward died at Westminster on 5 January 1066 and was buried the next day, when Harold Godwinson was crowned.

Edward's major building project was Westminster Abbey, the first Norman Romanesque church in England, consecrated on 28 December 1065; he was too weak to attend. Most historians regard him as an unlikely saint and his canonisation as political. Osbert of Clare, prior of Westminster, campaigned for it, and Pope Alexander III issued the bull on 7 February 1161. Edward was a national saint of England until about 1350, when Edward III preferred Saint George. His shrine in the abbey remains where Henry III placed it on 13 October 1269, the date of his feast.
edward-the-elder: Edward was the elder son of Alfred the Great and Ealhswith, who married in 868. His sister Æthelflæd married Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians. Alfred had taken the title King of the Anglo-Saxons after receiving the submission in London in 886 of all the English not under Danish rule. Edward was an ætheling, a prince eligible for kingship, but his accession was not assured, because his cousin Æthelwold was a son of Alfred's older brother and predecessor Æthelred I.

Alfred died on 26 October 899, and Æthelwold disputed the succession, seizing the estates of Wimborne and Christchurch in Dorset. He then rode to Northumbria, where the Danes accepted him as king, and Edward was crowned on 8 June 900 at Kingston upon Thames. Æthelwold was killed at the Battle of the Holme on 13 December 902, though the Danes held the field. In 910 a Mercian and West Saxon army defeated the Northumbrians at the Battle of Tettenhall, after which they did not go south of the Humber in his reign.

Æthelred of Mercia died in 911, and Edward took control of the Mercian lands around London and Oxford, while Æthelflæd ruled as Lady of the Mercians. With her he conquered the southern Danelaw in East Anglia and the Five Boroughs of Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford. After Æthelflæd died in June 918 her daughter Ælfwynn briefly succeeded her, but in December Edward took her into Wessex and imposed direct rule on Mercia. By the end of the 910s only Northumbria remained under Viking rule.

In 924 Edward faced a Mercian and Welsh revolt at Chester, and after putting it down he died at Farndon in Cheshire on 17 July 924. His eldest son Æthelstan succeeded him, and two younger sons later reigned as Edmund I and Eadred. William of Malmesbury judged him much inferior to his father in letters but incomparably more glorious in the power of his rule. Modern historians largely ignored him until the 1990s, partly because few primary sources survive. He is now seen as having destroyed Viking power in southern England and laid the foundations of a south-centred united English kingdom.
edward-viii: Edward was born on 23 June 1894 at White Lodge, Richmond Park, the eldest son of the Duke and Duchess of York, later George V and Queen Mary. He was baptised Edward Albert Christian George Andrew Patrick David and was known in the family as David. He entered the Royal Naval College, Osborne, in 1907, but when his father became king in 1910 he left the naval course early and went to Magdalen College, Oxford, for which his biographers think him intellectually unprepared. He left after eight terms without a qualification.

He became Prince of Wales on his 16th birthday and was invested at Caernarfon Castle on 13 July 1911, in a pageant devised by David Lloyd George. In 1914 he joined the Grenadier Guards. Lord Kitchener refused to let the heir to the throne serve at the front, but Edward visited the trenches several times and was awarded the Military Cross in 1916.

George V died on 20 January 1936. The next day Edward, accompanied by Wallis Simpson, watched the proclamation of his accession from a window of St James's Palace, which broke with custom. Ministers grew uneasy: his remark in South Wales that something must be done for the unemployed miners was seen as an attempt to steer policy, and they hesitated to send state papers to Fort Belvedere, fearing that guests might read them. He also insisted that his profile on coins face left, as his father's had, breaking the tradition of alternation.

On 16 November 1936 he told Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin that he wished to marry Simpson once she was free. Baldwin answered that his subjects would find the marriage morally unacceptable, largely because the Church of England opposed remarriage after divorce. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Cosmo Gordon Lang, insisted that Edward must go. Edward knew the government would resign if the marriage went ahead, and he abdicated after a reign of 326 days.

As Duke of Windsor, Edward married Simpson on 3 June 1937 at the Château de Candé, near Tours; George VI forbade the royal family to attend. In October 1937 they visited Nazi Germany against the advice of the British government and met Adolf Hitler at the Berghof, where Edward gave full Nazi salutes. After the fall of France he was appointed Governor of the Bahamas. After the war the couple lived in France, and he never again held an official role. He published a memoir, A King's Story, in 1951, and died in Paris on 28 May 1972, aged 77. He was buried at Frogmore, behind the Royal Mausoleum of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert.
edward-whymper: Edward Whymper was born in London on 27 April 1840, the second of eleven children of the artist and wood engraver Josiah Wood Whymper, and was trained as a wood engraver at an early age. In 1860 he toured the central and western Alps to produce commissioned drawings of alpine scenery.

In 1861 he climbed Mont Pelvoux, from whose summit he saw that it was overtopped by a neighbouring peak, the Barre des Écrins, which he climbed in 1864. Between 1861 and 1865 he made new ascents on the Mont Blanc massif and in the Pennine Alps, among them the Aiguille d'Argentière and Mont Dolent in 1864 and the Aiguille Verte in 1865, and designed a tent that bore his name for a hundred years.

Whymper failed eight times on the Matterhorn before 1865. That year, after Michel Croz left for another engagement, he planned an attempt on the eastern face with Lord Francis Douglas and the Zermatt guides Peter Taugwalder and his son of the same name. They were joined by Charles Hudson, Croz and the inexperienced Douglas Hadow, and reached the summit by the Hörnli ridge on 14 July 1865, days before an Italian party. On the descent Hadow slipped and fell onto Croz, dragging Douglas and Hudson to their deaths, and the rope parted between Taugwalder and Douglas.

A formal investigation found no proof that it had been cut, and the elder Taugwalder was acquitted. In 1867 he explored Greenland, bringing back fossil plants, and surveyed its coastline in 1872. In 1880 he climbed volcanoes in Ecuador, including the first ascent of Chimborazo, and studied altitude sickness; the Royal Geographical Society gave him its Patron's medal. In 1901, working with the Canadian Pacific Railway, he made the first ascents of Mount Whymper and Stanley Peak.

His account of the Matterhorn fills most of Scrambles amongst the Alps (1871), illustrated with his own engravings. He also published Travels amongst the Great Andes of the Equator (1892), How to Use the Aneroid Barometer (1881) and guides to Zermatt and Chamonix, and he engraved illustrations for John Tyndall and Florence Crauford Grove. He concluded that altitude sickness came from reduced atmospheric pressure and the expansion of gas in the body. He died alone at the Grand Hotel Couttet in Chamonix on 16 September 1911 and is buried in the English cemetery there.
edward-wilmot-blyden: Edward Wilmot Blyden was born on 3 August 1832 in Saint Thomas, Danish West Indies, to free black parents who claimed descent from the Igbo people of present-day Nigeria. Between 1842 and 1845 the family lived in Porto Bello, Venezuela, where he became fluent in Spanish. In 1845 he met the Reverend John P. Knox, a Dutch Reformed pastor, who became his mentor and encouraged his aptitude for oratory and literature.

In May 1850 Blyden went to the United States to enrol at Rutgers Theological College and was refused admission because of his race, as he was at two other colleges. Knox then encouraged him to go to Liberia, the colony set up by the American Colonization Society, and he sailed there later in 1850.

In Monrovia Blyden studied at Alexander High School, became its principal in 1858 and was ordained a Presbyterian minister that year. He edited the Liberia Herald in 1855 and 1856, and in Sierra Leone in the early 1870s he founded and edited the newspaper The Negro. In 1861 he became professor of Greek and Latin at Liberia College and later served as its president, from 1880 to 1884.

He was Liberia's Secretary of State from 1864 to 1865 under Daniel Bashiel Warner and Secretary of the Interior from 1880 to 1882 under Anthony W. Gardner, and he served as Liberian ambassador to Britain and France. He lost the 1885 presidential election as the Republican candidate. From 1901 to 1906 he directed the education of Sierra Leonean Muslims in Freetown.

Blyden believed that Black Americans could end their suffering from racial discrimination by returning to Africa and helping to develop it, and African Americans who wanted full civil rights in the United States criticised him for it. He called this redemptive role Ethiopianism, compared the diaspora's suffering to that of the Jews and supported the Zionist project.

Blyden is regarded by some as the father of Pan-Africanism and was among the first to articulate an African Personality. His major work, Christianity, Islam and the Negro Race (1887), argued that Islam was more unifying and fulfilling for Africans than Christianity, which he thought had a demoralising effect, although he remained a Christian. At first many doubted that an African had written it, and in later printings he added his photograph as the frontispiece. His ideas influenced Marcus Garvey, George Padmore and Kwame Nkrumah. Blyden died on 7 February 1912 in Freetown and was buried at Racecourse Cemetery.
edwin-barclay: Edwin James Barclay was a politician, poet and musician. His paternal grandparents moved from Barbados to Liberia with their children in 1865, part of a minority of Caribbean immigrants who shared with the Americo-Liberians a culture with an English base, considerable mixed-race ancestry and a common history. His father, Ernest Barclay, and his uncle Arthur Barclay became important Liberian politicians. At 19, in 1901, Edwin wrote a patriotic song, "The Lone Star Forever". A member of the True Whig Party, he served as secretary of state in the government of Charles D. B. King from 1920 to 1930.

Barclay became president in 1930, when King and Vice President Allen Yancy resigned after a League of Nations investigation implicated them in profiting from forced labour. He completed King's term and was first elected in his own right in 1931. One of his first decisions was to repeal the Port of Entry Law of 1864, which had restricted the economic activities of foreigners, and in the early 1930s concessions were signed with Dutch, Danish, German and Polish investors.

The Great Depression collapsed rubber prices and Liberia's revenues. In 1926 the government had granted a rubber concession to the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company and obtained a $5 million loan through a Firestone subsidiary. By 1931 Liberia could not meet its payments, and in 1932 the legislature declared a moratorium pending renegotiation. A League of Nations commission recommended financial help with foreign advisers in key posts; some members of the League advocated a form of international control, which the Liberian government resisted. A reorganisation plan under League supervision was put into effect in 1934, and Liberia kept its formal independence.

In 1937, under American pressure, Barclay withdrew the concession given to the German investors, who were accused of Nazi sympathies. After Japan occupied the rubber-producing areas of the Far East, Liberia became one of the few sources of natural rubber left to the Allies, and Barclay promised the United States all it needed. In 1942 Liberia signed a defence pact with the United States, which brought roads, airports and Roberts Field, a staging point on the South Atlantic air ferry route. President Franklin D. Roosevelt visited Liberia in January 1943, and Barclay addressed the United States Congress in May 1943.
Barclay retired on 3 January 1944 and was succeeded by William Tubman. He stood against Tubman in the presidential election of 1955 and received only about 1,100 votes. He died on 6 November 1955.
edwin-lutyens: Edwin Lutyens was born in Kensington, London, the tenth of thirteen children of Mary Theresa Gallwey and Captain Charles Augustus Henry Lutyens, an English soldier and painter. He grew up in Thursley, Surrey. Rheumatic fever in childhood kept him from formal schooling. He studied architecture at the South Kensington School of Art from 1885 to 1887, then joined the practice of Ernest George and Harold Peto, where he first met Herbert Baker. In 1888 he set up his own practice; his first commission was a private house at Crooksbury, Farnham.

At Crooksbury he met the garden designer Gertrude Jekyll, for whom he began the house at Munstead Wood in 1896. Their partnership shaped many of his country houses, which set hardy planting within terraces, stairs and balustrades. Edward Hudson's magazine Country Life made his houses widely known, and Hudson commissioned him for Lindisfarne Castle. Around 1900 his style turned to a more conventional classicism, seen in Julius Drewe's Castle Drogo in Devon.

New Delhi was chosen in 1911 to replace Calcutta as the seat of the British Indian government, and Lutyens worked on it from 1912 to 1930. He devised his own classical order, the Delhi Order, and based his layout on Mughal water gardens. The city was built of local red sandstone. He quarrelled repeatedly with the Viceroy, Viceroy Hardinge, who wanted Indian elements where Lutyens wanted classical architecture. He was knighted in 1918 and made a Knight Commander of the Order of the Indian Empire in 1930.

He was also one of three principal architects of the Imperial War Graves Commission and designed the Stone of Remembrance used in larger cemeteries and the Memorial to the Missing of the Somme at Thiepval. The Cenotaph began in 1919 as a temporary structure for the Allied Victory Parade; Lloyd George proposed a low catafalque, but Lutyens suggested a taller monument.

Lutyens was diagnosed with cancer in the early 1940s and died on 1 January 1944. His ashes lie in the crypt of St Paul's Cathedral. He received the Royal Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1921 and the Gold Medal of the American Institute of Architects in 1925. His design for a vast Roman Catholic cathedral in Liverpool, begun in 1933, was halted in the Second World War and only its crypt was completed. In 2015 all 44 of his surviving First World War memorials in Britain were listed for legal protection.
edwin-of-northumbria: Edwin was the son of Ælle, the first known king of Deira. His sister Acha was married to Æthelfrith, king of neighbouring Bernicia, and when Æthelfrith conquered Deira Edwin was forced into exile. Where he spent his childhood is not known; late traditions reported by Reginald of Durham and Geoffrey of Monmouth place him in Gwynedd, fostered by King Cadfan ap Iago. By the 610s he was in Mercia under the protection of King Cearl, whose daughter Cwenburg he married.

By around 616 he was at the court of Rædwald of East Anglia. Bede reports that Æthelfrith tried to have Rædwald murder his rival and that Rædwald meant to do so until his wife dissuaded him. Rædwald defeated Æthelfrith at the Battle of the River Idle in 616 and installed Edwin as king of Northumbria; Æthelfrith's sons went into exile in Dál Riata and Pictland.

Edwin ruled Deira and Bernicia, and after Rædwald's death he became the most powerful ruler in Britain. He expelled Ceretic from the British kingdom of Elmet. He allied with Eadbald of Kent and married his sister Æthelburg in 625, on condition that he convert. Edwin's rule rested on regular wars for tribute and slaves; by his death his realm probably stretched from the Humber and the Mersey north to the Southern Uplands and the Cheviots. His realm held York and Carlisle.

At Easter 626 an agent of Cwichelm of Wessex tried to assassinate him at York. Edwin promised to become a Christian if he defeated Cwichelm, and he was baptised with his chief men by Paulinus on 12 April 627. In Bede's account his priest Coifi and a counsellor who likened life to a sparrow's flight through a lit hall advised accepting the new faith.

From about 627 he was the most powerful Anglo-Saxon king, ruling Bernicia, Deira, much of eastern Mercia, the Isle of Man and Anglesey. Bede calls his overlordship imperium. His alliance with Kent, the subjection of Wessex and his recent successes added to his power, and the idea was later equated with that of a bretwalda.

Cadwallon ap Cadfan, his supposed foster-brother, appeared around 629 and was defeated, but he and Penda of Mercia rose against Edwin and killed him at the Battle of Hatfield Chase. Of his two grown sons by Cwenburg, Osfrith died at Hatfield and Eadfrith was captured by Penda and later killed. Tradition says his body was hidden in Sherwood Forest at a place that became Edwinstowe, with his head buried at York and the rest at Whitby. Bernicia and Deira separated again until Oswald, a son of Æthelfrith, killed Cadwallon and reunited Northumbria. Edwin was venerated as a saint.
edwin-smith-papyrus: The papyrus may have been a manual of military surgery. Its recto has 377 lines in 17 columns, and its verso 92 lines in five columns. Apart from the fragmentary outer column it is intact. It is written from right to left in black ink, with explanatory glosses in red. Most of it concerns trauma and surgery, with short sections on gynaecology and cosmetics on the verso, which also holds eight magic spells and five prescriptions. Two incidents in Case 8 and Case 9, as well as the spells, are the exceptions to its practical nature, and generic spells may have been used as a last resort in terminal cases.

The 48 cases are arranged by organ, from the head and neck through the arms to the torso, in descending anatomical order. They are typical cases, not individual ones. A title states the injury, for example a gaping wound in the head that has penetrated to the bone and split the skull. The physician examined by sight, smell, touch and the pulse, then judged the chances of survival and made one of three diagnoses: an ailment he would treat, one he would contend with, or one not to be treated.

Treatments include sutures for wounds of the lip, throat and shoulder, bandages, splints, poultices, honey to prevent infection and raw meat to stop bleeding. The papyrus contains the first known descriptions of the cranial structures, the meninges, the surface of the brain, the cerebrospinal fluid and intracranial pulsations, and it records that the side of the body affected relates to the location of a cranial injury.

Authorship is debated. One scribe wrote most of it and a second a few small sections, and it ends abruptly in the middle of a line. Archaic grammar and terminology suggest it copies an older manuscript, and James Henry Breasted speculated, while stressing it was pure conjecture, that the author might be Imhotep.

Edwin Smith bought it in Luxor in 1862 from a dealer named Mustafa Agha. After his death his daughter gave it to the New York Historical Society, where Caroline Ransom Williams recognised its importance and wrote to Breasted in 1920. His first translation appeared in 1930 and changed the understanding of the history of medicine. From 1938 to 1948 it was at the Brooklyn Museum, and it was then presented to the New York Academy of Medicine. In 2005 and 2006 it was exhibited at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and James P. Allen published the first complete English translation since Breasted's.
efrain-rios-montt: Efraín Ríos Montt was born on 16 June 1926 in Huehuetenango, in the highlands of western Guatemala, into a large ladino family of the rural middle class. He was rejected by the national military academy because of astigmatism, served as a private in the army, and entered the Polytechnic School in 1946. He graduated at the top of his class in 1950 and later trained in the United States and at the Italian War College. He ran for president in 1974 as candidate of the National Opposition Front. Most observers believe he won the popular vote, but the government halted the count and Congress chose General Kjell Laugerud. In 1978 he left the Catholic Church for an evangelical Protestant church.

Discontent with the rule of General Romeo Lucas García and with a result denounced as fraudulent led young officers to stage a coup in March 1982. On 23 March a three-person junta was installed under Ríos Montt, who had not planned the coup. It declared martial law, suspended the constitution and set up special tribunals.

On 9 June he forced the other members to resign and became sole head of state. The army's plan Victoria 82 included a pacification strategy called Fusiles y Frijoles, rifles and beans, which organised Civil Defense Patrols of indigenous villagers. In December 1982 Ronald Reagan met him in Honduras and praised his personal integrity. Ríos Montt alienated many Guatemalans, among them the military leadership, who objected to his promotion of young officers. His defence minister, Óscar Mejía Victores, overthrew him on 8 August 1983.

Ríos Montt founded the Guatemalan Republican Front in 1989 and served in Congress, and was president of Congress in 1995–1996 and 2000–2004. A constitutional ban on those who had taken power by a coup kept him from the presidency until the Constitutional Court approved his candidacy in 2003, when he came third.

Reports by the Catholic Church's REMHI project and the Historical Clarification Commission, co-sponsored by the United Nations, documented grave violations in the civil war, and the commission characterised the counter-insurgency as including acts of genocide. He admitted that the army had committed crimes during his term but denied ordering them. In 2013 a court sentenced him to 80 years for genocide and crimes against humanity, but the Constitutional Court quashed the sentence. He died of a heart attack in Guatemala City on 1 April 2018, before a retrial was completed.
egbert-of-wessex: Historians do not agree on Ecgberht's ancestry. His father was Ealhmund, thought to be the king of Kent who appears in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in 784. Offa of Mercia dominated Kent in the late 780s, and Ecgberht was forced into exile at the court of Charlemagne in Francia by Offa and by Beorhtric of Wessex. The Chronicle says he spent three years there, though many modern accounts assume a scribal error for thirteen. When Beorhtric died in 802, Ecgberht came to the throne of Wessex, probably with the support of Charlemagne and perhaps of the papacy.

Little is known of the first twenty years of the reign, but there is no evidence that Ecgberht submitted to the Mercian king Cenwulf, and Wessex seems to have kept its independence. In 825 he defeated Beornwulf of Mercia at Ellandun, now Wroughton near Swindon, a battle that ended Mercian domination of southern England. His son Æthelwulf went to Kent with a troop, and the men of Kent, Essex, Surrey and Sussex submitted. When East Anglia asked for his protection, Beornwulf and his successor Ludeca were killed invading it.

In 829 Ecgberht invaded Mercia and drove King Wiglaf into exile, and he issued coins as king of Mercia. The Chronicle says that he conquered Mercia and all that was south of the Humber, and that he was the eighth king to be bretwalda, or wide-ruler. Later that year he received the submission of the Northumbrian king, probably Eanred, at Dore, though one historian suggests the meeting was more likely a mutual recognition of sovereignty. In 830 he led an expedition against the Welsh, the high point of his influence.

In 830 Wiglaf regained the Mercian throne, probably by a rebellion against West Saxon rule, and Ecgberht's wider dominance ended. Wessex kept Kent, Sussex and Surrey, ruled by Æthelwulf as a subking, and the independent existence of the kingdoms of Kent and Sussex was over. In the south-west Ecgberht was defeated by the Danes at Carhampton in 836 but won a battle against them and the West Welsh at Hingston Down in 838.

He died in 839 and was buried at Winchester, as were his son Æthelwulf, his grandson Alfred the Great and his great-grandson Edward the Elder. His victories fundamentally changed the political landscape of Anglo-Saxon England, and his descendants ruled Wessex and later all England continuously until 1013.
egirdir: Eğirdir lies near the south end of Lake Eğirdir, on a peninsula that extends northwards into the lake, about 110 kilometres north of Antalya. A mountain called Eğirdirsivrisi, or Camili dağı, rises to 1,733 metres immediately to the southwest. To the northeast are two islands, Can Ada and Yeşil Ada, now joined to the mainland by a causeway. Yeşil Ada was formerly called Nis Ada, probably from the Greek word for island. The town was once called Eğridir, a Turkish form possibly borrowed from its old Greek name Akrotiri.

Numerous ancient coins suggest an early settlement, and the ancient settlement of Prostanna was probably on the nearby mountain. The Greek name Akroterion is first attested in 1438 but was probably used earlier, in Byzantine times. The Seljuks first conquered the town around 1080, and it was probably taken with Isparta in 1204 by Kilij Arslan III of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. Sultan Kayqubad I probably built its citadel during his reign in the 1220s-30s.

In the 1300s Eğirdir, also known as Falakābād, became the capital of the Hamidoğulları beylik. Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1332, described a great and populous city with fine bazaars, running streams, mosques and orchards beside a lake of sweet water, and mentioned merchant shipping on the lake. The principality lasted until 1381. Timur captured the town in 1403, and the Ottomans took control in 1417. Most of its population was Greek Orthodox until the population exchanges of the 1920s. Yeşil Ada once had a domed Christian basilica with frescoes dated stylistically to the 9th to 13th centuries.

Eğirdir is the seat of Eğirdir District in Isparta Province. Its castle is said to have been built by Croesus, king of Lydia, with additions by Romans, Byzantines and Seljuks. Residents fish in the lake throughout the year, and Yeşil Ada keeps stone houses from the Greek era alongside restaurants and guesthouses. The town joined the Cittaslow network on 4 February 2017.
egon-schiele: Egon Schiele was born on 12 June 1890 in Tulln, Lower Austria, the son of Adolf Schiele, the station master, and Marie Soukup. As a child he was fascinated by trains and drew them for hours. His father died when he was fourteen, and the family, which had been fairly wealthy, was left impoverished. He became a ward of his uncle Leopold Czihaczek, who recognised his talent and allowed him a tutor. In 1906 Schiele entered the School of Arts and Crafts in Vienna and soon moved to the Academy of Fine Arts, where the strict teaching of Christian Griepenkerl frustrated him so much that he left after three years.

In 1907 Schiele sought out Gustav Klimt, who mentored him, bought his drawings, arranged models and introduced him to patrons and to the Wiener Werkstätte. His earliest works, from 1907 to 1909, resemble Klimt's and show the influence of Art Nouveau. He held his first exhibition in Klosterneuburg in 1908 and founded the Neukunstgruppe with other students in 1909. From 1910 he began experimenting with nudes, and a style of emaciated, sickly-coloured figures, often with strong sexual overtones, emerged. He also explored themes of death and rebirth. In 1911 he met Wally Neuzil, who lived with him and modelled for some of his most striking paintings.

In April 1912 Schiele was arrested at Neulengbach on suspicion of kidnapping and seducing a girl of 13, and police seized more than a hundred drawings they considered pornographic. The charges were dropped, but he was found guilty of exhibiting erotic drawings in a place accessible to children. After 21 days in custody he was sentenced to a further three days, and in prison he drew his cell. He had his first solo show in Munich in 1913 and one in Paris in 1914. In 1915 he married Edith Harms and was called up for army service, working mostly as a clerk in a prisoner-of-war camp, and in 1918 he showed fifty works at the 49th Vienna Secession exhibition to great success.

In the autumn of 1918 the Spanish flu reached Vienna. Edith, who was six months pregnant, died of it on 28 October. Schiele, already ill, died three days later, on 31 October 1918, at the age of 28. In those three days he drew a few sketches of Edith. His work is noted for its intensity and its raw sexuality, and for the many self-portraits he produced, including nude self-portraits. The twisted body shapes and expressive line mark him as an early exponent of Expressionism.
egypt: Egypt spans the northeast corner of Africa and the southwest corner of Asia through the Sinai Peninsula, and covers 1,001,450 square kilometres. The climate is extremely arid, so population centres are concentrated along the narrow Nile Valley and Delta: about 98% of Egyptians live on 3% of the territory.

Apart from the Nile Valley the landscape is mostly desert, with a few oases such as Siwa, and parts of the Sahara and the Libyan Desert fall within it. Mount Catherine, at 2,642 metres on the Sinai Peninsula, is the highest mountain. The Suez Canal crosses the Isthmus of Suez and connects the Mediterranean Sea with the Indian Ocean by way of the Red Sea.

Evidence of rock carvings along the Nile and in the oases indicates early habitation. By about 6000 BCE a Neolithic culture had taken root in the Nile Valley, and the earliest known hieroglyphic inscriptions appeared on Naqada III pottery vessels dated to about 3200 BCE. Around c. 3150 BCE King Menes unified Egypt, establishing a succession of dynasties that ruled for three millennia.

The Old Kingdom (c. 2700 to 2200 BCE) saw the construction of the pyramids at Giza, and Ahmose I reunified the country after the Hyksos occupation, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom (c. 1550 to 1070 BCE). Its pharaohs included Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II.

Egypt came under foreign rule from the 6th century BCE. It was an early centre of Christianity and adopted Islam from the seventh century onwards. Cairo became the capital of the Fatimid Caliphate in the tenth century and of the Mamluk Sultanate in the 13th century, and Egypt became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1517.

Muhammad Ali established modern Egypt as an autonomous Khedivate in 1867. The country was then occupied by the British Empire and gained independence in 1922 as a monarchy, and after the 1952 revolution it declared itself a republic. Egypt signed the Camp David Accords in 1978, and the Sinai Peninsula was completely returned to it in 1982.

Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world, with about 120 million inhabitants, and Cairo is its capital and largest city. The 2011 revolution overthrew Hosni Mubarak. Islam is the official religion and Arabic the official language.
egyptian-blue: Egyptian blue is a pigment with the chemical formula CaCuSi4O10, also known as calcium copper silicate or cuprorivaite, and it is considered the first synthetic pigment. Its colour comes from calcium-copper tetrasilicate of the same composition as the natural mineral cuprorivaite. It was made by heating quartz sand, a copper compound, calcium carbonate and a small amount of alkali, either natron or ash of salt-tolerant plants, for several hours at 800 to 1,000 °C. The result consists of rectangular blue crystals with unreacted quartz and some glass. More alkali gave a harder product with more glass, and fine-textured pigment, which was lighter in colour, needed a second grinding and firing.

The ancient Egyptians held blue in high regard and wanted to imitate turquoise and lapis lazuli. Natural minerals such as azurite were rare and hard to work, so they made the pigment themselves. The earliest evidence, identified by the Egyptologist Lorelei H. Corcoran, is on an alabaster bowl of about 3250 BCE from Hierakonpolis, now in Boston. In the Middle Kingdom it decorated tombs, wall paintings, furnishings and statues, and under the New Kingdom it was used for many objects. It was made in cakes, slabs and balls; cakes found at Qantir and at the fort of Zawiyet Umm el-Rakham suggest they were traded and reshaped away from where they were made.

Egyptian blue also appears in the Near East, the Eastern Mediterranean and the limits of the Roman Empire, and it is unclear whether this was parallel invention or the spread of the technology. Roman sources report that a certain Vestorius moved production from Alexandria to Pozzuoli near Naples. The Romans called it caeruleum, and Vitruvius described grinding sand, copper and natron and heating small balls in a furnace in the first century BCE. Etruscan painters used it, and Raphael used it in his Triumph of Galatea.

No ancient Egyptian text describes its manufacture. Its use ended in the fourth century CE, when the method was lost. Humphry Davy investigated it in 1815, followed by W. T. Russell and F. Fouqué, and the first recorded use of the name Egyptian blue in English dates from 1809. Modern analysis has reconstructed how it was made. Its strong infrared luminescence lets researchers detect it on objects that look unpainted, and it has been traced on paintings as late as the sixteenth century.
egyptian-hieroglyphs: Hieroglyphs combined ideographic, logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with more than 1,000 distinct characters. They derive from proto-literate symbol systems of the Early Bronze Age, around the 33rd century BCE, such as the clay labels from Abydos attributed to a Predynastic ruler called Scorpion I. The first full sentence in mature hieroglyphs found so far is on a seal impression in the tomb of Seth-Peribsen, of the Second Dynasty. About 900 signs were in use in the Middle Kingdom, and by the Greco-Roman period there were more than 5,000.

Scholars have long debated whether the script arose independently or under the influence of Mesopotamian cuneiform. Geoffrey Sampson argued that Egyptian writing was probably invented under Sumerian influence, but the glyphs found at Abydos, dated between 3400 and 3200 BCE, have cast doubt on the older view that Mesopotamian writing came first.

The script has three kinds of sign: phonetic glyphs, including twenty-four single-consonant signs that work like an alphabet; logographs, which represent morphemes; and determinatives, silent signs at the end of a word that narrow its meaning. The writing normally does not indicate vowels, so some have called it an abjad. The same sign can be read in different ways according to context. Lines or columns are ordinarily read from right to left, and the direction in which animal and human figures face shows the reading order.

Cursive forms were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood, and simplified forms gave rise to the hieratic and demotic scripts. Hieroglyphs nevertheless continued beside them in monumental and formal writing. The Proto-Sinaitic script drew on them, and through it the Phoenician alphabet.

Hieroglyphs continued to be used under Persian rule and in the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. Monumental use ceased after Emperor Theodosius I closed all non-Christian temples in 391, and the last known inscription, the Graffito of Esmet-Akhom at Philae, dates from 394. Knowledge of the script was then lost completely. Medieval and early modern attempts failed because they assumed that the signs recorded ideas rather than sounds, and Athanasius Kircher in the 17th century was held back by belief in the mystical nature of the symbols.

The breakthrough came with the Rosetta Stone, found by Napoleon's troops in 1799, which gives the same text in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Silvestre de Sacy, Johan David Åkerblad and Thomas Young made some progress, and Jean-François Champollion completed the decipherment by the 1820s.
ehime-prefecture: Ehime Prefecture occupies the north-western part of the island of Shikoku and faces the Seto Inland Sea to the north. It borders Kagawa Prefecture to the north-east, Tokushima Prefecture to the east and Kōchi Prefecture to the south-east, and it also touches Hiroshima Prefecture for 74 metres on the island of Hyōtanjima. The interior has high mountains, and the long coastline has many islands in the Seto Inland Sea. Its westernmost arm, the Sadamisaki Peninsula, is the narrowest peninsula in Japan. Matsuyama is the capital, the largest city of the prefecture and the largest city on Shikoku.

Until the Meiji Restoration the area was known as Iyo Province. Since before the Heian period it was dominated by fishermen and sailors, who played an important part in defending Japan against pirates and the Mongol invasions. The name Ehime comes from the section of the Kojiki on the creation of the land, where Iyo Province is mythologically named Ehime, meaning lovely princess.

After the Battle of Sekigahara the Tokugawa shōgun gave the area to his allies, among them Katō Yoshiaki, who built Matsuyama Castle, the basis of the modern city of Matsuyama. The oldest extant hot spring in Japan, Dōgo Onsen, lies in Matsuyama; it is mentioned in the Nihon Shoki and has been used for over two thousand years.

The coastal areas around Imabari and Saijō have shipyards, including those of Japan's largest shipbuilder, Imabari Shipbuilding, as well as chemical industries, oil refining, paper and cotton textiles. Rural areas rely on farming and fishing and are known for citrus fruits such as mikan and iyokan and for cultured pearls. The novel Botchan by Natsume Sōseki draws on the author's experience in Matsuyama. Ehime University stands in the prefecture, and its natural parks include the Ashizuri-Uwakai and Setonaikai National Parks.
ehrenbreitstein-fortress: Ehrenbreitstein Fortress stands in Rhineland-Palatinate on the east bank of the Rhine, opposite the mouth of the Moselle, overlooking the city of Koblenz. The peak of the hill that shares its name is 118 metres above the river. The hill was first settled in the 4th millennium BCE, fortified in the 10th or 9th century BCE and held by a Roman fortification in the 3rd to 5th centuries CE. About the year 1000 a noble called Ehrenbert, or Erembert, built a castle on it, first called Burg Ehrenbertstein.

The castle was first mentioned in a surviving document in 1139 as a property of the Archbishop of Trier. Archbishop Hillin expanded it in 1152–1169. In the 16th century work began to turn it into a fortress able to withstand gunpowder weapons, and one of its first cannon was the nine-ton Greif of 1524. Philipp Christoph von Sötern built the palace Phillipsburg at its foot in 1625–1629. It held the Holy Tunic, the see's most valuable relic, from 1657 to 1794. In 1688 it withstood a siege by Louis XIV; around 1730 Balthasar Neumann added the Schönborn-Werke, a third ring of fortifications. French troops took it in 1759 but held it for three years.

French revolutionary troops conquered Koblenz in 1794 and besieged Ehrenbreitstein three times without success. A siege that began in 1798 starved the defenders, who handed over the fortress in 1799. Forced by the Treaty of Lunéville to withdraw from the right bank of the Rhine, the French blew it up in 1801. After the Congress of Vienna of 1815 the Rhineland became a Prussian province, and Prussia built the present fortress in 1817–1828 as the backbone of Festung Koblenz, paid in part by 15 million francs from France. It could be defended by up to 1,200 soldiers and was never attacked.

After the First World War the fortress escaped dismantling; the American General Henry Tureman Allen prevented its intended destruction in 1922, and the US Army used it as headquarters during the occupation of the Rhineland. It later served the French Army, was a refuge for archives and cultural objects in the Second World War, and passed to Rhineland-Palatinate in 1947.

The fortress is open to visitors, linked to Koblenz by a cable car. It houses several museums, among them the Haus der Fotografie and the Landesmuseum Koblenz, and serves for concerts and plays. Since 2002 it has formed the northernmost point of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Upper Middle Rhine Valley.
ehrenfried-walther-von-tschirnhaus: Tschirnhaus was born on 10 April 1651. He attended the Gymnasium at Görlitz and then studied mathematics, philosophy and medicine at the University of Leiden. He travelled in France, Italy and Switzerland and served in the army of Holland in 1672 and 1673. On his travels he met Baruch de Spinoza and Christiaan Huygens in the Netherlands, Isaac Newton in England, and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in Paris, with whom he kept up a lifelong correspondence. He became a member of the Académie Royale des Sciences in Paris.

The Tschirnhaus transformation, by which he removed certain intermediate terms from an algebraic equation, was published in the Acta Eruditorum in 1683. In 1682 he worked out the theory of catacaustics and showed that they were rectifiable; one catacaustic of a parabola is still called the Tschirnhausen cubic. In 1696 he was one of five mathematicians to send a solution to the brachistochrone problem set by Johann Bernoulli. He made lenses and mirrors, some now in museums, and built a large glassworks in Saxony where he constructed burning glasses and carried on experiments in 1687 and 1688.

His Medicina mentis (1687) combines deduction with empiricism and shows his link with the Enlightenment. At Leiden he began a correspondence with Spinoza, preserved in part, in which he raised objections to claims in the Ethics. He was one of the first to obtain a copy of the Ethics, and the only surviving pre-publication copy, in the Vatican Library, may have been his.

Back in Saxony, Tschirnhaus began systematic experiments with mixtures of silicates and earths at different temperatures to make porcelain, then available only as a costly import from China and Japan. In 1704 he showed porcelain to Leibniz's secretary and became supervisor of the young alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, who joined the work reluctantly by 1707. Kaolin from Schneeberg and alabaster advanced it, and Augustus II named him director of a porcelain factory he intended to found. Tschirnhaus died suddenly on 11 October 1708 and the project halted. Böttger announced the invention of porcelain on 28 March 1709 and headed the first European manufactory, though contemporaries such as Samuel Stöltzel in 1719 credited Tschirnhaus, and some others claim English makers produced porcelain earlier.
eichstatt: Eichstätt lies on both sides of the river Altmühl, in the heart of the Altmühl Valley Nature Park and in a valley of the Franconian Jura. The area is known for the quarries of Solnhofen Plattenkalk, a Jurassic limestone. The Berlin specimen of Archaeopteryx was found on the Blumenberg there by Jakob Niemeyer. The town is dominated by the Willibaldsburg, whose architect was the Augsburg master builder Elias Holl, and besides the cathedral it has 12 churches and 10 monasteries.

Saint Willibald founded the Diocese of Eichstätt in 741 on the site of an old Roman station, Aureatum or Rubilocus. The town received walls and a charter in 908. It was ruled by a prince-bishop and, within the Holy Roman Empire, was the seat of the Bishopric of Eichstätt until secularization in 1802. In 1806 it became part of the Kingdom of Bavaria, and in 1817 King Maximilian I granted the Principality of Eichstätt to his son-in-law Eugène de Beauharnais. An episcopal see was re-established in 1821, and the principality reverted to the Bavarian crown in 1855.

In 870 the remains of Saint Walpurga, an Anglo-Saxon missionary to the Frankish Empire, were moved from Heidenheim to Eichstätt. Her burial place there was enshrined in 1035 as the Benedictine Abbey of Saint Walburga, which continues today. Her bones were placed in a rocky niche that was said to exude a healing oil, and the oil drew pilgrims. Basilius Besler's botanical book Hortus Eystettensis, meaning Garden at Eichstätt, was first published in 1613. During World War II Allied prisoners of war were held at Oflag VII-B in Eichstätt; they attempted escapes and staged plays and music, including the premiere of Benjamin Britten's Ballad of Little Musgrave and Lady Barnard.

Eichstätt has a population of around 13,000 and is the capital of its district and the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Eichstätt. It is home to the Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt, founded in 1980, the only Catholic university in Germany, which the State of Bavaria granted full university rights including doctoral and Habilitation degrees.
eid-al-ghadir: Eid al-Ghadir, whose Arabic name means feast of the pond, is a major festival of Shia Muslims on 18 Dhu al-Hijjah, the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar. It commemorates the Event of Ghadir Khumm. Ten years after the Hijrah, Muhammad called on his followers to join his first and last pilgrimage, and Islamic scholars believe more than seventy thousand followed him to Mecca. On the return journey, on 18 Dhu al-Hijjah 10 AH, corresponding to March 632 CE, he delivered a sermon at Ghadir Khumm. He called up his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib and said that to whomever he was mawla, Ali was also mawla.

The word mawla has many meanings, among them friend and master. Because Muhammad first asked whether he had more authority over the believers than they had over themselves, many understand the word as master and the sermon as the designation of Ali as his successor and the first Imam. For this reason Shia Islam counts the date as one of its foundational events. The day has other names, including Eid al-Wilayah, the festival of guardianship. A hadith attributed to Muhammad and recorded by Ibn Babawayh calls Ghadir Khumm the best and highest of the festivals of his community.

Shia Muslims mark the day with prayers, sermons, gatherings, charity, congratulations and gifts, and some communities hold public celebrations and share food and sweets. Reported customs include greeting, shaking hands, wearing new clothes, using perfume and feeding others. According to historical narrations, Hassan ibn Ali held ceremonies at Kufa on the day, which Ali attended, and afterwards distributed gifts.

Some accounts hold that the commemoration was observed from the early centuries of Islam; it was first formally observed in the Buyid era. In the Safavid era it was among the largest religious festivals, and in the Qajar era an official greeting ceremony took place at court, a custom that continued in the Pahlavi era. In 2022 a festival ten kilometres long filled Valiasr Street in Tehran, and in 2024 the Iraqi Council of Representatives declared the day an official public holiday.
eidsvoll: Eidsvoll is a municipality in Akershus county, part of the traditional region of Romerike, and its administrative centre is the village of Sundet. The name comes from the genitive of Old Norse eið, here meaning a road passing around a waterfall, and vǫllr, meadow or field. People sailing down the Vorma from the districts around Lake Mjøsa, and people from Romerike sailing up it, both had to pass the Sundfossen waterfall, so the site became an important meeting place long before Christianity arrived. Until 1918 the name was spelled Eidsvold.

Eidsvoll is mentioned in Old Norse manuscripts. In the 11th century it became the site of the court and assembly, or ting, for the eastern parts of Norway, replacing Vang, now part of Hamar. Its position on the Vorma and Mjøsa made it a thoroughfare to the interior of the north. Agriculture was the main industry. Gold was found in 1758 in the eastern parts, which for a short time saw a minor gold rush, and the area is still called Gullverket. King Christian IV of Denmark opened Eidsvoll Verk in 1624 to smelt iron ore using the water power of the Andelva river.

Carsten Anker took over the works in 1794, when they were in decay because the surrounding forests, needed for charcoal, had been depleted. He restored them and made stoves and other iron goods. In 1811 he settled in Eidsvoll and rebuilt the manor house, now the Eidsvollsbygningen, where the constitutional assembly met to draft and sign the Constitution of Norway on 17 May 1814. The parish became a municipality on 1 January 1838. In 1854 Eidsvoll became the end of Norway's first railway line, from Oslo, and the transfer point for the steamship Skibladner to Hamar, Gjøvik and Lillehammer on Mjøsa.

Eidsvollsbygningen is a museum. Eidsvoll Church, a cruciform Romanesque stone building from about 1200, has been burned and rebuilt several times, and its wooden altarpiece dates from 1765. The pilgrim route Pilegrimsleden passes through the municipality, and the church is among its prominent stops. The municipality of Feiring was merged with Eidsvoll on 1 January 1964. Its arms, granted on 20 November 1987, show a balance as a symbol of justice, recalling the local court of the early Middle Ages. The poet Henrik Wergeland was brought up in Eidsvoll.
eifel: The Eifel is a middle mountain range in western Germany, eastern Belgium, south-eastern Netherlands and northern Luxembourg, covering about 5,300 km2 (2,000 square miles). It lies between Aachen to the north, Trier to the south and Koblenz to the east, bounded in the east and south by the valleys of the Rhine and the Moselle. It belongs to the Rhenish Massif, a rolling plateau formed by the erosion of the Variscan mountains, and its highest point is the volcanic cone of the Hohe Acht at 746.9 m (2,450 ft).

Volcanic activity began about 50 million years ago and continues into the geological present. It left cinder cones, basalt hills and volcanic lakes, among them the water-filled caldera of the Laacher See and the circular maars, of which the Pulvermaar is the largest.

The Buchenloch and Magdalena caves near Gerolstein show that Neanderthals and modern humans lived in the Eifel in the Old Stone Age, and the Magdalena Cave shows visits even at the height of the last ice age. The Iron Age Hunsrück-Eifel culture takes its name from the region, and the first smelting hut north of the Alps was built at Hillesheim in the 5th century BCE.

In Roman times the range between the Rhine, Meuse and Moselle was called Arduenna silva, the high forest. The Eifel was an important economic region, with lead, zinc spar, iron, limestone and building stone mined, and the Roman road from Trier to Cologne crossed it. The Eifel Aqueduct, one of the longest of the Roman Empire, carried water to Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, modern Cologne. The oldest record of the name Eifel dates only from the early Middle Ages, when the Frankish Eifelgau covered the sources of the Erft, Urft, Kyll and Ahr.

Part of the North Eifel has been the Eifel National Park since 2004, and four nature parks lie in the region. Much of it has limited infrastructure and few large industrial areas. Wine is grown along the Rhine, Moselle and Ahr valleys, and the Nürburgring racing course lies in the Eifel.
eight-banners: Nurhaci's forces were at first organised in small hunting parties of about a dozen men related by blood, marriage, clan or residence, as was the Jurchen custom. In 1601, with more men under his command, he reorganised them into companies of 300 households. Five companies made a battalion and ten battalions a banner. Four banners were created, Yellow, White, Red and Blue, each named after its flag, and in 1615 the number was doubled by adding bordered banners. The banner armies helped Nurhaci unify the fragmented Jurchen people, whom his son Hong Taiji renamed Manchu in 1635.

From the late 1620s the Jurchens placed allied and conquered Mongol tribes in the system, and in 1635 the Mongol Eight Banners were separated out. In 1631 artillerymen who had surrendered to Hong Taiji formed the Old Han Army under Tong Yangxing, and between 1637 and 1642 it became the Han Eight Banners, so that there were effectively twenty-four banner armies. The banners took part in the invasions of Joseon in 1627 and 1636. By 1644 an estimated two million people lived in the system. That year Dorgon and his bannermen joined the Ming defector Wu Sangui to defeat Li Zicheng at the Battle of Shanhai Pass and secure Beijing. Han defectors swelled the banners, and Manchus were only 16 percent of them in 1648.

In the Revolt of the Three Feudatories the Han Green Standard Army, not the bannermen, did most of the fighting. After the Ten Great Campaigns of the mid-18th century the quality of the banner armies declined, and by the 1730s bannermen neglected their duties while subsidising 1.5 million people strained the treasury. The banners failed to suppress the Taiping Rebellion, and regional armies such as the Xiang Army took over the defence of the empire. The system survived until the fall of the Qing in 1912, with a rump organisation continuing to 1924.

The smallest unit was the company, or niru, nominally of 300 soldiers and their families; fifteen made a jalan, and four jalan a banner of 60 companies, or 18,000 men. The three upper banners, both Yellow and the Plain White, were under the emperor, and the five lower banners under others. Membership became hereditary, and bannermen received stipends, land, grain rations and housing in garrison quarters, mostly in Beijing, and were tried by banner courts. Roughly half lived in Beijing, and some eighteen provincial garrisons were set up, the largest at Beijing, Xi'an and Hangzhou. Over time banner status became a marker of Manchu identity, even as the military strength of the banners vanished.
eighteenth-dynasty-of-egypt: The dynasty is classified as the first of the New Kingdom, the era in which ancient Egypt achieved the peak of its power, and is also called the Thutmoside Dynasty after its four pharaohs named Thutmose. Its conventional beginning is 1550 or 1549 BCE, though radiocarbon dating suggests a start a few years earlier. Ahmose I, the brother or son of Kamose, the last ruler of the 17th Dynasty, completed the campaign to expel the Hyksos rulers. His reign is seen as the end of the Second Intermediate Period. His consort Ahmose-Nefertari was deified after her death. He was succeeded by his son Amenhotep I.

Thutmose I extended Egypt's empire to Carchemish on the Euphrates in the north and beyond the fourth cataract of the Nile in the south. His daughter Hatshepsut, after a regency for her young stepson, became pharaoh in her own right and ruled for over twenty years. Thutmose III, a pharaoh of long reign and many campaigns, conquered large areas of the Near East in campaigns around 1450 BCE, as far as Syria and Mittani. Nubia, which the Egyptians called Kush, was administered through a Viceroy of Kush and supplied gold, ivory and cattle.

Amenhotep III's reign was a period of unprecedented prosperity and artistic splendour, attested by over 250 statues. His son Amenhotep IV changed his name to Akhenaten in the fifth year of his reign and moved the capital to Amarna. Under him the Aten, the sun disk, became the most prominent deity and eventually the only god, though scholars debate whether this was true monotheism. Later Egyptians saw the Amarna Period as an aberration. Tutankhaten came to the throne in 1334 BCE, restored the traditional cults and changed his name to Tutankhamun.

The last two rulers, Ay and Horemheb, rose from the ranks of court officials. Horemheb, a general, died without surviving children and named his vizier as heir, who became Ramesses I, the first pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty. The dynasty had two queens regnant, Hatshepsut and Neferneferuaten, usually identified as Nefertiti, which is unique among indigenous Egyptian dynasties. Nineteenth Dynasty king lists record the dynasty but omit Hatshepsut and the Amarna pharaohs, as repudiation of them had been state policy since Horemheb.
eighth-crusade: Louis IX of France kept his interest in crusading after the failure of the Seventh Crusade, in which the Mamluks captured him, and from 1254 to 1266 he sent aid to the settlements of Outremer. Under Baibars the Mamluks took a number of Frankish towns, including Antioch on 18 May 1268, and attacked Acre often, so that the loss of the whole Kingdom of Jerusalem seemed possible. Charles I of Anjou's victory at Benevento in 1266 brought Sicily under Capetian control, and Pope Clement IV proclaimed a new expedition in January 1266.

Louis decided at some point, probably by 1268, to begin with a campaign against Tunis. His confessor, Geoffrey of Beaulieu, said Louis was convinced that Muhammad I al-Mustansir was ready to convert to Christianity. The 13th-century historian Saba Malaspina believed Charles had persuaded him in order to secure the tribute Tunis's rulers had paid earlier Sicilian monarchs. The precise motive is unknown.

The fleet embarked from Aigues-Mortes on 2 July 1270, led by Florent de Varennes, the first Admiral of France. There was no significant fighting. An epidemic struck the camp near Tunis, and Louis's son John Tristan died on 3 August. Louis died on 25 August of dysentery, and his remains were treated by the mos Teutonicus, rendering the flesh from the bones, so that they could be carried home. His son Philip III, who had come as Count of Orléans, succeeded him.

The Treaty of Tunis was signed on 1 November 1270 by Philip III, Charles I of Anjou and Theobald II of Navarre for the Latin Christians and by al-Mustansir for Tunis. It guaranteed a truce and gave the Christians free trade and the right of monks and priests to live in the city, but no territory changed hands. Charles received one third of a war indemnity and a promise that Hohenstaufen refugees would be expelled.

The Crusaders left soon after. Edward of England arrived the day before they left, and the English returned to Sicily with the rest of Louis's force. On 22 November the combined fleet was destroyed in a storm off Trapani. Edward went on to Acre in April 1271 on what is called Lord Edward's Crusade, the last of the great crusades to the Holy Land. Baibars cancelled his plan to send Egyptian troops against the Franks in Tunis. Troubadours answered the failure with three planhs, songs of lament, for Louis IX.
einbeck: Einbeck lies in the district of Northeim, directly south of the Hube hills, where the Ilme flows into the Leine. The area has been inhabited since the Paleolithic. In the Early Middle Ages a number of villages stood along the Ilme before Einbeck was founded. It lies on the German Timber-Frame Road.

Einbeck is first mentioned on 1 January 1158 in a deed of Friedrich Barbarossa. A collegiate foundation, the stift of St Alexander, grew into an important sanctuary, and across a brook from it a market town developed at the end of the 12th century. It received a town charter in 1252, extended in 1279 by its sovereign, Heinrich Mirabilis. Written evidence for the export of Einbeck beer dates from 1351. The town joined the Hanse in 1368, extending sales from Antwerp to Riga and from Stockholm to Munich, and in the 14th and 15th centuries it was one of the largest cities of northern Germany.

A fire started by an arsonist almost destroyed the town in July 1540. It was rebuilt within about fifteen years, and a second fire in 1549 burned 580 houses. The plague struck in 1597, and in the Thirty Years' War enemy troops occupied the town in 1632 and 1641 and destroyed some hundred houses. Its autonomy shrank when the neighbouring village of Rotenkirchen became the administrative seat of the area.

After 1890 the firm of August Stukenbrok grew into the largest mail-order business in Germany. On 9 April 1945 the city manager handed the town to United States troops without permission from his superiors, and it survived the war physically undamaged.

The historic centre is a nearly complete late medieval half-timbered town, rebuilt after the fire of 1540, with the year of construction often carved into the frames. The Old Town Hall of the 16th century has three towers, and the Minster church of St Alexander is one of the largest Gothic hall churches in northern Germany. Einbecker Blaudruck, a fabric-printing business founded in 1638, is the oldest of its kind still existing in Europe. The town has about 32,000 inhabitants, including 46 villages incorporated since 1971.
einhard: Einhard came from the eastern German-speaking part of the Frankish Kingdom, from a family of landowners of some importance. His parents sent him to be educated by the monks of Fulda, one of the most impressive centres of learning in Frankish lands. Perhaps because his small stature limited his riding and sword-fighting, he concentrated on scholarship, especially mastering Latin. He was accepted into the court of Charlemagne around 791 or 792, where Charlemagne had gathered scholars and set up a royal school led by the Northumbrian scholar Alcuin.

Einhard evidently had talent as a builder and construction manager, and Charlemagne put him in charge of completing several palace complexes, including Aachen and Ingelheim. Although he was on intimate terms with Charlemagne, he never held office in his reign. In 814, when Charlemagne died, his son Louis the Pious made Einhard his private secretary. Einhard retired from court in the spring of 830, during the disputes between Louis and his sons.

He was married to Emma, of whom little is known; she took as active a part as he did, if not more, in managing their property. After her death on 13 December 835 he wrote to a friend that he was reminded of her loss in every action of the household.

He built churches at his estates in Michelstadt and Mulinheim and a basilica at Michelstadt, completed in 827. His servant Ratleic brought from Rome the bones of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, which were later moved to Mulinheim. Between 831 and 834 he founded a Benedictine monastery there and was its abbot until he died at Seligenstadt in 840.

His main work is the Vita Karoli Magni, written between 817 and 830, which gives direct information about Charlemagne's life and character. He relied heavily on the Royal Frankish Annals and took the Roman historian Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars as his model, adapting it for his own purposes. He wrote in praise of Charlemagne, whom he regarded as a foster-father and to whom he owed a debt in life and death.

The work therefore has a degree of bias: he took care to excuse Charlemagne in some matters, omitted others, and glossed over embarrassments such as the morality of the emperor's daughters, though he did not hide his concubines. His other surviving works are a collection of letters, an account of the translation and miracles of Marcellinus and Peter, and On the Adoration of the Cross.
einsatzgruppen: The Einsatzgruppen were formed under SS-Obergruppenführer Reinhard Heydrich. They began as the ad hoc Einsatzkommando that Heydrich formed to secure government buildings and documents after the Anschluss in Austria in March 1938. Two units were stationed in the Sudetenland in October 1938, where they confiscated documents, secured buildings and arrested as many as 10,000 Czech communists and German citizens. From September 1939 the Reich Security Main Office had overall command. For the invasion of Poland, Heydrich re-formed them to travel in the wake of the German armies, with personnel drawn from the SS, the Security Service, the police and the Gestapo.

For the invasion of the Soviet Union four Einsatzgruppen were created, each of 500 to 990 men, about 3,000 in all. Einsatzgruppen A, B and C were attached to Army Groups North, Centre and South, and Einsatzgruppe D to the 11th Army. In a letter of 2 July 1941 Heydrich ordered the execution of senior and middle-ranking Communist Party officials, people's commissars and Jews in party and government posts, and that pogroms begun spontaneously by the local population be quietly encouraged. The Wehrmacht supplied logistical support and took part in the killings.

The largest mass shooting took place on 29 and 30 September 1941 at Babi Yar, a ravine northwest of the centre of Kiev, where 33,771 Jews were murdered in two days. The Jews of Kiev had been told to report to a street corner, and many came laden with possessions, believing they were to be deported. In November 1941 about 25,000 Jews were shot in two days at Rumbula near Riga. Einsatzgruppe A reported to Himmler that it had murdered almost 140,000 people in five months, 136,421 of them Jews.

Historian Raul Hilberg called a renewed wave of killings from December 1941 into the summer of 1942 the second sweep. Himmler came to regard shooting as inefficient and demoralising for the troops, and the killing was transferred increasingly to gas chambers.

Hilberg estimated that the Einsatzgruppen and related units murdered 1.3 million of the 5.5 to 6 million Jews killed in the Holocaust. After the war, 24 senior leaders were prosecuted in the Einsatzgruppen trial of 1947 and 1948, one of the Subsequent Nuremberg Trials held under United States military authority. Fourteen death sentences were handed down, but only four were carried out, on 7 June 1951. Several defendants claimed to have received an order to kill all Soviet Jews before the invasion, but no evidence of such an order has been found. West Germany charged only about 100 former members, and the Ulm Einsatzkommando trial of 1958 brought their crimes to wider public awareness.
einsiedeln-abbey: The history of the abbey begins with Meinrad of Einsiedeln, born in 797 at Sulchen and educated at the abbey school on Reichenau Island. He became a monk and priest, and after attracting attention for reported miracles he set up a hermitage in the Einsiedeln forest in 828, seeking privacy. He was murdered by two robbers in January 861. Other hermits occupied the site over the next eighty years. In 934 Eberhard, formerly Provost of Strassburg, built the abbey and church there and became its first abbot. According to legend, Christ himself consecrated the church in 948 in honour of his mother, and the pilgrimage began as one to the Chapel of the Saviour.

In 965 Emperor Otto I named the third abbot, Gregory, a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, a title his successors held until the empire's dissolution in 1806. After a fire the church was enlarged in 1226, with the lower church built over the Chapel of the Saviour. In the 13th century the pilgrimage became more popular and better organised, and an enthroned Madonna on an abbey seal of 1239 is regarded as the oldest miraculous image. The pilgrimage turned gradually into a Marian one, and its oldest surviving reference dates from the early 14th century. Huldrych Zwingli studied at the abbey, which remained unaffected by the Reformation in Switzerland.

Discipline declined in the early 16th century until Abbot Ludovicus II, who held office from 1526 to 1544, restored stricter observance. Abbot Augustine I led the movement that created the Swiss Congregation of the Order of St. Benedict in 1602. Abbot Maurus rebuilt the church between 1704 and 1719, and the baroque ornamentation was finished in 1734. French revolutionary soldiers occupied the abbey in 1798, ending its status as an independent principality; the monks returned in 1801 and the abbey was reinstated on 19 February 1803 by the Act of Mediation. In the 1840s, fearing suppression, the monks sent a group to southern Indiana, which founded Saint Meinrad Archabbey.

Einsiedeln is a Benedictine monastery and a territorial abbey, so it lies outside any diocese and its abbot governs with the authority of a diocesan bishop. The Black Madonna in the Chapel of Grace draws pilgrims and visitors from across Switzerland and Europe. The library, founded in 934, holds around 230,000 printed books and 1,230 manuscripts, and the abbey received its own printing press in 1664. It also runs a school with a history of over a thousand years. Pope John Paul II consecrated the new high altar in the lower choir on 15 June 1984.
eirikr-hakonarson: The principal sources for Eiríkr's youth are Fagrskinna and Heimskringla. They relate that he was the son of Earl Hákon Sigurðarson and a woman of low birth, and that Hákon cared little for the boy and gave him to a friend to raise. When Eiríkr was eleven or twelve he refused to move his ship from beside Hákon's to make room for Hákon's closest friend Skopti, and Hákon ordered him away. The next winter Eiríkr hunted down Skopti's ship and killed him, his first exploit, commemorated by the skald Eyjólfr dáðaskáld. He then sailed to Denmark, where King Harald Bluetooth gave him the earldom of Romerike and Vingulmark.

A Danish invasion force was defeated at Hjörungavágr in 986, and according to Heimskringla Eiríkr commanded 60 ships there and gave quarter to many Jomsvikings. When Óláfr Tryggvason seized power in 995 Eiríkr was forced into exile in Sweden, where he allied himself with King Olof of Sweden and King Sweyn, whose daughter Gytha he married. He burned Staraya Ladoga, and Soviet archaeologists in the 1980s found evidence of a burning there in the late 10th century. In 1000 he, Sweyn and Olof ambushed Óláfr at Svolder. Eiríkr forced his iron-strengthened ship Járnbarðinn between the last ships of Óláfr's line, and the Norwegian ships were taken one by one until he captured the Long Serpent.

With his brother Sveinn Hákonarson, Eiríkr was grand earl of Norway under Sweyn Forkbeard from 1000 to 1012. Fagrskinna reports good peace and prosperous seasons. In 1014 or 1015 he joined Cnut's invasion of England, which landed at Sandwich in midsummer 1015.
