After Cnut won control of the north he gave Eiríkr Northumbria, and in 1017 Cnut divided England into four, with Northumbria going to Eiríkr.

Eiríkr is not mentioned in English documents after 1023. English sources say Cnut exiled him, but this is unlikely since Norse sources record no return. His successor Siward cannot be confirmed as earl until 1033, so his death falls between 1023 and 1033. Norse sources say he died of a haemorrhage after having his uvula cut, either just before or just after a pilgrimage to Rome.
eisenach: Eisenach lies on the Hörsel river, a tributary of the Werra, at the northern edge of the Thuringian Forest at an elevation of about 220 metres. The terrain is hilly, and mountainous to the south, where the land rises to 460 metres. The town grew up in the Middle Ages at the mouth of the Mariental valley, and from 1949 to 1990 part of its municipal boundary with Hesse formed the inner German border.

The origins of Eisenach are unknown. An 8th-century Frankish settlement near the Petersberg hill is regarded as its nucleus, but no written sources describe that period. According to legend, Louis the Springer began to establish the Wartburg castle above the settlement in 1067. The town was an early capital of Thuringia in the 12th and 13th centuries, and St Elizabeth lived at the court of the Ludowingians here between 1211 and 1228.

Between 1498 and 1501 the young Martin Luther attended the St George's Latin school in Eisenach. In 1521/22 Frederick the Wise hid him at the Wartburg to protect him from the Imperial ban, and there he translated the New Testament from Greek into German, an important step for the Reformation and for a consistent German standard language. Luther called Eisenach a clerical backwater, since it then had 300 monks and nuns per 1,000 inhabitants. The Lutheran Reformation was introduced in 1528, and in 1596 the town became a ducal residence again, for the house of Saxe-Eisenach.

In 1817 the Wartburg Festival brought together students who wanted a more liberal, constitutional state and the unification of Germany. Industry began early, and railways reached the town in 1847, 1849 and 1858. The Automobilwerk Eisenach was founded in 1896, and in the German Democratic Republic the Wartburg car was produced there.

Eisenach has about 42,000 inhabitants and is the main urban centre of western Thuringia. The Wartburg castle has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999. The Bachhaus, opened in 1906, was the first museum in the world dedicated to Johann Sebastian Bach, who was born in the town in 1685. The villa districts built for factory owners between 1850 and 1914 are among the largest of their type in Europe.
eisenerz: Eisenerz, whose name means iron ore, is a market town and old mining town in the Austrian state of Styria, about 109 kilometres north-west of Graz by rail. It lies in the deep Erzbach Valley, with the Pfaffenstein to the east, the Kaiserschild to the west and the Erzberg, the Ore Mountain, to the south. The town has a medieval fortified church, a Gothic building founded by Rudolph of Habsburg in the 13th century and rebuilt in the 16th. A few miles to the north-west stand Leopoldstein Castle and the small Leopoldstein Lake, whose dark green water is about 30 metres deep.
Copper smelting was a major activity at Eisenerz from the 15th century BCE to the 13th century BCE. Documents show the mines of the Erzberg being worked as early as the 12th century CE.

At the turn of the century the Erzberg furnished such rich ore that it was quarried in the open air like stone in the summer months. The mines employed two or three thousand workers in summer and about half as many in winter, and produced some 800,000 tons of iron a year. The Erzberg Railway, about 23 kilometres long and built on Abt's rack-and-pinion system, linked the town to the mines and descended to Vordernberg, a centre of the iron trade on the south side of the mountain. The town then had twenty-five furnaces producing iron and especially steel of high quality.

During World War II a subcamp of the Mauthausen concentration camp, Gsollgraben, stood next to the Erzberg and supplied slave labour to local industry. Its exact location and extent were first reconstructed in 2020 by a team of scholars at TU Graz.
eisleben: Eisleben was first mentioned in 997 as a market called Islebia, and in 1180 as a town. It is divided into the old town, the Altstadt, and the Neustadt, created in the fourteenth century for the town's miners. The counts of Mansfeld governed the area until the eighteenth century. In the Reformation Count Hoyer VI of Mansfeld-Vorderort stayed loyal to the Catholic faith, while the Mittelort and Hinterort branches of the family sided with Martin Luther. Count Albert VII of Mansfeld-Hinterort signed the Protestant Augsburg Confession in 1530 and joined the Schmalkaldic League. The German Peasants' War devastated the area.

In 1574 the surviving Mansfeld counts agreed with the Elector of Saxony to repay the family's large debts, though some properties were forfeited by 1579. The Hinterort branches died out in 1666 and the Mansfeld-Vorderort line in 1780, when Eisleben came directly under the Electorate of Saxony. After the Napoleonic Wars the Congress of Vienna assigned it to the Kingdom of Prussia. In 1947 it became part of the new state of Saxony-Anhalt, and from 1952 it belonged to the Bezirk Halle in the German Democratic Republic. It rejoined the re-created Saxony-Anhalt after reunification in 1990. On 6 June 1927 the American aviator Clarence D. Chamberlin landed in a wheat field outside the town, completing the first transatlantic passenger flight.

Martin Luther was born in Eisleben on 10 November 1483. His father, Hans Luther, was a miner, like many in the town, and the family moved to Mansfeld when Luther was a year old. He lived in Wittenberg for most of his life, but he preached his last sermon in Eisleben and died there in 1546. The town took steps to preserve its Luther memorials as early as 1689 and pioneered heritage tourism. In 1997 Luther's birth house and death house were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site, together with the Luther sites in Wittenberg. Luther was baptised in the town's church of Saint Peter and Paul, whose original font survives, and he preached his last sermons at Saint Andreas Church, both still in use.

At Helfta, now a district of the town, the counts of Mansfeld founded a monastery in 1258. It became known for powerful and mystical abbesses, among them Gertrude of Hackeborn, Gertrude the Great and Mechtild of Magdeburg, and was sometimes called the crown of German convents. It was destroyed in 1342, rebuilt the next year and secularised after 1542. Cistercian nuns have lived in the restored cloister since about 1999. The town had 22,668 inhabitants in 2020.
ekkathat: Ekkathat was born in 1718, in the reign of his uncle King Thaisa, a son of Prince Phon of the Front Palace, the later King Borommakot, and his consort Phlap. People of his time called him Khun Luang Khiruean, the king with skin disease, because of his chloasma. After the chief minister's death in 1753 he sided with his brothers Thammathibet and Uthumphon against the faction of three half-brothers known as the Three Princes. He was a Buddhist monk at Wat Lamut when his father lay dying in April 1758, and at the age of forty he left the monkhood to take the throne, being crowned in early June 1758.

His reign began with a plot: in December 1758 the chief minister and other conspirators, offended by the king's in-laws, recruited the monk Prince Thepphiphit to restore Uthumphon, and Thepphiphit was later exiled to Ceylon on a Dutch ship. In 1760 King Alaungpaya of Burma invaded with 30,000 men. Ekkathat, misinformed that the enemy was coming from three directions, divided his forces, and when the Burmese took Suphanburi in March the people begged Uthumphon to leave his temple and lead the defence, so that Ekkathat had to share his authority.

In 1764 King Hsinbyushin sent two armies of 20,000 men each, under Nemyo Thihapate from the north and Maha Nawrahta from the west. Ekkathat, who had been on pilgrimage to the Buddha's Footprint at Saraburi, ordered guns placed on the walls but made no serious reforms, and he called the governors of outlying cities to defend the capital, leaving their provinces to the invaders. The Burmese reached Ayutthaya in January 1766 and stayed through the rainy season, growing their own rice outside the flooded walls.

When the city fell, the Burmese killed its people indiscriminately and burnt its palaces, temples and houses. Ekkathat fled with his royal pages. According to Burmese chronicles he was shot by a random gunshot while escaping through a west gate; Siamese chronicles say he hid for more than ten days at Ban Chik Woods, next to Wat Sangkhawat, and died of starvation, his body being found there by a monk.
el-alamein: El Alamein is a city in the northern Matrouh Governorate of Egypt, on the Mediterranean Sea. It lies 106 kilometres west of Alexandria and 300 kilometres north-west of Cairo. The city is divided into three main areas: El Alamein, Cidi and the village of Tal El Eis. It has a hot desert climate, slightly less hot than the rest of Egypt because of the prevailing winds from the Mediterranean. Its economy rests on petroleum and on tourist areas with hotels and resorts, such as the town of Marina.

Two important battles of the Second World War were fought in the area. In the First Battle of El Alamein, from 1 to 27 July 1942, the Allies blunted the advance of Axis troops on Alexandria and stopped the Italian and German forces that were trying to outflank their position. In the Second Battle of El Alamein, from 23 October to 4 November 1942, Allied forces broke the Axis line and forced the Axis troops back to Tunisia.

Winston Churchill, then British Prime Minister, said of the victory: "Now this is not the end, it is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning." After the war he wrote: "Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein, we never had a defeat."

Military cemeteries lie on Tel el-Eisa Hill outside the town. The German cemetery is an ossuary built in the style of a medieval fortress, and the Italian War Memorial cemetery contains 5,200 graves. There is also a Greek cemetery at El Alamein. The Commonwealth Alamein Memorial and its attached war cemetery, maintained by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, hold the graves of soldiers from various countries who fought on the Allied side. Each summer many Egyptians travel to El Alamein and the North Coast to escape the heat of other cities.
el-alto: El Alto, Spanish for the high one and Patamarka in Aymara, lies next to La Paz in Pedro Domingo Murillo Province, on the Altiplano highlands. It has a cold climate, with cool days and nights that often approach or fall below 0 °C in winter. The El Alto–La Paz metropolitan area, formed by La Paz, El Alto, Achocalla, Viacha and Mecapaca, is the most populous urban area of Bolivia, with about 2.2 million people. The city contains the international airport that serves La Paz, and its autonomous government identifies 14 districts.

On 23 October 1548 Alonso de Mendoza, arriving from Laja, paused at the edge of the plateau at the spot now known as La Ceja and looked down on the valley of Chuquiago Marka, where the city of Nuestra Señora de La Paz would be founded. The Spaniards called the area the Altos de Nuestra Señora de La Paz, and it became a main route for migrants towards Chuquiago. The dry plain above La Paz was largely uninhabited until 1903, when new railways from Lake Titicaca and Arica reached the rim of the canyon. The La Paz terminus, railyards and depots were built there along with a settlement of railway workers, and a spur line down into the canyon opened in 1905.

An airfield was built in 1925 as a base for the new air force and attracted more settlement, and the first elementary school opened in 1939. El Alto began to grow tremendously in the 1950s, when the settlement was connected to La Paz's water supply, before which all water had been brought from La Paz in tanker vehicles, and building land in the canyon grew scarce and expensive.

Migration from the countryside to the La Paz region began with the rural reform of 1952 and increased in the 2000s. In March 1985 an administrative reform separated the district of El Alto from the city of La Paz, a date kept as the city's founding day. El Alto was incorporated as a city in 1987 and became the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of El Alto in 1994.

El Alto is a municipality within Murillo Province, governed by a mayor elected for five years and a municipal council of 11 members. Three lines of the Mi Teleférico cable car system connect it with central La Paz. A Neo-Andean architectural style, built from the mid-2000s onward, gives the city a distinct appearance, and a large open-air market operates in it. The city has long been a centre of the Bolivian gas conflict, and from 2003 access from La Paz to the airport and to oil and gas supplies was frequently blocked by protesting social leaders.
el-badi-palace: The name el-Badi', usually rendered the Incomparable, is one of the 99 Names of God in Islam and had also been used for a pavilion of the caliph's palace at Cordoba. The building stood on the northern edge of the Almohad kasbah of Marrakesh, where the earlier Saadian sultan Moulay Abdallah al-Ghalib had already built a palace. Its construction was probably paid for by the large ransom the Portuguese paid after the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578, and the sultan's wealth also came from the sugar trade with Europe and, after 1590, from control of the trans-Saharan routes.

The chronicler al-Ifrani says the work began in December 1578 and lasted fifteen years. The historian Gaston Deverdun pointed out that a Portuguese plan of 1585 already shows a finished palace, while al-Mansur was still buying marble in 1602, so the main building was probably done by the early 1580s and the decoration went on until his death.

The El Badi was a reception palace within a larger Saadian royal complex. It was built round a courtyard of 135 by 110 metres with a central pool of 90.4 by 21.7 metres, four sunken gardens and four further basins, a riad garden on a vast scale. A pavilion with a great cupola stood on each side; the western one, the Pavilion of the Fifty, served as the throne hall, with a fountain fed through silver figures of animals. The plan appears to develop that of the Court of the Lions in the Alhambra. The walls were of rammed earth covered with carved stucco, marble and zellij, and the Italian marble columns were traded for their weight in sugar.

After al-Mansur's death in 1603 the palace was not kept up. The first Alaouite sultan, Moulay Rashid, lived there briefly in 1668 and 1669. Its stripping probably went on over a long time, and Saadian elements, most likely from the palace, are found in buildings across Morocco, such as the Mausoleum of Moulay Isma'il in Meknes. The ruins now hold the 12th-century Almoravid minbar of the Kutubiyya Mosque.
el-cid: Rodrigo Díaz was born about 1043 at Vivar, a village some ten kilometres north of Burgos. His father, Diego Laínez, was a courtier and cavalryman. He was brought up at the court of Ferdinand the Great and served Ferdinand's son Sancho II of Castile, becoming commander and royal standard-bearer when Sancho came to the throne in 1065. The name El Cid comes from the Arabic sayyid, lord or master. Historians have found no contemporary record calling him Cid, though documents he signed himself use the cognomen Campeador, probably gained in Sancho's wars against his brothers.

Sancho was murdered in 1072 and the throne passed to his brother Alfonso VI. The Cantar de mio Cid says Rodrigo made Alfonso swear publicly at Santa Gadea in Burgos that he had no part in the plot, but the more reliable Historia Roderici does not mention it. In 1079 he beat the army of Granada and García Ordóñez at the Battle of Cabra, where Muslim troops hailed him as Sayyidi. He was then exiled, most likely because of an incursion into Toledo, held by Alfonso's vassal, and from 1081 served the kings of Zaragoza.

After the Almoravids defeated Alfonso at the Battle of Sagrajas in 1086, Alfonso recalled him, but he soon returned to Zaragoza. He defeated Berenguer Ramon II at the Battle of Tébar in 1090 and besieged Valencia after an uprising in October 1092. By May 1094 he had carved out a principality on the Mediterranean coast, ruling officially in Alfonso's name but in practice independently, over a city both Christian and Muslim.

In 1094 he inflicted on the Almoravids their first major defeat, on the plains of Caurte. His only son, Diego Rodríguez, died fighting them at Consuegra in 1097. Rodrigo died on 10 July 1099. His wife, Jimena Díaz, held Valencia until 1102, when the Almoravids took it, and she took his body to Burgos, where it now lies in the cathedral. A legend holds that she set his corpse on his horse Babieca to hearten the troops. The Cantar de mio Cid presents him as the ideal medieval knight, and Pierre Corneille's tragicomedy Le Cid drew on his story.
el-djem: Like almost all Roman settlements in ancient Tunisia, Thysdrus was built on a former Punic settlement. In a less arid climate than today's it prospered as an important centre of olive oil production and export, and it became the seat of a Christian bishopric, now listed among the Catholic Church's titular sees. By the early 3rd century, when the amphitheatre was built, it rivaled Hadrumetum, modern Sousse, as the second city of Roman North Africa after Carthage.

A revolt that began there in 238 failed. After Gordian committed suicide in his villa near Carthage, Roman troops loyal to the emperor Maximinus Thrax sacked the city. It appears on the 4th-century Peutinger Map. Recent excavations point to a richer economy than a simple commercial centre: remains of metallurgical, bone-working, moulding and sculpture workshops, and many terracotta statuettes and moulds, suggest that ceramics mattered locally, though no pottery workshop has yet been identified. Surveys of the countryside found rural settlements and small towns, and signs of ecological degradation from long, intensive land use. How far olive growing extended remains debated, since no ancient oil mills have been found.

The amphitheatre could seat 35,000 spectators. Only the Colosseum in Rome, with about 50,000, and the ruined theatre of Capua were larger. It was built under the proconsul Gordian, who was acclaimed emperor at Thysdrus about 238, and was used mainly for gladiator shows and small-scale chariot races. It stayed more or less whole until the 17th century, when its stones were used to build the nearby village of El Djem and were carried to the Great Mosque in Kairouan. During struggles with the Ottomans, cannon were used to flush rebels out of it. It was declared a World Heritage Site in 1979 and hosts an annual symphony festival.

Drifting sand has preserved much of the market city and the suburban villas around it, and some floor mosaics have been published, one showing the goddess Africa. Little field archaeology has been attempted, though aerial photographs have revealed a large racetrack stadium. The dry climate has preserved writings on papyrus. El Djem, in Mahdia Governorate, had 21,544 inhabitants at the 2014 census.
el-dorado: Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, saw golden ornaments worn by some inhabitants and became convinced that the lands held great wealth. European accounts drew on older legends of rich utopias across the Atlantic, such as the Isles of the Blessed and the Isle of Seven Cities. Ambrosius Dalfinger, a governor of Venezuela employed by the Welser banking family of Augsburg, looted golden trinkets around Lake Maracaibo from 1529 and was told they came from a tribe in the mountains.

No written reference to a place or person called El Dorado has been found before 1541, apart from a statement by Gonzalo de la Peña in testimony of July 1539. In 1541 the historian Oviedo recorded a story current among the Spaniards of Quito about a native ruler who went about covered in gold dust and washed it off each night. He did not say where this ruler lived. By the 1580s the story was firmly tied to the Muisca of the Colombian highlands, whose territory Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada had conquered in 1537.

Gonzalo Pizarro left Quito in February 1541 to find the golden king's country, with Francisco Orellana as second-in-command, and had local people tortured and killed when they could not guide him. In 1550 Charles V suspended all expeditions for nearly a decade. In 1560 Pedro de Ursúa set out down the Amazon with 370 Spaniards; on 1 January 1561 Lope de Aguirre led a mutiny that killed Ursúa, and the search was abandoned.

Antonio de Berrio, bound by his father-in-law Quesada's will to keep searching, crossed the Orinoco in 1584 and again in 1587, and heard of a great lake called Manoa in the Guianas. In March 1595 Sir Walter Raleigh reached Trinidad, captured Berrio at San José on 7 April and announced his own plan to find the golden city. Reports of a lake called Parime kept it on 17th-century maps.

Two Jesuits crossing the area in 1674 found no trace of Lake Parime. In 1800 Alexander von Humboldt reported that the tribes used the word for any large body of water and suggested that seasonal flooding around Lake Amucu lay behind the legend. After Robert Schomburgk visited Lake Amucu in 1836 the lake vanished from maps. El Dorado stayed in European culture as a symbol of fabulous wealth, appearing as an idealised society in Voltaire's Candide of 1759 and in Werner Herzog's 1972 film Aguirre, the Wrath of God. Objects tied to the tradition, including the Muisca raft, are in the Museo del Oro in Bogotá.
el-escorial: El Escorial stands at the foot of Mount Abantos in the Sierra de Guadarrama, about 45 kilometres north-west of Madrid. Philip II chose this austere site and ordered a grand edifice there to commemorate the Spanish victory over Henry II of France at the Battle of St Quentin in 1557. One of his personal aspirations was to be both a monk and a monarch, and the result was a three-storey, stronghold-like structure serving as royal residence and monastery.

Philip appointed Juan Bautista de Toledo architect-royal in 1559. Toledo had spent most of his career in Rome, where he had worked on St Peter's Basilica. Philip also intended the complex to be a necropolis for his parents, Charles I and Isabella of Portugal, for himself and for his descendants, and a centre of studies for the Counter-Reformation. Its design gave rise to a new style of Spanish Renaissance architecture, the Herrerian style.

The basilica of San Lorenzo el Real was first designed as a Latin cross, but Juan de Herrera changed the plan to a Greek cross with a full circular dome over the crossing. The dome, nearly 100 metres high, rests on four heavy granite piers with simple Doric pilasters, unlike the columns supporting the dome of St Peter's. Philip's own rooms lie beside the high altar, and include a window from which he could watch mass from his bed when gout incapacitated him.

The Royal Library was meant to be a monumental work of art, designed by Toledo and Herrera, who also designed its shelves. It was the first library on the continent to break with medieval design, and Domenico Fontana drew on it for the Vatican Library. Philip also gave the monastery some 7,500 relics in 570 reliquaries designed by Herrera.

The Pantheon of the Kings holds twenty-six marble sepulchres with the remains of kings and queens regnant of the Habsburg and Bourbon dynasties from Charles I onward, apart from Philip V and Ferdinand VI. Established with a community of Hieronymite monks, the monastery is now run by the Order of Saint Augustine. UNESCO declared the site a World Heritage Site on 2 November 1984.
el-fasher: El Fasher, also written Al-Fashir, is the capital of the North Darfur State, in the Darfur region of western Sudan, at an elevation of about 700 metres, 195 kilometres north-east of Nyala. It began as a caravan post and serves as an agricultural marketing point for the cereals and fruits grown in the surrounding region. Roads link it to Geneina and Umm Keddada. The climate is hot and arid, with a cool dry season from October to February, a hot season from March to May, and a short wet season from June to September that brings nearly all of the year's rainfall of about 210 millimetres.

The city's origins date to the late 18th century. Abdul Rahman el-Rashid, Sultan of Darfur, moved his itinerant court, the fashir, to a site called Rahad Tendelti while campaigning in northern Darfur, a vital area for settlement and grazing. The site was eventually renamed Al-Fashir, and a town grew up around the sultan's palace grounds. It fell to the British during the invasion of Darfur in November 1916.

Al Fashir University was created in 1990 by decree and opened in February 1991. Later the nearby camps of Abu Shouk and Al Salam for displaced people received United Nations aid, and the city experienced an economic and population boom, with rents and retail sales rising and the number of petrol stations tripling in three years. The city had 264,734 residents in 2006.

A series of sieges began in the city in April 2023, when civil war broke out in Sudan. The Rapid Support Forces besieged El Fasher from April 2024, and the United Nations warned that its civilians faced starvation and constant danger as the besiegers indiscriminately bombarded public areas such as the central marketplace. The city was taken by the Rapid Support Forces on 27 October 2025, and widespread killings and rape were reported after its fall.
el-geneina: Geneina, also written Al-Junaynah, is a city in West Darfur in the Dar Masalit region of Sudan. Its Arabic name means the little garden, a diminutive related to the word for paradise, and was given for its gardens, orchards and green fields. The name is also tied to Sultan Muhammad Bahr al-Din, the first to rule the city, nicknamed Enduka, a Masalit word implying extreme generosity. The city has a hot semi-arid climate, with a short wet season from mid-June to late September and a dry season covering the other nine months. Its economy rests on agriculture, pastoralism, trade and services; hashab forests near the city supply gum arabic, and cotton, sorghum, sesame and fruit are grown.

Geneina joined British Sudan at the end of 1919 through the Gilani Agreement, signed between the Masalit Sultanate and the United Kingdom. It has the largest group of Masalit people in Sudan and Darfur. During the war in Darfur they were heavily targeted, and the genocide against the Masalit drew the attention of the UN.

In early 2023 tensions grew between the Sudanese Armed Forces under Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces under Hemedti. On 15 April 2023 the Rapid Support Forces attacked Sudanese forces in Khartoum, Merowe and several cities of Darfur, among them Geneina. Clashes between Arabs and non-Arabs on the Chadian border at Foro-Baranga on 13 April had already left 24 people dead. The city came under siege by the Rapid Support Forces and allied militias by early June, and they took control on 22 June. Up to 15,000 people were reported killed in Geneina in what are called the Masalit massacres, mainly Masalit and other non-Arab people.

Geneina is the capital of West Darfur state. Many tribes live there, among them the Mahamid, Hausa, Zaghawa, Tama, Fur, Misseriya, Erenga and Baygo, and the Masalit are the most prominent, administering the area under the native administration system. The city has the University of El Geneina, with a College of Medicine, and a highway leads to Nyala.
el-greco: Doménikos Theotokópoulos, known as El Greco, was born on 1 October 1541, in either the village of Fodele or Candia on Crete, then part of the Republic of Venice. His father, Geṓrgios Theotokópoulos, was a merchant and tax collector. El Greco trained as an icon painter of the Cretan school, a leading centre of post-Byzantine art, and a document of 1563 already calls him a master, which implies that he belonged to the painters' guild of Candia and probably ran his own workshop.

Most scholars agree that El Greco went to Venice around 1567. A letter from the miniaturist Giulio Clovio calls him a disciple of Titian, and he took elements of Mannerism and of the Venetian Renaissance from artists including Tintoretto and Titian. In 1570 he moved to Rome, where he opened a workshop and, on Clovio's recommendation, was received as a guest at the Palazzo Farnese.

In 1577 he moved to Madrid and then to Toledo, the religious capital of Spain. Philip II of Spain was then struggling to find painters for the monastery-palace of El Escorial. Through his friendship with Luis de Castilla, whose father was dean of the cathedral, El Greco won his first large commissions in Toledo, among them nine paintings for the church of Santo Domingo el Antiguo, finished by September 1579, and El Espolio. He lived and worked in Toledo until his death on 7 April 1614.

El Greco gave imagination and intuition priority and discarded classicist ideas of measure and proportion. He held that colour mattered more than form. When Francisco Pacheco visited him in 1611 he reported that El Greco liked colours crude and unmixed, and believed in constant repainting. He also designed whole altars as architect and sculptor.

His contemporaries found his style puzzling, and the generations after his death, preferring the early Baroque, thought him incomprehensible and left him no important followers. Modern scholars regard him as so individual that he belongs to no conventional school, and see his influence in Velázquez and Goya. The number of works that are his own has been disputed: Wethey reduced the number to 285 authentic works, where José Camón Aznar had attributed between 787 and 829.
el-jadida: El Jadida is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, in the province of El Jadida in the Casablanca-Settat region, 96 kilometres south of Casablanca. An anchorage appears to have existed at the site throughout the Middle Ages and in ancient times, and a tradition traces the settlement to Phoenician founders in the 5th century BCE. The name Mazighan was first documented by the 11th-century Arab geographer al-Bakri. Over the centuries the place has also been called al-Breyja, Mazagão, al-Mahdouma and Mazagan.

In 1502 the Portuguese captain Jorge de Mello landed here, allegedly driven by a storm, and he and his crew took refuge in an abandoned tower called al-Briya. King Manuel gave permission for a fortress in 1505, but when the Portuguese army passed on its way to take Azemmour in 1513 it found only the old tower. In the summer of 1514 the Portuguese built a rectangular citadel with four towers at the more accessible Mazighan, designed by the brothers Diogo and Francisco de Arruda, and the place became known as Mazagão.

The Sa'dids began expelling the Portuguese from coastal fortresses, most significantly from Santa Cruz, present-day Agadir, in 1541. King João III then ordered the evacuation of Azemmour and Safi and concentrated on Mazagão, which was expanded in 1541 into the larger walled fortress that stands today. Portugal held it until 1769, when it abandoned Mazagão, its last territory in Morocco, destroying the Governor's Bastion. Most of the Portuguese inhabitants were sent to Brazil, where they founded Nova Mazagão, now Mazagão in the state of Amapá. Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah took the city over and it stood largely empty, called al-Mahdouma, the Ruined.

Under Sultan Abd al-Rahman, who reigned from 1822 to 1859, a mosque was built and damaged parts were rebuilt. In 1820 the city was renamed al-Jadida, the New, and it soon outgrew Azemmour, with a Jewish community taking part in its revival. After the French Protectorate began in 1912 it was developed as a tourist resort, with a casino by the 1930s, while Casablanca became the country's main port.

The fortress is star-shaped, about 250 by 300 metres, a response to Renaissance artillery, with massive walls averaging about 8 metres high and 10 metres thick. Its bastions are named for the Angel, St Sebastian, St Antoine and the Holy Ghost. Within stand the citadel, the Church of the Assumption and a Manueline cistern, converted to that use in 1541, whose floor is covered by a thin layer of water. The Portuguese Fortified City of Mazagan was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. An industrial complex at Jorf Lasfar, 20 kilometres to the south, processes phosphate and has been developed since the 1980s.
el-kurru: El-Kurru lies between the 3rd and 4th cataracts of the Nile, about 1.6 km west of the river, in what is now Northern state, Sudan. It was the first of the three royal cemeteries of the Kushite kings of Napata, Egypt's 25th Dynasty; later rulers were buried at Nuri. The site is divided into three parts by two wadis. The central part, apparently the oldest, holds tumulus tombs, rock-cut pits under circular mounds of gravel and rubble like the burials of the C-Group and Kerma, while rows of pyramids stand to the east and the queens' pyramids lie across the southern wadi.

The cemetery was used mainly from about 860 to 650 BCE. George Reisner dated its earliest tomb to the time of Sheshonq I; some scholars, such as Hakem and Török, place the first burials at the end of the Twentieth Dynasty, about 1070 BCE, while others, among them Kendall, broadly follow Reisner. The tombs grew from round mounds to square structures with offering chapels and then to pyramids. Piye's tomb (Ku.17), the first with a known name, about 750 BCE, has a vaulted chamber both rock-cut and built of masonry, and the tombs of Tantamani and Queen Qalhata are painted with scenes of the Egyptian underworld.

About 120 metres from the queens' pyramids, four rows of graves held the horses of Piye, Shabaka, Shebitku and Tantamani, buried upright with all their trappings. In the mid-4th century BCE an unnamed king built the largest pyramid of the site (Ku.1), which appears unfinished and unused. Almost every tomb was later robbed. In the medieval period, under the Christian kingdom of Makuria, a walled settlement stood here until about 1200, and Christian Nubians carved monograms, Christian symbols and many boats into pyramid Ku.1.

Reisner excavated the site in 1918 and 1919, and his assistant Dows Dunham published the report in 1950. Work resumed in 2013 under Geoff Emberling and Rachael J. Dann, with Sudan's National Council for Antiquities and Museums and the Qatar Sudan Archaeological Project.
el-lahun: The ancient name was rꜣ-ḥn.t, the mouth of the canal, and in Ptolemaic Egypt the place was Ptolemais Hormos. The pyramid of Senusret II has a core of stone walls filled with mudbrick and stands on a terrace cut from sloping ground. Mastabas, probably for members of the court, lie on its north side, with a subsidiary pyramid believed from its inscription to be that of Queen Atmuneferu. Cemeteries lie between pyramid and town, and the valley temple of the king's mortuary cult now lies under fields.

The town stood about 1.1 km from the pyramid at the desert's edge. It was laid out on a grid inside mudbrick walls, and a later wall set off a western third of rows of small single-room houses. The eastern part held medium and small houses and seven mansions of about 2,700 square metres, with granaries that could feed the whole town. A raised building called the acropolis was most likely the mayor's.

The site was lived in from the Middle Kingdom into the late Thirteenth Dynasty and again in the New Kingdom. Petrie, who coined the name Kahun, mapped the town and found the pyramid's entrance in 1889–1890, and returned in 1920. Ludwig Borchardt recorded the architecture in 1899 and found thousands of temple papyri, Nicholas B. Millet worked there with the University of Toronto from 1989 to 1997, and a Hungarian team under Zoltan Horvath works there now.

The papyri, about 1,000 fragments, deal with law, medicine, religion, astronomy, temple business and town affairs, including census lists and cases of debt. One records a Sothic date, month 8, day 16 of a year 7, which lets Egyptologists anchor the Middle Kingdom chronology on the seventh year of Senusret III. Seals on boxes, jars and bags give the names and titles of their owners. In 2009 Abdel Rahman el-Aydi and his team uncovered dozens of mummies dating from the 12th Dynasty to the 18th Dynasty in painted coffins near the pyramid, some later ones inscribed with texts from the Book of the Dead.
el-mirador: El Mirador lies in the north of the department of El Petén in Guatemala, within the Mirador-Calakmul Karst Basin. Its civic centre covers some 26 square kilometres and holds several thousand structures, with monumental architecture from 10 to 72 metres high. The region's seasonal swamps, called bajos, made its growth possible. Because tropical-forest soil holds few nutrients, the Maya imported mud from the swamps by the thousand tonnes to make terraces for farming, raised the soil's pH with lime, and added fresh mud when the ground was depleted. They grew corn, squash, beans, cacao, cotton and palms.

The site flourished from about the 6th century BCE to the 1st century CE and reached its height from the 3rd century BCE. It has about 35 triadic structures, large platforms topped with three summit pyramids, among them El Tigre at 55 metres and La Danta, which is about 72 metres tall with a volume of 2,800,000 cubic metres. Most buildings were faced with cut stone and decorated with large stucco masks of Maya deities. The archaeologist Carlos Morales-Aguilar finds alignments suggesting the city was planned from its foundation. Raised causeways, the sacbeob, 20 to 50 metres wide, joined its compounds and linked it to Nakbe, 12 kilometres away, and El Tintal, 20 kilometres away.

By about 150 CE El Mirador was abandoned, as were nearly all major sites in the area. A wall 3 to 8 metres high had been built around much of its West Group, which suggests a perceived threat. Soil erosion from deforestation may have played a part, since burning trees to make lime stucco needed great quantities of wood, and sterile clay 2 to 3 metres thick buried the nutrient-rich mud of the bajos. Around 700 CE parts of the site were reoccupied on a modest scale by scribes and artists; the Mirador Basin is the only known source of codex-style ceramics. By about 900 CE the area was again nearly completely abandoned.

Claudio Urrutia surveyed part of the basin in 1885, and Ian Graham made the first map in 1962. A detailed project began in 1978 under Bruce Dahlin and Ray Matheny and found that much of the construction predated the great Classic cities such as Tikal and Uaxactun. Richard D. Hansen began major investigation and conservation programmes in 2003, and he thinks the more than 45 mapped sites of the basin may have formed the earliest well-defined political state in Mesoamerica. The site's remote location has kept it from becoming a popular tourist destination.
el-nino: El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a single climate phenomenon that recurs in three phases: neutral, La Niña and El Niño. It involves fluctuations in sea surface temperature over the tropical Pacific and an accompanying atmospheric oscillation in surface air pressure between the eastern and western tropical Pacific. The switching between phases is irregular but cycles approximately every two to seven years. On average the tropical East Pacific is roughly 8 to 10 °C cooler than the West Pacific.

In an El Niño the trade winds weaken, warm water surges east and upwelling of cold water off South America is reduced or stops. A La Niña is the opposite, with an especially strong Walker circulation and eastern Pacific surface temperatures below average. Close to half of all years fall within neutral periods.

Jacob Bjerknes identified the close relationship between ocean temperatures and the strength of the trade winds in 1969. He proposed that the system was a positive feedback, in which changes in the ocean and the atmosphere reinforce each other, a process now called the Bjerknes feedback. He also tied it to an east–west overturning cell in the atmosphere that he named the Walker Circulation after Gilbert Walker, who had discovered the Southern Oscillation in the early twentieth century. The strength of the Southern Oscillation is measured by an index based on the difference in surface air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin. Variants have since been recognised, among them a Central Pacific form called Modoki, and the exact mechanisms of the oscillation are still being studied.

Evidence for El Niño events exists from the early Holocene, about 10,000 years ago, and coral about 13,000 years old carries chemical signatures of the warming and rain they bring. Events have occurred at two- to seven-year intervals for at least the past 300 years, though most were weak. Typical effects include below-average rainfall over Indonesia and northern South America and above-average rainfall in southeastern South America, eastern equatorial Africa and the southern United States.

Along the coasts of northern Peru and Ecuador it brings very wet weather and major flooding when the event is strong. Reduced upwelling hurts fishing, and developing countries that depend on agriculture and fishing are most affected. The events of 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16 caused widespread forest fires in the Amazon and Borneo. Cases of El Niño-type events in both the Pacific and Atlantic at once have been linked to severe famines caused by monsoon failure.
el-oro-province: El Oro is the southernmost of Ecuador's coastal provinces. To the north and east it borders the provinces of Guayas, Azuay and Loja, and to the west and south it is limited by the Pacific Ocean and the Peruvian Tumbes Region. It is divided into 14 cantons and includes the Jambelí Islands, the island of Santa Clara and the petrified forest of the Puyango River.

The Inca inhabited the area when Spanish settlement began in 1549. The Spanish found gold there, mined it and carried it to Spain. The mining was done by Indigenous slaves held captive mainly in the late 16th and 17th centuries, in the village of Zaruma, to which Philip II of Spain granted the title Villa de Sant Antonio del Zerro de Oro de Zaruma. An earthquake in January 1749 destroyed the mining area, and a local rebellion stopped the mining until the Spanish agreed to let the native people benefit from it. Spain imported gold from the area until independence in 1820.

After 1820 Ecuador emerged as an independent nation. In 1882 the province of El Oro was formed from the villages of Zaruma, Machala and Santa Rosa, with Zaruma as capital, and was named for its gold. Two years later the capital moved to Machala. Mining continued under companies that now paid taxes on the gold they took. As gold mining fell in value, the province became the major banana-growing area of Ecuador. Peru invaded and occupied most of it in the Ecuadorian-Peruvian War of 1941.

The economy rests mainly on exports of bananas and shrimp, with cacao and coffee as other crops. The population was 600,659 at the census of 2010, of whom 81.6 percent were mestizo, 7.8 percent white and 6.9 percent Afro-Ecuadorian.
el-pueblo-unido-jamas-sera-vencido: According to Sergio Ortega Alvarado, he composed the song after hearing a young man shout the phrase as he walked home through Santiago in June 1973. It was recorded for the first time in Chile at a large Quilapayún concert on the Alameda in Santiago, three months before the coup of Augusto Pinochet overthrew Salvador Allende and began the military dictatorship. Shortly before the concert Allende had appointed Ortega Cultural Ambassador of the Popular Unity government, a post he briefly shared with Víctor Jara, who was killed days after the coup. The first official release was on the live album Primer festival internacional de la canción popular, published by the DICAP label in June 1973, which Quilapayún closed with this song and "Las ollitas".

With Ortega's "Venceremos", the song is among the most successful of the Nueva canción chilena, or New Chilean Song, movement. It has a marching rhythm, and its chorus is a shout or slogan accompanied only by percussion. In the years after the coup it appeared on many albums, chiefly by Quilapayún and Inti-Illimani, who lived in exile in France and Italy respectively until the dictatorship ended, more than fifteen years later.

The song has been used in protests around the world, most with no direct link to the Chilean coup or to Latin America, and its words have been adapted or translated into many languages. In 1975 the American pianist Frederic Rzewski composed The People United Will Never Be Defeated!, a set of 36 piano variations on the theme. Iranian revolutionaries used the melody for a Persian song, "Barpakhiz", in 1979. In Argentina it was revived at the Resistance March of 1983 with new words demanding that the disappeared be returned, and the phrase was chanted at the White Night riots in San Francisco in 1979.

Others took up the words in later decades: the Ukrainian band GreenJolly paraphrased them in 2004 in the first days of the Orange Revolution, and a Cantonese version was played in the Hong Kong protests of 2019 and 2020. During the Latin American protests that began in Chile in 2019 the slogan became a motto of protesters in many countries.
elagabal: The name is the Latin form of the Arabic Ilah al-Jabal, God of the Mountain, written ʾĕlāhaʾgabāl in Aramaic; the Greeks called him Elagábalos and Roman coins and inscriptions consistently used Elagabalus from 218 onwards. The god kept Arab features in his names and images, and the Arab Emesan dynasty served as his priests. In the second century the cult spread to other parts of the Roman Empire, and a dedication to him has been found as far away as Woerden in the present-day Netherlands.

At Rome the god was identified with the Roman sun god Sol and known as Sol Invictus, the unconquered Sun. A temple called the Elagabalium was built on the east side of the Palatine Hill to house the stone, a black conical meteorite. The historian Herodian wrote that it was worshipped as though sent from heaven, and that worshippers saw in its markings a rough picture of the sun.

Herodian also described the emperor dancing round the altar to drums and cymbals while senators watched, and a great festival at each summer solstice, made popular by handouts of food. The stone rode through the city in a chariot drawn by six white horses with no driver, while the emperor ran backwards before it holding the reins and looking up at his god. His account strongly suggests that the cult drew on the Babylonian Akitu festival.

According to Cassius Dio, the emperor tried to unite Roman and Syrian religion under his god, whom he set even above Jupiter, giving him Astarte, Minerva or Urania as a wife. The most sacred Roman relics, among them the fire of Vesta, the Palladium and the shields of the Salii, were moved to the Elagabalium, and Jews, Samaritans and Christians were reportedly told to bring their rites there. Herodian says that after the emperor's murder in 222 his edicts were reversed and the cult went back to Emesa.
elagabalus: Elagabalus was the son of Sextus Varius Marcellus, an equestrian later raised to senatorial rank, and Julia Soaemias Bassiana, a cousin of the emperor Caracalla. His family belonged to the Arab Emesene dynasty of Roman Syria and held hereditary rights to the priesthood of the sun god Elagabal at Emesa, modern Homs, where he served as high priest from a young age. After Macrinus came to power he exiled Caracalla's family, including Julia Maesa and her grandson, to their estate at Emesa.

Maesa, with her adviser Gannys, plotted to overthrow Macrinus, and spread a rumour, which Soaemias publicly supported, that the boy was Caracalla's illegitimate son. On 16 May 218 the commander of the Third Legion Gallica proclaimed him emperor, and his forces defeated Macrinus at the Battle of Antioch on 8 June 218. The Senate acknowledged him and made Maesa and Soaemias Augustae. They were the first women allowed into the Senate and appear on many coins and inscriptions.

Elagabalus reached Rome in August or September 219. At the end of 220 he made Elagabal the chief deity of the Roman pantheon, above Jupiter, with himself as high priest. A temple, the Elagabalium, was built on the Palatine Hill for the god, who was represented by a black conical stone from Emesa. He also married the Vestal Virgin Aquilia Severa, a breach of Roman law and tradition. The sources name several wives and male favourites, but they are hostile and unreliable on these matters: Cassius Dio was a hostile contemporary, Herodian probably relied on him, and the Historia Augusta is much later.

Elagabalus alienated the Senate, the Praetorian Guard and the people through his foreign conduct and religious provocations. Maesa turned to her other daughter's son, Severus Alexander, who was made Caesar in June 221. When Elagabalus came to suspect that the Praetorians preferred his cousin, he ordered attempts on Alexander's life. On 13 March 222 the Guard attacked Elagabalus and his mother and killed them, and his body was thrown into the Tiber. His religious edicts were reversed, and damnatio memoriae was applied to his memory.

Modern scholars question the accuracy of the Roman accounts, suggesting that reports of sexual excess aimed to discredit him after his death and drew on Roman stereotypes of people from the East. Adrian Goldsworthy judges him an incompetent rather than a tyrant.
elam: Elam stretched across the far west and south-west of Iran, from the lowlands of Ilam and Khuzestan to a small part of southern Iraq. In classical writing it was also called Susiana, after its capital Susa. Ancient and modern authors disagree about its extent. Strabo treated Elam, the land of the Elymaei, as mainly the highland of Khuzestan and Susiana as a separate region, while some modern scholars place the centre of Elam at Anshan and in the highlands around it.

Knowledge of Elamite history is fragmentary and rests mainly on Mesopotamian sources. It is conventionally divided into the Proto-Elamite period, c. 3200 to c. 2700 BCE, and three periods of Elamite history: the Old Elamite, to c. 1500 BCE, the Middle Elamite, to c. 1100 BCE, and the Neo-Elamite, to 540 BCE. At least three early states, Anshan, Awan and Shimashki, merged to form Elam, whose strength lay in holding lowland and highland regions together under a coordinated, traditionally federated government. Finds at Susa of Indus carnelian beads and shells show trade with the Indus Valley Civilization from around 2500 to 2000 BCE.

The Middle Elamite period began with the Anshanite dynasties around 1500 BCE, whose kings took the title king of Anshan and Susa, and Susa's power peaked in this period. In the Neo-Elamite period Elamites fought unsuccessfully against the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and Iranian peoples such as the Parsu and the Medes migrated onto the plateau. The Assyrians destroyed the Elamite nation. Afterwards Teispes, son of Achaemenes, conquered Anshan in the mid 7th century BCE, forming a nucleus that would grow into the Persian Empire. A later Elamite kingdom, Elymais, lasted under Parthian suzerainty until the Sasanian Empire arose in 224 CE.

The Elamites practised polytheism, with a supreme triad of Inshushinak, Kiririsha and Napirisha. Their language is traditionally viewed as an isolate, written in a cuneiform adapted from Akkadian, though the earliest texts use a different script called Linear Elamite. Among the finds from Susa is a life-size copper statue of Queen Napir-Asu, made about 1300 BCE. Scholars hold that Elamite administrative traditions were an important foundation of the later Iranian administrative system.
elamite-language: Elamite, also called Hatamtite and formerly Scythic, Median, Amardian, Anshanian and Susian, was spoken by the ancient Elamites and is recorded in what is now south-western Iran from about 2600 BCE to 330 BCE. It is generally thought to have no demonstrable relatives, and the lack of relatives makes its interpretation difficult. Most linguists regard it as a language isolate, unrelated to Semitic, Indo-European or Sumerian, despite its adoption of the Sumerian-Akkadian cuneiform script. An Elamo-Dravidian family linking it to Brahui and the Dravidian languages was proposed in 1967 by Igor M. Diakonoff, but a reassessment published in 2023 reaffirmed that it lacks good evidence, and none of the proposed relationships has been accepted by mainstream historical linguists.

Elamite is divided into periods: Old Elamite (c. 2600 to 1500 BCE), Middle Elamite (c. 1500 to 1000 BCE), regarded as the classical period, Neo-Elamite (1000 to 550 BCE) and Achaemenid Elamite (550 to 330 BCE), the best-attested variety. It was written first in Proto-Elamite, the oldest known writing system from Iran (c. 3100 to 2900 BCE), which is not deciphered, and then in Linear Elamite, used for a brief time in the last quarter of the third millennium BCE and at least partly deciphered. Elamite cuneiform, adapted from Akkadian, was largely a syllabary of some 130 signs; its corpus is about 20,000 tablets and fragments, most from the Achaemenid era and mainly economic records.

It is an agglutinative language, mostly suffixing, with a noun class system that combines animate and inanimate nouns with personal classes matching the three persons of verbal inflection. Word order is subject, object, verb. A king might be written sunki-k, meaning I, a king, and sunki-r, a king in the third person.

The Persepolis Administrative Archives, found in the 1930s, are mostly in Elamite; the remains of more than 10,000 documents record administrative activity at Persepolis over more than fifty years, from 509 to 457 BCE, against only about 1,000 original records in Aramaic. Elamite was also used for official royal inscriptions, including the trilingual inscriptions of the Achaemenid Empire. The study of Elamite began with the publication of Achaemenid royal inscriptions in Europe in the early 19th century. Edwin Norris published the Elamite version of the Bisutun Inscription in 1855, and Jules Oppert published the first grammar in 1879. Archibald Henry Sayce is considered the first to use the name Elamite, in 1874.

The language may have remained in use after the Achaemenid period: several rulers of Elymais bore the Elamite name Kamnaskires in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. Arabic authors of the 8th to 13th centuries refer to a language called Khuzi in Khuzistan, possibly a late variant of Elamite, which probably went extinct in the 11th century.
elazig: Elazığ stands at the north-western corner of a valley about thirty miles long, known locally as Uluova, the Great Valley, and called Vosgetashd, the Golden Plain, by the area's Armenians. The plain lies at an altitude of 1,067 metres in the uppermost valley of the Euphrates. Lake Hazar and the reservoirs of several dams surround the city so closely that it resembles an inland peninsula. About five kilometres to the north-east, on a hill, lies Harput, a much older fortress town, of which Elazığ began as a suburb called Mezre.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Hurrians, who settled there about 2000 BCE. Harput and its region formed part of the kingdom of Urartu at its maximum extent, and may stand near Carcathiocerta, the first capital of the Kingdom of Sophene. Early Muslim geographers called it Ḥiṣn Ziyād. After the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 the region came under Turkish control, and it later passed between the Artuqids, the Sultanate of Rum, the Ilkhanate, the Aq Qoyunlu, the Safavids and the Ottomans.

Mezre was a small hamlet, the residence of the Çötelizades, a notable family exiled from Harput in the late eighteenth century. After Reşid Mehmed Pasha made it a garrison, it grew into a small town with a prosperous Armenian middle class, and in 1869 Krikor Ipekjian founded a silk factory there. In 1878 it became the centre of the Mamuret-ul-Aziz Vilayet. The name shortened to Elaziz, and in 1937 an order of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk turned it into Elazık, finally accepted as Elazığ.

In November 1895 government-backed Turks and Kurds massacred and plundered the Armenian villages of the plain, and many residents were killed during the Armenian genocide. Kurdish rebels took the town in the Sheikh Said rebellion of 1925. In the Republican period Elazığ grew into a modern city while Harput lay largely in ruins.

Elazığ is the capital of Elazığ Province and had 387,072 inhabitants in 2022, a mixed population of Kurds and Turks. Fırat University was founded there in 1975. The Keban Dam, built between 1966 and 1974, flooded formerly populated areas and affected more than 30,000 people, and many of those displaced settled in the city. Few historic monuments stand in the city itself, but Harput keeps its castle and the Ulu Camii, built in 1156 by the Artuqid sultan Fahrettin Karaaslan.
elba: Elba lies in the Tyrrhenian Sea about 10 km from the mainland town of Piombino and about 50 km east of Corsica. It is the largest island of the Tuscan Archipelago and the third largest in Italy, after Sicily and Sardinia. It is the largest remaining stretch of land from an ancient tract that once connected the Italian peninsula to Corsica.

The west is mountainous, dominated by Mount Capanne at 1,018 metres. The centre is a flat section only four kilometres wide, where the main towns stand. The east is the oldest part of the island, formed over three million years ago, and in its hills around Monte Calamita lie the iron deposits that made Elba known.

The island was first inhabited by the Ligures Ilvates and called Ilva. The Greeks named it Aethalia, from a word for smoky, after the fumes of its metal furnaces. The Etruscans began mining iron there, and the Romans settled after 480 BCE.

In the early medieval period the Ostrogoths and Lombards invaded, and the island passed to the Republic of Pisa. Genoa took it after the battle of Meloria, but Pisa regained it in 1292. It was then held for two centuries by the Appiani family, Lords of Piombino. In 1546 part of the island went to Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, who fortified Portoferraio and renamed it Cosmopoli, while the rest returned to the Appiani in 1577. In 1596 Philip II of Spain captured Porto Longone and had two fortresses built there, and that part came under Spain through the State of the Presidi.

After the Treaty of Fontainebleau Napoleon was conveyed to Elba on HMS Undaunted under Captain Thomas Ussher and arrived at Portoferraio on 4 May 1814. He kept a personal guard of 400 men and was nominally sovereign of the island, while French and British ships patrolled the nearby seas. During his nearly ten months there he carried out a series of economic and social reforms. On 26 February 1815 he escaped to France with about 1,000 men. The Congress of Vienna gave Elba to Tuscany, and in 1860 it joined the new Kingdom of Italy.

Elba is part of the province of Livorno and of the Arcipelago Toscano National Park. It is divided into seven municipalities, among them Portoferraio, the principal town, Capoliveri, Marciana and Porto Azzurro. It is a major tourist destination.
elbasan: Elbasan lies north of the river Shkumbin, between the Skanderbeg Mountains and the Myzeqe Plain in central Albania. Its name is derived from the Ottoman Turkish il-basan, meaning the fortress.

In the second century BCE a Roman trading post, recorded in Latin as Mansio Scampa, developed near a junction of two branches of the Via Egnatia, which connected the Adriatic coast with Byzantium. By the third or fourth century CE it had grown into a city protected by a fortress with towers, and it appears on late antique itineraries as Scampis or Hiscampis. It had a bishop, a cathedral and basilicas as early as the fifth century, and Emperor Justinian improved its fortifications.

The site seems to have been abandoned until the Ottoman army built a military camp there, followed by urban reconstruction under Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror in 1466. He built a four-sided castle with a deep moat and three gates in order to fight Skanderbeg. The town became the seat of the Sanjak of Elbasan, and in 1467 many Christians from Skopje, Ohrid, Serres and Kastoria were forcibly deported to it. Evliya Çelebi noted in the late 17th century that all the inhabitants spoke Albanian. The fortress was dismantled in 1832.

In 1909 an Albanian National Congress met in Elbasan and endorsed the use of the Latin alphabet rather than the Arabic script for Albanian. Industrial development began under Zog and culminated in the Communist period, with a steel complex built with Chinese assistance in the 1970s.

Elbasan is the seat of Elbasan County and the fourth most populous city of Albania. Its Saint Mary Orthodox Church, built in 1830 on the foundations of an older church, housed the first Albanian school of Elbasan in modern times, opened in 1909, and the first teachers' training college in Albania was founded in the city. Summer Day, a feast marking the end of winter, is marked with ballokume, a cornmeal cookie, and has been a national holiday since 2004.
elbe: The Elbe, Labe in Czech, rises on Mount Violík at 1,386 metres in the Giant Mountains and flows through Bohemia. At Mělník it is joined by the Vltava, which is longer and has a greater discharge, but the combined river keeps the name Elbe for historical reasons. It crosses the Czech-German frontier, flows through Dresden, Magdeburg and Hamburg, and reaches the North Sea at Cuxhaven. Its total length is 1,094 km, and its basin of 148,268 square kilometres lies almost wholly in Germany and the Czech Republic. From the sluice of Geesthacht downstream the river is subject to the tides.

The name was first attested in Latin as Albis. The Romans made only one serious attempt to move the border of their empire forward from the Rhine to the Elbe, and it failed with the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE, after which they never seriously tried again. In the Middle Ages the river formed the eastern limit of the empire of Charlemagne. From the early 6th century Slavic tribes known as the Polabian Slavs settled east of the Elbe and the Saale. In the 10th century the Ottonian dynasty began conquering these lands, and a slow process of Germanization followed, including the Wendish Crusade of 1147.

The river also divided western Germany from East Elbia, where serfdom prevailed longer and feudal lords held larger estates. Its navigable sections were essential to the success of the Hanseatic League in the late Middle Ages.

The Elbe has always been navigable by commercial vessels and provides trade links as far inland as Prague. Canals link it to the industrial areas of Germany and to Berlin, and the Elbe-Lübeck Canal and the Kiel Canal connect it to the Baltic Sea. At Magdeburg the Magdeburg Water Bridge carries a canal and its shipping over the river. Its catchment is inhabited by 24.4 million people.
elberfeld: Elberfeld lies on the banks of the Wupper. The area is first mentioned, as elverfelde, in a document of 1161. The first part of the name comes from an old Low German word for river, related to the name of the Elbe, so that elverfelde can be read as field on the river. The settlement received its town charter in 1610. Among those born there are the poet Else Lasker-Schüler, the mathematician and physicist Julius Plücker and the conductor Hans Knappertsbusch.

In 1726 Elias Eller and the pastor Daniel Schleyermacher founded a Philadelphian Society in the town. Its members later moved to Ronsdorf in the Duchy of Berg and became the Zionites, a fringe sect. In 1826 the industrialist and politician Friedrich Harkort had a trial suspension railway built and run in Elberfeld, on ground now occupied by the tax office. The Schwebebahn Wuppertal that was eventually built between Oberbarmen and Vohwinkel runs through the town.

In 1943 the Nazi regime sent forced labourers of the 3rd SS construction brigade to Barmen-Elberfeld. Wuppertal-Elberfeld is regarded as the city most devastated by the Allied strategic bombing of Germany in the Second World War. In a single primary raid 1,795 tons of explosives were dropped, destroying 352 hectares of built-up area, a level of devastation of 94 percent.

The district of Sonnborn was incorporated into Elberfeld in 1888. In 1929 Barmen, Elberfeld, Vohwinkel, Cronenberg and Ronsdorf were united as a single municipality officially called Barmen-Elberfeld, and the council of the new city voted to rename it Wuppertal, a change that took effect in 1930. Elberfeld is now the largest municipal subdivision of Wuppertal.
elbistan: Elbistan is a municipality and district of Kahramanmaraş Province, covering 2,201 square kilometres, with a population of 141,307 in 2022. In antiquity the town was known as Plasta and Plastentia, Armenian historians of the early eleventh century called it Ablasta, and Baldric of Dol says it was called Ablistan until the fifteenth century. The Dulkadirid ruler Alaüddevle Bozkurt Bey used Elbistan in official documents, and after the Ottoman conquest that form became usual. Albistan means the orchard in Arabic.

Settlement of the Elbistan plain goes back to prehistoric times. In 1947 an Anatolian hieroglyphic inscription stele, believed to date from the twelfth century BCE, was found near the village of Karahüyük. Modern settlement began in the middle of the tenth century, and the town seems to have been settled first by Armenian immigrants. By the end of the eleventh century it was the most important town on the plain, fortified against Turkish raiders and the seat of an Armenian bishop. According to Matthew of Edessa, in 1155 or 1156 Yaqub Arslan, the ruler of Cappadocia, uprooted the Christian population of Plastentia and nearby Gaihan, 70,000 people in all, and settled them in his own lands.

In 1256 or 1257 the Mongol commander Baidju killed 7,000 of the inhabitants and carried off the young men and women. In 1277 the Mamluks under Baybars defeated a Mongol army in the Battle of Elbistan, and the region became part of the Mamluk northern frontier. In 1337 Zeyneddin Karaca Bey captured the town from the Mamluks and made Elbistan and Marash the centre of the Beylik of Dulkadir. The Dulkadirids still paid homage to the Mamluks while seeking more autonomy, and controlled the region for 178 years until the Ottomans conquered it in 1515.

Under the Ottomans Elbistan was known in documents as vilayet-i Türkmân. The seventeenth-century traveller Evliya Çelebi recorded that Turkmens who had migrated from Bukhara lived in the mountains and towns, and some local chiefdoms had varying degrees of autonomy. The district's population is mostly Sunni Turkish, with a significant Alevi community. Its climate is dry-summer continental. The Elbistan coalfield supplies lignite to the power stations at nearby Afşin.
elblag: Elbląg lies in the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship in northern Poland, on the eastern edge of the Żuławy region. It stands on the river Elbląg, which connects Lake Drużno with the Vistula Lagoon about 10 km to the north, and it is about 55 km south-east of Gdańsk. Its name comes from the German Elbing, which the Teutonic Knights gave both to the river and to the citadel they established on its bank in 1237 to prevent the Old Prussian settlement of Truso from being reoccupied. The oldest known mention of the river or town is in the form Ylfing, in the report of the sailor Wulfstan from the end of the 9th century.

The Chronicon terrae Prussiae describes the founding of Elbing under Hermann Balk, after the knights built two ships, the Pilgerim and the Vridelant, and used them to clear the Vistula Lagoon of Prussians. In February 1440 the city hosted a convention that founded the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation. In 1454 the Confederation revolted against the Teutonic Knights and petitioned King Casimir IV of Poland, who signed the act of incorporation at Kraków in March 1454, which began the Thirteen Years' War. Elbing received privileges like those of Toruń and Gdańsk, including the right to mint Polish coins. In the Second Peace of Thorn of 1466 the Order renounced its claims and recognised the city as part of Poland.

Elbląg was a major port for English–Polish trade until the First Partition of Poland in 1772, when Prussia annexed it and its trading role weakened. The Elbląg Canal was commissioned during 19th-century industrialisation. French troops occupied the city without resistance in January 1807, and Napoleon held a parade there on 8 May. During the Second World War the Germans ran a prison, forced labour subcamps and three subcamps of the Stutthof concentration camp in the city. The Old Town was almost completely destroyed at the end of the war, in fighting that began on 23 January 1945, and the city passed to Poland. About 98 per cent of its new inhabitants were Poles expelled from the former eastern Polish areas annexed by the Soviet Union.

Elbląg has more than 120,000 inhabitants and is the capital of Elbląg County. Parts of the inner city were rebuilt gradually, and from around 2000 rebuilding began in a style imitating the earlier architecture, often over the old foundations and with old bricks. Surviving buildings include St Nicholas Cathedral, a 13th-century Gothic church that became a cathedral only in 1992.
elche: The neighbouring site of La Alcudia, ancient Ilici, had consolidated its urban structure by the early 5th century BCE and became the centre of power of a local Iberian group. Under Roman rule it was a colonia connected to maritime transport through the Portus Ilicitanus, and in late antiquity it became a bishopric. After the Treaty of Tudmir, and especially when Murcia became the new centre of Umayyad power in the 9th century, the site declined. A new Islamic city, Madinat Ilš, was founded on the present site, with walls dated between the second half of the 10th century and the first third of the 11th, refurbished in the 12th century under Ibn Mardanīsh, who ruled the Taifa of Murcia.

In the 13th century the taifa of Murcia became a vassal of Castile and was then conquered by Aragonese forces on behalf of Castile. The disputed rule over Elche was settled in favour of the Crown of Aragon by the Sentence of Torrellas in 1304 and the Treaty of Elche in 1305, and it joined the Kingdom of Valencia. In the 13th and 14th centuries the population remained mainly Muslim, and Elche also had a small but noted Jewish community. Townspeople opposed the creation of a lordship of Elche in 1470 and took part in the early 16th-century Revolt of the Brotherhoods. About 1563 the moriscos were 40 percent of the population, and an anti-seigneurial revolt broke out in the spring of 1766.

Elche is a city and municipality in the province of Alicante, in the Valencian Community. King Amadeo granted it the title of city in 1871. The espadrille industry developed in the 19th century, and local entrepreneurs later invested in leather footwear, so that the city became the centre of Spain's footwear industry. The Palm Grove, an urban orchard of more than 200,000 palm trees, was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 2000. It is the only palm grove in Europe with North African origins and the largest on the continent.

The Misteri d'Elx, a sacral-lyrical medieval drama dated from the 15th century, is performed every year in mid-August in the festivities of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. UNESCO declared it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2002. The Alejandro Ramos Folqués Archaeological and History Museum, in the Altamira Palace, shows the city's past from the Neolithic to the Islamic settlement, and holds finds from La Alcudia, where the Lady of Elche was found. The Basilica of Santa Maria was built in 1672, and the Calahorra Tower is the last relic of the old city walls.
elchingen: Elchingen is a municipality about 7 kilometres east of Ulm and Neu-Ulm. It consists of three parts: Thalfingen, Oberelchingen and Unterelchingen. The present municipality was formed in the Bavarian reorganisation of 1 May 1978 by joining the three. It lies on the A8 motorway between Stuttgart and Munich and on the railway between Ulm and Aalen.

In 1294 Konrad of Plochingen sold Elchingen, today Unterelchingen, to the Cistercian monastery of Salem, which kept it until secularisation in 1802. It never belonged to the Benedictine monastery of Elchingen, which was founded at the beginning of the twelfth century. A fire in 1395 destroyed all its authentic documents, so its probable consecration date of 15 August 1128 cannot be proved. In 1803 Oberelchingen, Unterelchingen and Thalfingen became Bavarian under the Principal Decree of the Imperial Deputation.

The conquistador Ambrosius Ehinger was born in Elchingen around 1500. He became a leading figure in the colony of Klein-Venedig in present-day Venezuela and was killed by native peoples in 1533 while searching for El Dorado.

On 14 October 1805 Napoleonic troops under Marshal Michel Ney defeated the Austrians at the Battle of Elchingen. The Battle of Ulm began the next day, and Karl Mack von Leiberich then had to capitulate. In 1806 Napoleon made Ney Duc d'Elchingen, and the name of Elchingen was engraved on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. For the region the victory ended Austrian supremacy and led to a reorganisation of the territory of Württemberg and Bavaria.

The former abbey church of St. Peter and Paul stands at the monastery of Oberelchingen, and the Catholic church of St. Laurentius in the centre of Thalfingen. A Swabian-Alemannic carnival custom is held every year in Oberelchingen.
eleanor-of-aquitaine: Eleanor was the eldest child of Duke William X of Aquitaine and Aénor de Châtellerault. She descended from a long line of dukes of Aquitaine going back to the 10th century, and twelfth-century Aquitaine was one of the wealthiest and most powerful vassal states in France, whose rulers gave only nominal allegiance to the French crown. Her father set out on pilgrimage to the Shrine of Saint James of Compostela in 1137 and died on Good Friday, 9 April, leaving her as duchess.

On 25 July 1137 Archbishop Geoffrey of Bordeaux oversaw her marriage to Louis, son of Louis VI of France. Her father-in-law died soon afterwards, making her queen of France. She accompanied Louis on the Second Crusade, which followed the fall of Edessa in December 1144. They had two daughters, Marie and Alix. After fifteen years of marriage, with no male heir, Pope Eugene III's earlier refusal of an annulment was reversed and the marriage was annulled in 1152 on grounds of consanguinity. Eleanor kept her lands, and in the same year she married Henry, Duke of Normandy.

Henry and Eleanor were crowned in England on 19 December 1154, the beginning of the House of Plantagenet. They had five sons and three daughters but became estranged. Henry imprisoned her for supporting the revolt of 1173 by their sons Young Henry, Richard and Geoffrey, and she was not released until his death on 6 July 1189. As queen dowager she acted as regent for Richard I during his absences. When Richard died in 1199 she warned John to secure his possessions and campaigned against the claim of Arthur I of Brittany, and John was crowned on 27 May 1199.

Eleanor died at Fontevraud on 31 March or 1 April 1204 and was entombed in the abbey crypt between Richard I and Henry II. Her tomb has a painted stone effigy of her wearing a crown, with an open book in her hands. During the French Revolution the abbey was sacked, and the human remains were scattered and have never been located. She had ten children and outlived eight of them.

Her descendants ruled various realms. Her grandchildren included Henry III of England, Henry I of Castile, Berengaria of Castile, Blanche of France and Emperor Otto IV. No image of her dates from her lifetime, so the portraits and carvings attributed to her are speculative.
eleanor-of-arborea: Eleanor, also known as Elianora de Serra Bas, was born around 1347 in Molins de Rei in Catalonia, the daughter of Marianus IV, judge of Arborea, and Timbors of Rocabertí, a Catalan noblewoman. She spent her first years in Oristano and at the castle of Goceano. Before 1376 she married Brancaleone Doria, a man of forty from an influential Genoan house that already held lands in Sardinia, as part of an anti-Aragonese alliance. She lived at Castelgenovese, now Castelsardo, where her sons Fredrick and Marianus were born. In 1382 she lent 4,000 gold florins to Nicolò Guarco, doge of Genoa, on terms that tied his daughter Bianchina to her eldest son.

In 1383 her brother Hugh III and his daughter Benedetta were murdered, an act attributed both to Aragon and its allies and to discontent with Hugh's harsh rule and heavy levies for mercenaries. Eleanor asked King Peter IV of Aragon to recognise her son Fredrick as heir and sent Brancaleone to court, where he was held as a hostage. Her brother-in-law Aimery VI of Narbonne claimed the throne for his own son. Back in Oristano, Eleanor punished the conspirators and proclaimed herself Judgess under the rules of her grandfather Hugh II, which let women succeed in the absence of male heirs. Peter IV in the end accepted Fredrick as judge, with Eleanor as regent.

She abandoned her brother's authoritarian methods, defended the judicate's borders and kept the Aragonese penned in a few coastal fortresses while reuniting almost the whole island, as her father had planned. Plague then undid this work, handing much of Sardinia to Aragon without a fight. In her last years she left affairs to her husband and to Marianus V, who had succeeded his brother Fredrick. Tradition holds that she died perhaps of plague, in an unknown place.

Her revision of the Carta de Logu, first issued by her father and revised by Hugh III, gave Arborea's laws and institutions a stable form, drawing on Roman-canonical, Byzantine and Bolognese legal traditions as well as Sardinian custom. The scholar Francesco Cesare Casula identified high reliefs in the church of San Gavino Monreale as the only contemporary portraits of Eleanor, Marianus IV, Hugh III and Brancaleone Doria. A statue of her stands in the Piazza Eleonora in Oristano.
eleanor-of-castile: Eleanor was born at Burgos, the second of five children of Ferdinand III of Castile and Joan of Ponthieu, probably towards the end of 1241. The courts of her father and of her half-brother Alfonso X of Castile were known for their literary atmosphere, and both kings encouraged a broad education of the royal children. In 1252 Alfonso revived an ancestral claim to the Duchy of Gascony, which Henry III of England countered with diplomatic and military moves. The two kings agreed that Eleanor would marry Henry's son Edward, who held the title of Duke of Gascony, and that Alfonso would transfer his Gascon claims to him. They were married at the monastery of Las Huelgas, Burgos, on 1 November 1254, when she was 13.

During the Second Barons' War Eleanor held Windsor Castle and baronial prisoners for Edward. After the royalist defeat at the Battle of Lewes in 1264 Simon de Montfort, suspecting that she was seeking troops from Castile, ordered her removed from Windsor, and she was confined at Westminster Palace.
