In 1270 she and Edward left to join Louis IX of France on crusade. They reached Acre in May 1271, where she gave birth to a daughter, Joan of Acre. In June 1272 an assassin wounded Edward in the arm with a dagger thought to have been poisoned.

As queen Eleanor acquired estates worth about £2,600 a year between 1274 and 1290, an unprecedented amount for an English queen, among them Leeds Castle. Some were bought from landholders who had fallen into arrears with Jewish moneylenders, which made her disliked and brought her into conflict with the church. She maintained the only royal scriptorium known in northern Europe at the time and was a patron of the Dominican friars. She bore between 14 and 17 children, of whom six survived to adulthood.

In late 1287, in Gascony, Eleanor was recorded as suffering from a double quartan fever, which suggests a strain of malaria. She died at Harby near Lincoln on 28 November 1290. Her embalmed body was carried to Westminster Abbey, and Edward ordered a memorial cross at each overnight stop between Lincoln and Westminster. These monuments, modelled on crosses in France that marked the funeral procession of Louis IX, stood at twelve places, ending at Charing. Only three survive, none complete, and the cross at Geddington is the best preserved.

Her later reputation was shaped by conflicting accounts. In 1586 the antiquarian William Camden first published in England the tale that she saved Edward's life at Acre by sucking the poison from his wound, and he attributed the crosses to Edward's grief for a heroic wife.
eleanor-of-england-queen-of-castile: Eleanor was born in the castle at Domfront in Normandy, the sixth child and second daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, after whom she was named. Her full siblings included Henry the Young King, Duchess Matilda of Saxony, Richard I, Geoffrey II of Brittany, Queen Joan of Sicily and John. In 1165 her marriage was arranged to Frederick V, Duke of Swabia, eldest son of the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa, but he died before it could take place.

Her marriage to Alfonso VIII of Castile was meant to secure Aquitaine's Pyrenean border for her parents, while Alfonso sought an ally against Sancho VI of Navarre. Her marriage treaty gave her direct control of lands, towns and castles across the kingdom, among them Aguilar de Campóo, Logroño and Calahorra. Of Eleanor of Aquitaine's daughters, she alone could wield influence like her mother's. Alfonso's will of 1204 provided that she would rule alongside their son if he died, and she persuaded him to marry their daughter Berengaria to Alfonso IX of León.

Around 1200 Alfonso began to claim that Gascony had been part of her dowry, though there is no documented foundation for the claim. He invaded it in her name in 1205 and gave up the claim in 1208. Her patronage drew troubadours and sages to the court; the Catalan poet Ramon Vidal de Besalu wrote about her, and Guillem de Bergued addressed a poem to her. In 1179 she took on the upkeep of the shrine of St Thomas Becket in Toledo cathedral.

Eleanor founded and supported the Abbey of Santa María la Real de Las Huelgas outside Burgos and its hospital for pilgrims, which served as a refuge and tomb for her family for generations. Her daughter Constance took the veil there. When Alfonso died in 1214 she was reportedly too grieved to preside at the burial, and Berengaria performed the honours. By his will she became regent for her son Henry I, with Berengaria as adviser. In poor health, she left most affairs to her daughter, and nobles feared she meant to hand over the regency. She died twenty-six days after her husband and was buried at Las Huelgas. Her great-grandson Alfonso X called her noble and much loved.
eleazar-lopez-contreras: José Eleazar López Contreras was born in Queniquea, Venezuela, on 5 May 1883, to Manuel María López Trejo and María Catalina Contreras Mora. His father died of malaria a few days after his birth, and his uncle Fernando María Contreras, a priest, became a father figure to him.

López supported Cipriano Castro in the Restorative Liberal Revolution and was wounded at the Battle of Tocuyito on 14 September 1899. Castro made him his aide-de-camp. He served as Minister of War under President Juan Vicente Gómez from 1931 to 1935.

Gómez entered a coma on 15 December 1935 and died two days later, after 27 years in power. López was his designated successor, and the cabinet voted to make him acting president to avoid a vacuum of power. The Congress elected him two weeks later to serve the rest of Gómez's term, and on 25 April 1936 it voted him a full term by 132 votes to 1. In February 1936 he announced a February Program promoting labour rights, education, better management of public funds, modernisation of agriculture and economic development, and a labour law followed that year.

On 2 January 1936 he announced that La Rotunda, the main political prison, would be demolished. He nationalised the large fortune Gómez had acquired in July 1936, although he had first opposed it and allowed over 90 of Gómez's relatives to leave the country with money. Petroleum workers began a strike in the Maracaibo region on 11 December 1936, which López ended by decree on 22 January 1937; oil production fell by 39% during it. In 1938 he ended oil concessions to private persons. In 1939 he accepted for Venezuela the ships Koenigstein and Caribia, which had fled Germany with Jews.

The constitution of 1936 restricted voting to literate men over 21, though over half of Venezuelans could not read, and in 1937 the Venezuelan Organizing Movement, the Progressive Republican Party and other left-wing groups were banned. López supported gradual democratisation while fearing competitive politics, and he was ideologically conservative. He cut the presidential term from seven years to five. He considered letting a civilian succeed him, but his military colleagues persuaded him otherwise, and Isaías Medina Angarita, his Minister of War, succeeded him.

Medina was overthrown in 1945, and both he and López were arrested and sent into exile. López stayed abroad even after an invitation to return in 1947 and came back only in 1951. He married three times and had eight children.He died on 2 January 1973.
election-commission-of-india: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body empowered to conduct free and fair elections to parliament, the state legislative assemblies, state legislative councils and the offices of the president and vice-president. It operates under Article 324 of the Constitution. In 1950 it was a single-member body. The Election Commissioner Amendment Act of 1989 made it a multi-member body, and the two other election commissioners were first appointed on 16 October 1989. It reverted to a single member on 1 January 1990, and the three-member structure returned on 1 October 1993.

The commission is headed by a chief election commissioner and two other election commissioners and is headquartered at Nirvachan Sadan in New Delhi. The chief election commissioner cannot overrule the other commissioners, and decisions are taken by majority vote. The chief serves a maximum of six years or until the age of 65. The post can be removed only through a process like the impeachment of a Supreme Court judge, while election commissioners can be removed by the president on the chief's recommendation. In the states and union territories a chief electoral officer supervises elections; district election officers, electoral registration officers and returning officers carry out the work in districts and constituencies.

The commission decides the dates for nominations, voting, counting and results. It prepares the electoral rolls, delimits constituencies, scrutinises candidates, allots ballot symbols, registers and recognises political parties, sets limits on campaign expenditure and issues a model code of conduct. That code was first issued during the 1960 Kerala assembly elections and adopted nationally for the 1962 general elections. It can cancel an election or order a repoll in cases such as rigging or violence. Electoral photo identity cards were introduced in 1993.

Voting machines were first trialled in 1982 at the by-election to Paravur assembly constituency in Kerala, and the commission introduced them in phases from the late 1990s. A voter-verified paper audit trail was trialled in 2011 and has been used in all elections since 2019 on an order of the Supreme Court. The none of the above option was introduced in 2014. In March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that election commissioners be appointed by a committee of the prime minister, the leader of the opposition and the chief justice of India; a law of 2023 put a union cabinet minister nominated by the prime minister in the chief justice's place.
elective-monarchy: The manner of election, the qualifications of candidates and the electors varied from case to case. Most elected monarchies practised hereditary succession in effect, so that the title stayed within the royal family, and many elected the next monarch only when the previous one died without an heir. Historically it was common for elective monarchies to become hereditary, whether legally or in practice, through the repeated election of a ruler's children, and for hereditary monarchies to acquire elective or semi-elective rules, particularly after dynastic crises.

Early examples include the kings of Macedon and Epirus, who were elected by the army, and the kings of the Roman Kingdom, who were elected by the Roman assemblies, with an interrex overseeing the vote. Gallic tribes were ruled by a rix elected for a year or longer from the relatives of past kings, and Visigothic Hispania elected its kings from the relatives of past kings until the Fourth Council of Toledo declared election the principle of succession in 633.

The Holy Roman Empire is perhaps the best-known case. Emperors were chosen by a small council of nobles, the prince-electors, though from 1440 to 1740 a Habsburg was always elected and the throne became unofficially hereditary. Bohemia's kings were elected by the Estates; in 1618 the Bohemians chose Frederick V, Elector Palatine, as king, and the Habsburgs treated this as rebellion, crushed it at the Battle of the White Mountain and abolished the elective monarchy. Hungary was an elective monarchy until 1687. In medieval France the first Capetian kings had their sons elected as co-kings, and the election became a formality that vanished after Philip II.

In Poland the electing of rulers goes back to the beginnings of the state. After Jadwiga inherited the throne in 1384, nobles elected Jogaila of Lithuania as her husband and co-king in 1386. The rules changed significantly in the 1570s and lasted until the Partitions of Poland, and there were thirteen royal elections in Poland-Lithuania from 1573 to 1764. The 1575 and 1576 election produced two proclaimed winners, and the nobility confirmed Stephen Báthory while avoiding war with Maximilian II of Habsburg.

Elective succession appears well beyond Europe. The Mongol Empire's Great Khan was chosen by the Kurultai, Silla elected its first king by a conference of elders in 57 BCE, and in Siam councils chose kings in 1824 and 1867. In England Parliament chose Henry IV in 1399 and, after the Glorious Revolution, enacted the Bill of Rights 1689, which chose William III and Mary II to replace James II. In 1787 Alexander Hamilton proposed to the Constitutional Convention that the President should be an elective monarch ruling for good behaviour, but the proposal was voted down. Some modern monarchies and the papacy keep elective forms.
electorate-of-cologne: Cologne was the Roman city of Colonia Agrippina in the province of Germania Inferior and had been a bishop's see since Roman times. In 953 the archbishops first gained notable secular power, when Bishop Bruno was appointed duke by his brother, Emperor Otto I. To weaken the secular nobility who threatened his power, Otto endowed Bruno and his successors with the prerogatives of secular princes, which began the electoral state.

It was formed from the temporal possessions of the archbishopric and came to include a strip along the left bank of the Rhine east of Jülich and the Duchy of Westphalia beyond Berg and Mark. It should not be confused with the archdiocese, whose spiritual authority was wider still.

By the end of the 12th century the archbishop was one of the seven electors of the emperor. He was also arch-chancellor of Italy, technically from 1238 and permanently from 1263 until 1803. At the Battle of Worringen in 1288 soldiers of the city captured the archbishop and forced him to grant it near-complete autonomy. He later moved to Bonn to escape conflicts with the city government, and in 1475 Cologne became a Free Imperial City, independent of him. Bonn was the electors' residence and the electorate's capital from 1597 to 1794.

In the 16th century two archbishops turned Protestant. Hermann von Wied resigned on converting, but Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg, who converted to Calvinism in 1582, tried to secularise the archbishopric. The election of a rival, Ernst of Bavaria, led to the Cologne War, in which the pope funded Italian and Spanish mercenaries, Bavaria sent troops to Ernst and the Protestant Netherlands backed Waldburg.

The war ruined most of the electoral economy, and the siege of Godesberg in late 1583 ended with the castle destroyed and most of its inhabitants killed. Waldburg gave up his claim, and Ernst's victory was the first major success of the Counter-Reformation in Germany. From 1583 to 1761 the archbishopric was effectively a secundogeniture of the Bavarian branch of the House of Wittelsbach.

French forces occupied the left bank territories from 1794 and formally annexed them in 1801. The Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 1803 secularised the rest, giving the Duchy of Westphalia to the Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt and Vest Recklinghausen to the Duke of Arenberg. Cologne was re-established as the seat of a Catholic archbishop in 1824 and is an archdiocese still.
electric-generator: Before the link between magnetism and electricity was found, electrostatic generators used moving charged belts, plates and disks to carry charge to a high-potential electrode. They produced very high voltage at low current and were never used for commercially significant power. Faraday discovered the principle of electromagnetic generators in 1831 and 1832: an electromotive force arises in a conductor that encircles a varying magnetic flux. His disk was inefficient and its voltage very low, and experimenters found that coils of many turns gave higher voltages, so wire windings became a basic feature of later designs.

Independently of Faraday, Ányos Jedlik began experimenting in 1827 with rotating electromagnetic devices, and his single-pole starter, finished between 1852 and 1854, embodied the principle of self-excitation. Hippolyte Pixii built one of the first dynamos in 1832.

A generator turns mechanical energy into electrical energy in an external circuit. Electromagnetic generators fall into two groups: dynamos, which give pulsing direct current through a commutator, and alternators, which give alternating current. A generator has a rotor and a stator forming a magnetic circuit, with a field produced either by coils or by permanent magnets, and an armature in which the changing field induces the current. Self-excitation means that part of the output feeds the field coils, so that remanent magnetism in the iron starts the machine and the field builds until the core saturates.

The Woolrich generator of 1844 was used by the firm of Elkingtons for commercial electroplating, and in the 1870s Siemens used dynamos to power electric arc furnaces. Direct current was later displaced because alternating current can be stepped to and from very high voltages to limit losses over long distances. J. E. H. Gordon built large two-phase alternators in 1882, and William Stanley Jr., of Westinghouse Electric, gave the first public demonstration of an alternator system in 1886. Sebastian Ziani de Ferranti designed the Deptford Power Station, completed in 1891, the first truly modern power station, which supplied high-voltage alternating current stepped down for each street.
electric-motor: Before electromagnetic motors, experimenters investigated motors that worked by electrostatic force. The first were simple devices described in the 1740s and 1750s by the Scottish monk Andrew Gordon and the American Benjamin Franklin. Their theoretical principle, Coulomb's law, was discovered but not published by Henry Cavendish in 1771 and independently by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785. The high voltages needed were hard to generate, and electrostatic motors were never put to practical use.

William Sturgeon invented the first commutator direct-current motor able to turn machinery in 1832. Thomas Davenport and Emily Davenport then built a motor which he patented in 1837, running at up to 600 revolutions per minute and powering machine tools and a printing press. Primary batteries were so costly that it was commercially unsuccessful and bankrupted them, and with no electricity distribution system there was no practical market. In 1879 Walter Baily demonstrated Arago's rotating magnetic fields, by manually turning switches on and off, as in effect the first primitive induction motor.

An electric motor turns electrical energy into mechanical energy, most often through the interaction of a magnetic field and the current in a wire winding, which produces torque on the shaft. An electric generator is mechanically identical but works in reverse. A motor has two mechanical parts, the rotor, which moves, and the stator, which does not. The stator core is built of thin insulated metal sheets called laminations, which reduce the losses from eddy currents. In a commutated motor a commutator reverses the current in the rotor windings every half turn, so that the torque always acts in the same direction; without it the rotor would stop.

Standardised motors provide power for industry. The largest, used for marine propulsion, pipeline compression and pumped storage, exceed 100 megawatts. Other uses are fans, blowers and pumps, machine tools, household appliances, power tools, vehicles and disk drives, and small motors are found in electric watches. In regenerative braking with traction motors, a motor can be used in reverse as a generator to recover energy otherwise lost as heat and friction. Since the 1980s the market share of direct-current motors has declined in favour of alternating-current motors.
electrolysis: The word electrolysis was introduced by Michael Faraday in 1834, from the Greek for amber, long associated with electrical phenomena, and for dissolution. The technique itself is older. In 1785 the Dutch scientist Martin van Marum used an electrostatic generator to reduce tin, zinc and antimony from their salts, without knowing what he was doing. In 1789 Adriaan Paets van Troostwijk and Jan Rudolph Deiman produced small amounts of hydrogen and oxygen from water in the same way. Luigi Galvani's experiments with frog legs in 1791 led Alessandro Volta to test his claims, which gave insight to Humphry Davy's ideas. In 1800 William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, with Johann Ritter also credited, showed the first sustained electrolysis of water using a voltaic pile.

Electrolysis passes a direct current through an electrolyte, a substance that contains free ions, producing chemical reactions at the electrodes and decomposing the material. It needs an electrolyte, two electrodes and an external power source, and a partition may keep the products apart. Positive ions move to the negative cathode and negative ions to the positive anode, where electrons are removed, which chemistry calls oxidation, and added, called reduction. Faraday's two laws state that the quantity of product is proportional to the current and that, with cells connected in series, the products are proportional to their equivalent weights. Graphite, called plumbago in Faraday's time, and platinum were chosen for anodes that should not react.

Davy's use of the method led him to discover potassium, sodium, barium, calcium and magnesium in 1807 and 1808. William Thomas Brande isolated lithium by electrolysis in 1821. Paul Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium in 1875, producing 3.4 mg. Henri Moissan prepared fluorine on 26 June 1886 and showed it to the Académie des sciences two days later, after many chemists, including Paulin Louyet and Jérôme Nicklès, had died trying to isolate it.

In 1886 Charles Martin Hall of America and Paul Héroult of France both filed for patents on electrolytic aluminium, Héroult in May and Hall in July. Hall obtained his patent by proving with letters to his family that his method predated the French filing, and the Hall–Héroult process cut the price of aluminium from four dollars to thirty cents a pound. The Castner–Kellner process for sodium hydroxide followed in 1890, and a Polish patent for electrolysis of copper and zinc was granted to Stanisław Łaszczyński in 1902. The modern chlor-alkali process, the electrolysis of brine, was developed in 1930 and supplies most of the chlorine and sodium hydroxide that industry needs. Electroplating deposits thin films of metal for decoration and use.
electromagnetic-induction: In his first experiment Faraday expected that when current began to flow in one wire a sort of wave would travel through the iron ring and cause an electrical effect on the opposite side. He saw a transient current, which he called a wave of electricity, when the battery was connected and another when it was disconnected.

Faraday explained induction with a concept he called lines of force, but scientists at the time widely rejected his theoretical ideas, mainly because they were not expressed mathematically. An exception was James Clerk Maxwell, who used them as the basis of his quantitative electromagnetic theory. Maxwell's differential equation for the time-varying case was called Faraday's law by Oliver Heaviside, and it is recognised today as one of the four Maxwell's equations. In 1834 Heinrich Lenz formulated the law that bears his name.

Faraday's law says that the emf induced in a closed circuit equals the rate of change of the magnetic flux enclosed by the circuit. By Lenz's law the induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change which produced it. Winding the wire into a tight coil of N identical turns multiplies the emf by N. The law covers two different phenomena: the motional emf produced by a magnetic force on a moving wire, and the transformer emf produced by a changing magnetic field. Maxwell drew attention to the distinction in 1861, and Albert Einstein noticed that both situations amount to relative movement between a conductor and a magnet, which was one of the principal paths that led him to special relativity.

Induction underlies electric generators, in which mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy, and transformers, in which a changing current in one wire sets up an emf in a second. It is also used in inductors, induction motors, induction cooking and welding, inductive charging and magnetic flow meters for conductive liquids.

Conductors in a changing or moving magnetic field also carry circular eddy currents. These are useful in eddy current brakes and induction heating, but in the cores of transformers, motors and generators they waste energy as heat. Engineers reduce them by building cores from stacks of thin laminations separated by nonconductive coatings, or from ferrite or iron powder at higher frequencies.
eleftherios-venizelos: Eleftherios Kyriakou Venizelos was born on 23 August 1864 at Mournies, near Chania, in Ottoman Crete, the son of the merchant and revolutionary Kyriakos Venizelos. When the Cretan revolution of 1866 broke out, the family fled to Kythira and then to Syros, returning only after an amnesty in 1872. He took a law degree at the University of Athens and from 1886 worked as a lawyer in Chania. In December 1891 he married Maria Katelouzou, who died in November 1894 after the birth of their second child; in mourning he grew the beard and moustache he kept for life. He married Helena Schilizzi in London in September 1921.

Venizelos entered Cretan politics in the elections of 2 April 1889 as a deputy of the island's liberal party, known for his eloquence and radical opinions. Cretans had risen repeatedly for enosis, union with Greece, and in the autonomous Cretan State under Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner he became minister of Justice in 1899. He insisted that the constitution make no reference to religion, so that all residents would feel represented, and clashed with the Prince over his promise to seek annexation from the Great Powers. On 10 March 1905 rebels led by Venizelos gathered at Theriso and declared the union of Crete with Greece.

Invited to Athens in 1909, he became Prime Minister in 1910 and founded the Liberal Party. His reforms, culminating in the 1911 Constitution, covered labour law, education and the army and navy. He brought Greece into the Balkan League before the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913, after which Greece had doubled its area and population. In the First World War he favoured the Allies, against the neutral policy of King Constantine I, producing the National Schism: a pro-Venizelos provisional government in the north confronted the royal government in Athens, and the population stayed polarised between Venizelists and royalists for decades.

Venizelos secured territorial concessions in Western Anatolia and Thrace after the war, but lost the election of November 1920, when anti-Venizelists took 246 of 370 seats, and he failed even to win a seat himself. He went into exile and represented Greece in the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Lausanne. After a landslide in 1928 he governed until 1932, seeking better relations with Greece's neighbours, signing agreements with Italy in 1928 and Yugoslavia in 1929, and dealing with refugees from Asia Minor and the Great Depression.

After coups in his support failed, he was sentenced to death in absentia in March 1935 and died in Paris on 18 March 1936. He was buried at Akrotiri near Chania. He is often called the Maker of Modern Greece, and the Liberal Party he founded outlived him.
elena-ceausescu: Elena Ceaușescu was born Lenuța Petrescu into a peasant family in Petrești commune, Dâmbovița County, in Wallachia. Her father was a ploughman, and she received only an elementary education. She moved to Bucharest with her brother and worked as a laboratory assistant and then in a textile factory. In 1939 she joined the Bucharest branch of the Romanian Communist Party and met Nicolae Ceaușescu, whom she married in December 1947. She obtained a degree in chemical engineering in 1957 and a doctorate in 1967, though there is anecdotal evidence that her thesis was written by a university professor.

After the Communists took power she worked as a secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and was an unimportant figure until her husband became General Secretary of the party. On a state visit to China in June 1971 she noted how Jiang Qing, Mao Zedong's wife, held a position of power, and she then began her own political rise.

She became a full member of the Central Committee in July 1972 and of the Politburo in June 1973, the second most influential person after her husband. She was elected to the Great National Assembly in March 1975, for Pitești, and in March 1980 became First Deputy Prime Minister, a post she kept until her death.

From the early 1980s she was the object of a cult of personality as intense as her husband's, which called her the Mother of the Nation. In science she was hired at the National Institute for Chemical Research in 1957 and became a member of the Romanian Academy's section for chemical sciences in 1974, and in 1978 the Royal Institute of Chemistry admitted her as a Fellow. After 1989 several scientists claimed she had forced them to write papers in her name and to share credit on patents.

She fled with her husband on 22 December 1989 after the events in Timișoara led to the Romanian Revolution, and they were captured at Târgoviște. At their trial she answered only a few questions. On the afternoon of 25 December 1989 they were turned over to a firing squad and executed, with their arms tied behind their backs. She was the only woman ever executed by the modern state of Romania. She was survived by her mother, her brother Gheorghe Petrescu and three children, Valentin, Zoia and Nicu, and was buried in Ghencea Cemetery.
elena-glinskaya: Elena Vasilyevna Glinskaya was the daughter of Prince Vasili Lvovich Glinsky and the Serbian princess Ana Jakšić. The Glinsky family claimed descent from Mamai, and by the 1520s from Genghis Khan. Her uncle Prince Mikhail Lvovich Glinsky changed sides from Lithuania to Moscow in 1508, and Grand Duke Vasili III gave the family Maloyaroslavets and Borovsk. Mikhail was imprisoned for trying to rejoin the Lithuanians and was released in 1527 at Elena's request. In 1525 Vasili resolved to divorce Solomoniya Saburova, who had borne no children, and marry Elena. The boyars and the Church opposed it, but they married on 21 January 1526. Their son Ioann, the future Ivan the Terrible, was born on 25 August 1530.

On his deathbed Vasili transferred power to her until Ivan, then three, could rule. The later chronicles of Ivan's court say he gave her the sceptre, while the Pskov Chronicle says he left Ivan's care to a small boyar council. Widows of Moscow rulers were never regents. By August 1534 Mikhail Glinsky was accused of poisoning Vasili and imprisoned, and he was eventually executed. Sigismund I attacked Moscow in 1534 while Crimean Tatar forces raided Ryazan, and an armistice was signed in February 1537.

In 1535 she carried out a currency reform that introduced a unified monetary system and the first kopek. She had counterfeiters punished with molten tin poured down the throat or the loss of their hands, and built a new wall around Moscow. In 1537 she had Andrei of Staritsa, Vasili's brother, arrested, and he died within half a year.

She died on 4 April 1538. Her son's governess, Agrippina Fedorovna Chelyadnina, was arrested in connection with her death. Some historians believe the Shuiskys, who took power afterwards, poisoned her, and recent studies of her remains tend to support that view.
elephanta-caves: The ancient history of Elephanta Island is unknown in both Hindu and Buddhist records. Archaeological finds suggest human settlement by possibly the 2nd century BCE, when Buddhists seem to have been the first occupants and raised a large stupa with seven smaller ones around it. Coins of the Western Satraps of the 4th century CE have been found on the island.

No surviving record of the Gupta era mentions the caves, so the century of their making has been disputed, with dates ranging from the late 5th to the late 8th century. Colonial-era historians attributed them to the Rashtrakutas in the 7th century or later, a theory later findings have discredited.

The Archaeological Survey of India and UNESCO place the temples in the 5th and 6th centuries. Contemporary scholars generally put their completion in the second quarter of the 6th century, as part of the artistic flowering of the Gupta era, and attribute them to King Krishnaraja of the Kalachuri dynasty, on numismatic evidence, inscriptions, construction style and the dating of other Deccan cave temples such as Ajanta.

The island, about 10 kilometres east of Mumbai, has five Hindu caves on its western hill and two Buddhist caves and stupa mounds on its eastern one, all hewn from solid basalt. Cave 1, the Great Cave, is 39.63 metres square in plan, with a hall of pillars and several entrances. The carvings, mostly in high relief, narrate Hindu legends and show Hindu and Buddhist ideas together. The best known are the three-faced Sadashiva, 5.45 metres high, Nataraja, lord of the dance, and Yogishvara, lord of yogis. The main temple and the other caves are laid out in a mandala pattern. Shaktism and Vaishnavism also appear in the art.

The Portuguese named the island Elefante, which became Elephanta, after elephant statues they found there. The Great Cave had been a Hindu place of worship until they arrived, when the island ceased to be an active one, and Cave 6 was used as a Christian church at some point between 1534 and 1682. Much of the sculpture has been defaced or damaged. James Burgess's publication of the site's condition in 1871 brought wider attention, British Indian officials began protecting it in 1909, and the Indian government restored the monuments in the 1970s. The Archaeological Survey of India now maintains them.
eleusinian-mysteries: The Mysteries had a basis in a Bronze Age agrarian cult, and some of their practices seem to have been influenced by the religion of the Mycenaean period. Excavations have shown a private building under the Telesterion in Mycenaean times, so the cult of Demeter may originally have been private. They were tied to the myth in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, from about 650 BCE. In it Persephone is seized by Hades, and Demeter searches for her and causes a drought. Zeus lets the daughter return, but she has eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld and must spend part of each year there.

Under Peisistratos of Athens the Mysteries became pan-Hellenic, and about 300 BCE the state took over their control, which was held by two families, the Eumolpidae and the Kerykes. The only requirements were freedom from blood guilt and the ability to speak Greek, and men, women and slaves could be initiated.

The Lesser Mysteries were held at Agrai in the month of Anthesterion, around February or March. Participants sacrificed a piglet to Demeter and Persephone and purified themselves in the river Ilisos, and became initiates, or mystae. The Greater Mysteries were held in Boedromion, around September or October, and lasted ten days. On the 18th of the month the procession left the Kerameikos and walked along the Sacred Way to Eleusis, calling Íakche. At Eleusis there was an all-night vigil, and initiates drank the kykeon, a drink of barley and pennyroyal.

On the 19th the initiates entered the Telesterion, where it is widely supposed that the rites had three elements: things done, a dramatic reenactment of the myth; things shown, a display of sacred objects by the hierophant; and things said. The penalty for divulging them was death, which is probably why almost nothing is known of them. Hippolytus of Rome wrote that the highest grade was shown an ear of grain reaped in silence. Initiates believed that they would have a better fate in the underworld.

Some scholars hold that the kykeon was a psychoactive drink, a hypothesis that continues to receive attention but was not well received by classicists. In 170 the Temple of Demeter was sacked by the Sarmatians and rebuilt by Marcus Aurelius. Julian was the last emperor to be initiated. Eunapius reports that the Mysteries were closed in 392 by Theodosius I, and that in 396 Alaric I, king of the Goths, looted the remains of the shrines. According to the historian Hans Kloft, elements of the cult survived in the Greek countryside, where Demeter's duties passed partly to Saint Demetrius of Thessaloniki.
eleusis: Eleusis stood on a height a short distance from the sea, opposite the island of Salamis, at the head of a bay on the Thriasian Plain. It lay on the road from Athens to the Isthmus of Corinth, in a very fertile plain. Caves on the coast were identified with the myth of the abduction of Persephone by Hades, and a sanctuary of Hades and Persephone, the Ploutonion, stood at the spot.

In tradition Eleusis was one of twelve independent states of early Attica and fought a war with Athens in the reigns of Eumolpus and Erechtheus. The Eleusinians were defeated and accepted the supremacy of Athens in everything except the management of the Mysteries. Eleusis became an Attic deme but kept the title of polis and the right to coin its own money. The Mysteries of Demeter and Kore were popular in the Greek-speaking world by about 600 BCE. They rested on the hope of life after death for initiates, and their central myth was Demeter's search for her daughter Persephone. Each year a procession travelled from Athens along the Sacred Way.

The Persians burned the old temple of Demeter during the Greco-Persian Wars, and rebuilding began under Pericles. Under the Romans the town prospered as initiation became fashionable among the nobility. Hadrian was initiated in about 125 and probably gave the town an aqueduct, completed in about 160. The Mysteries declined from the middle to late 4th century CE, and Alaric I destroyed Eleusis in 396 CE. Byzantine writers call it a small village, and in 1829 it had about 250 inhabitants.

The Telesterion, the hall of initiation, was the largest temple in Greece, and Ictinus, architect of the Parthenon, designed it. The Great Eleusinian relief of 440 to 430 BCE shows Demeter giving ears of wheat to Triptolemos. A Roman bridge over the Kephissus, carrying the Sacred Way, survives about one kilometre from the sanctuary. The poet Aeschylus was born at Eleusis. Elefsina is now a suburb of the Athens metropolitan area and an industrial centre.
eleuthera: Eleuthera refers both to a single island in the Bahamas and to its group of smaller islands, among them Harbour Island, Windermere Island, Man Island and Current Island. It forms part of the Great Bahama Bank, lies 80 km east of Nassau and is about 180 km long and in places little more than 1.6 km wide. At the Glass Window Bridge it is only about 30 feet across. Its eastern shore faces the Atlantic Ocean and its western side faces the Bank. The island has an estimated area of 457.4 square kilometres and 336 km of coastline, with pink sand beaches, outcrops of ancient coral reef and caves. Its highest point is 61 metres. The name comes from the Greek adjective eleutheros, meaning free.

The first settlers were possibly Taínos, also called Arawaks. A wooden ritual seat, a duho, made by the Lucayan people was found on the island in the nineteenth century and is in the British Museum. The island was known in the seventeenth century as Cigateo, said to mean distant rocky land; others derive the name from the Taíno word cigua, sea snail. It is believed to have been largely unoccupied when Puritan colonists arrived in 1648. Their difficulties left only a few settlers on the island and prevented them from creating the first European democracy in the Western Hemisphere. Preacher's Cave at the north end sheltered them in the mid-seventeenth century, and recent excavations there have found Arawak remains.

The island was agriculturally prosperous from 1950 to 1980, with a large pineapple crop for export. After the Bahamas became independent from Britain in 1973, new ownership laws changed its economy, and it has since become a popular tourist destination. Hurricane Andrew, a category 5 storm, severely damaged it in 1992, with an 18-foot tidal surge. A United States Navy submarine-detection station, NAVFAC Eleuthera, was commissioned on 1 September 1957 and closed on 31 March 1980. In March 2019 Disney Cruise Line bought the Lighthouse Point property, which opened to its guests on 6 June 2024.

The 2022 census recorded about 9,104 people on Eleuthera island, with further populations on Harbour Island and Spanish Wells. Governor's Harbour is the administrative capital, and Dunmore Town, Spanish Wells and Rock Sound are among the largest settlements. The Queens Highway runs the length of the island, and three airports serve it. Gregory Town holds an annual Pineapple Festival. The island's main economic activity is tourism.
elevator: Sources from later periods describe elevators as cabs hung on a hemp rope and powered by people or animals. In the industrial age their development was led by the need to move raw materials such as coal and lumber from hillsides, and this technology, with steel beam construction, produced today's passenger and freight elevators. In the mid-19th century steam-powered elevators in coal mines moved goods in bulk in mines and factories. In 1823 two London architects, Burton and Homer, operated a tourist attraction called the ascending room, which raised customers to a considerable height for a panoramic view.

An elevator is essentially a platform pulled or pushed upward by mechanical means. A modern one has a cab mounted in an enclosed shaft, the hoistway, and running on guide rails. In a traction elevator the cab is pulled up by steel ropes over a grooved pulley called a sheave, and a counterweight balances its weight; often two or three elevators are built so that their cars balance one another.

Hydraulic elevators use an underground cylinder and suit buildings of two to five floors. Other kinds include climbing elevators, which carry their own propulsion up masts and towers, and pneumatic elevators, which carry one to three passengers. Kone introduced the first machine-room-less elevator, the MonoSpace, in 1996, and the first vacuum elevator was offered commercially in Argentina in 2000.

Elevators lift materials in agriculture and manufacturing, as chain and bucket elevators, grain augers and hay elevators. In buildings they give access where ramps are not feasible, and high-speed elevators are common in skyscrapers. Before the Second World War most passenger elevators were run by operators using a rheostat connected to the motor.

In 1901 the engineer Charles G. Darrach proposed the first formula for judging the service an elevator system gives. In areas with many observant Jews a Sabbath elevator stops at every floor automatically, so that no button need be pressed, and the Eiffel Tower has double-deck Otis elevators built into its legs.
eli-whitney: Eli Whitney was born in Westborough, Massachusetts, on 8 December 1765, the eldest child of the prosperous farmer Eli Whitney Sr. and Elizabeth Fay, who died when he was 11. His stepmother opposed his wish to attend college, so he worked as a farm labourer and schoolteacher to save money, prepared at Leicester Academy, and entered Yale in 1789.

He graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1792 and, short of funds, accepted a post as a private tutor in South Carolina. Instead he was persuaded to visit Georgia, where Catherine Littlefield Greene, widow of the Revolutionary hero Nathanael Greene, invited him to her plantation, Mulberry Grove. Her manager, Phineas Miller, became his business partner.

At Mulberry Grove businessmen discussed the need for a machine to separate short-staple upland cotton from its seeds, work then done by hand at about a pound of lint a day. In a few weeks Whitney made a model: a wooden drum set with hooks that pulled the fibres through a mesh too fine for the seeds.

A single gin could clean up to 55 pounds a day. He applied for a patent on 28 October 1793 and received it on 14 March 1794. Resentment, the machine's simplicity and the primitive state of patent law led to infringement, and lawsuits consumed their profits. Their company ended in 1797. Cotton exports rose from under 500,000 pounds in 1793 to 93 million pounds by 1810.

By 1798 Whitney was nearly bankrupt, and in January he won a government contract to deliver between 10,000 and 15,000 muskets, though he had never made a gun. He first spoke of interchangeable parts ten months later. The arms were delivered only in 1809. Historian Merritt Roe Smith concludes that his 1801 demonstration of interchangeability was staged. The idea long predated him, and others achieved it in their armories first.

Whitney used his Yale connections, among them the Treasury Secretary Oliver Wolcott Jr., to build his arms business, and in 1817 he married Henrietta Edwards, daughter of the Connecticut political leader Pierpont Edwards. He died of prostate cancer in New Haven on 8 January 1825. His son, Eli Whitney III, took over the armory. Whitney's cotton gin made upland cotton profitable and strengthened the economic foundation of slavery. Cotton became the chief export of the United States, over half its value from 1820 to 1860.
elias-lonnrot: Elias Lönnrot was born on 9 April 1802 at Sammatti in the province of Uusimaa, then part of Sweden. His schooling was broken. He attended the Tammisaari Pedagogio in 1814–1815, studied at Turku Cathedral School until he left in the spring of 1818, and then worked as a tailor and singer in Sammatti and nearby villages. After two years as an apothecary student at Hämeenlinna, he enrolled in the Academy of Turku in October 1822 to study medicine. The Great Fire of Turku came in his first academic year, and the university moved to Helsinki, the newly established administrative centre of the Grand Duchy of Finland. He followed it and graduated in 1832.

Lönnrot became district doctor of Kajaani in eastern Finland, living at Paltaniemi, during a time of famine and pestilence there. He had begun writing about the early Finnish language in 1827 and collecting folk tales from rural people around the same time. In 1831 he was one of the founders of the Finnish Literature Society, which supported his collecting financially. He took extended leaves from his medical post and toured the countryside of Finland, Lapland and nearby parts of Russian Karelia. In recognition of his part in preserving Finland's oral traditions he was appointed to the Chair of Finnish Literature at the University of Helsinki in 1853.

His expeditions led to a series of books: Kantele (1829–1831), the Kalevala (1835–1836, the old Kalevala), an edited collection of epic poems gathered orally and representing a mythology for Finland, the Kanteletar (1840), a book of proverbs, Sananlaskuja (1842), and the enlarged second edition of the Kalevala in 1849, the new Kalevala. Lönnrot also compiled the first Finnish-Swedish dictionary, Finsk-Svenskt lexikon (1866–1880), with over 200,000 entries, many of its Finnish translations coined by him. His influence on Finnish scientific terminology was strong, and abstract terms that have Latin or Greek roots in most European languages appear in Finnish as native coinages, such as kielioppi for grammar and valtimo for artery.

In 1860 he published the first Finnish-language Flora Fennica, the first botanical work in Finnish rather than Latin. A second, expanded version, co-authored with Thomas Saelan, appeared in 1866. He died on 19 March 1884. The Kalevala was among the inspirations for J. R. R. Tolkien's Silmarillion and Lord of the Rings, and a Finnish commemorative coin of 2002 carries his image.
eliezer-ben-yehuda: Eliezer Yitzhak Perlman was born on 7 January 1858 in Luzhki, in the Vilna Governorate of the Russian Empire, to Yehuda Leib and Tzipora Perlman, who were Chabad hasidim. His native language was Yiddish. He studied Hebrew and the Hebrew Bible from the age of three at a cheder, and by twelve had read large parts of the Torah, Mishna and Talmud. His family hoped he would become a rabbi, and he was sent to a yeshiva, where he met the Hebrew of the Jewish Enlightenment. After graduating in 1877 he studied for four years in Paris, including at the Sorbonne. A conversation there with a Jew from Jerusalem who spoke Hebrew convinced him that Hebrew could be revived as the language of a nation.

In 1881 Ben-Yehuda joined the First Aliyah and settled in Jerusalem, then ruled by the Ottoman Empire, where he taught at a school of the Alliance Israélite Universelle. He sought a language that could replace Yiddish and regional dialects in daily life, and he wrote that Hebrew could live only if the nation was revived and returned to its fatherland. Before this, Hebrew had remained in continuous use in liturgy, study and writing. To supply missing terms he coined words from Semitic roots, and some became part of the language while others never caught on. He raised his son Ben-Zion entirely in Hebrew, making him the first native speaker of Hebrew in modern times.

He edited the newspapers HaZvi and Hashkafa. HaZvi was closed for a year after opposition from Jerusalem's ultra-Orthodox community, which objected to using the holy tongue for everyday speech. In December 1893 he and his father-in-law were imprisoned by the Ottoman authorities after accusations that they were inciting rebellion. He was a major figure in founding the Committee of the Hebrew Language, later the Academy of the Hebrew Language, and he began the first modern Hebrew dictionary.

Ben-Yehuda's first wife, Devora, died of tuberculosis in 1891, and three of his children died of diphtheria soon afterwards. He then married her younger sister, who took the name Hemda. He died of tuberculosis in December 1922, aged 64, and was buried on the Mount of Olives; 30,000 people attended his funeral. Hemda, a journalist and author, secured the completion of the dictionary in the following decades. The historian Cecil Roth is quoted as saying that before Ben-Yehuda Jews could speak Hebrew, and after him they did.
elijah: Elijah is known from the Books of Kings in the Hebrew Bible, which give no background for him beyond calling him a Tishbite. His name in Hebrew means My God is Yahweh. In the biblical account the kingdom once united under Solomon had divided into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the southern Kingdom of Judah. Omri, King of Israel, encouraged local altars and temples dedicated to Baal, an important deity of Canaanite religion, and secured his position by marrying his son Ahab to Jezebel, a worshipper of Baal and the daughter of the king of Sidon. The prophets, who held to a strict reading of the religious law, were not reconciled to these policies.

In the Books of Kings Elijah's challenge is direct. Baal was the Canaanite god responsible for rain, thunder, lightning and dew, so when Elijah announces a drought he challenges Baal, Jezebel, her priests, Ahab and the people of Israel. In 1 Kings 18 he defends the worship of Yahweh over that of Baal, and God is said to perform many miracles through him, including resurrection and bringing fire down from the sky. He is portrayed as leading a school of prophets known as the sons of the prophets, and after his ascension to heaven alive his disciple Elisha takes over as its leader.

Elijah is mentioned once more in 2 Chronicles 21:12, his last mention in the Hebrew Bible, as the sender of a letter to Jehoram of Judah that predicts a painful death. The Book of Malachi prophesies his return before the great and terrible day of the Lord. Scholars generally agree that a prophet named Elijah existed in Israel under Kings Ahab and Ahaziah, but they regard the biblical accounts as shaped by popular legend and later theological reflection.

In Jewish tradition Elijah is invoked at the Havdalah rite that ends the Sabbath, at the Passover Seder and at circumcisions, where a chair is set aside for him. The Talmud tells of rabbis who left difficult questions undecided until Elijah comes. In the New Testament John the Baptist is identified as the Elijah promised by Malachi, and Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration of Jesus. The Quran names him as a prophet and messenger who called his people from Baal to God, and the Druze also honour him. He is commemorated as a saint on 20 July in the Latin Church and on the same date by the Eastern Orthodox Church. Felix Mendelssohn's oratorio Elijah was first performed in 1846.
elisa-bonaparte: Elisa Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio, Corsica, the eldest surviving daughter of Carlo Buonaparte and Letizia Ramolino. In 1784 a bursary took her to the Maison royale de Saint-Louis at Saint-Cyr, which the Legislative Assembly closed in August 1792; she left with Napoleon to return to Ajaccio. The family later moved to Marseille, where she met Felice Pasquale Baciocchi, a Corsican nobleman and former captain. They married on 1 May 1797. Napoleon had doubts about the match because of Baciocchi's reputation as a poor captain.

On 19 March 1805 Napoleon gave her the Principality of Piombino, of strategic interest for its nearness to Elba and Corsica. In June the Republic of Lucca, occupied by France since 1799, was made a principality and added to the domain. Most power was exercised by Elisa, while her husband took a minor role and made military decisions. The people of Lucca resented the loss of independence and called her ironically la Madame.

In 1806 Napoleon added Massa and Carrara to her lands. She founded an Académie des Beaux-Arts at Carrara so that it might export marble statues, not only raw marble, and a bank to aid sculptors. She also nationalised clerical property, closed convents, laid out a botanical garden in 1811 and began a road and an aqueduct that were finished only after her fall.

On 3 March 1809 Napoleon made her Grand Duchess of Tuscany, with Florence as capital. Unlike at Lucca, the decree required her to carry out the decisions of Napoleon and his ministers. She arrived in Florence on 2 April and was coldly received by the nobility, amid resistance to conscription and new taxes. She commissioned busts of her family from Lorenzo Bartolini. Relations with Napoleon grew strained; in 1810 he demanded payment for the grants of Massa and Carrara, and she refused to pay a second time.

In 1814 Joachim Murat's Neapolitan army reached Florence and an Anglo-Austrian force under Lord William Bentinck took Lucca, so that Elisa fled on the night of 13 March and lost Tuscany. She was interned in the Austrian fortress of Brünn, freed in August and allowed to live in Trieste as Countess of Compignano. She financed archaeological digs near Villa Vicentina, probably caught a fatal illness at one, and died on 7 August 1820 at the age of 43, the only adult sibling of Napoleon not to outlive him. She was buried in San Petronio Basilica in Bologna.
elisabeth-christine-of-brunswick-wolfenb: Elisabeth Christine was born on 28 August 1691 in Brunswick, the eldest daughter of Louis Rudolph, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and Princess Christine Louise of Oettingen-Oettingen. At thirteen she was engaged to the future Charles VI through negotiations between her grandfather Anthony Ulrich and Empress Wilhelmine Amalia. As a Lutheran she at first opposed the marriage because it required her to become Catholic, but she gave in. Her mother-in-law, Empress Eleonore, tutored her in Catholicism and made a pilgrimage with her to Mariazell in 1706. She was converted in Bamberg on 1 May 1707 and had to swear the Tridentine Creed rather than the modified version she had hoped for.

Charles was then fighting in Barcelona for his claim to the Spanish throne against the French candidate Philip. Elisabeth Christine arrived in Spain in July 1708 and married him on 1 August 1708 in the church of Santa María del Mar. She was at once pressed to produce a son. When Charles left for Vienna in 1711 to succeed his brother Joseph I as emperor, he appointed her General Governor of Catalonia. She ruled alone until 1713, when the war ended with Philip recognised by Austria's allies, and she then joined her husband in Austria.

In Austria Charles VI allowed her no political influence, but she formed connections among ministers, notably Guido Starhemberg. She arranged the marriage in 1732 of her niece Elisabeth Christine to the Prussian crown prince, later Frederick the Great, and in 1739 that of her nephew Anthony Ulrich of Brunswick to Anna Leopoldovna. The rapprochement with Prussia she hoped for lasted only until the deaths of Frederick William I in May 1740 and of Charles in October. The pressure to bear a male heir dominated her marriage. A son, Leopold John, was born in 1716 but died at seven months. Doctors prescribed measures that damaged her health. Her children who lived to adulthood included Maria Theresa and Maria Anna.

Charles VI died in 1740. The large income he left her in his will was never paid because of the crisis of the state, but her daughter Maria Theresa provided for her court and gave her Schloss Hetzendorf near Vienna as a widow's seat. The traditional view that mother and daughter were close is not confirmed: their visits were formal. She died in Vienna on 21 December 1750. She was the longest serving Holy Roman Empress, and was the mother of Maria Theresa and grandmother of Joseph II, Leopold II and Marie Antoinette.
elisabeth-farnese: Elisabeth was born in Parma, the daughter of Odoardo Farnese, Hereditary Prince of Parma, and Countess Palatine Dorothea Sophie of Neuburg. She was the only child to survive infancy. Her father died in 1693, and her mother later married his younger brother Francesco, hoping for a male heir, but none came. Preparations were therefore made for the duchy to pass through the female line, and Elisabeth received proposals from Piedmontese and Modenese princes before her marriage to the widowed Philip V of Spain was arranged in 1714 by the Parmesan ambassador, Cardinal Alberoni.

Soon after reaching Spain, Elisabeth dismissed the Princesse des Ursins, the leader of the French party at court, and had her escorted over the border. She replaced the French party with her own followers, many of them Italian, and took part in the government meetings that Philip held in her apartments. The king suffered depressive episodes that left him unable to handle affairs, and during these she acted for him. After Alberoni's dismissal in 1719 she was effectively the sole ruler of Spain.

Her main interest was foreign policy, and her aim was to recover Spain's former Italian possessions and to find thrones for her sons. The seizure of Sardinia and Sicily led to the War of the Quadruple Alliance, in which she rode at the head of a division of the army, and which ended with those islands evacuated. Later she secured recognition of her son Charles as Duke of Parma in 1731, and after the Treaty of Vienna of 1738 he became ruler of Naples and Sicily. Her second son, Philip, became Duke of Parma in 1748.

Philip V died on 9 July 1746, and Elisabeth, now queen dowager, was exiled to the palace of La Granja in 1747 after she refused to give up influence. When Ferdinand VI died in 1759 she served as interim regent until her son Charles III arrived from Naples in 1760. She died at Aranjuez in 1766 and was buried beside her husband at San Ildefonso. Her art collection was divided among her three sons, and all later dukes of Parma descend from her son Philip, who founded the House of Bourbon-Parma. Frederick the Great wrote that she walked boldly towards her designs.
elisabeth-of-the-palatinate: Elisabeth was born at Heidelberg on 26 December 1618, the third of thirteen children and eldest daughter of Frederick V, Elector Palatine, and Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of James VI of Scotland and I of England. After her parents' short and unsuccessful reign in Bohemia they were forced into exile in the Netherlands in 1620. Elisabeth stayed with her grandmother Louise Juliana of Nassau in Heidelberg before moving to the Netherlands at the age of nine.

She studied philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, jurisprudence, history and modern and classical languages, as well as painting, music and dancing. Her siblings nicknamed her La Grecque, the Greek, for her skill in the ancient language. In 1633 King Władysław IV Vasa of Poland proposed marriage. He was a Catholic, and Elisabeth refused to give up her Protestant faith, a refusal she later boasted of as the refusal of a crown.

Elisabeth read Descartes's Meditations on First Philosophy in 1642, and her correspondence with him began in 1643 and lasted until his death in early 1650. In a letter of 6 May 1643 she asked how the soul, being only a thinking substance, could determine the bodily spirits to produce voluntary actions. Her objection was that if the mind is immaterial and has no extension, it cannot make contact with a body. Descartes compared the union to that of heaviness and bodies, and she was not satisfied. Jaegwon Kim cites her objection as the first causal argument for physicalism in the philosophy of mind.

At her request Descartes became her teacher in philosophy and morals, and in 1644 he dedicated his Principia to her. Elisabeth refused to publish her side of the exchange, which first appeared in 1879, and she left no philosophical works of her own. Some historians remark that she might have been a philosopher in her own right had she presented her position systematically. She also corresponded with the Quakers Robert Barclay and William Penn.

Elisabeth entered the Lutheran convent at Herford in 1660 and became its abbess in 1667. She was a Calvinist, which at first caused some distrust. She governed the convent and a surrounding community of 7,000 people. Under her it became a refuge from religious persecution and welcomed marginal sects such as the Labadists. She died in February 1680 and was buried in the Abbey Church of Herford.

Elisabeth has become a key subject in the feminist history of philosophy. Some scholars use her case to examine how women were excluded from the philosophical canon. She also used her court in exile at The Hague to build a network of women scholars that included Anna Maria van Schurman, Marie de Gournay and Lady Ranelagh.
elisha: According to the Books of Kings, Elisha was the son of Shaphat, a wealthy landowner of Abel-meholah. Elijah found him ploughing with twelve yokes of oxen and threw his mantle over his shoulders, investing him with the prophetic office. Elisha killed the yoke of oxen, boiled the flesh with the wood of his plough, shared the meal with his family and friends, and followed Elijah as his attendant. When Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind, Elisha asked to inherit a double portion of his spirit and picked up the fallen mantle. Some scholars read the request as reflecting inheritance custom; critics note that Elisha was already named successor and is said to have performed twice as many miracles as Elijah.

Elisha is described as active under the kings Joram, Jehu, Jehoahaz and Jehoash, and is often called the man of God. Using Elijah's mantle he recrossed the Jordan and purified the spring at Jericho. When the armies of Judah, Israel and Edom were suffering from drought in the campaign against Mesha, king of Moab, he foretold relief and victory. He multiplied a widow's oil, obtained a son for a woman of Shunem and revived the child when he died, and fed a hundred men with twenty loaves of barley. He cured the Syrian commander Naaman of leprosy and punished his own servant Gehazi. The narrative also says that two she-bears killed forty-two boys who taunted him for his baldness.

The stories also give him a political role. Elisha is said to have gone to Damascus and prophesied that Hazael would be king over Syria, and to have directed one of the sons of the prophets to anoint Jehu as king of Israel and commission him to cut off the house of Ahab. The deaths of Jehoram, Jezebel and Ahab's seventy sons followed. Scholars hold different opinions on the historical background, composition and social context of the Elisha narratives, which give unusual insight into the folk religion of the Kingdom of Israel.

On his deathbed Elisha was visited by Jehoash of Israel, who called him the chariot of Israel and its horsemen. Elisha had the king fire an arrow eastwards and predicted victory over the Arameans, and 2 Kings 13:25 records three victories by Jehoash. A body placed in Elisha's grave the following year is said to have revived on touching his remains. Elisha is also mentioned in the New Testament, where Jesus refers to Naaman's healing in Luke 4, and in the Quran, and he is venerated as a prophet in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
elizabeth-cady-stanton: Elizabeth Cady was born on 12 November 1815 into the leading family of Johnstown, New York. Her father, Daniel Cady, was one of the richest landowners in the state, an attorney who served one term in Congress and became a justice of the New York Supreme Court. Her mother, Margaret, was more progressive and supported the Garrisonian wing of the abolitionists. Elizabeth attended Johnstown Academy until fifteen, the only girl in its advanced classes in mathematics and languages. In 1840 she married the abolitionist agent Henry Brewster Stanton, omitting the word obey from the ceremony, and on their honeymoon in London they attended the World Anti-Slavery Convention, where male delegates barred women from taking part.

In 1851 Amelia Bloomer introduced her at Seneca Falls to Susan B. Anthony, and the two formed a partnership of decades, Anthony excelling at organisation and Stanton at ideas and writing. In 1860 Stanton argued in an hour-long speech for easier divorce, and Wendell Phillips tried to have the subject struck from the record. In 1863 she and Anthony founded the Women's Loyal National League, whose petition drive collected nearly 400,000 signatures for abolition. In 1868 they began the weekly newspaper The Revolution.

After the Civil War she and Anthony opposed the Fifteenth Amendment, and in the bitter arguments Stanton sometimes used elitist and racially condescending language, for which Frederick Douglass reproached her. In May 1869 she became first president of the National Woman Suffrage Association, which worked at the national level, while the rival American Woman Suffrage Association, led by Lucy Stone and Julia Ward Howe, followed a state-by-state strategy. When the two bodies united she became first president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, a largely honorary post.

Stanton wrote most of the first three volumes of the History of Woman Suffrage, a six-volume work of more than 5,700 pages written over 41 years, and The Woman's Bible, which holds that the Bible's attitude toward women reflects the prejudice of a less civilised age. In her last years she promoted educated suffrage. She died in New York City on 26 October 1902, eighteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote, and was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery.
elizabeth-charlotte-madame-palatine: Elizabeth Charlotte was born on 27 May 1652 in Heidelberg castle, the second child and only daughter of Charles I Louis, Elector Palatine, and Charlotte of Hesse-Kassel. Nicknamed Liselotte, she was raised in the Reformed Protestant faith. Her parents' marriage went badly, and in 1657 her father separated from her mother to marry Marie Luise von Degenfeld morganatically. She remained close to several of her thirteen half-siblings, the Raugrafen, and kept up a lifelong correspondence with two half-sisters, Louise and Amalie Elisabeth.

In 1671 she was married to Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, known as Monsieur, brother of Louis XIV and twelve years her senior. Her aunt Anna Gonzaga negotiated the contract, including the terms of her conversion to Catholicism. The wedding by proxy took place at Metz on 16 November 1671, the day after she renounced her Reformed faith, and she first met her husband on 20 November at Châlons. As his wife she was styled Madame. At first she became very close to the king, who enjoyed her wit, her dancing and her habit of long walks and hunting.

From about 1680 her husband's favourites, the Chevalier de Lorraine and the Marquis d'Effiat among them, intrigued against her and had her confidantes dismissed. Her relationship with the king cooled as Madame de Maintenon gained influence, and she withdrew into her writing room. The Duke died of a stroke at Saint-Cloud on 9 June 1701 after an argument with the king. When Louis XIV died on 1 September 1715, her son Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, had the Parlement of Paris overturn the king's will and became Regent, and she became first lady of the court. She had three children and died on 8 December 1722.

Liselotte is said to have written about 60,000 letters, two thirds in German and one third in French; about 5,000 survive, some 850 of them in French. They give vivid, often satirical accounts of court life, memories of her German childhood, gossip from across Europe and thoughts on literature and theatre. Writing to relatives in Germany also eased her melancholy and kept up her German, a link to her home and identity.

Selections first appeared in French in 1788 and in German soon after, and during the French Revolution she was read as a witness to the depravity of the old regime. An anonymous edition of 1791 presented her as the good, honest German woman. Through her children she was ancestress of the House of Orléans and of many European royal families, and has been called the Grandmother of Europe.
elizabeth-i: Elizabeth was born on 7 September 1533 at Greenwich Palace, the second child of Henry VIII born in wedlock to survive infancy. Her mother was Anne Boleyn. When she was two her parents' marriage was annulled, her mother was executed and Elizabeth was declared illegitimate; Henry restored her to the line of succession when she was 10. By 12 she could translate a religious work of her stepmother Catherine Parr into Italian, Latin and French.

After Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, his will named Lady Jane Grey, who was deposed after nine days. The Catholic Mary became queen and ordered everyone to attend Mass; Elizabeth outwardly conformed. During Mary's reign Elizabeth was imprisoned for nearly a year on suspicion of supporting Protestant rebels.

Elizabeth succeeded on 17 November 1558, aged 25, and relied on advisers led by William Cecil, whom she made Baron Burghley. One of her first acts was to establish an English church with herself as supreme governor, a settlement that would evolve into the Church of England. After Pope Pius V declared her excommunicated in 1570, several conspiracies threatened her life, all defeated with the help of the secret service run by Francis Walsingham. She never married, although she entertained suitors until she was about 50.

Her foreign policy was largely defensive. In August 1585 the Treaty of Nonsuch promised support to the Dutch rebels against Philip II and began the Anglo-Spanish War, in which Francis Drake raided Spanish ports and fleets. In Ireland, Crown forces used scorched-earth tactics, and an estimated 30,000 people starved to death during the Munster revolt of 1582.

Elizabeth died on 24 March 1603, the last and longest reigning monarch of the House of Tudor, and was succeeded by her first cousin twice removed, James VI of Scotland. A cult of personality had grown around her in the portraits, pageants and literature of the day. Some historians depict her as a short-tempered, sometimes indecisive ruler who enjoyed more than her share of luck, and towards the end of her reign economic and military problems weakened her popularity. After the short reigns of her half-siblings, her 44 years on the throne gave the kingdom stability and helped to forge a sense of national identity.
elizabeth-ii: Elizabeth was born at 2:40 am on 21 April 1926 at 17 Bruton Street in Mayfair, London, the first child of Prince Albert, Duke of York, later King George VI, and Elizabeth, Duchess of York, later Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. She was third in line to the throne behind her uncle Edward, Prince of Wales, and her father, but was not expected to become queen. Her sister, Princess Margaret, was born in 1930, and the two were educated at home, with lessons in history, language, literature and music.

On 6 February 1952 Elizabeth, aged 25, was in Kenya on the way to a tour of Australia and New Zealand when word came of her father's death. She kept Elizabeth as her regnal name and was proclaimed queen throughout her realms, becoming queen of seven independent Commonwealth countries and head of the Commonwealth. On 9 April 1952 she declared that the royal house would remain Windsor, though Philip had hoped for his own name. In 1960 the surname Mountbatten-Windsor was adopted for those of their male-line descendants who bear no royal titles.

She reigned as a constitutional monarch through the decolonisation of Africa, the Troubles in Northern Ireland, devolution in the United Kingdom, and its accession to the European Communities and later withdrawal. The number of her realms varied as territories gained independence and most realms became republics. She was advised by more than 170 prime ministers across her realms, and her events included her coronation in 1953 and the Silver, Golden, Diamond and Platinum jubilees. She made state visits to China in 1986, to Russia in 1994 and to the Republic of Ireland in 2011.

Elizabeth died at Balmoral Castle in Scotland at 3:10 pm on 8 September 2022, aged 96, and was succeeded by her eldest son, Charles III. She was the first monarch to die in Scotland since James V in 1542. Her coffin lay at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh and then in Westminster Hall, where an estimated 250,000 people filed past. Her state funeral was held at Westminster Abbey on 19 September, the first monarch's funeral service there since that of George II in 1760, and she was interred at Windsor with her husband Philip.
elizabeth-new-jersey: Elizabeth is the county seat of Union County, New Jersey. It covers about 13.66 square miles (35.37 km2), of which 1.34 square miles (3.46 km2) is water. It lies across Newark Bay from Bayonne and across the Arthur Kill from Staten Island, and is bordered to the north by Newark. Its street plan is largely circular, with circumferential and radial streets centred on the central railroad station.

The town was founded in 1664 by English settlers as Elizabethtown, part of the Elizabethtown Tract. It was not named for Queen Elizabeth I, as many assume, but for Elizabeth, wife of Sir George Carteret, one of the two original Proprietors of the colony of New Jersey. It served as the first capital of New Jersey. Its oldest neighbourhood, Elizabethport, depended on businesses serving seagoing ventures and was a thriving centre of commerce from the 1660s to the middle of the 20th century.

The cornerstone of St. John's Episcopal Church dates to 1706. The First Presbyterian Church was built from 1783 to 1793, replacing a building destroyed by the British in 1780. The newspaper The Daily Journal appeared from 1779 to 1992, and the police department was established in May 1858. Quality Hill, developed in the 1860s, was the most fashionable area, lined with mansions. Peterstown, developed at the end of the 19th century, was occupied first by German settlers and in the 1920s by newly immigrated Italians. The North End was built up in the 1920s for workers at the Duesenberg automobile plant, and the Goethals Bridge opened in 1928.

The 2020 census counted 137,298 people, against 124,969 in 2010 and 120,568 in 2000. The city is governed under the Mayor-Council system of the Faulkner Act. It is a hub of roads including the New Jersey Turnpike and Interstate 278, and NJ Transit trains run to Newark and New York. Newark Liberty International Airport lies partly within the city, as does the Port Newark-Elizabeth Marine Terminal.
elizabeth-of-hungary: According to tradition Elizabeth was born on 7 July 1207, possibly in the castle of Sárospatak in Hungary; another tradition says Pozsony, now Bratislava. She was brought as a child to the court of Thuringia to be betrothed to Louis IV, Landgrave of Thuringia, a union meant to strengthen alliances between the families. In 1221, at fourteen, she married Louis, and the marriage appears to have been happy. When Franciscan friars arrived in 1223 she learned the ideals of Francis of Assisi and began to live them. Louis did not object to her charity.

Louis died of a fever at Otranto on 11 September 1227, on his way to join the Sixth Crusade, a few weeks before the birth of their daughter Gertrude. His brother Henry Raspe became regent for her eldest son Hermann. After bitter arguments over her dowry she left the court at the Wartburg and moved to Marburg in Hesse. She made vows to her confessor Konrad von Marburg, including celibacy and obedience, and he is alleged to have treated her with great harshness, ordering beatings and the sending away of her three children.

With her dowry she built a hospital at Marburg, where she and her companions cared for the poor and sick. Her family tried to press her into remarrying, and she was more or less held at Pottenstein, the castle of her uncle Bishop Ekbert of Bamberg, but she kept her vow. Legends were attached to her, among them the miracle of the roses, which was first told of Elizabeth of Portugal and is absent from her earliest life.

Elizabeth died in Marburg on 17 November 1231, aged twenty-four. Healing miracles were soon reported at her grave in the hospital church, and after examinations held between August 1232 and January 1235 Pope Gregory IX canonized her in 1235. Her golden shrine in the Elisabethkirche in Marburg, a centre of the Teutonic Order, became a major German pilgrimage site in the 14th and early 15th centuries. She is patron saint of the Third Order of Saint Francis, though whether she formally joined the order is not settled, and she is often shown holding a basket of bread.
elizabeth-of-pomerania: Elizabeth was the daughter of Bogislaw V, Duke of Pomerania, and Elisabeth of Poland, whose parents were King Casimir III of Poland and Aldona of Lithuania. She married Charles IV on 25 May 1363 at Kraków, a year after the death of his third wife, Anne of Schweidnitz. The bride was 16 and the groom 47. Charles married her mainly for a diplomatic reason: the match helped to break the anti-Czech coalition led by Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria, in which Polish and Hungarian kings took part.
She was crowned Queen of Bohemia in Prague on 18 June 1363, and on 1 November 1368 Pope Urban V crowned her empress of the Holy Roman Empire in Rome.

Elizabeth is reputed to have been vigorous, self-confident and physically strong. Her relationship with Charles is described as good and harmonious, and it has been portrayed in art, as in the play A Night at Karlstein. When Charles fell seriously ill in 1371, she walked on foot to the cathedral and offered gifts in prayer for his health. She does not seem to have wielded political influence. She was tormented by the fact that Charles preferred his children from his earlier marriages, and she could not change his mind.

Her children were Anne of Bohemia, who married Richard II of England; Sigismund, later Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia and Hungary; John of Görlitz; Margaret, who married John III, Burgrave of Nuremberg; and two sons who died in infancy.

After Charles died in Prague on 29 November 1378, Elizabeth's stepson Wenceslaus IV, the son of Charles's previous wife, took the throne. She then cared for her own two surviving sons, above all the elder, Sigismund, whom she supported in his efforts to become king of Hungary. She outlived her husband by 15 years and died in Hradec Králové in 1393. She was buried beside him in St. Vitus Cathedral.
elizabeth-stuart-queen-of-bohemia: Elizabeth Stuart was born at Dunfermline Palace on 19 August 1596, the only surviving daughter of James VI and I and Anne of Denmark and the elder sister of Charles I. She was named for her godmother, Elizabeth I. After 1603 she was brought up in England, chiefly under Lord and Lady Harington at Coombe Abbey.

Part of the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was a scheme to kidnap her, place her on the throne as a puppet and raise her as a Catholic, a plan that failed when the plotters were betrayed. Her education covered natural history, geography, theology, languages, music and dancing, but not the classics, because her father thought Latin made women cunning.
