Many suitors sought her hand, among them Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden. A marriage to Philip III of Spain would have meant conversion, which the English court would not accept. The man chosen was Frederick V, Count Palatine of the Rhine, a senior prince of the Empire and a staunch Protestant. He arrived in England on 16 October 1612.

Her brother Henry, Prince of Wales, died on 6 November 1612, and the wedding took place on 14 February 1613 at the Palace of Whitehall, with festivities that cost nearly £50,000 and almost bankrupted the king. John Donne wrote a marriage song for the occasion. At Heidelberg Frederick built the Englischer Bau for her and began the Hortus Palatinus, laid out by her former tutor Salomon de Caus. She bore three children there.

In 1619 the Bohemian nobles deposed the Catholic Ferdinand and offered the crown to Frederick. Elizabeth urged him to accept. He was crowned in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague on 4 November 1619, and she was crowned three days later. Their reign ended with the defeat of the Bohemian Protestant armies at the Battle of White Mountain on 8 November 1620, which ended the first phase of the Thirty Years' War, and they became the Winter King and Queen.

Elizabeth left Prague before the defeat and bore her son Maurice at Custrin on 6 January 1621. The Palatinate was occupied, and at the invitation of the Prince of Orange the family settled at The Hague, where she bore eight more children. Frederick died on 29 November 1632. Elizabeth stayed at The Hague even after her son Charles Louis regained the Palatinate in 1648, and she worked to arrange marriages for her children.

After the Restoration she reached England on 26 May 1661. She died of pneumonia at Leicester House on 13 February 1662 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. When Queen Anne died in 1714, the last Stuart monarch, the British throne passed to Elizabeth's grandson George I, son of her daughter Sophia of Hanover, who began the rule of the House of Hanover.
elkab: Elkab lies on the east bank of the Nile at the mouth of the Wadi Hillal, about 80 kilometres south of Luxor, almost opposite Hierakonpolis. The site is a bay between sandstone cliffs to the north and south, and the same sandstone was used for its temples. In Greek it was called Eileithyias polis, the city of the goddess Eileithyia. It holds prehistoric and ancient Egyptian settlements, rock-cut tombs of the early Eighteenth Dynasty, temple remains from the Early Dynastic period to the Ptolemaic Kingdom, and part of the walls of a Coptic monastery.

In 1967 Pierre Vermeersch found well-stratified Epipaleolithic campsites, radiocarbon-dated to about 6400–5980 BCE, which are the type-sites of the Elkabian microlithic industry. The walled settlement of Nekheb was one of the first urban centres of the Early Dynastic period, and for a short time in the New Kingdom it eclipsed Nekhen (Hierakonpolis) on the opposite bank and became capital of the third nome of Upper Egypt.

The temple of Nekhbet was almost certainly founded in the late fourth millennium BCE; the sandstone temples of Nekhbet and Thoth that survive date mostly from the Eighteenth to Thirtieth Dynasties. The massive mudbrick walls, thought to have been built by Nectanebo II, enclose about 25,000 square metres and are still largely preserved. The town flourished in the Greco-Roman period. Coins from the first to the fourth century have been found, but it seems the city was demolished in 380, whether through military or political events.

James Quibell carried out the first scientific excavation at the end of the nineteenth century, mostly in the cemetery east of the town, where he found unmummified skeletons with their heads to the north. Belgian archaeologists took over the project in 1937 and have kept it since.

The tombs of the provincial governors of Nekheb include those of Sobeknakht II, an official credited with saving the Theban Sixteenth or Seventeenth Dynasty from near destruction by invaders from the Kingdom of Kush, of Ahmose, son of Ebana, an admiral in the wars against the Hyksos about 1550 BCE, and of Setau, a priest under Ramesses III. The hills around the site carry petroglyphs from the Predynastic to the Islamic period and short hieroglyphic texts, mostly of the Sixth Dynasty, that name inhabitants of the town.
ella-baker: Ella Josephine Baker was born on 13 December 1903 in Norfolk, Virginia, the second of three surviving children. After a race riot in Norfolk in 1910 her mother took the family back to her rural hometown near Littleton, North Carolina. Her grandmother, Josephine Elizabeth Ross, told her stories of slavery, including how she was whipped for refusing to marry a man her owner chose, and these gave Baker an early sense of injustice. She graduated from Shaw University in Raleigh as valedictorian.

In the 1930s she worked in Harlem for the Negro National News and joined the Young Negroes Cooperative League, founded by George Schuyler to build black economic power through collective networks, becoming its national director. She also taught consumer education, labour history and African history for the Works Progress Administration, and supported the campaign to free the Scottsboro defendants.

Baker began her long association with the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in 1938. She travelled widely in the South recruiting members, raising money and organising local chapters, and was named director of branches in 1943, the highest-ranking woman in the organisation. She pushed the NAACP to decentralise and in 1952 became president of its New York branch, which she led on school desegregation and police brutality. In 1953 she resigned to run for the New York City Council on the Liberal Party ticket, without success.

In 1957 she helped found the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, was one of three major organisers of the Prayer Pilgrimage for Freedom, and became its first staff person, as associate director. She ran its office as interim executive director until Wyatt Tee Walker took over in April 1960. That year she persuaded the SCLC to invite sit-in leaders to Shaw University, where the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was formed, and she worked to keep the students independent of older church-based leaders. In 1964 she helped organise the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, which challenged the all-white Mississippi delegation at the Democratic convention in Atlantic City.

Baker held that strong people do not need strong leaders, and promoted participatory democracy and group-centred leadership. She mentored Julian Bond, Diane Nash, Kwame Ture and Bob Moses. She remained an activist until her death on 13 December 1986, her 83rd birthday. Her papers are held by the New York Public Library, and the historian Barbara Ransby wrote a biography, Ella Baker and the Black Freedom Movement.
ellac: Ellac was the eldest son of Attila and Kreka. Several scholars derive the name from a word akin to Old Turkic älik, ilik or ilig, meaning prince or ruler, which would make it a title rather than a personal name. Priscus recounts that in 448 or 449 Onegesius was sent to the Akatziri, a Scythian or Hunnic people, to bring them into alliance with Attila. Their clans had different leaders, and Theodosius II tried to spread enmity among them with gifts. Attila subjected most of them and wished to make his eldest son their king, and Onegesius returned with Ellac, who had broken his right hand in a fall. Ellac also governed the other nations of Pontic Scythia.

After Attila died in 453 the empire was ruled in its remains by his sons Ellac, Dengizich and Ernak. According to Jordanes the heirs began to contest the kingship, each wanting to rule on his own, and demanded that the subject nations be divided among them by lot like household property. A coalition of Germanic peoples led by Ardaric, king of the Gepids, revolted against what it saw as slavery, meaning tribute and military service.

War was waged in Pannonia beside the river Nedao, where Goths, Gepids, Rugii, Suavi, Huns, Alans and Heruli fought, and the victory fell unexpectedly to the Gepids, who destroyed nearly 30,000 Huns and their allies. Ellac was killed. Priscus says Attila loved him above his other children and that he died after slaughtering many enemies. His brothers Dengizich and Ernak succeeded him. After the battle Attila's largely Germanic subject peoples began to reassert their independence, though not suddenly. According to Jordanes the Huns fled to parts of Scythia near the Danube, though some remained in Dacia Ripensis, Moesia and Thrace.
ellora-caves: The Ellora Caves are cut into the basalt cliffs of the Charanandri Hills, about 29 km north-west of Aurangabad. The 34 caves open to the public are 12 Buddhist (caves 1 to 12), 17 Hindu (caves 13 to 29) and 5 Jain (caves 30 to 34), and several of them are not strictly caves, since they have no roof. Eleven of the Buddhist caves are viharas, or monasteries with prayer halls. Cave 10, the Vishvakarma or Carpenter's cave, is a chaitya worship hall whose rock is finished to look like wooden beams, with a seated Buddha about 15 feet high. The Jain caves belong to the Digambara sect and stress the twenty-four tirthankaras.

Scholars disagree about the order of construction, in particular whether the Buddhist or the Hindu caves were carved first. The broad consensus described by Geri Hockfield Malandra and others sees a Buddhist phase from about 600 to 730 CE and a later Hindu and Jain phase from about 730 to 950 CE. The Rashtrakuta dynasty, which ruled from 753 to 982, built part of the Hindu and Buddhist caves. Funding came from royalty, traders and wealthy people of the region.

Cave 16, the Kailasha temple, is dedicated to Shiva and modelled on Mount Kailasha. Gateway, assembly hall, multi-storey main temple, surrounding shrines and a spire are all carved from one rock, and the work was completed in the 8th century with the support of King Krishna I. The Baroda inscription of 812 mentions that a great edifice was built on a hill by Krishnaraja at Elapura. Shrines in the complex honour Ganga, Yamuna, Saraswati, the ten avatars of Vishnu and many other deities, and relief panels summarise the two great Hindu epics.

Most Hindu caves were dedicated to Shiva and have a rock-cut linga-yoni within the shrine, surrounded by space for circumambulation. Cave 29, Dhumar Lena, was built around a natural waterfall, described as falling over Shiva's brow in the monsoon season. Cave 21 holds a large display of the seven mother goddesses. The caves served as temples and monasteries, and as a rest stop for pilgrims. The site also lay on an ancient trade route, which made it an important commercial centre in the Deccan. Today the Ellora Caves, with the nearby Ajanta Caves, are a protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.
ellwangen: Ellwangen lies in the valley of the Jagst, which runs through the town from south to north, between the foothills of the Swabian Alb and the Virngrund forest, part of the Swabian-Franconian Forest. It is in the district of Ostalbkreis, about 17 kilometres north of Aalen. The Virngrund was known in antiquity as Virgundia, and the town developed in the 7th century as an Alemannic settlement in the forest next to the Franconian-Swabian border.

In 764 Hariolf, a Frankish noble and Bishop of Langres, founded the Benedictine Ellwangen Abbey on a hill beside the settlement. A document of Louis the Pious named it Elehenuuwang in 814, and it became a Reichsabtei in 817. From 870 to 873 Saint Methodius, the Byzantine Greek "Apostle of the Slavs", was held at Ellwangen after Ermanrich, bishop of Passau, had arrested him; he was freed in 873 through the intervention of Pope John VIII. The abbey was exempt, answering directly to the pope, from 1124 or perhaps earlier, and its abbots were granted Reichsfreiheit in 1215. The office of Vogt passed from the counts of Oettingen to the counts of Württemberg in 1370.

In 1460 the abbey became an exempt house of secular canons under a prince-provost, with a chapter of 12 noble canons and 10 vicars. In 1588 and again from 1611 to 1618 about 450 people in Ellwangen were killed in witch-hunts. After the German Mediatisation of 1802 Ellwangen passed to Württemberg and became the seat of Neuwürttemberg; it became a district centre in 1803. The king of Württemberg wanted a Catholic diocese here and in 1812 founded an ordinary and a seminary, but they went to Rottenburg am Neckar in 1817, and the diocese was formed there in 1821.

In the First World War Germany ran a prisoner-of-war camp at Ellwangen in 1916 and 1917 for ethnic Polish officers of the Russian Army. In April 1945 American troops occupied the town, and from 1946 to 1951 a displaced persons camp held 3,000 Ukrainian refugees in the former tank school barracks.

Ellwangen has about 25,000 inhabitants. Its sights are the medieval town centre with its churches, notably Ellwangen Basilica, the Baroque pilgrimage church of Schönenberg and the castle, the last two on hills near the town. It is twinned with Langres in France and Abbiategrasso in Italy.
elmina: Elmina, called Edina in Fante, lies on a bay of the Atlantic on the south coast of Ghana, 12.2 km west of Cape Coast. Before the Portuguese arrived the town was called Anomansah, meaning perpetual or inexhaustible drink, because it stands on the peninsula between the Benya lagoon and the sea. The name Elmina means the mine and comes from the castle, São Jorge da Mina. By oral tradition the town was founded by Kwaa Amankwaa, a hunter looking for food, who found a stream and settled there; the exact origins are contested. His people founded the village of Anomansa near the Benya lagoon, which became Edina and belonged to the Eguafo kingdom until the late 16th century.

In the 1470s the Portuguese agreed with the king of Elmina to build the castle. In 1478 a Castilian fleet of 35 caravels and a Portuguese fleet fought the Battle of Guinea near Elmina for control of the trade in gold, slaves, ivory and melegueta pepper. The Portuguese won, and the Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1479 confirmed their sovereignty over most of the disputed West African territories. Diogo de Azambuja built the castle in 1482 as Portugal's headquarters in West Africa. The Portuguese first wanted gold, 8,000 ounces of which went to Lisbon from 1487 to 1489. Slaves followed, and ten to twelve thousand passed through Elmina from 1500 to 1535 alone.

Edina and neighbouring villages gained independence from Eguafo and Fetu by around 1570, governed by elders called braffoes and the castle's governor. The Dutch West India Company captured the castle in 1637, and in later centuries Elmina served mostly as a hub of the slave trade. It stayed Dutch until 1872, when the Dutch Gold Coast was sold to the British. The king of Ashanti, claiming to be suzerain, objected to the transfer and began the third Anglo-Ashanti war of 1873 to 1874.

Elmina is the capital of the Komenda/Edina/Eguafo/Abirem District, with a population of 33,576 in 2013. Its economy rests on fishing, salt production and tourism, and the castle and Fort Coenraadsburg, built by the Portuguese in 1555, are its main sights. The Bakatue Festival is held each July to mark the founding of the town, and the Edina Bronya Festival is a harvest festival held in January.
eloy-alfaro: José Eloy Alfaro Delgado was born in Montecristi, Manabí, on 25 June 1842. His father, Manuel Alfaro y González, was a Spanish Republican who came to Ecuador as a political exile. Alfaro aligned himself in youth with anticlerical liberalism and fought against Presidents García Moreno, Borrero, Veintemilla and Camaño, which earned him the name Viejo Luchador, the Old Warrior.

He spent a fortune acquired with the help of his Panamanian wife, Ana Paredes Arosemena, on these campaigns. He nearly drowned in the naval battle of Alajuela, saving himself by clinging to a barrel when his ship sank, and fought at Montecristi, San Mateo, Esmeraldas, Guayaquil, Cuenca and elsewhere. In exile in Central America he was given the rank of General de División by the Nicaraguan Congress.

In 1895, as head of the Radical Liberals, Alfaro deposed President Vicente Lucio Salazar and declared himself dictator on 5 June. He was named constitutional president from 17 January 1897 until 1 September 1901. The chief accomplishment of this government was the principle of secularism, and French architects were commissioned for public buildings in Quito.

In 1906 he led another revolt, deposing the elected President Lizardo García, and ruled as supreme dictator until 12 August 1911. He enacted freedom of speech, civil marriage and divorce, built public schools and introduced free secular education. He seized much Church property, expelled religious orders and barred new monasteries and convents, against the opposition of the Archbishop of Quito, Federico González Suárez. His chief public work was the Trans-Andean Railroad connecting Guayaquil to Quito.

His former supporters removed him from office in 1911. After an attempt to return to power he was exiled to Panama, came back on 4 January 1912, attempted another coup and was arrested by General Leonidas Plaza. On 28 January 1912 pro-Catholic soldiers shouting Muerte al indio Alfaro, backed by a mob, broke into his prison, dragged him and his colleagues through the streets of Quito and burnt the bodies at El Ejido.

His remains were buried in secret, later taken to Guayaquil, and in part re-interred in Montecristi on the initiative of President Rafael Correa. His effigy appeared on the 50-cent coin issued in 2000, and the Ecuadorian Army's military college bears his name.
eluru: Eluru lies on the eastern coastal plains on the banks of the Tammileru River, about midway between the Krishna and Godavari rivers and some 50 kilometres inland from the Bay of Bengal. The Tammileru flows through the city and empties into Kolleru Lake, a large shallow freshwater lake a few kilometres away that draws migratory birds between October and March. The Eluru Canal carries water from the Krishna River for irrigation. The city was historically known as Helapuri and Erla Uru before the British renamed it Ellore, and to avoid confusion with Vellore it was called Uppu Ellore, Salt Ellore, in the time of the Nizam.

The history of the area goes back to the second century CE. Vengi, near Eluru, was the capital of Andhra from the second century to the twelfth, ruled by the Salankayanas, the Vishnukudinas and the Eastern Chalukyas, and was capital of Andhradesa for longer than any other city in Andhra Pradesh.

The Salankayanas, feudatories of the Ikshvakus, ruled from the third to the fifth century, and an inscription of their first known king, Devavarman, records that he performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice to mark the founding of his kingdom. Eluru was later a prominent town under the Qutub Shahis in the 16th century and came under the Mughal Empire in the 17th. In 1689 the East India Company secured the renewal of its factory lease, including that for Eluru, after a dispute with the Mughals.

In 1894 farmers of Krishna district held a conference in Eluru to protest against higher water rates. Mahatma Gandhi visited the town after the Congress meeting of 1921 and opened the Gandhi Andhra Jateeya Mahavidyalayam, a national college. The Eluru municipality was first constituted in 1866, the district hospital began as a dispensary around 1858, and Eluru became the headquarters of West Godavari district in 1925. A museum is planned for copper plates of the 7th to 9th centuries.

Eluru is the headquarters of Eluru district in Andhra Pradesh and a municipal corporation, and had a population of 214,414 at the 2011 census. Weaving of rugs has been a trade since the 17th century, and the city is known for its wool pile carpets. It is also a trade hub for fish, rice, oilseeds, tobacco and sugar. In Eluru Buddha Park stands a 23-metre Buddha statue.
ely-cambridgeshire: Ely lies 14 miles (23 km) north-east of Cambridge, on a Kimmeridge Clay island of 23 square miles (60 km2) that rises to 85 feet (26 m), the highest land in the Fens. Because of this height it stood clear of the surrounding marshes and meres, fed by rivers such as the Witham, Welland, Nene and Great Ouse. It ceased to be an island only when the Fens were drained in the seventeenth century, though it is still called the Isle of Ely.

Eel fishing was central to the local economy. Bede, writing c. 731, explained the name Elge by the many eels caught in the marshes. In 1086 the abbot of Ely drew 24,000 eels from Stuntenei and 17,000 from Litelport. Wildfowling, peat cutting and the gathering of willow and rushes were also important before the drainage.

The town grew from a monastery founded in 673 by Æthelthryth (Saint Etheldreda), a queen and the daughter of King Anna. Danish invaders destroyed it in 870, and it was refounded in 970 under Ethelwold, Bishop of Winchester. By the Domesday survey of 1086 it was the second richest monastery in England, and the town held 110 households. The cathedral was begun in 1083. On 22 February 1322 the crossing collapsed, and the sacrist Alan of Walsingham rebuilt it as an octagon between 1322 and 1328, giving the building the name Ship of the Fens.

Charters from the time of King Edgar the Peaceful gave the abbey unusual freedoms, which later bishops used as the powers of a ruler, and the Isle of Ely was sometimes described as a county palatine. These rights were fully ended only in 1837. The abbey was dissolved in 1539. In 1555 two men from Wisbech, William Wolsey and Robert Pygot, were burnt for heresy at Ely during the persecutions under Mary I. Oliver Cromwell lived in the town from 1636 to 1646. William Camden in 1607 judged the place unhealthy, and the population was recorded as 3,000 in 1753, having been 800 households in 1563. The cathedral was restored by George Gilbert Scott from 1845 to 1870.

Ely is a cathedral city and civil parish in East Cambridgeshire. At the 2021 census the built-up area had 19,185 inhabitants. Its station, opened in 1845 on the Fen Line, is a hub with routes to King's Lynn, Peterborough, Norwich, Ipswich and Cambridge. The Stained Glass Museum stands inside the cathedral, and Oliver Cromwell's House is open to visitors. The city has been twinned with Ribe in Denmark since 1956. Its St Etheldreda's fair is the origin of the word tawdry, from cheap lace sold there.
elymians: The Elymians inhabited the western part of Sicily during the Bronze Age and classical antiquity. According to Thucydides they were refugees from the destroyed Troy. For Hellanicus of Lesbos they came from Italy, driven out by the Oenotrians. The Greek historian Philistus mentions a people of Ligurian origin without identifying it with the Elymians, and modern historians such as Heinrich Nissen and Karl Julius Beloch explored a Ligurian origin because of shared inscriptions and place names. The Elymian language is considered Indo-European, and the more generally supported opinion is that it was Italic, with similarities to Latin. No one has yet deciphered it.

The Elymians shared western Sicily with the Sicani, the Phoenicians and later the Greeks. In the archaeological record of the early Iron Age they cannot be told from their Sicani neighbours. Afterwards they adopted many aspects of the culture of the Greek colonists, raising the temple at Segesta and using the Greek alphabet to write their own language.

They kept friendly relations with Carthage but often came into conflict with the Greek colonies, above all Selinus. Boundary disputes with Selinus turned to open war several times after 580 BCE. The Elymians sought an alliance with Athens, which led to the Sicilian expedition of 415 to 413 BCE, and after its failure they encouraged the Carthaginians to attack Selinus in 409 BCE, which destroyed the city.

Their most important cities were Segesta, the political centre, Eryx, the modern Erice, a religious centre, and Entella. During the First Punic War they turned against Carthage and allied with Rome. They were granted a privileged status and exempted from taxes, said to recognise their claim of Trojan ancestry, which made them kin to the Roman people, who also claimed descent from the Trojans. Under Roman rule the Elymians largely disappear from view, presumably assimilated into the general Sicilian population.
email: Computer-based messaging between users of the same system became possible with the arrival of time-sharing in the early 1960s, and MIT's CTSS project produced a notable implementation in 1965. Most developers of early mainframes and minicomputers wrote similar but generally incompatible mail programs. In 1971 the first network mail was sent over the ARPANET, which introduced the address form still in use, with the @ symbol marking the user's system. A series of Requests for Comments then refined the conventions for sending mail messages over the File Transfer Protocol.

The term electronic mail has carried its modern meaning since 1975. The shorter e-mail was used from 1979, when the journal Electronics applied it to the United States Postal Service initiative E-COM, and CompuServe used the form EMAIL from April 1981, which helped to popularise it. The form without a hyphen is now the one recommended by style guides and required by the IETF.

Email systems rest on a store-and-forward model. Servers accept, forward, deliver and store messages, and neither the sender nor the recipient needs to be online at the same moment. A mail user agent hands a message to a mail submission agent, mail transfer agents pass it between hosts using the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, and mail delivery agents place it in a mail store. An agent that accepts a message must deliver it or send a bounce message back to the sender. Users read their mail through protocols such as POP, which suits downloading messages to one computer, or IMAP, which lets a mailbox be managed from several devices, or through a web interface.

The basic Internet message format was set out in RFC 822, published in 1982 and based on the earlier RFC 733 for the ARPANET; RFC 2822 replaced it in 2001 and RFC 5322 in 2008. Internet email was designed for 7-bit ASCII text. The Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, known as MIME, later made it possible to carry expanded character sets and attachments such as images.

Businesses, governments and non-governmental organisations adopted email widely, and it became one of the main parts of a change in workplace communication. A sponsored study of 2010 found that 83 per cent of United States knowledge workers thought it critical to their success and productivity.

Its low cost also brought problems. Unsolicited bulk email, called spam, made up as much as 30 per cent of all traffic by 2003, and the United States CAN-SPAM Act of that year was one of several laws that responded. Email has also served as a route for malware, and the volume of messages has led to concerns about overload among those who work with it daily.
emancipation-proclamation: The Constitution of 1787 did not use the word slavery but contained provisions about unfree persons, among them the Three-Fifths Compromise and the Fugitive Slave Clause. Between 1777 and 1804 every Northern state provided for abolition, but no Southern state did, and the enslaved population of the South grew to almost four million by the start of the Civil War. In May 1861 General Benjamin Butler refused to return three people who had fled to Union lines, calling them contraband of war.

Congress forbade the return of fugitives in March 1862 and abolished slavery in the District of Columbia on 16 April 1862. Lincoln first discussed a proclamation with his cabinet in July 1862, and Secretary of State William Seward advised him to wait for a major Union victory. The preliminary proclamation followed on 22 September 1862.

The final proclamation of 1 January 1863 was issued by Lincoln as Commander-in-Chief, as a war measure for suppressing the rebellion. It declared free all persons held as slaves in the states and parts of states then in rebellion, and stated that suitable men would be received into the armed service of the United States. It named ten states, from South Carolina to North Carolina, among them Virginia and Texas.

It did not cover the nearly 500,000 enslaved people in the border states of Maryland, Delaware, Missouri and Kentucky. Tennessee, under a Union military government, was not named, and 48 counties of what would become West Virginia, seven other Virginia counties, New Orleans and 13 nearby parishes were exempted. Where the Union army was already in place, commanders put it into effect at once. Estimates of those freed immediately range from about 20,000 to 75,000.

Copperhead Democrats, who opposed the war, denounced the proclamation as an unconstitutional abuse of presidential power. It made the end of slavery an explicit Union war aim and linked support for the South to support for slavery, which ended the Confederacy's hopes of recognition from Britain and France. The historian Richard Hofstadter ridiculed it as having the moral grandeur of a bill of lading, while William W. Freehling called it a warrior's new weapon.

Abolitionists feared it would lapse with the war, and Lincoln made a constitutional amendment part of his 1864 campaign. The 13th Amendment passed the Senate on 8 April 1864 and the House on 31 January 1865, and its ratification was completed on 6 December 1865. The proclamation was never challenged in court.
emancipation-reform-of-1861: Before 1861 Russia had three main categories of peasants: those on state lands, those on crown domains and those on private land. Only the privately owned were serfs, an estimated 38% of the population. They owed obligations to the state and to the landowner, who held great power over their lives. Landowners are estimated to have taken at least one third of income and production by the first half of the nineteenth century. Earlier rulers had considered reform. Paul I limited labour service to three days a week in 1797, but the law was not enforced, and a committee appointed by Alexander I in 1801 achieved only a ban on selling serfs without their families.

The Crimean War exposed the empire's weaknesses. On 30 March 1856 Alexander II told the marshals of the nobility that it was better to abolish serfdom from above than to wait for it to abolish itself from below. By 1859 a third of the landowners' estates and two thirds of their serfs were mortgaged to the state or to noble banks, which pushed them to accept emancipation.

The legal basis was the Emancipation Manifesto of 3 March 1861 (19 February in the Old Style calendar), with a set of acts called the Regulations Concerning Peasants Leaving Serf Dependence. It freed serfs on private estates and household serfs, more than 23 million people. They gained the rights to marry without consent, to own property and to run a business, and could buy land from their landlords.

The terms limited the peasants' independence. A two-year transition kept them bound to their former owners. Large parts of common land passed to the major landowners as otrezki, or cut-off lands. The peasants paid for their allotments in redemption payments: the government advanced 75% of the sum to the landowner and the peasants repaid it, with interest, over forty-nine years. The land belonged to the mir, the village commune, so an individual could not sell his share and leave.

Many peasants found the terms unacceptable, and in many places they doubted the manifesto was genuine. Troops were called in to disperse crowds. At the village of Bezdna on 12 April 1861 an official report counted 70 peasants dead and another 100 wounded. The state-owned serfs were freed in 1866 with larger plots, and in Georgia emancipation came in 1864. An 1881 decree made redemption compulsory, and the government cancelled the payments in 1907.

The reform brought new institutions, among them the zemstvo, an assembly of local government, and more independent courts and press. Sales of grain rose, and gentry landholdings fell from 80% to 50% while peasant holdings grew from 5% to 20%.
emden: Emden is an independent town and seaport in Lower Saxony in north-western Germany, on the River Ems close to the Netherlands border. It is the main town of the region of East Frisia. The exact date of its founding is unknown, but it has existed since at least the 8th century. Its town privilege and its coat of arms, the Engelke up de Muer, or Little Angel on the Wall, were granted by Emperor Maximilian I in 1495.

In 1542 Countess Anna von Oldenburg, who sought a religious third way between Lutheranism and Catholicism, invited the Polish noble John Laski to become pastor of a Protestant church at Emden. Pressure from Emperor Charles V forced her to ask him to leave for England in 1549. At the end of the 16th century Emden became the most important transshipment port on the North Sea, because of the Spanish blockade of Flemish and Brabant ports during the Dutch Revolt. Thousands of Protestant refugees came to the town, which was then predominantly Calvinist and in conflict with the Lutheran counts of East Frisia. The Synod of Emden in 1571 is generally considered the founding of the Dutch Reformed Church.

The Emden Revolution of 1595 made the town a distinct city-state under the protection of the Dutch Republic. It was very rich in the 17th century, and the political theorist Johannes Althusius served as its Syndic from 1604 to 1638. Prussia annexed Emden in 1744 under the Emden Convention of 14 March 1744, which recognised the privileges of the town and the regional estates after the local Cirksena dynasty died out. In 1752 Frederick the Great chartered the Emden Company to trade with Canton, but French capture of the town in 1757 ruined it.

The Dortmund-Ems Canal, built at the end of the 19th century, made Emden the seaport of the Ruhr area until the 1970s. Allied bombing during the Second World War destroyed most of the town centre, and on 6 September 1944 the largest raid destroyed approximately 80 percent of the buildings there.

Its main industries are automobile production and shipbuilding, and its harbour is one of the three main ports in Europe for car shipping. A university of applied sciences opened in 1973. Five German navy ships have been named after the town, among them the light cruiser SMS Emden of 1906.
emerald-buddha: The legend of the image is told in the Jinakalamali, the Amarakatabuddharupanidana and above all the Ratanabimbavamsa, a Pali chronicle by Brahmarājaprajña of the 15th century, whose oldest surviving manuscript dates only to 1788. According to the legend the sage Nagasena made the image in 43 BCE at Pataliputra, with the help of Vishnu and Indra. Historical sources instead place its appearance in the Lan Na kingdom of northern Thailand in 1434, when lightning is said to have struck a chedi at Wat Pa Yia in Chiang Rai and revealed a stucco-covered Buddha. The abbot saw green stone where the stucco on the nose had flaked off.

The Emerald Buddha is an image of the Buddha seated in meditation, about 66 centimetres high and 48 centimetres wide at the lap. It is made of a semi-precious green stone, described as jade or jasper, since emerald refers in Thai to its colour. The image has not been analysed to establish its composition or origin. Its posture suggests the late Chiang Saen or Chiang Mai school, not much earlier than the 15th century, although its meditation attitude resembles Buddha images of southern India and Sri Lanka, which has led some to suggest an origin there. It is clothed in gold and regarded as the sacred palladium of Thailand.

The legend says King Sam Fang Kaen of Lan Na wanted the image for Chiang Mai, but the elephant carrying it insisted three times on going to Lampang, where it stayed 32 years. In 1468 King Tilokaraj moved it to Chiang Mai. In 1552 it was taken to Luang Prabang, and Setthathirath of Lan Xang adopted it as his personal palladium; in 1564 he moved it to Vientiane, where it stayed 214 years. In 1779 the Siamese general Chao Phraya Chakri looted Vientiane and took it to Thonburi. He later founded the Chakri Dynasty as Rama I and built Wat Phra Kaew in Bangkok's Grand Palace.

The image wears three sets of gold seasonal decoration, two made by Rama I and one by Rama III. The king or a senior royal changes them at the start of each season. Early in the Bangkok period the image was paraded to relieve plague and cholera, but Rama IV ended the practice, believing that diseases are caused by germs.
emerita-augusta: Augustus founded the colony to resettle discharged soldiers from the veteran legions of the Cantabrian Wars, Legio V Alaudae, Legio X Gemina and possibly Legio XX Valeria Victrix. It stood near a crossing of the Guadiana river at the junction of several routes: Roman roads led west to Olisippo (Lisbon), south to Hispalis (Seville), north-west to the gold-mining area, and to Corduba (Córdoba) and Toletum (Toledo). One of the largest cities of Hispania, it controlled a territory of over 20,000 square kilometres and had three aqueducts and two fora, one municipal and one provincial.

The theatre, built in 16 and 15 BCE and dedicated by the consul Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, seated about 6,000 and was renovated around 330 to 340 under Constantine and his sons. Once Christianity became the sole state religion, plays were declared immoral and the theatre was abandoned and largely buried, leaving only the upper tiers visible. The amphitheatre, dedicated in 8 BCE, held about 15,000 for gladiatorial contests and beast hunts. The circus, begun around 20 BCE and some 400 metres long, could seat about 30,000 people, roughly the whole population of the city.

Water came from the Proserpina Dam, 5 km away, along the Los Milagros aqueduct, named because it seems a miracle that it still stands. The Temple of Diana, wrongly named on its discovery, served the imperial cult. A house on Mount San Albín holds the Cosmogonic Mosaic, and the Mithraeum nearby has yielded important remains of Mithraism. In the second half of the 6th century a Visigothic bishop built the Xenodoquio, a hospital and shelter for pilgrims to the shrine of the martyr Eulalia.

The Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida is one of the largest archaeological sites in Spain and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993. The Roman bridge over the Guadiana, 792 metres long and partly rebuilt after a flood in 1603, is one of the largest surviving bridges of antiquity. Finds from the city are kept in the National Museum of Roman Art in Mérida.
emil-hacha: Emil Dominik Josef Hácha was born on 12 July 1872 at Trhové Sviny in South Bohemia. He studied law at the University of Prague, finishing in 1896, and worked for the Country Committee of the Kingdom of Bohemia. Soon after the First World War began he became a judge at the Supreme Administrative Court in Vienna. After the Treaty of Versailles he served on the same court in Czechoslovakia, as judge in 1918 and deputy president in 1919, and in 1925 T. G. Masaryk chose him as its first president. He was a specialist in English common law and international law, translated English literature, including Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men in a Boat, and wrote poetry.

After the Munich Agreement Hácha was nominated on 30 November 1938 as successor to Edvard Beneš as President of Czechoslovakia, chosen as a Catholic and a conservative with no part in the governments that had led to partition. His short presidency, known as the Second Czechoslovak Republic, saw a shift from democracy to rule under an enabling act that gave the president and government new powers and restricted parliament. After Slovakia and Ruthenia seceded in March 1939, he was advised by the British ambassador to meet Hitler.

Hitler kept him waiting on the evening of 14 March 1939 and received him at 1:30 a.m. on 15 March. He told him that the German army was about to invade and offered a choice between co-operation, with autonomy for the Czechs, and a defeat by force. Accounts of the night differ. Joachim Fest wrote that Hácha suffered a heart attack after Göring's threat to bomb Prague, and that by four o'clock he had signed the country away. The French ambassador Robert Coulondre reported that the German ministers pressed pens into his hands, while Hitler's interpreter Paul Schmidt denied any such scenes.

After the occupation Hácha remained president of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, swore an oath to Hitler and worked beside the Protector Konstantin von Neurath. He signed legislation modelled on the Nuremberg Laws against Czech Jews and dissolved parliament. After Reinhard Heydrich was appointed Deputy Protector on 29 September 1941, he lost all remaining influence.

Prague was taken by the Red Army on 9 May 1945. Hácha was beaten and arrested by NKVD agents on 13 May and taken to Pankrác Prison, where he died on 27 June 1945 in circumstances described as mysterious. He was first buried in an unmarked grave at Vinohrady Cemetery.
emile-ollivier: Émile Ollivier was born on 2 July 1825 in Marseille. His father, Démosthène Ollivier, a vehement opponent of the July Monarchy, was banished after the coup d'état of December 1851 and returned only in 1860. Under the Second Republic his father's influence with Ledru-Rollin made Émile, at twenty-three and newly called to the Paris bar, commissary-general of the Bouches-du-Rhône. Less radical than his father, he suppressed a socialist uprising at Marseille, which won him the favour of General Cavaignac, who made him prefect. He was soon moved to a lesser prefecture and resigned to practise at the bar.

He returned to politics in 1857 as deputy for the Seine and joined the constitutional opposition. With Alfred Darimon, Jules Favre, Hénon and Ernest Picard he formed Les Cinq, which won some concessions from Napoleon III. Still a republican, he was prepared to accept the Empire in return for civil liberties. In the session of 1866 to 1867 he formed a third party backing a Liberal Empire. The sénatus-consulte of 8 September 1869 gave the chambers ordinary parliamentary rights, and the ministry of 2 January that followed was in fact led by Ollivier. A sénatus-consulte of 20 April 1870 made the Empire a constitutional monarchy, and a plebiscite on 8 May approved the amended constitution by nearly seven to one.

When Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was proposed for the Spanish throne in 1870, Ollivier let himself be won over by the war party and was outmanoeuvred by Bismarck. On 15 July he announced the Ems Dispatch to the Chamber. By 9 August the French army had lost at Wissembourg, Spicheren and Wörth, and his cabinet fell. He took refuge in Italy and returned in 1873 with his political power gone. His first wife, Blandine, was a daughter of Franz Liszt. In retirement he wrote the eighteen volumes of L'Empire libéral from 1895, his defence of his conduct. He died on 20 August 1913.
emilie-du-chatelet: Gabrielle Émilie Le Tonnelier de Breteuil was born in Paris on 17 December 1706, the only daughter among six children of Louis Nicolas le Tonnelier de Breteuil, who served at the court of Louis XIV. Her father held a weekly salon for writers and scientists and arranged for Bernard Le Bovier de Fontenelle to discuss astronomy with her when she was ten. By twelve she was fluent in Latin, Italian, Greek and German, and she studied mathematics, literature and science. On 12 June 1725 she married the Marquis Florent-Claude du Chastellet-Lomont; they had three children and later agreed to live separate lives in one household.

Her relationship with Voltaire began in 1733. In 1734, threatened with arrest after his Letters on the English, he settled at Cirey, her family's estate in Haute-Marne, which became their home and the main setting of their collaboration; the château was remodelled to include a laboratory. She studied mathematics with Pierre Louis Moreau de Maupertuis and corresponded with Alexis Clairaut, Leonhard Euler and Frederick II of Prussia.

In 1737 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris set a prize on the nature of fire. She disagreed with Voltaire's ideas and, without telling him, prepared her own entry. Her Institutions de Physique, published in 1740 and revised in 1742, was presented as a review of new ideas for her 13-year-old son and was translated into German and Italian in 1743. It helped make her a member of the Academy of Sciences of the Institute of Bologna in 1746. In 1741 she answered D'Ortous de Mairan point by point on the measure of forces vives, and he withdrew from the controversy.

Du Châtelet criticised John Locke, rejecting his aversion to innate ideas and holding that universal prior principles are the precondition of knowledge. Her preface to her adaptation of The Fable of the Bees argued strongly for women's education. She also wrote a critical analysis of the whole Bible and Discours sur le bonheur, which argues that illusions can serve happiness if one does not trust all of them.

In 1748 she became involved with the poet and officer Jean François de Saint-Lambert, and at 42 she feared she would not survive another childbirth. She worked intensively on her French translation of Newton's Principia with an extensive commentary, working with Alexis Clairaut, and completed it in 1749. She gave birth on 4 September and died on 10 September 1749. The translation appeared in 1756 and is still the standard French version.
emilio-aguinaldo: Emilio Aguinaldo was born on 22 March 1869 in Cavite el Viejo, now Kawit, the seventh of eight children. His father, Carlos Aguinaldo, was the community's appointed gobernadorcillo under Spanish rule, and the family was well-to-do. He studied at the Colegio de San Juan de Letran but could not finish because of a cholera outbreak in 1882. In 1895 he joined the Katipunan, the secret society led by Andrés Bonifacio that sought independence by armed force, taking the name Magdalo.

When the revolution broke out in August 1896 Aguinaldo marched from Kawit with 600 men and fought the Spanish at Imus. At Binakayan and Dalahican in November his men and those of Santiago Alvarez defeated Spanish forces, a victory regarded as the first major Filipino win over a colonial power. At the Tejeros Convention on 22 March 1897 he was elected president of a revolutionary government, though Bonifacio disputed the result.

After Aguinaldo ordered his arrest, Bonifacio and his brother Procopio were tried and executed by firing squad on 10 May 1897. Aguinaldo says he commuted the sentence to exile and withdrew the order under pressure from generals, and that Mariano Noriel acted hastily. From 24 June 1897 he had his headquarters at Biak-na-Bato. After the Spanish–American War began, Commodore George Dewey carried him from Hong Kong to Cavite, arriving on 19 May 1898. He promulgated the Declaration of Independence on 12 June 1898 and on 23 June set up a revolutionary government with himself as president.

The First Philippine Republic was established by the Malolos Constitution on 21 January 1899 and ended when American forces captured Aguinaldo at Palanan on 23 March 1901. In the American period he largely retired from public life and organised an association of veterans of the revolution. In 1935 he ran for president against Manuel L. Quezon and won 17.5 per cent of the vote.

After the Japanese invasion of 1941 he sided with Japan and on 1 February 1942 called on American and Filipino troops on Bataan to surrender. He was arrested in 1945 and charged with treason. He died on 6 February 1964. He is regarded in the Philippines as the country's first president and a national hero who designed the flag, though his part in the deaths of Bonifacio and of General Antonio Luna remains contested.
emilio-castelar: Emilio Castelar y Ripoll was born in Cádiz. At the age of seven he lost his father, who had taken part in the progressive agitations of the reign of Ferdinand VII and spent years in exile in England. In 1848 he began to study law in Madrid, then moved to the School of Philosophy and Letters, where he earned a doctorate in 1853. During the revolutionary movement of 1854 he gave his first speech, at a meeting of young liberals and democrats, and it placed him at once among the political vanguard. After the uprising of June 1866 a court martial condemned him to death by garrote in his absence, and he escaped to France.

The Revolution of 1868 let him return, and he took a seat in the Cortes as deputy for Zaragoza. In the Constituent Cortes of 1869 he led the republican minority that argued for a federal republic, and he attacked the monarchy of Amadeus of Savoy until it fell.

The federal republic was proclaimed on 11 February 1873, and Castelar became minister for foreign affairs. He disliked bloodshed, mob rule and military pronunciamientos. At the beginning of September 1873 he became chief of the executive, ruled by decree, reorganised an army that had dwindled to about 70,000 men and called out more than 100,000 conscripts against the 60,000 Carlists in arms and the cantonalists around Alcoy and Cartagena. He restored relations with the Vatican, and he handled the Virginius Incident with the United States without a rupture.

When the Cortes met on 2 January 1874 its intransigent majority passed a vote of censure, and he resigned. At daybreak on 3 January General Pavia forcibly ejected the deputies and called Marshal Serrano to form a provisional government.

After Alphonso XII was proclaimed king Castelar spent fifteen months in exile, then sat in every parliament until his death. He founded the daily newspaper El Globo in 1875 and wrote, among other works, Life of Lord Byron and The History of the Republican Movement in Europe. He died near Murcia on 25 May 1899, aged sixty-six, and his funeral in Madrid drew people of all classes and parties.
emilio-de-bono: Emilio De Bono was born in Cassano d'Adda, the son of Giovanni de Bono and Elisa Bazzi. He entered the Royal Italian Army as a second lieutenant in 1884 and fought in the Italo-Ethiopian War of 1887-1889. By the start of the Italo-Turkish War in 1911 he had reached the General Staff, and he received the Knight's Cross of the Military Order of Savoy for his conduct there. In the First World War he fought against Austria-Hungary on the Karst Plateau, at Gorizia, on the Piave and on Monte Grappa, and won three Silver Medals of Military Valour.

In the early 1920s De Bono helped organise the National Fascist Party and, as one of the four Quadrumvirs, organised the March on Rome. Afterwards he served as Chief of Police and Commander of the Fascist Militia. He was tried in 1925 over the death of the leftist politician Giacomo Matteotti, refused to implicate his superiors and was acquitted. Later that year he became governor of Tripolitania, where he was a key figure in anti-partisan policies, including poison gas and concentration camps, that killed tens of thousands of civilians and have been described as genocidal. In 1929 he became Minister of Colonial Affairs.

In November 1932 De Bono wrote, at Mussolini's request, a plan for an invasion of Ethiopia that was to be slow, cheap and safe. The army drew up a far larger plan of its own, and in 1935 De Bono became supreme commander of the operation. His forces crossed from Eritrea on 3 October, took Adowa on 6 October and captured Mek'ele on 8 November. He was made Marshal of Italy on 16 November, but Mussolini, impatient at the slow advance, relieved him in December and replaced him with Pietro Badoglio.

In 1940 De Bono commanded a defence corps in Sicily and opposed Italy's entry into the Second World War. On 24 and 25 July 1943 he was among the members of the Grand Council of Fascism who voted to oust Mussolini. After Mussolini was freed by German forces and set up the Italian Social Republic, De Bono and others who had voted against him were tried for treason at Verona. He was shot on 11 January 1944, aged 77, with Galeazzo Ciano, Luciano Gottardi, Giovanni Marinelli and Carlo Pareschi, and complained of being shot in the back as a traitor.
emilio-garrastazu-medici: Emílio Garrastazu Médici was born on 4 December 1905 in Bagé, in Rio Grande do Sul. On his father's side he was the grandson of Italian immigrants who went first to Uruguay and then to Brazil, and on his mother's side he descended from Basques. He entered military school at Porto Alegre in the 1920s and became a general in 1961. He was chief of staff to Artur da Costa e Silva from 1957 to 1960, military attaché to the US from 1964 to 1966 and, in 1967, chief of the National Intelligence Service.

In 1969, as commander of the Third Army, Médici was chosen as president by the military junta that followed Costa e Silva's stroke. Congress was reconvened to elect him, which it did by 313 votes to none, with 56 abstentions. He took the oath on 30 October 1969 and served until 15 March 1974. He ruled under the 1967 Constitution and Institutional Act Number Five, which gave the government sweeping powers to censor the press and restrict civil rights. His regime used torture, spied on opponents, many of whom disappeared, and enforced strict censorship; the period is often called the Years of Lead. The guerrilla movement of Carlos Marighella and Carlos Lamarca was mostly destroyed.

The same years saw the Brazilian Miracle, in which the economy grew about 10 percent a year. Large projects included the Trans-Amazonian Highway, the Rio-Niterói Bridge and the Itaipu Dam. External debt rose from 3.9 billion dollars in 1968 to over 12.5 billion in 1973, and the growth benefited mainly the richer classes: workers whose pay was tied to the minimum wage lost about half their purchasing power compared with 1960.

In 1974 Médici was succeeded by his chosen candidate, Ernesto Geisel, and retired from public life. He died of kidney failure on 9 October 1985, after a stroke, and was buried in the São João Batista Cemetery in Rio de Janeiro. In the 1980s the Catholic vicariate of São Paulo and Protestant ministers obtained thousands of classified documents detailing the use of torture during his term, which shocked many Brazilians who had not known of it. The Federal University of Rio de Janeiro in 2015 and the Federal University of Pelotas in 2024 revoked the honorary doctorates they had given him.
emir: Amir comes from the Arabic root a-m-r, meaning command, and meant lord or commander-in-chief. It came to be used as a title of leaders, governors and rulers of smaller states. The word entered English in 1593, from the French émir. It has been used in West Asia, East Africa, North Africa, West Africa, Central Asia and South Asia, and the feminine form is emira. From the start it was a military title, and in the ninth century it was also used for the ruler of a state, as in the Emirate of Sicily.

The caliphs first used the title Amir al-Mu'minin, Commander of the Faithful, to stress their leadership over the Islamic empire, especially its militia, and Shia Muslims still give it to the Caliph Ali. Various Muslim rulers later took it, sultans and emirs among them. The Abbasid caliph al-Radi created the post of Amir al-Umara, Amir of the Amirs, for Ibn Raik, and the title was used in various Islamic monarchies. In Lebanon the ruling emir formally used the style al-Amir al-Hakim, and Druze and Christians both held the title. The theocratic and hereditary leader of the Yazidi community, the Mîr of the Sheikhan principality, is known as an emir or prince.

In northern Nigeria the traditional rulers are called emirs, while the titular sovereign of the former Sokoto empire is styled Sultan of Sokoto, Amir al-Muminin. The title of emir has gradually given way to king among hereditary rulers who wish to stress their secular authority under the rule of law. Bahrain's monarch changed his title from emir to king in 2002, and the United Arab Emirates use sheikh rather than emir for their rulers of the individual emirates.

In certain decimally organised Muslim armies amir was an officer rank. In Mughal India the amirs commanded 1,000 horsemen, divided into ten units each under a sipah salar, and ten of them stood under one malik. In the imperial army of Qajar Persia there were ranks such as Amir Panj, commander of 5,000, and Amir-i-Tuman, commander of 10,000. Medieval Muslim states had posts such as amir al-hajj, commander of the pilgrim caravan to Mecca, and amir al-ʿarab, commander of the Bedouin tribes.

In the former Kingdom of Afghanistan Amir-i-Kabir meant great prince or great commander, and in imperial Persia Amir-i-Iel designated the head of a tribe. The son of a prince was an amirzade, from which the Persian princely title mirza comes. The Fatimid navy had a post called Amir al-Baḥr, commander of the sea, often mistaken for the origin of the English admiral. The titles of admiral actually derive from Medieval Latin forms of emir itself, first used for the amirs al-umara of Norman Sicily.
emir-abdelkader: Abd al-Qadir ibn Muhyi al-Din was born in the hamlet of el Guetna, in the Ottoman Regency of Algiers, about 25 kilometres west of Mascara, into a family of the religious and marabout elite. He claimed descent from Hasan ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, and belonged to the Qadiriyya Sufi brotherhood. He grew up in his father's zawiya and was educated in Islam, grammar, Quranic exegesis, hadith and jurisprudence. According to contemporary biographies he memorised the whole Quran at fourteen, becoming a hafiz.

The French navy blockaded Algiers from 1827 and invaded in 1830, and the French took Oran in January 1831. The tribes of the west fell into instability, and in 1832 Abdelkader was appointed emir. The Treaty of Tafna of 30 May 1837 gave him control of all of Oran Province, Titteri and more. In the peace that followed he built a broadly theocratic state with its capital at Tagdemt, divided into eight regions each under a caliph, and declined the title of sultan.

The peace ended in October 1839, and Bugeaud returned as governor-general in February 1841 with a strategy of annihilation by scorched earth. On 16 May 1843 the Duke of Aumale ransacked his itinerant capital, the smala. French columns in 1844 and 1845 suffocated hundreds of Algerians who had taken refuge in caves, including more than 500 of the Oulad Riah, of whom only 40 survived. He surrendered in December 1847.

The French government refused the promise made at his surrender and held him and about a hundred followers at Toulon, Pau and Amboise. Victor Hugo and others called for his release, and Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte freed him on 2 December 1852. He went to Bursa and in 1855 to Damascus, where in 1860 his intervention to halt the massacre of the Christian community earned him honours from several countries. There he wrote his main work, the Kitab al-Mawaqif. He died on 26 May 1883 and was buried in the mausoleum of Ibn Arabi. In 1966 his remains were moved to Algiers. His treatment of prisoners and civilians has often been cited as an early example of humane conduct in war.
emirate-of-cordoba: The Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom began in April 711, when an army under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and defeated the Visigoths at Guadalete. Iberia became a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, whose governors made Córdoba their capital. In 750 the Umayyads lost the caliphate in Damascus to the Abbasids. Abd al-Rahman I, a prince of the deposed family, spent six years on the run, and in 756 he refused to recognise Abbasid authority and became independent emir of Córdoba. He united local fiefdoms in campaigns that reached Toledo, Zaragoza, Pamplona and Barcelona and took over twenty-five years.

The emirs used the titles emir or sultan until the mid-10th century and nominally recognised the Abbasid caliphs, and their real control was always in question, especially along the Christian border. Abd al-Rahman III came to the throne in 912. Facing the rival Fatimid Caliphate in North Africa, he took the title of caliph in 929. He secured Melilla, Ceuta and Tangier, and brought the Christian kingdoms of the north under his influence by force.

Under Almanzor, chamberlain of Hisham II, the caliph's title became symbolic, and the state came to rest on a professional army often drawn from outside the peninsula. After Almanzor died in 1002, rival factions competed for power. The civil war known as the Fitna of al-Andalus followed, and in 1031 the caliphate collapsed into independent taifa kingdoms.

Under Umayyad rule Arabization and Islamization advanced significantly. Arabs were a minority who formed the ruling elite, Berbers a larger group, and indigenous converts to Islam, called Muwallads, became very numerous. Jews and Christians held the status of dhimmis, paying the jizya. The Umayyads promoted the Maliki school of law.

Córdoba was the cultural centre of al-Andalus. Its population probably passed 100,000 in the 10th century, and the royal library under al-Hakam II held an estimated 400,000 to 500,000 volumes. The caliph's workshops at Madinat al-Zahra produced silks, bronzes and carved ivory boxes. The period left the Great Mosque of Córdoba and Madinat al-Zahra, among the best-known works of Andalusi architecture.
emirates-mars-mission: The idea of a Mars mission came from a cabinet retreat of the United Arab Emirates at the end of 2013, and Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan announced it in July 2014. The Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre in Dubai designed and built the probe under an agreement with the UAE Space Agency, with Omran Sharaf as project manager and Sarah Al Amiri as deputy project manager and science lead. Emirati engineers assembled the spacecraft at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder, with support from Arizona State University and the University of California, Berkeley.

In April 2015 the public was invited to name it, and Hope, Al-Amal in Arabic, was chosen to send a message of optimism to young Arabs, in the words of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. The UAE minister of cabinet affairs gave the cost as 200 million US dollars.

The probe has a mass of 1,350 kilograms with fuel, about the size of a small car. It carries three instruments: a multi-band camera, the Emirates eXploration Imager; the Emirates Mars Infrared Spectrometer, which measures temperatures and the ice, water vapour and dust in the lower atmosphere; and the Emirates Mars Ultraviolet Spectrometer, which studies the upper atmosphere and the hydrogen and oxygen escaping from it.

Its high orbit, with a period of 55 hours, a periapsis of about 20,000 kilometres and an apoapsis of about 43,000 kilometres, was chosen to give a global view of the atmosphere through the day and the seasons. The team called Hope the first true weather satellite at Mars. It was to study dust storms, differences between regions and the loss of hydrogen and oxygen to space, and the data were to be shared with some 200 institutions.

Because of the coronavirus pandemic the probe was shipped to Japan in April 2020, and engineers spent two weeks in quarantine there. It was launched in July 2020 from the Tanegashima Space Center on a Mitsubishi H-IIA rocket, one of three missions sent to Mars in that launch window, with China's Tianwen-1 and the American Mars 2020. The journey of about 200 days covered 493 million kilometres.

On 9 February 2021 Hope fired its thrusters for about 27 minutes and entered orbit, the first interplanetary mission of an Arab country. The United Arab Emirates became the fifth country to reach Mars and the second, after India, to enter its orbit on the first try. On 10 March 2023 the orbiter made a fly-by of the Martian moon Deimos and returned the first close global images of it.
emma-goldman: Emma Goldman was born into an Orthodox Jewish family in Kaunas, then within the Russian Empire. The family later moved to the village of Papilė, where her father ran an inn. There she saw a peasant whipped with a knout in the street, an event that traumatised her and contributed to her lifelong distaste for violent authority.

In 1885 her sister Helena planned to move to New York to join their sister Lena. Their father refused to let Emma go, and he agreed only after she threatened to throw herself into the Neva River. She arrived at Castle Garden on 29 December 1885. On her first day she met Alexander Berkman, and heard Johann Most, the editor of Freiheit and an advocate of propaganda of the deed, who trained her in public speaking. She was drawn to anarchism after the persecution that followed the Haymarket affair.

After the Homestead Strike of 1892, Goldman and Berkman planned the killing of Henry Clay Frick, the manager of the Carnegie steel plant, as an act of propaganda of the deed. Frick survived and Berkman was sentenced to 22 years in prison. During the Panic of 1893 she spoke to a crowd of nearly 3,000 people in Union Square, and was imprisoned for inciting to riot.

After Leon Czolgosz shot President William McKinley in 1901, he said he had been inspired by a speech of hers, and she was arrested with twelve other anarchists. From 1903 she withdrew from public life and nursed, until opposition to the Anarchist Exclusion Act pulled her back. She founded Mother Earth in 1906, lectured across the country and was jailed for distributing information about birth control. In 1917 she and Berkman were sentenced to two years for conspiring to induce persons not to register for the draft. In the Red Scare they were arrested and deported to Russia in December 1919.

Goldman first welcomed the Bolshevik revolution, but she grew alarmed and, after the Kronstadt rebellion, denounced the Soviet Union for its violent repression of independent voices. She left the Soviet Union and published My Disillusionment in Russia in 1923, and lived in England, Canada and France, writing her autobiography Living My Life. In 1936 she went to Barcelona to support the anarchist revolution of the Spanish Civil War, where she edited the CNT-FAI Information Bulletin. She suffered a stroke on 17 February 1940 and died in Toronto on 14 May 1940, aged 70.

In her lifetime admirers called her a freethinking rebel woman, and detractors called her an advocate of politically motivated murder. After decades of obscurity, she was read widely again in the 1970s, when feminist and anarchist scholars revived interest in her.
emma-of-normandy: Emma was a daughter of the Norman ruler Richard the Fearless and Gunnor. King Æthelred of England married her in 1002 to pacify Normandy, since Viking raids on England had often been based there, and her brother Richard II, Duke of Normandy, hoped to improve relations with the English. On marriage she took the Anglo-Saxon name Ælfgifu, used in formal and official matters, and received properties of her own in Winchester, Rutland, Devonshire, Suffolk and Oxfordshire, as well as the city of Exeter. She had two sons with Æthelred, Edward the Confessor and Alfred Ætheling, and a daughter, Godgifu. When Sweyn Forkbeard conquered England in 1013 she and her children went to Normandy, returning after Sweyn died in 1014.

Æthelred died in 1016, and Cnut, Sweyn's son, held London until arrangements were made for him to marry Emma; she had tried to maintain Anglo-Saxon control of the city. Some scholars think the marriage saved her sons' lives. They married in 1017, and she became queen of Denmark in 1018 and of Norway in 1028. Her sons by Æthelred were sent to live in Normandy. With Cnut she had a son, Harthacnut, and a daughter, Gunhilda.

When Cnut died in 1035 Emma backed Harthacnut, who was in Denmark, against Harold Harefoot. In 1036 she called Alfred and Edward back from Normandy. Alfred was captured by Earl Godwin, blinded and died of his wounds, and Edward was met by armed opposition and fled. Emma went into exile at Bruges. Harthacnut became king in 1040, and after his death in 1042 Edward succeeded; in 1043 he accused her of treason and took her lands and titles, but soon relented and restored them.

Emma died in 1052 and was buried alongside Cnut and Harthacnut in the Old Minster, Winchester, and later moved to the new cathedral. During the English Civil War her remains were scattered by parliamentary forces and later reburied. Until 1043, writes Pauline Stafford, she was the richest woman in England.

She is the central figure of the Encomium Emmae Reginae, a praise of the queen and a critical source for the politics of the early 11th century. It names Æthelred only as a prince and does not mention that she had been his wife. Scholars now read it as an intervention in the politics of the Anglo-Danish court. A portrait in the New Minster Liber Vitae shows Cnut and Emma presenting a cross to the altar.
emmanuel-joseph-sieyes: Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès was born on 3 May 1748, the fifth child of a local tax collector of modest income in Fréjus. The family claimed some noble blood but were commoners. Frail health thwarted his ambition to be a soldier, and he turned to a religious career, spending ten years at the seminary of Saint-Sulpice in Paris. He read Locke, Hume, Voltaire, Rousseau and Diderot in preference to theology. After serving as secretary to the bishop of Tréguier, he followed him to Chartres in 1780 as vicar general, and became a canon and chancellor of the diocese. He resented how easily nobles advanced in the Church compared with commoners.

In 1788 Louis XVI proposed to convene the Estates-General, and Sieyès published What Is the Third Estate? in January 1789. It began: "What is the Third Estate? Everything. What has it been hitherto in the political order? Nothing. What does it desire to be? Something." It argued that the Third Estate represented the nation by itself. Though a priest, he was elected a deputy of the Third Estate for Paris. He proposed that the other orders join it, and on 5 June 1789 it took the name National Assembly.

In the Assembly he helped draft the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and argued for a single chamber and against a royal veto. In the Convention he voted for the death of Louis XVI. Asked what he had done during the Terror, he replied, "J'ai vécu" (I lived). He refused a place in the Directory in 1795 but became a director in May 1799.

Sieyès planned to overthrow the Directory and, in the coup of 18 Brumaire, he and his allies dissolved it, making Napoleon Bonaparte, Sieyès and Roger Ducos Consuls. The constitution he had long planned was remodelled by Bonaparte into the Constitution of the Year VIII. Sieyès soon retired from the consulship, became one of the first members of the Sénat conservateur and received an estate at Crosne from Napoleon. Expelled from the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences in 1816 for his role in the king's execution, he lived in Brussels until 1830 and died in Paris in 1836. In an unpublished manuscript of 1780 he had coined the term sociologie.
emmanuel-philibert-duke-of-savoy: Emmanuel Philibert was born in Chambéry on 8 July 1528, the only child of Charles III, Duke of Savoy, and Beatrice of Portugal to reach adulthood. His mother was sister-in-law to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, and he served in Charles's army in the war against Francis I of France, distinguishing himself by capturing Hesdin in July 1553. He became known as Testa di ferro, Ironhead, because of his military career.

His father died a month after Hesdin, in August 1553, and Emmanuel Philibert became Duke of Savoy. The honour was nearly empty, since the French had occupied and administered most of his hereditary lands since 1536. He continued to serve the Habsburgs in the hope of recovering them and served his cousin Philip II of Spain as Governor of the Netherlands from 1555 to 1559. In that post he led the Spanish invasion of northern France and won a victory at Saint-Quentin on 10 August 1557. He was also a suitor to Elizabeth Tudor, the future Queen Elizabeth I.

The Peace of Cateau Cambrésis, signed between France and Spain in 1559, finally restored his lands. He then married his first cousin once removed, Margaret of Valois, Duchess of Berry and sister of Henry II of France, and their only child was Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy. A skilled political strategist, he used various squabbles in Europe to regain territory from both the French and the Spanish, including the city of Turin, and he purchased two territories. He moved his capital from Chambéry to Turin and replaced Latin as the official language with French in the Duchy of Savoy and the Duchy of Aosta, and with Italian in the Principality of Piedmont and the County of Nice.

When his uncle Henry I of Portugal died on 31 January 1580, Emmanuel Philibert fought to press his claim to the Portuguese throne, but he soon realised that his position was fragile because Philip II took control of the country and united Spain and Portugal. He was trying to acquire the marquisate of Saluzzo when he died in Turin on 30 August 1580. He was buried in the Chapel of the Holy Shroud in Turin Cathedral, to which he had moved the Sindone in 1578.
emmeline-pankhurst: Emmeline Goulden was born in the Moss Side district of Manchester to politically active parents, and was introduced to the women's suffrage movement at 14. In 1878 she met Richard Pankhurst, a barrister who had advocated women's suffrage and other causes for years, and they married on 18 December 1879. After the National Society for Women's Suffrage split in 1888, she and her husband helped organise a new group dedicated to the vote for all women, married and unmarried. Richard died in July 1898 after a gastric ulcer.

By 1903 Pankhurst believed that years of moderate speeches and promises from MPs had achieved nothing, since suffrage bills in 1870, 1886 and 1897 had all been defeated. On 10 October 1903 she and colleagues founded the Women's Social and Political Union, open only to women and committed to direct action, with the motto deeds, not words. On 21 June 1908 500,000 people rallied in Hyde Park, but Prime Minister Asquith and leading MPs responded with indifference, and some members then escalated their actions, throwing rocks at the windows of 10 Downing Street.

The Union expelled Emmeline and Frederick Pethick-Lawrence over its tactics, and Adela Pankhurst left the group, a rift with her mother that was never healed. Members adopted arson and bombing, and more moderate organisations spoke out against the Pankhurst family. When the First World War began in August 1914, Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst halted militant activity until the fighting ended, and all imprisoned members were released. The Union became the Women's Party, and Emmeline later joined the Conservative Party and was selected as its candidate for Whitechapel and St Georges in 1927.

The Representation of the People Act of 1918 gave votes to women over 30 and to all men over 21. Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, only weeks before the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Act extended the vote to all women over 21 on 2 July 1928. She was commemorated two years later by a statue in Victoria Tower Gardens, beside the Houses of Parliament. Historians disagree about the effectiveness of her militant tactics, but her work is recognised as a crucial element in achieving women's suffrage in the United Kingdom.
emmendingen: Emmendingen lies on the Elz river, 14 km north of Freiburg im Breisgau, in the Breisgau between the foothills of the Black Forest and the Kaiserstuhl. The land is between 189 and 368 metres high. The Elz, flowing on the western edge of the town, divides near Riegel into the Old Elz and the Leopoldskanal, which was built in the middle of the 19th century. The nearby Kaiserstuhl, a range of volcanic hills, is considered one of the warmest places in Germany and is a wine-growing area.

The first mention of the town in a document dates to 1091, though it is much older. It was the seat of the counts of Hochberg, a cadet branch of the Margraviate of Baden. It received market rights from the emperor in 1418, and in 1590 Margrave Jacob III raised it to the status of a town and walled it. A neighbouring town, Nieder-Emmendingen, merged with it in 1883. The coat of arms shows the red bend on gold of the old arms of Baden, the symbol of the local lord, and a knight; seals earlier showed a ploughshare instead of the knight, and the present form was adopted in 1960.

The post was first established in 1745 as a Posthalterei. The Goethe Gymnasium was converted from a Latin School in 1667. The author Johann Georg Schlosser, a brother-in-law of Goethe, served for some years as Oberamtmann, the bailiff. His wife Cornelia, born Cornelia Friederica Christiana Goethe, was the only sibling of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, and they lived in a house on the main square which is now the municipal library.

Emmendingen is the capital of the district of the same name in Baden-Württemberg and has more than 26,000 residents. It lies on the Baden Main Line between Mannheim and Basel. The old town hall on the main square now houses the German Diary Archive, the only archive of diaries in Germany. A Jewish Museum stands on Castle Square, and a Jewish school offering courses on Jewish culture and history has been run since 2006 by the Jewish congregation together with an association for Jewish history and culture.
emmerich-am-rhein: Emmerich lies on the north bank of the Rhine, in the district of Kleve, and is the last German town on the river before it flows into the Netherlands, 4 kilometres to the north and 5 kilometres to the west. The town has a harbour and a quay on the Rhine. The municipality takes in villages such as Borghees, Dornick, Elten, Hüthum, Praest and Vrasselt, which were incorporated in 1969 and 1975.

Emmerich, formerly called Embrika and Emrik, was originally a Roman colony. Around the year 700 Saint Willibrord founded a mission there in the diocese of Utrecht, and the oldest documented name, Villa Embrici, dates from 828. The collegiate church of St Martini was built in 1040. In 1371 the town fell to the Duchy of Cleves, and in 1407 it joined the Hanseatic League. It passed to Brandenburg in 1609, a commune of French Huguenots was founded there in 1686, and in 1794 it was bombarded by the French under General Vandamme. It was assigned to the Duchy of Berg in 1806 and passed to Prussia in 1815.

The railway section from Oberhausen to Arnhem opened in 1856. On 7 October 1944 91 per cent of Emmerich was destroyed as a strategic bombing target of the Oil Campaign of the Second World War. Elten was annexed by the Netherlands from 1949 until 1963. The city has officially been called Emmerich am Rhein since 1 February 2001.

The Rhine Bridge, opened in 1965 and connecting Emmerich with Kleve, has a span of 1,228 metres and is the longest suspension bridge in Germany. The Rhine Museum holds 130 ship models and exhibitions on shipping and fisheries. Castle Borghees, expanded to its present form in the mid-18th century, is used as a cultural centre and is known for the love affair of Katharina Rickers, aged seventeen and later imperial countess of Wartenberg, with the Prussian king Friedrich I. The Holy Ghost Catholic Church of 1966 reflects the architecture of the Second Vatican Council era.
empedocles: Ancient accounts of Empedocles' life conflict, and the main sources come from the Hellenistic period, several centuries after his death. They agree that he was born in the early 5th century BCE in Akragas, a Greek city in Magna Graecia.
