Modern scholars accept that he came from a rich and noble family and that his grandfather, also named Empedocles, won the horse race at Olympia in the 71st Olympiad, in 496 to 495 BCE. Scholars think that other details, such as Aristotle's claim that he was the father of rhetoric and his tutelage under Pythagoras, which is chronologically impossible, were invented from readings of his poetry.

According to Diogenes Laërtius, Empedocles wrote two poems, On Nature and On Purifications, together about 5,000 lines, of which some 550 survive as quotations. He is generally considered the last Greek philosopher to record his ideas in verse. The Strasbourg papyrus holds a large part of On Nature, and scholars debate whether there were two poems or one.

He held that four unchangeable roots, fire, air, water and earth, make up all structures, and that different proportions of them produce different things. Two divine powers, Love and Strife, join and part them. He never used the word element, which seems first to have been used by Plato. The theory of the four elements became the standard doctrine for two thousand years. Like Pythagoras he believed in the transmigration of souls: humans were originally long-lived daimons who fell to earth after an unspecified crime and had to pass through 30,000 cycles of incarnation. He advocated vegetarianism, and proposed that we see because light streams out of our eyes.

According to Aristotle, Empedocles died at about 60, though other writers have him living as long as 109 years. Diogenes Laërtius records the legend that he threw himself into Mount Etna so that people would believe he had become a god, but the volcano cast back one of his bronze sandals and revealed the deceit. In Lucian's Icaro-Menippus an eruption carries him to the Moon. Friedrich Hölderlin's play Der Tod des Empedokles and Matthew Arnold's poem Empedocles on Etna treat his death, and Lucretius spoke of him with enthusiasm as a model. Galen regarded him as the founder of the Sicilian school of medicine.
emperor-bing-of-song: Zhao Bing was born on 12 February 1272, the seventh son of Zhao Qi, Emperor Duzong, and his concubine Lady Yu, who held the rank of xiurong. He was a younger half-brother of Zhao Xian, Emperor Gong, and of Zhao Shi, Emperor Duanzong. In 1274 he was enfeoffed as Prince of Xin, a title later changed to Prince of Guang and then Prince of Wei.

On 4 February 1276 the Mongol-led Yuan general Bayan took the Song capital Lin'an, present-day Hangzhou, and Emperor Gong surrendered. Zhao Shi and Zhao Bing escaped to the south with the help of officials including Yang Liangjie, Lu Xiufu, Zhang Shijie, Chen Yizhong and Wen Tianxiang. At Jinhua Zhao Shi became Grand Marshal and Zhao Bing Vice Grand Marshal, and on 14 June 1276 Zhao Shi was enthroned at Fuzhou as Emperor Duanzong.

After Duanzong died of illness in 1278, morale fell and soldiers began to desert. Lu Xiufu brought Zhao Bing to Meiwei in Gangzhou, in present-day Mui Wo on Lantau Island, Hong Kong, where he was enthroned under the era name Xiangxing and the place was renamed Xianglong County. The court then moved to Yamen, in present-day Xinhui District, Jiangmen, in Guangdong, to evade the Mongols. His reign lasted around 313 days.

The Mongols sent the general Zhang Hongfan against the Song remnants, and at the naval Battle of Yamen the Song forces under Zhang Shijie resisted fiercely but were wiped out. On 19 March 1279 Lu Xiufu, realising all was lost, carried the emperor to a cliff and both threw themselves into the sea.

A tomb at Chiwan, in Nanshan District, Shenzhen, was rediscovered in the 1960s; the identity of the body in it has not been authenticated, but in 1984 a joint Hong Kong and Shenzhen effort restored and enlarged the site. Local tradition in Guangdong holds that he named a vegetable soup served by monks at Chaozhou the Protect the Country Dish, later called patriotic soup in English, and its preparation became a way of honouring him.
emperor-daigo: Daigo was born on 6 February 884, the eldest son of Emperor Uda. His mother was Fujiwara no Taneko, daughter of the minister Fujiwara no Takafuji. She died before his accession, and he was raised by another consort of Uda, Fujiwara no Onshi, daughter of the former kampaku Fujiwara no Mototsune. His grandfather Emperor Kōkō had demoted his own sons to subjects, giving them the family name Minamoto, to reduce state expenses and their political influence. For that reason Daigo was named Minamoto no Korezane until 887, and his personal name was later changed to Atsuhito. Uda abdicated in 897, and Daigo formally acceded to the throne on 14 August 897.

The era name was changed in 898 to mark the beginning of the reign. Its notable feature was that Daigo governed himself, without a regency of the Fujiwara clan, although he was himself partly Fujiwara. In 901 the incident of Sugawara Michizane developed, but its details cannot be known because Daigo ordered the diaries and records of the period burned. In 906 Ki no Tsurayuki presented to the emperor the compilation of the Kokin Wakashū, a collection of waka poetry. Floods devastated the country in 929, and many people died.

On 21 July 930 lightning struck the Imperial Palace during a great storm and killed Senior Counselor Fujiwara no Kiyotsura and Taira no Mareyo among others. The deaths were construed as the revenge of the unsettled spirit of the late Sugawara Michizane. Daigo had 21 empresses, consorts and concubines and 36 children, and two of his sons later became emperors, Suzaku and Murakami. He also ordered the building of several halls at Daigo-ji, such as the Yakushi hall.

On 16 October 930 Daigo fell ill and, fearing that he would not survive, abdicated, and his son received the succession. In the early hours of 23 October he entered the Buddhist priesthood, taking the name Hō-kongō, and shortly afterwards he died, aged 46. He was buried in the precincts of Daigo-ji, which gave him his posthumous name. The site of his grave is known, and the Imperial Household Agency designates it as his mausoleum in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.
emperor-daozong-of-liao: Born on 14 September 1032 with the personal name Chala, he was the eighth emperor of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty and succeeded his father, Emperor Xingzong, in 1055. In 1066 he revived the official dynastic name Great Liao, first given by Emperor Taizong in 947, and the Sakyamuni Pagoda was built in 1056. In his early years the court was dominated by Xiao Ge and Xiao Ala; after the two fell out, Xiao Ge denounced Ala, and the emperor had him strangled in 1061 despite the pleas of the Empress Dowager Renyi.

In 1063 dissident nobles led by Zhongyuan and his son Nielugu ambushed Daozong on a hunting trip. He was wounded when his horse fell to crossbowmen, and his mother led the guards against the attackers. Nielugu was killed by a stray arrow, Zhongyuan took his own life, and all the conspirators and their families were executed. To reassert his legitimacy the emperor had to perform the traditional rebirth ceremony, and in 1070 he restructured the legal system to reflect the differences between Han and Khitan customs.

After 1072 the chancellor Yelü Yixin had no rival at court. With the Han scholar Zhang Xiaojie he fabricated evidence that Empress Xiao Guanyin had written erotic poems to a palace musician, Zhao Weiyi, and then a false confession by her son, Prince Jun, who was imprisoned and killed by Yixin's emissaries. Daozong soon regretted it. When Yixin tried in 1079 to have the emperor leave Jun's son Yelü Yanxi behind on a hunt, courtiers protested; Yixin was demoted in 1080 and sentenced to death a year later for trading prohibited goods with a foreign state.

Yanxi was groomed as heir, and Daozong showed him the armour and weapons of Abaoji to teach him the hardships of the dynasty's founding. The Song envoy Su Che, after a mission in 1089, found the emperor vigorous and the border at peace but judged the grandson weak. Daozong's reign was marked by corruption and lavish spending on palaces and Buddhist worship, and heavy taxes stirred revolts, most notably among the Jurchen, who would later found the Jin dynasty. He died on 12 February 1101.
emperor-gaozong-of-song: Zhao Gou was the ninth son of Emperor Huizong and a younger half-brother of Emperor Qinzong. When the capital Bianjing was besieged by the Jurchens, he was sent to their camp to negotiate, but was held for ransom and returned after the Jurchens came to doubt his identity. He was in Cizhou on a diplomatic mission when Bianjing fell, so he escaped the capture of his father, his half-brother and most of the imperial clan in the Jingkang Incident, and made his way south to Jiankang.

He was proclaimed emperor at Jiankang (present-day Nanjing) with the era name Jianyan, meaning Establishing the Fire, which suggested the continuation of the Northern Song, whose dynastic element was fire. The early reign was filled with Jurchen raids, and he moved from Yingtianfu to Yangzhou and then to Lin'an. On 26 March 1129 palace guards led by Miao Fu and Liu Zhengyan mutinied and forced him to abdicate in favour of his two-year-old son, Zhao Fu. The loyal army of Han Shizhong defeated the mutineers by 20 April 1129, and they were executed for treason.

Qin Hui, promoted in 1138, managed the talks with the Jin. Yue Fei and Han Shizhong were preparing to attack Kaifeng when Gaozong recalled Yue Fei with twelve gold plaques; Yue Fei was then imprisoned on a charge described as groundless and put to death. In the Treaty of Shaoxing the Song gave up all land north of the Huai River, was designated the insignificant state and paid a yearly tribute of 250,000 taels of silver and 250,000 packs of silk. One reason given is that a Jin defeat might have led to the release of Qinzong, who was in captivity, and so threatened Gaozong's throne.

In 1161 the Jin ruler Wanyan Liang declared war but lost at Tangdao and Caishi, and the Song ceased to be a vassal state, although it still paid tribute. In 1162, after reigning for more than 35 years, Gaozong abdicated in favour of his adopted son and distant cousin Zhao Shen, who became Emperor Xiaozong. As Taishang Huang, the Retired Emperor, he kept some power until he died of natural causes in 1187, at the age of 80. His reputation suffered for Yue Fei's death and the surrender of over half of Song China, and he was blamed with his father and half-brother for the dynasty's decline. Others note that the peace saved the Song economy from military costs it could not afford.
emperor-gaozong-of-tang: Li Zhi was born on 21 July 628, the ninth son of Emperor Taizong and the third son of Empress Zhangsun. He was named Prince of Jin in 631. When Empress Zhangsun died in 636, Taizong was touched by the grief Li Zhi displayed and favoured him from then on. Taizong came to doubt that Li Zhi, who was considered kind but weak in character, was strong enough to be emperor, and secretly discussed with Zhangsun Wuji making another son, Li Ke, crown prince. Zhangsun repeatedly opposed the idea, and Taizong did not carry it out.

Gaozong's first act as emperor was to cancel a second campaign against Goguryeo that Taizong had planned for late 649. In his early reign he greatly respected his uncle Zhangsun Wuji and Chu Suiliang and followed their advice, and the government was well organised. In 650 the general Gao Kan captured the Göktürk leader Ashina Hubo, whom the emperor spared and made a general. In 651 Ashina Helu broke away from Tang and took over the Western Turkic Khaganate, and the generals sent against him withdrew without engaging him.

The Tang conquered Baekje, Goguryeo and the Western Turkic Khaganate during the first part of his reign, but Baekje resisters besieged a Tang general at Sabi, and in 662 Su Dingfang withdrew from Pyongyang after a defeat on the Sasu River and heavy snowstorms. Throughout the 670s much of the territory was lost to the Tibetan Empire, Silla, the Khitans and Balhae. After a series of strokes left him incapacitated, Gaozong delegated all matters of state to Empress Wu from January 665, who was said to be hanging the curtain and listening to politics.

They were called the two saints, and historians debate whether she exerted undue influence or the two were equal partners. In 674 she took the title Empress of Heaven, and about 675 she submitted twelve suggestions, including that the Tao Te Ching be added to the reading of imperial university students; Gaozong praised and adopted them.

Gaozong died on 27 December 683, and power then passed entirely to Empress Wu as empress dowager and regent. He was interred at the Qian Mausoleum on 25 September 684, and she was buried there after her death in 705. She later became the only empress regnant in Chinese history. In Hui Islamic legend he is called Yung Wei, after the first era name of his reign, and is credited with building the first mosque in China, the Huaisheng Mosque in Guangzhou.
emperor-gaozu-of-tang: Li Yuan was born on 7 April 566. According to the official genealogy of the Tang ruling house, his ancestor in the seventh generation was Li Gao, founder of the state of Western Liang. His grandfather Li Hu served under the general Yuwen Tai and was given the Xianbei surname Daye. His father Li Bing died in 572, when Li Yuan inherited the title of Duke of Tang.

He kept the title after Yang Jian seized the Northern Zhou throne in 581 as Emperor Wen of Sui, whose wife, Empress Dugu, was Li Yuan's aunt. Under the Sui he became governor in the area of modern Shanxi, based at Taiyuan, and in 615 he was sent to garrison Longxi, where he gained experience in dealing with the Göktürks.

Emperor Yang of Sui grew dissatisfied with Li Yuan over his inability to stop incursions by the Eastern Turks and the growing strength of agrarian rebels. Li Yuan was also fearful because of prophecies that the next emperor would be named Li. Traditional accounts, compiled under his son Li Shimin, stress the son's role in urging the rebellion, but modern researchers have concluded that the initiative came from Li Yuan himself. He rose in July 617 and took the throne in 618 after Emperor Yang was killed at Jiangdu.

Gaozu's reign was spent uniting the empire. Aided by Li Shimin, whom he made Prince of Qin, he defeated rivals including Xue Rengao, Liu Wuzhou, Dou Jiande and Wang Shichong, and by 628 the Tang had united all of China. He restored much of the institutions of Emperor Wen, including the equal distribution of land, lowered taxes, and abandoned the harsh legal system of Emperor Yang.

A rivalry grew between the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin, who had the greater reputation in the army. In 626 Li Shimin ambushed and killed Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji at the Xuanwu Gate, and Gaozu passed the throne to him, becoming Taishang Huang, or retired emperor.

He exerted little influence afterwards, and in 630, hearing that Li Jing had defeated the Turkic khagan Jiali Khan, he held a celebration and played the pipa himself. He died on 25 June 635, before a summer palace that Taizong had begun for him was finished. His son honoured him as Gaozu, meaning high founder.
emperor-go-daigo: Go-Daigo was born on 26 November 1288, the second son of Emperor Go-Uda, and before his accession was known by his personal name Takaharu. His mother was Fujiwara no Chushi and his older brother was Emperor Go-Nijo. In 1308, at the death of Go-Nijo, Hanazono took the throne and Takaharu was made crown prince under the direction of the Kamakura shogunate. His ideal was the Engi era (901-923) under Emperor Daigo, a period of direct imperial rule, and he chose his own posthumous name during his lifetime so as to share it with that emperor.

Hanazono abdicated on 29 March 1318 and Go-Daigo succeeded. His plans against the shogunate were discovered in 1324, when the Rokuhara Tandai removed his associate Hino Suketomo in the Shochu Incident, and again in the Genko Incident of 1331, when Yoshida Sadafusa betrayed them. He hid the Sacred Treasures in a castle on Kasagiyama and raised an army, but the castle fell the next year. The shogunate enthroned Emperor Kogon and exiled him to Oki Province, where Emperor Go-Toba had been sent after the Jokyu War of 1221.

In 1333 Go-Daigo escaped with the help of Nawa Nagatoshi and raised an army at Senjo Mountain. Ashikaga Takauji, sent to destroy it, changed sides and took the Rokuhara Tandai, while Nitta Yoshisada besieged Kamakura. When it fell, the regent Hojo Takatoki and his family killed themselves, ending Hojo power. Back in Kyoto, Go-Daigo began the Kenmu Restoration, but hasty reforms, disputes over land rights and rewards and the exclusion of samurai from the political order caused complaint. In 1335 Takauji, disaffected, was ordered destroyed. Kusunoki Masashige proposed reconciliation in 1336, but the emperor refused, and Masashige's army was beaten at the Battle of Minatogawa.

Takauji entered Kyoto, Go-Daigo fled to Mount Hiei and, seeking reconciliation, sent the imperial regalia to the Ashikaga side. Takauji enthroned Emperor Komyo and began his shogunate with the Kenmu Law Code. In January 1337 Go-Daigo escaped the capital, the regalia he had handed over being counterfeit, and set up the Southern Court at Yoshino, which began the period of the Northern and Southern Courts. He sent his sons across the country against the Northern Court. He abdicated on 18 September 1339 in favour of Prince Noriyoshi, later Emperor Go-Murakami, and died the next day. His overthrow of the Kamakura shogunate was the last time an emperor held real power until the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
emperor-go-enyu: Go-En'yū, whose personal name was Ohito, was the second son of Emperor Go-Kōgon, the fourth emperor of the Northern Court. His mother was Fujiwara no Nakako, a daughter of Hirohashi Kanetsuna. His name means the Later Emperor En'yū, after the 10th-century Emperor En'yū. His consort was Sanjō Itsuko, a daughter of Sanjō Kintada, and their first son, Prince Motohito, later became Emperor Go-Komatsu. His first daughter was Princess Keiko (1381–1399) and his second son the prince-priest Dōchō (1378–1446).

In his own lifetime Go-En'yū and those around him believed that he occupied the throne from 9 April 1371 to 24 May 1382. In 1371 he received the rank of Imperial Prince by proclamation and at once became emperor on the abdication of Go-Kōgon. There was said to have been a disagreement between Go-Kōgon and the retired Northern Emperor Sukō over the crown prince; with the support of Hosokawa Yoriyuki, who controlled the shogunate, Go-Kōgon's son became emperor. Ashikaga Yoshimitsu had been named shōgun in 1368, and under his guardianship the Imperial Court was stabilised.

The years of his reign were counted by more than one era name. The Northern Court used Ōan, Eiwa, Kōryaku and Eitoku, while the Southern Court, whose rival emperor was Chōkei, used Kentoku, Benchū, Tenju and Kōwa, as the Meiji rescript later fixed them.

Go-En'yū abdicated in 1382 in favour of Go-Komatsu and began a cloistered rule without real power. He is said to have rebelled, attempting suicide and accusing Ashikaga Yoshimitsu and Itsuko, his consort, of adultery. In 1392 peace with the Southern Court brought the Period of the Northern and Southern Courts to an end. He died on 6 June 1393 and is enshrined with other emperors at the imperial tomb called Fukakusa no kita no misasagi in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.
emperor-go-kameyama: Emperor Go-Kameyama, whose personal name was Hironari, was born around 1347 and is counted as the 99th emperor of Japan in the traditional order of succession. He was the second son of Emperor Go-Murakami and Fujiwara Katsuko, better known as Kaki Mon'in. Little is known of his empress or other consorts. His empress was a daughter of Kitabatake Akinobu, and Imperial Prince Tsuneatsu is believed to have been his son. His name recalls the 13th-century Emperor Kameyama, with go meaning later, so he could also be called Kameyama the second.

Go-Kameyama came to the throne during the Nanboku-chō period, when rival claimants to the Chrysanthemum Throne gathered supporters in a Northern court and a Southern court. He became emperor of the Southern court in 1383, when Emperor Chōkei abdicated. On 15 October 1392, at the insistence of the peace faction among his own courtiers, he applied to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu for peace. He then returned to the capital and handed the Sacred Treasures to his Northern court rival, and in doing so he was understood to have abdicated.

Under the terms of the peace the Northern and Southern courts were supposed to alternate control of the throne. In 1412 Emperor Go-Komatsu reneged by abdicating in favour of his own son, and no Southern court claimant sat on the throne again.

After his abdication Go-Kameyama went into seclusion, but in 1410 he returned to Yoshino. He died on 10 May 1424, and the Imperial Household Agency recognises Saga no ogura no misasagi, in Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, as his tomb.

Since 1911 the Japanese government has declared the southern claimants to have been the rightful emperors, on the reasoning that the Southern court kept the three sacred treasures. This holds even though every later emperor, including Emperor Meiji, descended from the Northern court.
emperor-go-kogon: Emperor Go-Kōgon, whose personal name was Iyahito, was born on 23 March 1338. He was the second son of Emperor Kōgon of the Northern Court and the brother of his predecessor, Emperor Sukō. His mother was Hideko, a daughter of Sanjō Kinhide. His name means the Later Kōgon, and some older sources call him Emperor Kōgon the second. He had many children by several consorts, among them the future Emperor Go-En'yū, and several of his sons became imperial prince priests.

In 1351 Ashikaga Takauji briefly returned to the allegiance of the Southern Dynasty, and the Southern Court briefly consolidated control of the imperial line. The peace fell apart in April 1352, when the Southern Court abducted the retired Northern emperors Kōgon and Kōmyō, Emperor Sukō and the Crown Prince Tadahito from Kyoto to Anau, the seat of the Southern Court. No emperor remained in Kyoto, and Prince Iyahito became emperor in 1352 with the support of Ashikaga Yoshiakira. Pre-Meiji scholars date his reign from 1352 to 1371, and Go-Kōgon and those around him believed he held the throne from 25 September 1352 to 9 April 1371.

Public order in Kyoto was disturbed by the antagonism between the two courts. The Southern Court repeatedly recaptured Kyoto, and Go-Kōgon was forced to flee several times to Ōmi Province and other places. Around the time Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was named shōgun in 1368, the Southern Court's power weakened and order returned to Kyoto, though the emperor's own authority began to show its weakness.

On 9 April 1371 Go-Kōgon abdicated in favour of his son, who became Emperor Go-En'yū. He continued to rule as cloistered emperor until he died of illness on 12 March 1374. He is enshrined with other emperors at the imperial tomb Fukakusa no kita no misasagi in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto. His reign is dated under several era names, among them Kannō, Bunna, Embun, Kōan, Jōji and Ōan in the Northern Court's reckoning. A Meiji rescript later determined that the Southern Court had been the legitimate one, so the Northern emperors are counted as pretenders; Go-Kōgon's rivals there were Emperor Go-Murakami and Emperor Chōkei.
emperor-go-komatsu: Go-Komatsu was born on 1 August 1377. His personal name was Motohito, and he was the first son of Emperor Go-En'yū and of Tsūyōmonin no Itsuko, daughter of the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Sanjō Kimitada. He was raised in the turbulent Nanboku-chō period of rival northern and southern courts, in the mansion of Hino Sukenori. He succeeded as Northern Emperor when his father abdicated, and Go-En'yū then ruled as Cloistered Emperor with the help of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. His name recalls the ninth-century Emperor Kōkō, who was called the Emperor of Komatsu. The two were linked because each returned the throne to his own family.

Go-Komatsu was the sixth and last emperor of the Northern Court. In his own lifetime he and those around him believed that he had occupied the throne from 24 May 1382. In 1392 an envoy of the Ashikaga shogunate persuaded Emperor Go-Kameyama of the Southern Court to hand the Imperial Regalia to Go-Komatsu. Go-Komatsu then formally acceded to legitimate imperial power. The peace agreement provided that the northern and southern courts would alternate on the throne, on a ten-year plan, and effectively ended the Southern Court's claim to sovereignty.

The agreement was not kept. Go-Komatsu ruled for twenty years until he abdicated on 5 October 1412, and he was succeeded by his own son, Emperor Shōkō. All later emperors descended from the Northern Court. Go-Komatsu's reign as a legitimate emperor was reckoned by pre-Meiji scholars as 1392 to 1412, and the present imperial family descends from the three Northern Court emperors.

Until 1911 the Northern Court emperors were considered legitimate and the Southern Court illegitimate. The Southern Court is now considered to have been legitimate, mainly because it kept the three sacred treasures, and so Go-Komatsu is not regarded as a legitimate emperor for the first ten years of his reign. He died on 1 December 1433. His consort was Hinonishi Motoko, and his children included Shōkō, who died in 1428, and Prince Ogawa, Shōkō's crown prince, who died in 1425. He is enshrined with other emperors at the imperial tomb called Fukakusa no kita no misasagi, in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.
emperor-go-murakami: Go-Murakami, whose personal name was Noriyoshi, was a seventh son of Emperor Go-Daigo; his mother was Lady Renshi. He was named after the 10th-century Emperor Murakami, and the prefix go- means later, so he is sometimes called Murakami II. When Go-Daigo began the Kenmu Restoration, the still very young prince went in 1333 with Kitabatake Akiie to Tagajō in Mutsu Province to bring the eastern samurai back to their allegiance and destroy the remnants of the Hōjō clan.

In 1336 Ashikaga Takauji rose in rebellion, and after Takauji defeated the imperial side at Kyoto the prince returned to Mutsu. In 1337 Tagajō was attacked and he went west again, to Yoshino, fighting constantly. In October 1338 he was named Crown Prince.

He became emperor in September 1339 on the death of Go-Daigo, with Kitabatake Chikafusa as his adviser. He reigned from Sumiyoshi, Yoshino and other temporary locations. In 1348 Kō no Moronao attacked Yoshino and the court moved to Nishiyoshino, and in 1352 the emperor entered Otokoyama in Yamashiro Province.

In April 1352, after the Battle of Shichijō Ōmiya, Kusunoki Masanori recovered Kyoto from Ashikaga Yoshiakira, and the retired Northern emperors Kōgon, Kōmyō and Sukō were taken to Anau, where the Southern Court sat. Within twenty days Yoshiakira had retaken the city. The emperor was confined at Otokoyama but escaped to Kawachi Province during an attack and a few months later returned to Yoshino.

In 1361 Hosokawa Kiyōji and Kusunoki Masanori, who had returned to the Southern Court's allegiance, attacked Kyoto and held it briefly, but Yoshiakira quickly responded and they left in under twenty days.

The Southern Court tried to recover Kyoto again, but its power was weakening. By the emperor's death on 29 March 1368, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was in power and the throne had been moved to Sumiyoshi. His sons Yutanari and Hironari later became Emperor Chōkei and Emperor Go-Kameyama. His tomb, Hinoo no misasagi, lies in the precincts of Kanshin-ji temple in Kawachinagano, Osaka.
emperor-go-sanjo: Before his accession Go-Sanjō was known as Prince Takahito. He was named after his grandfather Emperor Sanjō, with go-, meaning later, added, so he is sometimes called the Later Emperor Sanjō or Sanjō II. His mother, Empress Sadako, was the third daughter of Emperor Sanjō. Both his parents were grandchildren of Fujiwara no Michinaga through their mothers, but his lack of a Fujiwara father's line meant he could afford to oppose the family. The Kampaku, Fujiwara no Yorimichi, neglected him, but Emperor Go-Suzaku had decreed that when Takahito's elder brother Chikahito was enthroned as Emperor Go-Reizei, Takahito would be heir.

Go-Reizei had no children of his own. When he died on 22 May 1068 at the age of 44, his younger half-brother received the succession. Yorimichi's younger brother Norimichi became kampaku, but Go-Sanjō was determined to rule personally. In 1070 he ordered a preliminary system of laws and a bureaucracy for regulating silk. In 1072, because the Ritsuryō system of centralized authority had largely failed by this time, he became interested in strengthening the finances of the Imperial Household. The eras of his reign were Jiryaku and Enkyū. In the court of the Daijō-kan, the Fujiwara held the main posts: Norimichi was kampaku and daijō-daijin, and Fujiwara Morozone was sadaijin.

In 1069, the first year of the Enkyū era, he issued the Enkyū Shōen Regulation Decree and called for a government office to certify the records of shōen estates. The Fujiwara grip on power was broken during and because of his reign, and their power continued to wane until 1150, when any semblance of it disappeared.

Go-Sanjō abdicated in favour of his son on 18 January 1073. On 11 May 1073 he entered the Buddhist priesthood with the name Kongō-gyō, and he died on 15 June 1073 at the age of 40. He is buried among the Seven Imperial Tombs at Ryōan-ji in Kyoto, and the Imperial Household Agency designates the site as his mausoleum. His consorts included Imperial Princess Kaoruko, a daughter of Emperor Go-Ichijō, and Fujiwara Shigeko, mother of the future Emperor Shirakawa. By Minamoto Motoko he had two sons, Prince Sanehito and Prince Sukehito, who founded the Go-Sanjō Genji line. His daughter Imperial Princess Tokushi married Emperor Horikawa.
emperor-go-toba: Go-Toba was the fourth son of Emperor Takakura and a grandson of Emperor Go-Shirakawa. He took the throne at the age of three, on 8 September 1183, after the child emperor Antoku had fled the capital and the cloistered former emperor Go-Shirakawa elevated Antoku's younger brother by decree. Because the imperial regalia were still held by Antoku, his accession became the first in history to omit the ritual transmission of the sacred treasures from one sovereign to the next. In 1192 Go-Shirakawa died and Minamoto no Yoritomo established the first shogunate, and the emperor became a figurehead. In 1198 Go-Toba abdicated in favour of his son, Emperor Tsuchimikado.

Abdication freed Go-Toba, who was eighteen, from what has been called the ceremonial prison of the imperial palace, and most of his activity as calligrapher, painter, musician, poet, critic and editor belongs to the years after it. He took pleasure in archery, horsemanship and swordsmanship, summoned swordsmiths to court, gave them honorary titles and learned their craft; his patronage is credited with beginning a golden age of Japanese bladesmithing.

His main contribution to literature was the Shin Kokinshu, the New Anthology of Ancient and Modern Waka, which he ordered and for which he revived the Office of Waka as headquarters and served as an editor. He also held many poetry parties and competitions. Fujiwara no Teika chose one of his poems as number 99 of the Hyakunin Isshu.

As cloistered emperor from 1198 to 1221, during the reigns of three emperors, Go-Toba held less power than earlier cloistered emperors of the Heian period. During this time he decreed that the followers of the Pure Land sect in Kyoto, led by Honen, be banished or in some cases executed. In 1221 the shogunate installed his three-year-old grandson as Emperor Chukyo, and Go-Toba rebelled in an attempt to reclaim the throne and overthrow the Kamakura shogunate, a conflict known as the Jokyu War.

Samurai around Kyoto supported him, but most samurai, particularly in the Kanto, backed the shogunate, encouraged by Hojo Masako, the widow of Yoritomo. The rebellion failed, Chukyo was replaced by Go-Horikawa, and Go-Toba was exiled to the Oki Islands. There he went on composing waka and prepared a private edition of the Shin Kokinshu, the Oki edition, dropping about 400 poems; he died and was buried on the islands.
emperor-guangwu-of-han: Liu Xiu, courtesy name Wenshu, was a sixth-generation descendant of Emperor Jing of the Western Han dynasty. His father, Liu Qin, was magistrate of Nandun County, near present-day Xiangcheng in Henan. In 22, with almost the whole empire in revolt against Wang Mang, his brother Liu Yan prepared a rebellion; the young men of their home territory of Chongling hesitated to join until they saw that the careful Liu Xiu was part of it.

Rebel leaders then set up a distant cousin, Liu Xuan, as the Gengshi Emperor in early 23, and Liu Xiu served as a general. He proved instrumental at the Battle of Kunyang, where a Xin army of some 430,000 men sent by Wang Mang was defeated.

The Gengshi Emperor feared Liu Yan's abilities and had him executed. Liu Xiu did not mourn openly, blamed himself and was spared. In autumn 23 he was sent to pacify the region north of the Yellow River, where a pretender named Wang Lang had been accepted as emperor in Handan. Liu Xiu was nearly killed, but gathered local allies and made a political marriage with Guo Shengtong, niece of Liu Yang, Prince of Zhending, who held 100,000 troops. He then merged agrarian rebel groups into his own forces and waited as the Chimei destroyed the Gengshi regime.

After his accession the Chimei, short of supplies, withdrew east; he blocked them at Yiyang and they surrendered, and he spared them. He then defeated regional powers such as Liu Yong, Peng Chong, Zhang Bu, Wei Xiao and Dou Rong, and reunified China in 36. In 37 he gave his generals large marquessates but few official posts, thereby avoiding friction. His reign was marked by thrift, efficiency and mild laws; in 38 he tabled a petition to restore the harsher criminal laws of the late Western Han.

In 41 he deposed Empress Guo, who had lost his favour, and made Yin Lihua empress, but he gave Guo's son the principality of Zhongshan rather than imprisoning her. In 48 a succession dispute split the Xiongnu, and both claimants, Punu and Bi, submitted to him.

In 49 he wrongly believed accusations against the general Ma Yuan, who died on campaign, and stripped him of his title; it was restored only later when Ma's daughter became empress to Emperor Ming. Guangwu died on 29 March 57 and was succeeded by Emperor Ming. His reconsolidation was called the resurgence of Guangwu, and its reforms, notably in land, gave the Han dynasty about two more centuries of life. Unusually for a founder, he did not kill the generals who had won his victories.
emperor-huan-of-han: Emperor Huan, born Liu Zhi in 132, was the son of Liu Yi, the Marquess of Liwu, and his concubine Yan Ming, and a great-grandson of Emperor Zhang. In July 146 the powerful official Liang Ji poisoned the young Emperor Zhi, who had called him an arrogant general. Many officials favoured Emperor Zhi's cousin Liu Suan, the Prince of Qinghe, but Liang Ji insisted on Liu Zhi, who was betrothed to his sister Liang Nüying and relatively young, so that he could be controlled. Liu Zhi took the throne on 1 August 146, at the age of 14.

Empress Dowager Liang remained regent, though her brother Liang Ji held more and more control. In 147 Emperor Huan married Liang Nüying, making her empress. In that year Liang Ji, with two eunuchs and with the emperor's clear approval, falsely accused the honest officials Li Gu and Du Qiao of plotting to replace him with Liu Suan; both were executed, and Liu Suan took his own life after being demoted. After the empress dowager died in 150, Liang Ji's violence and corruption grew.

In 159, after Empress Liang died, Emperor Huan learned that Liang Ji had sent assassins against the mother of a consort, and he conspired with five eunuchs to overthrow him. The imperial guards surrounded Liang Ji's house, and Liang Ji committed suicide. The Liang and Sun clans were arrested and slaughtered, and the confiscated property allowed taxes to be reduced by half for a year.

The eunuchs who had helped were rewarded with marquessates and posts of great power, and they became corrupt with the emperor's approval. In 159 he had the county magistrate Li Yun executed for a petition urging him to curb them. In 161 he offered minor offices for sale to pay for campaigns against Qiang rebellions. In 166 the governor Li Ying was arrested, and more than 200 university students who petitioned for his release were arrested as well; this was later called the first Disaster of Partisan Prohibition. The Hou Hanshu records that a Roman envoy reached Luoyang in 166 and was greeted by the emperor.

Emperor Huan died in January 168 without a son, aged 36, after reigning more than 21 years. Empress Dou chose the 11-year-old Liu Hong, who became Emperor Ling. Huan has largely been viewed as an emperor who might have had some intelligence but lacked wisdom, and his reign is held to have contributed greatly to the fall of the Eastern Han. The cycle of the eunuchs' rise and fall continued until the reign of Emperor Ling, when an army led by the regent He Jin and the noblemen Yuan Shao and Yuan Shu massacred the eunuchs in Luoyang.
emperor-jing-of-han: Liu Qi was born in 188 BCE, the eldest son of Emperor Wen, then Prince of Dai, and Consort Dou. After his father became emperor in November 180 BCE he was made crown prince in February or March 179 BCE, and his mother became empress. His mother was a Taoist who required her children and grandchildren to study Taoist doctrine, and she deeply influenced him. A member of his household, Chao Cuo, known for intelligence, ruthless efficiency and rhetorical talent, became a trusted adviser. Prince Qi had an epicurean lifestyle, and Emperor Wen once considered replacing him with his younger brother Liu Wu, Prince of Liang, but dropped the idea when many officials opposed it.

Emperor Wen died in July 157 BCE and Prince Qi became emperor. Many officials expected a poor ruler, but he proved capable. He continued his father's policy of non-interference with the people and cut taxes in half, to one thirtieth of the crop. He also reduced criminal penalties, and in 156 BCE cut the number of whip strokes after finding that his father's abolition of the mutilating punishments had caused more people to die from whipping. He kept the marriage treaties with the Xiongnu, which largely avoided conflict on the northern frontier.

The princes of the imperial clan, who often built up their own armies and resisted edicts, remained a problem. On Chao Cuo's advice Emperor Jing took commanderies and counties from the principalities of Chu, Zhao, Jiaoxi and Wu in 154 BCE. Wu rebelled in alliance with Chu, Jiaoxi, Zhao and three smaller principalities, in the Rebellion of the Seven States. Emperor Jing executed Chao Cuo in an attempt to appease the rebels, without effect. His commander Zhou Yafu cut the supply lines of the Wu and Chu forces, which collapsed from starvation. After the war the princes lost the right to appoint ministers for their fiefs, which strengthened central power.

Succession was troubled. He made his eldest son Liu Rong crown prince in 153 BCE but deposed him in 150 BCE after the intrigues of his sister Princess Liu Piao, and Liu Che, the future Emperor Wu, became crown prince. In 143 BCE Zhou Yafu was accused of what the interrogator called underground treason and killed himself in prison, an incident for which Emperor Jing was much criticised. He died in 141 BCE and was buried in the Han Yang Ling Mausoleum at Chang'an.

The joint reign of Wen and Jing, known as the Rule of Wen and Jing, is regarded as one of the golden ages of Chinese history, although Jing lacked his father's warmth and openness. In 2016 the earliest known traces of tea were announced from his mausoleum at Xi'an.
emperor-kanmu: Kanmu, whose personal name was Yamabe, was the eldest son of Prince Shirakabe, later Emperor Kōnin, and was born before his father came to the throne. His mother, Takano no Niigasa, was according to the Shoku Nihongi a 10th-generation descendant of Muryeong of Baekje. Because she was not of the imperial line and came from a clan of Korean origin, his succession could have been questioned, and Kanmu stressed her ancestry, including its descent from Dongmyeong of Goguryeo. He was named crown prince in 773 and succeeded when Kōnin abdicated in 781.

His reign, from 781 to 806, saw the emperor's powers reach their peak and the passage from the Nara period to the Heian period. Imperial sponsorship of Buddhism had politicised the clergy. In 784 Kanmu moved the capital from Nara to Nagaoka-kyō, a move said to have been meant to keep the powerful Nara monasteries out of state politics, since the great temples stayed behind. Disasters followed, including the flooding of half the city, and in 785 the chief architect of the new capital, Fujiwara no Tanetsugu, was assassinated. In 794 the capital moved again, to Heian-kyō, modern Kyoto, which marks the beginning of the Heian period.

His armies pushed the frontier outward. In 794 he appointed Ōtomo no Otomaro the first shōgun, a title meaning Barbarian-subduing Great General, and then Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, who subdued the Emishi in northern Honshu. After a defeat in 789 and a year of drought and famine he abolished national conscription in 792 in favour of provincial militias, which weakened the emperor's authority and led to a growth of private armies.

Kanmu sponsored the travels of the monks Saichō and Kūkai to China, from where they returned to found the Japanese branches of Tendai and Shingon Buddhism respectively. In 799 he conceived the Shinsen Shōjiroku, a genealogical record of the clans, completed in 814 under Emperor Saga. Three of his sons, Heizei, Saga and Junna, became emperors, and some descendants, the Kammu Taira, included Taira no Masakado and Taira no Kiyomori. The waka poet Ariwara no Narihira was his grandson.
emperor-komyo: Kōmyō, whose personal name was Yutahito, was the second son of Emperor Go-Fushimi. His mother was Neishi, a daughter of Saionji Kinhira. He was the second of the emperors of the Northern Court, though the first supported by the Ashikaga shogunate. His children included a daughter, Jōgakuin-dono (died 1422), and a son, Shuson.

In his own lifetime Kōmyō and those around him believed that he occupied the throne from 20 September 1336 to 18 November 1348. Ashikaga Takauji rebelled against Emperor Go-Daigo's Kenmu Restoration and entered Kyoto in 1336, and Go-Daigo fled to Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei. Prince Yutahito was enthroned as emperor, although he lacked the sacred treasures, and this began the Northern Court. On the 21st day of the 12th month Go-Daigo escaped to Yoshino and founded the Southern Court.

The years of Kōmyō's reign were counted in two ways: the Northern Court used Kenmu (continued), Ryakuō, Kōei and Jōwa, and the Southern Court Engen, Kōkoku and Shōhei, with Go-Daigo and Go-Murakami as its emperors. On 18 November 1348 he abdicated in favour of the eldest son of his older brother, the former claimant Emperor Kōgon, who became Emperor Sukō.

In April 1352, during the Kan'ō Disturbance, a family feud among the Ashikaga, the Southern Emperor Go-Murakami entered Kyoto and captured it. He carried away Kōmyō with Emperor Kōgon, Emperor Sukō and the Crown Prince Tadahito, and they ended in Anau, the seat of the Southern Court. After the Shōhei Reunification they were kept under house arrest in Yamato Province, in what is now the village of Nishiyoshino in Nara. In 1355 Kōmyō returned to Kyoto and entered a monastery. He died on 26 July 1380, at the age of 60.
emperor-meiji: Prince Mutsuhito was born on 3 November 1852 in a small house on his maternal grandfather's property at the north end of the Gosho, the palace compound in Kyoto, since birth was believed to be a source of pollution. His mother, Nakayama Yoshiko, was a concubine of his father, Emperor Kōmei. Under the Tokugawa shogunate the shōgun governed Japan, and a code of 1605 required emperors to devote their time to scholarship and the arts. Emperors almost never left the palace compound, and few lived long. All five of the future emperor's brothers and sisters died as infants.

By the early 1860s the shogunate faced threats from foreign powers and from young samurai known as shishi, who revered Emperor Kōmei. In 1863 they persuaded him to issue an Order to expel barbarians, which the shogunate could not enforce. When Mutsuhito became emperor after his father's death in 1867, the Boshin War followed, in which samurai, mostly from the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains, defeated the shogunate and restored power in his name. On 7 April 1868 he was presented with the Charter Oath, a five-point statement of the new government's nature, which he formally promoted.

The new leaders organised a Council of State and, in 1885, a cabinet led by a prime minister. In 1869 several daimyōs gave their lands to the emperor and were reappointed as governors, and in 1871 the domains were abolished and Japan organised into 72 prefectures. The daimyōs received salaries of ten percent of their former revenues and moved to Tokyo. The administration also abolished most privileges of the samurai and ended legalised discrimination against the burakumin. Documents of the reign include the Meiji Constitution of 1889 and the Imperial Rescript on Education of 1890. Japan defeated China in the First Sino-Japanese War and Russia in the Russo-Japanese War, and annexed Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910.

In 1911 several leftists, among them Shūsui Kōtoku, were executed on charges of plotting the sovereign's murder, known as the High Treason Incident. The emperor, suffering from diabetes, nephritis and gastroenteritis, died of uremia on 29 July 1912, aged 59, and his eldest son Yoshihito succeeded as Emperor Taishō. The Imperial Diet resolved to commemorate his role, and the Shinto shrine Meiji Jingū was built in Tokyo, though his grave is at Fushimi-Momoyama Castle in Kyoto.
emperor-muzong-of-liao: Yelü Jing, whose infant name was Shulü, was born on 19 September 931, the eldest son of Emperor Taizong, the second emperor of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty. He was the fourth emperor of the dynasty, coming to the throne in 951 after his cousin Emperor Shizong was murdered. He died on 12 March 969.

His reign was troubled by plots and rebellions against him from both the imperial clan and the Xiao consort clan. Muzong dismissed many of the ministers who had served Shizong and used force against those who rebelled. His brutal repression in the end restored stability and the authority of the throne.

The Later Zhou dynasty used Muzong's troubles to strengthen its hold on northern China, a region that had been under Khitan influence since earlier in the century. The Northern Han dynasty, under Liao protection, kept its independence. In 958 the Later Zhou attacked Liao positions in an attempt to regain the Sixteen Prefectures, and Muzong led a large army to the southern capital, at present-day Beijing. War was averted by the death of the Later Zhou emperor Chai Rong, and early the next year Muzong returned to his capital.

Midway through his reign the Northern Song dynasty replaced the Later Zhou, the last of the Five Dynasties. Relations between the Liao and the Northern Song stayed peaceful while Muzong lived: the two courts exchanged annual visits at the Chinese New Year, and profitable trade between them grew. Two questions remained open, the Sixteen Prefectures and the fate of the Northern Han, and neither was settled in his reign. Both led to war between the two states after his death.
emperor-qinzong: Zhao Huan was the eldest son and heir apparent of Emperor Huizong, and his mother was Huizong's empress consort, Empress Wang. In 1126 the forces of the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty began the first siege of Bianjing. Huizong intended to flee but was persuaded by his officials to abdicate first, and he took the title Taishang Huang, Retired Emperor.

Left to deal with the invasion, Qinzong appointed the general Li Gang to lead the defence, but later removed him in the hope of peace talks and sent his younger brother Zhao Gou to negotiate; Zhao Gou was captured and ransomed. The first siege ended after Qinzong gave a city to the Jurchens and agreed to pay annual tribute. Almost as soon as the Jin armies left, he went back on the deal and sent two armies, of 90,000 and 60,000 men, to relieve Taiyuan and strengthen Zhongshan and Hejian. Both were defeated by June.

Qinzong then sent a coded letter, sealed in candle wax, to two Jin ambassadors who were nobles of the former Liao dynasty, inviting them to join an alliance against the Jin. They handed it to the Jin ruler, Emperor Taizong, who accused Qinzong of breaking the treaty and sent a larger army. With Song forces posted across the country, the Jin breached the walls of Bianjing in 1127 in the Jingkang Incident, named for Qinzong's era.

Qinzong, Huizong and the rest of the family were taken prisoner, ending the Northern Song. They were reduced to commoners on 20 March 1127 and deported to Huining Prefecture on 13 May 1127. The Jurchens gave them the insulting titles Marquis Chonghun and Duke Hunde, and in 1141 changed Qinzong's to Duke of Tianshui Commandery. His brother Zhao Gou escaped south and founded the Southern Song as Emperor Gaozong.

The Treaty of Shaoxing of 1142 between Gaozong and the Jin ended Qinzong's chance of returning, and he lived on as a captive whom the Jin used as a hostage against the Song. He spent two thirds of his life in Jin territory. A later novel, Da Song Xuanhe Yishi, says he was trampled to death in a polo match staged to humiliate him, but this is largely fictitious. Qinzong and his father were blamed for the Song decline.
emperor-ruizong-of-tang: Li Dan was born on 22 June 662 as the fourth son of Emperor Gaozong and Empress Wu. His name and title changed several times in his youth: he was created Prince of Yin the year he was born, and later Prince of Yu, Prince of Ji and Prince of Xiang, before returning to Prince of Yu in 678, when his name became Li Dan. He was said to be known for humility, love for his siblings and skill in calligraphy. After Gaozong died in 683, his brother Emperor Zhongzong took the throne, but Empress Wu kept power as regent.

In 684 Empress Dowager Wu deposed Zhongzong when he showed signs of independence and replaced him with Li Dan. He was a figurehead: his name was not on the documents issued, and he was lodged in a separate palace and forbidden to move freely or meet officials. When she once offered to hand back imperial authority he declined, knowing she did not mean it. In October 690 he ceded the throne to his mother, who founded the Zhou dynasty and made him crown prince under the title Huangsi. In 698 Li Dan offered to yield that position to his brother Li Xian, who was recalled to Luoyang.

After the coup of 705 restored Zhongzong, Li Dan declined the honours offered to him. Zhongzong died on 3 July 710, allegedly poisoned by Empress Wei. Princess Taiping and Li Dan's son Li Longji then launched a coup that killed Empress Wei, and they persuaded Li Dan to take the throne again. His eldest son Li Chengqi declined to be crown prince, and Li Longji was chosen on account of his accomplishments.

Tension grew between Princess Taiping and Li Longji. In September 712 Ruizong abdicated in favour of Li Longji, who became Emperor Xuanzong, but kept the title of Taishang Huang and, at Princess Taiping's suggestion, superior power. In 713 Xuanzong, suspecting a coup, acted first, killed her associates and forced her to take her own life. Ruizong then yielded power entirely. He died at Baifu Hall in 716 and was enshrined in the imperial temple.
emperor-shenzong-of-song: Emperor Shenzong, whose personal name was Zhao Xu, was born on 25 May 1048 and was the sixth emperor of the Song dynasty. He reigned from 1067. He disagreed with the passive stance of his predecessors and wanted to raise the dynasty's prestige by conquest, in particular by recovering the Sixteen Prefectures. Conservatives such as Fu Bi and Sima Guang opposed his aims, fearing an expansion of monarchical power and wanting to keep the peace with the Western Xia and the Liao dynasty. Sima Guang, asked to head an Office of Expenditure Reduction, reported instead that defence consumed 83 per cent of the dynasty's cash income. In 1069 Shenzong made Wang Anshi head of government.

Wang Anshi's New Policies included the Seedling Law, the Law on the Exemption from Military Service and the Market Exchange Law, and they brought monopolies on salt, tea and jiu. Shenzong cut the army to fewer than 900,000 men and introduced the Baojia system of village defence. The policies gave him a large budget surplus, but the army did not improve, and Western Xia continued to defeat Song forces. After a drought in 1074 he removed Wang Anshi, who retired for good in 1076. Shenzong then led the Yuanfeng Reforms himself, and in 1082 he restored the Tang model of a government built around the Six Ministries.

In 1070 he invited 5,300 Muslim men from Bukhara to settle in China as mercenaries against the Liao, and in 1076 he sent campaigns against the Vietnamese ruler Lý Nhân Tông. Sima Guang published the Zizhi Tongjian in 1084.

A defeat at Yongle City in 1082, during the invasion of Western Xia, was a heavy blow to Shenzong. He berated his councillors in tears for not opposing the campaign, and his reforming zeal slowed as he favoured the conservatives, particularly Sima Guang. He died in early 1085, aged 36, of an unspecified illness, and his son succeeded him as Emperor Zhezong. Because Zhezong was a minor, Shenzong's mother Empress Gao ruled as regent. Her conservative faction, which included Sima Guang, Su Shi and Cheng Hao, defeated the faction of Cai Jue, repealed the New Policies and purged the court of reformers.
emperor-shirakawa: Shirakawa was born on 7 July 1053, the eldest son of Emperor Go-Sanjō and Fujiwara Shigeko. His personal name was Sadahito, and in his youth his relations with his father were cold but loving. He was proclaimed an imperial prince in 1068, when his father was enthroned, and became crown prince in 1069. Go-Sanjō abdicated in the twelfth month of Enkyū 4 (January 1073), and Shirakawa acceded at the age of 19.

A kampaku was in place, but Shirakawa tried to rule directly, as his father had. He attempted to regulate the shōen manor system and to weaken the influence of the sekkan lines of regents. In 1077 he had the temple Hosshō-ji built at Shirakawa in fulfilment of a sacred vow. It was the first of a series of sacred-vow temples created by imperial decree, and its nine-storey pagoda, begun in 1083, became the most elaborate temple structure sponsored by an emperor up to that time.

In 1081 the monks of Mount Hiei twice burned the temple of Miidera. When the empress Kenshi died in 1084, he was afflicted with great grief and for a time turned the administration over to his ministers. Go-Sanjō had wished Shirakawa's younger half-brother to succeed him, but the half-brother died of an illness in 1085, and Shirakawa's own son Taruhito became crown prince. On the day Taruhito was proclaimed heir, Shirakawa formally abdicated, on 3 January 1087, and took the title Daijō-tennō. Taruhito became Emperor Horikawa.

The retired emperor was the first to attempt what became customary cloistered rule: he exercised power indirectly from the Shirakawa-in, the White River Mansion, although the nominal offices of sesshō and kampaku continued to exist for a long time. In 1096, on the death of his daughter, he entered a monastery under the Dharma name Yūkan, becoming a hō-ō, the title of a former emperor who has become a monk.

After Horikawa's death his grandson became Emperor Toba, and Toba in turn abdicated to his son, who became Emperor Sutoku. By his death in 1129 Shirakawa had ruled as cloistered emperor through the reigns of three emperors who were effectively little more than figureheads. His posthumous name comes from the Shirakawa-in; another name for him was Rokujō no Mikado.
emperor-shizong-of-liao: Born on 29 January 919 with the personal name Wuyu, Yelü Ruan was the third emperor of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty. His father was Yelü Bei, the eldest son of Abaoji (Emperor Taizu), and in his father's absence he was raised by his uncle, Emperor Taizong. He went with Taizong on the campaign in China during which the emperor died in 947, and this let him quickly win the support of the military leaders.

As he returned to the capital, his grandmother, the Empress Dowager Yingtian, who wanted the throne for her third son, Yelü Lihu, denounced him and sent an army to intercept him. The Khitan nobles, knowing Lihu to be unfit to rule, refused to back her as they had done at Taizong's accession, and their firm support for Yelü Ruan's claim prevented a civil war among the Khitans. The new emperor sent both his grandmother and his uncle far from the capital; Lihu died in rebellion and the empress dowager of old age.

Shizong was known for his generosity and his martial skill, though also as a heavy drinker who loved to hunt. He adopted reforms that moved the Liao state towards a feudal society and consolidated power in a central government. In 951 he took the field to resist Chinese advances from the south.

That same year he was killed in a coup by members of the imperial clan who sought the throne, and Empress Zhen died with him. She had been a court lady of the Later Tang and bore him Yelü Zhimo, Prince of Ning. His second son, Yelü Xian, born on 1 September 948 to Empress Huaijie of the Xiao clan, later reigned as Emperor Jingzong.
emperor-shomu: Shōmu was born on 22 September 701, the son of Emperor Monmu and Fujiwara no Miyako, a daughter of Fujiwara no Fuhito. He was still a child when his father died, so his grandmother, Empress Gemmei, and his aunt, Empress Genshō, occupied the throne before him. In 724 Genshō abdicated, and her nephew received the succession. The era name was changed on 31 January 724 to mark his accession. His consort Kōmyō, a Fujiwara of non-royal birth, made him the first emperor whose consort was not born into the imperial household, and a new office for the queen-consort, the Kogogushiki, was created; it lasted into the Heian period.

A major smallpox epidemic raged through Japan from 735 to 737, with adult mortality of about 25 to 35 per cent. In 740 Fujiwara no Hirotsugu rebelled in Kyushu, reacting to the growing influence of Genbō and others. An imperial army of 17,000 under Ōno no Azumabito defeated him, and he was beheaded in Hizen Province. While the rebellion was still under way Shōmu left the capital Heijō-kyō and travelled east, probably fearing Fujiwara supporters in Nara. On 6 January 741 he proclaimed a new capital at Kuni-kyō, which was easy to defend and was linked with Tachibana no Moroe. In 744 the court moved to Naniwa-kyō, and in 745 the capital returned to Heijō-kyō.

In 741 Shōmu called for provincial temples and nunneries throughout the country, the closest anyone came to declaring Japan a Buddhist nation. In 743 he issued a rescript to build the Daibutsu, the sixteen-metre statue of the Buddha Vairocana at Tōdai-ji in Nara, and a law on perpetual ownership of cultivated lands. The Great Buddha took so much that later chroniclers accused him of exhausting the country's bronze and precious metals. He also commissioned the observance of the ohigan holiday at the spring and autumn equinoxes.

In April 749 Shōmu went in procession to Tōdai-ji and proclaimed himself a disciple of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. In July of that year, after a reign of twenty-five years, he abdicated in favour of his daughter Princess Takano, who became Empress Kōken, and took the tonsure as the first retired emperor to become a Buddhist priest. Kōmyō likewise became a nun. The Eye-Opening Ceremony of the Great Buddha took place at Tōdai-ji in April 752. Shōmu died on 4 June 756, aged 54. The Shōsōin, the treasure house of Tōdai-ji, holds about nine thousand objects connected with him and Kōmyō, furniture, games, instruments, clothing and Buddhist objects among them.
emperor-suko: Emperor Sukō was born on 25 May 1334. His personal name was originally Masuhito and was later changed to Okihito. His father was Emperor Kōgon, and his predecessor, Emperor Kōmyō, was his uncle, the younger brother of Kōgon. He was the third of the emperors of the Northern Court during the period of the Northern and Southern Courts.

In 1348 Sukō became Crown Prince and, in the same year, Northern Emperor on the abdication of Kōmyō. He occupied the throne from 18 November 1348 until 22 November 1351, while Kōgon ruled as a cloistered emperor. Meanwhile the rivalry between Ashikaga Takauji and Ashikaga Tadayoshi had begun, and in 1351 Takauji returned to the allegiance of the Southern Court, which forced Sukō to abdicate. The step was intended to reunify the imperial line.

The peace soon fell apart. In April 1352 the Southern Dynasty evacuated Kyoto and took with it the retired Northern emperors Kōgon and Kōmyō, Sukō himself and the Crown Prince Tadahito. Takauji responded by making Kōgon's second son, Prince Iyahito, emperor.

Sukō returned to Kyoto in 1357. His son Prince Yoshihito began to work with the shogunate to be named Crown Prince, but the shogunate chose the son of Emperor Go-Kōgon instead, the future Emperor Go-En'yū. Yoshihito founded the Fushimi-no-miya house, a collateral branch of the imperial family that was included in the succession to the Japanese throne until 1947.

Sukō died on 31 January 1398. Thirty years later, in 1428, his great-grandson Hikohito, adopted son of Emperor Shōkō, became Emperor Go-Hanazono, fulfilling Sukō's dearest wish. Sukō is enshrined at the Daikōmyōji no misasagi in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.
emperor-taizong-of-song: Zhao Jiong was born on 20 November 939 in Kaifeng and was known as Zhao Kuangyi before 960 and Zhao Guangyi from 960 to 977. When his elder brother took the throne as Emperor Taizu, he was appointed prefect of Kaifeng, where he gradually consolidated power, and he was Prince of Jin.

He succeeded in 976, when Taizu died aged 49 with no recorded illness. It was unusual for a brother rather than a son to succeed, which fuelled a popular belief that foul play was involved. Official history says their mother, Empress Dowager Du, had made Taizu promise that his brother would succeed him, and a Golden Shelf Promise was said to have been sealed; modern historians find no concrete evidence of murder but generally accept that the promise was fabricated by Taizong and Zhao Pu.

In the first three years of his reign Taizong intimidated the warlord Chen Hongjin and the Wuyue king Qian Chu into submission and personally led the campaign against the Northern Han in 979, flooding its cities by releasing the Fen River. Its ruler Liu Jiyuan surrendered, ending the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period and reunifying China proper for the first time in 72 years.

He then marched against the Liao dynasty. His siege of Yanjing failed, and at the Battle of Gaoliang River in 979 Liao cavalry destroyed his army; he was wounded by an arrow and had to ride back by carriage. A second campaign in 986, directed from Bianjing in three armies, failed through miscommunication, and the general Yang Ye died. A war in the south ended at the Battle of Bạch Đằng. The Sixteen Prefectures and northern Vietnam stayed outside Han control until the Ming. After 988 he turned to internal development: he widened the imperial examination system, compiled encyclopaedias, expanded the civil service and further limited the power of the jiedushi.

Taizong died on 8 May 997 after reigning for 21 years, and his third son became Emperor Zhenzong. He is remembered as hardworking and diligent. All later Northern Song emperors were his descendants, as was the first emperor of the Southern Song. After the Jingkang incident, when the Jurchen Jin took most of his line captive, Gaozong, who lacked an heir, chose a successor from the descendants of Taizu.
emperor-taizong-of-tang: Li Shimin was born in 598 at Wugong, in what is now Xianyang in Shaanxi. His father Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, was a general of the Sui dynasty and a nephew by marriage of the Sui founder, Emperor Wen, and the family was partly of Xianbei descent. In 613 he married the niece of the official Gao Shilian, the later Empress Zhangsun. He is traditionally regarded as a co-founder of the Tang because in 617 he encouraged his father to rebel against the Sui at Jinyang.

Under his father, Emperor Gaozu, he led campaigns to reunify the empire. Against Xue Ju he suffered what was recorded as his only defeat until the Goguryeo campaign of 645, when his assistants ignored his orders not to engage. His successes led to an intense rivalry with his elder brother Li Jiancheng, the crown prince, and the court divided into two factions.

Taizong took the throne in 626 and made his wife empress and their eldest son, Li Chengqian, crown prince. Within 19 days the Eastern Turkic leader Illig Qaghan reached the Wei river across from Chang'an, and Taizong had to negotiate with him in person, promising tribute. In 630 his general Li Jing defeated and captured the khan, destroying Eastern Turkic power, and Taizong took the title Khan of Heaven. His armies annexed Karakhoja in 640, Karasahr in 644 and Kucha in 648.

He employed capable chancellors such as Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui and Wei Zheng and tolerated criticism, and his era, Zhenguan (627 to 649), is regarded in tradition as a golden age and a model for later emperors. He also allowed Zoroastrianism, Judaism, Islam and Syriac Christianity to exist in the empire. After 642 officials split over the rivalry of Li Chengqian and his brother Li Tai.

Taizong fell seriously ill in the summer of 649, entrusted Li Zhi to Zhangsun Wuji and Chu Suiliang, and died at the Cuiwei Palace. His death was kept secret for three days, and Li Zhi took the throne as Emperor Gaozong. Six stone reliefs of his favourite horses were carved for his tomb between 636 and 649; four are now in the Beilin Museum in Xi'an and two in the Penn Museum in Philadelphia.
emperor-taizu-of-jin: Aguda, whose sinicised name was Min, was an eighth-generation descendant of Hanpu, the progenitor of the Wanyan clan. His father Helibo was chieftain of the clan, and his mother was a daughter of the chieftain of the Nalan tribe. He was born near the Ashi River, within present-day Harbin. He was known for his bravery and fought campaigns against rival Jurchen tribes at the command of the Liao. In 1109, in a widespread famine, he helped his father absorb starving warriors from other tribes. In 1113 he succeeded his elder brother Wuyashu as tribal leader. In 1112, when the Liao ruler Emperor Tianzuo ordered all the chieftains to dance for him on a fishing expedition, Aguda was the only one to refuse.

In early 1114 Aguda sent spies into Liao territory, with Wanyan Zonghan and Wanyan Xiyin as his chief advisers. In September he rallied about 2,500 tribesmen at Liushui and rebelled. His cavalry took Ningjiangzhou and defeated a Liao army of 7,000 at the Battle of Chuhedian in November. In January 1115 he proclaimed himself emperor, founded the Jin dynasty and took the regnal name Shouguo. In August his army took Huanglong Prefecture and, the account runs, defeated 700,000 Liao troops with 20,000 horsemen at the Battle of Hubudagang. By 1116 the whole Liaodong Peninsula was his, and between 1119 and 1122 his armies took all five Liao capitals.

The Northern Song regarded the Jin as natural allies, and between 1115 and 1123 the two states negotiated the Alliance Conducted at Sea: the Song would attack the Liao from the south, and the Jin would hand over the Liao's Sixteen Prefectures. During the war Aguda set up a government based on Jurchen tribal customs and organised agriculture under the Miŋgan Moumukə system. He also took in elements of Han Chinese culture and had his chancellor Wanyan Xiyin devise a Jurchen script.

Aguda died in August 1123, aged 56, a few months after a treaty with the Song that recognised each as an equal and required the Song to pay an annual tribute of 200,000 taels of silver and 300,000 bolts of silk. His younger brother Wuqimai, Emperor Taizong, succeeded him, captured Emperor Tianzuo in 1125 and ended the Liao, and soon afterwards the Jin made war on the Northern Song. Aguda was buried in the Rui Mausoleum at Dafangshan, outside Zhongdu, and in 1145 his descendant Emperor Xizong gave him the temple name Taizu.
emperor-taizu-of-liao: Abaoji was born in 872 in Southern Mongolia and had a turbulent childhood. His grandfather was killed in a conflict between tribes, his father and uncles fled, and his grandmother hid him for his safety. His father had been the elected chieftain of the Yila tribe. The Yaonian clan had dominated the leadership of the Khitan tribes since the 750s, but by the end of the ninth century leaders of the Yila were expressing dissatisfaction with the Yaonian khans.

Later Chinese historians record legends of his birth: his mother, Xiao Yanmujin, dreamt that the sun fell into her bosom, and the infant was said to have the body of a three-year-old and to have walked at three months.

Abaoji became chieftain of the Yila in 901 and in 903 was named Yuyue, commander of all Khitan forces, second only to the great khan. In 905 he led 70,000 cavalry into Shanxi to make a brotherhood with Li Keyong and pledged support against Zhu Wen. At the triennial council of 907 he demanded to be named khagan, and with the support of seven tribal chiefs and the acquiescence of the last Yaonian great khan he became khagan on 27 February 907.

Until 916 he faced constant uprisings, mostly led by cousins and brothers, whom he won over by persuading them that they would prosper as a dynasty and by giving them posts of influence. In 916 he declared himself Celestial Emperor in the Han style, adopted an era name and named his son Yelü Bei as heir apparent, which was a first among the Khitans and contrary to their notion of rule by merit.

He introduced a dual administrative system, with steppe peoples governed by steppe tradition and the settled population of Balhae and north China by a civil bureaucracy on Han protocols. He built a walled city in 918, ordered a Khitan large script in 920, and five years later had his brother Yelü Diela devise a second, more syllabic script.

In 926, while on campaign against Balhae, Abaoji demanded the Sixteen Prefectures from the Later Tang envoy Yao Kun, who said he could not grant them and was imprisoned. Abaoji died of illness on 6 September 926, having captured the whole Balhae state and left its ruling family as nobles of a new fiefdom. His borders reached the Yalu and Ussuri rivers and far onto the Mongolian Plateau, and he had not acted on a plan to move south.

Although Yelü Bei was heir apparent, the empress dowager Shulü Ping did not think him worthy and had her second son Deguang succeed, as Emperor Taizong. The dual system became a model for later steppe peoples.
emperor-taizu-of-song: Zhao Kuangyin was born in Luoyang to the military commander Zhao Hongyin and grew up excelling in mounted archery. In 949 he joined the army of Guo Wei, a military governor of the Later Han dynasty. When Guo Wei rebelled in 951 and founded the Later Zhou, Zhao was promoted to palace guard commander, and under Chai Rong, who became Emperor Shizong, he rose to command cavalry units. At the Battle of Gaoping he and Zhang Yongde led 4,000 elite palace troops to hold off a larger Liao army until reinforcements came. He became grand commander of the palace guards and built ties with other generals and officials. When Chai Rong died, the throne passed to his seven-year-old son Guo Zongxun.

In 960 the chancellor Fan Zhi sent him to meet a feared invasion by the Northern Han and the Liao. Forty li out, a rumour spread that a prophet had seen two suns fighting, meaning that the Mandate of Heaven had passed to Zhao. Soldiers woke him at night shouting that the army was without a master, and by the traditional account he took power reluctantly, refusing until they swore unconditional obedience. He ordered that the troops not loot the capital. The new dynasty took its name, Song, from the prefecture where he had commanded the army.

As emperor he conquered Later Shu, Southern Han, Southern Tang and Jingnan, and in 968 he led an army against the Northern Han, laying siege to Taiyuan before retreating when Liao cavalry came to its help. He expanded the imperial examination system so that most of the civil service was recruited through it. He also brought the military under control, inviting his generals to a banquet and persuading them to retire with estates and generous benefits; none refused.

Taizu reigned seventeen years and died in 976 aged 49. He was succeeded by his younger brother Zhao Kuangyi, Emperor Taizong, although he had two grown sons; traditional accounts stress the role of his mother in that decision, and it was accepted for nearly the whole reign. A popular folk story suggests that his brother murdered him. He is buried at the Yongchang Mausoleum near Gongyi. The throne passed from Taizong to his own descendants until 1161, when Emperor Gaozong, who had no heir, chose a descendant of Taizu to succeed him, and all later Song emperors descended from Taizu through his sons Zhao Dezhao and Zhao Defang.
emperor-tenmu: Tenmu was born Prince Ōama, the son of Emperor Jomei and Princess Takara, who later reigned as Empress Kōgyoku, and the younger brother of Naka no Ōe, the future Emperor Tenji. His date of birth is unclear, and little is known of his early life. During Tenji's rule Ōama was ambiguously favoured as successor but was gradually bypassed in favour of Tenji's son Prince Ōtomo. When Tenji fell ill in 671 he offered Ōama the succession. Ōama refused, perhaps fearing a plot, shaved his head and went to the Yoshino Palace as a monk.

Tenji died at the end of 671. In 672 Ōama learned that Ōtomo was plotting against him and fled east, which began the Jinshin War. The governor of Ise Province sent five hundred soldiers to close the Suzuka Barrier, and support came from Owari, Mino and local chieftains of eastern Japan. The Ōtomo clan of Yamato also sided with him. Prince Ōtomo was defeated and forced to commit suicide. Tenmu returned the court from Ōmi to Asuka and built the palace of Kiyomihara. Around 682 or 683 he seems to have chosen the site that became Fujiwara-kyō, Japan's first Chinese-style planned city.

He executed most of Tenji's top officials, redistributed offices among supporters and relied on his family. He left the posts of Minister of the Left and Minister of the Right vacant and created four new ranks at the top of the kabane noble titles. In 681 he ordered a new law code. He is likely the first Japanese ruler to use the title tennō in his lifetime. He raised Amaterasu above other ancestral kami, made the Ise Shrine the foremost shrine, and sponsored Buddhist rites and the building of Yakushi-ji.

Tenmu's health declined from the ninth month of 685, and he died on the ninth day of the ninth month of 686. Prince Ōtsu was charged with treason and executed that year, likely on the orders of Tenmu's consort Uno-no-sarara. Prince Kusakabe, the favoured heir, died in 689 after a mourning period of twenty-seven months. Uno-no-sarara then took the throne as Empress Jitō, and later passed it to Kusakabe's son Karu, who became Emperor Monmu. Because of his reforms, Tenmu's reign is often seen as the beginning of the Japanese imperial system.
emperor-uda: Uda was born on 10 June 866, a son of Emperor Kokō, whose mother was Empress Dowager Hanshi. Kokō had taken the throne after Emperor Yozei was forced to abdicate. In June 884 he gave the surname Minamoto to 26 princes and princesses of his line, demoting them to commoners, to reduce state expenses and their political influence. When Kokō fell seriously ill in 887, the regent Fujiwara no Mototsune stated the emperor's preference for Sadami over Prince Sadayasu, Yozei's brother. Sadami was the adopted son of Mototsune's half-sister Fujiwara no Yoshiko, a powerful court lady who strongly recommended him. He was made an imperial prince and crown prince, and was enthroned on 17 November 887.

Uda lacked experience, and Mototsune, regent for four emperors, held all power. Shortly after the enthronement Uda confirmed him as regent, then with Tachibana no Hiromi issued a second edict equating the kanpaku with the honorific title ako, which would have sidelined him. The court, dominated by the Fujiwara, did not accept this, and in June 888 he withdrew the edict. After Mototsune died in 891 Uda ruled directly. He founded Ninna-ji as an imperial temple in 894 and promoted men outside the main Fujiwara line, such as Minamoto no Yoshiari, Sugawara no Michizane and Fujiwara no Yasunori.

The reign saw the suspension of missions to Tang China, the compiling of the national histories Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku and Ruiju Kokushi, the consolidation or abolition of numerous government offices, and edicts protecting peasant land rights against powerful families and monasteries.

On 4 August 897 Uda proclaimed Crown Prince Atsuhito of age and abdicated the same day. It was long believed he did so to devote himself to Buddhism, but the act secured the succession in his own line before the Fujiwara could press a candidate of their own. He took the tonsure at Tō-ji in 899 and entered Ninna-ji as a monk. In January 901 Michizane was exiled to Dazaifu on suspicion of trying to put Uda's son Prince Tokiyo, his son-in-law, on the throne.

After the death of Fujiwara no Tokihira in 909 Uda regained influence, and he held a poetry contest at the palace on 22 April 913. He acted as regent to Emperor Suzaku after Daigo died in 930 and died on 3 September 931. His diary, the Kanpyo Gyoki, is an important source for the period, and his descendants became the Uda Genji.
emperor-wen-of-han: Liu Heng was the son of Emperor Gao and Consort Bo. In 196 BCE, after Emperor Gao defeated the rebellion of Chen Xi in the Dai region, he made Liu Heng Prince of Dai, with his capital at Jinyang, now Taiyuan. Dai lay on the border with the Xiongnu, and the principality probably served as a base against their raids. Later the grand empress dowager Lü, who held effective control of the imperial government, offered him the more prosperous Principality of Zhao. Prince Heng, rightly judging that she meant to give it to her nephew Lü Lu, politely declined and said he preferred to remain on the border.

After Grand Empress Dowager Lü died in August 180 BCE, officials slaughtered her clan and offered the throne to Prince Heng rather than to Prince Liu Xiang of Qi, because Xiang's maternal clan was domineering while the Bo clan was thought kind and humble. Aged 23, he accepted on 14 November 180 BCE. His nephew Emperor Houshao, seen as a puppet of Lü, was deposed and executed. Influenced by his wife Empress Dou, a Taoist, Wen governed with non-interference and relaxed laws. Tax rates were recorded as one thirtieth and one sixtieth, and warehouses were so full of grain that some of it decayed.
