In 179 BCE he abolished the law that allowed the arrest of the parents, wives and siblings of criminals, except in treason cases, and created an aid programme with loans, tax exemptions and stipends for widowers, widows, orphans and the old. The same year he made peace with Nanyue by writing humble yet assertive letters to its king, Zhao Tuo. In 167 BCE he banned facial tattooing and cutting off the nose or a foot, replacing them with whipping. He kept the heqin policy with the Xiongnu, giving a prince's daughter in marriage to their new chanyu Laoshang in 174 BCE.

Wen died in summer 157 BCE and was succeeded by Crown Prince Qi. His will cut the mourning period to three days and let his concubines return home. He was buried in the Baling mausoleum. His reign and that of his son Emperor Jing are known together as the Rule of Wen and Jing, noted for stability and relaxed laws, and he is counted among the most benevolent rulers in Chinese history. He was also listed among the Twenty-four Filial Exemplars, for tasting his mother's medicines before serving them to her.
emperor-wen-of-liu-song: Liu Yilong was born at Jingkou in 407, the third son of Liu Yu and his concubine Hu Dao'an, whom Liu Yu put to death in 409 for reasons lost to history. As a child he was given posts with staff to run them for him: defender of Jingkou at three, Duke of Pengcheng in 415 and, in 418, governor of the important Jing Province. When his father founded the Liu Song in 420 he became Prince of Yidu, and he was known as a student of the Confucian classics and histories and a good calligrapher. His eldest brother reigned as Emperor Shao until officials deposed him in 424.

At first he left power with the officials who had deposed his brother, Xu Xianzhi, Fu Liang and Xie Hui. But he resented that they had killed his two older brothers, and in 426, while publicly preparing a campaign against Northern Wei, he ordered them arrested and killed. His long reign, called the Yuanjia administration, is seen as a time of prosperity and strength, owed to his diligence and his choice of capable and honest officials.

Court quarrels marked his middle years. In 436, during a grave illness, the general Tan Daoji was arrested and executed with his sons on a false charge of treason; the traditional account plays down the emperor's part, but later events suggest his brother Liu Yikang acted with his approval. After an alleged plot of 445 involving Fan Ye, compiler of the Book of the Later Han, which the historian Wang Mingsheng thought far-fetched, Liu Yikang was reduced to a commoner, and in 451, fearing new plots during a Northern Wei invasion, the emperor had him killed.

Historians fault him for repeated failed attacks on Northern Wei and poor strategy, which weakened the state late in his reign. In 453, angered that the crown prince Liu Shao was using witchcraft to curse him, he planned to depose him; the plan leaked, and Liu Shao killed him on 16 March. Less than a year later another son, Liu Jun, defeated Liu Shao and took the throne as Emperor Xiaowu.
emperor-wen-of-sui: Yang Jian belonged to the northwestern Chinese military aristocracy, in the Yang clan of Hongnong, which had Han origins but had intermarried with the Xianbei for generations. His father Yang Zhong followed the general Yuwen Tai. Yang Jian was born in a Buddhist temple, and a Buddhist nun, Zhixian, raised him in his early years. At 14 he entered the army under Yuwen Tai, and in 557 he married Dugu Qieluo. In 573 his daughter Yang Lihua became the wife of the crown prince Yuwen Yun.

When the Northern Zhou emperor Xuan died in 580, Yang, as his father-in-law, took power as regent. General Yuchi Jiong rose against him, and within 68 days he was defeated, as was Wang Qian. Yang then began to eliminate the Yuwen clan and in spring 581 had Emperor Jing yield the throne, founding the Sui dynasty. He reorganised the government into five main bureaus, had Pei Zheng simplify the penal code, a reform later largely accepted by subsequent dynasties, and built a new capital, Daxing, to which he moved in 583. He also built the Guangtong Canal in 584.

In 588 he announced a campaign against the southern Chen dynasty under his son Yang Guang, and in spring 589 the Sui army captured the Chen capital Jiankang and took the Chen emperor captive, ending the Northern and Southern dynasties period. In the north he worked to divide the Göktürks, who by the end of his reign had split into an eastern and a western khaganate, and a campaign against Goguryeo in 598 ended in heavy losses. In 592 he reduced taxes and had land redistributed to poor farmers, and it was said that enough food was stored for 50 years.

In 600 Emperor Wen deposed his eldest son Yang Yong as crown prince and replaced him with Yang Guang. Empress Dugu died in 602. He died at Renshou Palace in 604 and was buried at the Tailing mausoleum. How he died is controversial: most traditional historians hold that Yang Guang had him killed, and Yang Guang took the throne as Emperor Yang.

The historian Sima Guang described him as cautious, hard-working and frugal, who lowered the burden of labour and tax on his people, but also as suspicious of his officials and even of his own sons. According to him the census rolls grew from under four million households to almost nine million during the reign. As a Buddhist, Wen encouraged the spread of Buddhism through the state.
emperor-wu-of-han: Emperor Wu, personal name Liu Che, was the 11th son of Liu Qi, the future Emperor Jing, and his consort Wang Zhi. His elder half-brother Liu Rong was made crown prince in 153 BCE, but the arrogance of Liu Rong's mother, Lady Li, gave Consort Wang and the young Liu Che the chance to win the emperor's favour. He took the throne in 141 BCE. Up to then the Han dynasty had followed a policy of non-intervention, and the heqin marriage alliances with the Xiongnu had failed to protect the borders. The non-interventionist rule had also let vassal states grow powerful, as in the Rebellion of the Seven States under Emperor Jing.

His reign lasted 54 years. To weaken the old noble classes he recruited young supporters from ordinary backgrounds into an inner court that reported directly to him, and he called on grassroots scholars such as Gongsun Hong to enter government. After the death of Grand Empress Dowager Dou in 135 BCE he had full control and began campaigns of territorial expansion in all directions but the sea. Han forces took Nanyue in 111 BCE and by 108 BCE completed the conquest of Gojoseon in what is now northern Korea and Manchuria. He adopted Confucian principles as the state ethic and started a school to teach future administrators the Confucian classics, though he also trusted officials known for harsh punishment.

In 139 BCE he sent Zhang Qian west to seek the Yuezhi as allies against the Xiongnu. Zhang was captured by the Xiongnu, escaped around 129 BCE, and returned to the capital Chang'an in 126 BCE. Although the Yuezhi refused to return, he established relations with several kingdoms, among them Dayuan and Kangju. After the Prince of Hunxie surrendered the Gansu region, regular embassies between Han and the Western Regions began. The Han waged war against the Dayuan in 104 BCE to obtain their horses. In the same year the Taichu calendar took effect, making the first month the start of the year.

Emperor Wu died on 29 March 87 BCE. At the height of the empire his borders spanned from the Fergana Valley in the west to northern Korea in the east and northern Vietnam in the south. The reforms that made Confucianism the state philosophy had an enduring effect throughout imperial China. He also developed the Imperial Music Bureau, introduced the practice of changing reign names, and worshipped the divinity Tai Yi. Michael Loewe called his reign the high point of the modernist policies that adapted ideas from the pre-Han period.
emperor-wu-of-jin: Sima Yan was born in 236, the eldest son of Sima Zhao and Wang Yuanji. Sima Zhao was then a mid-level official of Cao Wei and the son of the general Sima Yi. After Sima Shi died in March 255, Sima Zhao became regent and the paramount authority in the Wei government. His father hesitated between him and his brother Sima You as heir, but several high officials favoured Sima Yan. When Sima Zhao died on 6 September 265, Sima Yan became King of Jin the next day, and on 4 February 266 he forced Cao Huan to abdicate. On 8 February 266 he declared himself emperor of the Jin dynasty.

Believing that Cao Wei had been doomed by its weak princes, Emperor Wu made princes of many uncles, cousins, brothers and sons in February 266, each with independent military command. He also softened the penal law, but nobles received simple rebukes while commoners saw no real reduction. In 267 he made Sima Zhong crown prince, who appeared developmentally disabled, and in 272 chose Jia Nanfeng, daughter of Jia Chong, as his princess.

A revolt by the Xianbei chief Tufa Shujineng from 270 held his attention until Ma Long put it down in 279. He then sent a six-pronged attack on Eastern Wu, and Sun Hao surrendered on 1 May 280. After the conquest he ordered provincial governors to become purely civilian and regional militias disbanded. In 281 he took 5,000 women from Sun Hao's palace into his own and gave them more attention than state affairs.

As Emperor Wu grew ill in 289 he considered Yang Jun and his uncle Sima Liang as regents. After he wrote his will, Yang Jun seized it and promulgated another naming himself alone as regent. Emperor Wu died on 16 May 290. Historians commonly view him as benevolent but wasteful, too tolerant of the corruption of the aristocratic clans. His princes, given armies, fought the War of the Eight Princes soon after his death, which led to the uprisings of the Five Barbarians that destroyed the Western Jin.
emperor-wu-of-liang: Xiao Yan was born in 464, the third son of Xiao Shunzhi, who claimed descent from the Han prime minister Xiao He and belonged to the close circle of advisers around Xiao Daocheng, founder of Southern Qi in 479. Around 481 or 482 he married Chi Hui, and they had three daughters but no sons.

He began his career as military assistant to the Prince of Baling and later served on the staff of the prime minister Wang Jian. He became one of eight young officials in the literary arts befriended by Xiao Ziliang, Prince of Jingling, among them Fan Yun and Shen Yue. In 495 he fought Northern Wei troops on the frontline and distinguished himself.

After Xiao Baojuan became emperor of Southern Qi in 498, he executed several high officials, and Xiao Yan, then at his post in Yong Province, secretly prepared for civil war. Having overthrown Xiao Baojuan, he put his brothers and associates in important posts, collected ever higher honours and titles, and executed the brothers and cousins of the new emperor, Emperor He, one by one. In the spring of 502 he had Emperor He issue an edict giving him the throne, which ended Southern Qi and began the Liang dynasty. He soon had Emperor He put to death, though he treated the remaining descendants of Emperors Gao and Wu of Qi with honour, reasoning that they were of one family.

His early reign was regarded as Liang's prime. He was considered diligent and frugal, but he tolerated corruption by relatives. He established universities and extended the Confucian civil service examinations, requiring the sons of nobles to study and patronised the arts. Confucian in governing, he also embraced Buddhism, banned animal sacrifice and opposed executions, and was nicknamed the Bodhisattva Emperor. In 523 he replaced forged copper coins with iron ones.

In 547 the Eastern Wei general Hou Jing rebelled and surrendered nine provinces to Liang. Emperor Wu hesitated, but on the advice of Zhu Yi accepted and made Hou Prince of He'nan. Hou later rebelled, captured the capital Jiankang and held Emperor Wu and his successor, Emperor Jianwen, under close control, plunging the state into anarchy. His leniency towards the corruption of his clan and officials came at a heavy price, for few came to his aid. He died on 12 June 549, supposedly of hunger and thirst after Hou refused him honey. He is the namesake of the Liang Jeweled Repentance, a Buddhist text widely read in China and Korea.
emperor-wu-of-liu-song: Liu Yu was born on 16 April 363 at Jingkou, the son of Liu Qiao, a police officer said to descend from Liu Jiao, Prince of Chu under the Han, and Zhao Anzong, who died just after his birth. His father, too poor to raise him, thought of abandoning the child, but an aunt took him in and nursed him in place of her own son. He grew up strong and ambitious but poor and nearly unlettered, selling straw sandals and fond of gambling, and his village looked down on him. He became an officer under the general Sun Wuzhong.

After Huan Xuan seized the throne, Liu Yu and He Wuji led a plot of several simultaneous uprisings in 404; they surprised Huan Xuan's cousin Huan Xiu and took Jingkou, and Liu Yu won over the writer Liu Muzhi as his assistant. Having seen Huan Xuan fail, he moved slowly, at first sharing power with He Wuji and Liu Yi and repeatedly offering to resign his posts. When Lu Xun's forces attacked north in 410 while Liu Yu was taking the Southern Yan capital of Guanggu, he hurried back and refused to have Emperor An leave Jiankang.

He then removed rivals in his own coalition, defeating Liu Yi in 412 and killing Zhuge Zhangmin in 413. After Later Qin was destroyed he went back to Jiankang to prepare his own accession, leaving his 11-year-old son Liu Yizhen at Chang'an, where quarrels among the generals let Helian Bobo of Xia take the region, killing or capturing nearly the whole army at Qingni.

As emperor he honoured his stepmother as empress dowager and allowed those branded undesirable by public opinion a new chance. He had the deposed emperor, Sima Dewen, smothered with a blanket in 421 after he refused to take poison. He died on 26 June 422 and was buried in the Chuning Mausoleum, in present-day Nanjing, where two stone qilin of its spirit way survive. He is remembered as one of the great generals of the Northern and Southern dynasties: under him the southern empire came closest to reconquering the north, and his campaigns let the south defend along the Yellow River.
emperor-xian-of-han: Liu Xie was born in 181 to Emperor Ling and his consort Wang Rong. The jealous Empress He poisoned his mother soon after his birth, and he was raised by Emperor Ling's mother, Empress Dowager Dong, under the circumspect title Marquis Dong. His older half-brother Liu Bian, the empress's son, was judged insufficiently solemn, and Emperor Ling hesitated over naming Liu Xie crown prince instead. When Emperor Ling died in 189, Liu Bian was declared emperor, and Liu Xie was made Prince of Bohai and later Prince of Chenliu.

In 189 the warlord Dong Zhuo arrived in Luoyang as the court fell into chaos, forced Emperor Shao to yield, and enthroned Liu Xie at the age of eight. In 190, when a coalition led by Yuan Shao rose against Dong Zhuo, Dong forced the emperor to move to Chang'an and set fire to Luoyang. After officials led by Wang Yun and Lü Bu killed Dong in 192, his former subordinates Li Jue and Guo Si took control of the emperor. In 195 he escaped to the ruins of Luoyang, where officials starved.

In 196 Cao Cao entered Luoyang, shared power with the emperor's generals while in fact commanding, and moved the court to Xu. He issued edicts in the emperor's name and used him to lend legitimacy to his campaigns against rival warlords. In 200 Dong Cheng's plot against Cao Cao, based on a claimed secret edict, was discovered and he was killed; Cao Cao had Dong's pregnant daughter, an imperial consort, executed. In 215 Cao Cao had Empress Fu Shou killed, with her two sons, and made his own daughter Cao Jie empress.

Cao Cao died on 15 March 220, and his son Cao Pi soon forced Emperor Xian to abdicate, founding the state of Cao Wei. The former emperor became Duke of Shanyang with a fiefdom of 10 000 households and kept privileges such as not having to kneel when receiving edicts. He died in April 234 and was buried with Han ceremonies fit for an emperor, with the Wei emperor Cao Rui among the mourners. His dukedom lasted 73 more years under three further dukes. Such hereditary nobility for a deposed predecessor was known as two crownings and three respects.
emperor-xiaowen-of-northern-wei: Tuoba Hong was born on 13 October 467, the eldest son of Emperor Xianwen, then only thirteen, and Consort Li. He was made crown prince in 469, and his mother died the same year, probably forced to kill herself under the Northern Wei custom of putting crown princes' mothers to death. In 471 Xianwen, who favoured Taoist and Buddhist ideas, gave him the throne and became retired emperor, keeping real control. In 476 Empress Dowager Feng, resentful that Xianwen had executed her lover Li Yi, had him killed, most historians including Sima Guang believing by poison, and took the regency as Grand Empress Dowager.

Under the regency the court introduced the equal-field system in 485, in which the state owned the land and distributed it equally to taxpaying farmers, breaking the power of local magnates. With the Three Elders system for compiling population registers, it gave the state a stable fiscal base and lasted into the Tang dynasty. The Grand Empress Dowager also had the emperor's grandfather Li Hui and his clan killed on a false charge of treason in 478. By about 483 Xiaowen seemed largely in charge, though she kept substantial powers until her death, which he mourned for three years.

His sinicisation aimed to centralise a multi-ethnic state. In 493 he set out on a campaign against Southern Qi and, when Xianbei officials tried to stop him at Luoyang, offered to abandon it if the capital moved there. In 496 he ordered Xianbei surnames changed to Han ones, honoured eight Xianbei and five Han clans, and had offices given by clan status, over the objections of his official Li Chong. He also encouraged marriage between Xianbei and Han. His campaigns against Southern Qi in 495 and 497 to 498 were largely indecisive, though he took Wancheng and Xinye.

The reforms met resistance. In 496 Crown Prince Yuan Xun, unhappy with Han customs and Luoyang's heat, plotted to flee to Pingcheng and was deposed, and a second plot by Mu Tai and Lu Rui was crushed. In 497 Xiaowen made Yuan Ke crown prince and forced Yuan Xun to commit suicide. Already ill, he died on campaign on 26 April 499 after defeating the Southern Qi general Chen Xianda. His brothers kept his death secret until his body reached Luoyang, and Yuan Ke succeeded him as Emperor Xuanwu. By his will Empress Feng Run, whom he had found guilty of adultery, was forced to kill herself.
emperor-xiaozong-of-song: Zhao Shen was born Zhao Bocong, the second son of Zhao Zicheng, a sixth cousin of Emperor Gaozong. After the Jingkang Incident of 1127 Gaozong's father, eldest brother and most close relatives were captured by the Jin. Gaozong's only son, Zhao Fu, had died at about the age of two, so the emperor had his officials search for living descendants of the imperial family. Zhao Shen was found and adopted in April 1160, along with another relative, Zhao Qu.
Gaozong chose Shen over Qu as heir, it is said, because of his virtue: given ten maids, Qu touched every one and Shen not one. He was named crown prince in July 1162.

Gaozong abdicated on 24 July 1162 and kept power as Taishang Huang, so Xiaozong took full power only after Gaozong's death in 1187. He reached peace with the Jin in 1165, rehabilitated Yue Fei after death and cleared out the remnants of Qin Hui's faction. Under him trade missions to the ports of the Indian Ocean increased.

His was one of the few Southern Song reigns not dominated by powerful officials. He dismissed ministers who did not meet his expectations, and in 1166 an official, Mo Chi, criticised him for removing councillors after a few months; he praised the criticism but ignored it. He issued direct orders, called mi-pai, nei-pi and yu-pi, without consulting his councillors.

Xiaozong drove attempts to steady the paper currency, the huizi. In 1166 he bought back two million silver ounces' worth of circulating notes and burned them, and decreed that paper notes could pay taxes and fees. By limiting the quantity in circulation he stabilised the value in 1175; around 20 million strings of cash were in issue in 1186.

After Gaozong died in 1187 Xiaozong withdrew into mourning and handed government to his son Zhao Dun. In 1189 he abdicated in his favour as Emperor Guangzong and became Taishang Huang. He fell ill in 1194, and Guangzong refused to visit him or attend the funeral, which forced Guangzong to give up the throne to Xiaozong's grandson, Emperor Ningzong. He is remembered as an effective ruler under whom the Song prospered.
emperor-xizong-of-tang: Born Li Yan on 8 June 862 at the eastern palace in Chang'an, he was the fifth son of Emperor Yizong and his consort Wang, who held the highest rank among imperial consorts and died in 866. Created Prince of Pu in 865, he grew up with the eunuch Tian Lingzi as a constant companion. When Yizong fell gravely ill in 873, the eunuch commanders of the Shence Armies, Liu Xingshen and Han Wenyue, backed the young prince, and an edict in his father's name made him crown prince and renamed him Li Xuan. The powerful chancellor Wei Baoheng was soon exiled and forced to take his own life.

A drought-driven famine struck the heart of the realm early in the reign. The scholar Lu Xi urged tax relief, and an edict agreed, but no relief was said to have been carried out. Bands of the displaced gathered under Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao by 874–875. Peace talks failed when the general Song Wei seized and sent for execution Wang's envoy Shang Junzhang; Wang was later killed in battle, and his followers joined Huang, who marched south to Guang Prefecture and then north again.

Luoyang fell on 22 December 880. After his capture of Chang'an Huang declared a state of Qi and killed members of the imperial family and many officials. The Shatuo leader Li Keyong, pardoned and recalled, defeated Qi's armies from 882, Chang'an was retaken in 883, and Huang was killed by his nephew Lin Yan in 884.

Without taxes from the provinces, the court could not pay its armies. Tian Lingzi's attempt to take back the salt ponds of Huguo Circuit set its governor Wang Chongrong and Li Keyong against him, and around the new year of 886 they drove Tian and the emperor to Xingyuan. Zhu Mei and Li Changfu then proclaimed a distant relative, Li Yun, emperor, until Yang Fugong won back Wang and Li Keyong and Li Yun was killed. Xizong returned to Chang'an in the spring of 888 and died of illness a month later, on 20 April. His brother succeeded as Emperor Zhaozong, and the Tang fell in 907.
emperor-xuanzong-of-tang: Li Longji, later Emperor Xuanzong, was born at the eastern capital Luoyang in 685, the third son of Emperor Ruizong and his concubine Consort Dou. In 690 Empress Dowager Wu, later known as Wu Zetian, took the throne herself, interrupting the Tang dynasty, and imposed the surname Wu on Ruizong's family.

In 693 she had Consort Dou and Ruizong's wife killed after a false accusation of witchcraft. Li Longji's title was reduced and he was kept in the palace until 699. After Wu Zetian was overthrown in 705 he held posts under Emperor Zhongzong and cultivated ties with imperial guard commanders, fearing that Zhongzong's powerful wife Empress Wei would harm the dynasty.

When Zhongzong died suddenly in 710, traditional historians believed Empress Wei and her daughter had poisoned him. Li Longji acted with Princess Taiping and officers of the guard before the Wei faction could seize the throne, and Ruizong was restored. Li Longji became his heir, though his older brother Li Chengqi declined to be set above him. He then took the throne through a second coup against Princess Taiping, who held great influence over chancellors and officials.

The Kaiyuan era, 713 to 741, is usually viewed as one of the golden ages of Chinese history, a period of political stability, peace and economic prosperity, with advances in education, literature, music, painting, sculpture and religion. Capable chancellors such as Yao Chong served him, and he cut the number of chancellors to two or sometimes three.

In 714 he exiled the secret police officials of Wu Zetian's reign. In the Tianbao era, from 742, he turned to pleasure with his favourite concubine Yang Guifei, and power passed to Li Linfu, then her cousin Yang Guozhong, and the eunuch Gao Lishi. In 751 the Tang lost the Battle of Talas to the Abbasid Caliphate, and some tributaries turned to the Abbasids.

Military governors, most of them non-Han, took more regional power into their hands. One of them, An Lushan, who had defeated and again made vassals of the Khitan, began the Anshi Rebellion at Fanyang in 755. The rebels took Luoyang and, six months later, the capital Chang'an.

Xuanzong fled to Sichuan and abdicated in favour of Li Heng, Emperor Suzong, and as retired emperor he still intervened at times in the campaign against the rebel state of Yan. He sent messengers to the tomb of Zhang Jiuling, who had warned about An Lushan, to offer sacrifices. One of his poems, on passing through the old state of Lu with a sacrifice to Confucius, is included in Three Hundred Tang Poems.
emperor-yang-of-sui: Yang Guang was born in 569, the second son of Yang Jian, later Emperor Wen, and Duchess Dugu. When his father founded the Sui dynasty in 581 he became Prince of Jin and was later put in charge of the provinces north of the Yellow River. In 588 he commanded the five armies that invaded the Chen dynasty in the south and was widely praised for the success of the campaign. This and, according to the traditional account, his scheming against his elder brother Yang Yong made him crown prince in 600. Emperor Wen died in 604, and traditional historians generally thought, without direct evidence, that Yang Guang had ordered his murder.

Emperor Yang ruled from 604 to 618. He first put down a rebellion by his brother Yang Liang, then moved to Luoyang, which he made the eastern capital and where he ordered large building projects. He completed the Grand Canal and rebuilt the Great Wall. His expeditions brought the Sui to its largest extent, though the conquest of Champa cost thousands of soldiers' lives from malaria. In 609 he toured the conquered Tuyuhun territory and received 27 rulers of the western kingdoms at Zhangye. He was also a patron of the arts and increased the foreign orchestras at his court from seven to nine.

His campaigns against Goguryeo went badly. When he planned another in 614, officials disapproved but none dared oppose him, and many soldiers deserted. Conscription and heavier taxes to pay for the wars provoked unrest, and agrarian rebellions spread. In 615 he had Li Hun and Li Min and their clansmen put to death, worried by prophecies that a man named Li would become emperor.

With northern China in turmoil, Emperor Yang spent his last years at Jiangdu, now Yangzhou. His general Yuwen Huaji led a coup in which he was strangled, on 11 April 618. Traditional historians regard him as one of the worst tyrants in Chinese history and blame him for the Sui's short rule. In April 2013 a tomb discovered at Hanjiang in Yangzhou held a stone epitaph for the late Emperor Yang of Sui. It measures 4.98 by 5.88 metres, smaller than many tombs of non-royal people, which archaeologists explain by his sudden death. It had been robbed in antiquity, and no remains were found.
emperor-yuan-of-jin: Sima Rui was born in 276 in the Jin capital of Luoyang, the son of Sima Jin, heir to the princedom of Langya, and his wife Xiahou Guangji. After his father died on 9 March 290, Sima Rui became Prince of Langya.

During the War of the Eight Princes he remained aloof from politics to protect himself. In 304 he joined the campaign of Sima Yue against Sima Ying as a minor general. After Sima Ying's victory his uncle Sima Yao was executed, and Sima Rui fled back to his principality of Langya, advised by Wang Dao, whom he had befriended in the campaign.

In August 307 Sima Yue, victorious as regent for Emperor Huai, commissioned Sima Rui as military commander of parts of Yang Province south of the Yangtze, with his post at Jianye. Few southern gentry clans at first came to support an unknown prince, but on Wang Dao's counsel he visited He Xun and Gu Rong and invited them to serve him. It was said at the time that the Simas and the Wangs ruled equally.

After Luoyang fell to Han forces in July 311, he was proclaimed leader of the Jin alliance with authority to appoint and dismiss chief officials. He chose more than a hundred officials from the northern emigre families, known as the 106 Officials, and relied on them increasingly.

In 313 Sima Ye was declared emperor at Chang'an, and Jianye was renamed Jiankang to avoid his given name. Sima Rui took no action to aid him. After Chang'an fell in 316 he announced a campaign against Han but cancelled it, citing lack of supplies. He became King of Jin on 6 April 317 and, after Liu Cong executed Emperor Min on 7 February 318, declared himself emperor on 26 April 318. By 321 Jin rule north of the Yellow River had ended.

By 320 his relationship with Wang Dun, who controlled the western provinces, was at breaking point, and he surrounded himself with men who opposed the Wangs, such as Liu Wei and Diao Xie. Wang Dun marched on Jiankang in spring 322, claiming only to clean up the government, and defeated the emperor's forces. He killed Diao and others, and Yuan had to submit and grant him additional powers. Despondent and ill, Emperor Yuan died in January 323, and his son Sima Shao succeeded him as Emperor Ming.
emperor-yuryaku: The account of Yūryaku's life comes from the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, chronicles that mix legend and myth with possible historical fact. They record that he was born as Ōhatsuse no Wakatakeru, the fifth and youngest son of Emperor Ingyō, and was never named crown prince because he had two older living brothers. When his brother Emperor Ankō was assassinated, Ōhatsuse turned on his brothers as suspected conspirators: he killed Prince Shirahiko with a sword, and had Kurohiko burned to death.

The chronicles say that he also took Prince Ichinobe no Oshiwa, whom Ankō had wished to make his heir, and his brother Prince Mima out hunting and killed them. Ichinobe's sons fled to Harima and later became Emperor Kenzō and Emperor Ninken. He was then enthroned and made his palace at Asakura in Sakurai, Nara. The Kiki call his reign tyrannical and cruel, and say the public called him Emperor of Great Wickedness, though he improved after being admonished by the empress. He is also credited with encouraging agriculture, sericulture and handicrafts, and with writing poetry.

His name stands at the beginning of the Man'yōshū, and poems attributed to him are in that collection and the chronicles. In 1968 the iron Inariyama sword was recovered from a tomb, and X-ray study in 1978 revealed a gold-inlaid inscription of at least 115 Chinese characters. Its king Waka Takiru is thought to be Ōhatsuse-wakatakeru, and the Eta Funayama sword may carry the name too. If so, the power of the Great King already reached from Kyushu to the east by the later 5th century.

The Book of Song records that a King Bu sent envoys to the Chinese emperor Shun of Song in 477 and 478, announcing the death of King Kō and calling himself King of Wa; Bu is theorised to be Yūryaku. There is no evidence that the title tennō was used in his time, and his name was probably assigned later. Historians generally accept his existence. His actual grave is unknown, but he is venerated at a mausoleum in Habikino, Osaka, and enshrined at Katsuragi Ichigoshu Shrine in Gose, Nara.
emperor-zhaozong-of-tang: He was born Li Jie on 31 March 867 in the eastern palace at Chang'an, the seventh son of Emperor Yizong; his name was later changed to Li Min and, soon after he took the throne, to Li Ye. His mother, the concubine Consort Wang, appears to have died shortly after his birth. In 880 he followed his elder brother, Emperor Xizong, in flight from Chang'an before the rebels led by Huang Chao. On the journey the 13-year-old prince asked the eunuch Tian Lingzi for a horse; Tian refused and whipped his attendant, and Li Jie resented Tian deeply afterwards.

His accession in 888 raised great hopes, since he was considered intelligent, decisive and talented and wished to restore the imperial power lost under Xizong. He ordered a campaign against Tian Lingzi's brother Chen Jingxuan, military governor of Xichuan Circuit. In 891 he let Yang Fugong, with whom he had long been at odds, retire and then, on rumours of a plot, sent the guards against his mansion. Li Maozhen, military governor of Fengxiang Circuit, forced his own appointment as commander against the Yangs, and in summer 896 he attacked Chang'an.

The emperor fled to Hua Prefecture, where Han Jian controlled him, forced him to disband the guards under the imperial princes and slaughtered 11 of the princes. Back at court, the chancellor Cui Yin, an ally of Zhu Wen, planned with the emperor to slaughter the eunuchs, who in turn feared an emperor described as depressed, alcoholic and unpredictable. In winter 900, after he killed several attendants in a drunken rage, the eunuch Liu Jishu led troops into the palace, put him under house arrest and made his son emperor. He was restored in 901. His campaigns against Li Keyong, Chen Jingxuan and Li Maozhen only confirmed their power.

Zhu Wen came to control Chang'an, and after his nephew Zhu Youlun died in a polo accident late in 903 he suspected Cui Yin of a plot. In spring 904 his soldiers killed Cui and his associates, and Zhu forced the emperor to leave Chang'an for Luoyang.

Fearing that the emperor might rise against him, Zhu sent Jiang Xuanhui and others to the palace in the autumn of 904 to kill him. The emperor died on 22 September 904, aged 37; Zhu blamed two of his own officers and forced them to commit suicide. The emperor's son Li Zuo became Emperor Ai, and by 907 Zhu had taken the throne himself, ending the Tang dynasty and founding the Later Liang.
emperor-zhenzong-of-song: Zhao Heng was born on 23 December 968, the third son of Emperor Taizong. His personal name was first Zhao Dechang, then Zhao Yuanxiu in 983, Zhao Yuankan in 986, and finally Zhao Heng in 995. He became the third emperor of the Song dynasty in 997, and was succeeded at the end of his reign by his sixth son, Emperor Renzong.

His reign is noted for the consolidation of power and for prosperity, with the military further reinforced. It also began a policy towards the Khitan-led Liao dynasty in the north that ended in humiliation. In 1004 the Khitans made war on the Song, and Zhenzong led his army against them. Despite early successes he concluded the Chanyuan Treaty in 1005. It brought more than a century of peace, but the Song accepted a position inferior to the Liao and agreed to pay each year 100,000 ounces of silver and over 200,000 bolts of silk. This admission of inferiority troubled later Song foreign relations, and the payments slowly drained the treasury.

In 1011 and 1012 he ordered 30,000 bushels of quick-maturing rice seed shipped from Fujian to the lower Yangtze basin to improve agriculture. Champa rice reached China from Champa during his reign. In 1013 officials were evaluated by tax targets, usually set as averages of the highest and lowest collections of three years. Zhenzong stressed Taoism at court. During his reign the so-called Heavenly Texts, which glorified the Zhao family, were allegedly discovered. Imperial sacrifices at Mount Tai followed, and from 1013 to 1015 he issued decrees deifying the Jade Emperor as the highest ruler of Heaven.

In 1020 Zhenzong fell ill and could no longer handle the affairs of state. His wife, Empress Liu, was already established as the power behind the throne, and acted unofficially as regent for the last two years of his life. He died on 23 March 1022, and Renzong succeeded him, with real power remaining in the hands of Empress Liu, who became empress dowager.

Artefacts from the Tang and Song dynasties, some of which had belonged to Zhenzong, were excavated and came into the hands of the Kuomintang general Ma Hongkui, who did not publicise them. After his death his wife took them to Taiwan in 1971 and gave them to Chiang Kai-shek, who turned them over to the National Palace Museum.
emperor-zhezong: Zhezong was the sixth son of Emperor Shenzong. His original personal name was Zhao Yong, which he changed to Zhao Xu after his coronation. He came to the throne as a child under the supervision of his grandmother, Grand Empress Dowager Gao, who may have engineered his enthronement in order to become regent. Cheng Yi, a founder of Neo-Confucianism, was among his tutors; he proposed that li, or principle, was an innate property that could give moral guidance.

As regent, Empress Dowager Gao appointed conservatives such as Sima Guang as chancellor, and they halted and partly reversed the New Policies of Wang Anshi. Zhezong was powerless until her death in 1093, when he was able to reinstate the reforms and reduce the late Sima Guang's influence. By then, factionalism mattered more than the practicality of the reforms, and both conservatives and reformists engaged in infighting. His government lowered taxes.

In 1094 he changed the era name to Shaosheng, meaning continuing sagacity, to signal that Shenzong's reforms would continue, partly out of filial piety, and named the reformist Zhang Dun grand chancellor. Zhang Dun purged the conservatives and silenced dissent. The reformists took revenge for the earlier exile of Cai Que to Lingnan by exiling many conservatives there, and a blacklist of 37 conservatives barred them and their descendants from office. Zhezong changed the examinations to require candidates to support the reformist stance. He also ended negotiations with the Tangut-led Western Xia, and in the renewed war the Song consolidated borders, built fortifications and slowly took territory, expanding the dynasty to its widest territorial extent.

Zhezong fell ill in May 1099 with coughing and constipation, and the physician Geng Yu's treatments brought no lasting improvement. His infant son Zhao Mao died in 1099 after a short recovery. By 21 December the emperor was close to death. He died in Kaifeng on 23 February 1100 at the age of 23, and because his son had died prematurely he was succeeded by his younger half-brother Emperor Huizong. Huizong's mother, Empress Xiang, led a conservative restoration at court. The conflict between factions, which intensified under Zhezong, would contribute to the fall of the Northern Song in the 12th century.
emperor-zhongzong-of-tang: Li Xian was born in 656 as the seventh son of Emperor Gaozong and the third son of Empress Wu, later known as Wu Zetian. In 657 he was created Prince of Zhou. His name was later changed to Li Zhe. In 681, after Gaozong fell ill from pills made by alchemists, he briefly exercised imperial powers as crown prince, assisted by chancellors aligned with Empress Wu. Gaozong fell ill again at Luoyang in 683, summoned Li Zhe and transferred imperial powers to him, probably on Empress Wu's advice, and soon died.

Li Zhe took the throne as Emperor Zhongzong, but real power stayed with his mother, now empress dowager and regent. His reign lasted less than two months before she deposed him in favour of his younger brother, Emperor Ruizong. He was demoted to a princely rank and exiled to Fang Prefecture and Jun Prefecture in modern Hubei, under house arrest. On the way Princess Wei gave birth to a daughter, whom he wrapped in his own shirt, and she was named Li Guo'er, the child who was wrapped. He lived in fear that each messenger from the capital brought an order for his death, since Empress Dowager Wu had forced his brother Li Xian to suicide in 684.

In 697 the Khitan leader Sun Wanrong asked in a declaration why Wu Zetian kept Li Zhe in exile. Chancellors including Di Renjie urged her to recall him, and in 698 he returned to Luoyang. Li Dan offered to yield the position of crown prince, and Li Zhe was made crown prince on 24 October 698. On 20 February 705 the Shenlong Coup deposed Wu Zetian, and Zhongzong was restored three days later.

In his second reign most power lay with Empress Wei, her daughter Li Guo'er, who became Princess Anle, and Wu Sansi, a nephew of Wu Zetian. Empress Wei accused his eldest surviving son, Li Chongfu, of complicity in a death, and he was sent out of the capital under heavy guard. Zhongzong had repeatedly refused Li Guo'er's wish to be made crown princess.

He died on 3 July 710. According to traditional historians, Empress Wei and her partisans put poison in a cake because she wanted to rule as an empress regnant like Wu Zetian. She installed his son Li Chongmao, aged sixteen, as Emperor Shang. Two weeks later Princess Taiping and her nephew Li Longji, the future Emperor Xuanzong, overthrew Empress Wei and the young emperor, and Ruizong was restored.
empire-of-japan: After two centuries of the seclusion policy known as sakoku, Japan was forced open to trade when the American commander Matthew C. Perry arrived in 1854 and the Convention of Kanagawa was signed. Commercial treaties with Western countries followed, and their humiliating terms turned many against the Tokugawa shogunate, giving rise to the radical movement sonnō jōi, Revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians. After the Boshin War power was restored to the emperor from the shōgun, and the Charter Oath, made public at the enthronement of Emperor Meiji on 7 April 1868, set out the aims of the new government and the legal stage for modernisation.

Under the slogans Enrich the Country, Strengthen the Armed Forces and Promote Industry, Japan went through large-scale industrialisation and militarisation, often regarded as the fastest modernisation of any country to date. It joined the First World War on the Allied side in 1914, occupied the German-leased territory of Tsingtao and German islands in the Pacific, which in 1920 the League of Nations placed under Japanese administration as the South Seas Mandate. Hirohito came to the throne on 25 December 1926. During the 1920s the country moved toward a democratic system, but parliamentary government was not rooted deeply enough to withstand the economic and political pressures of the 1930s, when military leaders gained influence.

Japan occupied Manchuria in 1931 after the Mukden Incident and left the League of Nations in 1933. Its forces won large successes in the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Pacific War, notably the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, but from 1942, after Allied advances at Midway and Guadalcanal, Japan was on the defensive. After the dropping of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, it accepted the Potsdam Declaration on 14 August 1945, and the formal surrender was signed on 2 September.

The empire had three emperors, Meiji, Taishō and Shōwa. Its political system has been debated, since there was no single dictator, and terms proposed include militarism, totalitarianism and police state. Imperial Japan committed widespread war crimes in the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Second World War, among them the Nanjing Massacre, involving the deaths of millions. The Allied occupation under Douglas MacArthur lasted until 1952, when the Treaty of San Francisco took effect. A new constitution was ratified on 3 May 1947, ending the empire, and the armed forces were dissolved. The Japan Self-Defense Forces were created in 1954, and Okinawa was returned to Japan in 1972.
emporda: The Empordà is a natural and historical region of Catalonia. Its name derives from Empúries, Empòrion in Greek and Emporiae in Latin, meaning the markets, through the name of the medieval County of Empúries. The writer Josep Pla, born in the Baix Empordà, called the country around his native Palafrugell, between the Gavarres and the Montgrí, the Empordanet, a name still used for the Baix Empordà. The Montgrí Massif holds caves that sheltered Paleolithic people, among them two called Cau del Duc, and there are megaliths in the Gavarres and Cadiretes massifs and dolmens at Fitor.

Greeks settled at Roses, possibly a colony of Rhodes, in the 8th century BCE, and at Empúries at the beginning of the 6th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE the Iberian Indigetes built one of their main cities at Ullastret. Roman rule changed the settlement and use of the land, and Ullastret was abandoned in the 2nd century BCE. Invasions in the 3rd and 5th centuries impoverished the region and shrank its towns, and the Muslim occupation lasted less than sixty years, from 714 to 785.

The administration of the Carolingian Empire divided the conquered Catalan lands into counties. The north and the present Alt Empordà were organised around the County of Empúries, whose capital moved from Sant Martí d'Empúries to Castelló d'Empúries. Much of the rest belonged to the Bishop of Girona or to baronies of the Cardona family. The County of Empúries resisted royal power and was among the last to join the Crown of Aragon. Shipyards were working in the Empordà in the 10th century.

Since 1936 the Empordà has been divided into two comarques. Figueres, its main urban and economic centre, is the capital of Alt Empordà, and La Bisbal d'Empordà that of Baix Empordà. The region has nurtured several schools of painting, above all surrealism, with artists such as Salvador Dalí, Angel Planells, Joan Massanet and Evarist Vallès.
empress-dowager-cixi: Cixi was born Xingzhen of the Yehe Nara clan on 29 November 1835, probably in Beijing. Her father, Huizheng, belonged to the Bordered Blue Banner and held the title of third class duke. In 1851 she was among 61 candidates presented for selection as wives of the Xianfeng Emperor, and she was chosen as a concubine. She entered the Forbidden City on 26 June 1852 as a consort of the sixth rank, styled Noble Lady Lan, and in 1856 she gave birth to the emperor's son, Zaichun.

When Xianfeng died in 1861 her son became the Tongzhi Emperor, and she became co-empress dowager with his widow, Empress Dowager Ci'an. While the court waited at Rehe for an auspicious time to carry the coffin to Beijing, she conspired with officials and imperial relatives, and the two empresses ousted the eight regents the late emperor had appointed. Ruling from behind the curtain, they issued edicts for the boy emperor and changed his regnal title from Qixiang to Tongzhi. Cixi oversaw the Tongzhi Restoration, rejecting Western political institutions while supporting technological and military modernisation.

After Tongzhi died without a male heir she installed her nephew as the Guangxu Emperor; Ci'an remained co-regent until her death in 1881. After China's defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War, Guangxu launched the Hundred Days' Reform in June 1898 under the influence of Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. Cixi stepped in to stop it and placed him under house arrest for the rest of his life.

In 1900 she backed the Boxers and declared war on the Western powers, which led to the occupation of Beijing by the Eight-Nation Alliance and her flight to Xi'an. She returned in January 1902 and sponsored the New Policies, a programme more radical than the one she had stopped in 1898, including the abolition of the examination system in 1905. She died on 15 November 1908, a day after Guangxu, and was succeeded by her chosen heir, his nephew Puyi. Her tomb at Zunhua, Hebei, was looted in July 1928 by troops under Sun Dianying.

The widely held view is that she was a despot who contributed to China's slide into chaos and revolution, while some revisionist historians argue that she was scapegoated for structural problems and credit her with pragmatic reform.
empress-gi: Empress Gi was born in Haengju, in modern Goyang, in Goryeo, to a lower-ranked aristocratic family of bureaucrats. Her father was Ki Cha-o, and her maternal great-grandmother was Princess Consort Im of the Jangheung Im clan, a prominent Goryeo family. In 1333 she was among the teenage concubines sent to the Yuan court; the Goryeo king had to supply a certain number of young girls every three years, and marrying Goryeo women was considered prestigious. She was skilled at dancing, conversation, singing, poetry and calligraphy and quickly became the favourite concubine of Toghon Temür, who spent far more time with her than with his first empress, Danashiri.

Danashiri was executed on 22 July 1335 in a purge after the rebellion of her brother Tangqishi. When Toghon Temür tried to raise Gi to secondary wife, which went against the practice of taking secondary wives only from Mongol clans, opposition at court forced him to back down. Bayan, who held the real power in the Yuan, opposed it, as did the Empress Dowager, who thought her cunning. After Gi gave birth to a son, Ayushiridara, in 1339, whom the emperor chose as his successor, she was named secondary wife in 1340, and she became secondary empress that year after Bayan was purged.

As Toghon Temür lost interest in governing, Gi exercised power. Her brother Ki Ch'ŏl was appointed commander of the Mongol Eastern Field Headquarters, making him in effect the real ruler of Goryeo. Her son was designated Crown Prince in 1353, and she used the eunuch Park Bul-hwa as her agent in a campaign to make the emperor yield the throne to him, until the emperor learned of her aims and grew apart from her. In 1356 King Gongmin of Goryeo exterminated the Gi family in a coup and broke from the Yuan. Gi named Tash Temür as the new king and sent troops, but the Yuan army was defeated trying to cross the Yalu River.

Strife in the capital between supporters and opponents of the Crown Prince ended in 1364 when Bolud Temür occupied it and imprisoned Gi; her son fled to Köke Temür. Köke Temür overthrew Bolud Temür the next year, and Gi tried again to install her son as khagan, in vain. She became primary empress in December 1365, after the death of Bayan Khutugh. When the Yuan dynasty collapsed in 1368 she fled to Yingchang, in what is now Inner Mongolia, was soon captured, and died in 1369, a year before her husband. Her son became Biligtü Khan, an emperor of the Northern Yuan. She has been portrayed in the television series Shin Don in 2005 and Empress Ki in 2013-2014.
enabling-act-of-1933: Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933 and at once asked President Paul von Hindenburg to dissolve the Reichstag, with an election set for 5 March. On 27 February the Reichstag building caught fire. Hitler accused the communists of arson as part of a plot to overthrow the government and persuaded Hindenburg to enact the Reichstag Fire Decree, which abolished most civil liberties and enabled a violent crackdown, above all on the Communist Party. The Nazis gained five million votes in an election marked by intimidation by the Sturmabteilung (SA) but no absolute majority. On 7 March Hitler told the cabinet he intended an Enabling Act in the form of a constitutional amendment.

The act would let the cabinet enact laws, including ones departing from the constitution, for four years. As an amendment it needed two thirds of a quorum of two thirds of the Reichstag. Communist and some Social Democratic deputies had been arrested, so the Nazis needed the Catholic Centre Party. Its chairman, Ludwig Kaas, agreed on 22 March to support the law in return for assurances about his party, Catholic civil liberties and schools, and affiliated civil servants.

The Reichstag met late on 23 March in the Kroll Opera House, with SA men inside and outside. Its president, Hermann Göring, cut the required quorum from 432 to 378 by not counting the 81 absent Communist deputies. Only the Social Democratic leader Otto Wels spoke against the law, saying that no Enabling Act gave the Nazis the power to destroy ideas that were eternal and indestructible. The tally was 444 in favour and 94 against, all of the opposing votes Social Democratic, which was 83% of the deputies present. The Reichsrat assented that evening and Hindenburg signed.

The act completed the effect of the Reichstag Fire Decree and made Hitler's government a legal dictatorship, though the Weimar Constitution was never formally repealed. The Reichstag became a rubber stamp, and by mid-March the government was sending communists, trade union leaders and other dissidents to Dachau. On 14 July 1933 the Law Against the Formation of Parties made the Nazi Party the only legal party. Powers formally given to the cabinet were in practice exercised by Hitler, and the cabinet did not meet in full after 1938. The law was renewed in 1937 and 1939, when voters faced a single list of approved candidates.
encomienda: The word encomienda comes from the Spanish verb encomendar, to entrust. The institution began in the Middle Ages in the Christian reconquista of Spain, where adelantados were given the right to extract tribute from Muslims and other peasants in areas they conquered and resettled. It resembled a feudal relationship, with military protection traded for tribute or work, and was especially common among the military orders that guarded frontier land. It rewarded those who defeated the Moors, who were exiled in 1492 after the Granada War.

In 1501 Isabella I of Castile declared Native Americans subjects of the Crown and so legally equal to Castilians, which made enslaving them illegal except in narrow cases and allowed encomiendas, a bond reserved for full subjects. The Crown began formally granting encomiendas to conquistadors and officials in 1503, and Nicolás de Ovando set up the system on Hispaniola in 1502.

A grant gave an encomendero a number of people from a community, and Indigenous leaders had to mobilise the tribute and labour, paid in metals, maize, wheat and pork. In return the encomendero was to give instruction in Catholicism and Spanish and protect the people. Natives did not lose their land, which stayed with their communities. In practice conditions often resembled forced labour and slavery, and some encomenderos used extreme punishment and killing against resistance.

Grants were first held in perpetuity. Some women and some Indigenous elites held them: Cortés gave two of Moctezuma's daughters extensive encomiendas, and Inca rulers appointed after the conquest sought them. The system was used in the early Caribbean economies and later in the mining economy of Peru and Upper Peru, where it lasted from the 1530s to the eighteenth century. In 1594 Philip II extended it to the Philippines, with grants to local nobles.

Controversy began early. In 1510 an encomendero named Valenzuela murdered Indigenous leaders who had come to peace talks, and the Taíno cacique Enriquillo rebelled from 1519 to 1533. The Laws of Burgos of 1512-13 tried to regulate treatment. Bartolomé de las Casas, a priest and former encomendero, spent his life lobbying to abolish the system, which he thought enslaved the native people.

The New Laws of 1542 limited grants to two generations, gradually ended the system and repeated the ban on enslaving Native Americans. In Peru, Viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela tried to enforce them and was killed by rebellious encomenderos, while in Mexico Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza declined to apply them, saying he obeyed but did not comply.

After the mid-sixteenth century the Crown-managed repartimiento generally replaced the encomienda: native workers were allotted to settlers for a set period, usually several weeks, in an attempt to reduce abuses. The encomienda was abolished in Chile in 1789.
encyclopedie: The Encyclopédie, ou dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers began as a French translation of Ephraim Chambers's Cyclopaedia, first published in London in 1728. Around 1745 the Englishman John Mills and the German Gottfried Sellius undertook a translation that attracted the Parisian bookseller and printer André Le Breton. A prospectus issued early in 1745 gave the work, for the first time, the title Encyclopédie and promised five volumes by the end of 1748. The project grew far beyond that plan under Denis Diderot and, until 1759, Jean le Rond d'Alembert, and more than 140 people contributed at least one article.

D'Alembert's Preliminary Discourse set out a taxonomy of knowledge, adapted from Francis Bacon, in three branches: memory or history, reason or philosophy, and imagination or poetry. It made human reason, not religious or other authority, the measure of knowledge. The work was the first general encyclopedia to describe the mechanical arts in detail and the first to carry articles by named contributors. Much was compiled from other works, above all the Cyclopaedia.

Contributors included Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu, and the most prolific was Louis de Jaucourt, who wrote 17,266 articles, about a quarter of the whole. They were not a unified party but a varied group of men of letters, physicians, scientists and craftsmen. Articles such as Political Authority traced authority to ordinary people rather than to divinity. On slavery the work was ambivalent: some authors defended it, while Jaucourt attacked the slave trade.

The first edition had a print run of 4,225 copies, well above the average for French books. After the second volume, a royal edict of 1752 briefly suspended it, accusing it of destroying royal authority. In 1759 the government suspended its privilege on the initiative of the Parlement of Paris, but work continued in secret, helped by supporters including the minister Malesherbes and Madame de Pompadour.

By 1789 some 25,000 sets had been sold across Europe in its various editions, though the high price of the first edition, 980 livres, kept it from much of the middle class. Extracts, including the Preliminary Discourse, appeared in several languages. Its prestige helped establish encyclopedia as the general name for such works.
enewetak: Enewetak is a coral atoll of 40 islands in the Pacific, forming a legislative district of the Ralik Chain of the Marshall Islands. Its land area is under 5.85 square kilometres and no point is higher than 5 metres, and the islands surround a deep lagoon 80 kilometres in circumference. The atoll sits on a seamount of basalt formed in the late Cretaceous. Austronesian islanders settled the atoll, which has been inhabited since about 1,000 BCE. The Spanish explorer Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón reached it on 10 October 1529 and named it Los Jardines. The United States government spelled it Eniwetok until 1974.

Japan captured the Marshall Islands in 1914, and the League of Nations mandated them to Japan in 1920. In November 1942 the Japanese built an airfield on Engebi Island, and in January 1944 a brigade arrived to defend the atoll but could not finish its fortifications before the American attack. In the Battle of Eniwetok in February 1944 American forces took the atoll in a five-day amphibious operation. It then became a major naval advance base, with an average of 488 ships present daily in the first half of July 1944.

After the war the atoll came under American control as part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, until the Marshall Islands became independent in 1986. The Americans evacuated the residents many times, often against their will, and used the atoll as part of the Pacific Proving Grounds. Forty-three nuclear tests were fired there from 1948 to 1958. Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb test, took place in late 1952, vaporised the islet of Elugelab and created two new elements, fermium and einsteinium.

A cleanup began in 1977. Over three years the American military mixed more than 80,000 cubic metres of contaminated soil and debris with cement and sealed it in the crater of the nuclear test of 5 May 1958 on Runit Island, under a dome of 358 concrete panels. The United States declared the southern and western islands safe in 1980, and residents returned that year. In 2017 the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that rising seas were seeping into the dome. The Marshall Islands Nuclear Claims Tribunal made an award to the people of Enewetak in 2000, including 107.8 million US dollars for environmental restoration. The atoll had 296 residents in 2021.
engelberg: Engelberg lies in the Uri Alps and is surrounded by several summits. Titlis, at 3,238 metres, rises to the south, while the Walenstöcke and Ruchstock stand to the north and Hahnen and Wissberg to the east. The Engelberger Aa drains the valley into Lake Lucerne and leads up to the Surenen Pass, and the village stands at an average altitude of 1,020 metres.

The municipality is an exclave of the canton of Obwalden, entirely encircled by the cantons of Bern, Nidwalden and Uri. Besides the central village it includes Grafenort, Oberberg and Schwand. The nearest major city is Lucerne.

The place is first mentioned as Engilperc, in 1122, in connection with the founding of the abbey. Before that, local people already used the Alpine pasture of Trüebsee in common. In August 1815, when Nidwalden hesitated to accept the Federal Treaty, Engelberg quickly declared its support. Federal troops entered Nidwalden, which accepted the treaty on 18 August 1815, and Engelberg was incorporated into the canton of Obwalden.

From the middle of the 19th century Engelberg became a holiday destination, known for its mineral water, milk whey and fresh air. Families such as the Cattani, Hess and Odermatt built hotels. A broader road was constructed between 1872 and 1874 and the electric railway from Stansstad opened in 1898. The winter season began in 1903-1904, the Gerschnialpbahn funicular opened in 1913, and a cable car to Ober Trüebsee followed in 1927. The railway was extended to Lucerne in 1964 and the upper section of the Titlis cable car opened in 1967.

Engelberg is a municipality of 4,194 people. The official language is German, and most people speak a local form of Alemannic Swiss German. Tourism provides most of the work, and the village also hosts conferences.

Three sites are Swiss heritage sites of national significance: Engelberg Abbey with its library, archives and music collection, and the mansion and the Holy Cross chapel at Grafenort. The abbey includes a cheese factory and demonstration shop, and the Talmuseum shows the history of the area and Swiss rural life.
engelbert-dollfuss: Engelbert Dollfuss was born on 4 October 1892 into a poor peasant family near Texingtal in Lower Austria, and local parish priests helped to pay for his schooling. He enrolled at the University of Vienna to study theology but changed to law in 1912. In the First World War he was rejected as too short but insisted and was accepted, serving 37 months on the Italian Front with the Tyrolese militia and rising to first lieutenant. After the war he worked for the Lower Austrian Peasants' Union and became an unofficial leader of the Austrian peasantry. He was president of the Federal Railways from 1930 and Federal Minister of Agriculture and Forestry from March 1931.

On 10 May 1932 President Wilhelm Miklas offered him the chancellorship, and he took office on 20 May at the head of a coalition with a majority of one vote. In March 1933 the president of the National Council, Karl Renner, and his two vice presidents resigned in a dispute over voting procedure. Dollfuss declared the council unworkable, and from 7 March he governed by emergency decree under a wartime law of 1917. When the council tried to reconvene on 15 March, police barred the chamber. He banned the Communist Party on 26 May 1933 and the Austrian Nazi Party on 19 June, and in September 1933 formed the Fatherland Front, modelled on Catholic corporatist ideals and Italian fascism.

On 12 February 1934 armed resistance by the Linz Social Democrats to a search for weapons sparked the Austrian Civil War. Police and army used artillery, and the rising collapsed by 15 February with about 350 deaths. The Social Democrats were outlawed. A new constitution took effect on 1 May 1934, creating the Federal State of Austria as a one-party state.

Dollfuss opposed German demands for the unification of Austria with Germany, and Benito Mussolini guaranteed Austrian independence in August 1933. On 25 July 1934 a group of Austrian Nazis, including Otto Planetta and Franz Holzweber, entered the Chancellery in a coup attempt and shot him. The conspirators surrendered after the military threatened to blow up the building, and Planetta and Holzweber were hanged on 31 July. Mussolini mobilised troops on the Austrian border. About 500,000 people attended Dollfuss's burial in Vienna. His successor Kurt Schuschnigg kept the regime until the Anschluss of 1938.
engelbert-ii-of-berg: Engelbert was born in 1185 or 1186 at Schloss Burg, the younger son of Count Engelbert I of Berg and Margarete of Guelders, and was educated at the cathedral school in Cologne. From the age of twelve or thirteen he held the provostship of St. George in Cologne, and from 1199 to 1216 he was cathedral provost, besides other provostships in Cologne, Aachen, Deventer and Zutphen. Elected Bishop of Münster in 1203, he declined because of his age.

Pope Innocent III excommunicated him in 1206 for supporting his cousin, Archbishop Adolf of Altena, on the side of Philip of Swabia against Otto of Brunswick. He was pardoned in 1208 and in 1212, as penance, took part in the Albigensian Crusade. After the Battle of Bouvines in 1214 he gave his allegiance to the future Frederick II.

Elected archbishop on 29 February 1216 and consecrated on 24 September 1217, he found the rights and lands of the archdiocese in bad order and set out to recover them, chiefly against the Dukes of Limburg and their allies of Cleves, with alliances of his own with Brabant and Namur.

When his elder brother, Count Adolf VI of Berg, died on the Fifth Crusade in 1218, Duke Waleran III of Limburg claimed Berg for his son; Engelbert won the county in two feuds, and peace came in 1220. In 1222 he crowned the twelve-year-old Henry King of the Romans at Aachen. He granted town rights to many places, among them Attendorn, Siegen, Werl and Hamm, and it was said that he was more a monarch than a churchman.

His defence of the nuns of Essen Abbey against his cousin Count Frederick of Isenberg, their vogt, who was defrauding them, brought the conflict that ended his life. The attack may have been meant to capture rather than kill him. His body was carried to Cologne on a dung-cart and found to bear forty-seven wounds. The papal legate Cardinal Conrad of Urach declared him a martyr and had him buried in Cologne Cathedral on 24 February 1226, though no formal canonisation followed. In 1618 Archbishop Ferdinand of Bavaria set his feast on 7 November.
engelbrekt-engelbrektsson: Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson owned a mine and ironworks in the mining region of Bergslagen and came from the parish of Norberg in Västmanland. His family had migrated from Germany to Sweden in the 1360s, and its coat of arms shows three half-lilies formed into a triangle. He was dissatisfied with the offences of the Danish local bailiffs and with heavy taxation.

In 1434 he began a rebellion with the support of mine workers and peasants from his home area, in the setting of the Kalmar Union. The anger was directed at the king's bailiff in Västerås, Jösse Eriksson, who was blamed for the distress of the mining men. After Engelbrekt made formal complaints, an inquiry by Eric of Pomerania found Jösse's actions criminal, yet he was not replaced, and a large host of peasants marched to Västerås to protest. The Riksråd intervened peacefully but took no action against the bailiff.

The protests then turned violent and Dalecarlians besieged the bailiff's castle. The Riksråd dismissed Jösse and appointed Hans von Eberstein, but Engelbrekt was not satisfied because Jösse had not been prosecuted. Dalecarlians and Västmanlanders destroyed the castles of Borganäs and Köpingshus, many nobles joined, and the rebellion grew into a force sweeping the country.

In 1435 a Riksdag at Arboga, often considered the first in Sweden, appointed him Rikshövitsman, commander in chief. He could not withstand the nobility, who wanted to exploit the rebellion, and was pushed into the background. In 1436 the nobility and clergy supported Karl Knutsson Bonde, who supplanted him.

On 4 May 1436 Engelbrekt was murdered at Engelbrektsholmen, an islet in Lake Hjälmaren, by the nobleman Måns Bengtsson of the Natt och Dag family, whose father had been in a legal dispute with him over an illegal burning of a ship. Some historians consider it an assassination. He was buried at Saint Nicholas Church in Örebro.

He became a national hero, seen as a protector of the people and an opponent of the Kalmar Union. He himself held no national ideas, which would have been anachronistic, but the revolt gave peasants a voice in Swedish politics. It eroded the unity of the union and led to the expulsion of Danish forces from Sweden. A bronze statue by Carl Gustaf Qvarnström was unveiled in Örebro in 1865.
england: England covers about 62 per cent of the island of Great Britain, together with more than 100 smaller islands, among them the Isle of Wight and the Isles of Scilly. It shares land borders with Scotland to the north and Wales to the west. Most of the landscape is low hills and plains, with uplands in the north and west, including the Pennines, the Lake District and the Cheviot Hills. The highest point is Scafell Pike, at 978 metres. The Severn, at 350 kilometres, is the longest river flowing through England, and the Thames, at 346 kilometres, the longest entirely within it.

The earliest evidence of human presence is that of Homo antecessor, about 780,000 years ago. Humans repopulated the area roughly 11,000 years ago as the ice sheets receded, and Neolithic farmers from the Iberian Peninsula arrived around 4100 BCE. The Beaker culture, from around 2,500 BCE, brought clay vessels and bronze, and monuments such as Stonehenge and Avebury date from this time. The Romans founded the first cities and towns, among them London, Bath, York, Chester and St Albans, and built Hadrian's Wall across the north.

The name England comes from the Old English Englaland, the land of the Angles, a Germanic people who settled in the 5th and 6th centuries. The earliest recorded use, as Engla londe, is in a late-ninth-century Old English translation of Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People. England became a unified state in the 10th century.

After the Norman conquest of 1066 castles such as the Tower of London and Windsor Castle were built, and the University of Oxford was founded in 1096 and the University of Cambridge in 1209. The Kingdom of England, which included Wales after 1535, ceased to be a separate sovereign state on 1 May 1707 under the Acts of Union.

England is governed directly by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and has no devolved parliament of its own, unlike Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. A plan for regional devolution was dropped after the North East rejected it in a 2004 referendum. The population was 56,490,048 in the 2021 census, about 84 per cent of the United Kingdom's, with London as the largest city.

The Industrial Revolution began in 18th-century England, which became the first industrialised nation. The English language, the English legal system and association football originated there, and its parliamentary system has been widely adopted by other nations. The Bank of England was founded in 1694, and the National Health Service began on 5 July 1948, based on the Beveridge Report.
english-channel: The Channel is about 560 kilometres long and covers some 75,000 square kilometres, the smallest of the shallow seas around the continental shelf of Europe. Roman sources called it Oceanus Britannicus, the Ocean of the Britons. The English name comes from Middle English channel, borrowed from Old French chanel, and an Italian map of the mid-fifteenth century may be the first to use it. The French name, la Manche, has been used since at least the 17th century and is usually said to refer to a sleeve. The full Channel formed late in the Pleistocene, when at least two catastrophic glacial lake outburst floods between 450,000 and 180,000 years ago breached the ridge between the Dover and Calais regions.

Remnants of a Mesolithic boatyard have been found on the Isle of Wight, and wheat was traded across the Channel about 8,000 years ago. For nearly a thousand years the sea linked the Celtic Britons with Armorica, and Brittany was founded by British settlers during the Migration Period. The attack on Lindisfarne in 793 is generally taken as the start of the Viking Age, and raiders struck the Channel coast of England, as at Wareham and Portland. From the reign of Elizabeth I English policy aimed to keep any major power from controlling the Dutch and Flemish ports, and the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 began the Royal Navy's rise.

On 25 July 1909 Louis Blériot made the first aeroplane crossing, from Calais to Dover, a sign that the Channel was losing its role as a barrier. In May and June 1940, 338,000 Allied troops were evacuated from Dunkirk in Operation Dynamo, and the Germans failed to win the air supremacy that Operation Sealion, the projected invasion, required.

The Channel is the busiest shipping area in the world, and after collisions in 1971 the first radar-controlled traffic separation scheme was set up at Dover. Crossings have a long record of firsts: a balloon in 1785, a steamship in 1816, and the first observed swim, by Captain Matthew Webb on 24 and 25 August 1875, in 21 hours 45 minutes. Gertrude Ederle was the first woman to swim it, in 1926. The English shore is more populous than the French.
english-civil-war: The wars broke out in 1642, less than forty years after the death of Elizabeth I, who was succeeded by James VI of Scotland as James I of England, creating the first personal union of the two kingdoms. Accustomed to a weak parliament in Scotland, James was affronted by the constraints the English Parliament tried to place on him in return for money. His extravagance forced him to seek income outside Parliament. The English war was fought primarily over the proper balance of power between Parliament and Charles I. The Royalists held the countryside, the shires and the less developed north and west, and Parliament the industrial centres, ports and richer regions of the south and east.

In early January 1642, a few days after failing to capture five members of the House of Commons, Charles left the London area for the north. On 1 June the Lords and Commons approved the Nineteen Propositions, in which Parliament sought a larger share of power, and the king rejected them before the month was out. The first war ended in June 1646 with Royalist defeat and the king in custody. On 28 December 1647 he made a secret treaty with the Scots, the Engagement, under which they would invade England on his behalf, and Royalist uprisings and a Scottish invasion followed in 1648.

In December 1648 the Army carried out Pride's Purge, arresting 45 members of Parliament and keeping 146 out of the chamber. The remaining Rump Parliament set up a High Court of Justice to try Charles for treason, and Fairfax, a constitutional monarchist, refused to take part and resigned as head of the army. Oliver Cromwell landed at Dublin on 15 August 1649 to quell an alliance of Irish Confederates and English Royalists, whom his forces had already beaten at the Battle of Rathmines.

In 1650 Charles II was crowned King of Scotland, in return for agreeing to a Presbyterian church in both kingdoms, and the Anglo-Scottish war ended with a Parliamentarian victory at Worcester on 3 September 1651. Ireland and Scotland were incorporated into the Commonwealth, an arrangement that proved unpopular and was dissolved at the Restoration of 1660. Figures for casualties are unreliable, but a conservative estimate is some 190,000 dead out of a population of about five million. The wars popularised the terms Cavalier and Roundhead and brought a great growth in pamphlets and newsbooks, and the outcome set England and Scotland on course towards a parliamentary monarchy.
english-language: English is a West Germanic language of the Indo-European family that emerged in early medieval England. It is named after the Angles, one of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain after the end of Roman rule. Old English developed from West Germanic dialects originally spoken along the coasts of Frisia, Lower Saxony and southern Jutland by the Angles, Saxons and Jutes. It was spoken from c. 450 to c. 1150. From the 5th century the Anglo-Saxons settled Britain as the Roman economy and administration collapsed, and by the 7th century Old English had become dominant, replacing the Common Brittonic and British Latin previously spoken.

Old English was divided into two Anglian dialects, Mercian and Northumbrian, and two Saxon dialects, Kentish and West Saxon. Through the influence of the kingdom of Wessex and the educational reforms of King Alfred in the 9th century, West Saxon became the standard written variety, and the epic poem Beowulf is written in it. Early inscriptions used runes, and by the 7th century a Latin alphabet had been adopted.

Late Old English borrowed some grammar and core vocabulary from Old Norse. Middle English emerged in England under Norman control and borrowed vocabulary extensively from French dialects, the source of approximately 28 per cent of Modern English words, and from Latin, the source of another 28 per cent. Middle English then transformed, in part through the Great Vowel Shift, into Modern English. Speakers of the 21st century cannot understand Old English without special training.

English is the most spoken language in the world, primarily because of the global influence of the British Empire and the rise of the United States, though it is only the third-most spoken native language, after Mandarin Chinese and Spanish. It is the official language, or one of the official languages, of 57 sovereign states and 30 dependent territories. It is a co-official language of the United Nations and the European Union, and the de facto lingua franca of diplomacy, science, technology and international trade. Its grammar and phonology remain Germanic, as does most of its everyday vocabulary.
enheduanna: Enheduanna was the daughter of Sargon of Akkad, founder of the Akkadian Empire, who conquered Sumer and brought all of Lower Mesopotamia under his control. A few documents from her own lifetime show she was a historical person: a fragmentary alabaster disk with an inscription in her name and a relief that probably shows her, and cylinder seals belonging to her attendants, among them a hairdresser, Ilum-palil, and a steward, Adda. Her name is usually translated as The high-priestess is the Ornament of Heaven. High priestesses probably took a new name on entering office, so it would not be her birth name.

Her father, or possibly one of her brothers, appointed her high priestess of Nanna, the moon god and patron deity of Ur. The office was the most important in the Sumerian clergy and often carried heavy political weight. The priestess was regarded as the god's earthly spouse and took part in running the sanctuary and in rituals such as purification rites and food offerings.
