The appointment probably aimed to bind the conquered Sumerian south to the Akkadian dynasty.

Toward the end of the reign of Naram-Sin a certain Lugal-Ane came to power in Ur. As reconstructed from hints in her hymn Nin me šara, he demanded her confirmation of his rule. She refused, lost her office and was driven from the city, finding refuge probably at Ĝirsu. Naram-Sin put down the rebellion, and she probably returned to Ur. Later daughters of kings held the office, beginning with Enmenanna, the daughter of Naram-Sin.

Works attributed to her include The Exaltation of Inanna (Nin me šara), a hymn of 154 lines of which around one hundred copies are known, a Hymn to Inanna, the Sumerian Temple Hymns and two hymns to Nanna. Naming an author is rare in Mesopotamian literature, which is mostly anonymous.

Scholars debate whether she wrote them. None of the manuscripts dates from her lifetime. Most come from the Old Babylonian period, about six centuries later, and are in a later form of Sumerian. William W. Hallo and Åke Sjöberg asserted her authorship, while Miguel Civil and Jeremy Black doubted it. Her existence was rediscovered in 1927, when Sir Leonard Woolley excavated the Giparu at Ur and found the disk.
eniac: In June 1941 firing tables for United States Army artillery were being computed by graduate students using desk calculators and differential analyzers, under the supervision of John Mauchly. He began to explore electronics as a way of speeding the work and partnered with the research associate J. Presper Eckert. In August 1942 Mauchly proposed a fully electronic calculating machine, and the Army gave the University of Pennsylvania a six-month research contract for $61,700. The construction contract was signed on 5 June 1943, and secret work began at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering under the code name Project PX. Herman Goldstine persuaded the Army to fund the project and oversaw it, and John Brainerd was principal investigator.

ENIAC was a large modular machine made of panels with different functions. Twenty of them were accumulators, each able to add, subtract and hold a ten-digit decimal number. It could also branch according to the sign of a result, which was essential to its versatility. By the end of its operation in 1955 it contained 18,000 vacuum tubes, 7,200 crystal diodes and about five million hand-soldered joints. It weighed more than 30 short tons, was about 100 feet long and consumed 150 kilowatts. Input came from an IBM card reader and output from a card punch, and in 1953 a 100-word magnetic-core memory was added.

Several female mathematicians did most of the programming: Jean Jennings, Marlyn Wescoff, Ruth Lichterman, Betty Snyder, Frances Bilas and Kay McNulty. Tubes failed almost every day at first and left the machine unusable about half the time, mostly during warm-up and cool-down. Engineers reduced the failures to about one tube every two days.

Construction was complete in May 1945, and the machine first did practical work on 10 December 1945. Its first program was a study of the feasibility of the thermonuclear weapon. It was formally dedicated at the University of Pennsylvania on 15 February 1946 and called a Giant Brain by the press, at a cost of $487,000. The Army Ordnance Corps accepted it in July 1946. In 1947 it was transferred to Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland, where it operated continuously until 1955. In 1946 Mauchly and Eckert resigned from the university and formed the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation.
enki: Enki was first worshipped in Sumer. Early sources of the Fāra period associate him with Eridu, one of the oldest cities of Sumer, which was regarded as his home from the Early Dynastic Period. His temple there was the E-Abzû, the House of the Abzû, and he was called king of the Abzû and king of Eridu. He was already a major deity at the time of the earliest written sources.

Ea was originally a separate god, whose name is of unknown, possibly Semitic origin and first appears in personal names of the Old Akkadian period. The two were already syncretized in parts of Babylonia in the second half of the third millennium BCE, though it is uncertain when they were fully equated. The name Enki is usually translated as Lord of the Earth, but not all scholars accept this.

Enki was worshipped as the god of wisdom, crafts, fresh subterranean waters, springs and, by extension, incantations and magic, and as a creator. He was believed to reside in the Abzû, imagined as a region of fresh water beneath the earth. His symbols included the goat-fish, the ram-headed staff and the turtle. He is one of the few Mesopotamian deities with a recognisable iconography: streams of water flow from his body, often with fish in them, a feature first attested in the Old Akkadian Period.

His wife was Damgalnuna, and their children included Marduk, the patron god of Babylon, and Asalluhi, a god of incantations later merged with Marduk. His attendant was Isimud, who is shown with two faces. The sky god An is named as his father in several sources.

His cult was particularly influential in the Ur III and Old Babylonian periods, when he formed a triad at the top of the pantheon with Anu and Enlil, and was attested in almost all important cities of Babylonia. It spread to Mari early in the second millennium BCE, and into Hurrian and Hittite religion in Anatolia, where he could be invoked as a divine witness to treaties. With the rise of Babylon and Marduk his cult lost importance, but he remained a major god of first millennium BCE Babylonia.

In myth he is a crafty counsellor who solves difficult problems. Tradition regarded him as the creator of humankind from clay. In Atra-hasis he works with the mother goddess to create people and later opposes Enlil's attempts to destroy them in the flood. Berossos identified Ea with Kronos.
enlil: Enlil was a Mesopotamian god associated with wind, air, earth and storms. He is first attested as chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon and was later worshipped by Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians and Hurrians. His name combines the Sumerian EN, lord, with LÍL, whose meaning is disputed: it has been read as wind, as a spirit felt as a stirring of the air, or as a Semitic loanword. He was sometimes called Nunamnir and Kur-gal, the Great Mountain, and his symbol was a horned cap of up to seven pairs of ox-horns. With An and Enki he formed a triad linked with the fixed stars, his being those of the northern sky.

His main centre of worship was the Ekur, meaning Mountain House, at Nippur, believed to have been built by Enlil himself and to be the mooring-rope of heaven and earth. Priests tended his cult statue and laid out food as his daily meal. Rulers from all over Sumer travelled to Nippur to be legitimized and gave land and treasure to the temple. Nippur was the only Sumerian city-state that never built a palace, to show that Enlil was its king. Even when Marduk had superseded him, Babylonian kings still went to Nippur to seek recognition of their right to rule.

In the Sumerian account of creation Enlil is the son of An, the sky, and Ki, the earth, and separated them. The poem Enlil and Ninlil tells how he seduced Ninlil in several guises, and from these unions came the moon-god Nanna and the gods Nergal, Ninazu and Enbilulu. In the Akkadian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh he sends the flood because humans made too much noise and kept him from sleep. He was regarded as inventor of the mattock and patron of agriculture. His standing declined after Hammurabi conquered Sumer. After the Elamites attacked Nippur in 1230 BCE his cult declined, and about a hundred years later his role as head of the pantheon passed to Marduk.
enlil-bani: Enlil-bani was the 10th king of the 1st Dynasty of Isin, and the Ur-Isin king list gives him a reign of 24 years. According to two variant copies of a chronicle, a certain Ikūn-pî-Ištar ruled for six months or a year between Erra-imitti and Enlil-bani, and another chronicle that might have said more about his origins is too broken to read. The story of the gardener and the substitute king comes from the Chronicle of Early Kings, which tells that Erra-imitti died while eating hot porridge.

In a long inscription he claimed to have established justice in Nippur and Isin, to have lowered the barley tax from one-fifth to one-tenth and to have limited the service of the muškēnum to four days a month. His hold on Nippur was brief, as control of the city passed back and forth between Isin and Larsa, and Uruk broke away during his reign. As his power waned he may have had the chronicle edited to give his accession the colour of a tale, covering what may have been an ordinary usurpation.

He rebuilt the wall of Isin, recording the work on commemorative cones and naming it Enlil-bāni-išdam-kīn, "Enlil-bāni is firm as to foundation". He built the é-ur-gi7-ra, the dog house, temple of Ninisina, a palace, and temples for Nintinugga, for Sud, the goddess of Šuruppak, and for Ninibgal. He also delivered to Nippur two large copper statues for Ningal that Iddin-Dagān had made 117 years earlier but never sent.

A medical text in the Library of Ashurbanipal, on the condition "when a man's brain contains fire", ends with a note that its salves and poultices were left by Enlil-muballiṭ, sage of Nippur, in the second year of Enlil-bāni. Two hymns may be addressed to him, and two foundation nails record that he built or rebuilt a temple to the goddess Annunitum.
enmebaragesi: Enmebaragesi was the penultimate king of the first dynasty of Kish and, like his son and successor Aga, reigned at a time when Kish had hegemony over Sumer. His name is first written Mebarasi, and the prefix En is an honorific title that was not part of the original name. Interpretations of the rest differ: it can be read as Priest who permeates the throne or as Crown fit for a ruler. He is the earliest ruler on the Sumerian King List whose name is attested directly from archaeology.

The dating of his reign has been debated, with proposals ranging from the beginning of Early Dynastic I (c. 2900 to c. 2800 BCE) to Early Dynastic IIIa (c. 2600 BCE). Most scholars favour c. 2600 BCE, while others place the inscriptions slightly earlier, at c. 2700 BCE. Four inscriptions carry the name, but only one gives the title king: a vessel fragment of unknown provenance, in the Baghdad Museum, reading Mebarasi, King of Kish. Gianni Marchesi and Niccolò Marchetti propose that the other three refer to a non-royal person of the same name.

The Sumerian King List gives him a reign of 900 years and records him as the one who carried away the weapons of the land of Elam. It credits Kish with hegemony over northern Babylonia, including Nippur, Isin and Eresh, and large parts of the Diyala Region. A later tradition of Kishite expansion into Susiana and the Iranian plateau appears in an inscription of the Early Dynastic II king Enna-il. The Tummal Inscription, an Old Babylonian tablet, says that Enmebaragesi built the House of Enlil at Nippur and that his son Aga made the Tummal pre-eminent.

A version of the King List was once read as saying that Dumuzid the Fisherman of Uruk captured Enmebaragesi, but a newer translation reverses this: Enmebaragesi captured Dumuzid, subjugated Uruk and made Gilgamesh his vassal-king. Later literature tells it differently. The poem Gilgamesh and Aga has Aga of Kish besiege Uruk, and a praise poem of the Ur III king Shulgi credits Gilgamesh with defeating Enmebaragesi himself. One suggestion is that Enmebaragesi was put in the place of Aga because defeating the powerful founder of Kish's hegemony made Gilgamesh seem mightier.
enmerkar: Enmerkar is dated in modern references to about 2750 BCE and is credited in literary sources with building the city of Uruk and a reign of 420 years. The tradition of Enmerkar as founder of Uruk seems to go back to the Jemdet Nasr period (3100-2900 BCE), when a lexical list names him and his wife Enmerkarzi as builders of a town who made brick and dug irrigation canals.

Unlike his successors Lugalbanda and Gilgamesh, who appear in god lists and received offerings in the Ur III period, he does not seem to have been deified, and was remembered as the founder and first king of Uruk. Naram-Sin of Akkad later blamed him for failing to record his experience on a stele, and so for a defeat and the devastation of Akkad.

The Matter of Aratta is a group of four Sumerian poems about how Enmerkar won supremacy over the city of Aratta by nonmilitary means, to gain the favour of the goddess Inanna. The cycle began in the Ur III period (2112-2004 BCE) and aimed to present the Third Dynasty of Ur as heirs of Uruk's ancient rulers.

In Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, the king wants precious metals and stones that only Aratta has. On Inanna's advice he sends a messenger with a demand, and the lord of Aratta answers with three riddles, such as bringing a sceptre made of no existing material, which Enmerkar solves. When the messenger complains that the messages are too long to remember, Enmerkar pats clay and puts words on it like a tablet; the text says there had been no writing on clay before. In the Lugalbanda poems Enmerkar besieges Aratta, and his warchief Lugalbanda is left ill in a cave.

Scholars have asked whether the narratives have a historical basis, citing an archaic tablet from Uruk with the title Lord of Aratta. The Assyriologist Dina Katz argues that a historical explanation undermines the narrative's ideological purpose, and that the poem claiming writing as the invention of the founder of the first Sumerian city after the flood is a political and ethnic statement. A much later Greek legend told by Aelian names a king of Babylon, Euechoros, as grandfather of Gilgamos, and some scholars identify him with Enmerkar. David Rohl has proposed parallels with the biblical Nimrod, ruler of Erech, noting that the suffix kar in Enmerkar means hunter.
enmetena: Enmetena, also written Entemena, re-established Lagash as a power in Sumer. His reign lasted at least 19 years, and his personal god was Shul-utula. He controlled the cities of southern Mesopotamia from Badtibira to Uruk. One of his inscriptions records that he built or rebuilt the E-mush, a beloved temple at Badtibira, for the god Lugalemush, and set free the citizens of Uruk, Larsa and Badtibira.

His war with Il, king of Umma, is told on a foundation cone now in the Louvre, which recounts one of the earliest recorded border conflicts, between Lagash and Umma in the Early Dynastic III period. Il, it says, diverted water from the boundary channels of the gods Ningirsu and Nanshe and declared that the channels were his; but the gods Enlil and Ninhursang did not give them to him. Il was defeated, with the help of Lugal-kinishe-dudu of Uruk, successor to Enshakushanna. A second text of the same content, the Net cylinder, is in the Yale Babylonian Collection.

A clay nail found at Girsu commemorates the alliance with Lugal-kinishe-dudu, in which the two rulers 'established brotherhood'; it is the oldest known mention of a peace treaty between two kings. A statue of Enmetena in diorite, 76 centimetres tall, shows him in the dress of a devotee, with hands clasped at the chest, one of the earliest statues of a known king from Mesopotamia; it was stolen from the National Museum of Iraq in May 2003 and returned in 2010. A silver tripod vase he dedicated to Ningirsu, with a frieze of lions devouring ibexes and deer, is in the Louvre.

Foundation tablets in his name record his temple building. One of them says that he instituted liberty in Lagash, restored the child to its mother and the mother to her child and cancelled interest; it is the first known use of the word ama-gi, here translated as liberty. A plaque of bitumen bearing the name of Dudu, a priest of Ningirsu in his time, shows the eagle of Lagash holding two lions.
ennis: Ennis lies in the mid-west of Ireland on the River Fergus, north of where the river widens and enters the Shannon Estuary. Its Irish name, Inis, means island or river meadow, and it is short for Inis Cluana Rámhfhada, the island of the long rowing meadow, a reference to its position between two courses of the Fergus. The river is a well-known trout and salmon fishery, and at one time small sailing boats came up from the Shannon to berth in the centre of the town at Woodquay. The town centre consists of medieval narrow streets and laneways.

The history of Ennis is closely linked with the O'Brien dynasty, descendants of Brian Boru. In the 12th century the O'Briens, Kings of Thomond, left their seat of power in Limerick, and in 1210 they built Clonroad Fort as a royal residence on the Fergus. In 1240, after the arrival of Franciscan monks, King Donnchadh O'Brien ordered an extensive church built and donated it to the friars. The friary became a centre of theological study, with 600 students and 350 friars by 1375. Officially closed in 1540, it continued in a limited way until 1690, the last school of Catholic theology to survive the Reformation.

When Clare became a county in 1586 under Elizabeth I, Ennis was chosen as its administrative centre because of its central location and its association with the Earls of Thomond. It was granted the right to hold fairs and markets in 1610. Because it grew from a monastery and not a stronghold, it never had town walls and developed as a place of commerce, a market town and later a small manufacturing centre whose goods went by river to Clarecastle for shipping abroad. Textiles, milling, brewing and distilling were local industries. The Famine of 1845 and its aftermath cut the population by over 20 per cent through famine, disease and emigration.

Ennis is the county town of County Clare and its largest town, and a regional hub with the offices of Clare County Council. The Cathedral of Saint Peter and Saint Paul stands on the edge of the old town centre, and a market is held in the market square every Saturday. The West Clare Railway, a narrow-gauge line that ran from Ennis to the villages of the West Clare coast, closed in 1961. Ennis has been a centre of Irish traditional music and has hosted the Fleadh Nua each May since 1974. In 1997 it became Ireland's first Information Age Town.
enniskillen: Enniskillen is the largest town in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland, in the middle of the county between the Upper and Lower sections of Lough Erne. Its name comes from the Irish Inis Ceithleann, the island of Ceithlenn. Ceithlenn is a figure in Irish mythology who may have been a goddess, and local legend says she was wounded in battle by an arrow and tried to swim the river Erne, which surrounds the island, but never reached the far side. The name has been anglicised in many ways over the centuries, among them Iniskellen, Inishkillen and Iniskillin.

The oldest building is Enniskillen Castle, built by Hugh Maguire the Hospitable, who died in 1428, as the stronghold of a junior branch of the Maguires. The first watergate was built around 1580 by Cú Chonnacht Maguire. The English wanted the castle to support their plans for control of Ulster, and in February 1594 a force led by a Captain Dowdall captured it. Maguire then besieged it and defeated a relieving force at the Battle of the Ford of the Biscuits. He held the castle from 1595 to 1598, and the English finally took it in 1607.

The capture was followed by the Plantation of Ulster, in which native Irish lands were seized and given to planters loyal to the Crown. William Cole, originally from Devon, was appointed by James I to build an English settlement there in 1612. He became constable, strengthened the castle wall and built a house on the old foundation. The first Protestant parish church was built on the hilltop in 1627, and by 1630 the town had about 180 inhabitants, mostly English and Scottish settlers. Permanent bridges were not installed before 1688.

In the conflict that followed the ousting of James II by William III, Enniskillen and Derry were the focus of Williamite resistance in Ireland, including the nearby Battle of Newtownbutler. Enniskillen was the last town to fall before the Siege of Derry. As a result it became a garrison as well as a market town, and two regiments of the British Army were founded there, the Inniskilling Dragoons and the Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers.

Enniskillen is the county town of Fermanagh and had a population of 14,086 at the 2021 census. Its castle, Castle Coole and the nearby Florence Court are among its historic buildings, and St Macartin's Cathedral dates from 1840. In November 1987 a bombing at a Remembrance Day ceremony killed 11 people.
ennius: Very little is reliably known about the life of Quintus Ennius. His contemporaries hardly mentioned him, and much that is related may have been drawn from references to himself in his fragmentary writings. He was born in Rudiae, near modern Lecce, a partly Hellenised town founded by the Messapians, and could speak Greek and Latin as well as Oscan, his native language. According to Aulus Gellius he said this gave him three hearts, Greek, Oscan and Latin. He is also reported to have claimed descent from Messapus, a traditional king of his district. Some lines of the Annales suggest that he opened it by recalling a dream in which Homer told him his spirit had been reborn in Ennius.

Ennius first appears in public life in middle age, serving as a centurion in the Second Punic War. In Sardinia in 204 BCE he is said to have attracted the attention of Cato the Elder, who took him to Rome. There he taught Greek and adapted Greek plays for a livelihood, and his poems won the friendship of leading men, among them Scipio Africanus and Fulvius Nobilior, whom he accompanied on the Aetolian campaign of 189 BCE. He made the capture of Ambracia the subject of a play and of an episode of the Annales. Through the influence of Nobilior's son Quintus he obtained Roman citizenship. He lived simply on the Aventine Hill with the poet Caecilius Statius.

Ennius wrote tragedies and comedies in Greek and Roman style, along with minor works including the Epicharmus, Euhemerus, Hedyphagetica and Saturae. His chief work, the Annales, was a historical epic in fifteen books, later expanded to eighteen, covering Roman history from the fall of Troy to the censorship of Cato the Elder in 184 BCE. It was the first Latin poem to use the dactylic hexameter of Greek epic, which became the standard metre of the genre in Latin. It became a school text until the Aeneid of Virgil supplanted it, and about 600 lines survive.

Ennius died at about the age of 70, after producing his tragedy Thyestes, and wrote lines for his own bust: let no one weep for him, since he still lives, passing to and fro through the mouths of men.
enoch-sontonga: Enoch Mankayi Sontonga, a Xhosa, was born around 1873 in the city of Uitenhage in the Eastern Cape Colony. He trained as a teacher at the Lovedale Institution and then worked for eight years as a teacher and choirmaster at the Methodist Mission school in Nancefield, near Johannesburg. He married Diana Mgqibisa, the daughter of a minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and they had a son. She died in 1939.

The first verse and chorus of Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika, meaning God Bless Africa, were composed in 1897 and were originally intended as a school anthem. Some sources say he wrote the tune in the same year. The hymn was first sung in public in 1899, at the ordination of Reverend Mboweni, the first Tsonga Methodist minister. The Xhosa poet Samuel Mqhayi later wrote a further seven verses. Sontonga died on 18 April 1905 of gastroenteritis and a perforated appendix, a common cause of death at the time because of unsafe drinking water.

The song became better known after the choir of John Langalibalele Dube's Ohlange Institute used it, including at the meeting of the South African Native National Congress in 1912. The African National Congress adopted it as its official closing anthem in 1925. It was recorded in London in 1923 and published by the Lovedale Press in 1927. Tanganyika adopted a Swahili version as its anthem in 1961, Zambia took it in 1964, and Botswana and Zimbabwe used versions from 1980 until 1994, Zimbabwe's in Shona as Ishe Komborera Afrika.

For many years the site of his grave was unknown. It was located in the early 1990s in the Native Christian section of the Braamfontein cemetery; it had been listed under the name Enoch rather than Sontonga. On 24 September 1996 the grave was declared a national monument, and President Nelson Mandela unveiled a memorial there and posthumously bestowed the Order of Meritorious Service (Gold) on him.
enomoto-takeaki: Enomoto Takeaki was born on 5 October 1836 into a samurai family in the direct service of the Tokugawa clan, in the Shitaya district of Edo. He began learning Dutch in the 1850s and, after Commodore Matthew Perry forced the opening of Japan in 1854, studied at the shogunate's Naval Training Center in Nagasaki and at the Tsukiji Warship Training Center in Edo. At the age of 26 he was sent to the Netherlands to study western naval warfare and to procure western technologies. He stayed in Europe from 1862 to 1867 and became fluent in Dutch and English.

He returned on the Kaiyō Maru, a steam warship the shogunate had bought from the Netherlands. In Europe he had realised that the telegraph would be an important means of communication, and he began planning a line between Edo and Yokohama. At 31 he was made Kaigun Fukusōsai, the second highest rank in the Tokugawa Navy.

After Edo surrendered in 1868 during the Boshin War to forces loyal to the Satchō Alliance, Enomoto refused to hand over his warships. He escaped to Hakodate in Hokkaido with the rest of the Tokugawa Navy, eight steam warships and the strongest fleet in Japan, together with a few French military advisers led by Jules Brunet. He hoped to create an independent country there under the Tokugawa family, but the Meiji government refused to accept the partition of Japan. On 27 January 1869 the Tokugawa loyalists declared the Republic of Ezo and elected him president. Meiji forces defeated his fleet in the naval battle of Hakodate in May 1869, and after the Battle of Hakodate on 27 June 1869 the republic collapsed.

Enomoto was arrested, accused of high treason and imprisoned. The Meiji leaders, largely at the insistence of Kuroda Kiyotaka, saw that his talents and knowledge could be useful, and pardoned him in 1872. He became one of the few former Tokugawa loyalists to join the new ruling elite, dominated by men from Chōshū and Satsuma. He was made vice-admiral in 1874 and sent to Russia the next year to negotiate the Treaty of St. Petersburg, and in 1885 he helped Itō Hirobumi conclude the Convention of Tientsin with Qing China.

Enomoto became Navy Minister in 1880 and Japan's first Minister of Communications (1885 to 1888). He was also Minister of Education (1889 to 1890), Foreign Minister (1891 to 1892) and Minister of Agriculture and Commerce (1894 to 1897), and was made a viscount in 1887. He promoted Japanese emigration to the Pacific and to South and Central America, setting up an emigration section in the Foreign Ministry in 1891. He died in 1908 at the age of 72, and his grave is at the temple of Kisshō-ji in Bunkyō-ku, Tokyo.
enrico-dandolo: Enrico Dandolo was born in Venice around 1107, a member of the prominent Dandolo family and the son of the jurist Vitale Dandolo. His uncle, also named Enrico Dandolo, was patriarch of Grado. Little is known of him before his father's death in 1174, since Vitale lived into his nineties and his sons were not emancipated until then. His first important political role came in the crisis of 1171 and 1172 between Venice and the Byzantine Empire. He made trips to Constantinople as a ducal legate in 1183 and 1184, and in 1184 the emperor Andronicus I agreed to release imprisoned Venetians and restore their quarter.

Dandolo became doge on 1 June 1192, after Orio Mastropiero abdicated, as the second doge chosen by a council of forty electors. He was then old and blind. The commonly given birth year rests on Marino Sanuto the Younger, writing three centuries later, who stated that Dandolo was eighty-five at his election. How he lost his sight is not known: the Chronicle of Novgorod says the Byzantines blinded him, while Thomas F. Madden argues that a blow to the head between 1174 and 1176 caused cortical blindness. In 1194 he reformed the Venetian coinage, introducing the silver grosso, the first nearly pure silver, high-denomination coin minted in western Europe in over five centuries.

In 1202 envoys of the Fourth Crusade asked Venice for a fleet. The agreement set four silver marks for each knight and horse, with Venetians promising fifty armed galleys in return for half the spoils. The Crusaders could not pay the full 85,000 marks and still owed 34,000, so Dandolo proposed that they repay it from the spoils and help Venice retake Zara. Zara fell on 24 November 1202, and the Venetians were excommunicated, which Dandolo kept secret. The Crusaders then agreed to restore Alexius Angelus to the Byzantine throne, and Constantinople was conquered and sacked on 12 April 1204. Dandolo declined the imperial crown, accepted the title of despot, and Venice received three-eighths of the Byzantine Empire in the Partitio Romaniae.

Dandolo died in May or June 1205, reportedly from an infection caused by a hernia, and was buried in the Hagia Sophia. Accounts differ on what became of his tomb: the Byzantines are said to have thrown his remains into the Bosporus in 1261, or Mehmed II to have had Venetian tombs broken after 1453. His acquisitions lasted only until the collapse of the Latin Empire in 1261. His granddaughter Anna Dandolo married Stefan Nemanjić of Serbia in 1217, making him an ancestor of much of the later Nemanjić dynasty.
enrico-de-nicola: Enrico De Nicola was born in Naples and became known as a penal lawyer, graduating in law at the University of Naples in 1896. A Liberal, he was first elected a deputy in 1909. He was Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies in the Giolitti government from November 1913 to March 1914, and for the Treasury in the Orlando cabinet in 1919. On 26 June 1920 he was elected speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, an office he held until January 1924. With the advent of fascism he retired from political life. King Victor Emmanuel III appointed him senator in 1929, but he refused to take his seat.

De Nicola returned to his law practice and took an interest in politics again only after the fall of Italian Fascism. After Benito Mussolini fell from power in 1943, the king tried to separate the monarchy from the Fascist regime, and De Nicola was perhaps the most influential mediator in the transition that followed. Victor Emmanuel later abdicated, Umberto became king as Umberto II, and a referendum was won by the republicans. The Constituent Assembly elected De Nicola Provisional Head of State on 28 June 1946 with 80 percent of the votes at the first round. Giulio Andreotti recalled that he was modest and hesitated over accepting.

On 25 June 1947 he resigned, citing health reasons, but the Constituent Assembly re-elected him the next day. After the Italian Constitution took effect he was formally named President of the Italian Republic on 1 January 1948. He declined to stand in the first constitutional election that May, in which Luigi Einaudi was elected. In 1948 De Nicola became a senator for life as a former head of state, and he was later elected President of the Senate and of the Constitutional Court. He died at Torre del Greco, in the province of Naples, on 1 October 1959. He was unmarried and had no children.
enrico-fermi: Enrico Fermi was born on 29 September 1901 in Rome, the third child of Alberto Fermi, a division head in the Ministry of Railways, and Ida de Gattis, an elementary school teacher. As a boy he built electric motors with his brother Giulio, who died during an operation in 1915. At a market in Campo de' Fiori he found a 900-page Latin physics book, and with his friend Enrico Persico he built gyroscopes. He finished high school in July 1918, having skipped a year, learned German to read scientific papers, and took first place in the entrance examination of the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa.

In 1926, at 24, Fermi won one of the first three chairs in theoretical physics in Italy, at the Sapienza University of Rome. His team there, which included Edoardo Amaldi, Emilio Segrè and Franco Rasetti, was nicknamed the Via Panisperna boys. He applied the exclusion principle to an ideal gas, a formulation now called Fermi-Dirac statistics, and developed a theory of beta decay using a particle he named the neutrino. After finding that slow neutrons were more easily captured by nuclei, he bombarded thorium and uranium and concluded he had made new elements; this earned the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics, although the products were later shown to be fission fragments.

Fermi left Italy in 1938 to escape the racial laws that threatened his Jewish wife, Laura Capon, and arrived in New York on 2 January 1939 to take a post at Columbia University. In the Manhattan Project he led the team at the University of Chicago that built Chicago Pile-1, which went critical on 2 December 1942. He was present at the Trinity test on 16 July 1945. After the war he opposed development of a hydrogen bomb on moral and technical grounds and testified for J. Robert Oppenheimer at the 1954 hearing.

Fermi died of inoperable stomach cancer at his home in Chicago in November 1954, aged 53. Fermilab, the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and the synthetic element fermium are named after him. Emilio Segrè called him the last person who knew all of the physics of his day.
enrique-lister: Enrique Líster Forján was born on 21 April 1907 at Ameneiro in A Coruña. A stonemason, he spent his adolescence in Cuba and returned to Spain in 1925, when he joined the Communist Party of Spain (PCE). His revolutionary activity forced him into exile until the proclamation of the Second Spanish Republic in 1931. Between 1932 and 1935 he trained at the Frunze Military Academy in the Soviet Union.

When the Spanish Civil War began in 1936 he joined the Fifth Regiment, and in October he led a mixed brigade in the failed Republican counteroffensive at Seseña. As commander of the 11th Division he helped stall the Nationalist attack on the Jarama and took a large part in the Republican victory at the Battle of Guadalajara, and his division fought at Brunete, Belchite and Teruel. The historian Antony Beevor cites 4,300 casualties out of 13,353 men at Brunete and quotes the chief Soviet adviser reporting that the division fled and that about 400 of those fleeing were shot on 24 July.

The division's failure to take Fuentes de Ebro in August 1937, in which the International Tank Regiment lost most of its tanks, left lasting hatred between Líster and his corps commander Juan Modesto, who blamed him. Later Líster led the V Army Corps in the Battle of the Ebro and the Catalonia Offensive. As late as September 1938 he claimed that Franco's own troops thought him incompetent.

After the war Líster took refuge in Moscow and fought in the Second World War as a Red Army general, taking part in the relief of Leningrad in January 1944. In 1946 he became a general of the Yugoslav People's Army, and he also served in the Polish People's Army. According to Christopher Andrew and Oleg Gordievsky he was among the Soviet advisers sent in 1959 to organise the Committees for the Defense of the Revolution in Cuba.

After the PCE condemned the Soviet intervention in Czechoslovakia in 1968 he broke away and in 1973 founded the Spanish Communist Workers' Party (PCOE). He returned to Spain in 1977, rejoined the PCE, and dissolved the PCOE into it after Santiago Carrillo's expulsion in 1986. He wrote four books, among them Nuestra guerra (1966) and Memorias de un luchador (1977), and died in Madrid on 8 December 1994.
enryaku-ji: Enryaku-ji is a Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei in Ōtsu, overlooking Kyoto. It was founded in 788, in the early Heian period, by Saichō, also known as Dengyō Daishi, who introduced the Tendai sect of Mahayana Buddhism to Japan from China. With the support of Emperor Kanmu, Saichō ordained a hundred disciples in 807. He kept strict discipline on the mountain, and his monks lived in seclusion for twelve years of study and meditation. The best students were then kept on in the monastery, and others went into government posts. The founders of Jōdo-shū, Jōdo Shinshū, Sōtō Zen and Nichiren Buddhism all spent time at the monastery.

At its peak Enryaku-ji was a huge complex of as many as 3,000 sub-temples with a powerful army of warrior monks, the sōhei. In the tenth century succession disputes broke out between Tendai monks of the line of Ennin and those of Enchin. They produced rival centres at Enryaku-ji and at Mii-dera, known as the Mountain Order and the Temple Order. Warrior monks were used to settle the disputes, and Tendai leaders hired mercenary armies that threatened rivals and even marched on the capital to enforce monastic demands.

The warlord Oda Nobunaga ended this militancy in 1571, as part of a programme to remove all potential rivals and unite the country. He attacked Enryaku-ji, levelled its buildings and killed monks. The present structures date from the late sixteenth century to the first half of the seventeenth, when the temple was rebuilt after a change of government. The most significant reconstruction, that of the main hall, took place in 1642 under Tokugawa Iemitsu. Only one minor building survived, the thirteenth-century Ruri-dō, or Lapis Lazuli Hall. Some buildings were moved from other temples, notably Mii-dera.

Most of the buildings stand in three areas: Tō-dō, the East Pagoda, which holds the most important buildings, Sai-tō, the West Pagoda, and the more isolated Yokokawa. Enryaku-ji is the headquarters of the Tendai sect and part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto. It is also the centre for the practice of kaihōgyō, undertaken by the so-called marathon monks.

On 4 April 2006 Enryaku-ji performed a ceremony for former leaders of the Yamaguchi-gumi, the largest yakuza organisation in Japan, and received crime-related money for it, despite a request from the Shiga Prefectural Police to stop. After newspaper reports the temple faced a nationwide scandal, and on 18 May all its representative directors resigned.
ensenada: Ensenada, meaning inlet, lies on the Bahía de Todos Santos on the Pacific coast of Baja California. Guadalupe Island, off the coast, has been a wildlife sanctuary since 1975, and the waters hold gray whales, northern elephant seals, Guadalupe fur seals and California sea lions. The city has no rivers, only streams that flow after heavy rain, and a mild semi-arid climate cooled by the California Current. Rainfall averages 280 millimetres a year and falls mainly in winter. The city lies some 108 kilometres south of the border with the United States.

When the first European explorers arrived the region was inhabited by Yuman-Cochimí speaking peoples, among them the Kiliwa, Paipai and Kumeyaay, who still exist. The Kumeyaay had a village on the city's site called Pa-tai. Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo reached the bay by sea, and a founding in 1542 under the name San Mateo is recorded.

In 1602 Sebastián Vizcaíno, mapping the coast in search of safe harbours for galleons returning from Manila to Acapulco, renamed it Ensenada de Todos Santos. Jesuits made the first permanent settlement, and Dominicans took over after the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1768. William Walker, the self-declared president of the Republic of Baja California, briefly took the town in 1853-54.

In 1882 the small community of Rancho Ensenada de Santos was made the capital of the northern part of the Baja California Territory. The English Mexican Land and Colonization Company tried to develop the area, and the town grew with the mines in the surrounding mountains, but the Mexican Revolution left the area devastated.

The capital was transferred to Mexicali in 1915, and in 1930 the population was only 5,000. Prohibition in the United States then sent Americans and Canadians south in search of entertainment and alcohol, and the Hotel Riviera del Pacífico opened in 1930. Ensenada flourished from the early 1950s, when it had 20,000 inhabitants, and had a construction boom in the 1950s and 1960s.

Ensenada is the municipal seat of Ensenada Municipality and the third-largest city of Baja California. It has a major port and is a tourist destination and a base for research institutions. About 90 percent of Mexican wine comes from the nearby Guadalupe and Calafia valleys. Spanish is the main language.
enshakushanna: His name is also read Enshagsagana, En-shag-kush-ana and En-šakušuana. The Sumerian King List gives him a reign of 60 years. A dedication tablet in the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg names his father as Elilina, possibly King Elulu of Ur. His title, en ki-en-gi lugal kalam, may be translated as lord of Sumer and king of all the land, and may imply en of the region of Uruk and lugal of the region of Ur; it could correspond to the later title King of Sumer and Akkad.

His reign is known above all for his campaigns. He is said to have conquered Hamazi, Akkad, Kish and Nippur. A stone bowl at Nippur records that he sacked Kish and Akshak and dedicated their statues, precious metals, lapis lazuli, timber and treasure to the god Enlil, and fragments of three more bowls from Nippur repeat that he gave Enlil the treasure of sacked Kish.

Many scholars attribute to him the destruction layers at Palace A and the Plano-Convex Building at Kish, and Federico Zaina notes the evidence of violent destruction of the city at the end of the ED IIIb period. Besides his wars in the north, one of his year names was "Year in which En-šakušuana defeated Akkad", which would place this war shortly before the rise of the Akkadian Empire.

He may have been succeeded in Uruk by Girimesi, but the leadership of Sumer seems to have passed for a time to Eannatum of Lagash. Lugal-kinishe-dudu was later allied with Entemena, a successor of Eannatum, against Umma, the chief rival of Lagash.
ensisheim: Ensisheim is a commune in the Haut-Rhin department in north-eastern France. People lived in the area long before the town existed. A Neolithic burial site near it yielded the skeleton of a man of about 50 whose skull showed two trepanation operations, one fully healed and the other partly, so that he had survived both. Researchers from Freiburg University reported in 1997 that the remains date to between 5100 and 4900 BCE, which makes it one of the earliest clear examples of the practice. The village is first mentioned in 768, as Enghisehaim.

In the second half of the 13th century Rudolph I of Germany built a castle at Ensisheim that came to be known as the Königsburg. Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg was held captive there for seven years until his death in 1293. On 28 October 1444 the Pact of Ensisheim, connected with the Battle of St. Jakob an der Birs, was signed in the town by the Confederation, Zurich and the French mercenaries.

On 7 November 1492 a meteorite fell into a field close to the town. Sebastian Brant, author of The Ship of Fools, used the occasion to write Loose Leaves Concerning the Fall of the Meteorite, in which he sought to influence Maximilian of Austria, and the king went on to pursue a war against France. The administrative and legal functions of the town brought it a prosperity that peaked between the end of the 16th and the early 17th century. It had a mint from 1585 to 1634, the most significant in Alsace after Strasbourg.

The war that began in 1618 brought decline. The imperial administration left Ensisheim in 1630, and the town was pillaged seven times between 1631 and 1638. After the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the Habsburg possessions passed to the French Crown, which set up a Royal Chamber and then, in 1662, a Provincial Council. When imperial troops returned in 1674 the council withdrew to Breisach, and Marshal Turenne retook the town the following year. Ensisheim was afterwards only the chief town of a bailliage until the Revolution. At the start of the 20th century the extraction of potash brought it a new rise.

The meteorite, which fell in 1492, can still be seen in the town's museum, the Musée de la Régence. The composer Léon Boëllmann was born in Ensisheim. The town is twinned with Markdorf in Germany, Castroville in Texas and Otjiwarongo in Namibia, and it belongs to the Communauté de communes du Centre Haut-Rhin.
entebbe: Entebbe lies on a peninsula on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, in what is now Wakiso District. Its name comes from the Luganda word entebbe, meaning seat or chair. It was probably given because a Baganda chief sat there to judge legal cases. The site was cultural ground for the Mamba clan, and was called entebbe za Mugula after Mugula, the title of a chief of a subdivision of that clan. The town covers 56.2 square kilometres, of which 20 are water.

Entebbe became a British colonial administrative and commercial centre in 1893, when Sir Gerald Portal, a colonial Commissioner, used it as a base. It was the seat of government of the Protectorate of Uganda until independence in 1962, and State House, first the residence of British governors, later became the president's office and residence. The National Botanical Gardens were laid out in 1898, and Entebbe Golf Club, established in 1900, is the oldest golf course in East Africa. Kigungu, near the town, is the historical site where the first Catholic missionaries, Brother Amans and Father Lourdel, landed to establish their faith in Uganda.

Entebbe International Airport has been the scene of events known well beyond Uganda. Queen Elizabeth II left Africa from it in 1952 when she learned of her father's death and that she had become queen. On 4 July 1976 soldiers of the Sayeret Matkal, Paratroopers Brigade and Golani Brigade of the Israeli Army freed more than 100 hostages after a hijacking by a group of Palestinian and German militants. This was Operation Entebbe.

The airport is Uganda's largest commercial and military airport, and Kampala has replaced Entebbe as the seat of power. The town has a population recorded at 69,958 in the census of 2014. It is home to the Uganda Virus Research Institute, a government body whose research centres on infectious diseases such as HIV, tuberculosis and malaria, and to the Uganda Wildlife Education Centre, which also serves as the national zoo, and Nkumba University.
entre-rios-province: Entre Ríos lies in the Mesopotamia region of Argentina. It borders the provinces of Buenos Aires to the south, Corrientes to the north and Santa Fe to the west, and Uruguay to the east. The land is almost completely flat, with hills of some 100 metres at most, in two systems of low hills, the Cuchilla de Montiel in the west and the Cuchilla Grande in the east. The name means 'between rivers': the Paraná River and its delta lie to the west and south, and the Uruguay River to the east.

The first inhabitants were the Charrúa and the Chaná. Spaniards entered in 1520, when Juan Rodríguez Serrano went up the Uruguay River in search of the Pacific Ocean. The first permanent Spanish settlement was founded in what is now La Paz Department at the end of the 16th century. Juan de Garay, after founding Santa Fe, explored the territory and called it la otra banda, 'the other bank'. Colonists from Santa Fe Province settled on the Bajada del Paraná, the site of the present capital, in the late seventeenth century. In 1783 Tomás de Rocamora explored the area, gave official status to many of its towns and was the first to call it Entre Ríos.

In 1853 a meeting of all the provinces except Buenos Aires made Paraná the capital of the Argentine Confederation, and the provincial capital moved to Concepción del Uruguay. Urquiza encouraged immigration through colonization contracts and set up agricultural colonies of European settlers, mainly Volga Germans, Russians, Italians, Swiss and French. At the 1903 census, 153,067 of the province's 425,373 inhabitants were immigrants. Urquiza was assassinated in 1870, probably on the orders of his former supporter Ricardo López Jordán.

The capital is Paraná, with 391,000 inhabitants, on the Paraná River opposite the city of Santa Fe. The province has 17 departments and a bicameral legislature. Since 1999 it has belonged, with Córdoba and Santa Fe, to the association known as the Center Region. El Palmar and Predelta national parks lie within it, and its agriculture includes rice, soybeans, wheat, maize, citrus and cattle.
enuma-elish: Enūma Eliš has about a thousand lines and is recorded on seven clay tablets, each holding between 115 and 170 lines of cuneiform. Most of Tablet V has never been recovered, but the rest of the text is almost complete. The earliest manuscript, excavated at Assur, dates to the 9th century BCE. The poem was once thought to have been composed in the reign of Hammurabi, but most scholars now consider that unlikely, because in the Old Babylonian period Marduk was not the head of the pantheon. The rise of Marduk is generally dated to the Second Dynasty of Isin, when Nebuchadnezzar I brought his statue back from Elam. Some late Assyrian versions replace Marduk with Ashur.

The poem begins when only Apsu and Tiamat existed, their waters mingled. Their children, the younger gods, disturbed Apsu, who planned to destroy them, but Ea put him to sleep with a spell and killed him. Within Apsu, Ea and Damkina created Marduk. Tiamat then made eleven monsters and made the god Kingu her consort and chief of her war party. When no other god could face her, Marduk accepted the challenge on condition that the gods proclaim him supreme.

In single combat Marduk entangled Tiamat in a net, filled her mouth with the Evil Wind and shot an arrow into her heart. He split her body in two and made the sky from one half. Humankind was made from the blood of Kingu to serve the gods. The gods built Babylon and the temple Esagila for Marduk, and the poem ends with a hymn giving him fifty names.

The tablets were found between 1848 and 1876 in the ruins of the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh by Austen Henry Layard, Hormuzd Rassam and George Smith, who published a form of the myth in 1876. Interest grew because of similarities to the book of Genesis, such as a watery chaos before creation and seven tablets set against seven days. L. W. King collected the texts in 1902.

A ritual text of the Seleucid period states that the poem was recited at the Akitu festival, but scholars debate whether this reading occurred and which text was meant. Most consider that the festival included a re-enactment of Tiamat's defeat as a renewal of order.
enver-hoxha: Enver Hoxha was born in Gjirokastër, in southern Albania and then part of the Ottoman Empire, in October 1908. His father, Halil Hoxha, was a Shia Muslim cloth merchant who travelled widely in Europe and the United States, and the family belonged to the Bektashi Sufi order. He was named after Enver Pasha, a leading figure of the Young Turk Revolution. He studied at the Gjirokastër Lyceum from 1923, and when it closed he received a state scholarship to continue at the Albanian National Lyceum in Korçë, where he studied until 1930.

The Communist Party of Albania was founded on 8 November 1941, and the two Yugoslav envoys chose Hoxha from the Korça group as a Muslim representative among the seven members of its provisional Central Committee. The Albanian Communists repudiated a Greater Albania agreement when the Yugoslav Communists disagreed with it, and the Balli Kombëtar, which condemned them, then sided with Nazi Germany, leaving the Communists in the lead of the fight for liberation.

In power from 1944, Hoxha admired Joseph Stalin. Between 1945 and 1950 the government consolidated power through policies that included extrajudicial killings of anti-communists. The Agrarian Reform Law of August 1945 took land from beys and large landowners without compensation, cutting their share from 52 per cent of the land to 16 per cent. In February 1951, after a bombing at the Soviet embassy in Tirana, 23 intellectuals were arrested; one was killed during interrogation and the other 22 were executed without trial under Hoxha's orders.

Albania joined Comecon on 22 February 1949 after the break with Yugoslavia. When Stalin died in March 1953, Hoxha had the people of Tirana kneel in the main square and swear an oath of eternal fidelity. Aid fell under Khrushchev, and Albania later turned to China, then severed ties with the Chinese Communist Party after the Sino-Albanian Split of 1976 to 1978. In 1966 he led the Cultural and Ideological Revolution, which sought to remove the influence of religion; the Jesuit Order had been banned in 1946 and the Franciscans in 1947.

After 1968 travel abroad was forbidden to all but those on official business, and at one point every third Albanian had been questioned by the Sigurimi or held in a labour camp. Hoxha died on 11 April 1985 and was succeeded by Ramiz Alia.
enver-pasha: İsmail Enver was born in Constantinople on 23 November 1881. His father Ahmed was either a Gagauz bridge-keeper in Monastir or an Albanian small-town public prosecutor in the Balkans, and his mother Ayşe Dilara was a Tatar. He grew up in Monastir (Bitola) from the age of six and in 1902 graduated from the Ottoman Military Academy, becoming a mektebli, an officer with a formal military education. His classmate there was Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk), and the two developed a rivalry.

Through his uncle Halil Kut he became the twelfth member of the Ottoman Freedom Society, which merged with the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP). On his return to Monastir in 1906 he formed a CUP cell there and brought Ottoman officers into the organisation.

In July 1908 Ahmed Niyazi went into the mountains from Resne and called for the restoration of the constitution of 1876, and Enver and others followed with guerrilla bands, helping to start the Young Turk Revolution against Sultan Abdul Hamid II. He and Niyazi were hailed as heroes of freedom. When Italy invaded Tripolitania on 29 September 1911, Enver went to Libya, mobilised about 20,000 troops and took command of the Benghazi zone, though the outbreak of the Balkan Wars recalled him and Italy took control of Libya. A coup in 1913 brought the CUP to power and Enver became Minister of War, with Talaat in charge of the civil government.

He was an architect of the Ottoman-German alliance. Without informing the cabinet he allowed the German warships Goeben and Breslau into the Dardanelles, and on 29 October 1914 Admiral Souchon bombed Russian ports in the Black Sea, after which Russia and Britain declared war. At the Battle of Sarikamish in the winter of 1914–1915 he pressed an attack in the mountains despite objections, and a large part of the 90,000-strong army froze to death or was killed. He blamed Armenian soldiers for the defeat and later initiated the deportations and massacres of Western Armenians, culminating in the Armenian genocide. In 1918 he planned an Army of Islam in the Caucasus, halted at the Battle of Sardarabad.

The Sultan dismissed Enver as War Minister on 4 October 1918, and after the Armistice of Mudros he escaped by German submarine to Odessa with seven other CUP leaders. He was tried in absentia in 1919–20 for plunging the country into war without a legitimate reason, for the forced deportation of Armenians and for leaving without permission, and was condemned to death. In 1921 he went to Moscow and was sent to Bukhara to help suppress the Basmachi Revolt, but he defected and became the rebels' commander, hoping to realise his pan-Turkic aims. He was killed in 1922, and his remains were reburied in Turkey in 1996.
enzo-of-sardinia: Enzo, also called Enzio, was the son of Emperor Frederick II by Adelaide, a member of the Swabian House of Urslingen and a relative of Duke Conrad I of Spoleto. He was the second of the emperor's illegitimate sons and reputedly his favourite until the birth of Manfred. He resembled his father and shared his love of the arts. When Ubaldo Visconti died in 1238, the Doria family of Genoa, seeking to keep the Giudicato of Logudoro from Pisan control, persuaded Frederick to marry Enzo to the widow, Adelasia of Torres. The marriage gave him Logudoro and Gallura, the northern half of Sardinia, and he was knighted at Cremona and granted the Sardinian royal title, last held by Barisone II of Arborea.

In July 1239 Enzo became imperial vicar general in Lombardy and general legate in Romagna, and left Sardinia, never to return. He shared his father's excommunication that year and fought in the war against Pope Gregory IX and the Lombard League. He retook Jesi, Frederick's birthplace, and in 1241 took part in the capture of a papal fleet at the Battle of Giglio in the Tyrrhenian Sea, in which churchmen bound for a council in Rome were taken. He was briefly captured by the Milanese at Gorgonzola. His marriage was annulled in 1245 or 1246, and in 1247 he took part in the failed Siege of Parma and attacked Reggio.

On 26 May 1249, campaigning for the Ghibelline cities of Modena and Cremona against Guelph Bologna, he was defeated and taken at Fossalta. Despite his father's demands, Bologna kept him as a knightly prisoner in the palace now called Palazzo Re Enzo, and every attempt at escape or rescue failed.

Enzo died on 14 March 1272 after more than 22 years in captivity and was buried in the Basilica of San Domenico. By then he was one of the last Hohenstaufen heirs. A lover of falconry, he was nicknamed Falconello, and in prison he wrote poems, of which two canzoni and a sonnet survive. Giovanni Pascoli wrote of him in Canzoni di re Enzio (1909), and the Bentivoglio family of Bologna claimed descent from him.
eoka: Cyprus was conquered by the Ottoman Empire in 1571, and control passed to the British Empire on 4 June 1878 after the Russo-Turkish War. British censuses recorded a Greek Cypriot majority throughout, with Turkish Cypriots the smaller community. The organisation was headed by Georgios Grivas, a Greek Army officer from Cyprus who had led the anti-Nazi and anti-communist resistance group Organization X in occupied Greece. He took the nom de guerre Digenis, after the Byzantine hero Digenis Akritas.

Grivas arrived to stay in early November 1954. He recruited from the Cyprus Farmers' Union in the villages and from two youth movements, the Church-controlled OHEN and the nationalist PEON, in the towns. The armed wing consisted of mountain groups in hidden camps and town groups, supported by a National Front of Cyprus that supplied intelligence and weapons.

Archbishop Makarios III and Grivas disagreed over method: Makarios wished to limit the campaign to sabotage without loss of life, while Grivas aimed at continual harassment of the British, believing that British repression would alienate the population and give Greece a case before the United Nations. The armed struggle began just after midnight on 31 March to 1 April 1955 with eighteen bomb attacks, accompanied by a proclamation signed Digenis. Grivas at first forbade attacks on Turkish Cypriots.

Governor John Harding arrived on 3 October 1955 and declared a State of Emergency on 26 November. After talks with Makarios failed, the British exiled him to the Seychelles on 9 March 1956, which brought a general strike and a sharp rise in attacks.

Violence between the communities grew as Grivas began targeting Turkish Cypriot policemen, and the Turkish Cypriot organisation TMT emerged. After the MacMillan Plan, which Greek Cypriots rejected, he cancelled a further truce on 7 September 1958 and ordered attacks on British people, in which eight were killed in the next two months. Makarios hinted that he would accept an independent Cyprus.

After the Zurich and London agreements Makarios became the first president of the Republic of Cyprus and staffed the government and civil service with EOKA members. Extremists of both communities remained armed, and the new state collapsed after Makarios changed the constitution unilaterally. In 2012 the Foreign Office released documents in which colonial officials admitted torture and abuse between 1955 and 1959. The Republic of Cyprus regards EOKA's members as freedom fighters and marks 1 April as a national anniversary, while a Turkish Cypriot textbook calls the campaign barbaric and illegal. A memorial museum was created in Nicosia in 1960.
epaminondas: Epaminondas was born at Thebes to a family of high standing which, by tradition, claimed descent from the mythical Spartoi. The Pythagorean Lysis of Tarentum, who had fled persecution in Magna Graecia and lived in his father's house, taught him philosophy and influenced him deeply. Ancient writers describe him as patriotic, incorruptible and modest, living in voluntary poverty. He never married, and his lifelong companion was Pelopidas.

After its victory in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BCE Sparta followed an aggressively unilateral policy toward the rest of Greece. In 382 BCE the Spartan commander Phoebidas, taking advantage of civil strife in Thebes, seized the Theban acropolis, the Cadmeia, and the anti-Spartan party was forced to flee. Epaminondas was allowed to remain, because his philosophy and poverty made him seem harmless.

The exiles regrouped in Athens and prepared to liberate the city, while Epaminondas prepared the young men of Thebes to fight. A small group of exiles led by Pelopidas slipped into the city and killed the leaders of the pro-Spartan government, and with Epaminondas and Athenian hoplites they surrounded the Spartans on the Cadmeia, who surrendered on condition of marching away unharmed. In 371 BCE Epaminondas won the battle of Leuctra, where his decision to refuse his right flank, the first recorded use of such a tactic, let a smaller force defeat the Spartan phalanx.

The next year the Thebans invaded the Peloponnese to break Spartan power. The historian Hans Beck argues that Thebes made no effort to create an empire or bind its allies in a stable organisation. The poem on his tomb, as Pausanias records it, credits him with the restoration of Messene and the walls of Megalopolis.

At Mantinea in 362 BCE Epaminondas was hit in the chest by a spear while pressing forward with his troops. Carried to camp still alive, he asked which side had won, and on hearing that the Boeotians had, said that it was time to die. He was buried on the battlefield. Within a few years Athens replaced Thebes at the head of Greek politics. Thebes was defeated by Philip II at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and three years later Alexander the Great destroyed the city after a revolt. Cicero called Epaminondas the first man of Greece.
ephesus: Ephesus was an ancient Greek city on the coast of Ionia, in present-day Selçuk in İzmir Province, Turkey. People lived in the surrounding area by the Neolithic, about 6000 BCE, and Hittite sources name Apasa as the capital of the kingdom of Arzawa, which some scholars identify with the later Ephesus.

The city was founded as an Attic and Ionian colony in the 10th century BCE on Ayasuluk Hill. Legend names its founder as Androklos, a prince of Athens who left home after the death of his father King Kodros, and who joined the twelve cities of Ionia together in the Ionian League. Ephesus took part in the Ionian Revolt against Persian rule, in the Battle of Ephesus of 498 BCE. After Alexander the Great defeated the Persians at the Battle of Granicus in 334 BCE he was greeted warmly in Ephesus. The city passed to Lysimachus in 290 BCE and, as part of the kingdom of Pergamon, to the Roman Republic in 129 BCE.

Ephesus was a major centre of early Christianity. The apostle Paul lived there for three years from 52 to 54 CE, and the Acts of the Apostles tells of a mob raised by the silversmith Demetrius, who feared for the trade in silver shrines of Artemis. Ephesus remained the most important Byzantine city in Asia after Constantinople in the 5th and 6th centuries, and Justinian I built the basilica of St John. The Goths destroyed the city in 263, and the harbour was slowly silted up by the Küçükmenderes River, so that the city declined as a port.

In 1304 the town surrendered to a Turkish warlord, Sasa Bey, and was then ceded to the Aydinid principality, which stationed a navy in the harbour of Ayasuluğ. Ephesus was abandoned by the 15th century.

The Temple of Artemis, completed around 550 BCE, once had over 100 marble pillars, and only one column stands. The Library of Celsus was built about 125 and held nearly 12,000 scrolls, and the Great Theatre may be the largest of the ancient world. Excavation began in 1863 under John Turtle Wood, and the Austrian Archaeological Institute, founded in 1898, still leads it. The ruins were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.
ephor: The word ephoros means one who oversees. The ephors were a board of five magistrates of ancient Sparta, elected each year, with judicial, religious, legislative and military powers. Ancient sources gave two accounts of their origin. Herodotus, followed by Xenophon, Plato and Isocrates, traced the office to the lawgiver Lycurgus. Aristotle said the king Theopompos created it, and Cicero and Plutarch followed him. Modern scholars think the second account derives from a lost work by the exiled king Pausanias, who may have disliked the ephors, and most place the ephorate in Theopompos's time, during the Messenian Wars. Yurij Andreev points out that ancient Thera also had ephors, and suggests that the office existed earlier in some form.

All Spartan citizens could be elected, and the office was the only one open to every man between 30 and 60 years of age. Ephors could not be re-elected. Elections took place near the autumn equinox, when the Spartan year began: candidates passed before the assembly, and a jury shut in a building judged who was greeted with the loudest shouts. Aristotle called this method childish. One ephor, the eponymous ephor, gave his name to the year, and the Spartans kept a list of them.

Ephors presided over the assembly, acted as judges in the supreme civil court and handled foreign relations and treaties. Two accompanied a king on campaign and could put him on trial. According to Plutarch they declared war on the helots each autumn, so that any Spartan could kill one without guilt, and they watched the sky every eight years to judge whether a king had offended the gods. They supervised the education of Spartan boys and chaired the congress of the Peloponnesian League. Aristotle observed that, since ephors often came from poor families, they were liable to corruption, and Plato called them tyrants.

Policy could change when a single ephor changed his vote. In 403 BCE Pausanias persuaded three ephors to send an army to Attica, reversing the policy of Lysander. Cleomenes III abolished the office in 227 BCE, and four of the five ephors died in his coup. After the Battle of Sellasia in 222 BCE the Macedonian king Antigonus III Doson restored it. The ephorate lasted under Roman rule into the second century CE, when Hadrian probably abolished it. Several cities of Spartan ancestry, among them Taras, Thera and Cyrene, also had ephors.
ephorus: Ephorus was born in Cyme in Aeolia and, with the historian Theopompus, was a pupil of Isocrates in rhetoric. Little else is known of his life. He does not seem to have made much progress as a speaker, and at the suggestion of Isocrates himself he took up literary composition and the study of history. According to Plutarch, he declined an offer from Alexander the Great to join the Persian campaign as official historian. His son Demophilus also became a historian.

His main work was a universal history in 29 books. Demophilus edited the whole and added a thirtieth. It began with the days of the Heraclids and came down to the taking of Perinthus by Philip of Macedon in 340 BCE, covering more than seven hundred years, and it included a summary description of the Sacred Wars. Polybius says that Ephorus was the first historian to write a universal history. Each book had its own prooimion, and the work, probably called simply Historiai, followed a thematic rather than a strictly chronological order.

Besides the universal history he wrote the Epichorios logos, a patriotic essay praising the traditions of Cyme, a book on inventions, Peri heurematon, and a work on style, Peri lexeos. Other titles are attributed to him, though it is doubtful whether they were separate works or only extracts from the Histories. Of all these only isolated fragments survive. He also reported that a comet split in two in the winter of 372–373 BCE, a claim that Seneca the Younger, the ancient source for the report, rejected because nobody else had recorded it.

The work was highly praised and widely read in antiquity, and later historians drew on it freely. It is generally believed to be the main or sole source for the account by Diodorus Siculus of Greek history between 480 and 340 BCE, one of only two continuous narratives of the period that survive. Strabo valued Ephorus's geographical investigations and quoted him at length in his Geographica, praising him as the first to separate the historical from the geographical element. Polybius credited him with knowledge of naval warfare but ridiculed his account of the Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE as showing ignorance of land operations.

Ancient writers regarded him as able and thorough but somewhat dull. He drew a sharp line, though not always, between myth and history, and he saw that a profusion of detail is grounds for suspicion in reports of distant history. His style was high-flown and artificial, and he often sacrificed truth to rhetorical effect. Dionysius of Halicarnassus judged that he and Theopompus were the only historians whose language was accurate and complete.
epic-of-gilgamesh: The literary history of Gilgamesh begins with five Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, some of which may date to the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2100 BCE. These circulated independently and were later used as source material for a combined epic in Akkadian. The earliest surviving version of that epic is the Old Babylonian one, from about the 18th century BCE, named after its first words, Shūtur eli sharrī, Surpassing All Other Kings. Only a few of its tablets survive.

The later Standard Babylonian version, in twelve tablets, was compiled by Sîn-lēqi-unninni at some point between the 13th and 10th centuries BCE. Its opening words are Sha naqba īmuru, He Who Saw the Deep. About two-thirds of it have been recovered, and some of the best copies came from the ruins of the library of the 7th-century BCE Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. The twelfth tablet is probably a later addition, a near copy of an earlier Sumerian tale of Enkidu's journey to the Underworld.

Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, oppresses his people, and the gods create Enkidu, a wild man, to stop him. Enkidu is civilised through sexual initiation with Shamhat and travels to Uruk, where he challenges Gilgamesh to a contest of strength. Gilgamesh wins, and the two become friends. Together they journey to the Cedar Forest and kill its guardian, Humbaba. When Gilgamesh spurns the goddess Ishtar, she sends the Bull of Heaven against him, and the two heroes kill it. The gods then sentence Enkidu to death by a fatal illness.

Grief at Enkidu's death drives Gilgamesh to seek the secret of eternal life. He meets Utnapishtim and his wife, the only humans to survive the flood sent by the gods, and learns that death was ordained as humanity's share while life remained in the gods' hands.

About 15,000 fragments of Assyrian tablets were found in the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh by Austen Henry Layard, Hormuzd Rassam and W. K. Loftus in the early 1850s. George Smith, hired by the British Museum, read translated fragments to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in 1872 and published fuller translations in 1875 and 1876. The hero's name was first read as Izdubar, before the cuneiform signs could be pronounced accurately. Samuel Noah Kramer reassembled the Sumerian poems. In 1998 Theodore Kwasman identified a fragment in the British Museum containing the first lines of the epic. Andrew George's two-volume critical edition appeared in 2003.
epicurus: Epicurus was born in February 341 BCE in the Athenian settlement on Samos, to Neocles and Chaerestrate, both Athenian-born. He studied under a Samian Platonist named Pamphilus, probably for about four years. After the death of Alexander the Great, Perdiccas expelled the Athenian settlers from Samos to Colophon, and Epicurus joined his family there after his military service. He studied under Nausiphanes, a follower of Democritus, and around 311 BCE began teaching in Mytilene.

Platonism dominated higher education in his lifetime, and over half of the forty Principal Doctrines flatly contradict Plato. Epicurus held that the universe is eternal and consists of matter and void. Matter is made of atoms with only shape, size and weight, and there are infinitely many worlds. Unlike Democritus, he proposed that atoms may swerve from their course, which allows free will. He took sense perception as the foundation of knowledge and the soul as mortal and material: death is nothing to us, since when we are, death is not come.

In ethics he was a hedonist who redefined pleasure as the absence of suffering and aimed at ataraxia, untroubledness. He sorted desires into natural and necessary, natural but not necessary, and unnatural and unnecessary, and valued friendship above power or wealth. He did not deny the gods but denied that they take part in human affairs.

Diogenes Laërtius records, on the authority of Epicurus's successor Hermarchus, that he died painfully in 270 BCE, aged seventy-two, of a stone blockage of the urinary tract, yet kept teaching. Of some 300 works only the Principal Doctrines and three letters survive whole, with parts of On Nature found among the Herculaneum papyri. Most of what is known comes through later writers such as Lucretius.

Epicureanism flourished in the late Roman Republic but had died out by late antiquity. Poggio Bracciolini found a copy of Lucretius's On the Nature of Things in 1417, and Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655) revived a modified atomism that influenced Robert Boyle and John Locke.
epimenides: Epimenides came from Knossos or Phaistos in Crete. While tending his father's sheep he is said to have fallen asleep for fifty-seven years in a cave sacred to Zeus, and to have woken with the gift of prophecy. According to Diogenes Laërtius, he met Pythagoras in Crete, and the two went to the Cave of Ida. His countrymen later honoured him as a god and held that he lived nearly three hundred years. Another story says he was captured in a war between the Spartans and the Knossians and put to death because he refused to prophesy favourably for his captors.

Diogenes Laërtius relates that when a pestilence raged in Athens the Pythonic oracle told the Athenians to fetch Epimenides from Crete. He set sheep on Mars Hill and had altars raised where they lay down, which was held to explain the anonymous altars of the city. Plutarch writes that he purified Athens after the pollution brought by the Alcmeonidae, and that his knowledge of sacrifice and his reform of funeral practice helped Solon in reforming the Athenian state. He would accept only a branch of the sacred olive and a promise of lasting friendship between Athens and Knossos.

Athenaeus also mentions him in connection with the self-sacrifice of Aristodemus and Cratinus, a story some in antiquity thought to be fiction. He was also said to have prophesied at Sparta on military matters.

Pausanias reports that when Epimenides died his skin was found covered with tattooed writing, which was odd because the Greeks reserved tattooing for slaves. Some modern scholars have taken this as evidence that he was heir to the shamanic religions of Central Asia. His skin was said to be kept at the court of the ephors in Sparta.

Several prose and verse works, now lost, were attributed to him, among them a theogony, an epic on the Argonautic expedition, prose works on purifications and sacrifices, a cosmogony, oracles and a work on the laws of Crete. His Cretica is thought to be quoted twice in the New Testament. The Epistle to Titus cites a line calling the Cretans always liars and attributes it to a prophet of their own, whom Clement of Alexandria identified as Epimenides. The saying created a paradox of self-reference like the liar paradox, known as the Epimenides paradox. James Rendel Harris argued that the passage in Acts 17:28, in Him we live and move and have our being, derives from the same poem.
epirus: Classical Epirus lay roughly between the Pindus Mountains in the east and the Ionian Sea in the west, and between the Acroceraunian Mountains in the north and the Ambracian Gulf in the south. The region is rugged, with steep limestone ridges parallel to the sea, so that the valleys are mostly suited to pasture rather than large-scale farming. The highest point is Mount Smolikas, at 2,637 m. The main river is the Vjosë, and the only large lake is Lake Pamvotis, on which Ioannina stands.

In the early 1st millennium BCE the fourteen Epirote tribes, among them the Chaonians, the Molossians and the Thesprotians, spoke a strong west Greek dialect. They lived in small villages rather than city-states, and their region was a frontier contested with Illyrian peoples. Epirus had religious importance through the oracle of Dodona, regarded as second only to Delphi. Thucydides called the Epirotes barbarians, while Herodotus and Pausanias described them as Greeks. From 370 BCE the Molossian Aeacidae dynasty built a centralised state, and in 359 BCE the Molossian princess Olympias married Philip II of Macedon and became the mother of Alexander the Great.

Epirus became part of the Roman Republic in 146 BCE, and under Trajan it became a separate province. After 1204 it was the centre of the Despotate of Epirus, a successor state of the Byzantine Empire, and in the 15th century the Ottoman Empire conquered it. In the 18th century Ali Pasha of Tepelena, who became governor of Ioannina in 1788, ruled a de facto independent Pashalik of Yanina, until the Ottoman government reasserted control in 1821. After the First Balkan War southern Epirus, including Ioannina, joined Greece, while northern Epirus was assigned to Albania.

The region is divided between the Greek region of Epirus, whose seat is Ioannina, and the Albanian counties of Gjirokastër and Vlorë. The Greek region covers only part of classical Epirus. Livestock keeping is the main industry, and the Vikos Gorge is the centrepiece of the Vikos-Aoös National Park.
epona: The name Epona, 'Great Mare', comes from Gaulish. It derives from the Proto-Celtic word *ekʷos, 'horse', with an augmentative suffix often found in names of deities, such as Sirona and Matrona. Some scholars suggest instead that the ending refers to sacred water. Horses mattered greatly to Gallic life: Vercingetorix sent his horses away rather than let them be captured or killed. Iconography suggests that before Roman contact Epona was a peaceful divinity of fertility and protection rather than of war. Some scholars compare her with Rhiannon of the Welsh Mabinogion, but Ronald Hutton is sceptical, since Rhiannon is a much later literary creation.
