In Gaul Epona was worshipped as a mother goddess who watched over horses, donkeys, mules and their riders, and she was probably also a protector of horse-breeding and of grooms, muleteers, charioteers and travellers. Altars to her were commonly placed in stables. Apuleius, in The Golden Ass, describes a shrine to her in a niche of a stable post, wreathed with fresh roses, and Juvenal links her to stables.

Some objects dedicated to her suggest a funerary role, and Fernand Benoît proposed that her images expressed a theme of victory over death. A story attributed to Pseudo-Plutarch tells how a man named Fulvius Stellus, who hated women, had a daughter by a mare, who was called Epona.

As Gaul was made Roman, Epona became a protector of cavalry. Military units recruited from Gaul, Lower Germany and Pannonia spread her cult across the Roman Empire, and she was the only Celtic divinity ultimately worshipped in Rome itself. A rustic calendar from Guidizzolo in Italy gives her feast day as 18 December, though this may have been only local. She was invoked for the emperor as Epona Augusta or Epona Regina.

Most evidence comes from eastern and north-eastern Gaul and the Rhineland, in the form of votive objects, small statues and Latin inscriptions, many made by cavalrymen in fulfilment of a vow; objects found by springs and wells suggest she was also seen as a healer. In Hispania she was known as Epane, and her cult probably spread along the copper-mining towns of the Sierra Morena. Folklorists have linked the May Day hobby-horses of Padstow and Minehead and the Welsh Mari Lwyd to her, but there is no firm evidence for this.
equal-rights-amendment: On 25 September 1921 the National Woman's Party announced a campaign for a constitutional amendment guaranteeing women equal rights with men. Its first text forbade any political, civil or legal disabilities or inequalities on account of sex or of marriage. Alice Paul, the party's head, believed that the Nineteenth Amendment would not be enough to ensure equal treatment, and in 1923 at Seneca Falls, New York, she revised the wording. In its early decades middle-class women largely supported it, while those speaking for the working class often opposed it, arguing that employed women needed special protections regarding working conditions and hours.

The text approved by Congress has two operative sections. The first provides that equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex; the second gives Congress power to enforce it by appropriate legislation. The resolving clause required ratification by three-fourths of the states within seven years. Supporters held that it would end legal distinctions between men and women in divorce, property and employment. Opponents argued that it would remove protections from women, expose them to conscription and combat roles, and threaten alimony and housewives' Social Security benefits.

After pressure from the women's movement, including NOW's the disruption of a Senate hearing in February 1970 and the Women's Strike for Equality that August, Representative Martha Griffiths reintroduced the amendment in 1971. It went to the states on 22 March 1972. Hawaii ratified it that same day, 22 states ratified it during 1972 and eight more early in 1973, but only five between 1974 and 1977. In Illinois, supporters of Phyllis Schlafly lobbied legislators with homemade bread, jams and apple pies. South Dakota voted in 1979 that its own ratification would lapse at the original deadline.

The amendment has been reintroduced in every session of Congress since 1982; in 1983 it fell six votes short of two-thirds on the House floor, its last floor vote. From the mid-1990s supporters pursued a three-state strategy, citing the Twenty-seventh Amendment, ratified in 1992 after pending since 1789. Lawsuits followed on both sides from 2019. On 17 January 2025, three days before leaving office, President Joe Biden declared the amendment the law of the land, but the declaration had no formal effect, and the National Archives said it did not intend to certify it.
equatoria: Equatoria is the southernmost region of South Sudan, along the upper reaches of the White Nile and the border with Uganda, Kenya and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Juba, the national capital and largest city of South Sudan, lies within it. Its people belong to numerous ethnic groups, among them the Azande, Bari, Acholi, Madi, Moru, Lokoya, Otuho and Pari, and they are traditionally peasants or nomads. Juba Arabic and English are the common languages. Equatoria now consists of the states of Central, Eastern and Western Equatoria.

In the 19th century Egypt controlled Sudan and chose the British explorer Samuel Baker to establish the Equatoria province, which he did in 1870. He was to set up trading posts along the White Nile, with Gondokoro, near present-day Juba, as an important centre. Equatorian groups such as the Azande, Bari, Lokoya, Otuho and Pari resisted outsiders, and King Gbudwe of the Azande encouraged resistance. Charles George Gordon governed from 1874 and founded more posts. In 1878 he was succeeded by Emin Pasha, who made his headquarters at Lado.

In 1881 Muhammad Ahmad proclaimed himself the Mahdi, and by 1883 the Mahdists had cut off outside communications. A relief expedition under Henry Morton Stanley, the Advance, set out in February 1887 and lost two thirds of its personnel on the way through the Ituri Forest. Emin had been deposed by his own officers in August 1887, and the Mahdists had overrun most of the province. After the Anglo-Egyptian force under Lord Kitchener overthrew the Mahdist State in 1898, Equatoria was administered by the British. Missionaries ran limited schools and clinics there.

On 18 August 1955 No. 2 Company of the Equatoria Corps, the southernmost unit of the Sudan Defence Force, mutinied at Torit rather than move north, and similar mutinies followed at Juba, Yei, Yambio and Maridi. This marked the beginning of the first civil war in southern Sudan, and the rebellion later became known as Anya Nya. The war ended with the Addis Ababa Agreement, signed on 27 March 1972, which gave the South autonomy in three provinces, Equatoria, Bahr el Ghazal and Upper Nile. Fighting resumed in 1983, and the second civil war lasted until 2004.
erasmus: Desiderius Erasmus is reported to have been born in Rotterdam on 27 or 28 October. He was named after Erasmus of Formiae, whom his father Gerard favoured, and although he is closely associated with the city he lived there for only four years and never returned. Orphaned and poor, the sickly, bookish teenager was forced by poverty into the consecrated life, entering the novitiate in 1487 at the canonry of Stein near Gouda and professing his vows as a canon regular of St Augustine in late 1488.

In 1493 his prior arranged for him to become Latin Secretary to the Bishop of Cambrai, Henry of Bergen, on account of his skill in Latin. He then went to Paris to study theology. His years of increasing literary output followed his contact in 1499 with a reformist English circle that included John Colet and Thomas More. He travelled widely, for study, employment and patronage, and to see his books through the press in Paris, Venice, Louvain and Basel.

Erasmus was the most popular and most printed author of the early sixteenth century, and by the 1530s his writings accounted for 10 to 20 per cent of book sales in Europe. In his New Testament project his Annotations, modelled on a work by Lorenzo Valla, grew to include a revised Vulgate text, his own Latin translation, an accompanying Greek text and Paraphrases of the whole New Testament except Revelation. He also wrote On Free Will, The Praise of Folly and The Complaint of Peace.

He remained a member of the Catholic Church all his life and was committed to reforming it from within. He advocated peaceable concord and pastoral tolerance on matters of indifference, and held what he understood as the traditional doctrine of synergism, which Martin Luther and John Calvin rejected in favour of monergism. His middle-road approach disappointed and even angered partisans in both camps.

When his strength began to fail, Erasmus accepted an invitation from Queen Mary of Hungary, Regent of the Netherlands, to move from Freiburg to Catholic Brabant. In 1535 he moved back to Basel in preparation and saw his last major works, notably Ecclesiastes, through publication. He died on 12 July 1536 after an attack of dysentery. He was later called the Prince of the Humanists.
eratosthenes: Eratosthenes was the son of Aglaos and was born in Cyrene, a city founded by Greeks in the second half of the 7th century BCE, which came under Ptolemaic rule after the death of Alexander the Great. By the late 260s BCE he had gone to Athens to study. According to Strabo, he was taught Stoicism there by Zeno of Citium, and he also studied under Arcesilaus of Pitane, head of the Platonic Academy. He stayed in Athens for some twenty years, writing Platonikos, an inquiry into the mathematics and music in Plato's philosophy, poems, and works on chronology and on the winners of the Olympic Games.

In 246 BCE Ptolemy III succeeded his father. The reigning librarian of Alexandria, Apollonius of Rhodes, was forced into retirement, and Eratosthenes, known as a scholar and poet in the tradition of Callimachus, was summoned from Athens to replace him. The post included tutoring the future Ptolemy IV Philopator. Eratosthenes was closely associated with Archimedes, who addressed his Method of Mechanical Theorems to him as a letter. According to the Suda, his sight failed in old age and he starved himself to death. His epitaph laments that he was buried in a foreign land and not at Cyrene.

His best-known measurement is the circumference of the Earth. As Cleomedes reports it, at noon on the summer solstice the sun shone straight down a well at Syene, while at Alexandria a vertical rod still cast a shadow of about 7.2 degrees, one fiftieth of a circle. Taking the distance between the cities as about 5,000 stadia, he multiplied by fifty to reach roughly 250,000 stadia. The method was sound, though two false assumptions, that Syene lay on the Tropic of Cancer and on the same meridian as Alexandria, happened to cancel each other out.

His three-volume Geography, which survives only in fragments, mostly in Strabo, mapped the known world, divided the Earth into five climate zones and used parallels and meridians to place more than 400 cities. He is credited with coining the word geography. In his Chronographies he dated the fall of Troy to 1184/1183 BCE. The sieve of Eratosthenes, which finds prime numbers by marking off the multiples of each prime, carries his name, though one scholar holds that he named an older method. Admirers called him Pentathlos, the all-rounder.
erbil: Erbil lies on a plain beneath the mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan. The modern town stands on a tell topped by an Ottoman fort, and the Citadel of Erbil and the Mudhafaria Minaret are at its heart. The name comes from the Sumerian Urbilum, through Assyrian Arbaʾilu, and in classical antiquity it was Arbela. Settlement may date back to the 5th millennium BCE. Because the site has been so heavily occupied it has never been properly excavated, though surveys of the western slope found pottery from the Neolithic to the Middle Bronze Age and more from later periods.

The earliest literary mention is in the archives of Ebla, which record two journeys to Irbilum by a messenger around 2300 BCE. Erridupizir, king of Gutium, captured the city in 2150 BCE. After the fall of the Ur III empire it became a power in its area, was conquered by Shamsi-Adad and regained independence. By the Middle Assyrian Empire it lay within the Assyrian zone, and its patron deity was Ishtar of Arbela. After the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE Darius III is said to have fled to the city, and the battle is sometimes inaccurately called the Battle of Arbela.

Between the mid-second century BCE and the early 2nd century CE Erbil was the capital of Adiabene, whose royal family, notably Queen Helena, converted to Judaism. Its people turned gradually to Christianity, with Pkidha traditionally its first bishop around 104, and it became a centre of Syriac Christianity. The Turkmen Begtegenid emirs ruled it from 1131 to 1232, most notably Gökböri, one of Saladin's leading generals. The Mongols took the citadel after a six-month siege following the fall of Baghdad in 1258, its Assyrian defenders were massacred on 1 July 1310, and Timur's forces destroyed the city in 1397. The Ottomans took it in 1851.

Erbil is the capital and most populated city of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and of the Erbil Governorate. The Citadel of Erbil was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014. The city's archaeological museum holds a large collection of pre-Islamic artefacts, particularly of Mesopotamian art. The parliament of Iraqi Kurdistan was established there in 1970.
ercole-consalvi: Ercole Consalvi was born in Rome on 8 June 1757, the son of Mario Giuseppe Consalvi, Marquess of Toscanella, and Countess Claudia Carandini of Modena. The family descended from the Brunacci of Pisa; his grandfather had taken the Consalvi name to inherit a fortune. After his father's death in 1763 he was placed in the care of Cardinal Andrea Negroni. He studied with the Piarists and at the seminary in Frascati founded by Cardinal Henry Benedict Stuart, who helped him to high office in the Roman Curia, and he took doctorates in civil and canon law at La Sapienza in 1789.

When the French Revolutionary Army invaded Italy in 1798, Consalvi was jailed in the Castel Sant'Angelo, but he was soon released and joined Pope Pius VI in exile. He was secretary of the conclave in Venice that elected Pope Pius VII, who made him cardinal-deacon and secretary of state in August 1800. He introduced free trade in the Papal States, withdrew depreciated money and admitted many laymen to government offices. He was ordained subdeacon and deacon in December 1801, but never priest or bishop.

His opposition to the Papal States joining the Continental System forced his resignation in June 1806. After France annexed the Papal States in 1809 he was taken to Paris, refused a pension of 30,000 francs from Napoleon, and in 1810 was one of thirteen black cardinals stripped of property and status for refusing to attend Napoleon's marriage to Archduchess Marie Louise. Confined at Reims, he rejoined the pope in 1813 and persuaded him to retract the concessions of the Concordat of Fontainebleau. Exiled again to Béziers, he was freed on 2 April 1814 and reappointed secretary of state.

As papal plenipotentiary he set out a policy of papal neutrality, first stated at the Neapolitan revolt of 1821. For the rest of Pius VII's pontificate he was the virtual ruler of Rome, concluding another concordat with France in 1817 and helping to re-establish the English College in 1818. A highly cultivated man devoted to music and archaeology, he laid out promenades along the Tiber, restored ancient monuments and filled the museums with statues from excavations. He secured the Protestant sculptor Thorvaldsen's commission for Pius VII's tomb in St Peter's. He died on 24 January 1824 and is buried in San Marcello al Corso.
ercole-i-d-este: Ercole was born on 26 October 1431 in Ferrara, the son of Niccolò III d'Este and Ricciarda of Saluzzo. From 1445 to 1460 he was educated at the Neapolitan court of Alfonso, king of Aragon and Naples, where he studied the military arts and chivalry and acquired a taste for architecture and the fine arts in the manner of antiquity.

In 1471 he became duke on the death of his half-brother Borso, with the support of the Republic of Venice, taking advantage of the absence in Mantua of Borso's son Niccolò. Niccolò later attempted a coup while Ercole was away from Ferrara; it was crushed, and Niccolò and his cousin Azzo were beheaded on 4 September 1476. In 1473 Ercole married Eleonora d'Aragon, daughter of Ferdinand I of Naples.

The War of Ferrara, fought from 1482 to 1484 against Venice, which was allied with Pope Sixtus IV, arose from disputes over the salt monopoly. It ended with the Peace of Bagnolo. Ferrara escaped destruction or absorption into the papal dominions, but the war was a humiliation for Ercole, who lay sick and immobilised while the besieging army destroyed Este properties around the city.

Afterwards he stayed neutral in the Italian War of 1494 to 1495 and tried to improve relations with the papacy. He reluctantly agreed to the marriage of his son Alfonso to Lucrezia Borgia, daughter of Pope Alexander VI, which brought notable territorial gifts.

He admired the preacher Girolamo Savonarola, also from Ferrara, and about a dozen letters between them survive from the 1490s. Ercole tried without success to have him freed by the Florentine church authorities; Savonarola was burned in 1498. In 1503 or 1504 Ercole asked his newly hired composer Josquin des Prez for a musical testament, and the result was a Miserere built on Savonarola's prison meditation Infelix ego.

Ercole's patronage was in part a political and cultural statement, and he was the only Italian ruler to style himself divus on his coinage, like a Roman emperor. He staged plays with elaborate scenery and musical intermezzi, among the first purely secular theatre in Europe since antiquity, and built a musical establishment that for some years was the finest in Europe. Composers such as Alexander Agricola, Jacob Obrecht, Heinrich Isaac, Adrian Willaert and Josquin des Prez worked for him or dedicated music to him; Josquin's Missa Hercules dux Ferrariae takes its theme from the syllables of the duke's name.

He brought Ludovico Ariosto into his household. Under his direction Ferrara roughly doubled in size, in a planned extension that was the first executed urban project of the Renaissance, with walls and buildings by the architect Biagio Rossetti. Ercole died on 25 January 1505, and his son Alfonso became duke.
erdene-zuu: Abtai Sain Khan, ruler of the Khalkha Mongols and grandfather of Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, ordered the building of Erdene Zuu in 1585, after meeting the 3rd Dalai Lama and the declaration of Tibetan Buddhism as the state religion of Mongolia. The monastery, at Kharkhorin in Övörkhangai Province, belongs to the Gelug sect of Tibetan Buddhism. Stones from the nearby ruins of the thirteenth-century Mongol capital of Karakorum were used in its construction. The planners meant the surrounding wall to resemble a Tibetan Buddhist rosary of 108 stupas, 108 being a sacred number in Buddhism.

The temple walls of the monastery were painted, and its Chinese-style roof was covered with green tiles. It stands within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape World Heritage Site. It was damaged in 1688 in one of the many wars between the Dzungars and the Khalkha Mongols, and local people dismantled the wooden fortifications of the abandoned monastery. According to tradition, a local disciple named Bunia made several unsuccessful attempts in 1745 to fly with a device of his own invention, similar to a parachute.

The communist leader Khorloogiin Choibalsan ordered the monastery destroyed in a political purge that destroyed hundreds of Mongolian monasteries and killed more than ten thousand monks. Three small temples and the external wall with the stupas survived. By 1944 Joseph Stalin pressured Choibalsan to keep the monastery, with Gandantegchinlen Monastery in Ulaanbaatar, as a showpiece for visitors such as the US Vice President Henry Wallace, to show that the communist regime allowed freedom of religion. In 1947 the temples became museums, and for four decades Gandantegchinlen was Mongolia's only functioning monastery. After the fall of communism in 1990 the monastery was handed to the lamas, who restored it as a place of worship; it is also a museum open to visitors.
erechtheion: The classical Erechtheion is the last of a series of buildings on the north side of the Acropolis, the earliest dating to the late Bronze Age Mycenaean period. Before the Persian destruction of Athens in 480 BCE a temple probably stood on the site. The building accounts for 409 to 404 BCE survive, which allows an unusually secure dating of the work, but no primary evidence shows when construction began. Work seems to have ended in 406 to 405 BCE, with some mouldings left unfinished. The overseers Philokles and Archilochos are named, while the architect is unknown; Mnesikles, Kallikrates and Iktinos have all been proposed.

Its asymmetrical plan does not follow the canon of Greek temples. This is attributed to the irregular site, to the complex cults it housed, or to the possibility that it is part of a larger symmetrical design that was never completed. It is built of Pentelic marble with a frieze of blue Eleusinian limestone, to which white marble figures were attached. Its best-known feature is the Porch of the Maidens, where six sculpted female figures carry the roof. Their identity is debated, and copies found at Tivoli in 1952 showed that they carried phialai.

The building probably held a collection of religious objects rather than serving one deity. Scholars place there the old image of Athena Polias, altars of Poseidon and Erechtheus, the tomb of Kekrops, a saltwater well, and nearby the sacred olive tree of Athena. Official decrees call it only the temple on the Acropolis within which is the ancient statue.

After damage in antiquity the building was converted to Christian use, by the late 6th or 7th century as a three-aisled basilica. Under Frankish rule from 1204 it became a bishop's residence, and under Ottoman control it is traditionally said to have been the garrison commander's harem, though Turkish sources do not support this. Lord Elgin removed one of the caryatids, which ended up in the British Museum, and cannon fire in the siege of 1826 to 1827 felled the Maiden Porch and the west facade.

Spon and Wheler's account of 1682 first identified the building with Pausanias's Temple of Athena Polias. Stuart and Revett published accurate drawings in 1787, which spread the Ionic style among architects. Kyriakos Pittakis made the first reconstruction, and Nikolaos Balanos a second in 1902 to 1909. His steel joints caused damage, and the Acropolis Restoration Service was set up in 1975.
erfurt: Erfurt lies in the wide valley of the River Gera, in the southern part of the Thuringian Basin, north of the Thuringian Forest and in the middle of a line of six large Thuringian cities that runs from Eisenach through Gotha, Erfurt and Weimar to Jena and Gera. The town stands on the Via Regia, a medieval network of trade and pilgrim roads. The Thuringi inhabited the area around 480 and gave their name to Thuringia around 500.

The town is first mentioned in 742 as Erphesfurt, when Saint Boniface wrote to Pope Zachary that he had established three dioceses in central Germany, one of them in a place long inhabited by pagan natives. Zachary confirmed them the next year, though in 755 Erfurt was brought into the diocese of Mainz.

Although it belonged to none of the Thuringian states, it quickly became the economic centre of the region and joined the Hanseatic League. In the Holy Roman Empire it was part of the Electorate of Mainz. Around 1500 it had 18,000 inhabitants and was one of the largest cities in the Empire. The Erfurt Treasure, a hoard of coins and goldsmiths' work, is assumed to have belonged to Jews who hid it in 1349, at the time of the Black Death pogroms.

Meister Eckhart entered the Dominican monastery in Erfurt around 1275. Martin Luther began his studies at the university in 1501, entered St Augustine's Monastery as a friar in 1505, and was ordained in Erfurt Cathedral in 1507. The city adopted the Protestant Reformation early, in 1521. Erfurt passed to Prussia in 1802, was handed over to the French on 16 October 1806, and became the Principality of Erfurt, directly subject to Napoleon. In 1850 it saw the failed Erfurt Union of German states. From 1949 to 1990 the city was part of East Germany.

Erfurt is the capital and largest city of Thuringia, with about 216,000 inhabitants. Its old town is one of the best preserved medieval city centres in Germany, with about 25 churches and monasteries, many Gothic, which earned it the nickname Thuringian Rome. The Merchants' Bridge over the Gera carries houses, and Erfurt Cathedral holds the bell Gloriosa, the largest free-swinging medieval bell in the world. The Old Synagogue, the Erfurt Mikveh and the Stone House form the UNESCO World Heritage Site Jewish-Medieval Heritage of Erfurt. The Petersberg Citadel is one of the largest and best preserved town fortresses in Central Europe.
eric-bloodaxe: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle describes Eric only as Harold's son, and Norwegian histories and Icelandic sagas identify him as a son of the Norwegian king Harald Fairhair. The sagas are of limited historical value. Heimskringla names his mother as Ragnhildr, daughter of Eric, king of South Jutland, and says he was fostered by the hersir Thórir son of Hróald. It also tells that at the age of twelve he began a career of piracy, harrying the Baltic coasts, Scotland, Wales, Ireland and France. The origin of his nickname Bloodaxe is uncertain. The sagas usually explain it as referring to his killing of half-brothers, while Fagrskinna ascribes it to his violent reputation as a raider.

According to Heimskringla, Harald appointed his sons as client kings and intended Eric, his favourite, to inherit the throne. Eric killed his half-brothers Ragnvald and Bjørn Farmann and, when Harald died, defeated the combined forces of Olaf and Sigrød, ruling Norway from 932 to 934. His rule was reputedly harsh, and the nobility turned against him. His half-brother Haakon, who had been raised at the court of King Æthelstan, returned and ousted him, and Eric fled to Britain.

The English sources show Eric as King of Northumbria more firmly, though they give scanty detail and a confused chronology. His first reign, from 947 or 948 to 948, followed Eadred's attempt to bring the Northumbrians under his control. He was driven out, and Amlaíb returned. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports that in 952 the Northumbrians drove out King Olaf and accepted Eric, son of Harold, and in 954 they expelled him again. Coins minted at York bear his name, in two types, with the moneyers Ingalger and Radulf. The Life of St Cathróe of Metz says that his wife at York was a relative of the saint, probably of British or Scottish descent, whereas Egils saga names her Gunnhild.

The Flores historiarum of Roger of Wendover says that Eric was treacherously killed at Stainmore, betrayed by Earl Oswulf, by Earl Maccus, together with his son Haeric and his brother Ragnald, and that King Eadred then ruled the region. Fagrskinna cites the Eiríksmál, a poem said to have been commissioned by his widow Gunnhild, in which Eric is welcomed to Valhöll by Odin. The Rey Cross on Stainmore, an Anglo-Scandinavian cross possibly of the 10th century, has been linked to the battle, though no evidence supports this. In the sagas Eric became a mixture of history, folklore and political propaganda, a powerful warrior who was cruel and unpopular as a ruler.
eric-hobsbawm: Eric Hobsbawm was born in 1917 in Alexandria, Egypt, the son of Leopold Percy Hobsbaum, a Jewish merchant from the East End of London, and Nelly Hobsbaum, from an Austrian Jewish family. A clerical error at birth changed the spelling of his surname. His early childhood was spent in Vienna and Berlin, and English was his first language. His father died in 1929 and his mother in 1931, and he and his sister Nancy were adopted by an aunt and uncle. He joined a socialist pupils' association in Berlin in 1931, and in 1933, as the Nazi Party came to power, the family moved to London.

Hobsbawm attended King's College, Cambridge, from 1936 and joined the Communist Party of Great Britain through the university's Socialist Club. He took a double-starred first in history and wrote his doctoral dissertation on the Fabian Society. In the Second World War he served in the Royal Engineers and the Army Educational Corps. MI5 opened a file on him in 1942, and he says its monitoring affected his career. In 1947 he became a lecturer at Birkbeck College, University of London, where he was reader from 1959 and professor from 1970. He helped found the journal Past and Present in 1952 and retired in 1982 as emeritus professor.

He remained in the Communist Party after the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956 but ceased political work by the end of that decade. After 1968 he was a leading figure in its Eurocommunist faction. Outside academic writing he wrote a jazz column for the New Statesman under the name Francis Newton. He became president of Birkbeck in 2002, received the Balzan Prize in 2003, and died on 1 October 2012 at the age of 95.

Hobsbawm analysed what he called the dual revolution, the political French Revolution and the British Industrial Revolution, and he coined the term long nineteenth century, running from 1789 to 1914. His tetralogy comprises The Age of Revolution, The Age of Capital, The Age of Empire and The Age of Extremes, the last on the short twentieth century. A recurring theme was social banditry, which he placed in its social and historical context instead of treating it as spontaneous primitive rebellion. He also edited the volume that introduced the influential idea of invented traditions. His later writings include On Empire (2008) and How to Change the World (2011).
eric-iv-of-denmark: Eric was born about 1216, the second legitimate son of King Valdemar II of Denmark and his second wife, Berengária of Portugal. In 1218 his older half-brother Valdemar the Young was crowned co-ruler and heir and made Duke of Schleswig. After Valdemar's early death in 1231, Eric was crowned king at Lund Cathedral on 30 May 1232 as his father's co-ruler and heir, and gave the Duchy of Schleswig to his younger brother Abel. When their father died in 1241, Eric took the throne. His brothers included Abel and Christopher, who would both be kings of Denmark after him.

Eric's reign was marked by conflict with his brother Abel, who seems to have wanted an independent position and was supported by the counts of Holstein, and with the Church. The Scanian peasants rebelled against his heavy taxes, including one on ploughs, a measure of a man's wealth, which gave him the name Ploughpenny. His quarrel with Abel began in 1242 and ended in a truce in 1244, with plans for a joint crusade to Estonia.

Meanwhile the religious orders claimed immunity from his taxes, and in 1245 a papal nuncio met the king and bishops at Odense, with excommunication threatened for anyone who infringed the Church's privileges. In 1249 Eric confiscated the properties of Niels Stigsen, Bishop of Roskilde, including the growing town of Copenhagen, and the bishop fled and died at Clairvaux Abbey the same year, despite the intervention of Pope Innocent IV.

Fighting with Abel resumed in 1246, when Eric invaded Holstein. Abel and the Holsteiners, backed by Lübeck, raided Jutland and Funen the following year. Eric retook Ribe, occupied Svendborg and captured Arreskov Castle, taking his brothers Christopher and Canute prisoner, and a truce arranged by his sister Sophie left him in firm control of Denmark. Scanian peasants rose again in 1249. After securing Estonia that year, Eric marched into Holstein in 1250, and Abel invited him to his house at Gottorp.

There the duke's chamberlain and others seized the king, bound him and rowed him out on the Schlien, where he was beheaded with an axe and his body dumped in the water. Fishermen found it the next morning, and in 1257 it was moved to St Bendt's Church, Ringsted. Abel was sworn in as king and denied any part in the murder. He was himself killed within a year and a half, and Christopher succeeded him.
eric-of-pomerania: Erik was born at Darłowo, then called Rügenwalde, in Pomerania. He was named Bogislaw at birth and was the son of Wartislaw VII, Duke of Pomerania. Queen Margaret I, his great-aunt, wanted her three kingdoms to remain united and chose him as her heir. In 1389 he was brought to Denmark to be raised by her, and his name was changed to the more Nordic-sounding Erik. On 8 September 1389 he was hailed as king of Norway at the Ting in Trondheim.

He was proclaimed king in Denmark and then in Sweden in 1396, and on 17 June 1397 he was crowned king of the three countries in Kalmar cathedral. A union treaty drafted at the same time established the Kalmar Union, although Margaret remained the de facto ruler until her death in 1412.

In 1417 Erik made Copenhagen a royal possession, which secured its status as the capital of Denmark. From 1423 to May 1425 he made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, where he was dubbed a Knight of the Holy Sepulchre. Almost the whole of his sole rule was shaped by conflict with the counts of Schauenburg and Holstein over South Jutland. His choice of war over negotiation led to a devastating conflict that ended without conquests and cost him the areas he had won.

In 1429 he introduced the Sound Dues, paid by all ships passing through the Sound into or out of the Baltic, which lasted until 1857. He built the fortress of Krogen at the narrowest point to enforce them. They gave the crown a large, stable income and helped the town of Elsinore flourish, but they challenged the Baltic powers, especially the Hanseatic cities. From 1426 to 1435 he was at war with the Hanseatic League and Holstein, and the Peace of Vordingborg of 17 July 1435 exempted the Hanseatic cities from the dues and ceded Schleswig to the count of Holstein. In 1434 Swedish farmers and mine workers rose in the Engelbrekt rebellion, which the Swedish nobility used to weaken him.

When the Danish nobility refused to accept his choice of Bogislaw IX of Pomerania as his successor, Erik left Denmark for Visborg Castle on Gotland. The councils of Denmark and Sweden deposed him in 1439, and Norway followed in 1440, with a formal deposition in 1442. His nephew Christopher of Bavaria was chosen as king.

From 1449 to 1459 Erik ruled Pomerania-Rügenwalde, a small partition of Pomerania-Stolp, as Erik I. He died at Darłowo Castle in 1459 and was buried in St Mary's Church there. His epithet of Pomerania was a pejorative, meant to suggest that he did not belong in Scandinavia.
eric-the-victorious: Eric is the first Swedish king in a consecutive succession who is attested in sources independent of each other, which is why Sweden's list of rulers usually begins with him. His original territory lay in Uppland and neighbouring provinces; the extent of his kingdom is unknown, but it may have reached down the Baltic coast as far south as Blekinge. The Flateyjarbok credits his success to an alliance with free farmers against an earl-class nobility. He probably introduced the system of universal conscription known as ledung in the provinces around Lake Mälaren, and in all probability founded the town of Sigtuna, where the first Swedish coins were later minted for his son Olof.

The sagas tell of his nephew Styrbjörn the Strong, said to be a son of Eric's brother Olof. When the Swedes refused to accept Styrbjörn as co-ruler, Eric gave him 60 longships, and Styrbjörn became ruler of Jomsborg and an ally of the Danish king Harold Bluetooth, whose daughter Tyra he married. He returned to Sweden with an army and was defeated by Eric at the Battle of Fýrisvellir near Uppsala. According to one saga, Eric first sacrificed to Odin and promised to give himself to Odin in ten years if he won. Two skaldic verses by Thorvaldr Hjaltason describe the battle, and the runestones of Hällestad and Sjörup mention a battle at Uppsala, though they may be from the next century.

The oldest narrative, by Adam of Bremen around 1075, differs substantially from the sagas. It says Eric invaded Denmark against King Swein Forkbeard, who was forced to flee to Norway, England and finally Scotland, and that Eric kept Denmark for a time. Saxo Grammaticus likewise says Eric ruled Denmark for seven years. Details of the conquest have been questioned, and the historian Peter Sawyer calls Adam's account a gross distortion, but Sture Bolin considers the conquest likely. Adam also reports that Eric, at first hostile to Christianity, accepted baptism and later reverted to the religion of his ancestors.

Adam's account places Eric's death between 992 and 995, and Snorri Sturlasson says he died in Uppsala. The sources name several wives, Sigrid, Świętosława, Gunhild and Aud, of whom two or three may be the same woman under different names. His only historically attested child is Olof Skötkonung, who died in 1022 and is considered the first ruler documented as accepted by both the Swedes around Lake Mälaren and the Geats around Lake Vättern.
eric-williams: Eric Eustace Williams was born on 25 September 1911. His father, Thomas Henry Williams, was a minor civil servant and a devout Roman Catholic; his mother, Eliza Frances Boissiere, belonged to the mixed French Creole and African de Boissière family. He attended Queen's Royal College in Port of Spain, where he excelled at studies and football, and in 1932 won an island scholarship to St. Catherine's Society, Oxford. He took a first in 1935, ranking first among that year's history graduates, and completed his doctorate in 1938 under Vincent Harlow. In his autobiography Inward Hunger he described the racial discrimination he met at Oxford.

His thesis was published in 1944 as Capitalism and Slavery. It attacked the view that moral and humanitarian motives had been the key to British abolition and argued that economic change drove it; it owed much to C. L. R. James. He joined Howard University in 1939 and in 1944 the Anglo-American Caribbean Commission, and in 1948 he returned to Trinidad as deputy chairman of its Caribbean Research Council. After the Commission did not renew his contract in 1955 he gave public lectures at Woodford Square, which he called the University of Woodford Square. On 15 January 1956 he founded the People's National Movement. In the election of 24 September 1956 it won 13 of 24 elected seats, and he became Chief Minister.

He supported a West Indies Federation but turned against it after the Democratic Labour Party's victory in the federal elections of 1958. After Jamaica withdrew, he took Trinidad and Tobago out on the strength of a resolution of 15 January 1962, remarking that 'one from ten leaves nought', and the federation was dissolved. Independence followed on 31 August 1962. In April 1970, during the Black Power protests, he declared a state of emergency, and part of the defence force mutinied before surrendering on 25 April.

Williams died on 29 March 1981 at his official house in Port of Spain, aged 69. Later scholars have disputed Capitalism and Slavery: David Brion Davis called the decline thesis discredited, and Seymour Drescher's Econocide argued that Britain's sugar economy was thriving in 1807. Others note that Williams also treated the decline of sugar from the 1820s and the sugar duties of the 1840s, and that this part of his argument still influences the historiography. His papers are in the Eric Williams Memorial Collection at the University of the West Indies, named to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1999.
erich-ludendorff: Erich Ludendorff was born on 9 April 1865 at Kruszewnia near Posen, in the Prussian Province of Posen, the third of six children of a family descended from Pomeranian merchants. He was commissioned as a junior officer in 1885 and entered the War Academy in 1893. The next year he was recommended for the General Staff, and from 1904 to 1913 he directed the Mobilisation Section of the Great General Staff in Berlin under Alfred von Schlieffen, where he helped oversee development of the Schlieffen Plan. In 1910 he married Margarethe Schmidt.

At the outbreak of war in 1914 Ludendorff was deputy chief of staff of the German Second Army. When the brigade commander was killed, he led the assault that took Liège, and he received the Pour le Mérite. He was then made chief of staff to Paul von Hindenburg on the Eastern Front. Nine days after their arrival the Eighth Army surrounded most of a Russian army at Tannenberg and took 92,000 prisoners. On 29 August 1916 Hindenburg became head of the Supreme Army Command and Ludendorff First Quartermaster General with joint responsibility. From then they directed Germany's whole strategy and war effort, and put army officers into the economy and the ministries.

Their command supported unrestricted submarine warfare, begun in February 1917, and helped Lenin and about thirty other exiles return to Russia from Switzerland by train. On the Western Front they introduced an elastic defence in depth and, with Russia out of the war, launched Operation Michael on 21 March 1918. It made large advances but lost as many men as it killed, and among the dead was Ludendorff's eldest stepson. By late 1918 a string of defeats culminated in the Hundred Days Offensive of the Allies, and Kaiser Wilhelm II forced Ludendorff to resign.

After the war Ludendorff became a prominent nationalist leader and promoted the stab-in-the-back myth, which blamed Germany's defeat on a treasonous conspiracy of Marxists, Freemasons and Jews. He took part in the failed Kapp Putsch of 1920 and Adolf Hitler's Beer Hall Putsch of 1923, and stood unsuccessfully in the 1925 presidential election. In his last years he studied military theory, and his best-known work, The Total War, argued that a nation's whole resources should remain ready for mobilisation, because peace was merely an interval between wars. He died of liver cancer in Munich on 20 December 1937 and was given, against his wishes, a state funeral organised and attended by Hitler.
erich-muhsam: Erich Mühsam was born in Berlin on 6 April 1878, the third child of Siegfried Seligmann Mühsam, a Jewish pharmacist, and his wife Rosalie. The family soon moved to Lübeck, where he attended the Katharineum-Gymnasium, a school known for harsh discipline. In January 1896 he wrote an anonymous piece denouncing a teacher, and when his authorship was discovered he was expelled for socialist activities. He finished school in Parchim. His father made him study pharmacy, which he abandoned for a literary life, and in 1900 he moved to Berlin, where he joined the communal group Neue Gemeinschaft and met the anarchist Gustav Landauer.

In 1904 Mühsam withdrew to an artists' commune in Ascona and began writing plays, the first being Die Hochstapler. He edited anarchist journals, was under constant police surveillance, and in 1908 moved to Munich, where he wrote cabaret songs that became among his best-known work. In 1911 he founded the newspaper Kain, which ridiculed the state and opposed capital punishment and theatre censorship.

In 1915 he married Kreszentia Elfinger. Early in the First World War he wrote in support of Germany, but renounced that position by the end of 1914 and later took part in strikes against the war. He was arrested in April 1918 and held until 3 November 1918.

In the revolution that followed Mühsam refused a ministry offered by Kurt Eisner and worked with Landauer, Ernst Toller and others for workers' councils. After Eisner's assassination the Bavarian Soviet Republic was proclaimed, and it lasted only six days before communists led by Eugen Levine overthrew it. When Freikorps troops took Munich, Landauer was killed and Mühsam was arrested and sentenced to fifteen years in fortress confinement. In prison he wrote the play Judas and many poems. After his release under the amnesty of 1924 he founded the journal Fanal in 1926 and satirised the Nazis, notably in the short story Die Affenschande.

Mühsam was arrested without charge on 28 February 1933, hours after the Reichstag fire, and Joseph Goebbels named him among Jewish subversives. Over the next seventeen months he was held at Sonnenburg, Brandenburg and Oranienburg camps and repeatedly beaten and tortured. On the night of 9 July 1934 he was killed, and his body was found hanging in a latrine the next morning. An official Nazi report of 11 July called it suicide in protective custody; his widow, Zenzl, said the body bore signs of strangulation. Later accounts named the former Dachau commander Theodor Eicke as the murderer.
erie-canal: Before railroads, water transport was the cheapest way to ship bulk goods: a mule that could carry about 250 pounds could draw a barge of as much as 60,000 pounds along a towpath, and a canal could cut transport costs by about 95 percent. A canal from the Hudson River to the Great Lakes was first proposed in the 1780s, and the New York State Legislature authorised construction in 1817 after a survey in 1808. Opponents, referring to its chief supporter, Governor DeWitt Clinton, called the project Clinton's Folly and Clinton's Big Ditch.

The original canal ran 363 miles from Albany to Buffalo, cut 40 feet wide and 4 feet deep, with the soil piled on the downhill side to form a towpath. Animals pulled slip scrapers to move earth, and all labour depended on human and animal power or the force of water. Irish labourers and German stonemasons built it, and aqueducts carried it across rivers. It opened on 26 October 1825, and toll revenue covered the state's construction debt within the first year.

Feeder canals soon extended it into a system, including the Champlain Canal north from Troy and the Oswego Canal to Lake Ontario. The planned annual tonnage of 1.5 million tons was exceeded at once, and a First Enlargement from 1834 widened the canal to 70 feet and deepened it to 7 feet; it was declared complete in 1862.

Freight boats were pulled by horses and mules walking on a single towpath. Packet boats carried passengers at up to five miles per hour, more frequently than stagecoaches. The canal greatly lowered costs: a barrel of flour from Rochester to Albany fell from $3 to 75 cents. It brought cheaper food to eastern cities and let the East ship manufactured goods west, and gave New York City a strong advantage over all other US ports. Irish immigrants formed communities in towns along its route.

A continuous railway reached Buffalo by 1842, and passengers soon switched to it, yet in 1852 the canal carried thirteen times more freight tonnage than all the railroads in New York State combined. Between 1905 and 1918 the Barge Canal was built, and over half the original route was abandoned. Commercial traffic declined in the later 20th century, and the canal is now used mainly by recreational craft.
erigavo: Erigavo, in Somali Ceerigaabo, stands on the Sanaag escarpment in northern Somalia. Somali sources explain the name as ceeri, a place where water collects, and gaabo, short or low, and some writers link ceeri to ceeriyaan, mist or fog. About 2 kilometres west the massif rises to Shimbiris, the highest point in Somaliland at about 2,460 metres, and remnant juniper woodlands lie about 10 kilometres north, above a sharp drop to the Gulf of Aden coastal plain.

The altitude gives a mild semi-arid climate with average annual rainfall of about 435 millimetres, falling mostly in the Gu rains of April to June and the Deyr of October and November. The area is a centre for collecting and trading frankincense, from Boswellia carteri and Boswellia frereana, and livestock trade is central to local livelihoods.

The settlement is several centuries old. Modern Erigavo was founded by the Musa Ismail sub-clan of the Habr Yunis as a home well for passing nomads and caravans. In July 1945 Sheikh Bashir, a religious leader, led a rebellion against British authority in the Somaliland protectorate, attacking Burao. He called on religious figures in Erigavo to join, and people there rose with rifles and spears. The British reinforced the town, fired on the crowds in two local actions and arrested minor religious leaders. On 7 July British forces found Bashir and his second-in-command, Alin Yusuf Ali, at Bur Dhab and killed them, but resistance continued, especially at Erigavo and Badhan.

In the last years of the Barre regime the town saw conflict between the Somali National Movement insurgency and government reprisals, and reports record killings and arrests in 1989. After Somaliland's declaration of 1991, local reconciliations culminated in the Erigavo Peace Charter of 31 August 1993. In mid-December 2024 armed clashes between Somaliland security forces and SSC-Khaatumo fighters displaced many people, and in January 2025 Puntland's president urged dialogue.

Erigavo is the administrative seat of the Sanaag region and its main commercial hub, administered by Somaliland and also claimed by Puntland. Published estimates of its population vary with the area counted, from about 30,000 for the town in a 2013 assessment to 180,000 for the district in a 2011 text. Its clans include the Habr Je'lo, Habr Yunis, Warsangali and Dhulbahante. A road of about 284 kilometres links it to Burao, and onward to the Port of Berbera, and Sanaag University has its seat in the town.
erik-the-red: According to the Icelandic sagas, Erik Thorvaldsson was born in the Jæren district of Rogaland, Norway, the son of Thorvald Asvaldsson. Thorvald was banished from Norway for manslaughter and sailed west with his family, including the ten-year-old Erik. They settled in Hornstrandir in north-western Iceland, where Thorvald died before 970. Erik later married Þjódhild Jorundsdottir and built a farm called Eiríksstaðir in Haukadalr. Tradition gives them at least three sons, among them Leif Erikson. Erik most likely earned his epithet from the colour of his hair and beard.

Like his father, Erik was exiled. His thralls caused a landslide on a neighbouring farm, and a kinsman of the owner, Eyjolf the Foul, killed them. Erik killed Eyjolf and Hrafn the Dueller. He moved to the islands of Brokey and Öxney, where a quarrel with a man named Thorgest over his father's carved pillars ended in the deaths of Thorgest's two sons. At the Thorsnes Thing, Erik and his allies were outlawed from Iceland for three years.

Erik used the time to explore Greenland, whose coast the outlaw Snæbjörn galti had visited some years before and which, by tradition, Gunnbjörn Ulfsson had sighted nearly a century earlier. He rounded Cape Farewell and sailed up the western coast. On his return he gave the land an appealing name, saying that people would be drawn to it if it sounded favourable. In 985 he went back with colonists: of 25 ships that left, 14 arrived. They founded the Eastern Settlement, in what is now Qaqortoq, and the Western Settlement near present-day Nuuk.

At Brattahlíð, near present-day Narsarsuaq, Erik held the title of paramount chieftain of Greenland and became wealthy and respected. The Eastern Settlement grew to about 5,000 inhabitants along Eriksfjord and neighbouring fjords. Erik remained a follower of Norse paganism, while his wife and his son Leif became Christians. When Leif sailed for Vinland, Erik fell from his horse on the way to the ship and took it as a bad omen. He died in a winter epidemic, brought by a group of immigrants who arrived in 1002. The colony lasted until the Little Ice Age made the land marginal for European ways of life in the 15th century, with raids, conflict with the Inuit and abandonment by Norway also playing a part.
eritrea: Eritrea lies between latitudes 12° and 18°N on the Red Sea, with a total area of approximately 117,600 square kilometres that includes the Dahlak Archipelago and several of the Hanish Islands. A branch of the East African Rift bisects the country. A hot, arid coastal plain gives way to cooler and more fertile highlands that reach up to 3,000 metres and are a northern extension of the Ethiopian Highlands. The highest point is Emba Soira, at 3,018 metres.

Fossil remains known as Madam Buya, found at an Eritrean site by Italian anthropologists, have been dated to 1 million years old. Tools from the Barka Valley dating from 8,000 BCE appear to give the first concrete evidence of settlement, and excavations near Agordat found the pre-Aksumite Gash Group, with ceramics dated to between 2,500 and 1,500 BCE. Parts of Eritrea were likely part of the Land of Punt around 2,000 BCE, known from Egyptian records of trade expeditions.

The Kingdom of Aksum, centred in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, was established in the first or second century CE, and the Persian prophet Mani considered it one of the four great powers of the world. It adopted Christianity around the middle of the fourth century. From the 12th century the Zagwe and Solomonid dynasties held fluctuating control over the plateau and the Red Sea coast. In the 16th century the Ottomans failed to conquer the Ethiopian Highlands and were limited to the Eritrean coastline.

The coast came under the Khedivate of Egypt in May 1865 and passed to Italy in February 1885, and Italian Eritrea was formed in 1889. After British administration from 1942, Eritrea federated with Ethiopia under a UN decision of 1952, and Ethiopia annexed it in 1962. Eritrea won de facto independence in 1991 and de jure independence in 1993 after a referendum.

Asmara is the capital and largest city. The name Eritrea derives from the Greek name for the Red Sea, the Erythraean Sea, and was formally adopted in 1890. The country has nine recognised ethnic groups, each with a distinct language, and Tigrinya is the most widely spoken. Most people are Christian or Muslim. On 8 July 2017 the entire city of Asmara, with its Art Deco, futurist and modernist buildings from the Italian period, was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
eritrean-liberation-front: Under a United Nations resolution Eritrea became part of Ethiopia in 1952 with its own autonomous government. Emperor Haile Selassie dismantled that autonomy step by step: the Eritrean Trade Union was outlawed in 1953, the National Assembly ceased to exist in 1956, and Amharic replaced Arabic and Tigrinya as the official language. The Eritrean Liberation Movement, founded in 1958 among students and workers, organised protests but proved unable to move to armed struggle. Egypt meanwhile trained Eritreans, among them Idris Muhammad Adam, at a camp in Alexandria modelled on the methods of Algeria's national liberation front.

The ELF was openly founded in Cairo in July 1960 by Idris Muhammad Adam and other intellectuals and students, mostly Muslim, and it adopted Pan-Arab beliefs. Hamid Idris Awate, a former soldier of the Italian colonial era, opened the fighting on 1 September 1961 in the western lowlands near Sudan, its safe haven; after his death in June 1962 his group merged with the ELF. Ethiopia annexed Eritrea on 14 November 1962. Armed by Arab states and others, the front grew to 2,000 fighters by 1965, organised in four, later five, Zonal Commands.

Ethiopia's counter-offensive of 1967 and 1968, backed by Israel and the United States, destroyed hundreds of villages and deepened the split between Muslims and Christians within the front, which saw massacres of Christian fighters. In 1971 Isaias Afwerki and others broke away, and their factions formed the Eritrean People's Liberation Front in August 1973; the ELF began war on them in February 1972. After the Derg overthrew Haile Selassie in 1974, the two fronts briefly joined in attacking Asmara in January 1975, but by 1977 the EPLF had overtaken the ELF.

After Ethiopia, with Soviet help, recovered most of Eritrea in 1978, a failed ELF counter-offensive revived the quarrel with the EPLF. The ELF fled into Sudan, where it lost its weapons and broke up. The war of independence went on under the EPLF, and Eritrea became fully independent on 24 May 1991.
eritrean-peoples-liberation-front: In 1967 thirty-three members of the Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF), among them Isaias Afwerki and Romodan Mohammed Nur, trained for six months in China. On their return they strengthened the front but also sharpened its feuds. Many young dissidents, disillusioned with feuding leaders, left the ELF, and the Eritrean People's Liberation Front emerged from them in August 1973. Led by Isaias and Ramadan, it found refuge in the mountains of Sahel and gave its members political as well as military training, with the same education for all.

Internal dissent was put down by Isaias, and eleven members were executed in August 1974. The front's First Congress in January 1977 elected Romodan Mohammed Nur secretary-general and called for women's rights, literacy in every language and borders based on Italy's colonial treaties. Between 1975 and 1977 the ELF and EPLF overran most of Eritrea, but a counteroffensive in 1978, backed by Soviet support that eventually exceeded $11 billion, forced a strategic withdrawal. In a second civil war from August 1980 the EPLF, helped by the Tigray People's Liberation Front, defeated the ELF.

Between February and June 1982 more than 80,000 Ethiopian troops failed to crush the front in the Red Star Campaign. Its army grew from about four hundred men into a force of divisions and brigades, nearly a third of it women, though few women held command. It also used child soldiers between 1979 and 1983, a policy dropped after criticism. At the Unity Congress of 1987 Isaias became secretary-general and the movement abandoned most of its Marxist–Leninist ideology for a National Democratic Program.

In March 1988 the EPLF destroyed the strongest Ethiopian garrison in northern Eritrea at the Battle of Afabet, which has been likened to Điện Biên Phủ. In 1990 it took the port of Massawa; Ethiopian bombing that followed destroyed many historic Islamic buildings there. Allied with the TPLF, it helped bring down the Derg in May 1991. At its Third Congress, in Asmara in 1994, the front, then 95,000 members strong, became the People's Front for Democracy and Justice.
eritrean-war-of-independence: Eritrea was an Italian colony from 1882 until the Allies conquered it in 1941, and then a British Military Administration until 1951. In 1952 the United Nations decided to federate Eritrea with Ethiopia, which was to keep its own parliament under the Ethiopian crown. Eritrea's autonomy was curtailed during the 1950s as Unionist parties gained influence in the Eritrean Assembly. Exiles led by Idris Muhammad Adam founded the Eritrean Liberation Front in Cairo in 1961, and on 1 September 1961 Hamid Idris Awate and his companions fought Ethiopian troops and police at Adal. In 1962 Emperor Haile Selassie dissolved the federation and the Eritrean parliament and annexed the country.

In the 1960s the Eritrean Liberation Front, mostly Muslim and based in the lowlands, drew arms from Arab states, while many highland Christians distrusted it. The Ethiopian army answered by burning villages and shooting suspects. In 1970 splinter groups left the front, among them Christian fighters led by Isaias Afwerki, and in August 1973 two of them formed the Eritrean People's Liberation Front. The two organisations fought a civil war until popular pressure made them cooperate in 1975. After Haile Selassie was ousted in 1974, the Marxist Derg sent a peasant army of 100,000 against the rebels in 1975, and it was largely routed.

Between 1975 and 1977 the fronts held all of Eritrea except Asmara, Massawa, Assab and Barentu. After the Ogaden War the Ethiopian army, backed by Cuba, regained much of this ground, and in 1978 the Eritrean People's Liberation Front withdrew to the mountains of Sahel and held Nakfa. The Red Star Campaign of 1982, with more than 80,000 troops, failed to take it. In 1988 the front captured Afabet, and in February 1990 it took Massawa. Once the Soviet Union ended its support for Mengistu Haile Mariam, Ethiopian morale fell, and the garrison in Asmara disintegrated, letting the front enter the city on 24 May 1991.

Israel trained Ethiopian counter-insurgency forces, the United States assisted Haile Selassie until the revolution, and the Soviet Union and Cuba aided the Derg after the Ogaden War. Iraq, Syria, Libya, the Palestine Liberation Organization and Sudan supported the Eritreans to varying degrees. Talks mediated by Jimmy Carter in 1989 produced a deal that collapsed. At a conference in July 1991 the new Ethiopian transitional government recognised Eritrea's right to a referendum. In April 1993 the Eritrean people voted almost unanimously for independence, and on 28 May 1993 the United Nations admitted Eritrea to membership.
erlangen: Erlangen lies on the edge of the Middle Franconian Basin, in the floodplain of the Regnitz river, which divides the city into two halves of about equal size. The Regnitz valley was a passage from north to south in prehistory: a blade scraper found at Spardorf is attributed to the Gravettians and put at about 25,000 years old, and farming and settlement can be traced only from the end of the Neolithic, between 2800 and 2200 BCE, because the soils are barren.

The town is first mentioned in a document in 1002. It belonged first to the diocese of Würzburg and from 1017 to the archdiocese of Bamberg, and in 1528 the first Lutheran priest was appointed and the Reformation introduced. The town was completely deserted in 1634 after the destruction of the Thirty Years' War, and its population reached 500 again only in 1655.

Margrave Christian Ernst founded the new town for French religious refugees in 1686, with Protestant congregations only. In 1742 Margrave Frederick of Brandenburg-Bayreuth endowed a university for Bayreuth, which was moved to Erlangen in 1743. It was poorly funded and drew little approval at first, and Margrave Charles Alexander of Brandenburg-Ansbach put it on a broader footing. Student numbers stayed below 200 and fell to about 80 when the margraviate was incorporated into the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1810. Closure was averted because Erlangen had the only Lutheran theological faculty in the kingdom.

After the Second World War the Siemens companies Siemens & Halske and Siemens-Schuckert Werke settled in the undamaged city, helped by the existing Siemens-Reiniger-Werke site. The population passed 100,000 in 1974, making Erlangen a major city by the German statistical definition, and with Nuremberg, Fürth and Schwabach it forms one of Bavaria's metropolises. Much of daily life is still shaped by the Friedrich Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg and Siemens.
erligang-culture: The primary site, Zhengzhou Shang City, was discovered at Erligang, inside the modern city of Zhengzhou in Henan, in 1951. Later work showed that it was part of an ancient city enclosed by a roughly rectangular wall about 7 kilometres round. The walls were of rammed earth, a technique going back to the Longshan culture, and are estimated to have been 20 metres wide at the base and 8 metres high. Large workshops lay outside them: one for bone, one for pottery and two for bronze vessels. Because the modern city stands on the ancient one, excavation there is impossible, and most knowledge of the culture comes from other sites.

The culture was centred in the Yellow River valley. In its early years it spread rapidly as far as the Yangtze, then gradually shrank from that peak. Its largest excavated site is Panlongcheng on the Yangtze in Hubei, found in 1954 and excavated in 1974 and 1976. Zhengzhou had no local copper or tin, and sites such as Panlongcheng probably served to secure distant metal. The composition of the Panlongcheng bronzes matches ore from Tonglushan, which indicates that their copper came from there.

Erligang bronze casting grew out of the style and techniques of the earlier Erlitou culture, centred 85 kilometres west of Zhengzhou. Erligang was the first archaeological culture in China to cast bronze vessels widely, and its vessels were used far more and were more uniform in style than those of Erlitou.

Many Chinese archaeologists hold that the ancient cities of Yanshi and Zhengzhou were among the early capitals of the Shang dynasty named in traditional histories, and they call the culture early Shang. Many other scholars, Western archaeologists among them, point out that no writing has been found at Erligang sites, unlike at the later settlement of Anyang, to link the remains with traditional accounts written a millennium later.
erlitou-culture: The Erlitou culture was widely spread throughout Henan and Shanxi and later appeared in Shaanxi and Hubei. It may have evolved from the Longshan culture. Most archaeologists consider it the first state-level society in China. The site of Erlitou, discovered in 1959 by Xu Xusheng, is the largest associated with it, with palace buildings and bronze smelting workshops. It lies on the Yi River, a tributary of the Luo. The city measured 2.4 by 1.9 kilometres, though flood damage has left only 3 square kilometres.

The site's growth is divided into four phases. In Phase I it covered 100 hectares and was a rapidly growing regional centre of several thousand people. Urbanization began in Phase II, when it grew to 300 hectares with around 11,000 people. A palace area of 12 hectares was marked off by four roads, and a bronze foundry controlled by the elite lay to its south. Tracks of vehicles found near the palace are the earliest evidence of wheeled wagons in China.

The city peaked in Phase III with perhaps 24,000 people, and its palatial complex was surrounded by a rammed-earth wall two metres thick. Palace 1, the largest, covered 9,600 square metres. In Phase IV the population fell to around 20,000 although building continued. Bronze production and other elite goods ceased at the end of that phase, as the Erligang city of Zhengzhou was founded 85 kilometres to the east. There is no evidence of destruction by fire or war, but the palaces were abandoned and Erlitou became a village of 30 hectares.

Erlitou was the earliest large-scale bronze-producing culture in China, using the section-mould process for ritual vessels. More than ten kinds of vessel have been found, along with tools, bells, weapons and animal-faced plaques. The earliest bronze ding was found in its fourth phase, and the first bronze dagger-axe, or ge, appeared there. There are no copper resources on the Luoyang Plain, and the ore may have come from the Zhongtiao Mountains of southern Shanxi. Jade was worked into ritual blades and dagger-axes, and symbols on pottery are considered markings or proto-writing.

Chinese archaeologists generally identify the culture with the later part of the Xia dynasty, since its place and period fit the traditional accounts. Some Western scholars argue that this is premature, because no contemporary written records link them.
ermanaric: The name Ermanaric is built from a Proto-Germanic root meaning 'universal' and the element for 'ruler' found in many Gothic royal names; the Gothic form is reconstructed as Airmanareiks. He is known from two Roman sources: the contemporary historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who calls him a most warlike king ruling wide and fertile regions, and the sixth-century Getica of Jordanes. Ammianus says he took his own life when the Alani and the Huns invaded his lands in the 370s, and that a certain Vithimiris was then elected king.

Jordanes places Ermanaric over the realm of Oium, part of Scythia inhabited by the Goths, and calls him a Gothic Alexander who ruled all the nations of Scythia and Germania. He tells how the king had a young woman, Sunilda, put to death with horses as punishment for her husband's treason; her brothers Sarus and Ammius then wounded him so badly that he could not resist the Huns. Jordanes adds that he ruled successfully until his death at the age of 110.

Historians disagree on the size of his realm. Herwig Wolfram holds that it stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea and east to the Ural Mountains. Peter Heather doubts that he ruled all the Goths except the Tervingi, since such an empire would be larger than any known Gothic political unit, would have left more traces, and rests on sources not reliable enough to take at face value. Edward Gibbon accepted the ancient accounts and credited him with subduing the Heruli, Venedi, Sclaveni, Antes and Aestii.

Ermanaric became a figure of Germanic heroic legend as Eormenric in Old English and Jǫrmunrekkr in Old Norse. Beowulf speaks of Eormenric's wiles and hatred, and the poem Deor calls him a cruel king with a wolfish mind who ruled the Goths far and wide. The death of Svanhildr and his killing by Jonakr's sons recur in the Ragnarsdrápa, Hamðismál, the Prose Edda, the Volsunga Saga, the Gesta Danorum and the Nibelungenlied. In the Thidreks Saga a treacherous counsellor, Bicke, leads him to execute his own wife, and in German poems about Dietrich of Bern he is Dietrich's uncle, who drove him into exile.
ernest-augustus-duke-of-brunswick: Ernest Augustus was born on 17 November 1887 at Penzing near Vienna, the youngest of six children of the Hanoverian pretender Ernest Augustus, Duke of Cumberland, and Princess Thyra of Denmark. Prussia had deposed his grandfather George V of Hanover in 1866. When the reigning Duke of Brunswick died in 1884, the younger Welf line ended and the duchy would by house rules have passed to his father.

Otto von Bismarck had the Bundesrat rule that the claimant, who had never renounced his claim to Hanover, would disturb the peace of the empire. Prince Albrecht of Prussia became regent, followed after 1906 by Duke Johann Albrecht of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. An offer by the Cumberlands in 1906 to renounce their claims in favour of the younger Ernest Augustus was rejected.

His elder brother George died in a car accident on 20 May 1912, and Emperor Wilhelm II sent condolences. The duke sent his surviving son to Berlin to thank the emperor, and there Ernest Augustus met Wilhelm's only daughter, Princess Victoria Louise of Prussia. They married on 24 May 1913 in what was the last great gathering of European sovereigns before the First World War, attended by King George V, Queen Mary and Tsar Nicholas II.

Having sworn allegiance to the German Empire and accepted a commission in the Zieten Hussars, he saw his father renounce the Brunswick claim on 27 October 1913. The Bundesrat voted the next day to admit him, and he took possession of the duchy on 1 November. During the war he rose to major-general. In 1917 the Titles Deprivation Act removed his father's British dukedom and his own title as a Prince of the United Kingdom, effective in 1919.

He was forced to abdicate on 8 November 1918. When his father died in 1923 he did not become Duke of Cumberland but headed the House of Hanover for thirty years, living mainly at Blankenburg Castle and Cumberland Castle in Gmunden. He never joined the Nazi Party, but he donated funds and was close to several of its leaders.

In the mid-1930s Hitler asked the couple to arrange a match between their daughter Frederica and the Prince of Wales; they refused, thinking the age difference too great. Frederica married Prince Paul of Greece in 1938 and became queen consort in 1947. In 1945 the family moved from Blankenburg to Marienburg Castle in the British zone shortly before Blankenburg passed to the Red Army. He died at Marienburg in 1953 and was buried at Herrenhausen in Hanover.
ernest-augustus-elector-of-hanover: Ernest Augustus was born on 20 November 1629 at Herzberg Castle near Göttingen, in the Principality of Calenberg. His parents were George, Duke of Brunswick-Calenberg, and Anne Eleonore of Hesse-Darmstadt. On 30 September 1658 he married Sophia of the Palatinate at Heidelberg. She was the daughter of Frederick V of the Palatinate and Elizabeth Stuart, and a granddaughter of King James I of England. Sophia had been betrothed to his older brother George William, who did not want her; when she married Ernest Augustus instead, George William ceded to him his claim to Lüneburg.

Ernest Augustus had little chance of succeeding his father, and the couple lived at the Hanover court of his eldest brother Christian Louis. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 had agreed that the rule of the Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück should alternate between the churches, with Protestant bishops drawn from the House of Welf. When the see fell vacant in 1662, the family appointed him Prince-Bishop. He and Sophia moved to Iburg Castle, and in 1667 began building Osnabrück Palace, which they entered in 1673. Christian Louis died childless in 1665, and Ernest Augustus succeeded to Lüneburg, while George William kept Celle. In 1679 he inherited Calenberg from his brother John Frederick, and in 1680 the family returned to Hanover.

In 1683 he introduced primogeniture, over the protests of his five younger sons, so that his territory would not be divided again and as a precondition for obtaining the electorship. He took part in the Great Turkish War on the side of Emperor Leopold I. In 1692 the Emperor appointed him prince-elector, the ninth, raising the House of Hanover to electoral dignity; the elevation took effect in 1708, when the Imperial Diet confirmed it.

Ernest Augustus died in 1698 at Herrenhausen Palace and was succeeded by his eldest son George Louis, later King George I of Great Britain. His main residences were the Leineschloss in Hanover and Herrenhausen, a summer residence outside the city, where he and Sophia had the Great Garden enlarged after Italian and Dutch models, one of the most distinguished baroque formal gardens of Europe.
ernest-augustus-i-duke-of-saxe-weimar-ei: Born on 19 April 1688, he was the eldest surviving son of Johann Ernst III, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, and Sophie Auguste of Anhalt-Zerbst. When his father died in 1707 he became co-ruler with his uncle Wilhelm Ernst, but only in name, and he began to govern only on his uncle's death in 1728. In 1716 he married Eleonore Wilhelmine of Anhalt-Köthen, who bore him eight children. After her death in 1726 he did not mean to marry again, but the death of his only surviving son Johann Wilhelm in 1732 led him to marry Sophie Charlotte of Brandenburg-Bayreuth in 1734.

His spending helped ruin the duchy. Short of money, he had wealthy subjects arrested without cause and freed only once they gave up their fortunes or paid heavy ransoms. Some of them sued him before the imperial court in Vienna and the Imperial Chamber Court at Wetzlar; he lost every case, and the long proceedings ended in the duchy's bankruptcy. He kept an army far too large for the duchy and hired some of its soldiers out to the Electorate of Saxony and the emperor. He built Schloss Belvedere and the Rococo palace at Dornburg, and at his death he left 1,100 dogs and 373 horses.

On the death of Wilhelm Heinrich, Duke of Saxe-Eisenach, in 1741, he inherited the Eisenach and Jena lands as the only surviving kinsman. Primogeniture, confirmed by Emperor Karl VI in 1724, prevented their division. The two parts, around Weimar and Eisenach, were not joined by land, and the union was at first only personal. He moved to Eisenach for its hunting woods, leaving his heir in Weimar.

Following the French model of absolutism, he dissolved the privy council of nobles. In 1746 the citizens of Eisenach presented him with a memorandum accusing him of constant offences against traditional rights, and some of his plans could not be carried through. He died on 19 January 1748, leaving a ruined duchy to his son Ernst August II, who was still under age.
ernest-augustus-king-of-hanover: Ernest Augustus was born on 5 June 1771 at Buckingham House, London, the fifth son of George III and Queen Charlotte. As a boy he lived on Kew Green with his younger brothers Adolphus and Augustus and a tutor. At fifteen he was sent with them to the University of Göttingen in his father's Electorate of Hanover, partly, according to the historian John Van der Kiste, to limit the influence of the extravagant Prince of Wales. He proved a keen student, but all three princes fell into debt. Serving with Hanoverian forces near Tournai against Revolutionary France, he received a disfiguring facial wound.

On 23 April 1799 George III created him Duke of Cumberland and Teviotdale. Although a lieutenant general in both the British and Hanoverian armies, he stayed in England and took a seat in the House of Lords, where he became a leader of the right wing of the Tories. In 1815 he married his twice-widowed cousin Frederica of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, against the wishes of Queen Charlotte. The marriage proved happy. The death of Princess Charlotte in 1817 gave him some prospect of the throne, but his brother Edward, Duke of Kent, fathered the future Queen Victoria in 1819.

On 31 May 1810 he was wounded in an apparent attack while asleep, and his valet Joseph Sellis was found dead with his throat cut. The inquest, under the foreman Francis Place, returned a unanimous verdict of suicide. His political foes spread persistent allegations that he had murdered the valet.

William IV died on 20 June 1837. Victoria succeeded to the British throne, but Hanover's Salic law barred women, so Ernest became King of Hanover. This ended the personal union begun in 1714. Hanover now had a resident ruler for the first time since George I. Many Hanoverians were liberal and would have preferred Adolphus, but he and the Duke of Sussex refused to stand against their elder brother.

A new constitution had been granted in 1833, without Ernest's consent, and he had protested. On arrival he dissolved the Parliament, suspended the constitution on 5 July and, by a patent of 1 November 1837, declared it void while upholding the laws passed under it. The earlier constitution of 1819 was restored.

He dismissed the Göttingen Seven, professors who protested, among them the Brothers Grimm. He put down an attempted revolution in 1848, and Hanover joined the German customs union in 1850 despite his reluctance. He remained heir presumptive to Victoria until the birth of her daughter in November 1840. He died on 18 November 1851, aged 80, and was succeeded by his son George V. He was mourned in Hanover and rests in a mausoleum in the Berggarten of Herrenhausen.
ernest-i-duke-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha: Ernest was born on 2 January 1784, the eldest son of Francis, Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, and his second wife, Countess Augusta of Reuss-Ebersdorf. His youngest brother Leopold became the first king of Belgium, and his sister Victoria was the mother of Queen Victoria. When his second son Albert married the queen in 1840, Ernest became both her uncle and her father-in-law. His father fell gravely ill, and Ernest was proclaimed an adult on 10 May 1803 to share in the government. He succeeded as Ernest III in 1806, but French troops occupied the duchy. After the Peace of Tilsit in 1807 it was restored to him, through Russian pressure, since his sister Juliane was married to the brother of the Russian tsar.

After 1813 Ernest was a Prussian general and fought against Napoleon at Lützen and Leipzig, then commanded a Prussian corps. Following Waterloo, the Congress of Vienna gave him an area of 450 square kilometres with 25,000 inhabitants around St. Wendel, named the Principality of Lichtenberg in 1816. He sold it to Prussia in 1834.

When Duke Frederick IV of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg died without an heir in 1825, the Ernestine duchies were redistributed. Ernest was then divorcing his first wife Louise, the late duke's niece, and the other branches used this to bargain against his inheriting Gotha. In the compromise of 12 November 1826 he received Gotha but ceded Saalfeld to Saxe-Meiningen, and became Ernest I, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha.
