He had given Coburg a constitution in 1821 and did not interfere in the government of Gotha. In Coburg he built the court theatre in its new building and shaped the Schlossplatz, and he is remembered for the economic, educational and constitutional development of his lands.

Ernest married Louise of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg in 1817. They had two sons, Ernest II, born in 1818, and Albert, born in 1819. The marriage was unhappy, and they separated in 1824 and were divorced on 31 March 1826; the sons stayed with their father. In 1832 he married his niece Marie of Württemberg, and they had no children. He also had three illegitimate children. He died on 29 January 1844 and was first buried in the Morizkirche, then moved to a new mausoleum in the Friedhof am Glockenberg. Through Albert and his marriage to Queen Victoria the house of Coburg gained a significant international position.
ernest-i-duke-of-saxe-gotha: Ernest was born on 25 December 1601, a surviving son of Johann II, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, and Dorothea Maria of Anhalt. His father died in 1605 and his mother in 1617, and he was brought up strictly: gifted and precocious but not physically strong, and early marked by the piety of his time. A devout Lutheran, he allied with Sweden in 1631 and fought at Lech, Nördlingen, Lützen and the siege of Nuremberg. After the Peace of Prague of 1635 he withdrew from warfare to concentrate on administration and recovery. In 1640, under the partition treaty with his brothers, he received Gotha.
On 24 October 1636 he married his younger cousin Elisabeth Sophie of Saxe-Altenburg, and when the last duke of that line died childless in 1672 the two duchies were united.

After the Thirty Years' War Ernest freed his land from debt by careful economy, reduced taxation and left a considerable sum in the treasury at his death. He gave much attention to public security and to an efficient judiciary, and other states took up his regulations as models. He banned torture and dueling, and was a foe of alchemy, though he supported witchcraft trials. His laws forbade secret betrothals and tried to regulate dress, yet promoted agriculture, commerce, learning and art. He rebuilt Friedenstein Palace in Gotha, whose collections began with him, and founded a library that became one of the largest in Germany.

With Veit Ludwig von Seckendorf and Andreas Reyher he issued the Schulmethodus of 1642, which called for compulsory, graded schooling. It was said that no one in his land could not read and write, and the Gotha gymnasium drew pupils from Sweden, Russia, Poland and Hungary. He also increased the funds of the University of Jena. His religious zeal won him the nickname Praying Ernest. He interceded with the emperor for his Austrian co-religionists, supported the Lutheran church in Moscow and sent an embassy to introduce Lutheranism into Abyssinia, which failed.

Ernest died on 26 March 1675 and was buried in the crypt of St. Margarethenkirche on the Neumarkt, the first of the House of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg to lie there. He and Elisabeth Sophie had 18 children, of whom nine reached adulthood. Frederick I inherited Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, and the other sons became dukes of Coburg, Meiningen, Römhild, Eisenberg, Hildburghausen and Saalfeld. He died with the name of father and saviour of his people, and Oliver Cromwell is said to have counted him among the most sagacious of princes.
ernest-ii-duke-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha: Ernest was born at Ehrenburg Palace in Coburg on 21 June 1818, the elder son of Ernest III, Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, and Princess Louise of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg. His only full sibling, Prince Albert, was born fourteen months later, and the two were raised as though they were twins. In 1826 their father became Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha through an exchange of territories. On 3 May 1842 Ernest married Princess Alexandrine of Baden at Karlsruhe; the marriage produced no children, though he fathered at least three illegitimate ones.

Ernest succeeded on 29 January 1844. He was extravagant and in debt throughout his reign, and in 1848 there were calls to nationalise most of his property. Timely concessions, a constitution promulgated at Gotha in 1849 and his habit of mingling with the people helped him keep his throne. In 1852 the constitutions of the two duchies were joined into one, turning a personal union into a real union.

In the First Schleswig War he sent 8,000 men and led a Thuringian contingent; as commander of a German corps he was instrumental in the victory over Danish forces at Eckernförde on 5 April 1849. He may have hoped to be chosen German Emperor by the Frankfurt Parliament, but urged King Frederick of Prussia to take the position. In 1850 he brought about a Berlin conference of German princes.

He opposed the marriage of his nephew Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, to Princess Alexandra of Denmark, and in 1863 attended the liberal Frankfurt Conference. After King Otto of Greece was deposed in October 1862, the British government put Ernest forward as a possible successor, but he would not give up his duchies and the negotiations failed.

Ernest began as a proponent of German liberalism and made his duchy a refuge for political exiles from other German states. He later supported the Prussians in the Austro-Prussian and Franco-Prussian Wars, which cost him standing as a possible leader of a political movement. After Albert's death in 1861 he published anonymous pamphlets against members of the British royal family, and Queen Victoria disliked his plans to write memoirs. Because he had no children, his nephew Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, was designated heir after the Prince of Wales renounced his rights. Ernest died at Reinhardsbrunn on 22 August 1893, and Alfred succeeded him.
ernest-ii-duke-of-saxe-gotha-altenburg: Ernest was born in Gotha on 30 January 1745, the third but second surviving son of Frederick III, Duke of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, and Luise Dorothea of Saxe-Meiningen. The death of his elder brother Frederick in 1756 made him heir to the duchy. His mother took great care over the training of Ernest and his younger brother August and had them taught by a select group of teachers. In 1768 and 1769 the two princes travelled through the Netherlands, England and France, where Ernest met leading figures in politics, science and the arts. In 1769 he married Princess Charlotte of Saxe-Meiningen; they had four sons.

Ernest succeeded his father in 1772. He promoted schools, the economy, the theatre, art collections, libraries and the natural sciences, and his duchy came to rank first among the Saxon duchies in Thuringia. His private interests were astronomy and physics. He named the clockmaker Johann Andreas Klindworth court mechanic and brought the astronomer Franz Xaver von Zach to Gotha, where together they founded the observatory that became a European centre of astronomy. Gotha drew visitors of note, among them Goethe, who came several times. Under the influence of the French Revolution he thought of abdicating and emigrating, had land bought near Montgomery in Ohio and in 1796 commissioned Joseph Ramée to design a country house, but he remained in Gotha.

A cousin of King George III through his aunt's marriage to Frederick, Prince of Wales, he was made a knight of the Order of the Garter in 1790. He became a Freemason in 1774 and Grand Master of the Landesloge of Germany in 1775. In 1783 he joined the Bavarian Illuminati under the name Quintus Severus or Timoleon, and in 1787 he gave its founder, Adam Weishaupt, asylum in Gotha.

Ernest died in Gotha on 20 April 1804 and was buried wrapped in a white cloth on the island in the palace park. His will asked that the observatory survive as the only visible sign of his existence. His subjects regarded him as a man with magical powers, and a legend still told in Gotha says that he could banish fire. After his death the Garter insignia were handed back to the order.
ernest-louis-grand-duke-of-hesse: Ernest Louis was born on 25 November 1868 at the New Palace in Darmstadt, the elder son of Louis IV, Grand Duke of Hesse and by Rhine, and Princess Alice, daughter of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. His younger sister Alix married Tsar Nicholas II of Russia. His childhood was marked by loss: his only brother, Prince Friedrich, who had haemophilia, died in a fall when Ernest Louis was four, and in 1878 a diphtheria epidemic killed his sister Marie and then his mother, who died on 14 December.

Ernest Louis succeeded his father in 1892, aged twenty-three. On 19 April 1894 he married his first cousin Princess Victoria Melita of Edinburgh, a match Queen Victoria had encouraged. The marriage was unhappy, and it ended in divorce on 21 December 1901 by a verdict of the Supreme Court of Hesse. Their daughter Elisabeth died of typhoid fever in 1903, aged eight. On 2 February 1905 he married Princess Eleonore of Solms-Hohensolms-Lich; the marriage was harmonious and produced two sons, Georg Donatus and Louis.

Throughout his life he was a patron of the arts and founded the Darmstadt Artists' Colony. He also wrote poems, plays, essays and piano compositions. He commissioned a new mausoleum in 1903, consecrated on 3 November 1910, to which the remains of his father, mother and siblings were moved.

During the First World War Ernest Louis served as a general of the infantry at Kaiser Wilhelm II's headquarters. His sister Alexandra, wife of Nicholas II, and another sister, Elizabeth, widow of Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich, were murdered by the Bolsheviks in July 1918. At the end of the war a workers' and soldiers' council in Darmstadt declared him deposed. He accepted the loss of his throne but refused to formally abdicate.

He died after a long illness at Schloss Wolfsgarten, near Darmstadt, on 9 October 1937, aged 68, and was buried beside his daughter near the New Mausoleum. On the day of his funeral, 16 November, his widow, his eldest son Georg Donatus, his daughter-in-law and their children, except Johanna, were killed in an air crash at Ostend on their way to the wedding of his younger son Louis.
ernest-renan: Joseph Ernest Renan was born on 27 February 1823 at Tréguier in Brittany, into a family of fishermen. His father, the captain of a small cutter and an ardent republican, died when he was five, and his sister Henriette, twelve years older, became the moral head of the household. He was educated at the ecclesiastical seminary of Tréguier, and in 1838 Félix Dupanloup brought him to Paris. In 1840 he moved to the Saint-Sulpice Seminary to study philosophy. Studying Hebrew and Syriac from 1844, he concluded that the second part of the Book of Isaiah differs from the first in date and that the Book of Daniel was written centuries after its setting. In October 1845 he left Saint-Sulpice and became a teacher.

In 1847 Renan won the Volney prize for his General History of Semitic Languages and took his degree as agrégé de philosophie. In 1856 he married Cornélie Scheffer, and they had two children, Ary and Noémi. In 1869 he stood for the liberal opposition at Meaux but was not elected. The Franco-Prussian War was a turning point: Germany, which he had seen as the home of disinterested science, now appeared to him as an invader. In the 1870s he rallied to the French Third Republic. In 1883 he published the autobiographical Souvenirs d'enfance et de jeunesse, which with the Life of Jesus is the work by which he is chiefly known.

His Histoire des origines du christianisme, published between 1863 and 1881, ran from the Life of Jesus through The Apostles and Saint Paul to Marc-Aurèle, and he later wrote a five-volume Histoire du peuple d'Israël. He held that races differ by instinct and that the Semitic race was inferior to the Indo-European, calling Semites an incomplete race. He nevertheless disputed in 1883 that Jews form a unified biological race, and criticised German ethnic nationalism. He supported colonial expansion.

Anatole France called him the incarnation of modernity, and Nietzsche and Jacob Burckhardt attacked his interpretations. A monument to him unveiled in 1903 in the cathedral square of Tréguier was read as a challenge to Catholicism and caused widespread protests.
ernesto-cardenal: Ernesto Cardenal was born into an upper-class family in Granada, Nicaragua; his brother Fernando Cardenal also became a priest, and the poet Pablo Antonio Cuadra was his first cousin. He studied literature in Managua, then in Mexico from 1942 to 1946 and in New York City from 1947 to 1949. Back in Nicaragua he took part in the April Revolution of 1954 against Anastasio Somoza García, a failed coup in which many of his associates died. After a deep mystical experience on 2 June 1956 he entered the Trappist monastery of Gethsemani in Kentucky, where the poet-priest Thomas Merton was master of novices, and in 1959 he left to study theology in Cuernavaca, Mexico.

Cardenal was ordained a priest in Granada in 1965 and went to the Solentiname Islands, where he founded a Christian, almost monastic community of mainly peasants. An artists' colony grew from it, and The Gospel in Solentiname was written there. He worked closely with the Sandinista National Liberation Front against Anastasio Somoza Debayle. In 1977 the National Guard raided Solentiname and burned it down, and Cardenal fled to Costa Rica. He described himself as a Marxist who believes in God.

On 19 July 1979, after the liberation of Managua, the new Sandinista government named him Minister of Culture, and his brother Fernando became Minister of Education. When Pope John Paul II visited in 1983 he scolded Cardenal at Managua airport for refusing to resign. On 4 February 1984 the pope suspended him a divinis, and the suspension lasted until Pope Francis lifted it in 2019. His ministry was closed in 1987 for economic reasons, and he left the Sandinista Front in 1994.

Cardenal's early poetry dealt with life and love; later works such as Zero Hour were tied to Marxist ideas and the killing of the guerrilla leader Augusto César Sandino, and his later verse drew on science and evolution. His honours include the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade in 1980 and the Queen Sofia Prize for Ibero-American Poetry in 2012. He died on 1 March 2020 after heart and kidney problems. At his request his remains were cremated and buried in the community he had founded on the Solentiname Islands.
ernesto-geisel: Ernesto Beckmann Geisel was born on 3 August 1907 in Bento Gonçalves, Rio Grande do Sul, to German Lutheran immigrants. His father, Guilherme Augusto Geisel, was a German teacher from Herborn who had emigrated to Brazil in 1883 at the age of 16; his mother, Lydia Beckmann, was born in Brazil to parents from Osnabrück. German was spoken at home. Most people in Bento Gonçalves were Italian immigrants, and Geisel later recalled the contrast between his parents' strict upbringing and the freer life of his Italian friends. In 1940 he married Lucy Markus, the daughter of an army colonel.

Geisel entered the army in 1921, together with his brother Orlando, and in 1928 graduated first in his class from the Military School of Realengo, joining an artillery unit. He took part in the Revolution of 1930, lived through the Estado Novo and its overthrow in 1945, and was military attaché in Uruguay in 1946–47.

Promoted to brigadier general in 1960, he took part in the military coup of 1964 that overthrew President João Goulart and served as chief of the military staff of President Humberto de Alencar Castelo Branco until 1967. He became an army general in 1966 and in 1969 president of the state oil company Petrobras.

In 1973 President Emílio Garrastazu Médici chose Geisel as his successor, after manoeuvring between hard-liners and the more moderate supporters of Castelo Branco. His brother Orlando, Minister of the Army, and General João Baptista de Oliveira Figueiredo, chief of Médici's military staff, supported him. Congress elected him by 400 votes to 76 against Ulysses Guimarães of the opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement, and he was inaugurated on 15 March 1974.

With his chief of staff Golbery do Couto e Silva he devised a plan of gradual relaxation of authoritarian rule, which he called abertura and distensão: in his words, the maximum of development possible with the minimum of indispensable security. Torture of left-wing opponents continued, as the 1975 murder of Vladimir Herzog showed. In October 1977 he dismissed the Minister of the Army, General Sylvio Couto Coelho da Frota, who had tried to become a candidate for the succession.

The oil crisis of 1973 cut growth from more than 10 per cent a year to 5 or 6, and the foreign debt rose, but Geisel kept up heavy investment in infrastructure and atomic energy. Abroad he established relations with the People's Republic of China, Angola and Mozambique, signed a nuclear agreement with West Germany in 1975, and in April 1977 renounced the military alliance with the United States. In 1985 he supported the opposition candidate Tancredo Neves, which eased military resistance to his presidency.
ernesto-sabato: Ernesto Sabato was born on 24 June 1911 in Rojas, Buenos Aires Province, the tenth of eleven children of Italian immigrants from Calabria. In 1924 he moved to La Plata for secondary school, where the professor Pedro Henríquez Ureña was an early inspiration, and in 1929 he began studying physics and mathematics at the Universidad Nacional de La Plata. As a student he took part in the university reform movement, and in 1933 he was elected general secretary of the Communist Youth Federation. In 1934 he began to doubt communism and Joseph Stalin's regime, and he left a congress in Brussels to avoid being sent to the International Lenin School in Moscow.

Sabato earned his doctorate in physics in 1938 and, through the help of Bernardo Houssay, a fellowship at the Curie Institute in Paris, where he also met the surrealists. He worked briefly at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and returned to Argentina in 1939. In 1943, after what he called an existential crisis, he left science for good to become a writer and painter. His first book, Uno y el Universo (1945), was a series of essays criticising the apparent moral neutrality of science. In 1948 he published his first novel, El túnel, in the magazine Sur, after several publishers rejected it; Albert Camus admired it and had Gallimard publish a French translation.

Sabato's novels are El túnel (1948), Sobre héroes y tumbas (1961), regarded as his masterpiece, and Abaddón el exterminador (1974). His essays cover metaphysics, politics and tango. He was a critic of Peronism, and in 1956 published El otro rostro del peronismo. His honours include the Miguel de Cervantes Prize and the Legion of Honour. At the request of President Raúl Alfonsín he presided over the commission, CONADEP, that investigated the forced disappearances of the Dirty War of the 1970s, and its findings were published in 1984 as Nunca Más. He died on 30 April 2011 at Santos Lugares, two months short of his hundredth birthday.
ernst-ii-duke-of-saxe-altenburg: Ernst was born on 31 August 1871, the fourth child and only son of Prince Moritz, youngest son of Georg, Duke of Saxe-Altenburg, and of Princess Augusta of Saxe-Meiningen. His father's death on 13 May 1907 made him first in line to the duchy, which he inherited when his uncle Ernst I died without surviving male issue. In 1898 at Bückeburg he married Princess Adelaide of Schaumburg-Lippe; their children included Georg Moritz, Hereditary Prince of Saxe-Altenburg.

In the First World War Ernst refused honorary posts at the Kaiser's headquarters, which would have been far safer. Giving up his courtesy rank of Generalleutnant, he took command of his duchy's regiment, the 153rd (8th Thuringian) Infantry, which fought at the Battle of Mons. When Paul von Reichenau was killed in 1914 Ernst replaced him at the head of the 15th Infantry Brigade. In 1915 he received the Pour le Mérite and command of the 8th Infantry Division, which he led at the Battle of the Somme. Illness ended his field service late in 1916.

A lover of science, he had a wireless station fitted in his castle at Altenburg at the start of the war to communicate with airships, and he was considered an expert in aeronautics. He was among the first German princes to see that great changes were coming and reached an amicable settlement with his subjects. He was forced to give up the government of the duchy on 13 November 1918.

Ernst retired with a moderate fortune to a Berlin hotel, and his marriage ended in divorce in 1920. On 15 July 1934 he married his long-time companion Maria Triebel at Schloss Fröhliche Wiederkunft in Wolfersdorf, where he had set up an observatory in 1922. He joined the Nazi Party on 1 May 1937. After the Second World War he was the only former reigning German prince to accept citizenship of the German Democratic Republic, keeping the use of his confiscated palace. He became the last survivor of the princes who had reigned until 1918 and died there on 22 March 1955.
ernst-johann-von-biron: Ernst Johann von Bühren was born at Kalnciems in Semigallia in 1690, the second son of Cornet Karl von Bühren. His grandfather had been a groom to Jacob Kettler, Duke of Courland, and received a small estate. He studied at the academy of Königsberg but was expelled for riotous conduct.

In 1714 he sought a place in Russia without success and returned to Mitau, where a sister who served Anna, regent of Courland, helped him to a place at court. He then supplanted the ruling minister, Peter Bestuzhev, in Anna's favour and had him disgraced and banished. In 1723 he married Benigna Gottlieb von Trotha genannt Treyden, who shared his later exile.

After Anna became Empress of Russia in 1730, Biron was appointed grand chamberlain and made a count of the Empire, receiving an estate at Wenden; his name was now written Biron, and he is said to have adopted the arms of the French ducal house of that name, to which he had no connection. When the Council tried to secure an aristocratic constitution, Anna crushed the Dolgoruki and Galitsin nobles and relied on him.

He is said to have caused over 1,000 executions and the exile of 20,000 to 40,000 people to Siberia, and Russians called the period the Bironovshchina. He was nonetheless an able administrator who kept order. In June 1737 the Courland estates were pressed, with bribes, into electing him duke after the Kettler line died out, and he was invested at Warsaw in 1739.

On her deathbed Anna named him regent for the infant Ivan VI, and a declaration signed by 194 dignitaries confirmed it on 26 October 1740. Anna died on 28 October. At midnight on 19 November 1740 Field Marshal Münnich seized him in his bedroom. A commission condemned him on 11 April 1741 to death by quartering, commuted by the regent Anna Leopoldovna to banishment at Pelym in Siberia, and his property was confiscated. Empress Elizabeth later moved him to Yaroslavl.

Peter III summoned him to court in 1762, and in 1763 Catherine II restored him to Courland, which he bequeathed to his son Peter in 1769. The last years of his rule were described as just and even benevolent, though autocratic. He died on 29 December 1772 at Rastrelli's palace in Mitava, and his wife outlived him by ten years.
ernst-rohm: Ernst Röhm was born on 28 November 1887 in Munich, the youngest of three children of Emilie and Julius Röhm, a railway official. His family had no military tradition, but in 1906 he entered the Royal Bavarian 10th Infantry Regiment as a cadet. In the First World War he was seriously wounded in the face in September 1914 and again in the chest at Verdun in 1916, and he received the Iron Cross First Class. After the war he stayed in the Reichswehr and was a senior member of Franz Ritter von Epp's Freikorps, which overturned the Munich Soviet Republic by force on 3 May 1919.

In 1919 Röhm joined the German Workers' Party, which became the Nazi Party, and became a close associate of Adolf Hitler. In the Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923 he led the Reichskriegsflagge militia, which occupied the War Ministry in Munich for sixteen hours. He broke with Hitler in 1925 over the party's course and in 1929 and 1930 advised the Bolivian Army. Hitler recalled him, and on 5 January 1931 he became chief of staff of the Sturmabteilung (SA), then over a million strong, which continued violence against communists, rival parties and Jews. After Hitler became chancellor in 1933, Röhm was named a Reichsleiter and, on 2 December 1933, a Reichsminister without portfolio.

Röhm and other radicals called for a second revolution against capitalism, and he wanted the Reichswehr merged into the SA, by then over three million men, under his command. The army and Hitler's industrial backers saw this as a threat. In June 1934 SS leaders Heinrich Himmler and Reinhard Heydrich assembled fabricated evidence of a plot, and on 30 June SS men arrested Röhm at the Hanselbauer Hotel in Bad Wiessee. In Stadelheim Prison in Munich he refused a pistol offered for suicide and was shot on 1 July 1934.

The killings of 30 June to 2 July, called the Night of the Long Knives, took more than 200 other lives, including Gregor Strasser and General Kurt von Schleicher, most of them with little connection to Röhm. A decree of 3 July declared them legal acts of self-defence.
ernst-toller: Ernst Toller was born on 1 December 1893 to a Jewish family in Samotschin, Germany, now Szamocin in Poland. His father, Max Toller, was a pharmacist, and his parents also ran a general store. At the outbreak of the First World War he volunteered for the German Army. After 13 months on the Western Front he suffered a complete physical and psychological collapse. His first drama, Transformation (Die Wandlung, 1919), was drawn from his wartime experiences.

Toller took part in the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic of 1919 together with anarchists such as Gustav Landauer and B. Traven and his own party, the Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany. He served as president from 6 to 12 April. He issued numerous decrees, almost none of which were carried out, among them the socialisation of the press and of the mining industry, a legally binding eight-hour working day and a limit of 100 marks a day on bank withdrawals. On 13 April 1919 the Communist Party seized power under Eugen Leviné, and in May the republic was defeated by the Freikorps.

Toller was tried for his part in the revolution, with Max Weber and Thomas Mann testifying on his behalf, and was sentenced to five years in prison. He served in Stadelheim, Neuburg and Eichstätt and, from February 1920, mostly in the fortress of Niederschönenfeld, where he spent 149 days in solitary confinement and 24 days on hunger strike. The plays he wrote in prison, among them Masse Mensch (1921) and The Machine Wreckers (1922), were not performed for him to see until after his release in July 1925. Hoppla, We're Alive!, directed by Erwin Piscator, depicts a revolutionary released from a mental hospital who finds his comrades compromised.

After the Nazis came to power in 1933 Toller was exiled from Germany. He made a lecture tour of the United States and Canada in 1936 and 1937 and settled in New York, where he joined other exiles. His early plays were produced there, The Machine Wreckers in 1937 and No More Peace in 1938, but their style seemed outmoded and the poor reception added to his discouragement. Depressed, separated from his wife and short of money, having given all he had to refugees of the Spanish Civil War, he died by suicide on 22 May 1939. W. H. Auden's poem In Memory of Ernst Toller appeared in 1940. His work has been in the public domain since the copyright expired on 31 December 2009.
eros: Eros is the ancient Greek god of love and sex, whose name means desire. In the earliest sources, the cosmogonies, the earliest philosophers and texts on the mystery religions, he is one of the primordial gods involved in the coming into being of the cosmos. In Hesiod's Theogony, from about 700 BCE, he is the fourth god to exist, after Chaos, Gaia and Tartarus, while Parmenides makes him the first of all. In The Birds, a comedy by Aristophanes of 414 BCE, he springs from an egg laid by Night. In later sources he is the son of Aphrodite, and the poet Simonides made him her son by Ares.

Eros is usually shown as a handsome young man, though sometimes as a mischievous boy in the company of his mother, and he is winged and carries a bow and arrows with which he makes mortals and gods fall in love. Ovid gives him two kinds of arrow, golden ones that bring love and lead ones that bring aversion, as in the story of Apollo and Daphne. His role in myth is mostly to prompt love, and he has little mythology of his own beyond the story of Eros and Psyche, told in Apuleius's Latin novel The Golden Ass, in which Psyche, the deified human soul, wins him after tasks set by Aphrodite and is made immortal by Zeus.

A cult of Eros existed in pre-classical Greece but was much less important than that of Aphrodite. In Athens he shared a popular cult with her, and the fourth day of every month was sacred to him. In late antiquity he was worshipped by a fertility cult in Thespiae, where the Thespians held the Erotidia, festivals of Eros. The Samians consecrated a gymnasium to him, and the Lacedaemonians and Cretans sacrificed to him before battle, thinking victory depended on the friendship of those who stand side by side.

Later satirical poets showed Eros as a blindfolded child, the forerunner of the chubby Renaissance Cupid. The Romans called him Cupid or Amor. In art he appears as a putto, an image that seems to have influenced the figure of the cherub in Christian art of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, and the later Cupid became a major symbol of Valentine's Day. The ancient motif of Eros stung by bees, found in the Anacreontea and in Theocritus, was retold many times in antiquity and the Renaissance.
errol-barrow: Errol Walton Barrow was born on 21 January 1920 in the parish of Saint Lucy, the son of the Rev. Reginald Grant Barrow, an Anglican priest whose advocacy for poor black labourers led to his transfer to St. Croix and later his deportation from there, and Ruth Albertha O'Neal. He spent his first six years in St Croix, then grew up in Bridgetown under the influence of his uncle Dr. Charles Duncan O'Neal, founder of the Democratic League. He attended Harrison College and won the Island Scholarship in 1940, but in December 1940 enlisted in the Royal Air Force with 11 other Barbadians, the Second Barbadian Contingent.

As a navigator with 88 Squadron he flew 48 operational sorties between 23 September 1944 and 26 March 1945, supporting ground forces at Arnhem and in the Battle of the Bulge, and after the war was personal navigator to Air Chief Marshall Sir William Sholto Douglas in occupied Germany. He then studied at the London School of Economics and read law at the Inns of Court. Elected to parliament for the Barbados Labour Party in 1951, he broke with it and in April 1955 joined 21 others in adopting the constitution of the Democratic Labour Party; he lost his seat in 1956 and returned in a by-election in 1958.

His governments accelerated industrial development, expanded tourism to reduce dependence on sugar and introduced National Health Insurance and Social Security. He led the founding of the Caribbean Free Trade Association in 1965, which became the Caribbean Community under the Treaty of Chaguaramas. The party lost in 1976 after a dispute over constitutional amendments and an economic downturn. In opposition he condemned the United States invasion of Grenada in 1983.

In May 1986 the party won 24 of 27 seats, after a campaign remembered for his Mirror Image speech, and he openly criticised President Reagan. He collapsed and died at his home on 1 June 1987, and an act of Parliament in 1998 named him one of the National Heroes of Barbados.
erzberg: The Erzberg lies at Eisenerz in the central-western part of Austria, 60 km north-west of Graz and 260 km south-west of Vienna. It is the largest iron ore deposit in Austria, with estimated reserves of 235 million tonnes of ore. The deposit lies at the northern fringe of the eastern greywacke zone, a band of Paleozoic metamorphosed sedimentary rocks that runs east to west through the Austrian Alps. Most of the siderite is hosted in Silurian and Devonian marbles of the Noric nappe, and the ore, made up of siderite, ankerite and ferrous dolomite, holds on average 21% iron.

Iron has been mined at the Erzberg for more than 1,300 years. A document once held by the Oswaldikirche, the Catholic church of Eisenerz, dated the start of mining to 712, although this is unconfirmed. At first the ore was dug at the surface: limonite found close to the surface was mined in the 12th century under exploitation rights granted by territorial rulers, and it was smelted in small forges near the pits, where the miners lived at little more than subsistence.

Underground mining with hammer and pick began in the 16th century on the orders of the Austrian emperor. The upper part of the mountain was worked by the townsfolk of Vordernberg and the lower part by the people of Innerberg, the former name of Eisenerz. Forges known as Radwerke, their bellows driven by water wheels, were built in the valleys of Eisenerz and Vordernberg and drew further settlement. Ore was at first carried down to them by hand on sleighs, the Sackzug, with women assisting, before horses and carts came into use, and from 1810 to 1870 the shafts and tunnels were fitted with rails and miners' carts.

Black powder was tried on the mountain in 1720 and dynamite in 1870, and from 1876 electrical cables connected the blasting caps. From 1906 the miners used carbide acetylene lamps and percussion drills driven by compressed air. Underground mining gave way to open-pit terraces from 1890. Mine trucks appeared in 1951 and had replaced the carts and rails by 1963, and later automation and remote control of the work cut the workforce sharply.

The mine produces around 3.2 million tonnes of iron ore a year, which is shipped to Voestalpine AG in Linz and south to the smelter at Donawitz. Its old tunnels can be visited by a tourist train, and the site is the scene of the annual Erzberg Rodeo, a hard enduro motorbike race.
erzincan: Erzincan is the capital of Erzincan Province in eastern Turkey. Historically it was called Yerznka in Armenian, and its ancient region was Acilisene, the site of the Peace of Acilisene, by which in 387 CE Armenia was divided into two vassal states, one dependent on the Byzantine Empire and a larger one on Persia. For a time the city was called Justinianopolis in honour of Emperor Justinian. A pre-Christian shrine of the Armenian goddess Anahit stood at Erez.

By the eleventh century Acilisene was a metropolitan see with 21 suffragans, the height of its splendour, which ended with the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071. Marco Polo called Erzincan the noblest of cities and said its people were Armenians. In 1243 it was destroyed in fighting between the Seljuks and the Mongols. In the summer of 1500 about 7,000 Qizilbash gathered there at the invitation of Ismail I, who was founding the Safavid dynasty.

Ottoman forces captured the city in 1514. Evliya Çelebi visited in 1647 and recorded 48 neighbourhoods, seven mosques and eleven hamams. During the Armenian genocide, at least 150,000 Armenians from Erzincan and the surrounding area were transported through the city in 1915 and 1916, where transit camps fed the killing site at the nearby Kemah gorge. Of about 37,000 Armenians in Erzincan and its suburbs before the First World War, most were killed. Russian forces under General Nikolai Yudenich took the city in July 1916, and Kâzım Karabekir regained it on 13 February 1918.

On 27 December 1939 a sequence of seven violent shocks, the largest of magnitude 7.8, destroyed the city completely. By the end of the year 32,962 people had died from the earthquakes and floods. The old site was abandoned and a new town was founded a little further north.

Erzincan had 150,714 inhabitants in 2022. The city is majority Turkish Sunni, with a Kurdish Alevi minority. It has cold, snowy winters and hot, dry summers, and mulberry plantations were used for sericulture in the early twentieth century.
erzurum: Erzurum lies in eastern Turkey, 1,900 metres above sea level. It is the largest city and capital of Erzurum Province, and the site of ancient Theodosiopolis. Its Armenian name was Karin, and the present name arose after the Seljuk conquest that followed the Battle of Manzikert in 1071. When the neighbouring commercial city of Artze was sacked by the Seljuks in 1048/49, its Christian inhabitants moved to Theodosiopolis and called it Artsn Rum, Artze of the Rûm, meaning the Romans, a name from which Erzurum is derived. The city has a double-headed eagle as its coat of arms.

Under the Artaxiad and Arsacid kings of Armenia, Karin was the capital of a canton in Upper Armenia. After Armenia was partitioned between the Eastern Roman Empire and Sassanid Persia in 387, the Romans fortified the city and named it Theodosiopolis after Emperor Theodosius I. As the chief military stronghold on the empire's eastern border it was fiercely contested between Byzantines and Persians, and Anastasius I and Justinian I both strengthened its defences. The Umayyad general Abdallah ibn Abd al-Malik conquered it in 700 or 701, and it became the capital of an emirate and a base for raids into Byzantine territory. The Byzantine commander Theophilos Kourkouas captured it in 931 and again in 949, and Basil II rebuilt its defences in 1018.

After 1071 the Seljuk Turks held the city, and the Saltukids ruled an Anatolian principality centred on it from 1071 to 1202. Melike Mama Hatun, sister of Nâsırüddin Muhammed, was ruler from 1191 to 1200. The city fell to a Mongol siege in 1242 and was looted. It later belonged to the Ilkhanate, the Timurid Empire and the Turkmen confederations, then to Safavid Persia, until the Ottomans under Selim I took it in 1514 after the Battle of Chaldiran. Nader Shah took it in 1733, and it returned to the Ottomans after his death in 1747. Russian forces occupied it in 1829, in 1878 and in 1916, and each time except the last it was returned.

The Armenian population of about 40,000 was deported and killed en masse during the Armenian genocide of 1915, and when Russian forces took the city in 1916 scarcely 200 Armenians were left alive. In 1919 Mustafa Kemal Atatürk resigned from the Ottoman army in Erzurum, and the Erzurum Congress of that year was one of the starting points of the Turkish War of Independence.

Little of medieval Erzurum survives beyond scattered buildings, among them the citadel and the 13th-century Çifte Minareli Medrese, the Twin Minaret madrasa. Atatürk University, established in 1950, is among the largest universities in Turkey, and the nearby Palandöken Mountain draws visitors for winter sports. Small workshops make souvenirs from Oltu stone.
esagila: The Esagila, also spelled Esangil, took its Sumerian name, É-SAǦ-ÍL.LA, to mean temple whose top is lofty. It was dedicated to Marduk, the protector god of Babylon, and lay south of the ziggurat Etemenanki. Esarhaddon, king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 681 to 669 BCE, reconstructed it, claiming to have built it from the foundation to the battlements, a claim corroborated by dedicatory inscriptions found on the stones of the temple's walls.

The temple held the statue of Marduk, surrounded by cult images of the cities that had fallen under the hegemony of Babylon from the 18th century BCE. It also contained a small lake called the Abzu by the Babylonian priests, a representation of Marduk's father Enki, the god of the waters, who lived in the Abzu, the source of all fresh waters.

The complex, completed in its final form by Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BCE) around earlier cores, was the centre of Babylon. It had a large court of about 40 by 70 metres, containing a smaller court of about 25 by 40 metres, and then the central shrine, made of an anteroom and the inner sanctum that held the statues of Marduk and his consort Sarpanit.

According to Herodotus, Xerxes had a statue removed from the Esagila when he flooded Babylon in 482 BCE, desecrated the temple and sacked the city. Alexander the Great ordered restorations, and the temple was maintained through the 2nd century BCE as one of the last strongholds of Babylonian culture, including literacy in cuneiform. As Babylon was gradually abandoned under the Parthian Empire the temple decayed in the 1st century BCE.

Robert Koldewey rediscovered it under a heap of debris in November 1900, and serious examination began in 1910. The rising water table has obliterated much of the sun-dried brick and other oldest material. The Esagila tablet, copied from older texts in 229 BCE, describes the temple in its first fifteen lines before turning to Etemenanki, and has aided reconstruction. George Smith described the tablet in 1872.
esarhaddon: Esarhaddon was the third king of the Sargonid dynasty, and his name in Akkadian, Aššur-aḫa-iddina, means Ashur has given me a brother. Sennacherib's first choice of heir was his eldest son Ashur-nadin-shumi, whom he made ruler of Babylon around 700 BCE. The Elamites captured the prince at Sippar in 694 BCE and probably executed him. Sennacherib then raised his second surviving son, Arda-Mulissu, to crown prince, but in 684 BCE replaced him with Esarhaddon, a younger son. The reason is unknown, but Arda-Mulissu was deeply disappointed. Esarhaddon later wrote that his brothers went mad and drew their swords in the middle of Nineveh.

On about 20 October 681 BCE Arda-Mulissu and another brother, Nabû-šarru-uṣur, killed Sennacherib in a temple at Nineveh. Their supporters fell out, delaying a coronation, and Esarhaddon raised an army and met his brothers' forces at Hanigalbat, where most of the soldiers deserted to him. He then marched on Nineveh unopposed, after a six-week war of succession. His brothers' attempt left him distrustful of officials, governors and male relatives, and he often sought the advice of oracles and priests. His mother Naqiʾa, his wife Esharra-hammat and his daughter Šērūʾa-ēṭirat held more influence than women had in earlier Assyrian history.

He sponsored building and restoration in Babylonia on a far greater scale than any predecessor, probably to show the benefits of Assyrian rule. He faced Urartu under Rusa II and the Cimmerians, and after defeating the Median kings Eparna and Shidirparna many Medes swore allegiance to Assyria. His first invasion of Egypt, in 673 BCE, failed, and his health was deteriorating.

In 671 BCE he marched again with a much larger army, and a prophecy at Harran predicted success. He conquered Egypt. A conspiracy followed in 671-670 BCE, and he performed the substitute king ritual to avert evil. In 669 BCE Egypt rebelled, and Esarhaddon died at Harran in about November 669 BCE, apparently of natural causes, on his way to campaign against it a third time.

Esarhaddon arranged for his sons to succeed him peacefully, Ashurbanipal as ruler of the empire and Shamash-shum-ukin as king of Babylon. Ashurbanipal finished the campaign against Egypt in 667 BCE. Historians generally regard Esarhaddon as gentler than Sennacherib and as one of the most successful Assyrian kings, and according to the Assyriologist Karen Radner he emerges more clearly as an individual than any other Assyrian king because court correspondence from his reign survives.
esch-sur-alzette: Esch-sur-Alzette lies in the south-west of Luxembourg, on the border with France, in the valley of the Alzette, which flows through the city. It is usually called just Esch, and the full name distinguishes it from the village of Esch-sur-Sûre, 45 kilometres further north. Luxembourg City is roughly 15 kilometres to the north-east.

The town was first mentioned on 12 April 1128, in a message to Pope Honorius II. For a long time it was a small farming village in the valley. That changed when important amounts of iron ore were found in the area in the 1850s. With the development of the mines and the steel industry the population multiplied tenfold in a couple of decades, and the workers came from across Europe, making Esch a multicultural community. The steel company ARBED was founded in 1911.

In the 1970s, as a result of the steel crisis, the mines and many of the blast furnaces were shut down. The last one, at Esch-Belval, stopped operating for good in 1997, and an electric furnace fed with scrap metal replaced the blast furnaces. In 2001 a film company built a huge backdrop on the Terre Rouge, a former steelworks site, a copy of sixteenth-century Venice with a 600-metre Grand Canal. Films such as The Merchant of Venice were shot there until it was torn down in 2007.

Esch-sur-Alzette is the second most populous commune of Luxembourg, with a population of about thirty-eight thousand. The industrial wasteland at Belval is being redeveloped as a new town quarter, and the area around the old blast furnaces hosts structures of the University of Luxembourg, research centres and the national archives. Esch has a conservatory of music and the longest shopping street in Luxembourg. It was a European Capital of Culture for 2022, together with Kaunas and Novi Sad.
esen-taishi: Esen was the son of Toghon, the Oirat taishi, of the Choros clan. The title, derived from a Chinese term, was the highest rank among the Mongols below that of khan, which Toghon could not hold because he was not of the lineage of Genghis Khan. In the 1420s Esen led three successful campaigns against Eastern Moghulistan, twice capturing its ruler Uwais Khan. In the 1430s he fought beside his father against the Khalkha taishi Arughtai, who died in 1434. Toghon then installed Taisun as a puppet Great Khan of the Northern Yuan and married him to Esen's elder sister.

After Toghon died in 1438 Esen inherited his title. In 1443 and again in 1445 Oirats attacked Hami, an oasis that acknowledged Ming suzerainty, and its prince came to the Oirat camp in 1448. In 1445 Esen forced the leaders of the Shazhou and Qizhin guards in western Gansu to accept Mongol titles. By 1447 he had conquered two of the three Uriankhai guards and driven the third to migrate, giving him control from present-day Xinjiang to Korea.

Oirat tributary missions to Beijing, in fact commercial, grew from around a hundred men to more than two thousand. In 1448 a mission falsely claimed over three thousand members and was granted one fifth of the gifts it demanded; the court then rejected a marriage between Esen's son and the imperial family that Chinese interpreters had promised without authority. In July 1449 Esen invaded. Emperor Yingzong of Ming led an army reportedly of half a million men, which was massacred at the Tumu postal station on 1 September. Esen besieged Beijing from 27 to 30 October but withdrew, and in September 1450 the emperor was taken back to China.

Esen and Taisun fell out over the choice of Taisun's successor. Taisun allied with the Ming and with Esen's subordinate Alag, but his brother Agbarjin defected to the Oirats in the winter of 1451. Esen defeated Taisun, who fled and was killed by a local chieftain in early 1452. Esen proclaimed Agbarjin khan and soon murdered him. In a letter of 1453 to the Ming court he styled himself Tian-sheng Khagan of the Great Yuan.

Chinese accounts attribute the revolt against him to his lavish living and heavy drinking. He had also refused the title of taishi to Alag, granting it to his own son Amasanj. Esen was defeated and was killed by a man named Bukun, whose father he had ordered put to death, and the Oirat state collapsed.
eshnunna: Eshnunna was an ancient city and city-state in central Mesopotamia, in the Diyala Valley north-west of Sumer proper but securely within the Sumerian cultural milieu. Its modern site is Tell Asmar in Iraq. The city's tutelary deity was Tishpak, though Sin, Adad and Inanna of Kiti were also worshipped there. Because it controlled trade routes it was a gateway between Mesopotamian and Elamite culture, with access to horses from the north, copper, tin and other metals and precious stones. A pendant of copal from Zanzibar was found in a grave there, and a small number of seals and beads of the Indus Valley civilisation.

Inhabited since the Jemdet Nasr period, around 3000 BCE, Eshnunna was a major city in the Early Dynastic period. Its first known rulers were vassal governors under the Third Dynasty of Ur. Ituria, one of them, built a temple to the deified Shu-Sin in a new lower town. His son Šu-ilišu in 2026 BCE replaced the Ur III calendar with a local one and styled himself king instead of governor.

After Ur fell, Eshnunna was for about fifteen years the independent state of Warum. Ishbi-Erra of Isin defeated an invader from Subartu around 2010 BCE and installed Nur-ahum as ruler. Kirikiri then ousted Nur-ahum and founded a line with his son Bilalama, who gave his daughter Me-Kubi in marriage to Tan-Ruhuratir of Elam and tried to stay on good terms both with Elam and with Ilum-muttabbil of Der, though the two were at war. A fire later destroyed the palace, perhaps after a foreign invasion. After the city was captured by Hammurabi it was ruled by vassal governors under Babylon. In the 12th century BCE the Elamite ruler Shutruk-Nakhunte conquered it and carried statues from the site to Susa.

The ruins form the mound of Tell Asmar, about 50 miles north-east of Baghdad. A team of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago led by Henri Frankfort excavated it in six seasons between 1930 and 1936. They concentrated on the palace and the temple of Shu-Sin and on the Abu Temple, whose phases helped to define the three parts of the Early Dynastic period. The Tell Asmar Hoard, twelve gypsum temple statues in a simplified geometric style with greatly enlarged inlaid eyes, was found in its Square Temple.

The Laws of Eshnunna, found on two tablets at Shaduppum (Tell Harmal) and a fragment at Tell Haddad, were written around the reign of King Dadusha. They are similar to the Code of Hammurabi, though the date when the laws were composed is unknown.
esperanto: Before Esperanto, Johann Martin Schleyer (1831–1912) had created Volapük as a neutral universal second language. His movement gained widespread and active use in the 19th century, which showed there was demand for such a language. When the Volapük movement collapsed from within, many of its speakers joined the Esperanto movement, which was linguistically simpler and lacked central control, and many former Volapük clubs became Esperanto clubs.

L. L. Zamenhof, a Jewish ophthalmologist from Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire, created Esperanto in the late 1870s and early 1880s. After several earlier versions, he self-published the first book of grammar, the Unua Libro, on 26 July 1887, under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'. He called the language simply the international language. Early speakers grew fond of the pseudonym and began to use it as the name of the language. Besides his native Yiddish and Russian, Zamenhof studied German, Hebrew, Latin, English, Spanish, Lithuanian, Italian, French, Aramaic and Volapük.

The language sits between naturalistic constructed languages, which imitate existing ones, and a priori ones. About 80% of its vocabulary derives from Romance languages, and the remainder chiefly from Germanic, Greek and Slavic languages. New words are formed through extensive use of prefixes, suffixes and compounds, so a smaller set of words can express a great deal. Its default word order is subject–verb–object, and adjectives may stand before or after their nouns. One 2010 typological study concluded that Esperanto is somewhat European in character, but considerably less so than the European languages themselves.

The Universal Esperanto Association has a consultative relationship with the United Nations and UNESCO, which recognised Esperanto as a medium for international understanding in 1954. The League of Nations tried to promote its teaching in member countries, but the resolutions were defeated, mainly by French delegates who saw no need for it. No country has officially adopted it. It has entered the education systems of Hungary and China, and Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest had a department of Interlinguistics and Esperanto from 1966 to 2004.

Esperanto has an estimated 2,000 native speakers and, by two estimates, around 100,000 users. Reform proposals began with Zamenhof's own in 1894 and with Ido in 1907, and several later constructed languages were based on it. Poland added Esperanto to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2014.
espiritu-santo: Espiritu Santo, usually called Santo, has an area of 3,955.5 square kilometres, although Efate, where the capital Port Vila stands, has a larger population. It lies in Sanma Province in the region of Melanesia in the Pacific. Luganville, on the south-east coast, is the only true town on the island and the second-largest settlement in Vanuatu. Vanuatu's highest peak, the 1,879-metre Mount Tabwemasana, rises in the west-centre of the island, and most of the interior is far from the limited road network. More than 30 local languages are spoken, and the chief system continues strongly in most areas, whatever people's religion.

A Spanish expedition of three ships led by Pedro Fernandes de Queirós landed in 1606 at Big Bay on the north side. Queirós named the land La Austrialia del Espíritu Santo, honouring the Spanish king's descent from the House of Austria, and believed he had reached the Great Southern Continent. A local chief tried to chase the explorers back to their ships and was killed in an exchange of arrows and musket fire.

Queirós announced a city, Nova Jerusalem, but in early June, with provisions running low, the ships left. His second-in-command, Luis Váez de Torres, sailed west and found the strait between New Guinea and northern Australia that bears his name. Europeans did not return for 160 years: Louis de Bougainville came in 1768 and James Cook in 1774.

In the 19th century Australian, British, French and German settlers came to the New Hebrides. Britain and France declared the islands neutral in 1878, and in 1906 a joint Condominium replaced their naval commission. During the Second World War American naval and air forces made Santo a large base, with airfields built by the Seabees. The liner SS President Coolidge, converted to a troop ship, hit a sea mine and sank off the island, and the Americans dumped equipment at what is called Million Dollar Point.

Between May and August 1980, during the transfer of the New Hebrides to independent Vanuatu, Jimmy Stevens's Nagriamel movement, allied with private French interests and backed by the Phoenix Foundation and American libertarians, declared the island independent. The Republic of Vemerana was proclaimed on 28 May, and Luganville was renamed Allonneaupolis. After independence on 31 July 1980, Papua New Guinea's army suppressed the rebellion at the new government's request.

Most people are Christians, with Presbyterian, Roman Catholic and Anglican churches the largest, and the Nagriamel movement has followers at Fanafo. The shipwreck and reefs draw divers. The island is home to endemic birds such as the Santo mountain starling and to two protected areas, the Loru Conservation Area and the Vatthe Conservation Area. James A. Michener set Tales of the South Pacific there in fictionalised form.
essad-pasha-toptani: Essad Toptani was born in Tirana in 1863, the son of Ali Toptani and Vasfije Alizoti, and belonged to the Toptani family, a prominent landowning noble family that helped found the city. Under Ottoman rule he served as a kaymakam and commanded the gendarmerie in Tirana. In 1908 at Janina he joined the Young Turks and sat in the Ottoman parliament. On 27 April 1909 he was the main messenger of four Young Turk members who told Sultan Abdul Hamid II that he was deposed, saying that the nation had deposed him; the sultan called him a wicked man.

In 1912 Toptani and Syrja Vlora argued for Albanians in the Ottoman parliament for an end to government force and for good governance, and during the Albanian revolt he undertook to organise the uprising in Central Albania and Mirdita. On 30 January 1913 Hasan Riza Pasha, commander of Shkodër, was ambushed and killed by men disguised as women, thought to be two of Toptani's officers, and Toptani has been accused of involvement. He continued the resistance until April 1913, when he turned the fortress over to Montenegro after a long siege, hoping for Montenegrin support for his rule in central Albania. In July 1913 the Vlora family persuaded him to become minister of the interior in the provisional government.

He led a faction in the Peasant Revolt against Prince Wilhelm. On 19 May 1914 forces under the Dutch gendarmerie officer Johan Sluys shelled his house in Durrës and he surrendered; he was sent to Bari and banned from returning. After the outbreak of the First World War he signed the secret Treaty of Niš with Serbia's prime minister Nikola Pašić on 17 September 1914. With Italian and Serbian backing he took Durrës without a fight by 3 October 1914, and he served as prime minister until 1916. Austria-Hungary later occupied much of the country and he fled to France and England.

Avni Rustemi shot Toptani dead in Paris on 13 June 1920 as he left the Hotel Continental. He was buried in the Serbian military section of the Thiais cemetery. Many Albanians regard him as a traitor and a symbol of treason. Edith Durham described him as a relic of the Middle Ages, like the swashbucklers who sold their services to rival rulers. A street in Belgrade is named after him.
essaouira: Essaouira lies on the Atlantic coast of western Morocco, in a bay partly sheltered by the island of Mogador, which makes it one of the best anchorages on the Moroccan coast. Its Arabic name aṣ-Ṣwiṛa is the diminutive of a word meaning wall or rampart. Until the 1960s it was generally known by the Portuguese name Mogador, probably a corruption of Amegdul, a name mentioned by the 11th-century geographer al-Bakrī. The place has been occupied since prehistoric times.

The Carthaginian navigator Hanno visited in the 5th century BCE and established the trading post of Arambys. Around the turn of the 1st century BCE and CE the Berber king Juba II of Mauretania set up a factory making Tyrian purple dye from shells found on the rocks and nearby islands. In 1506 King Manuel I of Portugal ordered a fortress built, the Castelo Real de Mogador, which fell to the local Regraga fraternity in 1510. In 1629 France tried to colonise Mogador under Admiral Isaac de Razilly, but the settlers withdrew after a few days.

The present city was built by the 'Alawid sultan Mohammed III, who wished to reorient his kingdom towards the Atlantic and to trade with European powers. For twelve years he directed the French engineer Théodore Cornut and other Moroccan and European architects and technicians. The harbour entrance, with the Porte de la Marine, was built by an English renegade known as Ahmed el Inglizi. Mohammed III closed the harbour of Agadir in 1767 so that southern trade would pass through Essaouira, and he encouraged Moroccan Jews to settle and handle the European trade. Until the end of the 19th century Essaouira was Morocco's principal port, receiving goods that came by caravan from sub-Saharan Africa through Timbuktu and Marrakesh.

On 16 August 1844 the French Navy under the Prince de Joinville bombarded and briefly occupied Mogador in the First Franco-Moroccan War. From 1912 to 1956 the city was part of the French protectorate of Morocco.

Essaouira has 82,962 inhabitants, according to the count of 2024. Its medina was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. The Jewish quarter, the mellah, contains many old synagogues, and the town has a large Jewish cemetery; in 1867 a visiting French botanist reported that Jews made up half of the population of 12,000.
essen: Essen lies at the centre of the Ruhr, the largest urban area in Germany, and is its second-largest city after Dortmund. The Emscher flows through the north of the city and the Ruhr River, dammed to form Lake Baldeney and Lake Kettwig, through the south. The oldest archaeological find is the Vogelheimer Klinge, a blade dated to between 280,000 and 250,000 BCE, found in 1926 during the building of the Rhine-Herne Canal. A megalithic tomb found in 1937 is described as Essen's earliest preserved architecture.

Around 845 Saint Altfrid, later Bishop of Hildesheim, founded a community for women, with his relative Gerswit as first abbess. It was a residence and school for the daughters and widows of the higher Saxon nobility, and members other than the abbess were not obliged to take vows of chastity. In 1216 Emperor Frederick II called the abbess Elisabeth I a Princess of the Empire. Essen received a town charter in 1244, but in 1290 King Rudolph I restored the abbesses to full sovereignty. Charles IV granted the title of free imperial city in 1377, yet disputes between city and abbey continued until the abbey's dissolution in 1803.

During the Thirty Years' War the Protestant city and the Catholic abbey were opposed. In 1623 the princess-abbess Maria Clara von Spaur directed Catholic Spaniards against the city, and a law of 1624 aimed to make the city Catholic again, and churchgoing was strictly controlled. She fled to Cologne when the Dutch stormed Essen in 1629. Mining rights were granted to the abbess in the fourteenth century, a silver mine opened in 1354 and coal mining began in 1450. Prussia annexed the territory in 1802.

Industrialisation, above all the iron works of the Krupp family, made Essen one of Germany's chief coal and steel centres. Alfred Krupp built the mansion Villa Hügel in 1873. Heavy industry declined in the late twentieth century.

Essen is the tenth-largest city in Germany, with 573,618 inhabitants. The Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex, whose Shaft XII is in Bauhaus style, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001. Essen Minster, the former abbey church, keeps the Golden Madonna of Essen, made around 980 and regarded as the oldest known sculpture of the Madonna. The city was European Capital of Culture on behalf of the Ruhr in 2010.
essenes: The Essene movement likely arose as a distinct group among Jews in the time of Jonathan Apphus, driven by disputes over Jewish law and the belief that Jonathan's high priesthood was illegitimate. Most scholars think the Essenes seceded from the Zadokite priests. They attributed their interpretation of the Torah to an early leader, the Teacher of Righteousness, possibly a legitimate high priest. Josephus names them as one of the three sects of Jewish philosophy, with the Pharisees and Sadducees. Josephus and Philo give their number as about four thousand, living in many towns of Judaea, while Pliny the Elder places them above Ein Gedi on the west side of the Dead Sea.

Josephus and Philo describe a strictly communal life, often compared to later Christian monasticism. Property was held in common, a leader was elected and obeyed, and the Essenes owned no slaves and did not trade. They were forbidden to swear oaths or sacrifice animals, and carried weapons only against robbers. Many groups were celibate, though Josephus mentions another order that married after a three-year engagement. After a three-year probation a new member swore to practise piety and righteousness and to preserve the books of the Essenes and the names of the angels. They believed in the immortality of the soul, ate communal meals and practised ritual immersion in water.

The Dead Sea Scrolls, found at Qumran on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea, are commonly believed to be the Essenes' library, and Qumran is believed to have been home to an Essene community. The scrolls include parts of the Hebrew Bible and sectarian works such as the Community Rule, the Damascus Document and the War Scroll. The link is disputed: Norman Golb argues that the ruins were a fortress, and Lawrence Schiffman calls the community Sadducean. The conventional view is that the Essenes disappeared after the First Jewish–Roman War, which destroyed Qumran, though no direct source supports this. Some scholars see their influence on Mandaeism and early Christianity.
esslingen-am-neckar: Esslingen am Neckar lies on the Neckar, about 14 kilometres south-east of the centre of Stuttgart, in Baden-Württemberg, and is the seat of the District of Esslingen. Archaeological evidence shows settlement since the Neolithic period. In the 1st century CE the region became part of the Roman Empire. The place-name ending -ingen points to a settlement of a kinship group led by a man called Azzilo, Hezzilo or Hetsilo, and the name first appears in 856 as Ezlinga.

Esslingen is first mentioned in 777, in the will of Abbot Fulrad of Saint-Denis, chaplain of Pippin and Charlemagne. He bequeathed to his monastery the sixth cell on the river Neckar, and he also brought the bones of Saint Vitalis to Esslingen, which made it a destination for pilgrims and led to its growth. Around 800 it became a market town, and it received city rights in 1229 under Emperor Frederick II.

The Neckar bridge, which still stands, made Esslingen a major centre of trade on the route between Italy, Switzerland and northern Germany. Taxes from the bridge and market, and exports of the region's wines, led to further growth. Between the 13th and 16th centuries the Free Imperial City was often in conflict with the Counts of Württemberg. About half the population died of famine or epidemics in the Thirty Years' War between 1618 and 1648. In the Napoleonic era it lost its independence and became part of the Duchy of Württemberg.

Industrialisation in the 19th century, with glove manufacturing, textiles and metalworking, shaped the city's growth, and the first train ran from Cannstatt to Esslingen on 20 November 1845. US troops occupied the city in April 1945, and it suffered very little damage in the war, so the medieval character of its centre is largely preserved.

The old town keeps part of its defensive wall, including the Dicke Turm, or fat tower, above the vineyards, a market square ringed by half-timbered buildings, and the Altes Rathaus, the old city hall. The city lies on the German Timber-Frame Road and is the seat of the Esslingen University of Applied Sciences.
estates-general-france: The first national assembly was summoned in 1302 by King Philip IV, who was in conflict with Pope Boniface VIII. During his reign it was assembled several times to grant him subsidies, which became the most frequent reason for calling it. It always included the clergy, the nobility and the commoners, and the king summoned it to grant subsidies or to give aid and counsel, though its makeup and powers varied greatly.

In the 14th and first half of the 15th centuries only the Third Estate was elected, and only by the privileged towns, the bonnes villes. The country districts were not represented, and the lay and ecclesiastical lords were chosen and summoned directly by the king.

In the 14th century the king could not in theory levy general taxation without the consent of the lords and the towns, so the Estates were summoned often. From 1355 to 1358, under John II, they controlled the voting of taxes and their administration. In the later 15th century the taille, aids and gabelle became permanent, and the Estates lost the power of the purse.

At the Estates of 1484 the deputies sided with Anne de Beaujeu over the regency and voted the taille for two years only, on the promise that they would be summoned again. The promise was not kept, and they did not meet again until 1560. The Wars of Religion and shortage of money then revived them, at Orleans in 1560, Pontoise in 1561, and Blois in 1576 and 1588. The meeting in Paris in 1614 was the last for over a century and a half; dissensions between the three orders weakened it, and it dissolved before finishing its work.

The Estates had no share in legislation, which belonged to the king alone. Their initiative lay in presenting complaints and petitions, gathered in cahiers de doléances, which the king usually answered by an ordinance.

The Estates General met again at Versailles on 5 May 1789, after an Assembly of Notables in 1787. The Third Estate, about 25 million people, had 578 representatives, but voting by orders meant that its votes counted no more than those of each smaller estate. After a deadlock over procedure, Abbé Sieyès moved on 28 May that the Third Estate proceed alone, and on 17 June it declared itself the National Assembly. It took the Tennis Court Oath on 20 June, and on 9 July it reconstituted itself as the National Constituent Assembly.
este-veneto: Este gives its name to the Este culture, a proto-historic culture that ran from the late Italian Bronze Age, in the 10th or 9th century BCE, to the Roman period in the 1st century BCE, and that was located in the present territory of the Veneto. During the Iron Age the town was a major centre of the Veneti, who left inscriptions on funerary and votive objects. In the late 3rd century BCE Este fell peacefully under the sway of Rome and became a Roman colony under the name of Ateste. After the Battle of Actium, Augustus settled soldiers of two legions in its territory. In Late Antiquity the town was devastated by barbarian invasions, especially that of Attila, and reduced to a rural village.

It revived only after the 10th century, when the Obertenghi family came to rule a vast area including Este and began to call themselves the House of Este. Azzo II d'Este built a castle there and named his family after it. The family held the town until 1240, when it moved its capital to Ferrara. Ezzelino da Romano III conquered Este in 1238 and 1249, and in the 14th century the Scaligeri, the Carraresi and the Visconti disputed it, until it surrendered to Venice in 1405. Under Venice it grew economically, apart from the plague of 1630. It passed to the Austrian Empire after the Napoleonic Wars and was annexed by the Kingdom of Italy after the Third Independence War of 1866.

Este is a town and comune of the Province of Padua, at the foot of the Euganean Hills, and a centre for farming, crafts and industry. Its sights include the Duomo of Este, the Museo Nazionale Atestino, the Villa Contarini and the Castello Carrarese.
estella-lizarra: Estella, in Basque Lizarra, lies south-west of Pamplona in the autonomous community of Navarre, close to the border with La Rioja and Álava. It stands near a great meander of the Ega. The town was founded in 1090, when the place beside the fortified settlement of Lizarra received a charter from the Pamplonese king Sancho Ramirez.

The town became a landmark on the Way of St. James, the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, and thrived on its position and on the mix of peoples settled there. Navarrese kings called in settlers, chiefly Occitans from Auvergne and Limousin, and they lived alongside Jews and the original Navarrese inhabitants. The wealth that resulted produced a flourishing Romanesque architecture, represented by the Church of San Pedro de la Rúa, the Palacio de los Reyes de Navarra and the Church of San Miguel, among others.

A Jewish community is recorded from the 11th century. Many Jews from Andalusia came because of the privileges granted there, among them the Granada poet Moses ibn Ezra. The Jews were expelled from Estella in 1498. In the 19th century the town was long the headquarters of Don Carlos, who was proclaimed king there in 1833, and a major base of the Carlists in their wars.

Tomás de Zumalacárregui was appointed commander in chief there. When the Third Carlist War began in 1872 Estella became the court of Carlos de Borbón y Austria-Este, called Carlos VII by his supporters, and virtually the capital of Carlist Spain until liberal troops took the town on 16 February 1876, when the Carlists there surrendered.

Between 1927 and 1967 Estella was the terminus of the Ferrocarril Vasco-Navarro, a railway running as far as Bergara, which was electrified in 1938, a feat for the time. The town holds the cycling race GP Miguel Induráin each year. Its Romanesque churches and palace are the chief remains of its medieval prosperity on the pilgrim road.
estonia: Estonia lies in the Baltic region of Northern Europe, bordered by the Gulf of Finland to the north, the Baltic Sea to the west, Latvia to the south and Russia to the east. Its territory covers 45,335 square kilometres and includes the mainland, the larger islands of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, and over 2,300 other islands and islets. Its indented coastline stretches for 3,794 kilometres and is notable for the limestone cliffs of the north coast.

The terrain is generally flat, with an average elevation of about 50 metres. The highest peak, Suur Munamägi in the Haanja Upland, reaches 318 metres. Bogs and mires cover 23.2% of the land, and there are over 1,560 natural lakes, the largest being Lake Peipus on the border with Russia.

The oldest known settlement is Pulli, on the banks of the Pärnu, dating to the Mesolithic. The Kunda culture is linked to the earliest human habitation in the Mesolithic, and ceramics of the Narva culture appear around 5300 BCE. The Bronze Age began around 1800 BCE and saw the first hill fort settlements, and the Iron Age began around 500 BCE. The name Estonia has been connected to the Aesti, a people first mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus around 98 CE, though historians differ on whom he meant.

Scandinavian sagas describe the early 7th century defeat and killing of Ingvar Harra, King of the Swedes, by Estonian Vikings. In about 1030 Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise of Kievan Rus' captured Tartu, and the Sosols destroyed this foothold in 1061. Estonians from the island of Saaremaa, known as Oeselians, joined seaborne raids, and in 1187 Oeselians, Curonians or Karelians sacked Sigtuna, then a major city of Sweden. The indigenous population was one of the last pagan civilisations in Europe to adopt Christianity, after the Northern Crusades of the 13th century.

Estonia is a unitary parliamentary republic. The 101-member Riigikogu is elected for four years, and the president is chosen by the Riigikogu or an electoral college. In 2005 Estonia became the first country to introduce nationwide binding internet voting in local elections. It adopted the euro on 1 January 2011.

The population is nearly 1.4 million. Ethnic Estonians were 88% of the population before World War II, dropped to 61% by 1989 under Soviet immigration, deportations and executions, and rose to 69% by 2006. The Estonian Cultural Autonomy law of 1925 was unique in Europe at the time.
estonian-declaration-of-independence: The manifesto was drafted by the Salvation Committee, which the elders of the Estonian Provincial Assembly (Maapäev) had elected. Its three members were Konstantin Päts, Jüri Vilms and Konstantin Konik. The Committee acted as the executive body of the democratically elected Assembly during World War I, as Russian Bolshevik troops retreated from Estonia and the German army advanced towards it. The proclamation was first intended for 21 February 1918 but was delayed until the evening of 23 February, when the text was printed and read aloud in public in Pärnu.

On 24 February 1918 the manifesto was printed and distributed in the capital, Tallinn, then also called Reval. The declaration was made in the main hall of the local branch of the State Bank of the Russian Empire, which later became part of the head office of the Bank of Estonia. It is the founding act of the independent democratic Republic of Estonia, and 24 February has been kept since then as Estonian Independence Day, the national day.

The German Empire did not recognise the new democratic republic and occupied the country. After the defeat of the Central Powers in November 1918, Germany withdrew its troops and on 19 November formally handed power to the Estonian Provisional Government. The Bolshevik invasion and the Estonian War of Independence followed. On 2 February 1920 Estonia and Bolshevik Russia signed the Tartu Peace Treaty, and in 1921 the republic gained international recognition and joined the League of Nations.
estonian-defence-league: The league grew out of the Omakaitse, or Citizens' Defence Organisation, Estonia's first armed home guard, formed in 1918 against the disorder that followed the Russian Revolution. It took the name Estonian Defence League on 11 November 1918 and served as a national guard in the War of Independence. On 1 December 1924 it helped oppose an attempted Communist coup, after which it was developed for national defence. A magazine, Kaitse Kodu!, followed in 1925, and the first Defence League Festival was held in Tallinn on 19–20 June 1926.

Women's Home Defence was given statutes in 1927, the scouts of the Young Eagles were invited to join in 1928, and the girls' organisation Home Daughters was founded in 1932; the statutes the government approved in 1931 are still in force. After the Soviet invasion of 17 June 1940 the government had to order members to hand in all their weapons within 48 hours. Many damaged them first and hundreds were hidden. The 43,600 members were released from their oaths on 24 June, and on 29 June the league's property passed to the Communist Party of Estonia.

Former members kept in touch in secret. In 1941 some joined the forest brothers and the Omakaitse units of the Summer War, which were placed under German field commanders. A league in exile was founded in the United States in 1974 by Avdy Andresson. The league was refounded at Järvakandi on 17 February 1990, its legal rights were restored on 4 September 1991, and on 28 April 1992 it became part of the Defence Forces.

A law of 1999 set out its tasks, structure and cooperation with the army and police. It is divided into four Territorial Defence Districts of fifteen regional units called malevs, which mostly follow the county borders, and each district would form a battalion on mobilisation. Members help fight wildfires, serve as assistant police and have taken part in peace support operations in the Balkan states. Since 2000 the league has again organised the Victory Day parade each 23 June.
estonian-war-of-independence: During the Russian Revolution of 1917 the provincial legislature of the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia, the Maapäev, proclaimed itself the highest authority in Estonia, and the local Bolsheviks dissolved it. Its Salvation Committee issued the Estonian Declaration of Independence in Tallinn on 24 February 1918, but German troops entered the city the next day and did not recognise the provisional government. Between 11 and 14 November 1918, after Germany's capitulation, German representatives handed over political power to it. On 16 November it called for voluntary mobilisation, with Konstantin Päts as Minister of War and Aleksander Tõnisson as commander of an army that at first made up one division.

On 28 November 1918 the Soviet 6th Red Rifle Division attacked Narva taking it the next day. By the end of the year the 7th Red Army held a front 34 kilometres east of Tallinn. Colonel Johan Laidoner became commander in chief and Finland delivered 5,000 rifles and 20 field guns.
