On 31 December a Royal Navy squadron under Rear Admiral Sir Edwyn Alexander-Sinclair arrived with 6,500 rifles and 200 machine guns, and Finnish volunteers followed in January. The Estonian army halted the Red advance between 2 and 5 January 1919 and counter-attacked on 7 January, using armoured trains. It freed Tapa, Rakvere, Narva on 18 January and Tartu, and drove the Red Latvian Riflemen from Valga on 31 January.

Fighting continued into Russia and Latvia. The Estonian Petseri Battle Group took Pskov on 25 May, with the White Russian Northern Corps. The war against the Baltische Landeswehr began on 5 June 1919, after Laidoner demanded that German forces under General Rüdiger von der Goltz withdraw. The Landeswehr took Cēsis on 6 June. In the Battle of Cēsis from 19 June, the Estonian 3rd Division, with a Latvian regiment, held off the Iron Division and on 23 June recaptured Cēsis. A ceasefire on 3 July, at the Entente's demand, restored the Latvian government of Kārlis Ulmanis.

In autumn Estonia supported the Northwestern Army's offensive towards Petrograd, as the Entente demanded, and when it failed disarmed and interned the remnants. Fierce battles at Narva followed from November, with 120,000 Soviet troops facing 40,000 Estonians, and the Red Army suffered 35,000 casualties. The peace treaty was concluded on 31 December 1919, and the ceasefire took effect on 3 January 1920. The war ended in the Treaty of Tartu in 1920.
estonians: Archaeological research shows that the area of Estonia was first inhabited about 13,000 to 11,000 years ago. Some recent linguistic estimates suggest that Finno-Ugric speakers reached the Baltic Sea considerably later, perhaps in the Early Bronze Age around 1800 BCE. It has also been argued that Western Uralic tribes reached Fennoscandia first, giving rise to the Sámi, and arrived in the Baltic region later, which led to the formation of the Baltic Finnic peoples, from whom Estonians and Finns descend.

The Roman historian Tacitus mentioned the Aesti in 98 CE, and the name is thought to be related to Eesti. The oldest known endonym is maarahvas, meaning land people or country folk, which was used until the middle of the 19th century. The oldest known book in Estonian, the Wanradt–Koell Catechism, was printed in 1535. The ruling elites stayed predominantly German in language and culture after the conquest of the early 13th century.

Some ethnic awareness preceded the national awakening of the 19th century. Bible translations appeared in 1739, books and brochures in Estonian rose from 18 in the 1750s to 54 in the 1790s, and by 1800 more than half of adult Estonians could read. The first university-educated intellectuals to identify as Estonians appeared in the 1820s, among them Friedrich Robert Faehlmann, Kristjan Jaak Peterson and Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald. By the end of the 1860s Estonians were unwilling to accept German cultural and political hegemony.

Estonians speak Estonian, a Finnic language related to Finnish, Karelian and Livonian. Historically and culturally the country divides into Northern and Southern Estonia, and the South Estonian dialects, including Võro and Seto, are often considered a separate language. About 1.1 million ethnic Estonians live worldwide, mostly in Estonia, with diaspora communities in Finland, the United States, Sweden, Canada and the United Kingdom. Large numbers fled over the Baltic Sea in 1944 as the Soviet army occupied Estonia.
eswatini: Eswatini is a small landlocked kingdom of 17,364 square kilometres, no more than 200 km from north to south and 130 km from east to west, the second smallest country in continental Africa. It is bordered by South Africa on the north, west and south and by Mozambique on the east, where the Lebombo Mountains rise to about 600 m. Four regions run from north to south by elevation: the Highveld, the Middleveld, the Lowveld and the Lubombo plateau. The capital Mbabane is on the Highveld, and Manzini, the main commercial and industrial city, is in the Middleveld.

Artefacts show human activity from the Early Stone Age, around 200,000 years ago. The earliest known inhabitants were Khoisan hunter-gatherers, who were largely replaced by Nguni speakers during the Bantu migrations. Agriculture and iron use date from about the 4th century. The Swazi trace their origins to the Embo-Dlamini, a branch of the Embo-Nguni who settled near Delagoa Bay in Mozambique, where the Embo were a small chiefdom led by Chief Langa.

The Swazis established their kingdom in the mid-18th century under Ngwane III. The country and its people take their name from Mswati II, the 19th-century king under whom the kingdom was expanded and unified. Its boundaries were drawn in 1881 during the European Scramble for Africa. After the Second Boer War the kingdom, as Swaziland, was under British rule from 1903 until it regained full independence on 6 September 1968. In April 2018 the king changed the official name to the Kingdom of Eswatini, the name commonly used in the Swazi language.

Eswatini is an absolute monarchy under a constitution adopted in 2005, with Mbabane as executive capital and Lobamba as legislative capital. Its head of state is the king, or ngwenyama, meaning lion, who by tradition reigns with his mother, the ndlovukati, or she-elephant. SiSwati and English are the official languages, and most people are ethnic Swazi. The traditional homestead centres on a cattle byre, which has ritual as well as practical meaning as a store of wealth and a symbol of prestige.
esztergom: Esztergom is a city with county rights in Komárom-Esztergom County, 46 kilometres north-west of Budapest. It lies on the right bank of the Danube, which forms the border with Slovakia at this point. The Roman town was called Solva, and the medieval Latin name was Strigonium. Antonio Bonfini derived the name from Istrogranum, the city at the confluence of the Ister (the Danube) and the Gran (the Hron), and this remains popular, while Pavel Jozef Šafárik proposed a Slavic word meaning a guarded place.

Excavations show that Castle Hill and its surroundings have been inhabited since the end of the Ice Age, some 20,000 years ago. The first people known by name were Celts, who settled about 350 BCE. After Roman conquest it became an important frontier town of Pannonia, known as Salvio Mansio, Salvio or Solva. In the 9th century the territory was mostly under Frankish control and may have formed part of Great Moravia.

Esztergom was the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary from the 10th century until the middle of the 13th, when King Béla IV moved the royal seat to Buda. Part of the royal palace was built under King Béla III, whose wife, a daughter of Louis VII, brought French architects who raised the building at the end of the 12th century. Charles I of Hungary was crowned there in 1301. The Ottoman sultan Suleiman besieged the city in 1543, and a stone table with Ottoman Turkish writing on the Danube bank commemorates the siege. The Ottoman wars left the city devastated, and it was repopulated in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, mostly by Hungarians with some Germans and Slovaks.

Esztergom is the seat of the primate of the Catholic Church in Hungary. Esztergom Basilica was built to plans by Pál Kühnel, János Páckh and József Hild from 1822 to 1869. Its dome is 71.5 metres high, and it incorporates the Bakócz Chapel, the only chapel to survive from the Middle Ages, which was taken apart into 1,600 pieces and rebuilt inside. The Christian Museum, in the Primate's Palace, holds the largest ecclesiastical collection in Hungary, and the Cathedral Library, built in 1853, holds about 250,000 books and several codices.
etchmiadzin-cathedral: Armenian church tradition places the foundation between 301 and 303, after King Tiridates III adopted Christianity as the state religion, although scholars have proposed other dates. The church stood near the royal palace in what was then the capital, Vagharshapat, and is believed to have been built on the site of a pagan temple. Excavations under the main altar in the 1950s found an Urartian stele of the 8th to 6th centuries BCE and an amphora that has been interpreted as part of a Zoroastrian fire temple.

The city and the cathedral were almost completely destroyed in an invasion by the Sasanian king Shapur II around 363. In 450 the Sasanian king Yazdegerd II built a fire temple inside it in an attempt to impose Zoroastrianism. The core of the present building was built in 483/4 by Vahan Mamikonian, after a Persian invasion had severely damaged the church.

The cathedral has a cruciform plan, four free-standing piers and four projecting apses, semicircular inside and polygonal outside. The roof is mostly flat apart from a central cupola with a conical roof on a polygonal drum. It measures 33 by 30 metres, with the dome rising about 34 metres. The core is built of grey stone, and the 17th-century additions are in bright red. Reliefs on the northern facade, including a standing Saint Thecla and Paul the Apostle, are among the most discussed sculptures of early medieval Armenia.

In 1441 a council voted to re-establish the catholicosate at Etchmiadzin, and the cathedral was restored between 1441 and 1443. Shah Abbas I plundered it in 1604. Renovation began in 1627 under Catholicos Movses, who walled the complex, and belfries were added from 1653 to 1682. A sacristy was built at the east end in 1868.

The cathedral is usually considered the first cathedral of ancient Armenia and is often called the oldest cathedral in the world. Scholars generally hold that the first church of the country stood at Ashtishat, and Robert W. Thomson argues that Etchmiadzin was nevertheless a holy shrine from the earliest Christian times. Its plan was copied in 19th-century Armenian churches, such as the Ghazanchetsots Cathedral in Shushi.

During the Armenian genocide about 70,000 refugees gathered in the Etchmiadzin district by the end of 1918. In 2000 UNESCO listed the cathedral with the churches of St Hripsime, St Gayane and Shoghakat and the ruins of Zvartnots as a World Heritage Site. The museum holds manuscripts and relics.
etchu-province: Etchū Province (Etchū no Kuni, also abbreviated Esshū) lay in what is now Toyama Prefecture, in the Hokuriku region of Japan. It bordered Noto and Kaga Provinces to the west, Shinano and Hida Provinces to the south, Echigo Province to the east and the Sea of Japan to the north. Its land was divided into eight districts, among them Imizu, Himi, Nei, Niikawa and Tonami, some of which were later split or dissolved.

Etchū began as part of the ancient Koshi Province, one of the original provinces listed in the Nihon Shoki. Under the reforms of the Taihō Code in 701 CE, Koshi was divided into Echizen, Etchū and Echigo. In 702 the four western districts of Etchū, Kubiki, Kosi, Uonuma and Kambara, were transferred to Echigo. Etchū annexed Noto Province in 741, and Noto was separated again in 757. In 746 the poet Ōtomo no Yakamochi became its governor, or kokushi, and left many references to the region in the poetic anthology Man'yōshū.

The provincial capital and provincial temple of the Nara period stood in what is now the city of Takaoka. Four shrines claim the title of Ichinomiya, two in Takaoka, one in Nanto and one in Tateyama. The Engishiki ranked Etchū a superior country in importance and a middle country in distance from the capital, yet it never developed a powerful local gōzoku clan and was usually controlled by stronger neighbours.

In the Muromachi period the Hatakeyama clan held the post of shugo but preferred to stay in Kyoto and rule through deputies such as the Jinbō and Shiina clans. In the Sengoku period the Hatakeyama moved their power base to Nanao Castle in Noto, and Etchū was contested by Uesugi Kenshin and the Oda clan, with the Ikkō-ikki helping to play one side against the other.

Oda Nobunaga's general Shibata Katsuie and his deputy Sassa Narimasa conquered the area. They were later replaced by Maeda Toshiie under Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The Maeda retained control through Kaga Domain during the Edo period, and in the mid-Edo period Nei District and much of Niikawa District were separated from Kaga as the 100,000 koku Toyama Domain, ruled by a branch of the Maeda.

After the Meiji Restoration and the abolition of the han system in 1871, Etchū was divided into four prefectures, named Kanazawa, Toyama, Nanao and Niikawa, which were merged into Ishikawa Prefecture in 1876. In 1883 Ishikawa was divided, and the four original districts of Etchū became the new Toyama Prefecture. The name Etchū Province continued to appear in official documents for some administrative purposes, and it is named explicitly in treaties of 1894 between Japan and the United States and between Japan and the United Kingdom.
etemenanki: It is unclear when Etemenanki was first built. Andrew R. George argues that it dates from between 1500 and 1000 BCE, because a Middle Assyrian copy of the Creation Epic, Enûma Eliš, already refers to a ziggurat at Babylon. Other scholars see a longer history of successive construction, destruction and reconstruction reaching back to the reign of Hammurabi. Sennacherib destroyed Babylon in 689 BCE and claimed to have destroyed the Etemenanki. Restoration of the city took 88 years, begun by the Assyrian king Esarhaddon and continued by Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II, who rebuilt the ziggurat beside the temple of Marduk, Esagila.

A cuneiform tablet from Uruk dated to 229 BCE, a copy of an older text known as the Esagila tablet, describes the tower as seven stages high with a square base 91 metres on each side. Robert Koldewey's excavations after 1913 confirmed a mudbrick structure, with large stairs on the south side where a triple gate connected it with Esagila, and a larger gate on the east leading to the processional way. Modern scholars dispute the stated height of 91 metres; Fenollós and colleagues propose about 54 metres, or 66 with the temple at the top.

A stele in the Schøyen Collection, identified in 2003 as the oldest known depiction of the ziggurat, dates to 604 to 562 BCE. It shows the high first stages with paired flights of steps, five further stepped stages and the temple on top. Foundation cylinders of Nabopolassar, found in the 1880s, record that Marduk told him the ziggurat was badly buckled and ordered him to found it on the breast of the netherworld and make its top vie with the heavens. Herodotus described a tower of eight stages in the 5th century BCE, but his account is probably second hand.

When Alexander the Great captured Babylon in 331 BCE he ordered repairs to the ziggurat, but he found no progress when he returned in 323 BCE, and his death prevented the work. Later chronicles record several attempts to rebuild it, each preceded by clearing the last debris. The Seleucid crown prince Antiochus I made a sacrifice in preparation, stumbled on the rubble, and angrily ordered his elephant drivers to destroy the last remains. No later references to the Etemenanki survive from antiquity. Some scholars propose it as the ziggurat that may have influenced the biblical account of the Tower of Babel.
eteocretans: The name comes from the Greek eteós, true, and Krḗs, Cretan. In the epic, Odysseus, home again and posing as a grandson of Minos, describes Crete as a land of ninety cities where language is mingled with language: Akhaians, great-hearted Eteocretans, Kydones, Dorians in three clans and Pelasgians. In the first century the geographer Strabo, citing Staphylos, placed the Eteocretans in the south of the island with their town at Prasos, where the temple of Diktaian Zeus stood, and judged them and the Kydones probably native, the other peoples incomers.

About half a dozen inscriptions in Greek letters survive from eastern Crete, five of them clearly Eteocretan. More than half come from Praisos and the rest from Dreros. Two Dreros texts are bilingual with Greek. Found in a Hellenistic cistern beside the temple of Apollo Delphinios, they are written in the archaic Cretan alphabet of the late 7th or early 6th century BCE and record official religious and political decisions. The longer was found in 1936, published by Henri Van Effenterre in 1946 and lost during the occupation of Crete in the Second World War.

The three Praisos inscriptions, published by Margherita Guarducci in 1942 and kept at Heraklion, run from the archaic Cretan alphabet to the Ionic alphabet of probably the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. A text from Psychro is listed by some, though some scholars have called it a modern forgery, a view since challenged.

The language remains untranslated. Van Effenterre suggested that the word inai meant it was decided, matching a formula of the Greek texts, and that one Dreros text concerned offerings of goat cheese to Leto. It has no established link to Indo-European or Semitic languages. Raymond A. Brown proposed an Aegeo-Asianic family joining it with Minoan and Tyrrhenian, but linguists such as Helmut Rix and Carlo De Simone have disputed a Tyrrhenian link. It may descend from the Minoan language of Linear A, but while Linear A is undeciphered the question stays open, and Yves Duhoux has insisted that the two be studied separately.
eteocypriot-language: Eteocypriot is an extinct non-Indo-European language spoken in Cyprus by a non-Hellenic population during the Iron Age. Its name means true or original Cypriot, parallel to Eteocretan, and modern scholars use both names for the non-Greek languages of those places. It was written in the Cypriot syllabary, a script derived from Linear A by way of the Cypro-Minoan variant known as Linear C. The language came under pressure from Arcadocypriot Greek from about the 10th century BCE and died out in about the 4th century BCE.

Several hundred inscriptions in the Cypriot syllabary cannot be read as Greek, though not all of them need be non-Greek. Texts of clearly non-Greek content come from at least two places: Amathus, which has yielded several, among them a bilingual, and Golgoi, the present-day Athienou, where a few short inscriptions were found. The scholar Markus Egetmeyer has suggested that the language of Golgoi, which he calls Golgian, may differ from that of Amathus. Apart from a small vocabulary known from bilingual inscriptions the language is unknown, and its syntax and any inflection or agglutination remain unclear.

The best-known Eteocypriot inscription is the Amathus bilingual, a black marble slab found on the acropolis of Amathus about 1913 and dated to around 600 BCE. Its Eteocypriot text, in Cypriot signs, runs from right to left, and its Greek text, in the Attic dialect and in capital letters, from left to right. Cyrus H. Gordon translated the Greek as a dedication: the city of the Amathusans honoured the noble Ariston, son of Aristonax. Gordon held that the bilingual proves that the signs have the same sound values in Eteocypriot texts as in Cypriot Greek ones.

With so few texts, the origin of the language and its speakers is much debated. Some have linked it to Etruscan and Lemnian, to Hurrian, to Northwest Semitic, to an unknown pre-Indo-European language, or to the language of the poorly understood Cypro-Minoan inscriptions of Bronze Age Cyprus, which share with Eteocypriot a genitive suffix, -o-ti. None of these links is proven, and partial translations depend largely on the language group the translator assumes.
eth-zurich: The Swiss Confederation created the institution as a polytechnic school, and it began giving lectures on 16 October 1855 at various sites around Zurich. It started with six faculties: architecture, civil engineering, mechanical engineering, chemistry, forestry, and an integrated department for mathematics, natural sciences, literature and the social and political sciences. The creation of a federal university was heavily disputed. Liberals advocated a federal university, while conservatives wanted universities to remain under cantonal control, fearing an increase in liberal political power. At first the school shared the buildings of the University of Zurich. It is still known locally as the Polytechnikum, or simply Poly.

From 1905 to 1908, under the presidency of Jérôme Franel, the school restructured its courses to those of a university and gained the right to award doctorates; the first were awarded in 1909. It received its present name, Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule, in 1911. A reorganisation in 1924 grouped it into 12 departments, and it now has 16. The main building was constructed from 1858 to 1864 under Gustav Zeuner, with Gottfried Semper, then a professor of architecture at the school, as its architect. Its south wing was allocated to the University of Zurich until that university built its own main building, and Semper's building was enlarged and given its cupola around 1912 to 1914.

ETH Zurich is a federal institute under the direct administration of the Swiss government. With the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne and four research institutes it forms the ETH Domain. It has two campuses in Zurich, Zentrum, which grew around the main building, and Hönggerberg, and since 2007 one department in Basel. Undergraduates face the Basisprüfungen, intensive first-year examinations in mathematics, physics and engineering subjects that must be passed within two attempts. Doctoral candidates are hired as paid employees in professors' laboratories. The institution counts 22 Nobel laureates among its students, faculty and researchers, including Albert Einstein.
ethan-allen: Ethan Allen was born in Litchfield, Connecticut Colony, the first child of Joseph and Mary Baker Allen, and grew up in Cornwall with five brothers, among them Ira and Heman, who also became prominent in early Vermont history. He was forced to end his studies when his father died. In 1762 he became part owner of an iron furnace in Salisbury and married Mary Brownson. In the late 1760s he became interested in the New Hampshire Grants. Governor Benning Wentworth had sold land west of the Connecticut River, but in 1764 George III resolved the competing claims of New York and New Hampshire in New York's favour, and New York demanded fees that approached the original purchase price.

Resistance to New York led to the formation of the Green Mountain Boys in 1770, at the Catamount Tavern in Bennington, with Allen as Colonel Commandant and his cousins Seth Warner and Remember Baker as captains. In 1772 Allen, his brothers and Baker formed the Onion River Company to buy land around the Winooski River, which later became Burlington. After the battles of Lexington and Concord, Allen agreed to help Connecticut militiamen plan the capture of Fort Ticonderoga, and he was elected to lead the expedition. The Green Mountain Boys captured the fort in May 1775.

The Boys later elected Seth Warner to command their regiment, and Allen was given no position at all. On 8 September 1775 Schuyler sent Allen and John Brown to win support among the inhabitants and Indians near Montreal. Allen's attempt on Montreal failed and he was captured. He was held in solitary confinement and chains aboard HMS Gaspée, then shipped to England on the merchant vessel Adamant. Most of what is known of his captivity comes from his own account. He was released in a prisoner exchange in 1778.

Allen reached Salisbury on 25 May 1778 and found that his brothers Heman and Zimri had died. He returned to the territory, which had declared independence in 1777, and served as one of the judges deciding whose property fell under Vermont's Banishment Act against Tories. He lobbied Congress for Vermont's recognition and took part in controversial negotiations with the British over making Vermont a separate British province. He wrote accounts of his wartime exploits that were widely read in the 19th century, together with philosophical treatises and political documents. He died on 12 February 1789 and was married twice, fathering eight children.
ethiopia: Ethiopia is a landlocked country in the Horn of Africa, covering 1,104,300 square kilometres. Within it is a vast highland complex of mountains and dissected plateaus, divided by the Great Rift Valley and surrounded by lowlands, steppes or semi-desert. The Ethiopian Highlands are the largest continuous mountain ranges in Africa, and Lake Tana in the north is the source of the Blue Nile.

The terrain ranges from deserts along the eastern border to tropical forests in the south and extensive Afromontane areas in the north and southwest. The country includes Dallol, described as the world's hottest settlement. Endemic species include the gelada, the walia ibex and the Ethiopian wolf. Ethiopia has the second-largest number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Africa.

Ethiopia is regarded as one of the earliest sites of anatomically modern humans. The Omo remains, excavated in the southwest, are dated to around 200,000 years ago, and Omo-Kibish I is the oldest anatomically modern Homo sapiens skeleton currently known. The hominid Lucy, Australopithecus afarensis, found in the Awash Valley in 1974, is estimated to have lived 3.2 million years ago. A 30,000-year-old rock shelter at Fincha Habera in the Bale Mountains, at 3,469 metres, is the earliest known permanent human occupation at high altitude.

The Kingdom of D'mt extended over Eritrea and northern Ethiopia from about 980 BCE, and the Kingdom of Aksum maintained a unified civilisation for 900 years; Christianity arrived there in 330 CE. After Aksum collapsed in 960, the Zagwe dynasty ruled the north-central region until Yekuno Amlak overthrew it at the Battle of Ansata in 1270, inaugurating the Solomonic dynasty. Under Emperor Amda Seyon I (r. 1314 to 1344) the empire expanded against neighbouring Muslim territories, and the Ethiopian-Adal War (1529 to 1543) weakened it.

Under Emperor Menelik II, Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 and remained independent during the Scramble for Africa. Italy invaded in 1936, and the country was liberated by the British Army in 1941; full sovereignty was restored in 1944. The Derg, a military junta, took power in 1974 after deposing Emperor Haile Selassie and ruled for nearly 17 years. Ethiopia is now a federal parliamentary republic.

It is a multi-ethnic state with more than 80 ethnic groups, of which the Oromo, Amhara, Somali and Tigrayans are the four largest. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is the largest denomination of Christianity, the most widely professed faith. Its capital, Addis Ababa, hosts the headquarters of the African Union Commission.
ethiopian-empire: After the Kingdom of Aksum fell in the 10th century, the Ethiopian Highlands passed to the Zagwe dynasty, Agaw rulers from the Lasta region. Later church texts denied that the dynasty had pure Solomonic descent, and most Christians regarded the Zagwe as usurpers, although their rock-hewn churches at Lalibela were the high point of a tradition begun in late Aksumite times. Yekuno Amlak, an Amhara nobleman from Bete Amhara, rebelled with the support of the Orthodox Church, which he promised a semi-independent standing, and defeated the Zagwe king at the Battle of Ansata.

He was on the throne by 1270. He claimed descent from Dil Na'od, the last king of Aksum, and so, through the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon, from Menelik I. This claim was set out in the 14th-century Kebra Nagast. Yekuno Amlak kept friendly relations with Muslim neighbours, writing to the Mamluk Sultan Baybars, and built the church of Genneta Maryam.

Under Amda Seyon I (1314–1344) and Dawit I (1382–1413) the empire expanded and for a time dominated the Horn of Africa. It reached its peak under Zara Yaqob (1434–1468), who built churches and monasteries, encouraged literature and replaced regional warlords with administrative officials. The Adal Sultanate then threatened the empire, and the jihad of Imam Ahmed Gran ended in his defeat in 1543 with Portuguese help. The Oromo migrations cost the empire much of its southern territory, and the Ottomans took Massawa and occupied parts of the north from 1557. In the 1630s Fasilides founded Gondar, beginning the Gondarine period of relative peace.

After the deaths of Iyasu II in 1755 and Iyoas I in 1769 came the Zemene Mesafint, when regional warlords held the real power. Tewodros II (r. 1855–1868) ended it and died during the British Expedition to Abyssinia. Menelik II, from Shewa, annexed lands to the west, south and east, so that by 1898 Ethiopia had its modern borders, and in 1896 his victory at the Battle of Adwa kept Italy to Eritrea. Italy occupied the country after the Second Italo-Ethiopian War of 1935, using mustard gas, and Haile Selassie went into exile in May 1936. On 27 August 1942 he abolished the legal basis of slavery. Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia under a United Nations resolution of 2 December 1950.

The 1973 Wollo famine, discontent in the cities and high fuel prices led to a revolt in February 1974. A committee of officers known as the Derg dismantled the imperial government and deposed and imprisoned Haile Selassie on 12 September 1974, ending the monarchy. Geʿez literature, with the Kebra Nagast among its works, had its most productive period under the Solomonic dynasty. The 1931 and 1955 constitutions introduced a parliament of two chambers.
ethiopian-highlands: The Ethiopian Highlands, also called the Abyssinian Highlands, are a rugged mass of mountains extending from Ethiopia into Eritrea. They form the largest continuous area of such elevation in Africa, with little of the surface below 1,500 metres and summits reaching 4,550 metres, which has earned them the name Roof of Africa. The Main Ethiopian Rift divides them into a north-western portion, the Abyssinian Massif, and a south-eastern one, the Harar Massif. The north-western part includes the Semien Mountains, whose summit Ras Dashen is the highest peak in Ethiopia, and Lake Tana, the source of the Blue Nile.

The highlands began to rise about 75 million years ago, as magma from the Earth's mantle uplifted a broad dome of the ancient rocks of the Arabian-Nubian Shield. A flood basalt plateau began to form about 30 million years ago.

Altitude gives a country near the equator an unexpectedly temperate climate, and the highlands catch the monsoon rains of the Indian Ocean in a rainy season from June to mid-September. These rains make the Nile flood in summer, a phenomenon that puzzled the ancient Greeks, for whom summer was the driest season. The hillsides have fertile soil and are heavily populated, largely by farming communities. In the south lay the Kingdom of Kaffa, a medieval and early modern state from which the coffee plant was exported to the Arabian Peninsula; the word coffee is traced to Kaffa. Among the Amhara people of the north, genetic adaptation to low atmospheric pressure has been found that may have developed within the past 5,000 years.

Most of Ethiopia's major cities lie at about 2,000 to 2,500 metres, including the capital Addis Ababa and the historic capitals Gondar and Axum. Other towns of the highlands include Bahir Dar, with its island monasteries on Lake Tana, the old walled city of Harar and Mek'ele. The Simien Mountains and Bale Mountains are national parks. The slopes are home to endemic animals such as the walia ibex, the gelada baboon, the mountain nyala and the Ethiopian wolf.
ethiopian-orthodox-church: The church is the largest of the Oriental Orthodox churches and the first indigenous Christian church of sub-Saharan Africa. Tradition and early writers report apostolic missions to the lands now called Ethiopia, and the New Testament tells of a royal official baptised by Philip the Evangelist. The church was administratively part of the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria from the first half of the 4th century until 1959, when Pope Cyril VI of Alexandria granted it autocephaly with its own patriarch.

Its name, Tewahedo, is a Ge'ez word meaning united as one. It refers to the miaphysite belief, shared by the Oriental Orthodox churches, that in Christ divinity and humanity are united in one nature, against the two-natures doctrine decreed by the Council of Chalcedon in 451.

Union with the see of Alexandria continued after the Arab conquest of Egypt, and Coptic patriarchs sent bishops to Ethiopia. In 1439, in the reign of Zara Yaqob, a religious discussion between Giyorgis and a French visitor led to an embassy from Ethiopia to the Vatican.

A period of Jesuit influence, which broke the connection with Egypt, followed an initiative of Portugal, which was in conflict with the Ottoman Empire and the Sultanate of Adal over the trade route to India by the Red Sea. An Ethiopian envoy, the Armenian Mateus, was sent to Portugal in 1507, and an embassy under Dom Rodrigo de Lima reached Ethiopia in 1520. In the 19th century the first Amharic translation of the Bible appeared. Emperor Haile Selassie reformed the church's finances and clergy appointments in 1942 and founded the Theological College of the Holy Trinity Church in 1944.

Services are held in Ge'ez, the liturgical language, while sermons are usually given in the local language. The sanctuary of a church houses the tabot, an altar slab dedicated to the patron saint, which is carried in procession on holidays; it is the tabot, not the building, that is consecrated. Churches are either basilican, as at Axum, or round or oblong in a native style, and eleven rock-hewn churches stand at Lalibela. Church music is traced to Saint Yared.

The church keeps 250 fasting days, 180 of them obligatory for lay people, on which no meat or animal products are eaten. It holds that its church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Axum houses the original Ark of the Covenant, a claim that international scholars doubt. Its biblical canon is larger than most, including Jubilees and Enoch.
ethiopian-peoples-revolutionary-democrat: During the Ethiopian Civil War the front was a rebel group fighting the Derg, the military regime led by Mengistu Haile Mariam that had been effectively in power from 1974 until it was replaced by the People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia in 1987. The Derg was responsible for the deaths of tens of thousands of opponents without trial in the Qey Shibir, and the 1983 to 1985 famine killed 400,000 people.

The front was formed by the union of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian People's Democratic Movement. It was later joined by the OPDO, the Oromo members of the TPLF and two other movements, and by a small body of Derg officers captured by the TPLF at Shire in February 1989, which was disbanded after the Transitional Government of Ethiopia was established. After the collapse of the People's Democratic Republic in the early 1990s the front gained support from the United States.

The front was an alliance of four parties: the TPLF in Tigray, the Amhara Democratic Party, the Oromo Democratic Party and the Southern Ethiopian People's Democratic Movement. It was led by a council and an executive committee chosen every three years by a congress, and government and party structures were closely intertwined. The other regions were governed by parties created or heavily influenced by the front, such as the Afar National Democratic Party and the Ethiopian Somali People's Democratic Party.

Revolutionary democracy replaced Marxism–Leninism as its official ideology in the early 1990s, because of the international situation after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991. It held that a vanguard party should rule because it represents the people, and it treated the peasantry as the main class in Ethiopia. Most of its top leaders had belonged to the Marxist–Leninist League of Tigray. The front also set goals of rapid export-based economic growth, close cooperation with the United States on foreign and defence policy and with China on economic and trade policy, and privatisation of state-owned enterprises. Some observers say it never held a well-defined unified ideology.

The front dominated Ethiopian politics from 1991 to 2019. Meles Zenawi led it until 20 August 2012, followed by Hailemariam Desalegn until 27 March 2018 and then Abiy Ahmed. In November 2019 the front was dissolved, and Abiy Ahmed merged three of its member parties, not including the TPLF, into the Prosperity Party, founded on 1 December 2019.
etihad-airways: The emirate of Abu Dhabi had been a joint owner of Gulf Air with Bahrain, Qatar and Oman, and Abu Dhabi's airport was one of Gulf Air's bases until the United Arab Emirates withdrew in 2005. In July 2003 Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who wanted an airline for Abu Dhabi, issued an Amiri decree establishing Etihad Airways as a national airline. Sheikh Ahmed bin Saif Al Nahyan founded it with start-up capital of 500 million dirhams. Etihad means union or unity in Arabic and stands for the unity of the seven emirates. Services began with a ceremonial flight to Al Ain on 5 November 2003, and commercial operations started on 12 November with flights to Beirut.

In June 2004 the airline ordered six Boeing 777-200s and 24 Airbus aircraft, including ten A380s, worth US$8 billion. James Hogan, formerly chief executive of Gulf Air, led it from 2006, and it reported its first full-year net profit, of US$14 million, in 2011.

From December 2011 Etihad built an equity alliance of minority stakes in other carriers: 29.21 percent of Air Berlin, 40 percent of Air Seychelles, 49 percent of the Serbian carrier that became Air Serbia, and in 2014 49 percent of Alitalia. Losses on Air Berlin and Alitalia mounted, and both partners later went bankrupt, which led Etihad to cut back its investments.

Etihad is owned by Abu Dhabi and has its head office in Khalifa City, Abu Dhabi, near the airport that serves as its hub; the head office and training centre were completed in 2007. A board of seven independent non-executive members governs the airline under its founding legislation. Besides passenger services it runs Etihad Cargo and Etihad Holidays.

The airline was title sponsor of the 2009 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, and it introduced a three-room cabin called The Residence on its A380s, which was then the only one of its kind on any airline. The Etihad Guest frequent flyer programme began on 30 August 2006.
etosha-pan: The Etosha Pan is an endorheic salt pan, a hollow in the ground where water collects or a deposit of salt remains after the water has evaporated. It forms part of the Cuvelai-Etosha Basin in the north of Namibia. Etosha means Great White Place in Oshindonga, and the pan has a characteristic white and greenish surface spreading over 4,800 square kilometres. The pan is believed to have developed through tectonic activity over about ten million years.

Around 16,000 years ago, when ice sheets were melting across the northern hemisphere, a wet-climate phase in southern Africa filled Etosha Lake. It is assumed that the Kunene River fed the lake in the distant past, but movements of tectonic plates changed the direction of the river, and the lake ran dry, leaving a salt pan. Today the Ekuma River, the Nipelo River, the Cuvelai River and the Omurambo Ovambo River are its only seasonal sources of water. Little river water or sediment reaches it, because water seeps away into the riverbed along its 250-kilometre course.

In the colonial era the first non-Africans to explore the area were the Europeans Charles John Andersson and Francis Galton, in 1851. The pan is mostly dry clay, split into hexagonal shapes as it dries and cracks, and is seldom seen with even a thin sheet of water. After heavy rains it floods with a layer of water about 10 cm deep, heavily salted by the mineral deposits. In good rainy seasons flamingos arrive in their thousands, and great white pelicans also breed there. The hypersaline pan supports brine shrimp and extremophile micro-organisms, and blue-green algae give it its colour.

The surrounding area is dense mopane woodland, with herds of elephants on the south side. Mopane trees host the mopane worm, the larva of the moth Gonimbrasia belina, an important source of protein for rural communities. The savanna around the pan is home to zebra, wildebeest, gemsbok, springbok, eland, black rhinoceros, bush elephants, lions, leopards and giraffes. The pan and its surroundings are protected as Etosha National Park, Namibia's second-largest wildlife park, covering 22,270 square kilometres. The pan lies wholly within the park and is a Ramsar wetland of international importance.
etruria: Etruria was a region of Central Italy bounded by the rivers Arno and Tiber, covering most of what is now Tuscany, northern Lazio and north-western Umbria. It is usually divided into Northern and Southern Etruria. Northern Etruria ran from the Arno south to the Albegna and east to the Apennines, Inner Etruria was the Perugia area in western Umbria, and Southern Etruria took in the southern edge of Tuscany and northern and central Lazio up to the gates of Rome. Etruscan colonies lay beyond: Etruria Padana in Emilia-Romagna and the southern edges of Lombardy and Veneto, and Etruria Campana in southern Lazio and Campania.

Etruscan culture centred on many city-states that arose during the Villanovan period in the ninth century BCE and were very powerful in the Orientalizing and Archaic periods. By 650 BCE the Etruscans were a dominant culture in Italy, ahead of peoples such as the Ligures, and their influence reached the Po Valley, Latium and Campania. Their trade extended to Egypt, whether directly or through Greek or Phoenician sailors; fine Egyptian faience cups have been found in the Tumulus di Montefortini at Comeana. Between 600 and 500 BCE twelve city-states formed a loose confederation, the Etruscan League, which met in the Etruscan language. The cities of Etruria included Caere (Cerveteri), Clusium (Chiusi), Tarquinii (Tarquinia), Veii, Volaterrae (Volterra), Arretium (Arezzo), Perusia (Perugia), Vulci and Volsinii.

Rome stood outside Etruria, separated from its early boundary by the Ciminian Forest, yet a series of Etruscan kings ruled it until 509 BCE, when the last, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was removed and the Roman Republic was established. The Etruscans are credited with influencing Roman architecture and ritual, and under their kings the Capitolium, the Cloaca Maxima and the Via Sacra were built. Etruria was assimilated into the Roman Republic in the 4th century BCE, and Latin replaced Etruscan as the official language.

In the Augustan organisation of Roman Italy, Etruria was the seventh region, Regio VII, bounded by the Tiber, the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Apuan Alps and the Apennines, roughly the same area as before Roman rule. The name lived on: the Grand Duchy of Tuscany styled itself in Latin Magnus Ducatus Etruriae, and the Kingdom of Etruria was a short-lived client state of Napoleon I between 1801 and 1807. George Dennis explored its ruins in the 1840s and published Cities and Cemeteries of Etruria in 1848, and D. H. Lawrence wrote Sketches of Etruscan Places.
etruscans: Literary texts in Etruscan have not survived and the language is only partly understood, so what is known about the Etruscans depends heavily on later and generally disapproving Roman and Greek writers. These writers differed about the origin of the people, some holding that they were native to central Italy and others that they were Pelasgians. The consensus among modern scholars is that the Etruscans were an indigenous population. The earliest identifiably Etruscan culture dates from about 900 BCE, in the Iron Age Villanovan culture. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus they called themselves Rasenna, from Rasna, the people, and the Greeks called them Tyrrhenians, which gave the Tyrrhenian Sea its name.

In the last Villanovan phase, about 770 to 730 BCE, the Etruscans entered close relations with the first Greek settlers in southern Italy and took over writing, a new way of banqueting and a heroic funerary ideology. The earliest known Etruscan inscriptions date to about 700 BCE, in a script derived from the Euboean alphabet. The mining and trade of copper and iron enriched them, and in the sixth century BCE their interests clashed with Greek colonists, so that they allied themselves with Carthage. According to legend, a league of 12 cities formed between 600 and 500 BCE.

Their territory reached its fullest extent about 500 BCE, shortly after the Roman Kingdom became the Roman Republic. The conflict between Veii and Rome began in 482 BCE, and from the late 4th century BCE the Etruscans succumbed to Rome in the Roman–Etruscan Wars. They were granted Roman citizenship in 90 BCE, and by 27 BCE the whole territory belonged to the Roman Empire.

Authority lay with individual cities and probably with individual families, and the city-state was the political unit. The government is thought to have changed from monarchy to an oligarchic republic in the sixth century BCE. The married couple stood at the centre of a monogamous society, and the great family tombs held members of a family over long periods. Elite families grew rich through trade with the Celts to the north and the Greeks to the south, and filled their tombs with imported luxuries. The economy rested on agriculture, mining and metalworking, and Mediterranean trade; Populonia was a major centre of iron smelting.
euboea: Euboea, or Evia, is the second-largest Greek island in area and population after Crete. It is about 180 kilometres long and varies in breadth from 50 to 6 kilometres, and a mountain range runs along its whole length. The Euripus Strait, only 40 metres wide at Chalcis, separates it from Boeotia. Tides in the strait have been noted since classical times, the current running like a river first one way and shortly afterwards the other. The name Euboea means the land of the well-fed oxen, and the Italian Negroponte comes from a Greek phrase for to the Euripus, taken as Black Bridge.

Its two principal cities, Chalcis and Eretria, were settled by Ionian Greeks from Attica and founded many colonies in Magna Graecia and Sicily, such as Cumae and Rhegium, and on the coast of Macedonia. They fought one of the earliest major wars in Greek history, the Lelantine War. The Persians utterly ruined Eretria in 490 BCE. Athens, which valued the island's grain and cattle, invaded Chalcis in 506 BCE and settled 4,000 Attic Greeks on its lands, and the whole island gradually became an Athenian dependency. It regained independence by 410 BCE, fell under Philip II of Macedon after Chaeronea in 338 BCE and was incorporated into the Roman Republic in the second century BCE. Aristotle died at Chalcis in 322 BCE.

After the Fourth Crusade, Lombard families divided the island into three baronies, the Triarchy of Negroponte. The Venetian Republic secured control of its commerce in the War of the Euboeote Succession of 1256 to 1258 and had full sovereignty by 1390. On 12 July 1470 Mehmed II took the city of Negroponte after a bloody siege, and the island passed to the Ottoman Empire, which called it Eğriboz. It returned to Greece at the end of the Greek War of Independence in 1830.

The island had 204,818 inhabitants at the census of 2021. Southern Euboea still has Arvanite communities, and Sarakatsani and Vlachs live in the mountains of the centre and north. Two bridges link Chalcis with the mainland.
eucharist: Christians believe that the rite was instituted by Jesus Christ at the Last Supper, the night before his crucifixion, when he gave his disciples bread and wine. Passages in the New Testament state that he told them to do this in memory of him. According to the synoptic Gospels the meal was a Passover meal. The First Epistle to the Corinthians gives the earliest account and shows how early Christians observed what Paul the Apostle called the Lord's Supper.
The Didache, which most scholars date to the late 1st century, gives instructions for baptism and the Eucharist, and Ignatius of Antioch called the Eucharist the flesh of the Saviour Jesus Christ.

The name comes from the Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving. The term Lord's Supper came into popular use after the Protestant Reformation, and Communion also began with groups that originated in the Reformation. Most churches treat the rite as a sacrament, others, such as the Anabaptists, as an ordinance. Christians generally recognise a special presence of Christ in the rite but differ on how and where.

The Catholic Church teaches that by the consecration the substances of bread and wine become those of the body and blood of Christ, while their appearances remain. The Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches agree that an objective change occurs but leave the manner a mystery. Lutherans hold that the body and blood are really present in, with and under the bread and wine, Reformed Christians a real spiritual presence, and the Plymouth Brethren a memorial.

In the Eastern churches the service is called the Divine Liturgy, in two parts: the Liturgy of the Catechumens, ending in a Gospel reading, and the Liturgy of the Faithful, in which the Eucharist is offered and received. The Syriac churches observe the Holy Qurbana, whose main East Syriac anaphora is that of Addai and Mari, and the Liturgy of Saint James; both go back at least to the third century. In the Catholic Church the sacrifice Jesus made once on the cross is believed to be made present at every Mass. The belief that Jews desecrated the consecrated host fed medieval anti-Jewish violence, and was related to the blood libel.
euclid: Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria, writing many centuries later. According to Proclus he lived shortly after several of Plato's followers and before Archimedes, during the rule of Ptolemy I (r. 305/304–282 BCE). His birth date and birthplace are unknown, and his death is speculated to have been about 270 BCE. He is often presumed to have been educated by Plato's disciples at the Platonic Academy in Athens, though Michalis Sialaros calls this mere conjecture. Pappus says Apollonius studied with Euclid's students in Alexandria, which has been taken to mean that Euclid taught there.

He is often called Euclid of Alexandria to distinguish him from Euclid of Megara, a pupil of Socrates, with whom he was conflated in medieval Byzantine sources. Medieval Arabic sources give a detailed biography, but it is unverifiable. The best-known anecdote, that he told Ptolemy there is no royal road to geometry, is questionable, since a similar story is told of Menaechmus and Alexander the Great.

Euclid is best known for the Elements, a treatise in thirteen books. It is traditionally divided into plane geometry (books 1–6), basic number theory (books 7–10) and solid geometry (books 11–13). Much of its content comes from earlier mathematicians such as Eudoxus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. The classicist Markus Asper concludes that Euclid's achievement lay in assembling accepted knowledge into a cogent order and adding new proofs to fill gaps.

Book 1 begins with 20 definitions and ten assumptions, five postulates and five common notions, the fifth postulate being the parallel postulate. It includes the earliest surviving proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Book 7 contains the Euclidean algorithm for finding the common divisor of two numbers, and book 9 the proposition, now called Euclid's theorem, that there are infinitely many prime numbers. The Optics, the earliest surviving Greek treatise on perspective, the Data and the Phaenomena also survive. The Conics, Pseudaria, Porisms and Surface Loci are lost.

Euclid is generally ranked with Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga among the leading mathematicians of antiquity. The system of the Elements dominated geometry until the early 19th century, when non-Euclidean geometries were discovered. The Elements is often considered, after the Bible, the most frequently translated, published and studied book in the Western world, and it was the dominant mathematical textbook in the medieval Arab and Latin worlds. Its first English edition appeared in 1570, published by Henry Billingsley and John Dee.
euclids-elements: The Elements was written about 300 BCE by the Greek mathematician Euclid and is the oldest extant large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics. Scholars believe it is largely a compilation of propositions drawn from earlier mathematicians such as Eudoxus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus, and it is hard to separate Euclid's own work from theirs, because the Elements superseded much earlier Greek mathematics that is now lost. The historian Michalis Sialaros, however, argues that its tight structure suggests Euclid wrote it himself. The version available today also contains later additions, probably by editors such as Theon of Alexandria in the 4th century.

The work is traditionally divided into plane geometry in books I to VI, basic number theory in books VII to X and solid geometry in books XI to XIII. Book I opens with 20 definitions and then gives five postulates and five common notions as the logical basis of what follows. The fifth postulate, the parallel postulate, is less straightforward than the first four, and the question of its independence from them led to the development of non-Euclidean geometry. Book I also contains the earliest surviving proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Proposition 5, on the base angles of an isosceles triangle, was known in the Middle Ages as the pons asinorum, the bridge of asses.

Book VII begins the number theory with the Euclidean algorithm. Book XII uses the method of exhaustion to show that a cone is a third of the corresponding cylinder, and Book XIII constructs the five Platonic solids and proves that they are the only regular polyhedra. Two further books, XIV and XV, were not written by Euclid but were transmitted with the manuscripts.

The Islamic world received the work from the Byzantine Empire around 760, and it was translated into Arabic under Harun al-Rashid and later by Ishaq ibn Hunayn, revised by Thābit ibn Qurra. In about 1120 the English monk Adelard of Bath translated it into Latin from an Arabic version. Erhard Ratdolt printed it in 1482, and since then it has appeared in over a thousand editions. The first English edition, by Henry Billingsley in 1570, had a preface by John Dee, and a Chinese edition appeared in 1607 by Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi. In the 19th century it fell out of favour as a school textbook, though Charles Dodgson defended it in Euclid and His Modern Rivals of 1879.
eucratides-i: Eucratides was probably born around 210 to 205 BCE, the son of Heliocles and Laodice, as shown on his coinage. His mother wears a royal diadem on the coins, which points to royal descent, while his father is bare-headed. It is unclear whether he was a Bactrian nobleman who raised a rebellion or, according to some scholars, a cousin of the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes trying to regain Bactria. Tarn held that Laodice was a daughter of Seleucus II Callinicus, a view that Narain and other modern authors have challenged.

Eucratides took power by overthrowing the Euthydemid dynasty in Bactria, possibly while Demetrius I was conquering north-western India. The king he dethroned was probably Antimachus I. The Roman historian Justin places his accession at about the time Mithridates began to rule the Parthians, which is known to be 171 BCE. Mithridates I took Tapuria and Margiana from Demetrius around 170 BCE and then tried to conquer Bactria itself, but Eucratides checked him.

With his western border secured, Eucratides conquered parts of India, campaigning as far south as Barigaza, present-day Bharuch. Justin says he was besieged for four months by Demetrius, king of the Indians, and that he defeated 60,000 enemies with 300 soldiers; which Demetrius is meant is uncertain. His bilingual coins are found widely across northern India and Pakistan. The city of Eucratideia on the Oxus was probably named for him, and may have been Ai-Khanoum or Dilbarjin.

Justin reports that Eucratides was murdered on his way back from India by his son, who drove a chariot over his blood and left the corpse unburied. This may be a misreading, and the killer may have been the Euthydemid prince Demetrius II, since patricide was uncommon in the Hellenistic age. A civil war among the dynasty's members probably followed. His successors were Eucratides II and Heliocles I, the last Greek king to rule in Bactria, and the Greco-Bactrians lost the lands north of the Hindu Kush to the Yuezhi.

Ai-Khanoum, his capital, was likely destroyed at the end of his reign, about 145 BCE. The seal of Da Afghanistan Bank, the central bank of Afghanistan, bears one of his coins with the Greek legend of the great king Eucratides.
eudokia-angelina: Eudokia Angelina was born around 1173, a daughter of Alexios III Angelos and Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera. Around 1190, while her father was in exile in Syria, her uncle, the emperor Isaac II Angelos, arranged her marriage to Stefan, the second son of Stefan Nemanja, Grand Župan of Serbia. In 1196, when her father-in-law retired to a monastery, her husband became ruler of Serbia; he is known as Stefan the First-Crowned.

According to the Byzantine historian Nicetas Choniates, Stefan and Eudokia quarrelled and separated, each accusing the other of adultery, and in 1200 or 1201 she was banished from Serbia. She fled on foot, with only the clothes she wore, to the court of Stefan's brother Vukan, ruler of Zeta, who took her in and provided for her. When she had recovered she went to Dyrrachium, and a Byzantine ship took her back to her father in Constantinople. Her repudiation has been taken as a sign of the decline of Byzantine power and prestige.

In Constantinople she became the mistress of the future emperor Alexios V Doukas. On 12 April 1204, as the crusaders of the Fourth Crusade stormed the city, she and her mother fled with him into Thrace. At Mosynopolis, where her deposed father was staying, she was allowed to marry Alexios V, but Alexios III then had him arrested and mutilated, to her fury. Alexios V was later captured by the crusaders.

Leo Sgouros, the independent ruler of Corinth, offered asylum to Alexios III and his family in 1204, and Eudokia became his wife, her third marriage. Blockaded in the citadel of Corinth, Sgouros killed himself in 1207 or 1208. Eudokia is thought to have died around 1211. By Stefan she had four children: Stefan Radoslav, King of Serbia from 1228 to 1234; Stefan Vladislav, King of Serbia from 1234 to 1243; Sava II, Archbishop of the Serbian Orthodox Church from 1263 until his death in 1271; and Komnena Nemanjić.
eudoxus-of-cnidus: Eudoxus, son of Aeschines, was born and died in Cnidus, a city on the south-west coast of Anatolia, and the years of his birth and death are not fully known. According to Diogenes Laërtius, he studied mathematics with Archytas of Tarentum and medicine with Philiston the Sicilian. At 23 he went with the physician Theomedon to Athens to study with followers of Socrates, walking about 7 miles (11 km) each way from Piraeus to attend lectures. Friends then paid for him to spend 16 months in Egypt studying astronomy and mathematics. He travelled to Cyzicus and the court of Mausolus, gathering students, and later returned to Athens; according to some sources he headed the Academy while Plato was in Syracuse and taught Aristotle.

Back in Cnidus he served in the city assembly, built an observatory and wrote on theology, astronomy and meteorology. He was probably the source of most of Book V of Euclid's Elements, which defines when two ratios are equal without needing a common unit of measure, allowing rigorous treatment of incommensurable magnitudes. He developed Antiphon's method of exhaustion, a forerunner of integral calculus, and used it to prove that the volumes of spheres are as the cubes of their radii and that a cone is one third of a cylinder on the same base and height.

In astronomy he introduced concentric spheres to account for the planets' motions, answering a question reported of Plato about what uniform motions could explain their apparent wandering. In reconstructions the Moon and Sun have three spheres each, the five visible planets four each, and the fixed stars one, 27 in all. Callippus later added seven. Because the spheres are concentric, the system cannot explain changes in a planet's brightness. Aristotle attributes to Eudoxus an argument that pleasure is the ultimate good.
eugene-de-beauharnais: Eugène Rose de Beauharnais was born in Paris on 3 September 1781, the son of Viscount Alexandre de Beauharnais and Marie-Josèphe Rose Tascher de la Pagerie, both born in Martinique, who separated when he was three. His father, a general in the early Revolutionary Wars, was guillotined on 23 July 1794 after losing the Siege of Mainz. Eugène soon joined the Revolutionary Army as an orderly to General Lazare Hoche. He served as aide-de-camp to his stepfather in Italy, followed him to Egypt, where he was wounded at the Siege of Acre, and commanded the chasseurs of the Consular Guard.

Napoleon was crowned King of Italy on 26 May 1805, after his brother Joseph and then Louis had refused the throne, and on 7 June he announced Eugène as Viceroy of Italy. After Austerlitz Napoleon arranged Eugène's marriage to Princess Augusta of Bavaria, daughter of King Maximilian I Joseph, and adopted him on 12 January 1806. He was excluded from the French succession but declared heir presumptive to the Italian throne. As viceroy he built fortifications, roads and public works and introduced the Napoleonic codes.

In 1809 he commanded the Army of Italy, lost the Battle of Sacile against Archduke John, then won at the Piave and at Raab and fought at Wagram. In 1812 he led IV Corps in the invasion of Russia, fighting at Borodino and the Berezina, and after Napoleon and Joachim Murat left he took command of the remnants of the Grande Armée.

In 1814, despite Murat's defection and pressure from his father-in-law, he refused to change sides, and he fought a series of retreats up the Po Valley. After Napoleon's abdication he signed the Convention of Schiarino-Rizzino on 16 April, and a rising in Milan on 20 April ended his hope of being crowned. He gave up the kingdom at Mantua on 23 April.

Eugène retired to Munich in June 1814 and then returned to Paris on his mother's death, where Louis XVIII and Alexander I of Russia received him honourably. He gave up politics and stayed neutral during the Hundred Days. On 14 November 1817 he became Duke of Leuchtenberg and Prince of Eichstätt. He lived in Munich managing estates and adding to his art collection. He died there on 21 February 1824, aged 42. Two of his daughters became queen consort of Sweden and empress of Brazil. Historians consider him one of Napoleon's most able relatives.
eugene-delacroix: Ferdinand Victor Eugène Delacroix was born on 26 April 1798 at Charenton-Saint-Maurice, near Paris. His mother, Victoire Oeben, was the daughter of the cabinetmaker Jean-François Oeben. His legal father died in 1805 and his mother in 1814, leaving him an orphan at sixteen. In 1815 he began training with Pierre-Narcisse Guérin in the neoclassical style of Jacques-Louis David. The impact of Théodore Géricault's Raft of the Medusa stimulated him to paint The Barque of Dante, accepted by the Paris Salon of 1822; the public and officials largely derided it, yet the State bought it for the Luxembourg Galleries.

His Chios Massacre showed dying Greek civilians rounded up for enslavement by the Ottoman Empire and expressed support for the Greek cause. The state bought it, though critics deplored its despairing tone. The Death of Sardanapalus of 1827–28, drawn from a play by Lord Byron, shows the besieged king watching as his servants, concubines and animals are killed. In 1832 he travelled to Spain and North Africa on a diplomatic mission to Morocco shortly after the French conquered Algeria, and produced over 100 paintings and drawings of North African life.

Liberty Leading the People, painted in 1830, shows armed Parisians marching under the tricolour behind a symbolic figure of Liberty. The French government bought it, but by 1832 officials judged it too inflammatory and removed it from view; after the Revolution of 1848 Louis Napoleon put it on display. From 1833 Delacroix received many commissions to decorate public buildings in Paris, among them the ceiling of the Galerie d'Apollon at the Louvre from 1848 to 1850 and frescoes at Saint-Sulpice from 1857 to 1861.

Delacroix died on 13 August 1863 after a severe throat infection, with his housekeeper Jeanne-Marie le Guillou by his side, and was buried at Père Lachaise Cemetery. His will forbade any representation of his features. At the sale of his work in 1864, 9,140 works were attributed to him, including 853 paintings and 6,629 drawings. Renoir and Manet copied his paintings, and Degas bought his portrait of Baron Schwiter.
eugene-v-debs: Eugene Victor Debs was born on 5 November 1855 in Terre Haute, Indiana, to parents who had emigrated from Colmar in Alsace. His father owned a textile mill and a meat market. Debs left high school at 14 and took a job cleaning grease from freight engines for the Vandalia Railroad, and later worked as a locomotive fireman. As editor of the official journal of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen he at first held that labour and capital were friends and opposed strikes. He was elected to the Indiana General Assembly as a Democrat in 1884 and married Katherine Metzel in 1885.

Debs was instrumental in founding the American Railway Union, one of the first industrial unions. In 1894 workers at the Pullman Palace Car Company, whose wages had been cut by twenty-eight percent, appealed to its convention. Debs warned that a boycott was too risky, but the members refused to handle Pullman cars and he joined the strike, which spread to most lines west of Detroit. President Grover Cleveland used the army, and Debs was convicted of defying a court injunction and served six months in the jail at Woodstock, Illinois. There he read socialist writings and was visited by the editor Victor L. Berger, and he came out a socialist.

He helped found the Social Democracy of America in 1897, the Social Democratic Party in 1898 and the Socialist Party of America in 1901. He ran for president in 1900, 1904, 1908, 1912 and 1920. His best result was 6.0 percent of the popular vote in 1912. In June 1905 he joined Bill Haywood and others in Chicago in founding the Industrial Workers of the World, although the socialist party and the union later drifted apart.

On 16 June 1918 Debs spoke at Canton, Ohio, urging resistance to the military draft. He was arrested on 30 June and charged with sedition. He addressed the court himself, and was found guilty on 12 September and sentenced to two ten-year terms, and he lost his citizenship. In 1920 he ran for president from the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary, with campaign pins reading Convict No. 9653, and received 914,191 votes, 3.4 percent. President Warren G. Harding commuted his sentence in December 1921, though his citizenship was not restored in his lifetime.

His health had been undermined by prison. He was admitted to Lindlahr Sanitarium in Elmhurst, Illinois, and died on 20 October 1926. His only book, Walls and Bars, a critique of the prison system, was published after his death.
eugenia-charles: Mary Eugenia Charles was born on 15 May 1919 in the fishing village of Pointe Michel, Dominica, the youngest of four children. Her family belonged to the so-called coloured bourgeoisie, descendants of free people of colour who had become wealthy landowners, and her father served as Mayor of Roseau and as a Senator. Interested in law after watching the colonial magistrate's court, she studied at the University of Toronto and the London School of Economics and was called to the bar in London. She returned as Dominica's first woman lawyer, specialising in property law.

Charles entered politics in the 1960s, writing anonymous newspaper columns against restrictions on press freedom. In 1968 her group merged with another to form the Dominica Freedom Party, which she led from 1969 to 1995. She sat in the House of Assembly from 1970 and became Leader of the Opposition after 1975. She supported full independence from British rule in 1978. The party won the 1980 election, and she became prime minister on 21 July 1980, also serving as foreign minister until 1990 and finance minister throughout.

In 1981 she faced two coup attempts: a mercenary plot to restore Patrick John, stopped by American agents in New Orleans, and an attack on the police headquarters led by Frederick Newton, commander of the military, who was executed in 1986. In October 1983, as chair of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States, she appealed to the United States for intervention in Grenada after the execution of Maurice Bishop, and appeared with Ronald Reagan in support of the invasion. She won re-election in 1985 and 1990 and began the citizenship by investment programme in 1991.

Charles retired in 1995, and her party lost that year's election. She received the Order of the Caribbean Community in 2003 and died on 6 September 2005, aged 86, after surgery in Martinique. She was known as the Iron Lady of the Caribbean and as Mamo Charles, and she was the first woman prime minister in the Caribbean. Historians Eudine Barriteau and Alan Gregor Cobley have argued that her image as a commanding, charismatic figure has overshadowed assessments of her accomplishments.
eugenius: Eugenius was a Christian, a former teacher of grammar and rhetoric and a magister scriniorum. He became an acquaintance of the magister militum Arbogast, who was of Frankish origin and the de facto ruler of the western part of the empire, after being introduced by Arbogast's uncle Richomeres. Three months after the death of Valentinian II, Arbogast raised him to the rank of augustus at Lyons on 22 August 392. A Roman and a Christian was more suitable as emperor than a Frankish pagan, and the Roman Senate was more likely to support him.

Eugenius was unrecognised by the eastern emperor Theodosius I. He replaced the administrators Theodosius had placed in the highest civil offices with men from the senatorial class loyal to himself. Virius Nicomachus Flavianus the Elder became praetorian prefect, his son prefect of the city. Pagan senators persuaded him to use public money to rededicate the Temple of Venus and Roma and to restore the Altar of Victory in the Senate house, and the appointment of a pagan as prefect revived the pagan cause. Historians disagree about his actual beliefs, though he was at least publicly a Christian. These policies strained relations with Theodosius and with Bishop Ambrose, who left Milan when the court arrived.

He also renewed old alliances with the Alamanni and Franks. He marched to the Rhine, where he impressed the Germanic tribes by parading his army before them, and afterwards recruited Alamannic and Frankish units.

Two embassies Eugenius sent to Theodosius asking for recognition received vague answers. In January 393 Theodosius made his eight-year-old son Honorius augustus of the West, showing that he regarded Eugenius's elevation as illegitimate. In spring 393 Eugenius and Arbogast marched their army into Italy. Theodosius advanced from Constantinople and met them at the Battle of the Frigidus in the Vipava Valley on 6 September 394. The battle lasted two days, was marked by unusually strong winds and ended in victory for Theodosius. Eugenius was captured and executed, and his head was displayed in Theodosius' camp. Arbogast took his own life the next day.
eulalia-of-merida: Eulalia of Mérida was born at Augusta Emerita, the capital of Lusitania and the modern Mérida in Spain, and died there on 10 December 304 during the persecution of Christians under Diocletian. Other views place her death in the time of Trajan Decius, in the years 249–51. There is debate over whether Saint Eulalia of Barcelona, whose story is similar, is the same person. Until the proclamation of James, son of Zebedee, as patron, she was invoked as the protector of Christian troops in the Reconquista and as patron of the territories of Spain during their formation.

In the hagiographic account she was a devout Christian girl of twelve to fourteen whose mother kept her in the countryside because all citizens were required to avow faith in the Roman gods. Eulalia ran away to the court of the governor Dacian at Emerita, professed herself a Christian, insulted the pagan gods and the emperor Maximian, and challenged the authorities to martyr her. The judge's flattery and bribes failed.

The poet Prudentius, who wrote in the fifth century according to the account, devoted the third book of his Peristephanon, a work on martyrs, to her. He gives her words that Isis, Apollo, Venus and Maximian himself are nothing, being works of human hands. In the story she was stripped by soldiers, tortured with hooks and torches and burnt at the stake, dying of smoke. A dove is said to have flown from her mouth, frightening the soldiers away, and a miraculous snow covered her body.

A shrine was soon built over her tomb, and by 350 her veneration was already popular among Christians. Prudentius's poem increased her fame, and relics were distributed through Iberia. Bishop Fidelis of Mérida rebuilt a basilica in her honour around 560, and her shrine was the most popular in Visigothic Spain.

Around 780 King Silo transferred her body to Oviedo, where it lies in a coffin of Arab silver given by Alfonso VI in 1075. In 1639 she was made patron saint of Oviedo. She also appears in Thieleman J. van Braght's Martyrs Mirror of 1660. She is often linked with Saint Julia of Mérida, said to have been a girl martyred at Mérida in 304 in the same persecution, whose feast day is also 10 December.
eulogius-of-cordoba: The year of Eulogius's birth is not known, but it must have been before 819, since he was already a respected priest by 848. His family belonged to the senatorial class and had held land at Córdoba since Roman times. He and his five brothers were educated under the guardianship of their mother, Isabel. His youngest brother, Joseph, held high office in the palace of Abd ar-Rahman II, two others traded as far as Central Europe, and one sister became a nun. Christians under the emirs kept their churches on payment of tribute, but held a subordinate status.

Eulogius studied at the monastery of St. Zoilus and with Abbot Speraindeo, was ordained by Bishop Reccafred of Córdoba and came to head the city's chief church school. With his friend and fellow student Paulus Alvarus, later his biographer, he exchanged letters in prose and verse that they afterwards agreed to destroy. In 848 he visited monasteries in northern Iberia, among them San Zacharias, and brought back texts of Augustine, Horace, Juvenal and Virgil.

When the emirate began to prosecute Christians in 850 for speaking against Muhammad, the bishop and priests of Córdoba, Eulogius among them, were imprisoned; in jail he read the Bible to his companions. His writings record events in Iberian Christianity from 848 to 859, above all the lives of those executed. Around 857 he copied into his Liber apologeticus the Storia de Mahometh, whose rendering of verse 37 of Sura al-Ahzab is the earliest account of the Quran in a language other than Arabic.

In 859 Leocritia, a convert from a noble Muslim family, sought his protection from her parents. He hid her among friends, but they were discovered and condemned. Eulogius was beheaded on 11 March 859 and Leocritia four days later. He had been chosen for the see of Toledo but was never consecrated. Paulus Alvarus's Life records a dove seen above his body. He is buried in the Cathedral of Oviedo, and his feast day is 11 March.
eumenes-i: Eumenes was the son of another Eumenes, the brother of Philetaerus, the founder of the Attalid dynasty, and of Satyra, daughter of Poseidonius. Philetaerus had no children, and adopted him to become his heir. Although Pergamon was nominally under Seleucid control, it enjoyed considerable autonomy under Philetaerus, and Eumenes succeeded him as dynast of the city in 263 BCE.

On his succession Eumenes revolted against the Seleucids, perhaps encouraged by Ptolemy II, who was at war with them. He defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus I near the Lydian capital of Sardis in 261 BCE, freed Pergamon and greatly enlarged its territory. In the new possessions he established garrison posts: Philetaireia, named after his adoptive father, in the north at the foot of Mount Ida, and Attaleia, named after his grandfather, northeast of Thyatira near the sources of the river Lycus. He also extended his control south of the river Caïcus to the Gulf of Cyme.

To show his independence he struck coins with the portrait of Philetaerus, where his predecessor had still shown Seleucus I Nicator. No further hostilities involving Pergamon are recorded for the rest of his rule, although the Seleucids and Ptolemies continued to fight and the Galatian Gauls plundered the region. If he kept Pergamon free of the Gauls, it was probably because he paid them tribute.

Eumenes never took the title of king, but he exercised all of a king's powers, and, like other Hellenistic rulers, was honoured with a festival in Pergamon, the Eumeneia. It is not known whether he had children. An inscription at Thespiae mentions a Philetaerus son of Eumenes, whom some regard as his son, dead before Eumenes himself died in 241 BCE. Eumenes adopted his first cousin once removed, Attalus I, who succeeded him as ruler of Pergamon.
eumenes-ii: Eumenes II Soter was the eldest of four sons of King Attalus I Soter and Queen Apollonis of Pergamon, and a member of the Attalid dynasty. He was presumably born before 220 BCE. He refused to marry a daughter of Antiochus III when he saw that Antiochus was about to go to war with the Romans, and he married Stratonice, daughter of Ariarathes IV, king of Cappadocia. Their son was named Attalus III.

Eumenes became king in 197 BCE. Like his father he worked with the Romans against Antigonid and especially Seleucid expansion in Asia Minor towards the Aegean. After the Second Macedonian War he helped Rome and the Achaean League against the Spartan tyrant Nabis. In the Roman-Seleucid War he warned Rome of Antiochus's ambitions by sending his brother Attalus II ahead, and then sided with the Romans. At the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE he commanded the right flank, and his fleet fought the Seleucids at sea.

By the Peace of Apamea in 188 BCE he received Phrygia, Lydia, Pisidia, Pamphylia, parts of Lycia and the Thracian Chersonese. By dividing Asia Minor between their allies Rhodes and Pergamon, the Romans made sure that neither would grow too powerful.

In 183 BCE he fought the Bithynian king Prusias I, was at first defeated, and won after receiving Roman support. He also fought Pharnaces I of Pontus, who sued for peace around 179 BCE after suffering losses.

In the Third Macedonian War he helped the Romans defeat Perseus of Macedon at the Battle of Pydna. Afterwards the Romans suspected him of conspiring with Perseus. He sent his brother Attalus II to Rome with congratulations, and in 167 BCE the Romans made an abortive attempt to put Attalus on the Pergamene throne. Eumenes set out to plead his case in person but was ordered to leave Italy as soon as he landed at Brundusium. Ties of kinship proved strong, and he remained king.
