When Eumenes's health weakened, Attalus II became co-ruler in 160 BCE. Because Eumenes's son was a minor, Attalus took the throne and in 158 BCE married Stratonice. Eumenes raised his state to a powerful monarchy, and under him Pergamon became a flourishing city that welcomed scholars, among them Crates of Mallus, founder of the Pergamene school of criticism. He adorned it with splendid buildings, including the great altar with the frieze of the Battle of the Giants, and expanded the Library at Pergamon, one of the great libraries of the ancient world and traditionally associated with the creation of parchment. He also built a stoa on the Athenian acropolis.
eumenes-of-cardia: Eumenes was a native of Cardia in the Thracian Chersonese, the son of a prominent citizen named Hieronymus, who was a friend of Philip II of Macedon. Philip employed him as private royal secretary, probably in 342 BCE. Although Macedonians looked down on the post, Eumenes oversaw all written communications and kept a close relationship with the king. He stayed in the post under Alexander the Great, accompanied him to Asia and began military and diplomatic missions after the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE. After the death of Hephaestion in late 324 BCE he became commander of the companion cavalry, and at the Marriages at Susa he married Artonis, daughter of the satrap Artabazus II.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE Eumenes helped end the quarrel between the infantry under Meleager and the officers at Babylon. Perdiccas became regent and Eumenes his adviser. In the Partition of Babylon he was given Cappadocia and Paphlagonia, which he first had to subdue. In 321 BCE he defeated Craterus at the Battle of the Hellespont. After Perdiccas was murdered, the generals at Triparadisus condemned Eumenes to death, with Antigonus as the executioner. Antigonus defeated him at the Battle of Orkynia in 319 BCE and confined him in Nora.

Eumenes escaped, probably by agreeing terms with Antigonus in 318 BCE, and then accepted an offer of alliance from Polyperchon, who was also supported by Olympias. In Cilicia he won the loyalty of the commanders of the Silver Shields, veterans who had fought with Alexander, by claiming that Alexander had appeared in a dream and by setting up a tent for the dead king with a throne, diadem and sceptre. He then marched to the upper satrapies and joined the satraps there, though Peucestas disputed his command. He defeated Antigonus at the Battle of Paraitakene, and the Battle of Gabiene was indecisive.

At Gabiene Eumenes inflicted heavier casualties but lost the army's baggage, including the treasure the Silver Shields had gathered over 30 years and their women and children. The Silver Shields agreed with Antigonus to hand over Eumenes in return for their baggage. Antigonus executed him. Historians see Eumenes as an excellent commander and an able propagandist, hampered by divided command and disloyal subordinates. His defeat is seen as the end of the Argead loyalists. Bosworth holds that his duel with Antigonus did more than anything to define the shape of the Hellenistic world, and Green writes that with his death the fiction of a unified empire was exploded.
eunuch: The Greek word eunoûkhos is first attested in a fragment of the comic poet Hipponax of the 6th century BCE. The earliest records of castration carried out to produce eunuchs come from the Sumerian city of Lagash in the 2nd millennium BCE, and in China eunuchs are recorded from about 2,000 BCE.

They were usually servants or slaves, castrated so that they would be less threatening attendants in a royal court, where access to the ruler could bring influence. Tasks that seem humble, such as dressing the ruler or relaying messages, could give a eunuch the ruler's ear. They were thought to have no loyalties to the army, the aristocracy or a family of their own, and so to be less interested in founding a dynasty.

In the Neo-Assyrian Empire a eunuch was called ša rēš šarri, the one who stands by the head of the king. In the Achaemenid Empire the eunuch Bagoas was vizier to Artaxerxes III and Artaxerxes IV and the main power behind the throne until Darius III killed him. In the later Roman Empire, after Diocletian and Constantine adopted an eastern court model, emperors were surrounded by eunuchs who held bureaucratic posts and shielded them from their administrators.

In China eunuchs ran the imperial household, and under the Ming dynasty the official Zheng He at times outranked even the Grand Secretaries. In Korea the naesi served the king, with 140 in the palace under the Joseon dynasty until the system was repealed in 1894. Some Muslim rulers in the Indian sultanates used eunuchs as harem guards and advisers, and Malik Kafur became a general under Alauddin Khalji. The Galli, priests of Cybele, were eunuchs.

The Bible mentions eunuchs often; in Matthew 19, Jesus speaks of men who are eunuchs from birth, made so by others, or who have made themselves so for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Boys castrated before puberty kept a high voice and became castrati, who replaced women where women were forbidden to sing in church. They were very popular in 18th-century opera seria. Alessandro Moreschi, the last eunuch of the Sistine Chapel Choir, died in 1922, and his is the only sound recording of a castrato. The practice was ended in 1878 by Pope Leo XIII.
eupen: Eupen and its St. Nikolaus Chapel are first mentioned in 1213 as part of the Duchy of Limburg. After the Battle of Worringen in 1288 the duchy was annexed by John I, Duke of Brabant. Brabant and Limburg passed to Burgundy in 1387, and Eupen was burnt to the ground during the war against the Duchy of Guelders. The Austrian House of Habsburg inherited the town in 1477. Charles V granted it two markets a year in 1544. Rebels burnt Eupen in 1582, during the Eighty Years' War, without taking control of it, and bubonic plague reached it in 1635 with devastating consequences.

The town obtained its own court of law in 1648 and city rights in 1674, and textile manufacture was introduced six years later. Revolutionary France took Eupen in 1794 and made it part of the Département Ourthe. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 it became part of the Prussian Rhine Province, and in 1871 it passed with Prussia's possessions into the German Empire, flourishing as a spa town.

The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 transferred Eupen and the nearby municipality of Malmedy from Germany to Belgium. Construction of the Vesdre Dam began in 1938 and finished in 1950, creating Lake Eupen. Nazi Germany annexed Eupen and Malmedy in 1940, and American forces reached the town in September 1944, when it became a centre of fierce fighting in the Battle of the Bulge. In 1980, after a state reform ten years earlier, the German-speaking Community of Belgium was established and Eupen became its capital. German remains the official language, and the town is also the capital of the Euroregion Meuse-Rhine.
euphrates: The Euphrates is about 2,780 km long, the longest river of West Asia, and drains an area of about 440,000 km2 across six countries. It begins where the Kara Su and the Murat Su meet near the town of Keban in southeastern Turkey, both rising northwest of Lake Van. It flows through Syria and Iraq and joins the Tigris in the Shatt al-Arab, which empties into the Persian Gulf. In Syria the Sajur, the Balikh and the Khabur join it; in Iraq it has no more natural tributaries. Most of its water comes from rain and melting snow, with peak flow in April and May.

Early villages arose in the upper reaches from the eleventh millennium BCE, among them Abu Hureyra, Jerf el Ahmar, Mureybet and Nevalı Çori, where farming depended on rainfall. Settlement of lower Mesopotamia began in the 6th millennium BCE and is associated with irrigation. In the Uruk period, in the 4th millennium BCE, truly urban settlements appeared, and Habuba Kabira on the Syrian Euphrates is read as an Uruk colony.

From the Early Dynastic period, from about 3100 BCE, southern Mesopotamia held competing city-states such as Uruk, Kish and Sippar, many of them on canals of the Euphrates and Tigris that have since dried up. Ebla, Mari and Tell Leilan rose in the north from the mid 3rd millennium. The Akkadian Empire, from 2335 to 2154 BCE, and the Ur III empire first united large parts of the basin under one ruler. Babylonia absorbed the southern city-states under Hammurabi in the early to mid 18th century BCE.

After the First World War the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 required Turkey, France for Syria and the United Kingdom for Iraq to agree on the river's use. The Hindiya Barrage in Iraq, finished in 1913, was the first modern water diversion structure in the Tigris–Euphrates system. Syria completed the Tabqa Dam in 1973 and Turkey the Keban Dam in 1974, and later dams have changed the river's seasonal flow.

The name Euphrates comes through Greek and Old Persian from Elamite, from the cuneiform name read Buranun in Sumerian and Purattu in Akkadian. Mandaean scriptures treat the river as the earthly form of a heavenly flowing river. In the Hebrew Bible Jacob crosses it on his way back to Canaan, and Genesis names a river Phrath among the rivers of Paradise, identified with it. In Islamic tradition a hadith says the Last Hour will not come until the river uncovers a mountain of gold. Today Euphrates Lake in Syria is a main source of drinking water for Aleppo.
euphrosyne-of-polotsk: Euphrosyne was born Predslava, between 1101 and 1104, into the Rurik family that ruled the principality of Polotsk, in what is now Belarus. She was the granddaughter of Vseslav, prince of Polotsk, and her father was Prince Svyatoslav (Georgy) Vseslavich of Vitebsk. Historical sources are scarce and unsure on whether Georgy was Svyatoslav's Christian name or his elder brother's.

She refused all proposals of marriage and, without her parents' knowledge, ran away to the convent where her aunt was abbess. She took the name Euphrosyne. With the blessing of the Bishop of Polotsk she lived near the Sophia cathedral, copying books and giving the money she earned to the poor.

Around 1128 Bishop Elias of Polotsk entrusted her with setting up a convent. At the newly built Savior-Transfiguration convent at Seltse she taught young women to copy books, sing, sew and do other handicrafts. A cathedral was built through her efforts in 1161 and survives today. She also founded a monastery dedicated to the Mother of God and two churches. The Church of the Holy Saviour still stands and is considered the most precious monument of early Belarusian architecture.

The Cross of Saint Euphrosyne, a six-armed golden cross decorated with enamels and precious stones, was made at her request by a local master, Lazar Bohsha, and presented to the Church of the Holy Saviour in 1161. It disappeared in 1941 during the evacuation of the museum and was last seen in Mogilev; searches in the early 1990s, including private collections in the United States, did not find it.

Late in life she made a pilgrimage to Constantinople and the Holy Land. Patriarch Michael II of Constantinople gave her an icon of the Theotokos, now called the Virgin of Korsun, and King Amalric I of Jerusalem received her. She died in the Holy Land. After Saladin's conquest of Jerusalem in 1187 monks carried her body to Kiev, to the Monastery of the Caves, and her relics were returned to Polotsk only in 1910.

Her feast day is 23 May. Since 1984 she has been one of the 15 patron saints of Belarus, and she is the only virgin saint of East Slav origin. A convent of Saint Euphrosyne stands in Polotsk and a church in Minsk, and churches in London, Toronto, Vilnius and South River, New Jersey, bear her name.
eurasia: Eurasia is the largest continental area on Earth, comprising all of Europe and Asia. The concept of Europe and Asia as distinct continents dates back to antiquity and is largely cultural, and their borders have historically been subject to change. The ancient Greeks, for example, originally included Africa in Asia but classified Europe as separate land. The division is a historical social construct, since neither fits the usual definition of a continent. Eurasia is connected to Africa at the Suez Canal, and the two are sometimes combined as Afro-Eurasia, the largest contiguous landmass on Earth.

It spans from Iceland and the Iberian Peninsula in the west to the Russian Far East, and is bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Arctic Ocean to the north and the Pacific Ocean to the east. It covers around 55 million square kilometres, about 36.2 per cent of the Earth's land area, and contains around 70 per cent of the human population. All of the 100 highest mountains on Earth are in Eurasia, in the Himalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush, Pamir, Hengduan and Tian Shan ranges. Geologically it formed between 375 and 325 million years ago, when Siberia, Kazakhstania and Baltica merged.

Humans first settled in Eurasia from Africa 125,000 years ago. The landmass has hosted many ancient civilisations, including those based in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and China. In the Axial Age, in the middle of the first millennium BCE, a continuous belt of civilisations stretched through the Eurasian subtropical zone from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and this belt became the mainstream of world history for two millennia.

New connections between the subregions of Eurasia emerged from the Age of Discovery onwards, beginning with the new maritime routes the Iberians found in the 1490s. The completion of the Suez Canal in 1869 paved the way for direct passage through the Indo-Mediterranean and for the wave of Western European New Imperialism that dominated Africa and Asia until the middle of the 20th century. The communist presence in Eurasia, driven primarily by the Soviet Union, then dominated much of the continent until the end of the Cold War in 1991.
eureka-rebellion: Victoria separated from New South Wales on 1 July 1851, and in August news spread that Thomas Hiscock had found more gold 3 kilometres west of Buninyong. The colony's population rose from 77,000 in 1851 to 198,496 in 1853. On 16 August 1851 Lieutenant-Governor Charles La Trobe reserved all land rights on the goldfields to the crown and introduced a mining licence of 30 shillings a month, levied on time spent on the fields rather than on gold found.

In October 1854 James Scobie was murdered outside the Eureka Hotel at Ballarat. An inquest found no evidence against the hotel's owners, amid allegations that the magistrate, John D'Ewes, who held shares in the hotel, had a conflict of interest. Two days after a protest meeting on 15 October, a gathering of about 10,000 men near the hotel ended with it set alight. On 11 November a crowd of more than 10,000 at Bakery Hill founded the Ballarat Reform League under the Chartist John Humffray.

Police and soldiers of the 40th (2nd Somersetshire) and 12th (East Suffolk) Regiments of Foot reinforced the government camp. On 29 November around 10,000 people met at Bakery Hill, where the Eureka Flag was flown for the first time. A licence search the next day led to rioting and eight arrests, and Peter Lalor, standing on a stump with a rifle, proclaimed liberty and called for volunteers to be sworn into companies.

Rede sent 276 soldiers and police under Captain Thomas against the stockade at dawn on Sunday 3 December, when its garrison was seen to be low; they marched off in silence at about 3:30 am. Lalor claimed that the government forces fired first, but the other surviving accounts suggest the first shot came from the rebels. The battle ended the rebellion.

Martial law was proclaimed, and first-hand accounts tell of shots fired from the government camp toward the diggings that killed or wounded a woman, her infant and several men. Of about 120 people detained, thirteen, among them Timothy Hayes and Raffaello Carboni, were tried for high treason. A commission's report of 27 March 1855 was scathing about the goldfields' administration, and the licence gave way to an export duty and a one-pound miner's right that carried a vote.

The rebellion's meaning is contested: it has been read as a revolt against imperial tyranny, against burdensome taxation, of labour against a privileged class, or as republicanism. Some historians think its fame inflated, others see a turning point in Australian history.
euric: Euric was born between 420 and 430, the third son of King Theodoric I, who died in 451 at the Battle of the Catalaunian Fields. His brothers Thorismund and Theodoric II reigned before him. Nothing is known of his youth; he likely grew up in the Gothic capital Toulouse and served in the Roman army. Gothic succession at the time was not fixed, and power was won through violence and the support of the aristocracy. Euric murdered Theodoric II at Toledo in 466. The act was driven by his thirst for power, not by objection to his brother's Roman sympathies. Sidonius Apollinaris described him as determined and intelligent, but also a tyrannical pursuer of Catholic bishops.

At first Euric continued his brother's foreign policy, but he sought to end the alliance with the Western Roman Empire. The defeat of the joint Roman fleet against the Vandals in 468 gave him the chance to declare himself an independent monarch in Gaul, and Gothic militias in Spain revolted. Emperor Anthemius failed to form an anti-Gothic coalition, and Euric destroyed an imperial army sent from Italy. In 469 an attempt on northern Gaul failed against the Gallo-Romans and the Franks under Childeric I, with a great loss near Orléans. Later he defeated an army sent by Riothamus, helped by the betrayal of the Gallic prefect Arvandus, won a battle near Arles and took Berry.

In 472 he conquered most of Hispania; only the northeast, around Barcelona, stayed Roman. An attempt on Italy failed in 473 through the diplomacy of Emperor Glycerius. In 475 Emperor Julius Nepos, who needed Gothic support, gave up Provence and the Barcelona region and recognised Euric's full independence in place of the status of foederati. In the same year Clermont surrendered after a long siege and its bishop, Sidonius Apollinaris, sued for peace.

Earlier Visigothic kings had ruled officially as legates of the Roman emperor; Euric was the first to declare complete independence. He was among the more learned Visigothic kings and the first to codify his people's laws. The Code of Euric, probably issued around 476, set down traditional laws that had been kept in the memory of designated specialists. He employed Gallo-Roman nobles at court, such as Leo of Narbonne. He died of natural causes in 484, when his kingdom covered a third of modern France and almost all of Iberia, except Galicia, which the Suebi ruled.
eurico-gaspar-dutra: Dutra was born in Cuiabá, Mato Grosso, on 18 May 1883. At the age of 19 he falsified his birth year to 1885 so that his physical condition would match his age and ease his entry into the army. He studied in Rio Grande do Sul and at the Military Academy in Rio de Janeiro, from which he was expelled in 1904 for taking part in an uprising linked to the Vaccine Revolt, but he was pardoned, returned and finished the course in 1906. He graduated first in his class at the School of General Staff in 1922.

His early career was spent largely in putting down revolts. He fought the uprising known as the 18 Fort in 1922, took part in the repression of the São Paulo revolution of 1924, fought in the Revolution of 1930 and then, as a colonel, against the Constitutionalist Revolution in São Paulo in 1932. He stood out in the reaction to the communist rising of 1935, known as the Intentona Comunista, and became Minister of War in 1936, holding the post until 1945.

During the Second World War Dutra was among the Brazilian military leaders who opposed alignment with the Allies and a deeper involvement in the conflict. Once Brazil had sent forces to fight beside the Allies, and with civil society pressing for democratisation, he accepted the end of the regime begun in 1930 and took part in the deposition of Getúlio Vargas in October 1945. Vargas then announced his support for Dutra, the army's candidate, against the air force candidate Eduardo Gomes in the elections that followed.

The fifth constitution of Brazil was enacted on 18 September 1946, returning the country to democratic rule. His government closed the casinos and banned gambling, and created the Social Service of Industry and the Social Service of Commerce. In 1947 it broke off diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union, and the Ministry of Labour intervened in many unions. The Salte Plan, proposed that year, concentrated on health, food, transport and energy. Work began on the Paulo Afonso hydroelectric plant and on the highway linking Rio de Janeiro to São Paulo, and in 1948 his government set up the Superior School of War with American support.

After leaving the presidency Dutra stayed active in politics and ran again in the indirect presidential election of 1964, when he received only 0.55 per cent of the vote against General Humberto de Alencar Castelo Branco. He died in Rio de Janeiro on 11 June 1974, aged 91, and was buried in the São João Batista Cemetery. He is remembered as the first president of the Fourth Brazilian Republic, which followed the Vargas regime.
euridice-peri: Euridice was written for the marriage of King Henry IV of France and Maria de' Medici, and Ottavio Rinuccini based its libretto on books X and XI of Ovid's Metamorphoses. Peri and Rinuccini had already written Dafne in 1597, which is lost. Because libretto and score were dedicated to the new queen, some scholars see a parallel between Orfeo and Euridice and the royal couple, while others note that Henry IV would not even travel to Florence to fetch his bride.

Peri himself sang Orfeo at the first performance, and many other roles went to members of Giulio Caccini's entourage, among them his daughter Francesca Caccini. Some of Peri's music was replaced by Caccini's. When Caccini learnt that Peri meant to publish the opera with these pieces, he hurried to finish his own setting of the same libretto and had it published first. In his preface Peri notes that all his music was complete by the first performance.

The opera opens with a melody sung by La Tragedia, the Tragic Muse. Nymphs and shepherds gather to celebrate the wedding of Orfeo and Euridice, until Dafne brings news that Euridice has died from the bite of a venomous snake. Orfeo vows to rescue her, and Arcetro tells how Venus carried him off in her chariot. At the gates of the underworld Venus urges him to sway Pluto with his voice. Orfeo pleads with the deities of the underworld, almost entirely in recitative, succeeds, and the couple return and rejoice.

Peri sought a vocal style half sung and half spoken: lines close to speech over a sustained accompaniment for calmer passages, and stronger, quicker melodies over changing harmonies for impassioned scenes, where exclamations are set with unprepared dissonances and unexpected movements in the bass. He used range, register and the frequency and power of cadences to set characters and moods apart. Critics have found no musically outstanding passages in the score, but even his detractors grant that it laid sound principles for operatic composition, establishing the dual resource of aria and recitative and using solo, ensemble and choral singing.
euripides: Traditional accounts say that Euripides was born on Salamis around 480 BCE, the son of Cleito and of Mnesarchus, a retailer. An oracle said the boy was fated to win crowns of victory, and his father had him train as an athlete, but he turned to the stage and studied painting and philosophy under Prodicus and Anaxagoras. Tradition gives him two unhappy marriages and a retreat to a cave on Salamis. These details derive almost entirely from unreliable sources: folklore, the parody of comic poets, and clues gleaned from his plays.

Euripides first competed at the City Dionysia in 455 BCE and did not win first prize until 441 BCE. The Bacchae and Iphigenia in Aulis were performed in 405 BCE and won first prize after his death. Ancient scholars credited him with ninety-five plays; nineteen attributed to him survive more or less complete, though Rhesus is often thought not to be his. More of his plays survive than of Aeschylus and Sophocles together.

His plays show a shift of outlook: high tragedy in Medea and Hippolytus, a patriotic phase at the start of the Peloponnesian War, disillusion with war in Hecuba and The Trojan Women, romantic plays such as Ion and Helen, and despair in Orestes and The Bacchae. Aristotle called him the most tragic of poets, and Aristophanes mocked his intellectualism in The Frogs.

Tradition says that he retired to the court of King Archelaus in Macedonia and died there in 406 BCE, after being attacked by the king's hounds. Some modern scholars think he may never have visited Macedonia, or went there drawn by incentives offered to other artists. Plutarch tells that Athenian prisoners after the Sicilian expedition won food and drink by performing his lyrics. In the Hellenistic Age he became a cornerstone of literary education, with Homer, Demosthenes and Menander. In 2022 a papyrus found at Philadelphia in the Faiyum was found to hold new fragments of his Ino and Polyidus.
euripus-strait: The Euripus Strait separates the Greek island of Euboea in the Aegean Sea from Boeotia on the mainland, and joins the North Euboean Gulf to the South Euboean Gulf. Its principal port is Chalcis on Euboea, at the strait's narrowest point. Tidal flows are very weak in the Eastern Mediterranean, but the strait is an exception. The current reverses approximately four times a day and peaks at about 12 kilometres an hour, northwards or southwards, so that lesser vessels are often unable to sail against it. Near the moment of reversal vortices form and make passage more precarious.

The name comes from the Ancient Greek eúrīpos, meaning any strait or narrow sea where the flux and reflux is violent. The Swiss scholar François-Alphonse Forel advanced the understanding of the phenomenon through his study of seiches, but the problem was solved completely only by D. Eginitis, director of the Athens Observatory, who published his conclusions in 1929.

The Euripus was closed by a dike of coarse sediment until about 6000 years ago, when an unrecorded earthquake opened it. Herodotus mentions it in his account of the Battle of Artemisium in 480 BCE, which implies that large fleets of triremes could sail through. Diodorus Siculus reports that in 411 BCE the Euboeans closed the strait by mostly rebuilding the dike, so as to become part of Boeotia rather than an island subject to Athenian hegemony. Gaps had to be left for the tides, and the narrowness of the passage made the current much more intense. Only a single passage, wide enough for one ship, remained navigable. Strabo later wrote of a bridge two plethra long.

Procopius reports that under Emperor Justinian I there were two channels, the large original one and a narrow cleft to the east that could be crossed on a single plank. The fortress there was called Euripus, which became Egripos by 1204; the Latins who occupied it in 1205 altered the name to Nigriponte. Venetian records of 1408 and 1439 note a reef under the wooden bridge and erosion around its pilings. Evliya Çelebi wrote that the narrow channel was first opened enough for a galley in the late sixteenth century and was still barely wide enough in 1668.

Two road bridges cross the strait at Chalcis. The Old or Sliding Bridge lies at the narrowest point, where the strait is only 38 metres wide; a retractable bridge was built there in 1858, replaced by a rotating one in 1896, and the existing bridge dates from 1962 and was refurbished in 1998. The Euripus Bridge, a cable-suspended bridge with a span of about 215 metres, was built south of the town in 1992.
eurocommunism: Eurocommunism was a trend within several Western European communist parties, prominent in Italy and Spain and to a lesser extent in France, whose members said they had developed a theory and practice of social transformation more relevant to Western Europe than Marxism-Leninism. The origin of the term was much debated in the mid-1970s. According to Perry Anderson its main theoretical foundation was Antonio Gramsci's writing, which questioned the sectarianism of the left and encouraged communist parties to seek social alliances.

The crushing of the Prague Spring in 1968 was a turning point. The Italian Communist Party and the Communist Party of Spain firmly denounced the occupation, and the French party criticised a Soviet action publicly for the first time in its history. Détente also played a part: with war less likely, Western communists felt less pressure to follow Soviet orthodoxy.

The Italian and Spanish parties adopted Eurocommunism most enthusiastically, and the Finnish party was dominated by Eurocommunists, while most of the French party stayed aligned with Moscow, apart from a brief turn in the mid-to-late 1970s. In 1976 Enrico Berlinguer of the Italian party spoke in Moscow of a pluralistic system and of a socialism possible only in Italy.

His Historic Compromise with the Christian Democrats ended with the kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro in 1978. Santiago Carrillo of the Spanish party wrote Eurocomunismo y estado in 1977 and took part in drafting the democratic constitution as Spain emerged from the dictatorship of Francisco Franco. In 1977 Berlinguer, Carrillo and Georges Marchais of the French party met in Madrid and set out the new way.

The parties embraced public-sector middle-class workers and new movements such as feminism and gay liberation, and the idea spread to parties outside Europe, including those of Japan, Australia and Mexico. After the Soviet Union dissolved many parties split. Some became social democrats, as the Italians did in the Democratic Party of the Left, while others moved into green politics or kept some communist positions.

Critics argued that the Eurocommunists did not break decisively with the Soviet Union, the Italian party taking that step only in 1981 after the repression of Solidarność in Poland, and that they lacked a clear strategy and identity, claiming to differ from both Soviet communism and social democracy while resembling one or the other. The Trotskyist Ernest Mandel saw them as nationalist movements that had abandoned internationalism, and Enver Hoxha called Eurocommunism anti-communism. Mikhail Gorbachev named it in his memoirs as an influence on glasnost and perestroika.
europe: Europe covers approximately 10,186,000 square kilometres, or 2% of Earth's surface, which makes it the second-smallest continent in the seven-continent model. It is commonly considered to be separated from Asia by the watershed of the Ural Mountains, the Ural River, the Caspian Sea, the Greater Caucasus, the Black Sea and the Turkish straits.

This eastern boundary is somewhat arbitrary and inconsistent compared with any clear-cut definition of a continent, and before it was adopted the border had been redefined several times as a series of rivers, seas and straits. Europe has a higher ratio of coast to landmass than any other continent, and warm Atlantic currents such as the Gulf Stream give much of it a temperate climate.

The earliest hominin discovered in Europe is Homo erectus georgicus, which lived roughly 1.8 million years ago in Georgia. Neanderthals appeared about 150,000 years ago and disappeared from the fossil record about 40,000 years ago, with the Iberian Peninsula as their final refuge. Modern humans seem to have appeared around 43,000 to 40,000 years ago, though there is evidence that Homo sapiens arrived around 54,000 years ago.

The culture of Europe takes ancient Greece and ancient Rome as crucial shared roots, particularly through their Christian successors. The fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE and the Christian consolidation of Europe after the Migration Period marked the Middle Ages.

The Italian Renaissance spread across Western Europe, and from the Age of Discovery, led by Spain and Portugal, European powers colonised the Americas, almost all of Africa and Oceania, and the majority of Asia between the 16th and 20th centuries. The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain at the end of the 18th century. Both world wars began and were fought to a great extent in Europe, and the Cold War divided the continent along the Iron Curtain until the Revolutions of 1989.

Europe had a total population of about 745 million in 2021, roughly a tenth of the world's people, and is politically divided into about fifty sovereign states. Russia is the largest and most populous, spanning 39% of the continent. The political map derives largely from the reorganisation after the Napoleonic Wars in 1815, and parliamentary democracy is now the prevalent form of government.
European integration has advanced since the founding of the Council of Europe in 1949, and the European Union, a supranational entity with 27 member states, represents the majority of the continent.
european-commission: The European Commission traces its origin to the High Authority of the European Coal and Steel Community, proposed by the French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman on 9 May 1950. The first Commission was the nine-member High Authority under President Jean Monnet, which took office in Luxembourg City on 10 August 1952. The Treaties of Rome of 1958 created the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community, whose executives were called Commissions rather than High Authorities, because some states, France among them, wished to limit the executive's power by giving more to the Council.

The three executives existed side by side until 1 July 1967, when the Merger Treaty combined them into a single administration under President Jean Rey. His Commission completed the customs union in 1968. Walter Hallstein is nevertheless seen as the first president of the modern Commission.

The Commission headed by Jacques Delors from 1985 to 1995 is credited with giving the Community direction. In his first term he rallied support for the single market, and he later urged economic, monetary and political union. His successor Jacques Santer led a Commission that was forced to resign by the European Parliament in 1999 after a fraud and corruption scandal, the first mass resignation of a College of Commissioners. The European Anti-Fraud Office was created in response.

Romano Prodi took office in 1999, when the Amsterdam Treaty had increased the Commission's powers, and the Treaty of Nice of 2001 gave the president more power over the composition of the College. José Manuel Barroso became president in 2004 and had to reshuffle his College after Parliament objected. Jean-Claude Juncker held the presidency from 1 November 2014 to 30 November 2019, and his Commission saw the General Data Protection Regulation pass.

The Commission was set up as an independent supranational authority. It is composed of a College of Commissioners, one from each member state, who are bound by oath to act for the Union as a whole. The president is chosen by the European Council and must win the approval of the European Parliament, which can dissolve the College by a two-thirds vote of no confidence. The Commission alone has the right of legislative initiative and ensures that treaties and law are upheld, for which it is known as the Guardian of the Treaties. It is divided into Directorates-General, each headed by a director-general responsible to a commissioner, and is based mainly in Brussels, in the Berlaymont building, and in Luxembourg City.
european-communities: The European Coal and Steel Community was created first. Following its proposal in 1950 in the Schuman Declaration, Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany signed the Treaty of Paris in 1951. It was to combine the members' coal and steel industries in a single market, to increase prosperity and lessen the risk of war between them. After attempts at a European Defence Community and a European Political Community failed, the members returned to economic matters. In 1957 the Treaties of Rome created the European Atomic Energy Community, which worked on nuclear cooperation, and the European Economic Community, which was to create a customs union and general economic cooperation and later led to a single market.

The three Communities shared some institutions from the start, including the Common Assembly and the Court of Justice, but each had its own executive. The Merger Treaty of 1967 gave the Council and Commission of the Economic Community responsibility for the other two as well, abolishing the Councils of the Coal and Steel Community and Euratom, the Euratom Commission and the High Authority. From then on the three were known collectively as the European Communities, although they remained separate in law.

The six founders were known as the Inner Six. The first enlargement came in 1973 with the accession of Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom, and Greece, Spain and Portugal joined in the 1980s. The Maastricht Treaty, signed on 7 February 1992 and in force from 1 November 1993, created the European Union and made the Communities its institutional core and first pillar. The Economic Community was renamed the European Community, and the Parliament gained legislative power equal to the Council's on Community matters under the codecision procedure.

The Treaty of Paris had a fifty-year limit, and the Coal and Steel Community ceased to exist in 2002, its work continuing within the European Community. The Treaty of Lisbon, in force in 2009, merged the pillars and abolished the European Community, making the European Union its legal successor. Euratom, which had no time limit, continues to exist as a separate entity governed by the Union's institutions. Some bodies kept the old name for a long time: the Court of Justice was formally the Court of Justice of the European Communities until 2009.
european-court-of-auditors: The Court was created by the Budgetary Treaty of 1975 and formally established on 18 October 1977, holding its first session a week later. At that time it was not a formal institution but an external body designed to audit the finances of the European Communities. It replaced two separate audit bodies, one that dealt with the finances of the European Economic Community and Euratom and one that dealt with the European Coal and Steel Community.

The Court had no defined legal status until the Treaty of Maastricht made it the fifth institution, the first new institution since the founding of the Community. This gave it new powers, such as the ability to bring actions before the European Court of Justice. At first its audit power covered only the European Community pillar of the Union, but under the Treaty of Amsterdam it gained the full power to audit the finances of the whole Union. The Parliament refused to sign off the Commission's handling of the budget in 1984 and in 1999, and the second refusal forced the resignation of the Santer Commission.

Despite its name the Court has no jurisdictional functions. It is an external audit agency that checks whether the Union's budget has been implemented correctly and funds spent legally and with sound management, and it reports in annual, specific and special reports. It must be consulted, though its opinion is never binding, before legislation with financial implications is adopted. When it finds a fault it informs the European Anti-Fraud Office. Each member state nominates one member, formally appointed by the Council of the European Union after consulting the Parliament, for a renewable term of six years. The members elect one of themselves as president for three years. The Court is based in Luxembourg.
european-economic-area: In the late 1980s the member states of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), led by Sweden, began looking at options to join the European Economic Community. Authors give several reasons: the economic downturn of the early 1980s and the Community's Europe 1992 agenda, pressure from large multinational firms that threatened to move production abroad, and the end of the Cold War, which made membership less controversial for neutral countries. Jacques Delors, then President of the European Commission, did not want the Community to enlarge, fearing it would hinder the completion of internal market reform and monetary union. In January 1989 he proposed a European Economic Space, later renamed the European Economic Area.

The EEA Agreement was signed at Porto on 2 May 1992 by the seven EFTA states, the European Community and its twelve member states. Switzerland's voters rejected ratification in a referendum on 6 December 1992, and Switzerland is instead linked to the Union by bilateral agreements. The agreement entered into force on 1 January 1994. Austria, Finland and Sweden left EFTA and joined the European Union on 1 January 1995, and Liechtenstein's participation was delayed until 1 May 1995.

The agreement extends the four freedoms of the single market, the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital, to Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. These states adopt most EU legislation on the single market, such as social policy, consumer protection, environment and company law, but not the Common Agricultural Policy or the Common Fisheries Policy, which Norway and Iceland see as an important reason not to join the Union. They are not represented in the European Parliament or the Commission, but they take part in shaping new legislation at an early stage.

No joint court or authority was set up. An EEA Joint Committee amends the agreement to include new EU legislation, and a council meets twice a year. The EFTA Surveillance Authority at Brussels acts as guardian of the agreement for the EFTA states, and the EFTA Court at Luxembourg resolves disputes among them. A plan for a joint court was dropped after the European Court of Justice held in Opinion 1/91 that it would violate the treaties.
european-economic-community: The Community had its roots in the European Coal and Steel Community, created by the Treaty of Paris in April 1951 to integrate its members' economies and prevent future war. Proposals for a European Defence Community and a European Political Community followed, but the French Parliament rejected the defence community. Jean Monnet, president of the High Authority of the coal and steel community, resigned in protest and began work on alternatives based on economic rather than political integration.

After the Messina Conference in 1955, Paul-Henri Spaak prepared a report on a customs union, which formed the basis for negotiations at the Val Duchesse conference centre in 1956. They led to the signature of the Treaty of Rome on 25 March 1957.

The Hallstein Commission held its first formal meeting on 16 January 1958. Early achievements included common price levels for agricultural products in 1962 and the removal of internal tariffs on certain products in 1968. A crisis over the financing of the Common Agricultural Policy led President Charles de Gaulle's France to pursue an empty chair policy until the Luxembourg compromise of 29 January 1966 allowed members to use a veto on matters of national interest. The Merger Treaty, in operation from 1 July 1967, combined the institutions of the three communities.

De Gaulle vetoed British membership, and the applications of Denmark, Ireland, the United Kingdom and Norway were suspended. After Georges Pompidou succeeded him, negotiations began in 1970, and Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom joined on 1 January 1973. Greece, Spain and Portugal followed, each after restoring democracy. The European Parliament was first directly elected in June 1979. The Maastricht Treaty entered into force on 1 November 1993, renaming the Community the European Community within the new European Union; the Treaty of Lisbon abolished it in 2009.

The Community's preamble committed it to preserving peace and liberty and laying the foundations of an ever closer union among the peoples of Europe. Western Europeans also feared that poverty would leave populations open to communist propaganda, and hoped prosperity would reconcile states such as France and Germany. Its institutions were the Council, the Commission, the Parliament, the Court of Justice and, from 1975, the Court of Auditors, and from 1967 they served all three communities. After Maastricht they became the institutions of the European Union.
european-free-trade-association: The European Free Trade Association was set up in 1960 as an alternative trade bloc for European states that were unable or unwilling to join the European Economic Community. The convention was drawn up in Stockholm and provided for the progressive removal of customs duties on industrial products, leaving agricultural and fisheries products aside. Seven states founded it: Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, often called the Outer Seven in the 1960s, in contrast to the Inner Six of the Community.

The main difference from the early Community was that it had no common external customs tariff. Each member remained free to set its own duties on goods from outside the association and to make its own free trade agreements with other countries.

Membership changed as members left for the Community. Finland became an associate member in 1961 and a full member in 1986, and Iceland joined in 1970. The United Kingdom and Denmark left in 1973 on joining the Community, and Portugal left to join it in the 1980s. Liechtenstein joined in 1991; until then Switzerland had represented its interests. Austria, Sweden and Finland joined the European Union in 1995, leaving Norway and Switzerland of the founders. Norway's governments twice sought to join, but referendums rejected membership in 1972 and in 1994. Switzerland rejected membership of the European Economic Area in a referendum in 1992.

The Agreement on the European Economic Area was signed in Porto in 1992 and took effect on 1 January 1994. It lets Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway take part in the internal market of the European Union without belonging to it, applying almost all its market legislation except on agriculture and fisheries. Because the European Court of Justice ruled in Opinion 1/91 that the EU's institutions could not hold such powers over non-members, the EFTA Surveillance Authority and the EFTA Court were created for this purpose. The Portugal Fund, a low-interest loan of US$100 million from the members, began in February 1977 to support Portugal's development after the Carnation Revolution and was dissolved in January 2002.

The association is not a customs union, though it has a coordinated trade policy, and its members have jointly concluded free trade agreements with the European Union and with many other countries. A revised treaty, the Vaduz Convention, was signed on 21 June 2001 and took effect on 1 June 2002. Switzerland, outside the Economic Area, has instead a set of bilateral agreements with the European Union. Citizens of its member states can live and work in the other member states. The association also originated the Hallmarking Convention and the Pharmaceutical Inspection Convention, both open to other states.
european-russia: European Russia is the western part of Russia, set apart from Siberia by the Ural Mountains, the Ural River and the Miass River. It spans roughly 40 per cent of Europe's landmass and is divided into six federal districts. Moscow, the capital and the most populous city entirely within Europe, and Saint Petersburg, the cultural capital, both lie within it. Most of the country's population lives here, and it is the most densely populated region of Russia.

The historical population of the region was composed of Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Germanic, Turkic, Jewish, Scythian, North Caucasian, Hunnic and Baltic peoples. Some theories hold that early Eastern Slavs arrived in what is now western Russia in the middle of the first millennium CE. The Vyatichis lived around the Oka river and the Severians in the west of central Russia, while Finno-Ugric, Baltic and Turkic tribes were also present, and many of the Turkic and Finno-Ugric peoples were absorbed by the Slavs.

According to the Sofia First Chronicle, Veliky Novgorod was one of the first Rus' regions, in 859. A Rus' Khaganate formed in the late 8th and early to mid-9th centuries, and the region was a place of operations for Varangians, eastern Scandinavian adventurers, merchants and pirates. From the late 9th to the mid-13th century a large section of European Russia was part of Kievan Rus', whose lands were trade routes linking Scandinavia, the Byzantine Empire, Volga Bulgaria, Khazaria and Persia.

Through contact with the Byzantine Empire the Slavic culture of the Rus' gradually adopted the Eastern Orthodox religion, though elements of East Slavic paganism and Christianity overlapped and sometimes produced a double faith in Muscovite Rus'. Many sources say that Ryazan, Kolomna, Moscow, Vladimir and Kiev were destroyed by the Mongol Empire. After the Mongol invasion Muscovite Rus' arose.

European Russia covers an area of over 3,969,100 square kilometres, about 80 per cent of the population of Russia. A majority of its people are Slavic, and Christianity is the dominant religion. Twelve of the sixteen Russian cities with over a million inhabitants lie within it, among them Moscow, Saint Petersburg, Kazan, Nizhny Novgorod and Volgograd.
european-union: Visions of European unity existed well before the 19th century but gained ground as a reaction to the First World War. In 1920 John Maynard Keynes proposed a European customs union, and in 1923 the Paneuropean Union, the oldest organisation for European integration, was founded under Richard von Coudenhove-Kalergi. On 5 September 1929 Aristide Briand, Prime Minister of France, called in a speech at the League of Nations for a federal Europe to settle the historic Franco-German enmity. By the end of the following world war integration was seen as an antidote to the extreme nationalism that had caused it, and on 19 September 1946 Winston Churchill, speaking at the University of Zürich, repeated his calls for a European Union and a Council of Europe.

The Union's beginnings are traced to the Inner Six states, Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, at the start of modern European integration in 1948. Treaties created the Western Union, the International Authority for the Ruhr, the European Coal and Steel Community, the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community, which increasingly merged. In 1969 a single currency became an official objective.

The European Union was established, along with its citizenship, when the Maastricht Treaty came into force in 1993, and the Treaty of Lisbon gave it a single international legal personality in 2009. It grew through the accession of 22 further states from 1973 to 2013. The flag of 12 golden stars on blue was designed in 1955 for the Council of Europe and adopted by the European Communities in 1986. In 2020 the United Kingdom became the only member state to leave.

The Union combines supranational and intergovernmental decision-making. It acts only within the competences the treaties give it, and only where the member states acting alone cannot achieve an objective. Regulations are enforceable at once in every member state, while directives must be put into national law. A country joining must meet the Copenhagen criteria set in 1993: a stable democracy that respects human rights and the rule of law, a functioning market economy and acceptance of EU law. The internal market rests on the free movement of people, goods, services and capital, and passport controls have been abolished within the Schengen Area. The Union was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.
eurotas: The Evrotas is the main river of Laconia and one of the major rivers of the Peloponnese. It is 82 kilometres long and drains a basin of 2,239 square kilometres. Its springs lie just northwest of the border between Laconia and Arcadia, near Skortsinos, and it is fed by tributaries from Mount Taygetos on the west and Mount Parnon on the east. The valley lies in a rift. Analysis of bore holes shows that it was a lake in the Pliocene. In classical times ancient authors described it as swampy but very fertile, and it was used mainly for fruit trees, especially olives. Earlier names of the river were Bomycas and Himeras, and in the Middle Ages it was called Iri.

Greek legend made Lelex, king of the Leleges, the ancestor of the peoples of the valley, and his son or grandson Eurotas the last of the line. Eurotas had a daughter, Sparta, who married an outsider, Lacedaemon. The name Lacedaemon was probably that of the Mycenaean state. A drowned town off Pounta and the island of Pavlopetri, surveyed from 1968 and again in 2009, was occupied from the late Neolithic into Byzantine times and was mainly Early Bronze Age.

On the left bank, opposite Sparta, a ridge holds the Menelaon. A survey found that the whole ridge had been covered by a walled Mycenaean town of the late Bronze Age. Excavators concluded that in the later fifteenth century BCE it was the principal settlement of Laconia, and the dedications to Menelaus and Helen found there from the Archaic period identify it with the Homeric Sparta. Classical Sparta lay on the west bank about halfway down the valley. The Spartans made little use of the left bank, and the main traffic went south to the port of Gytheio. Pausanias believed that the Eurotas and the Alpheios in Arcadia shared a source and were connected underground.

Much of the water of the Evrotas is drawn off for irrigation, mainly of citrus crops, and the river is almost dry in summer, though it floods in winter. The plain of Elos near the mouth is particularly fertile. The final 10 kilometres of the river run through alluvial soil that did not exist in antiquity, and the old coastline lay farther inland. Modern Laconia covers the valley, and its seat is Sparta, as in ancient times.
eurystheus: In Greek mythology Eurystheus was king of Tiryns, one of three Mycenaean strongholds in the Argolid, though Homer and Euripides cast him as ruler of Argos. He was the son of King Sthenelus and Nicippe, and a grandson of the hero Perseus. He married Antimache, daughter of Amphidamas of Arcadia, and they had seven children, among them Admete.

The myths explain his rule through a contest between Hera and Zeus. Heracles' stepfather Amphitryon was also a grandson of Perseus, and since Amphitryon's father was older than Eurystheus' father he might have inherited the kingdom, but Sthenelus had banished him. When Zeus proclaimed that the next-born descendant of Perseus should rule, Hera thwarted him by delaying the birth of Alcmene's child Heracles and having Eurystheus born prematurely at seven months.

Eurystheus imposed the Twelve Labours on Heracles, which were penance for Heracles' murder of his own family in a fit of madness sent by Hera. Mythographers also note that the two families had been rivals for the throne of Mycenae. After Heracles brought back the skin of the Nemean Lion, which he wore, Eurystheus was so frightened that he hid in a bronze winejar below ground, and from then on gave his orders through a herald, Copreus. He hid in the jar again when Heracles returned with the Erymanthian Boar and with Cerberus.

He also refused to count some labours. He did not count the Hydra, since Heracles' nephew Iolaus had helped him, nor the Augean stables, since Heracles had bargained for payment. This is said to have extended what may once have been ten labours to the canonical twelve. The ninth task, the belt of Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons, was set at the request of his daughter Admete.

After Heracles died, Eurystheus remained bitter and tried to destroy Heracles' children, the Heracleidae, led by Hyllus, who fled to Athens. He attacked the city but was soundly defeated, and he and his sons were killed. Accounts differ over who killed him and what became of his body, though it is widely told that Hyllus did. The Athenians believed his burial site remained on their soil and protected the country against the descendants of Heracles, who traditionally included the Spartans and Argives.

He appears as a character in the play Heracleidae by Euripides, where he speaks prophetically of his burial in Attica. After his death Atreus and Thyestes, whom he had left in charge during his absence, took over the city, and Atreus exiled Thyestes and became king, while Tiryns returned to the kingship of Argos.
eustace-ii-count-of-boulogne: Eustace, also known as Eustace aux Gernons, Eustace with long moustaches, was the son of Eustace I of Boulogne and Matilda of Louvain. His first wife was Goda, a daughter of King Æthelred the Unready and sister of King Edward the Confessor of England. In 1047 he joined the rebellion of Godfrey III, Duke of Lower Lorraine, against the Holy Roman Emperor Henry III, and he married Godfrey's daughter Ida of Lorraine. The next year Pope Leo IX excommunicated him for marrying within the prohibited degrees of kinship, possibly at Henry III's request. The rebellion failed, and in 1049 Eustace and Godfrey submitted to the emperor.

In 1051 Eustace visited Edward the Confessor. On the way back his men put on mail coats as they approached Dover, and in the brawl that followed some twenty townsmen and a similar number of his men were killed. The historian Tom Licence comments that Eustace was either anticipating trouble or intending to start a fight. Edward accepted his account and ordered Earl Godwin to ravage the town; Godwin refused and raised an army, and in the confrontation that followed he and his sons were forced to flee England.

Eustace then took part in the Norman Conquest of 1066 and fought at Hastings, though sources differ on his conduct. The contemporary chronicler William of Poitiers wrote that Eustace, turning in flight with 50 knights, urged Duke William to retire and was then struck between the shoulders and barely escaped. Other sources place him with William at the Malfosse incident after the battle. His large grants of English land suggest he contributed in other ways too, perhaps by providing ships. Some have suggested that he was the patron of the Bayeux Tapestry.

In the following year, probably dissatisfied with his share of the spoil, Eustace helped the men of Kent in an attempt to seize Dover Castle. The conspiracy failed and he forfeited his English fiefs, but he was later reconciled with William, who restored part of them. He is one of the few proven companions of the Conqueror. Eustace died around 1087 and was succeeded by his son Eustace III. His second son, Godfrey of Bouillon, was a leader of the First Crusade, and another son, Geoffrey fitz Eustace, married Beatrice de Mandeville.
euthydemus-i: Euthydemus was an Ionian Greek from one of the cities called Magnesia in Ionia, though it is uncertain whether it was Magnesia on the Maeander or Magnesia ad Sipylum. According to Strabo and Polybius he was the father of Demetrius I. He is thought to have been originally a satrap of Sogdia, and he usurped power from Diodotus II. William Woodthorpe Tarn proposed that he was the son of a Greek general named Antimachus or Apollodotus and married a sister of Diodotus II.

Little is known of his reign before Antiochus III the Great attacked him. He tried to resist on the river Arius, the modern Harirud, and although he commanded 10,000 horsemen he lost the battle and retreated. He then held out in the fortified city of Bactra against a long siege. Antiochus finally recognised him, and around 206 BCE offered one of his daughters to Euthydemus's son Demetrius; as part of the treaty Euthydemus gave Antiochus Indian war elephants.

Polybius records that Euthydemus argued that he had never revolted against the king but had destroyed the descendants of those who had, and warned that nomads on the steppe threatened both kings. Coin finds show intense activity at fortresses in north-western Bactria, and he seems to have first built the Derbent Wall, the Iron Gate, a stone wall of 1.6 to 1.7 kilometres with towers and a central fortress guarding a pass. He issued a very large coinage in gold, silver and bronze at two mints, with his profile on the obverse and a seated Heracles on the reverse.

An inscription from the Kuliab area of Tajikistan, dated 200 to 195 BCE, records a Greek named Heliodotus dedicating an altar to Hestia for Euthydemus and his son Demetrius, whom it praises for fine victories; it suggests that Demetrius was a junior partner in rule. Demetrius succeeded him and invaded north-western South Asia. Later kings, Agathocles and Antimachus I, put Euthydemus on their coins with the epithet Theos, God, and nomadic tribes of Central Asia imitated his coins for decades after his death. A bust in the Torlonia Collection once identified as him is now judged a Roman Republican portrait.
euthymius-of-tarnovo: Euthymius was born around 1325, between 1320 and 1330, possibly into the eminent Tsamblak family of the capital, Tarnovo. Educated at the monastery schools in and around the city, he became a monk and around 1350 joined the Kilifarevo Monastery, drawn by the fame of Theodosius of Tarnovo, who made him his first assistant in 1363. The two went together to Tsarigrad, where Theodosius died soon afterwards. Euthymius then lived at the Studion monastery and at the Great Lavra of Athanasius the Athonite on Mount Athos, under the influence of Gregory the Sinaite, Gregory Palamas, Callistus Philotheus and John Kukuzelis.

The Byzantine Emperor John V Palaiologos exiled him to the island of Lemnos. On his release he went to the Bulgarian Zograf Monastery on Mount Athos, where he first planned his spelling reforms and corrections to the translations of church books. Around 1371 he returned to Bulgaria and founded the Holy Trinity Patriarchal Monastery near Tarnovo, the home of the Tarnovo Literary School. He laid down rules of spelling and corrected badly translated religious books against their Greek originals, and the corrected texts became models for the churches of Bulgaria, Serbia, Romania and Russia.

Elected patriarch in 1375 on the death of Patriarch Joanicius, Euthymius, an ascetic, set out to fight heresy and moral decay, and metropolitans and hegumens across the Orthodox world asked him to interpret theological matters. There are 15 known works by him, among them lives of Saint Ivan of Rila and Saint Petka of Tarnovo, praises and letters. His literary disciples included Gregory Tsamblak, Metropolitan of Kiev, Cyprian, Metropolitan of Moscow, Joasaph of Bdin and Constantine of Kostenets.

In the spring of 1393 Suleyman Çelebi, son of the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I, laid siege to Tarnovo. With Tsar Ivan Shishman away at the fortress of Nikopol, Euthymius was entrusted with the city's defence. Tarnovo fell on 17 July 1393 after a three-month siege. According to Gregory Tsamblak its churches were turned into mosques and 110 notable citizens and boyars were massacred, but the patriarch was spared and sent into exile, possibly to the Bachkovo Monastery, where he is supposed to have died. The Bulgarian church became subordinate to the Patriarchate of Constantinople until 1870. Euthymius was canonised and is remembered on 20 January.
eutin: Eutin is the district capital of Eastern Holstein in Schleswig-Holstein and is surrounded by lakes of the Holsteinische Schweiz, among them the Großer Eutiner See, the Kleiner Eutiner See, the Kellersee and the Ukleisee, many of them ringed by forest. The name, originally Utin, is of Slavic origin, and its meaning is not quite clear; it probably comes from the personal name Uta.

The Slavic Obotrites settled eastern Holstein in the 7th or 8th century and built a castle on Pheasant Island in the lake now called the Großer Eutiner See. In the twelfth century Dutch settlers populated the originally Slavic settlement. Eutin became a market town in 1156 and received town rights in 1257. Because Lübeck was an imperial free city, Eutin became the seat of the Prince-Bishopric of Lübeck.

When the bishopric was secularised in 1803, Eutin passed to the Duchy of Oldenburg. The Greater Hamburg Act of 1937 moved it from the Free State of Oldenburg to the Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein. People born in Eutin include Wilhelm, Duke of Oldenburg, born in Eutin Castle in 1754 and ruler from 1784, the philosopher Friedrich Adolf Trendelenburg and the composer Carl Maria von Weber, born in 1786. The poet and classicist Johann Heinrich Voss and the poet Matthias Claudius worked in the town.

The town has some 17,000 inhabitants. In honour of Weber an open-air theatre was built in the park of Eutin Castle in 1951, where operas are performed each July and August at the Eutin Opera Summer Festival. Standard German and Low German are both in common use, and the usual greeting is moin.
eva-peron: Eva Perón was born into poverty in the Pampas, the youngest of five children. Her mother, Juana Ibarguren, had been supported by the children's father, Juan Duarte, until he abandoned them, leaving only a document declaring that the children were his, which let them use the Duarte surname. Juana moved the family to a one-room apartment in Junín, where mother and daughters worked as cooks in the houses of local estancias. The records of her birth conflict: a civil registry certificate gives 1922 and a baptismal certificate 1919, and it is thought that in 1945 she had a forged birth certificate made for her marriage.
In 1934, at 15, she ran off with a young musician to Buenos Aires. The relationship ended quickly, but she stayed and found work on the stage and radio, eventually becoming a film actress.

She met Colonel Juan Perón on 22 January 1944 at a gala in the Luna Park Stadium to raise money for victims of the San Juan earthquake. He won the presidency in 1946 with 54 per cent, and she campaigned heavily for him on her weekly radio show.

In 1947 she made a much-publicised Rainbow Tour of Europe, meeting Francisco Franco and Pope Pius XII. As first lady she was powerful in the Peronist trade unions, ran the Ministries of Labor and Health, the Eva Perón Foundation and the Female Peronist Party, and on women's suffrage made radio addresses and wrote in her newspaper Democracia, though the power to grant the vote was beyond her. In 1951 she was chosen as candidate for vice-president, but opposition from the military and the middle class, with her failing health, forced her to withdraw.

She fainted in public on 9 January 1950 and had surgery three days later; it was reported as an appendectomy, but she had advanced cervical cancer. In 1952 Congress gave her the title Spiritual Leader of the Nation. She died on 26 July 1952 at the Unzue Palace, aged 33, and flags flew at half-staff for ten days. Pedro Ara embalmed her body, which was displayed at the headquarters of the CGT for almost two years. After the coup of 1955 overthrew Juan Perón it was lost to him; in 1971 it was flown to Spain, and it returned to Argentina in 1974. She became the subject of the musical Evita in 1976, and many Argentines have kept her image in their homes.
evagoras-i: Evagoras claimed descent from Teucer, the son of Telamon and half-brother of Ajax, and his family had long ruled Salamis. During his childhood Salamis came under Phoenician control and he was exiled. While in Cilicia he gathered fifty followers and returned secretly to take the throne. Expecting a Persian response to recapture Cyprus, he cultivated the friendship of the Athenians and gave refuge to Conon after the Battle of Aegospotami.

For a time Evagoras kept friendly relations with the Achaemenid Empire and secured the aid of Artaxerxes II for Athens against Sparta. He took part in the Battle of Cnidus of 394 BCE, providing most of the resources, and the Lacedaemonian fleet was defeated through his efforts. For this the Athenians placed his statue beside that of Conon in the Kerameikos.

From 391 BCE relations with the Persians were strained and the two were virtually at war. With Athenian help and that of the Egyptian king Hakor, Evagoras extended his rule over most of Cyprus, crossed to Anatolia, took several Phoenician cities including Tyre, and persuaded the Cilicians to revolt.

The Peace of Antalcidas of 387 BCE, which he refused to accept, led Athens to withdraw its support. In 385 BCE the Persian generals Tiribazus and Orontes invaded with a much larger army, but Evagoras cut off its supplies and the starving troops rebelled. The war then turned when his fleet was destroyed at the Battle of Citium, and he fled to Salamis, where he held out under blockade and made peace by exploiting a quarrel between the two generals. He remained nominally king as a Persian vassal paying yearly tribute.

Evagoras was assassinated in 374 BCE by a eunuch acting from private revenge, and his son Nicocles succeeded him. In Isocrates's Panegyricus he is a model ruler who promoted the welfare of his state through Greek refinement, and many people are said to have migrated from Greece to Cyprus because of his rule. Diodorus Siculus and Xenophon are less uniformly complimentary. He has also been called a pioneer of adopting the Greek alphabet in Cyprus in place of the older Cypriot syllabary.
evelyn-baring-1st-earl-of-cromer: Evelyn Baring was born on 26 February 1841, the ninth son of Henry Baring, of the family that founded Barings Bank. He entered the Royal Military Academy at 14 and was commissioned in the Royal Artillery at 17, serving first on Corfu, where he taught himself Greek and Italian. He was aide-de-camp to Sir Henry Storks in the Ionian Islands, Malta and Jamaica, attended the Staff College and worked at the War Office. In 1872 he went to India as private secretary to his cousin Lord Northbrook, the viceroy, and found a gift for administration. In 1879 he was British controller in the Dual Control of Egypt's bankrupt finances, and pressed for the deposition of Khedive Ismail.

After the Anglo-Egyptian War of 1882 he returned as agent and consul-general, with a mandate for minor reforms and a prompt withdrawal, but argued for continued occupation. Under the Granville Doctrine, British officials could install cooperative Egyptian ministers and dismiss those who refused British directives, a system known as the Veiled Protectorate. He disbanded the Egyptian army and raised a new one on British lines, and once finances were stable by 1887 made Cairo give up any plan to reconquer the Sudan. Careful budgets and irrigation brought considerable prosperity, but Egypt grew more dependent on cash crops.

Fearing that education bred nationalism, as he believed it had in India, he cut the education budget, closed specialised colleges and raised school fees. The historian Afaf Lufti al-Sayyid-Marsot argues that he held subject races incapable of self-government. He also argued that Islam degraded women and promoted unveiling, ideas that shaped later debate. After the Denshawai Incident of 1906 he resigned in April 1907, officially for his health, and Parliament voted him £50,000.

He had been made Earl of Cromer in 1901 and a Member of the Order of Merit in 1906. In retirement he published Modern Egypt (1908) and Ancient and Modern Imperialism (1910), joined the free-trade wing of the Unionist Party in the House of Lords and led the Men's League for Opposing Woman Suffrage. In 1916 he chaired the Dardanelles Commission, a strain that the historian John Grigg wrote in effect killed him. He died on 29 January 1917 and is buried in Bournemouth.
everglades: The Everglades comprise the southern half of the Kissimmee-Okeechobee-Everglades watershed. The system begins near Orlando with the Kissimmee River, which empties into the vast but shallow Lake Okeechobee. In the wet season water leaving the lake forms a slow-moving river 97 kilometres wide and over 160 kilometres long, flowing south across a limestone shelf to Florida Bay. Before drainage the area was a web of marshes and prairies of about 10,000 square kilometres.

The climate has two seasons: a dry season from November to April and a wet season from May to October, which brings about 70 per cent of the annual rainfall. The primary feature is the sawgrass marsh, together with tropical hardwood hammocks, pineland, the Big Cypress Swamp and the mangroves of the Ten Thousand Islands. Fire, mostly started by lightning in the wet season, helps to maintain these ecosystems.

Humans reached the Florida peninsula about 15,000 years ago. Before European colonisation the region was dominated by the Calusa and Tequesta, who declined gradually under Spanish colonisation. The Seminole, formed mostly from Creek people, assimilated other peoples and created a new culture after being forced from northern Florida into the Everglades during the Seminole Wars of the early 19th century. Having adapted to the region, they were able to resist removal by the United States Army. The first written record was on Spanish maps by cartographers who had not seen the land, which named the area Laguna del Espíritu Santo.

Draining the Everglades was proposed as early as 1837, and in 1848 migrants who wanted to develop plantations proposed it again; but no work of this type was attempted until 1882. Land developers sold 20,000 lots in a few months in 1912, though many settlers found that the peat kept burning and that crops wilted. Hurricanes in 1926 and 1928 made Lake Okeechobee breach its levees, killing thousands, and the government turned to flood control. A dike 106 kilometres long was built around the southern edge of the lake between 1930 and 1937.

In 1947 Congress formed the Central and Southern Florida Flood Control Project, which built 2,300 kilometres of canals, levees and water control devices. Water was diverted to the growing Miami area, and portions of the Everglades became farmland, mainly for sugarcane. About half of the original Everglades has been developed as agricultural or urban land. From the 1970s conservation groups gave the ecosystem notable attention, and UNESCO and the Ramsar Convention designated it a Wetland Area of Global Importance. Congress approved the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan in 2000.
evian-accords: The Algerian War began in 1954 out of a growing nationalist movement. The National Liberation Front (FLN) called for independence in its Declaration of 1 November 1954, and the French government led by Pierre Mendès France declined, under pressure from the pieds-noirs and the political situation in France. The war escalated until 1958, when the Fourth Republic ended and Charles de Gaulle came to power. On 16 September 1959 de Gaulle acknowledged the principle of self-determination for Algeria and recognised the FLN as the intermediary for negotiating independence. A referendum on self-determination followed on 8 January 1961, and negotiations between the French government and the FLN took place at Évian between 7 and 18 March 1962.

The agreements, set out on 18 March 1962 at Évian-les-Bains between the French government and the Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic, ran to 93 pages in five chapters. They covered a cease-fire, the release of prisoners and recognition of Algeria's full sovereignty, with a referendum on independence and the recognition of the FLN as a legal political body. French mining titles were guaranteed, French companies were to have preference for new ones and Saharan hydrocarbons were to be bought in francs, in return for French technical, cultural and economic aid.

French forces were to be withdrawn over two years, apart from the naval base at Mers El Kébir, leased to France for fifteen years, and a number of military airfields. The pieds-noirs and Algeria's Sephardi Jews were guaranteed religious freedom and property rights and given the choice between French and Algerian citizenship after three years. Disputes could go to the International Court of Justice, and no sanctions were to follow for acts committed before the cease-fire.

The cease-fire came into force on 19 March 1962. In a referendum on 8 April 1962 the French electorate approved the Accords with almost 91% in favour, 17,866,423 votes to 1,809,074. On 1 July Algerians voted 5,975,581 to 16,534 for independence, and de Gaulle pronounced Algeria independent on 3 July. The Secret Army Organisation (OAS) had opposed the talks with bombings and attempts on de Gaulle's life, including the Petit-Clamart attack in August 1962.

The Provisional Government's authority was challenged by the Political Bureau led by Ahmed Ben Bella, and after two months of civil conflict Ben Bella became the first president of the Democratic and Popular Republic of Algeria on 22 September 1962. France left Mers El Kébir in 1967. The historian Alistair Horne notes that events overtook most provisions: the exodus of almost all of the million-strong European community made the transition clauses a dead letter, and the killing of many Muslim harkis who had served with the French Army contravened the amnesty.
evliya-celebi: Dervish Mehmed Zillî, known as Evliya Çelebi, was born in Constantinople on 25 March 1611 to a wealthy family from Kütahya. His father was a jeweller attached to the Ottoman court, and his mother was an Abkhazian relation of the future Grand Vizier Melek Ahmed Pasha. He received a court education from the imperial scholars and studied music with the Khalwati dervish 'Umar Gulshani. A devout Muslim who opposed fanaticism and could recite the Quran from memory, he served as a clergyman and entertainer at the court of Sultan Murad IV but refused employment that would keep him from travelling.

His journal-writing began in Constantinople with notes on buildings, markets and customs, and from 1640 it was extended by accounts of his travels. These became the ten-volume Seyahatnâme, written in a mixture of vernacular and high Turkish, which remains an accessible reference on life in the 17th-century Ottoman Empire. Its first volume deals only with Constantinople and the last with Egypt. The journeys it describes include Anatolia, the Caucasus and Crete (1640), Kurdistan, Iraq and Iran (1655), Hungary in the campaigns of 1663 and 1664, the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1671, and Egypt, Ethiopia and the Sudan (1672 to 1675).

He collected samples of the languages of each region, some thirty Turkic dialects among them, and the Seyahatnâme holds the only written specimens of Ubykh outside the linguistic literature. Of the Parthenon in 1667 he wrote that it was like an impregnable fortress not made by human agency.

Many descriptions in the Seyahatnâme are exaggerated or inventive, or rest on misreadings of other sources, but the notes remain a useful guide to the culture of the period. He took part in raids on the Habsburg frontier in Hungary in 1663 in which people were captured and sold into slavery, and described such sales in graphic detail. A 2019 study by Mustafa Çapar argues that his reputation for objectivity toward minorities is only partly deserved, since he judged peoples chiefly by religion and often used demeaning language about non-Muslims.

Evliya Çelebi died in 1684, and it is unclear whether he was in Constantinople or Cairo. No English translation of the whole work exists; Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall translated the first two volumes in 1834.
