evora: Évora lies at an altitude of 300 metres in the Alentejo, a region of wide plains in southern Portugal, 140 kilometres from Lisbon and 80 kilometres from Badajoz at the Spanish border. It is considered the historic capital of the Alentejo. Its old town, still partly enclosed by medieval walls, covers about one square kilometre. The name Ebora, used by the Celtici, who made the town their regional capital, probably comes from a Celtic word for yew trees.

The Romans conquered the town in 57 BCE and expanded it into a walled town, and Julius Caesar called it Liberalitas Julia. It grew because it lay at the junction of several important routes, and Pliny the Elder mentioned it as Ebora Cerealis for its surrounding wheat fields. The Corinthian temple at its centre dates from the first century and was probably raised in honour of Augustus. In 715 the Arab commander Tariq ibn-Ziyad conquered it and it became Yāburah. Gerald the Fearless took the town by surprise attack in September 1165, and it came under King Afonso I of Portugal in 1166.

In the Middle Ages, especially the fifteenth century, it was one of the most dynamic cities of Portugal, and the court lived there for long periods. It flourished under Manuel I and John III as a centre of humanists and artists, among them the playwright Gil Vicente. It became an archbishopric in 1540, and the Jesuits founded its university in 1559. The Marquis of Pombal closed the university in 1759, and it reopened only in 1973. On 29 July 1808, in the Peninsular War, a French and Spanish division routed an outnumbered Portuguese and Spanish force at the Battle of Évora, and the attackers stormed the town.

Évora is the seat of the Évora District and had 53,591 inhabitants in 2021. Its historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Its monuments include the Roman temple, the Gothic cathedral, mainly built between 1280 and 1340, and the Chapel of Bones, covered entirely with human bones, in the Church of São Francisco. The Prata Aqueduct, built between 1531 and 1537, once ran nine kilometres to bring water to the city.
evreux: In late antiquity the town, attested in the fourth century CE, was a small regional centre of the Roman province of Gallia Lugdunensis. Julius Caesar wintered eight legions in the area during the conquest of Gaul. The name Évreux comes from the Eburovices, a Gallic tribe that lived there, whose name derives from the Gaulish eburo, meaning yew tree. Remains of a Roman theatre, a palace, baths and an aqueduct have been found at Le Vieil-Évreux, the Roman Gisacum, 5.6 kilometres to the south-east.

The first known counts of Évreux descended from an illegitimate son of Richard I, duke of Normandy. The line died out in the male line with the death of Count William in 1118, and Henry I of England burned the city in 1119. In 1200 Amaury VI de Montfort-Évreux ceded the title to King Philip II. In 1307 Philip IV gave it to his brother Louis d'Évreux, and in 1317 Philip the Tall raised it into the peerage of France. Louis's son Philip d'Évreux became king of Navarre by marriage to Joan II of Navarre. Charles the Noble ceded Évreux to Charles VI of France in 1404. The city was heavily damaged in the Second World War, and most of its centre was rebuilt.

Évreux lies in the valley of the Iton, and arms of the river run through the town. Évreux Cathedral has been the seat of the bishops of Évreux since its traditional founder, Saint Taurin, who most probably worked between 375 and 425. The earliest parts of the present mostly Gothic building date from the eleventh century, and the octagonal central tower from the late fifteenth. In the Middle Ages the town was also a centre of Jewish learning, whose scholars, among them Samuel ben Shneor and Moses of Évreux, are quoted in the medieval notes to the Talmud known as the Tosafot.
ewe-people: The largest Ewe population is in Ghana, about 6.0 million, and the second largest in Togo, about 3.1 million. They speak Ewe, which belongs to the Gbe family, and are related to the Fon, Gen, Ogu, Mahi and Aja. All Gbe-speaking peoples regard the Adja as the mother tribe. The Ewe were formerly known as the Dogboawo, after Dogbo, the first town they founded when they broke away from the Aja Confederacy before moving west and founding the walled city-state of Notsie. They may have come from Ketu, a place recalled in their oral history. Archaeological evidence suggests that some of their ancestors were in their present homelands as early as the thirteenth century.

Oral tradition describes the harsh king Agɔ Akɔli of Notsie, thought to have ruled in the seventeenth century. His high-handedness ended in the escape and dispersal of the Ewe to their present homes. Their experience of him is said to have made them refuse support to despotic rulers.

The Ewe lived between the powerful slave-trading kingdoms of Asante, Dahomey and Oyo. They suffered raiding and also sold war captives to Europeans. In 1784 they fought Danish colonial interests, who tried to build coastal forts.

After the slave trade ended they prospered from farming cotton and rice and exporting palm oil and copra. German Lutheran missionaries arrived in 1847, and the Germans named the colony Togoland. Their lands were divided between German and British colonies and, after the First World War, between British and French administrations. British Togoland, renamed Trans Volta Togoland, later voted in a plebiscite supervised by the United Nations to join the newly independent Ghana. French Togoland became the Republic of Togo and gained independence on 27 April 1960. Efforts to unite the Ewe in a single country since the colonial period have not succeeded.

The Ewe are patrilineal and live in towns and villages built of lineages, each led by a male elder. Decisions were traditionally made by a council of elders, and in regional matters the chief traditional priest held the main power. Their traditional religion is Vodun, in which Mawu is the creator god who made many lesser deities. About 89 per cent of Ewe have converted to Christianity, although many keep their ancestral rites. Women are traditionally the main traders.

The Ewe are known for strip weaving, and Ewe weavers supplied cloth to many peoples of West Africa. Their drumming, tied to their religion, uses an ensemble led by the atsimevu drum, and war music and dance, such as Agbekor and Agbadza, are among their best-known forms.
exarchate-of-ravenna: Justinian I's reconquest of Italy from the Ostrogoths took Ravenna in 540, and the long Gothic War ended in 552 to 554 under the general Narses. On 13 August 554 the Pragmatic Sanction returned the prefecture of Italy to Roman rule, though Sicily and Dalmatia were separated from it. In 568 the Lombards under King Alboin invaded northern Italy, took Milan in 569 and Pavia in 572 and seized about two thirds of the imperial lands. Duchies at Spoleto and Benevento followed.

In 576 Justin II sent his son-in-law Baduarius, who was defeated and killed, and in 580 Tiberius II reorganised the scattered holdings into five provinces. The presence of an exarch at Ravenna is first attested in 584, and the exarchate is dated from then.

The exarch was the emperor's military governor with full powers, chosen from among his generals or trusted officials. Under him the imperial lands were organised in duchies, among them Rome, Venetia, Naples, Calabria, Perugia and the Pentapolis, mostly coastal cities, since the Lombards held the interior. The Exarchate in the strict sense reached from the Po to Rimini and included Forlì. Sicily was governed separately, and Corsica and Sardinia belonged to the Exarchate of Africa. War led commanders to centralise power, and civil authorities disappear from the sources from the second half of the 7th century.

From then the aristocracies' tendency to autonomy and the growing role of the Church of Rome weakened imperial authority. Fiscal and religious conflicts between the papacy and Byzantium hastened the breakup; the local armies tended to defend the pope and might turn on an exarch who plotted against him. Liguria was lost to the Lombards in 640. Ravenna remained the seat of the exarch until the revolt of 727 over iconoclasm. By 740 the exarchate comprised Istria, Venetia, Ferrara, Ravenna, the Pentapolis and Perugia.

Eutychius, the last exarch, was killed by the Lombards in 751. In 752 King Aistulf conquered the Pentapolis. After the Franks drove the Lombards out four years later, Pope Stephen II claimed the territory, and Pepin the Short gave the conquered lands to the papacy, a donation confirmed by Charlemagne in 774 that began the temporal power of the popes. Byzantine control was reduced to southern Italy, reorganised later as the Catepanate of Italy at Bari. The old militias of the exarchate are seen as forerunners of the armed burghers of the medieval Italian cities, and the independent traditions of its archbishoprics fed the rise of the communes three centuries later. Some see the loss of Ravenna as a possible end of Late Antiquity.
exeter: Exeter stands on the eastern bank of the River Exe, on a ridge backed by a steep hill, at the point where the river, just joined by the River Creedy, opens onto a wide flood plain and estuary. Historically this was the lowest bridging point of the Exe, which was tidal and navigable up to the city until weirs were built. Its name comes from the Old English Escanceaster, the river's name with the suffix -ceaster, used for fortresses and fortified towns.

Coins from the Hellenistic kingdoms suggest a settlement trading with the Mediterranean as early as 250 BCE. About 55 CE the Romans established a fort of 42 acres here, named Isca, which was the south-western end of the Fosse Way and the base of the 5,000-man Second Augustan Legion. A community of natives and soldiers' families grew up around it as the tribal capital of the Dumnonii. When the fortress was abandoned about 75, its large bathhouse was replaced by a forum and a basilica.

Little is known of Exeter between the Roman withdrawal from Britain around 410 and the seventh century, when the Saxons held it. Danish Vikings briefly captured it in 876, and Alfred the Great drove them out the next summer. He made it one of the four burhs of Devon and rebuilt its walls on the Roman lines, which let it repel a siege in 893. Æthelstan strengthened the walls about 928 and drove out the remaining Britons. The Danes plundered the city in 1003, let in by the French reeve of Emma of Normandy, who had been given Exeter as part of her dowry.

Exeter was made a county corporate in 1537. In 1549 it withstood a month-long siege by the Prayer Book rebels, who burnt two of its gates and tried to undermine its walls before they were defeated by the army of Edward VI. It became an affluent centre of the wool trade. The Industrial Revolution largely bypassed it for lack of nearby coal, and in 1778 a new bridge replaced the 500-year-old Old Exe Bridge. Much of the city centre was rebuilt after the Second World War.

Exeter is a cathedral city and the county town of Devon, with Exeter Cathedral founded in the mid 11th century. It is home to the University of Exeter, which received its royal charter in 1955. The Exeter Book, a codex of Old English poetry, is kept in the cathedral. The city has over 1,800 listed buildings, many medieval, Tudor and Georgian, and was made a UNESCO City of Literature in 2019. The Exeter Ship Canal, first built about 1566, is one of Britain's oldest artificial waterways.
exeter-new-hampshire: Exeter lies in Rockingham County, where the Exeter River becomes the tidal Squamscott River over a set of falls. For thousands of years before European colonisation the area was inhabited by Pennacook Abenaki villagers, who called the place M'Squamskook, meaning Falls at the Place of the Salmon. About 100 Pennacook returned each spring to fish at the falls and to raise corn, pumpkins and pigeons. The town covers about 20 square miles, and its highest point, 250 feet above sea level, is on Great Hill in the south-west.

On 3 April 1638 John Wheelwright, a clergyman exiled from the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bought the land from the sagamore Wehanownowit. He brought about 175 people and named the town after Exeter in Devon, England. On 4 July 1639 thirty-five freemen signed the Exeter Combination, a document Wheelwright wrote to set up their own government. Exeter was one of the four original townships of the province, and it first included Newmarket, Newfields, Brentwood, Epping and Fremont. The Gilman family, who arrived from Hingham, Massachusetts, built the first sawmill in 1647 and became lumbermen, shipbuilders, merchants and statesmen.

In 1774 the rebellious Provincial Congress met in the Exeter Town House after Governor John Wentworth banned it from Portsmouth, and in July 1775 the provincial records were brought to Exeter, which stayed the capital for 14 years. The 1790 census recorded 81 free African Americans there, 4.7 per cent of the town, and several, such as Jude Hall, had earned their freedom in the Revolutionary War. The Exeter Manufacturing Company began making cotton textiles in 1827, and the Boston & Maine Railroad arrived in 1840. According to the former governor Hugh Gregg, the Republican Party was conceived at a meeting of abolitionists led by Amos Tuck in Exeter on 12 October 1853.

Exeter had 16,049 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It was the county seat until 1997, when county offices moved to Brentwood. Phillips Exeter Academy, founded in 1781 by John Phillips on land given by the Gilman family, occupies much of the centre; its campus was designed by the firm of Ralph Adams Cram between 1908 and 1950, and its library of 1971 by Louis I. Kahn. The American Independence Museum, the Exeter Historical Society and the Congregational Church, founded in 1638, are among its sites of interest.
expedition-of-the-thousand: The expedition was an ambitious and risky venture, aiming to conquer with about a thousand men a kingdom with a larger regular army and a more powerful navy. It was the only action jointly decided by the four Fathers of the Fatherland, Giuseppe Mazzini, Giuseppe Garibaldi, King Victor Emmanuel II and Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, who pursued divergent goals. Mazzini, a republican, wanted to liberate southern Italy and Rome. Garibaldi wanted to conquer the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the king's name and go on towards Rome. Cavour wanted to avoid taking Rome so as not to offend his ally Napoleon III, who protected the Papal States.

In 1860 Sicilian independentism was the one force willing to take up arms against the Bourbons. A revolt began in Palermo on 4 April and was quickly repressed, but it led to further demonstrations. Cavour thought the expedition risky, yet he openly supported it only when its chances of success were significant.

In March 1860 the exile Rosolino Pilo urged Garibaldi to lead an expedition, and by May Garibaldi had gathered 1,089 volunteers. They left Quarto near Genoa on the night of 5 to 6 May. Garibaldi landed at Marsala on 11 May, helped by the presence of two Royal Navy ships in the port, which deterred the Bourbon ships from interfering. On 14 May at Salemi he assumed the dictatorship of Sicily in the name of Victor Emmanuel II, and about a thousand Sicilian volunteers joined him.

Garibaldi occupied Palermo on 21 June, and the news drew support abroad. Workers in Glasgow and Liverpool gave days of work, and Alexandre Dumas brought weapons. On 7 July he proclaimed himself Dictator of Sicily. Reinforcements formed the Southern Army. After Milazzo on 20 July he prepared the crossing to the mainland, entered Basilicata on 2 September, and advanced on Naples without obstacles.

Plebiscites in October 1860 brought the south into the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. Garibaldi left Naples on 9 November 1860, six months and three days after setting out, and returned to Caprera. Spain and the Russian Empire broke off diplomatic relations with Piedmont-Sardinia.

Many expectations were disappointed, especially in Sicily, where farmers and the poor faced higher taxes and compulsory conscription. Brigandage later required some 140,000 Piedmontese troops to hold the former kingdom. Some historians trace the Southern Question to the enterprise.
expo-58: Expo 58 was the eleventh world's fair hosted by Belgium and the fifth in Brussels, after those of 1888, 1897, 1910 and 1935. Belgium won the bid in 1953 over other European capitals such as Paris and London, and the government of Prime Minister Achille Van Acker gave up the national celebrations due in 1955 to put more money into the fair. Nearly 15,000 workers spent three years building the site on the Heysel Plateau, reusing many buildings of the 1935 fair. The theme, Bilan du monde, pour un monde plus humain, drew on faith in technical and scientific progress and on post-war debates over the ethical use of atomic power.

More than forty nations took part, with over forty-five national pavilions besides those of Belgium and the Belgian Congo. King Baudouin opened the Atomium, a giant model of an iron crystal's unit cell, with a call for world peace and social and economic progress. In the Philips Pavilion the Poème électronique was played from 425 loudspeakers placed as designed by Iannis Xenakis and Le Corbusier. The Czechoslovak pavilion, visited by 6 million people, was named the best of the fair, the Soviet pavilion showed Sputnik prototypes and a model of the nuclear-powered icebreaker Lenin, and the American one showed America the Beautiful, a 360° film by Walt Disney Productions.

The Belgian Congo section was meant above all to display the civilising work claimed for Belgian colonialism, and its village indigène was recognised by the Congolese as a human zoo. The Ministry of Colonies exhibited 598 Congolese, educated city dwellers who were made to wear primitive clothing and were kept by an armed guard from speaking to the visitors. An eight-month-old baby, Juste Bonaventure Langa, died during the exhibit. In mid-July the Congolese protested at their treatment and demanded to be sent home, which ended the exhibit.

The fair ran from 17 April to 19 October 1958. It was tied to major redevelopment works in Brussels, whose boulevards were turned into urban motorways; a new terminal was added to the Melsbroek national airport, on land of the municipality of Zaventem, and the tram lines built to serve the site from Brussels remained in service. The Atomium, meant to last only the six months of the fair, was never taken down. During the fair someone tore a corner from a page of the autograph of Mozart's Requiem, which was on display.
expressionism: Expressionism arose in poetry and painting in Northern Europe around the beginning of the 20th century as a modernist movement that presents the world from a subjective perspective, distorting it for emotional effect. It developed as an avant-garde style before the First World War and remained popular under the Weimar Republic, especially in Berlin. The word was used in its modern sense as early as 1850, but the Czech art historian Antonin Matějček is said to have coined it in 1910 as the opposite of Impressionism. Precursors included Friedrich Nietzsche, Edvard Munch and Vincent van Gogh.
In 1905 four German artists led by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner formed Die Brücke in Dresden, and in 1911 Der Blaue Reiter was formed in Munich by artists including Wassily Kandinsky.

The movement is hard to define because it overlapped with other modernist currents such as Futurism, Cubism and Surrealism. It is generally described as a reaction to the dehumanising effect of industrialisation and the growth of cities, and as a rejection of realism and of the styles of Naturalism and Impressionism. Instead of an agreeable impression of a subject, the artists sought vivid emotional reactions through powerful colours and dynamic compositions. They were influenced by Munch, van Gogh and African art, and knew the Fauves of Paris. Kandinsky believed that simple colours and shapes could convey moods and feelings, which pushed him toward abstraction.

The style extended to architecture, literature, theatre, dance, film and music. Oskar Kokoschka's playlet Murderer, The Hope of Women of 1909 is often called the first expressionist drama. German film produced The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari of 1920 and Fritz Lang's Metropolis of 1927. In music the term was probably first applied in 1918, to Arnold Schoenberg, and the Second Viennese School of Schoenberg, Anton Webern and Alban Berg are counted among the expressionists. In architecture Bruno Taut's Glass Pavilion of 1914 and Erich Mendelsohn's Einstein Tower in Potsdam are cited.

Paris became a gathering place for expressionists, many of them foreign-born Jewish painters such as Chaim Soutine and Marc Chagall, dubbed the School of Paris. The movement declined in Germany with the rise of Adolf Hitler in the 1930s. After the Munich exhibition Entartete Kunst of 1937, American museums began to acquire expressionist works. After the Second World War figurative expressionism influenced artists around the world, including the Boston and New York figurative expressionists, and the abstract expressionism of the 1950s. Neo-expressionism was an international revival that began in the late 1970s. Expressionism in architecture was re-evaluated more positively only in the 1970s.
expulsion-of-the-jews-from-spain: Jews had lived in the Iberian Peninsula since at least Roman times. Violence grew in the 14th century: the Shepherds' Crusade massacred the communities of Pamplona and Estella-Lizarra in 1321, the Black Death brought attacks on Jewish quarters in Catalonia, and supporters of Enrique de Trastámara killed Jews in Toledo in 1355. After the massacres of 1391 many Jews converted, and by 1415 scarcely 100,000 still practised their faith in Castile and Aragon. Suspicion that converts kept Jewish practices in secret helped bring about the Spanish Inquisition in 1478.

The first inquisitors reached Seville in November 1480 and pronounced 700 death sentences there in the first years. Judging that converts could not be kept from Judaism while they met their Jewish relatives, they won an order in 1483 sending the Jews of the dioceses of Seville, Córdoba and Cádiz to Extremadura.

Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile signed the Alhambra Decree at Granada on 31 March 1492, shortly after the fall of the Emirate of Granada, with orders that it not be made public until 1 May. The expulsion was to be final and allowed no exception of age or birthplace. Jews had until 10 August to leave on pain of death and confiscation, and anyone who hid them risked losing all their goods. They could sell their property but take the proceeds only as bills of exchange or goods, not gold, silver, arms or horses. The decree gave as its reason that contact with Jews led converts back to Judaism. Isaac Abravanel's offer of money to the king failed.

Many converted to stay. Modern estimates of those who left range from 40,000 to 200,000 and remain debated. Many first went to Portugal, which forced conversion in 1497, or to Navarre, which expelled its Jews in 1498; others went to North Africa and the Italian states. The Inquisition pursued suspected crypto-Jews into the 18th century. In the Ottoman Empire Sultan Bayezid II ordered the exiles welcomed, and within a few generations its cities became the heart of the Sephardic world, where communities kept Judaeo-Spanish for centuries. In 2015 the Cortes Generales passed a law letting descendants of the expelled become Spanish citizens.
extraterritoriality: Pre-modern states generally claimed sovereignty over persons rather than over land, which created personal jurisdiction. When people moved across borders under territorial jurisdiction, some came under laws of countries where they did not live. In the 13th and 14th centuries Genoa, Venice and Pisa obtained extraterritoriality for their merchants in the Pera and Galata quarters of Constantinople, in Egypt and in the Barbary states. The Ottoman Empire concluded capitulations with Western nations from the sixteenth to the early nineteenth century. They ceased to have effect in Turkey in 1923 by the Treaty of Lausanne and in Egypt in 1949.

In Qing China jurisdiction depended on status rather than geography; Banner people, for example, stood outside the jurisdiction of local civil administrators. British merchants, who before 1842 could trade only at Canton, distrusted the Qing legal order for its collective responsibility and its capital punishment of accidental manslaughter. After the Lady Hughes affair of 1784 East India Company officials generally spirited Britons away before Qing officials could act. The Qing commissioner Qiying readily conceded extraterritorial privileges at the Treaty of Nanking of 1842, and the Supplementary Treaty of the Bogue of 1843 provided that Britons be punished under English law, only in the treaty ports. Other powers followed, as in the American Treaty of Wanghia of 1844, and the most-favoured-nation clause spread the rights further.

Shanghai was the most important treaty port, with its Mixed Court and the British Supreme Court for China. Japan recognised extraterritoriality in treaties of 1858 with the United States, Britain, France, the Netherlands and Russia, and Siam granted it to Britain in the Bowring Treaty of 1855.

Western powers began to consider giving up their rights as legal reform progressed. Japan persuaded them that its legal system was sufficiently modern, and treaties signed from 1894 took effect in 1899, ending extraterritoriality there. Siam ended it by about 1930 and cancelled the rights completely in treaties of 1937 and 1938. In China the Nationalist government announced in 1929 its aim of abolishing it. Several countries agreed that year to give up their rights, but Britain, the main holder, negotiated slowly until the Japanese invasion of 1937. The United States and Britain signed treaties ending their rights in 1943, and the Cairo Conference of November 1943 formally ended extraterritoriality, the foreign concessions and the unequal treaties.
extremadura: Extremadura lies in the central-western part of the Iberian Peninsula and is crossed from east to west by the Tagus and Guadiana rivers. It is formed by the two largest provinces of Spain, Cáceres and Badajoz, and is bordered by Portugal to the west. Its highest point is Calvitero, 2,401 metres, in the Sistema Central. The climate is mostly hot-summer Mediterranean, with very hot dry summers. The name is explained in two ways: as a Latin phrase for the lands south of the river Duero, or as extremo, 'extreme', with the Spanish suffix -dura, for the outer regions of the kingdoms of León and Castile.

In Roman times the area belonged to the province of Lusitania, whose capital was Mérida. The Umayyads conquered it in the early 8th century, and after the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba most of it passed to the Taifa of Badajoz. León, Castile and Portugal advanced across it in the 11th and 12th centuries, with setbacks caused by the Almoravid and Almohad advances. After the Almohad defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, Alfonso IX of León took Alcántara, Cáceres, Mérida and Badajoz between 1214 and 1230, and the military orders of Santiago and Alcántara took Trujillo and Medellín. The last fortresses of Lower Extremadura fell by 1248.

Between 1570 and 1572 the Crown relocated about 11,000 moriscos from Granada into the region; their expulsion began in 1609 and had reached 12,776 people by 1611. The Portuguese Restoration War of 1640 to 1668 brought pillage and raids to both sides of the frontier. The first railway in the region opened in September 1863, from Elvas to Badajoz. After 1955, and more heavily after 1961, emigration removed nearly 40 per cent of the population. A statute of autonomy was enacted in 1982.

Extremadura is an autonomous community of Spain with Mérida as its capital and Badajoz as its largest city. It covers 41,633 square kilometres and has about one million inhabitants, the lowest population density of the Spanish autonomous communities. Spanish is the only official language, while Fala, a Galician-Portuguese language, is specially protected. The region is known for Iberian ham from pigs fed on acorns, and for the Monfragüe National Park, designated in 2007.
exxonmobil: ExxonMobil is the largest direct successor of John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil. One of its two roots, the Vacuum Oil Company, was founded in 1866, acquired by Standard Oil in 1879 and divested in 1911 when Standard Oil was broken up under a legal order. In 1931 Vacuum Oil merged with the Standard Oil Company of New York (Socony), and the combined company later became known as Mobil.

The other root was Standard Oil's New Jersey subsidiary, called Jersey Standard, which after the breakup kept the Standard Oil name across much of the eastern United States. It grew by acquiring Humble Oil in the 1930s and became the dominant oil company on the world stage. Because it did not own the Standard Oil name throughout the country, it sold its products under three brands, Esso, Enco and Humble Oil, and in 1972 it chose the single name Exxon.

The two companies agreed in 1998 to merge, and the deal closed on 30 November 1999. The new name joined the trade names of both predecessors. In legal terms Exxon was the surviving company and bought Mobil, rather than a new company being created, and Exxon's NYSE ticker symbol changed from XON to XOM. ExxonMobil Chemical was created in 1999 by joining the chemical businesses of both firms.

In 1989 an Exxon tanker discharged about 11 million US gallons (42,000 m3) of oil into Prince William Sound in Alaska, oiling 1,300 miles (2,100 km) of remote coastline. The Exxon Valdez spill remains one of the largest in American history. In the late 1980s Mobil hired units of the Indonesian army to guard its gas project in Aceh, and the units were accused of human rights violations. The company left Indonesia in 2001 and settled the resulting lawsuit in 2023, without admitting wrongdoing. In 2022 the company combined its separate downstream and chemical divisions into a Product Solutions division and formed a Low Carbon Solutions division.

ExxonMobil is vertically integrated across the oil and gas industry, from exploration and extraction to refining and retail, and has a large chemicals business producing plastics and synthetic rubber. It markets fuel under the brands Exxon, Esso and Mobil. Exxon is used only in the United States, while Esso and Mobil are used in most other countries. Since 2008 Mobil has been the only brand for the company's lubricants. Its headquarters are at Spring, Texas, a suburb of Houston, where the company moved from Irving.
ey-iran: Ey Iran is an Iranian patriotic song. The music was composed by Ruhollah Khaleghi and the lyrics were written by Hossein Gol-e-Golab. It was created during World War II, after the Allied occupation of Iran in September 1941 that followed the Anglo-Soviet invasion and overthrew Reza Shah. Gol-e-Golab was inspired to write a poem on Iranian nationalism when he saw Allied flags waving from an Iranian military barracks in Tehran.

He later said that a confrontation between a British soldier and an Iranian officer encouraged him further. In his words, the footsteps of the invading armies in the streets in 1944 were enough to rattle any patriot, and Khaleghi's music, despite all the political opposition, found its way into the hearts of the people.

The piece was first performed over two consecutive nights on 27 October 1944 at the military primary school on Istanbul Street, with Gholam-Hossein Banan as the soloist. The audience was enthusiastic and called for several encores. Its popularity led the Minister of Culture to commission a studio recording, which was broadcast daily on Radio Tehran.

In the transitional period after the 1979 Iranian Revolution the song briefly served as the country's de facto national anthem under the interim government. After the Islamic takeover several people involved in its preparation were imprisoned and public performance was discouraged, but the melody kept circulating and served as a morale-boosting symbol during the Iran–Iraq War.

Since 1979 the song has been widely used in anti-Islamic Republic marches and other demonstrations by the Iranian diaspora abroad, and as a symbol of Iran's pre-1979 identity. In 1990 Golnoush Khaleghi, the composer's daughter, arranged a new version while in Tehran for the 25th anniversary of her father's death. It appeared on the album May Nab, released by Sorush Publications, with a monologue performed by Rashid Vatandoust.
ezana: Ezana, written 'Ezana in Ge'ez, ruled the Kingdom of Aksum. Tradition states that he succeeded his father Ella Amida, called Ousanas in Greek, while still a child, and that his mother, Sofya, served as regent until he came of age. He is one of the best-documented rulers of Aksum, and Stuart Munro-Hay ranked him as the best known of the Aksumite kings before Kaleb.

In his early life he considered himself a son of Ares, but later inscriptions show a growing attachment to Christianity. He was converted by his tutor Frumentius, who became head of the Ethiopian Church. A surviving letter from the Roman emperor Constantius II, addressed to Ezana and his brother Saizana, asked that Frumentius be sent to Alexandria to be examined for doctrinal errors; Munro-Hay assumes that Ezana refused or ignored the request.

Ezana launched several military campaigns and recorded them in inscriptions. A pair of Ge'ez inscriptions on a stela found at Meroë is evidence of a campaign in the fourth century, either in his reign or by a predecessor such as Ousanas. Some authorities read them as proof that the Aksumites destroyed Meroë, others point to archaeological evidence of Meroë's economic and political decline around 300, and others see the stela as Aksumite aid to put down a Nuba revolt. No conclusive evidence decides between these views. His Greek inscription styles him king of Aksum, of the Himyarites, of the Ethiopians and of other peoples. He is credited with erecting several stelae and obelisks.

Coins minted in his reign carry the Greek motto meaning 'May this please the country', which Munro-Hay saw as a sign of royal concern for the people's wishes. They show a change from a disc and crescent to a cross, and coins bearing his name found in India in the late 1990s point to trade contacts there. His name is absent from the king lists although it appears on coins.

Tradition names Abreha and Asbeha as the rulers when Christianity was introduced, and these may be later names for Ezana and his brother, or their baptismal names. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Catholic Church regard Ezana and Saizana as saints, with feast days on 1 October and 27 October.
ezra: The Book of Ezra and the Book of Nehemiah are the oldest sources for Ezra's activity, and the two were originally written as one scroll. According to the Hebrew Bible he was a descendant of Seraiah, the last High Priest to serve in Solomon's Temple. Whether he was himself a High Priest is disputed: the Greek 1 Esdras says he was, and rabbinic sources are divided. In the seventh year of the reign of Artaxerxes, the Achaemenid king sent him from Babylon to Jerusalem to teach the laws of God to any Israelite who did not know them.

The Book of Ezra describes him leading a group of Judean exiles to Jerusalem and enforcing observance of the Torah. When he learned that Jewish men had married foreign women, he tore his garments in despair and confessed the sins of Israel. Despite opposition he enforced the dissolution of those marriages. Later, after Nehemiah, a Jewish cupbearer of the king, had rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem as its governor, Nehemiah had Ezra read the Torah to the assembled people, who entered a covenant to keep its laws.

Jewish tradition holds that Ezra wrote the Books of Chronicles and that he is the prophet Malachi. It credits him with establishing the Great Assembly, forerunner of the Sanhedrin, which is credited with shaping features of traditional Judaism such as Torah reading and the Amidah. Christian tradition also regards him as the author of Ezra and Chronicles. In Islam he is known as Uzair and is mentioned in the Qur'an. A fourth book of Ezra, written around 100 CE, presents him as a seer who restores the law destroyed with the Temple.

The text does not say which Artaxerxes sent Ezra, and scholars place his mission under Artaxerxes I or Artaxerxes II. Most favour the first, though Ezra and Nehemiah seem to know nothing of each other, and some date Ezra some fifty years after Nehemiah. There is no consensus on his historicity or mission. Some regard him as a historical figure whose life was embellished, others as a literary creation modelled partly on Moses. Traditions of his burial vary: Josephus says he was buried in Jerusalem, while others name a tomb near Basra or the Syrian village of Tadef near Aleppo.
